Raw parameters are at chance, as step 5 predicts. Their largest standardized gap, 0.34, is the size expected from noise alone. A standardized feature has variance 1, so its mean over 150 networks has variance \(1/150\), and the difference of two such means has variance \(2/150\), a standard deviation of \(\sqrt{2/150} = 0.115\). The largest of 17 such gaps is typically two to three times that.
Canonical order recovers most of the signal, with one feature carrying most of it (Figure 12.4, left). Second moments do better with fewer features, because they need no tie-breaking between units with nearly equal \(v_j\). Probe outputs are best. The property changes the function the network computes, and probe outputs measure that function directly, without passing through any parameterization.






Figure 12.4: Left: for each representation of 100 tanh networks per hypothesis (\(t = 0.2\) against \(t = 0.8\)), the standardized mean gap of every feature. Right: accuracy of the linear meta-classifier on 100 further networks per hypothesis (seed 1). Raw parameters carry no mean signal; invariant representations do.





12.6.6 Check yourself

Would the raw means vanish for a network with ReLU units instead of tanh? (Not by this argument. ReLU is not odd, so the sign flip is not a symmetry; only the permutations remain. They force every unit slot to have the same mean, but that common mean can differ between \(t_0\) and \(t_1\).)
Why does a linear meta-classifier on the sum \(\sum_ju_j\) fail for tanh networks, even though the sum is permutation invariant? (The sign flips still apply: \(\mathbb E[u_j] = 0\) for every \(j\), so the sum has mean zero under both hypotheses. An invariant feature needs to be even in each \(u_j\), like \(u_ju_j^\top\).)

12.7 Code: check every result by computation and simulation
The script code/property_inference.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. The binomial advantages are exact sums. The population fit and the sandwich covariance of the logistic regression are computed by Gauss–Hermite quadrature on a \(40\times40\) grid. Shadow and target models are trained in batches with NumPy: logistic regressions by Newton’s method, tanh networks by full-batch gradient descent. From the repository root:

What to take from it. Four things stand out. First, more data helps the property attacker: the same release that hides each record better as \(n\) grows reveals the property better. Second, the Gaussian picture predicts real attacks: two numbers computed from the population, \(\theta'\) and \(\Sigma_1\), predict the meta-classifier’s accuracy across a 20-fold range of \(n\) and an 8-fold range of gaps. Third, hiding the group column does not hide the property: the logistic regression never sees the group, and still leaks the property as well as a tenth of its records would. Fourth, representation matters before access does: the same networks are opaque to a linear attacker in raw form and transparent once the hidden-unit symmetries are removed.

title: 12  Property inference
text:
12.8 References

Ateniese, Mancini, Spognardi, Villani, Vitali & Felici, “Hacking Smart Machines with Smarter Ones: How to Extract Meaningful Data from Machine Learning Classifiers” (International Journal of Security and Networks, 2015). The first property-inference attack: shadow models trained with and without the property, and a meta-classifier on their parameters. Read it for the recipe and its threat model.
Ganju, Wang, Yang, Gunter & Borisov, “Property Inference Attacks on Fully Connected Neural Networks using Permutation Invariant Representations” (CCS 2018). The permutation problem for neural networks, neuron sorting, and the DeepSets meta-classifier. The source of Section 12.6.
Suri & Evans, “Formalizing and Estimating Distribution Inference Risks” (PoPETs 2022). The property game as a test between two training distributions, and leakage measured in records. Exercise 3 follows their definition.
Zhang, Tople & Ohrimenko, “Leakage of Dataset Properties in Multi-Party Machine Learning” (USENIX Security 2021). Black-box property inference from query outputs, including properties of attributes that were removed from the training data.
Mahloujifar, Ghosh & Chase, “Property Inference from Poisoning” (IEEE S&P 2022). An attacker who can add a few records to the training set can make a property far easier to infer.
Melis, Song, De Cristofaro & Shmatikov, “Exploiting Unintended Feature Leakage in Collaborative Learning” (IEEE S&P 2019). Properties of other participants’ data, inferred from the updates they share during collaborative training.
Salem, Cherubin, Evans, Köpf, Paverd, Suri, Tople & Zanella-Béguelin, “SoK: Let the Privacy Games Begin! A Unified Treatment of Data Inference Privacy in Machine Learning” (IEEE S&P 2023). Property inference as one game among the others of this part.
Zaheer, Kottur, Ravanbakhsh, Póczos, Salakhutdinov & Smola, “Deep Sets” (NeurIPS 2017). The \(\rho(\sum_j\phi(u_j))\) form of permutation-invariant functions.
van der Vaart, Asymptotic Statistics (1998), ch. 5. Asymptotic normality of M-estimators and the sandwich covariance \(H^{-1}GH^{-1}\), with the regularity conditions this chapter skips.

Rules of thumb

Property inference gets easier with more data, membership inference harder. What matters for a property is \(\sqrt n\,|t_1 - t_0|\).
A property changes about \(n|t_1 - t_0|\) records at once. Defences sized for one record do not cover it.
Removing the sensitive column does not remove the property. Whatever correlates with it moves the model.
Train the meta-classifier on a representation that respects the model’s symmetries: canonical order, sums over units, or outputs on probe inputs.
Report accuracy for property attacks: there is one secret per dataset, not a population of targets.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1 Why this matters
A language model trained on scraped text sees phone numbers, addresses, keys and private messages. Ask it to continue “Anna Smith’s phone number is” and it may finish the sentence with the real number. Nobody queried a database and nothing was leaked by a breach: the number is stored in the weights, and it comes out through the model’s normal interface. That is what training-data extraction means. Membership inference (Membership inference) asks “was this record in the training set?” and needs the record in hand. Extraction asks for more: the attacker gets the record itself, often without knowing it existed.
This chapter answers three questions, in order. The first is what it means for a model to memorize a string. There are several definitions, from “greedy decoding reproduces it when you prompt with the text that preceded it in training” to “some prompt makes the model emit it”, and they differ in what the attacker must already know. Once you know what to measure, the second question is which strings get memorized. Two things decide it: duplication and model capacity. A string repeated often, or seen by a model large enough to give it a context of its own, comes back verbatim. The third question is how you measure memorization and how an attacker finds it. Planted random secrets called canaries, and a score called exposure, measure how much a model has memorized a secret you put there yourself. Generate-rank-verify pipelines find real training data among a model’s samples.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.1.1 The one idea: the rank of the secret under the model
A language model is a distribution over strings: it gives every possible string a probability. Memorization is the model putting a training string far above the other strings that could have stood in its place. To make that precise, fix the context in which the secret appears, say “my pin is”, and list all possible fillers \(r\) (all five-digit pins) in order of the model’s probability \(p(r \mid \text{context})\), most likely first. The rank of the true secret is its position in that list. It is also the number of guesses an attacker needs if they try fillers from most to least likely, so a low rank means the model has done most of the attacker’s work.
Every measure in this chapter reads that rank, in a different way. Greedy extraction, which writes out the model’s single most likely next symbol at each step, reproduces the secret when the secret’s next symbol is the top choice, rank 1, at every step. Exposure compares the secret’s rank with the size of the space, on a logarithmic scale: it is \(\log_2\) of the number of candidates minus \(\log_2\) of the rank, which counts how many halvings of the search the model has saved the attacker, in bits. Sampling-based extraction, which draws random outputs from the model, hits the secret quickly when the secret has high probability, and high probability is what puts it near the top of the list.
Table 13.1 lists the results of the chapter and where each is used.

The chapter builds on four earlier ones, and restates what it uses from them where it uses it. Algorithmic stability and generalization defined memorization as self-influence and showed that atypical examples are memorized most. Information theory introduced min-entropy and guessing, which give exposure its meaning. Threat models and privacy games set up attacks as games, and membership inference introduced the likelihood-ratio tests and reference models that extraction attacks reuse. The defence that bounds every quantity here, differential privacy, starts in Part 3.
The running example. Every experiment uses one toy that runs in seconds. The training set is a contact list: each line is a user name made of three random syllables, a space, and a five-digit pin, such as toneka 14524. There are 5,000 background lines, each seen once, and 600 secret lines, 100 each duplicated 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 times: 11,300 lines and 146,900 symbols in all, counting the end of each line. The model is a character \(n\)-gram language model with add-\(\alpha\) smoothing, which predicts each character from the few characters before it by counting (Fact 2 below says exactly how). The order \(n\) (the model sees the last \(n - 1\) characters) plays the role of model size: an order-3 model stores 2,734 distinct \(n\)-grams and an order-8 model 54,614. It is the smallest model that has every property this chapter needs: a probability for every string, greedy decoding, sampling, and a capacity you can turn up. When a context is written out, _ stands for a space: gule_ is the five characters before the first digit of migule 16430.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
13.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

13.2.1 Fact 1 — A language model is the chain rule
A language model never scores a whole string at once. It answers one smaller question many times: given everything written so far, how likely is each possible next symbol? Write \(p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\) for the probability it gives to the next symbol \(x_t\) after the symbols \(x_{<t} = x_1 \dots x_{t-1}\) that come before it. To get the probability of a whole string \(x = x_1\dots x_L\) of length \(L\) after a prompt \(c\), you multiply these one-step probabilities. That is the chain rule of probability: the chance that the first symbol is \(x_1\), and then the second is \(x_2\) given the first, and so on, is the product of the conditional chances. Taking logarithms turns the product into a sum: \[p(x \mid c) = \prod_{t=1}^{L}p(x_t \mid c, x_{<t}), \qquad \ln p(x \mid c) = \sum_{t=1}^{L}\ln p(x_t \mid c, x_{<t}). \tag{13.1}\]
For the pin 16430 after the prompt migule, the model multiplies five numbers: the probability of 1 after migule_, of 6 after migule_1, of 4 after migule_16, of 3 after migule_164, and of 0 after migule_1643.
The negative of the log in base 2, \(-\log_2p(x \mid c)\), is called the log-perplexity of \(x\) in bits. It measures how surprised the model is by \(x\): a string the model finds likely has low log-perplexity, and each extra bit means the model found it half as likely. Every score in this chapter (exposure, the probability that a sample reproduces a string, the ranking of generations) is built from this sum of per-symbol log-probabilities.


13.2.2 Fact 2 — An \(n\)-gram model is a table of counts
An order-\(n\) model looks only at the last \(n - 1\) symbols, which it calls the context \(c\). Training is nothing more than counting: for every context \(c\) and every possible next symbol \(w\), the model stores the count \(N(c, w)\) of times \(w\) followed \(c\) in the training text. The natural prediction would be the fraction of times \(w\) followed \(c\), but that gives probability 0 to anything never seen, and one zero in the chain rule makes a whole string impossible. Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing fixes this by pretending every symbol was seen \(\alpha\) extra times in every context. With an alphabet of \(V\) symbols, the \(\alpha\) is added to each of the \(V\) counts, so the total grows by \(\alpha V\): \[p(w \mid c) = \frac{N(c, w) + \alpha}{N(c) + \alpha V}, \qquad N(c) = \sum_wN(c, w). \tag{13.2}\]
Three consequences of this formula do most of the work in the chapter.
The first is that training is counting. A line of text passes through a sequence of (context, next symbol) pairs, and training on it adds 1 to each of those counts. Training on \(k\) copies of a line adds \(k\) to each, and changes no other count.
The second is that smoothing does not change the most likely symbol. In a fixed context \(c\), every count gets the same \(+\alpha\), and the denominator \(N(c) + \alpha V\) is the same for every \(w\). So the symbol with the largest count still has the largest probability: \(\arg\max_wp(w \mid c) = \arg\max_wN(c, w)\), where \(\arg\max_w\) means “the \(w\) that makes this largest”. Greedy decoding, which emits the most likely symbol, therefore just follows the largest counts.
The third is what happens at a context that occurs only in the copies of one line. Say the line has been inserted \(k\) times and its context \(c\) appears nowhere else. Then the line’s own next symbol has count \(k\), every other symbol has count 0, and the total is \(N(c) = k\). Putting those counts into Equation 13.2 gives \[p(\text{true} \mid c) = \frac{k + \alpha}{k + \alpha V}, \qquad p(\text{other} \mid c) = \frac{\alpha}{k + \alpha V}. \tag{13.3}\] The two share a denominator, so the true symbol is \((k + \alpha)/\alpha\) times as likely as any other, whatever \(V\) is. A context never seen at all has every count 0, and gives every symbol \(\alpha/(\alpha V) = 1/V\).
The toy uses \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(V = 39\) symbols: 26 letters, 10 digits, the space, a start symbol and an end-of-line symbol, \(26 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 39\). Table 13.2 evaluates Equation 13.3. For one copy, \(\alpha V = 3.9\), so \(p(\text{true} \mid c) = 1.1/4.9 = 0.2245\) and \(p(\text{other} \mid c) = 0.1/4.9 = 0.0204\), a ratio of \(1.1/0.1 = 11\). The last column turns the ratio into bits, \(\log_2 11 = 3.46\): one copy makes the true digit as much more likely than any rival as 3.46 halvings would.

So a single copy already makes the true digit 11 times more likely than any other. That is the mechanism of memorization in this toy: a context that belongs to one training line alone, followed by that line’s next symbol.


13.2.3 Fact 3 — Guessing in order of probability takes “rank” guesses
Let a secret \(r\) come from a finite set \(\mathcal R\) of possible values, with \(|\mathcal R|\) elements. An attacker who has a score for every candidate, here the model’s probability, should guess candidates from the highest score down, because each guess then has the best remaining chance of being right. The number of guesses this takes is the rank of the true secret: the number of candidates at least as likely as it, \[\operatorname{rank}(r) = \big|\{r' \in \mathcal R : p(r') \ge p(r)\}\big|, \tag{13.4}\] counting \(r\) itself and every candidate tied with it (ties are counted against the attacker, who may have to try them all first).
Without a model, the attacker has no reason to prefer one order over another. A uniform secret is then equally likely to sit at each position \(1, \dots, |\mathcal R|\) of whatever order is used, so the number of guesses is on average the middle position, \((|\mathcal R| + 1)/2\). Information theory measures the same difficulty with one guess. The best single guess is the most likely value, and it succeeds with probability \(\max_rp(r)\), which Information theory calls the vulnerability. Its negative logarithm, the min-entropy \(H_\infty = -\log_2\max_rp(r)\), expresses that difficulty in bits: a secret with \(H_\infty\) bits is as hard to guess in one try as a uniform choice among \(2^{H_\infty}\) values. A uniform 5-digit pin has \(10^5\) equally likely values, so \(H_\infty = \log_2 10^5 = 5\log_2 10 = 16.61\) bits.
The rank is what the rest of the chapter measures. Exposure is defined from the rank of a secret among all secrets of its format, and greedy decoding asks for rank 1 among the possible next symbols at every step.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.3 Verbatim, approximate, discoverable, extractable

13.3.1 Context
“The model memorized its training data” can mean several things. A model that completes a famous quotation has memorized it, but so has every reader, and nothing private leaked. A model that emits a phone number seen once in training has leaked it. Some definitions assume the attacker knows the beginning of the training string. Others ask whether any prompt at all brings it out. Before measuring anything you need to say which notion you measure, because the numbers differ by orders of magnitude.


13.3.2 Statement
Let \(f\) be a language model trained on a dataset \(D\) of documents, and let \(\mathrm{greedy}_f(c)\) be the string produced by greedy decoding from the prompt \(c\): at each step, append the most likely next symbol. The definitions below are parallel options that differ in what the attacker gets to use and in how close the output must be.

Extractable (Carlini et al. 2021): a string \(s\) is extractable from \(f\) if there is some prompt \(c\), any prompt at all, such that \(\mathrm{greedy}_f(c)\) begins with \(s\).
\(k\)-eidetic (Carlini et al. 2021): \(s\) is \(k\)-eidetically memorized if it is extractable and it appears in at most \(k\) documents of \(D\). Small \(k\) is the dangerous case: a secret seen once and given back.
Discoverable (Carlini et al. 2023, named by Nasr et al. 2023): if the training data contain \([p \,\|\, x]\), a prefix \(p\) followed by a suffix \(x\), then \(x\) is discoverably memorized if prompting with that same prefix makes greedy decoding produce the suffix: \(\mathrm{greedy}_f(p)\) begins with \(x\).
Approximate (Ippolito et al. 2023): \(x\) is approximately memorized if \(\mathrm{greedy}_f(p)\) is within distance \(\tau\) of \(x\) in some string distance \(d\). In this chapter’s toy \(d\) is the number of wrong digits and \(\tau = 1\), so a pin with at most one wrong digit counts. Definitions 1 to 3 are verbatim: the output must match exactly.

Two relations follow directly from the definitions. Discoverable is a special case of extractable, with the training prefix as the prompt, and an exact match is a special case of a close one: \[\text{discoverable} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{extractable}, \qquad \text{verbatim} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{approximate}. \tag{13.5}\]
Real systems sample rather than decode greedily, so it is useful to know how many samples bring a string out. Each sample is a fresh, independent try that produces the string \(x\) with its probability \(p = p(x \mid c)\) after the prompt \(c\), like a biased coin that lands heads with probability \(p\). The chance that at least one of \(m\) samples is \(x\) is one minus the chance that all of them miss, \(1 - (1 - p)^m\), and this is at least \(1 - e^{-mp}\). Asking that to be at least \(1 - \beta\), for a small failure probability \(\beta\), gives a sample budget: \[m \ge \frac{\ln(1/\beta)}{p} \quad\text{samples suffice to extract } x \text{ with probability at least } 1 - \beta. \tag{13.6}\]


13.3.3 Derivation
Discoverable implies extractable. If \(\mathrm{greedy}_f(p)\) begins with \(x\), then \(c = p\) is a prompt that makes the model emit \(x\), which is the definition of extractable. The converse fails: an extractable string may come out after a prompt that is not its training prefix, or after a prompt the attacker cannot know, while its own prefix leads elsewhere.
Verbatim implies approximate. A verbatim match has distance \(0\), and \(0 \le \tau\).
Samples needed. The idea is to compute the probability that every sample misses, and bound it by an exponential that is easy to solve for \(m\).

One sample hits with probability \(p\). A temperature-1 sample from \(c\) draws each next symbol with exactly the model’s probabilities \(p(x_t \mid c, x_{<t})\). By the chain rule (Equation 13.1), the chance that it writes out exactly \(x\) is the product of those probabilities, which is \(p = p(x \mid c)\).
All \(m\) samples miss with probability \((1 - p)^m\). Each sample misses with probability \(1 - p\), and the samples are independent, so the misses multiply.
Replace \(1 - p\) by \(e^{-p}\). The curve \(e^{-p}\) is convex, and the straight line \(1 - p\) is its tangent at \(p = 0\) (both equal 1 there, with slope \(-1\)). A convex curve lies above its tangent lines, so \(1 - p \le e^{-p}\), and raising both sides to the power \(m\) gives \((1 - p)^m \le e^{-mp}\).
Solve for \(m\). The miss probability is then at most \(\beta\) as soon as \(e^{-mp} \le \beta\). Taking logarithms, \(-mp \le \ln\beta\), that is \(m \ge \ln(1/\beta)/p\).



13.3.4 Interpretation
The definitions answer different threat models. Discoverable memorization assumes an attacker who holds the training prefix. That is a strong assumption, but it makes the quantity easy to measure: prompt with every training prefix and compare the output with the true suffix. Extractable memorization fits the real attacker, who has only the model, but it is hard to measure, because you would have to search over all prompts. So the discoverable rates are what papers report on open models, and attacks then show how much of that an outsider can actually reach.
Verbatim matching is a weak notion of leakage, because it misses near copies. A model that emits a phone number with one digit changed, or a paragraph with its punctuation changed, has leaked it to any reader. Ippolito et al. (2023) show that a filter blocking verbatim training text is easy to bypass with prompts that change the style, while the approximate copies still come out. A verbatim rate is therefore a lower bound on the leak, not a measure of it.
Greedy decoding is a convenience for measurement; real deployments sample. Equation 13.6 converts a probability into an attack budget. For a string with probability \(10^{-3}\) after its prefix and 99% confidence (\(\beta = 0.01\)), the budget is \(\ln(100)/10^{-3} = 4.605/0.001\), so the string comes out within about 4,600 samples.


13.3.5 Example: one secret, six model sizes
Take the secret line migule 16430, inserted 4 times, and prompt each model with its prefix migule. Greedy decoding gives 07 followed by an end of line at order 3, 81554 at order 4, 14032 at order 5, and the true 16430 at orders 6, 7 and 8. The order-5 output gets the first and fourth digits right and the other three wrong, so it is not approximately memorized either. The reason the switch happens at order 6 is Fact 2. An order-6 model reads five characters of context, and from the first digit on its contexts (gule_, then ule_1, and so on) occur in this line and nowhere else. In such a context the line’s own next digit has count 4 and every rival digit has count 0, so greedy decoding, which follows the largest count, emits the line’s digit every time. Shorter contexts, such as the four characters ule_ an order-5 model reads, are shared with other lines, whose digits can outvote the four copies.
Sampling gives a graded version of the same picture. At order 5, the probability that one sample from the true prefix reproduces a secret’s pin, averaged over the 100 secrets of each group, is \(1.4 \times 10^{-3}\) at 4 copies and \(0.142\) at 32 copies. With \(\beta = 0.01\) that means 3,252 and 31 samples for a 99% chance of extracting the pin. These are the exact budgets, the smallest \(m\) with \((1 - p)^m \le \beta\); Equation 13.6 gives slightly larger ones, since it replaces \(1 - p\) by the larger \(e^{-p}\). For \(p = 0.142\), for instance, \(\ln(0.01)/\ln(1 - 0.142) = 4.605/0.153 = 30.1\), which rounds up to 31. Repetition turns a needle in a haystack into the model’s favourite answer.


13.3.6 Check yourself

Can a string be extractable but not discoverable? (Yes. Another prompt, say a different name that shares the last syllables, may lead greedy decoding into it while its true prefix leads elsewhere.)
A model emits a training string with probability \(10^{-6}\) after its prefix. Is it memorized? (Not in the greedy sense, and by Equation 13.6 an attacker needs about \(\ln(100)/10^{-6} \approx 4.6 \times 10^6\) samples for 99% success. Whether that counts as a leak depends on the attacker’s budget, which is why exposure, which uses the rank rather than the probability, is useful.)

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.4 Duplication and model size: the copies a string needs
text:
13.4 Duplication and model size: the copies a string needs

13.4.1 Context
Carlini et al. (2023) measured discoverable memorization on a family of open models and found that it grows log-linearly with three things: the number of times a string is duplicated in the training set, the size of the model, and the length of the prompt. Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel (2022) found that a sequence repeated 10 times is generated about 1,000 times more often than one seen once. The \(n\)-gram toy lets you derive why, for every string, from counts.


13.4.2 Statement
The idea is a vote. Greedy decoding follows the largest count at each step (Fact 2). Each copy of a line adds one vote for the line’s own next symbol in every context the line passes through. So the line comes out when, at every step, its own votes plus whatever the rest of the corpus already gave its symbol beat the strongest rival symbol. The number of copies needed is set by the step where the rival is furthest ahead.
To write this down, let \(s\) be a training line with prompt \(p\) and secret suffix \(x = x_1\dots x_L\), inserted \(k\) times. Let \(c_t\) be the context at step \(t\) (the last \(n - 1\) symbols of the prompt followed by the first \(t - 1\) symbols of the suffix, \(p\,x_{<t}\)), and let \(N_-(c, w)\) be the counts in the rest of the training set, without the copies of \(s\). At step \(t\), the gap is how far the strongest rival \(w \ne x_t\) is ahead of the true symbol in those counts, \(\max_{w \ne x_t}N_-(c_t, w) - N_-(c_t, x_t)\). Assume each context \(c_t\) occurs only once within \(s\), so a copy of \(s\) adds to the true pair \((c_t, x_t)\) and to no rival pair \((c_t, w)\); this holds for almost every line. Then greedy decoding from \(p\) emits \(x\) if and only if \(k \ge k^*(s)\), where the copies needed are the largest gap plus one: \[k^*(s) = \max_{t \le L}\Big[\max_{w \ne x_t}N_-(c_t, w) - N_-(c_t, x_t)\Big] + 1. \tag{13.7}\] There is one refinement for ties. Greedy decoding breaks a tie toward the symbol with the lowest code, so at a step where the true symbol has the lower code, a tie is already a win, and the bracket is reduced by one there.
Over a population of lines, the fraction memorized at \(k\) copies is then the fraction of lines whose \(k^*\) is at most \(k\): \[\Pr[\text{discoverably memorized at } k \text{ copies}] = \Pr[k^*(s) \le k]. \tag{13.8}\] In particular, a line whose contexts are unique to it (\(N_- = 0\) everywhere, so every gap is 0) has \(k^* = 1\): it is memorized from a single copy.


13.4.3 Derivation

Greedy picks the largest count. By Fact 2, adding \(\alpha\) to every count does not change which count is largest, so at context \(c_t\) greedy decoding emits \(\arg\max_wN(c_t, w)\), the symbol with the largest count.
What the copies add. Training is counting (Fact 2), so \(k\) copies of \(s\) add \(k\) to \(N(c_t, x_t)\). By the assumption that \(c_t\) occurs once in \(s\), they add nothing to \(N(c_t, w)\) for \(w \ne x_t\). With the copies, the true symbol’s count is \(N_-(c_t, x_t) + k\) and each rival’s is still \(N_-(c_t, w)\).
Winning one step. The true symbol wins strictly when its count beats the largest rival count, \(N_-(c_t, x_t) + k > \max_{w \ne x_t}N_-(c_t, w)\). Moving \(N_-(c_t, x_t)\) to the right, this is \(k > \text{gap}_t\), with \(\text{gap}_t\) the bracket in Equation 13.7. Since \(k\) and the gap are whole numbers, that is \(k \ge \text{gap}_t + 1\).
Every step must win. Greedy decoding stays on the line’s path \(c_1, c_2, \dots\) only while it keeps emitting the true symbols. One wrong symbol puts it in a different context, from which in general it does not return to \(x\). So \(x\) comes out exactly when every step wins, that is when \(k \ge \text{gap}_t + 1\) for every \(t\), which is \(k \ge \max_t(\text{gap}_t + 1)\), Equation 13.7.
Unique contexts. If \(N_-(c_t, \cdot) = 0\) for every \(t\), every gap is \(0 - 0 = 0\), so \(k^* = 1\).
The population rate. Each line is memorized at \(k\) copies exactly when \(k^*(s) \le k\). The fraction of lines memorized is therefore the fraction for which this holds, which is \(\Pr[k^*(s) \le k]\) for a line drawn at random from the population.

Figure 13.1 draws steps 3 and 4 for one line.






Figure 13.1: For one secret line inserted once, an order-5 model: at each step of its pin, the count of the true next digit (blue) and of its strongest rival (orange) in the rest of the training set. The label is the gap plus one, the copies that step needs. The line needs as many copies as its hardest step.





13.4.4 Interpretation
Duplication works as a vote. Each copy is one more vote for the line’s continuation in every context it passes through, and a line comes out when it outvotes the rest of the corpus at its most contested step.
Model size works by splitting the vote. A longer context is a finer partition of the training positions: fewer positions share any one context of length 7 than of length 2. So the rival counts in a longer context are smaller, while the line’s own \(k\) votes stay with it in every context it passes through. In the limit every line has contexts of its own and \(k^* = 1\). This is the toy version of “larger models memorize more”: a larger model can afford to give rare strings their own parameters.
For the same reason, rare data are exposed first. A line whose name shares few syllables with other names reaches a context of its own sooner. This is the pattern Algorithmic stability and generalization found for self-influence, how much a model’s prediction on a training example changes when that one example is removed: atypical examples can only be fitted by memorizing them, so they have the largest self-influence.
Deduplication is the cheapest defence, because it lowers \(k\) for every repeated string. Lee et al. (2022) found that models trained on deduplicated data emit memorized text about ten times less often, without losing quality, and Kandpal et al. (2022) found that deduplication sharply lowers the success of extraction attacks. It does nothing for singletons in a high-capacity model, where \(k = 1\) already and \(k^* = 1\).

The script prompts each of the 600 secrets with its true prefix (the name and the space), decodes five symbols greedily, and compares them with the pin. Figure 13.2: Discoverable memorization against copies of the secret in the training set, for \(n\)-gram models of order 3 to 8, on an independent draw of the corpus. Left: greedy decoding reproduces the pin exactly. Right: at most one digit is wrong. Both rise with duplication and with order, and the approximate rate is only slightly higher.



The approximate rates are barely above the verbatim ones. In this toy, a pin either sits in contexts of its own and comes out whole, or it loses a contest early, after which greedy decoding is in the wrong context and wanders off. Natural text has many near-ties (synonyms, punctuation), and that is where approximate memorization adds the most (Ippolito et al. 2023).
The real experiment of Carlini et al. (2023) has the same shape at scale. Take GPT-Neo models from 125 million to 2.7 billion parameters and GPT-J (6 billion), all trained on the Pile, a large public collection of web and book text. Sample training sequences, grouped by how many times they are duplicated in the Pile. Prompt each model with the first 50 tokens and decode 50 tokens greedily. Count exact matches. They found that the largest model reproduces at least 1% of its training data this way, and that the rate rises log-linearly with model size, duplication and prompt length. The toy replaces tokens by characters, parameters by the context length and the Pile by a contact list, and keeps the measurement.


13.4.6 Check yourself

In Figure 13.1, why does the line need as many copies as its worst step, and not the sum over steps? (The copies count at every step at once: each copy adds one to every pair on the line’s path. So \(k\) copies close every gap up to \(k\), and the largest gap decides.)
Does deduplication help an order-8 model on this corpus? (Barely. Its singletons are already memorized 98% of the time, because their contexts are unique. Deduplication works by lowering \(k\), and here \(k^* = 1\).)

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.5 Canaries and the exposure metric

13.5.1 Context
Discoverable memorization is all or nothing: the secret comes out or it does not. An auditor wants a graded answer: how much closer to the secret does the model put an attacker? Carlini et al. (2019, “The Secret Sharer”) proposed planting canaries, random secrets of a fixed format such as “my pin is” followed by five random digits, in the training data, then measuring where the trained model ranks the planted secret among all secrets of the same format. Because the canary is random and planted, you know the right answer and the size of the space, so you can quantify memorization exactly.


13.5.2 Statement
A canary has a format \(s[\cdot]\) with a hole, and a randomness space \(\mathcal R\) of values that can fill the hole. Here \(s[r]\) is “my pin is \(r\)”, with \(r\) one of the \(|\mathcal R| = 10^5\) pins. A value \(\hat r\) is drawn uniformly at random from \(\mathcal R\), and \(s[\hat r]\) is inserted \(k\) times into the training data. After training, order all of \(\mathcal R\) by the model’s probability \(p(r \mid \text{"my pin is"})\); the rank of \(\hat r\) is its position in that order (Fact 3), the number of guesses an attacker who follows the model needs.
The exposure turns the rank into a number of bits saved. Without the model, the attacker faces all \(|\mathcal R|\) candidates, which is \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) bits of search. With the model, it faces \(\operatorname{rank}(\hat r)\) candidates, \(\log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r)\) bits. The exposure is the difference: \[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \log_2\operatorname{rank}(\hat r). \tag{13.9}\]
Two properties follow from this definition directly. Because the rank lies between 1 and \(|\mathcal R|\), the exposure lies between 0 and \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\), with the maximum when the canary is the model’s top candidate. And exposure counts guesses saved: an attacker who guesses in the model’s order needs \(\operatorname{rank}(\hat r) = 2^{\log_2|\mathcal R| - \mathrm{exposure}}\) guesses instead of \(|\mathcal R|\), so each bit of exposure halves the work.
The third property is what makes exposure an audit tool: you know how it behaves when nothing was memorized. If the model does not depend on \(\hat r\), for instance because the canary was never inserted, then \(\hat r\) is just a random point in a fixed ordering, and a high exposure is unlikely. Precisely, for every \(e \ge 0\), \[\Pr\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r) \ge e\big] \le 2^{-e}, \tag{13.10}\] and, when no two candidates tie, its average is a fixed small number of bits: \[\mathbb E\big[\mathrm{exposure}(\hat r)\big] = \log_2|\mathcal R| - \frac{\log_2(|\mathcal R|!)}{|\mathcal R|} \;\longrightarrow\; \log_2e = 1.4427 \text{ bits}. \tag{13.11}\]
So exposure is \(-\log_2\) of a p-value. A p-value is the probability, under the assumption that nothing happened, of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one observed. Here it is the probability that a canary that was never inserted would look at least this memorized, and Equation 13.10 says it is at most \(2^{-\text{exposure}}\).


13.5.3 Derivation
Range and guesses. The rank is between 1 and \(|\mathcal R|\), so \(\log_2\operatorname{rank}\) is between 0 and \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\). Subtracting from \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) gives an exposure between \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) and 0. Solving Equation 13.9 for the rank gives \(\operatorname{rank} = 2^{\log_2|\mathcal R| - \mathrm{exposure}}\).
Null distribution. The idea is that, without the canary, the model’s scores are fixed before \(\hat r\) is drawn, so \(\hat r\) lands at a uniformly random position in their order.

The order is fixed. If the model was trained without the canary, its scores \(p(r \mid \cdot)\) are fixed numbers that do not depend on \(\hat r\). With no ties they order \(\mathcal R\) into positions \(1, \dots, |\mathcal R|\).
The canary’s position is uniform. \(\hat r\) is uniform on \(\mathcal R\) and independent of the scores, so its position is equally likely to be any of \(1, \dots, |\mathcal R|\).
Count the positions with high exposure. By Equation 13.9, exposure \(\ge e\) means \(\log_2\operatorname{rank} \le \log_2|\mathcal R| - e\), that is \(\operatorname{rank} \le |\mathcal R|2^{-e}\). There are \(\lfloor|\mathcal R|2^{-e}\rfloor\) such positions (the whole numbers up to that bound), each with probability \(1/|\mathcal R|\), so the probability is \(\lfloor|\mathcal R|2^{-e}\rfloor/|\mathcal R| \le 2^{-e}\).
Ties only help the bound. The rank counts every candidate at least as likely as \(\hat r\), so a tie can only raise the rank of \(\hat r\). A higher rank means a lower exposure, so the probability of a high exposure can only fall, and the bound still holds.
The mean. With the rank uniform on \(1, \dots, |\mathcal R|\), the average of \(\log_2\operatorname{rank}\) is \(\frac{1}{|\mathcal R|}\sum_{i=1}^{|\mathcal R|}\log_2 i\). A sum of logarithms is the logarithm of the product, and \(1 \cdot 2 \cdots |\mathcal R| = |\mathcal R|!\), so this is \(\log_2(|\mathcal R|!)/|\mathcal R|\); subtracting it from \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) gives Equation 13.11. For the limit, Stirling’s approximation of the factorial (derived in Section E.2) says \(\ln N! = N\ln N - N + O(\ln N)\), where \(O(\ln N)\) is a correction that grows no faster than a multiple of \(\ln N\). Dividing by \(N\ln 2\) to get base-2 logarithms per candidate, \(\log_2(N!)/N = \log_2N - 1/\ln 2 + O(\ln N/N) = \log_2N - \log_2e + O(\ln N/N)\), since \(1/\ln 2 = \log_2 e\). The correction vanishes as \(N\) grows, so the mean exposure tends to \(\log_2 e\).

A space of four candidates makes all of this concrete. With \(|\mathcal R| = 4\) the rank is 1, 2, 3 or 4 with probability \(\frac14\) each, and the exposure is \(2 - \log_2(\text{rank})\):



Table 13.4: The four equally likely exposures of a canary from a space of four candidates that was never inserted.

The third entry is \(2 - \log_2 3 = 2 - 1.585 = 0.415\). The mean is \(\frac14(2 + 1 + 0.415 + 0) = 0.854\), which matches \(2 - \log_2(24)/4 = 2 - 4.585/4\), since \(4! = 24\). The probability of exposure at least 1 is \(\frac12 = 2^{-1}\) (ranks 1 and 2), and of exposure at least 2 is \(\frac14 = 2^{-2}\) (rank 1 only): the bound is tight at integer exposures.


13.5.4 Interpretation
Exposure is a membership test with a known null. “Was this canary inserted?” is a membership question (Membership inference), and the exposure is the score of a test that says “inserted” when the exposure is at least a threshold \(e\). By Equation 13.10 that test has false positive rate (the chance of saying “inserted” about a canary that was not) at most \(2^{-e}\). In membership inference, calibrating a test means training shadow models, extra models trained with and without a record, to learn how the score behaves for non-members. Here none are needed: the randomness of the canary does the calibration, playing the role that the population of non-members plays in membership inference.
Exposure is also guessing work saved, in the sense of Fact 3. A uniform canary has min-entropy \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\): before seeing the model, the attacker’s best single guess succeeds with probability \(1/|\mathcal R|\). After the model, the attacker who guesses in the model’s order needs \(2^{\log_2|\mathcal R| - \mathrm{exposure}}\) tries. Carlini et al. (2019) note that exposure close to \(\log_2|\mathcal R|\) means the secret can actually be extracted, for example by a shortest-path search: treat each digit position as a step, weight each choice of digit by its negative log-probability, and find the cheapest path through the model’s predictions, which is the most likely pin.
For large spaces exposure has to be estimated, because enumerating \(\mathcal R\) is impossible for, say, a 9-digit number. Two estimators replace enumeration. The first is sampling: score \(m\) random candidates and use the fraction of them at least as likely as the canary as the estimate of \(\operatorname{rank}/|\mathcal R|\). It cannot resolve exposures above \(\log_2m\), because a canary above all \(m\) sampled candidates only tells you its rank fraction is below about \(1/m\). The second is extrapolation: fit a distribution to the sampled scores and read off its tail beyond the canary’s score; Carlini et al. (2019) fit a skew-normal, a normal distribution with an extra parameter that lets one tail be heavier than the other. The fit is only as good as its tail, and the tail is exactly the part you cannot sample.
Ties hide memorization. A model that has never seen the canary’s contexts gives every candidate the same score. Every candidate is then tied with all the others, so every rank is \(|\mathcal R|\) and every exposure 0. On this corpus the order-8 model without a canary gives every pin exactly the same probability after “my pin is”, and the exposure of every candidate is 0.
Finally, canaries test defences, not only models. Because you control what was planted, you can compare exposure across two training runs that differ in one thing. Train with and without deduplication, and the change in exposure measures what deduplication bought. Train with a differentially private algorithm (Part 3), and exposure near the null mean says the planted secrets were not memorized; Carlini et al. (2019) found that private training kept their canaries at the exposure of canaries never inserted. Plant canaries, unlearn them, and measure exposure again, and you have a test of an unlearning method. Auditing differentially private training uses the same tool, with canaries designed to be as exposed as possible.


13.5.5 Example: one canary, three model sizes
The script plants “my pin is 58745” and computes the exact exposure by scoring all \(10^5\) pins. Table 13.5 gives it for orders 2, 3 and 4.

The jump from \(k = 0\) to \(k = 1\) follows from Fact 2: what matters is whether a digit of the canary sits in a context that only the canary’s copies fill. No background line contains s_, an s followed by a space, because names end in a vowel. So the three orders behave differently.
At order 2 the model reads one character of context, and the first digit’s context is a single space, shared by all 11,300 lines. No digit of the canary has a context of its own, so one copy is a single vote among thousands, and it moves the exposure by \(0.41 - 0.40 = 0.01\) bits.
At order 3 the first digit’s context is s_, which occurs only in the canary. By Fact 2 and Table 13.2, one copy makes the first digit 11 times as likely as each other first digit, a factor worth \(\log_2 11 = 3.46\) bits. The exposure goes from 0.89 to 4.05, a rise of \(4.05 - 0.89 = 3.16\) bits: close to 3.46 but not equal, because the rank also depends on how the other pins’ scores are spread.
At order 4 the first two digits have unique contexts, is_ and s_5, worth about \(2 \times 3.46 = 6.92\) bits. The exposure goes from 3.76 to 9.98, a rise of \(9.98 - 3.76 = 6.22\) bits.
The remaining digits share their contexts with the 5,000 background pins and move only as the copies outvote them. Figure 13.3 shows the same movement on the full distribution of scores, and Figure 13.4 averages several canaries.

Each insertion pushes the canary further into the right tail, past more and more of the other pins.

The null in practice. For a pin that was never inserted, the derivation predicts a uniform rank. For orders 2, 3 and 4 the scores have no ties, so the exposures of all \(10^5\) uninserted pins are exactly the uniform-rank values: mean 1.443 bits, against 1.4426 from Equation 13.11, and a fraction \(0.03125 = 1/32 = 2^{-5}\) with exposure at least 5, exactly on the bound Equation 13.10.

13.5.6 Check yourself

An auditor plants one canary, trains, and measures exposure 10 bits on a space of \(10^9\). What is the chance a non-inserted canary scores that high? (At most \(2^{-10} = 1/1024 \approx 0.001\), by Equation 13.10. The size of the space does not enter.)
Why does the order-2 model barely react to the canary even at 64 copies? (Every context it sees is a single character, shared with thousands of training positions. The 64 votes are a small fraction of the counts in each context. The model is too small to give the canary anything of its own.)

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.6 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify
text:
13.6 Extraction without the prefix: generate, rank, verify

13.6.1 Context
The attacker of Section 13.3 had the training prefix. A real attacker has only the model. Carlini et al. (2021) showed how such an attacker extracts training data from GPT-2: generate a large number of samples, rank them by how likely they are to be memorized, and check the top of the ranking. The checking step is easy for whoever has the training data (a search) and, for an outside attacker, can be done against public sources. The hard step is the ranking, and it is a hypothesis test: for each sample, decide between two explanations of why the model produced it.


13.6.2 Statement
A model can find a string likely for two different reasons. The string may be ordinary, the kind of text any model of the language would find likely, or the model may have memorized it from its training set. Only the second is a leak. So for a generated string \(x\), test \(H_0\): “\(x\) is likely because text like it is common” against \(H_1\): “\(x\) is likely because the target model memorized it”. To score the two explanations you need a model of each. A reference model \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\), trained on data from the same distribution but not on the target’s training set, stands in for “common text”, the distribution under \(H_0\). The target model \(p_\theta\) itself stands in for \(H_1\). The best evidence for memorization is then how much more likely the target finds \(x\) than the reference does, which on a log scale is a difference. The most powerful test at every false positive rate ranks generations by this log-likelihood ratio, \[\Lambda(x) = \ln p_\theta(x) - \ln p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x), \tag{13.12}\] not by \(\ln p_\theta(x)\) alone.


13.6.3 Derivation

The two hypotheses give two probabilities. Under \(H_0\) the string has probability \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\), and under \(H_1\) it has probability \(p_\theta(x)\).
The best test thresholds their ratio. The Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing says that, among all tests with a given false positive rate (the fraction of \(H_0\) strings wrongly flagged), the one with the highest true positive rate (the fraction of \(H_1\) strings caught) flags a string when the likelihood ratio \(p_\theta(x)/p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) is above a threshold. The reason is a budget argument: each flagged string costs false positives in proportion to \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}(x)\) and gains true positives in proportion to \(p_\theta(x)\), so for a fixed budget of false positives you catch the most by flagging the strings with the largest ratio first.
Take logarithms. The logarithm is increasing, so it keeps the order of the ratios, and thresholding the ratio is the same as thresholding its logarithm, Equation 13.12.
Why raw likelihood falls short. Ranking by \(\ln p_\theta(x)\) alone is the same as using Equation 13.12 with \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\) constant, as if every string were equally common a priori. That assumption is wrong exactly for strings that are likely under any model, such as boilerplate, licences and famous quotations, and those are the strings raw likelihood puts first.

This is the same move as the per-example calibration of Membership inference: there, a record’s raw loss under the target model is compared with the loss that models which did not see the record would give it.


13.6.4 Interpretation
Raw likelihood finds the common, not the private. The most likely generations of a large model are text that appears everywhere: software licences, news boilerplate, number sequences. These are in the training data, but extracting them reveals nothing. A reference model knows them too, so their ratio is close to 1 and the difference in Equation 13.12 cancels them.
The reference can be crude. Carlini et al. (2021) used three: a smaller model of the same family, the length of the text after compression with zlib (a general-purpose compressor, so the compressed length is a model-free measure of how predictable the text is), and the target’s own likelihood on the lowercased text. Each gives a different idea of “generic”, and each catches strings the others miss.
What the attacker cares about is precision, not recall. An attacker who checks the top 100 candidates by hand cares about how many of those are real training data, the precision of the top of the ranking, not about how many of all memorized strings it eventually finds. A high precision among a few flagged strings is a high true positive rate at a tiny false positive rate, the same operating point that matters in membership inference.


13.6.5 Example: extracting secrets from the contact-list model
The attacker samples 20,000 lines from the order-6 model, starting each at the beginning of a line. To make the ranking problem realistic, 50 public lines (think of a published directory) are added 100 times each to the target’s training set; the attacker’s own reference data, an independent contact list of 5,000 lines from the same generator, also contain them. The reference model is trained on those reference data. A generation counts as a hit if it is a private training line: in the target’s training set and not public.
Of the 20,000 samples, 14,852 are distinct. Among them are 197 private training lines and all 50 public lines. By duplication group, the samples contain none of the secrets inserted 1, 2 or 4 times, 11% of those inserted 8 times, 86% of those inserted 16 times and all of those inserted 32 times. Compare the discoverable rates at order 6 (Table 13.3): 8% of the singletons and 65% of the lines seen twice come out when you hold their prefix. Without the prefix, a sample must first produce the right name before it can produce the pin, and only heavily duplicated lines make their names likely enough. What this attack extracts is much less than what is discoverable.
Ranking matters (Figure 13.5). Among the top 100 distinct generations by target likelihood, 45 are private training lines; the rest are mostly the 50 public lines, which, repeated 100 times each, are the most likely strings the model knows. Ranking by Equation 13.12, 85 of the top 100 are private training lines, because the reference model also finds the public lines likely and cancels them.






Figure 13.5: Fraction of the top-ranked distinct generations that are private training lines (solid) or public lines (dashed), from 20,000 samples of an order-6 model trained with 50 public lines repeated 100 times. Ranking by likelihood puts the public lines first. Ranking by the likelihood ratio to a reference model trained on other data puts the private lines first.





13.6.6 The production attack in prose
Nasr et al. (2023) carried this to deployed models. Their measurements separate the two notions of Section 13.3, discoverable and extractable. On open models whose training data are public (Pythia, GPT-Neo and others), they measured how much of what an attacker generates is verbatim training data, by checking every 50-token window of the output against a suffix array of the training set, an index that finds any substring of a huge text quickly. For closed models, whose training data are unknown, they built a 9-terabyte auxiliary corpus of public web text and counted 50-token matches against it as a lower bound.
The aligned chat model they attacked, ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo), rarely emitted training data when used normally: alignment training, a later stage that fine-tunes the model to follow instructions, had taught it to answer as an assistant, not to continue documents. Their divergence attack asked it to repeat a single word forever. After many repetitions the model diverged from the chat behaviour and began to emit text that looked like pretraining documents, and a sizeable part of that text matched the web corpus verbatim. They report that the attack made the model emit training data at a rate about 150 times higher than normal use, and that about 200 US dollars of queries extracted over 10,000 unique memorized training examples, including personal contact details. The structure is the one of this chapter: generate (with a prompt that escapes the aligned behaviour), verify (against a corpus), and estimate the total from what was found.


13.6.7 Check yourself

Why are none of the secrets inserted 4 times generated, although at order 6 76% of them are discoverably memorized? (An unprompted sample must first produce the secret’s name. With 343,000 possible names, a sample hits a particular one only if that name is likely, which takes many copies.)
When would ranking by raw likelihood be as good as the ratio? (When nothing is generically likely: if every string had the same prior probability, \(p_{\mathrm{ref}}\) would be constant and the two rankings would agree.)

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
section: 13.7 Code: check every number by computation and simulation
text:
13.7 Code: check every number by computation and simulation
The script code/memorization.py builds the contact list, trains the \(n\)-gram models by counting, and runs every experiment in this chapter: greedy and sampled extraction from true prefixes, the copies needed \(k^*\) for every secret, exact and estimated exposure of canaries over all \(10^5\) pins, and the generate-rank-verify attack. Every model is a small typed dataclass of sorted count arrays, so scoring all \(10^5\) pins is one vectorized lookup. From the repository root:
uv run python code/part02-attacks/memorization.py

What to take from it. Four things stand out. First, the count formula is exact: \(k^*\) from Equation 13.7 predicts which secrets greedy decoding reproduces in every cell, ties included, because it is a restatement of how greedy decoding reads counts. The migule 16430 row shows the mechanism in one line: the secret, inserted 4 times, would need 151 copies at order 3, 43 at order 4 and 9 at order 5, but only 1 from order 6 on, which is why greedy decoding reproduces it from order 6. Second, duplication and model size both matter, and they trade off against each other: a small model needs dozens of copies, a large one needs one. Third, exposure behaves like a p-value. Without the canary, exposures follow the uniform-rank law exactly; with it, each digit of the canary that has a context of its own adds about 3.5 bits at one copy, the \(\log_2 11\) of Fact 2. Fourth, the attacker without the prefix gets less, and needs a reference. Only heavily duplicated secrets come out of unprompted samples, and ranking by the likelihood ratio nearly doubles the precision of the top 100, from 0.45 to 0.85.

title: 13  Memorization and training-data extraction
text:
13.8 References

Carlini, Liu, Erlingsson, Kos & Song, “The Secret Sharer: Evaluating and Testing Unintended Memorization in Neural Networks” (USENIX Security 2019): canaries, the exposure metric, its estimation by sampling and skew-normal extrapolation, and extraction of planted secrets by search.
Carlini et al., “Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models” (USENIX Security 2021): extractable and \(k\)-eidetic memorization; the generate-rank-verify attack on GPT-2 with perplexity, reference-model, zlib and lowercase ranking.
Carlini, Ippolito, Jagielski, Lee, Tramèr & Zhang, “Quantifying Memorization Across Neural Language Models” (ICLR 2023): memorization measured by prompting with training prefixes; log-linear growth with model size, duplication and prompt length.
Nasr et al., “Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models” (2023): discoverable against extractable memorization, measurement on open models against their training sets, and the divergence attack on an aligned chat model.
Kandpal, Wallace & Raffel, “Deduplicating Training Data Mitigates Privacy Risks in Language Models” (ICML 2022): how the rate of regenerated sequences grows with duplication.
Lee et al., “Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better” (ACL 2022): near-duplicate detection at scale and its effect on emitted training text and model quality.
Ippolito et al., “Preventing Generation of Verbatim Memorization in Language Models Gives a False Sense of Privacy” (INLG 2023): approximate memorization and why verbatim filters fail.
Feldman, “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail” (STOC 2020): why rare examples must be memorized for accuracy, which explains why they are exposed first.
Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed. draft), ch. 3: \(n\)-gram language models, smoothing and perplexity.

Rules of thumb

Memorization is a rank: the secret above the strings it could have been.
Duplication is a vote in every context the string passes through; the most contested context decides.
Larger models split contexts and give rare strings their own parameters, so they memorize more and from fewer copies.
Deduplicate first: it is cheap and helps, but not for singletons in a high-capacity model.
Report exposure, not just extraction: it is graded and has a known null.
Rank generations against a reference, never by raw likelihood.
An attacker without the prefix gets less than the discoverable rate suggests, but production attacks show “less” is still thousands of records.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1 Why this matters
A phone keyboard learns from what its users type. The raw text never leaves the phones. Instead, a server sends the current model \(\theta\) to each phone, the phone computes the gradient of the loss on its own few examples, and only that gradient goes back. The server averages the gradients of many phones and takes a step. This is the setting of federated learning (FL), and it is often described as private because “the data stay on the device”. Later parts study FL itself. This chapter asks one question about it: what does a single client’s gradient reveal about the client’s data?
The answer is: often, everything. A gradient is not a summary statistic chosen to hide the data. It is the derivative of a loss with respect to millions of parameters, and many of those derivatives are simple functions of the input. This chapter shows four ways to read the data back out of the gradient, going from the exact to the approximate. The first is exact recovery: for a fully connected layer with a bias, dividing one row of the weight gradient by one entry of the bias gradient gives back the layer’s input, with no search at all. The second is label recovery: the signs of the last layer’s gradient name the label, so the label can be taken off the list of unknowns. The third handles layers where no such closed form exists. You guess an input, compute the gradient it would produce, and move the guess until that gradient matches the one you saw. This is Deep Leakage from Gradients (DLG). The fourth asks what happens when the client sends the average gradient of a whole batch of examples. Averaging mixes the examples together, but much less than you might hope.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.1.1 The one idea: a gradient is a sum of outer products
Why should a gradient contain the input at all? Take a fully connected layer, which computes \(a = Wx + b\): each output \(a_j\) is a weighted sum of the inputs \(x_k\), with weights \(W_{jk}\), plus a bias \(b_j\). The weight \(W_{jk}\) multiplies the input \(x_k\), so a small change in \(W_{jk}\) changes \(a_j\) by \(x_k\) times that change. The loss \(\ell\) in turn responds to a change in \(a_j\) at some rate, \(\gamma_j = \partial\ell/\partial a_j\), which depends on everything that happens after this layer. The chain rule multiplies the two rates: the loss changes with \(W_{jk}\) at the rate \(\gamma_jx_k\). Collecting these numbers into a matrix with the shape of \(W\), the gradient of the loss with respect to \(W\) is \[\nabla_W\ell = \gamma\,x^\top, \qquad \gamma = \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial a}. \tag{14.1}\] A matrix whose \((j, k)\) entry is \(\gamma_jx_k\) is called the outer product of \(\gamma\) and \(x\). Here it is the outer product of what flows backward (\(\gamma\)) with what flowed forward (\(x\)). Row \(j\) is the input \(x\) multiplied by the single number \(\gamma_j\), so the layer’s input sits, unchanged up to a scale, in every row of the gradient. Every attack in this chapter exploits that. With one example the scale can be divided out. With a batch of \(B\) examples the gradient is a sum of \(B\) such outer products, and the attacker’s job is to pull the sum apart.
Table 14.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 14.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.









Result
Where it is used




\(\nabla_W\ell = \gamma x^\top\), \(\nabla_b\ell = \gamma\) (Toolkit)
Every attack below; per-example gradients in later parts


Exact recovery \(x = (\nabla_W\ell)_{j,:}/(\nabla_b\ell)_j\)
Inverting any model whose first layer is fully connected with a bias

Removing the label from the unknowns; label leakage in batches

How much batching protects, and why it is not a defence








14.1.2 The setting and the game
The server is honest-but-curious in the sense of Threat models and privacy games: it runs the training protocol as specified, sends the real model and does not tamper with anything, and only analyses what it receives. Its access is the transcript, the strongest level of that chapter: it sees each client’s own update, which is more than the final model, and it knows the architecture and every parameter of \(\theta\) because it chose them. A client holds a batch of \(B\) labelled examples \((x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_B, y_B)\). Its training loss is the average of the \(B\) per-example losses, and what it sends is the gradient of that average with respect to all the parameters \(\theta\). Since the derivative of an average is the average of the derivatives, this is the average of the per-example gradients: \[g = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i, y_i). \tag{14.2}\]
This is the reconstruction game of that chapter, played on one client. A game there has three parts: a challenger who draws a hidden secret, an adversary who sees only what the threat model allows, and a score for the adversary’s guess. Here the challenger draws the batch from the population and the secret is the inputs. The adversary sees \((\theta, g)\) and outputs reconstructions \(\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B\), and its gain is how close they come to the true inputs. We measure closeness by the relative error \(\|\hat x - x\|/\| x\|\): the length of the mistake as a fraction of the length of the input, so that 0 is a perfect reconstruction and 1 is a mistake as large as the image itself. Each true example is matched to its closest reconstruction, because an average does not change when you reorder the examples, so the gradient carries no record of which example came first.
The baseline is a guess from the population alone, such as the average image of a shape, which knows nothing of the client’s own position, noise or pixels. The attacks below either recover the client’s exact pixels or, for large enough batches, produce blends; there is little in between.
The model. All experiments use a network with one hidden layer, written in NumPy. An input \(x \in \mathbb R^d\) first goes through a fully connected layer (\(W_1\), \(b_1\)) that gives one number \(a_j\) per hidden unit. An activation \(\sigma\) is applied to each unit, giving \(h\). A second fully connected layer (\(W_2\), \(b_2\)) turns \(h\) into one score \(z_k\) per class, called a logit. The softmax turns the logits into probabilities by exponentiating and normalizing, \(p_k = e^{z_k}/\sum_{k'}e^{z_{k'}}\), so that every \(p_k\) is positive and they sum to 1. The loss is the cross-entropy, minus the log of the probability the model gives to the true label \(y\), which is small when the model is confidently right. In one line: \[a = W_1x + b_1, \quad h = \sigma(a), \quad z = W_2h + b_2, \quad p = \mathrm{softmax}(z), \quad \ell = -\ln p_y, \tag{14.3}\] with \(m\) hidden units, \(K\) classes, \(W_1 \in \mathbb R^{m\times d}\) and \(W_2 \in \mathbb R^{K\times m}\). The activation \(\sigma\) is either the ReLU \(\max(a, 0)\), which passes positive values and replaces negative ones by 0, or the sigmoid \(1/(1 + e^{-a})\), which squashes every value smoothly into \((0, 1)\). The inputs are synthetic \(8\times8\) grey-scale images (\(d = 64\)) of \(K = 4\) shapes (a horizontal bar, a vertical bar, a diagonal and a square outline), shifted at random and with pixel noise. The network has \(m = 32\) hidden units and is at its random initialization, as in the first round of training. Counting the \(64\cdot32\) weights and 32 biases of the first layer and the \(32\cdot4\) weights and 4 biases of the second, it has \(64\cdot32 + 32 + 32\cdot4 + 4 = 2{,}212\) parameters, so the gradient has 2,212 entries, against 64 unknown pixels per example.
What this chapter assumes. Gradients, stochastic gradient descent (SGD), minibatches and the limits of non-convex optimization are in Optimization. The threat-model vocabulary and the games are in Threat models and privacy games. The facts this chapter needs from both are restated where they are used. For a different route to reconstruction, from noisy answers to many queries rather than from one gradient, see Reconstruction attacks.
Conventions. \(e_y\) is the \(y\)-th standard basis vector: 1 in position \(y\) and 0 elsewhere, the “one-hot” encoding of the label. \(\odot\) is the elementwise product, which multiplies two vectors entry by entry. For a matrix \(A\), \(A_{j,:}\) is its \(j\)-th row. Gradients are column vectors and \(\nabla_W\ell\) has the shape of \(W\). We write \(\gamma_1 = \partial\ell/\partial a \in \mathbb R^m\) and \(\gamma_2 = \partial\ell/\partial z \in \mathbb R^K\) for the backward signals at the two layers: how fast the loss changes with each hidden unit’s pre-activation and with each logit. Texts on backpropagation usually write these signals as \(\delta\); this book keeps \(\delta\) for the privacy parameter of the later parts.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
14.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

14.2.1 Fact 1 — The gradient of a fully connected layer is an outer product
This is the fact behind the whole chapter: in a fully connected layer, the gradient of each weight is the backward signal of its output times the input it multiplies. Let \(a = Wx + b\) with \(W \in \mathbb R^{m\times d}\), and let \(\gamma = \partial\ell/\partial a\) be the backward signal. Then \[\nabla_W\ell = \gamma\,x^\top, \qquad \nabla_b\ell = \gamma. \tag{14.4}\]
Why. Write out one output: \(a_j = \sum_kW_{jk}x_k + b_j\). The weight \(W_{jk}\) appears in \(a_j\) only, with coefficient \(x_k\), so \(\partial a_j/\partial W_{jk} = x_k\). The loss depends on \(W_{jk}\) only through \(a_j\), so the chain rule gives \(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial W_{jk}} = \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial a_j}\frac{\partial a_j}{\partial W_{jk}} = \gamma_jx_k\), which is the \((j, k)\) entry of \(\gamma x^\top\). The bias \(b_j\) enters \(a_j\) with coefficient 1, so \(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial b_j} = \gamma_j\cdot1\).
A concrete case. With \(m = 2\), \(d = 3\), \(\gamma = (-0.3279, 0.9838)\) and \(x = (0.5, 1, 0.2)\), the two rows of \(\nabla_W\ell\) are \(-0.3279\,x = (-0.1640, -0.3279, -0.0656)\) and \(0.9838\,x = (0.4919, 0.9838, 0.1968)\). Both are multiples of \(x\). This is the worked example of Table 14.2.
Every attack in this chapter uses this fact. The point to keep is the split between the two factors: \(\gamma\) depends on everything above the layer (the rest of the network, the loss, the label), but the factor \(x^\top\) does not. Whatever the rest of the network does, it can only rescale the rows, never change their direction.


14.2.2 Fact 2 — Softmax with cross-entropy has gradient \(p - e_y\)
At the last layer the backward signal has a very simple form: the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot label. In words, raising the logit of a wrong class \(k\) raises the loss at the rate \(p_k\), the probability the model already gives that class, and raising the logit of the true class lowers the loss at the rate \(1 - p_y\). With \(p = \mathrm{softmax}(z)\) and \(\ell = -\ln p_y\), \[\gamma_2 = \frac{\partial\ell}{\partial z} = p - e_y. \tag{14.5}\]
Why. Write the loss without the fraction. Since \(p_y = e^{z_y}/\sum_ke^{z_k}\), its log is \(z_y - \ln\sum_ke^{z_k}\), so \(\ell = -z_y + \ln\sum_ke^{z_k}\). Now differentiate in one logit \(z_k\). The first term depends only on \(z_y\), so it contributes \(-1\) when \(k = y\) and 0 otherwise, which is \(-\mathbf 1[k = y]\). The second term is the log of a sum, and the derivative of \(\ln u\) is \(u'/u\): here \(u' = e^{z_k}\), so the term contributes \(e^{z_k}/\sum_{k'}e^{z_{k'}} = p_k\). Together, \(\partial\ell/\partial z_k = p_k - \mathbf 1[k = y]\), which is entry \(k\) of \(p - e_y\).
A concrete case. With logits \(z = (-0.35, 0.295)\) and \(y = 1\) (the first class), the first probability is \(p_1 = e^{-0.35}/(e^{-0.35} + e^{0.295}) = 1/(1 + e^{0.645}) = 1/(1 + 1.906) = 0.3441\), so \(p = (0.3441, 0.6559)\) and \(\gamma_2 = (0.3441 - 1, 0.6559) = (-0.6559, 0.6559)\). The entries sum to 0, and only the true class is negative.
This sign pattern is what label recovery uses. The softmax never gives a probability of exactly 0 or 1, since every \(e^{z_k}\) is positive, so \(0 < p_y < 1\). The entry at the true label is therefore \(p_y - 1 < 0\), and every other entry is \(p_k > 0\).


14.2.3 Fact 3 — Backpropagation and averaging
To use Fact 1 at the first layer you need its backward signal \(\gamma_1\), and that is obtained by sending \(\gamma_2\) back through the network, which is what backpropagation does. Each hidden unit \(j\) feeds every logit \(z_k\) through the weight \(W_{2,kj}\), so it collects the logits’ signals weighted by those connections, \(\sum_k\gamma_{2,k}W_{2,kj}\). That sum is how fast the loss changes with the unit’s output \(h_j\). The unit’s output is \(h_j = \sigma(a_j)\), so to get the rate with respect to \(a_j\) you multiply by the activation’s slope \(\sigma'(a_j)\). In vector form: \[\gamma_1 = (W_2^\top\gamma_2)\odot\sigma'(a). \tag{14.6}\] The second half of the fact concerns batches: the gradient of an average loss over a batch is the average of the per-example gradients.
Why. \(z_k = \sum_jW_{2,kj}h_j + b_{2,k}\), so \(h_j\) enters each \(z_k\) with coefficient \(W_{2,kj}\), and the chain rule sums over the logits: \(\frac{\partial\ell}{\partial h_j} = \sum_k\gamma_{2,k}W_{2,kj} = (W_2^\top\gamma_2)_j\). Then \(h_j = \sigma(a_j)\) multiplies this by \(\sigma'(a_j)\). The claim about batches holds because differentiation is linear: the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives, and a constant factor \(\frac1B\) comes out unchanged.
A concrete case. For ReLU the slope is \(\sigma'(a_j) = \mathbf 1[a_j > 0]\): 1 if the unit is switched on, 0 if it is switched off. So a unit that is switched off on an input has \(\gamma_{1,j} = 0\) and, by Fact 1, a zero row in \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\). For a batch, Fact 1 applied to each example and then averaged gives the first-layer gradient \(\frac1B\sum_i\gamma_{1,i}x_i^\top\): a sum of \(B\) outer products, one per example.
Label recovery uses this fact to know which rows of the weight gradient can be negative, and every batch result below uses the averaging.

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer
text:
14.3 Exact recovery from a fully connected layer

14.3.1 Context
The server sees \(g\). Is there any computation, short of a search, that gives back the client’s input? For the most common first layer of all, a fully connected layer with a bias, there is: one division. The observation goes back at least to Phong et al. (2018), who pointed it out for exactly this federated setting.


14.3.2 Statement
Suppose the client sends the gradient of a single example, and the first layer is fully connected, \(a = W_1x + b_1\). By Fact 1, row \(j\) of the weight gradient is the input \(x\) scaled by the number \(\gamma_{1,j}\), and entry \(j\) of the bias gradient is that same number \(\gamma_{1,j}\). Dividing the first by the second removes the scale. So for every unit \(j\) with \((\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j \ne 0\), \[x = \frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j}. \tag{14.7}\] Moreover, since every row is a multiple of the same vector, \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\) has rank one (all its rows lie on a single line), and that line, its row space, is the line through \(x\).


14.3.3 Derivation

Apply Fact 1 (Equation 14.4) to the first layer. It gives the two pieces the server sees: \((\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:} = \gamma_{1,j}\,x^\top\) and \((\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j = \gamma_{1,j}\).
Divide one by the other. When \(\gamma_{1,j} \ne 0\), the ratio is \(\gamma_{1,j}x^\top/\gamma_{1,j} = x^\top\). Nothing about the rest of the network enters: the depth, the activations above, the loss and the label all sit inside the number \(\gamma_{1,j}\), and that number cancels.
Read off the rank. All rows of \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell = \gamma_1x^\top\) are multiples of the same vector \(x^\top\). A matrix whose rows are all multiples of one nonzero vector has rank one, so (as long as \(\gamma_1 \ne 0\)) the rank is one and the row space is spanned by \(x\).



14.3.4 Interpretation
The attack is exact and costs nothing. It needs no optimization, no prior knowledge of what the data look like, and no knowledge of the label. It also checks itself: every unit with a nonzero bias gradient gives the same answer, so if all the usable ratios agree, the attacker knows it has the input.
The same division works at any fully connected layer whose input you want. Applied deeper in the network, it gives that layer’s input, an intermediate feature vector. Applied at the first layer, the input is the data itself.
Three things can stop it, and only one of them stops it fully. With ReLU, units that are switched off on \(x\) have \(\gamma_{1,j} = 0\) and give nothing, but a single active unit is enough. Without a bias there is no denominator, but the rank-one structure still gives the direction of \(x\), so \(x\) is known up to one scalar, and a one-dimensional search finds that scalar (Exercise 2). A convolutional first layer is what really breaks the outer-product form. A convolution applies the same small filter at every position of the image, so its gradient is a sum of outer products over all the image patches rather than a single one, and no division separates them. That is why images fed to convolutional networks need the search of Section 14.5. A batch of more than one example also breaks the formula, as Section 14.6 shows, but only partly.
Figure 14.1 shows the attack on one image.






Figure 14.1: Exact recovery from the first-layer gradient of a ReLU network with 32 hidden units. Left: the client’s \(8\times8\) input. Middle: \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\), one row per hidden unit and one column per pixel (blue positive, red negative), next to \(\nabla_{b_1}\ell\). Every nonzero row is the image times the matching bias entry; switched-off units give zero rows. Right: one row divided by its bias entry, which is the input exactly.





14.3.5 Example: a network you can compute by hand
Take \(d = 3\) inputs, \(m = 2\) ReLU units and \(K = 2\) classes, with \[W_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.4 & -0.2 & 0.1\\ 0.3 & 0.5 & -0.4\end{pmatrix},\quad b_1 = \begin{pmatrix}0.1\\ -0.1\end{pmatrix},\quad W_2 = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{pmatrix},\quad b_2 = 0, \tag{14.8}\] and the example \(x = (0.5, 1, 0.2)\) with label \(y = 1\) (the first class). Table 14.2 walks through the forward pass, the backward pass and the attack.
