The server never sees \(a\), \(h\), \(z\) or \(p\). From the two gradient rows alone it divides and reads off \(x\), twice. Both units are on here (\(a = (0.12, 0.47)\) is positive in both entries), so the ReLU slope is 1 for both and \(\gamma_1\) is just \(W_2^\top\gamma_2\).
On the images. For one \(8\times8\) image and the 32-unit ReLU network, 13 of the 32 units are switched on and have a nonzero bias gradient. Every one of the 13 ratios equals the image to a relative error of at most \(6.7\times10^{-17}\), which is rounding error. To check the rank, look at the singular values of \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell\): they measure how much of the matrix lies along each of its independent directions, so a rank-one matrix has exactly one that is not zero. Here they are \(1.6155\) and then nothing: the second is \(9.5\times10^{-17}\) times the first. The gradient is rank one, as the statement says.


14.3.6 Check yourself

The network has 20 layers above the first one and a custom loss. Does Equation 14.7 still hold? (Yes. Everything above the first layer only changes \(\gamma_1\), and \(\gamma_{1,j}\) cancels in the ratio. All that matters is that the first layer is fully connected with a bias.)
For a ReLU network, which units are useless to the attacker, and could all of them be useless? (Units switched off on \(x\) have \(\gamma_{1,j} = 0\). All units are useless only if every unit is off or every active unit has \((W_2^\top\gamma_2)_j = 0\), which for a random network essentially never happens; the image above had 13 usable units out of 32.)

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.4 Label recovery from the last layer
text:
14.4 Label recovery from the last layer

14.4.1 Context
The gradient depends on the label too, and the label is often the most sensitive part: the diagnosis, the word typed next, the class of a photo. Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen (2020) noticed that the label can be read off the last layer in closed form. Their attack, iDLG (“improved DLG”), then searches only for the input, which makes the search of Section 14.5 easier and more reliable.


14.4.2 Statement
There are three versions of the rule, depending on what the last layer has and how many examples the gradient covers. All three come from Fact 2: the last layer’s backward signal is \(p - e_y\), a vector of probabilities with 1 subtracted at the true label.
From the bias, for one example. By Fact 1 the last layer’s bias gradient equals its backward signal, \(\nabla_{b_2}\ell = p - e_y\). Every entry is a positive probability except the one at the true label, where subtracting 1 makes it negative. So the label is the position of the smallest entry, the only negative one: \[y = \arg\min_k(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.9}\]
From the weights, for one example. The weight gradient tells the same story. By Fact 1, row \(k\) of \(\nabla_{W_2}\ell\) is \(\gamma_{2,k}\) times the hidden activations \(h\). If those activations are never negative (\(h \ge 0\) and \(h \ne 0\), as for ReLU or the sigmoid), multiplying by them keeps the sign of \(\gamma_{2,k}\). So \(y\) is the only row of \(\nabla_{W_2}\ell\) whose entries are non-positive, and in particular the only row with a negative sum.
Counts, for a batch. With \(B\) examples the bias gradient is the average of \(p_i - e_{y_i}\) over the batch. The \(e_{y_i}\) parts add up to the label histogram: their \(k\)-th entries sum to \(n_k\), the number of examples of class \(k\). The \(p_i\) parts add up to the model’s total predicted probability for class \(k\), \(\sum_ip_{ik}\). So the histogram is that total minus \(B\) times the bias gradient: \[n_k = \sum_{i=1}^Bp_{ik} - B\,(\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k. \tag{14.10}\] An attacker who does not know \(\sum_ip_{ik}\) replaces it by \(B\bar p_k\), where \(\bar p\) is a guess of the model’s average prediction, and rounds to the nearest integer.


14.4.3 Derivation

Bias. Fact 1 at the last layer gives \(\nabla_{b_2}\ell = \gamma_2\), and Fact 2 (Equation 14.5) gives \(\gamma_2 = p - e_y\). Softmax probabilities lie strictly between 0 and 1, so \((\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_y = p_y - 1 < 0\) and \((\nabla_{b_2}\ell)_k = p_k > 0\) for \(k \ne y\). The smallest entry is therefore at \(y\).
Weights. Fact 1 gives \((\nabla_{W_2}\ell)_{k,:} = \gamma_{2,k}\,h^\top\). With \(h \ge 0\), row \(y\) is \((p_y - 1)h^\top\), a negative number times non-negative entries, so it is \(\le 0\) entrywise. Every other row is \(p_kh^\top \ge 0\). Summing a row multiplies \(\gamma_{2,k}\) by \(\sum_jh_j\), which is positive because \(h \ge 0\) and \(h \ne 0\), so the sum keeps the sign of \(\gamma_{2,k}\).
Counts. By Fact 3 the batch gradient is the average of the per-example ones, so \(\nabla_{b_2}\ell = \frac1B\sum_i(p_i - e_{y_i})\). Its \(k\)-th entry is \(\frac1B\big(\sum_ip_{ik} - n_k\big)\), because \(e_{y_i}\) has a 1 in position \(k\) exactly when example \(i\) has class \(k\), so \(\sum_ie_{y_i}\) counts the examples of each class. Multiply by \(B\) and solve for \(n_k\).



14.4.4 Interpretation
For one example the rule makes no errors. It is exact for every network that ends in softmax and cross-entropy with a bias, at any point of training, because the sign argument never depends on how good the model is. On 1,000 random images and random networks, both the bias rule and the weight rule name the label correctly 1.000 of the time.
For a batch, the gradient leaks the label histogram. Equation 14.10 is exact, so the only uncertainty is the total prediction \(\sum_ip_{ik}\), and the attacker can estimate it well: it knows the model, so it can run the model on data of its own from the same population and average the predictions. The true counts are integers, and a number within \(\frac12\) of an integer rounds to that integer. So rounding gives the exact counts whenever the estimate of \(\sum_ip_{ik}\) is off by less than \(\frac12\) for every class (Exercise 4). The cruder guess \(\bar p_k = 1/K\), which assumes the model spreads its predictions evenly over the classes, does worse, because even an untrained network is not uniform.
The label matters for inversion as well. Knowing \(y\) removes a discrete unknown from the search. Zhu et al. (2019) optimized a soft label (a probability vector standing in for the unknown label) jointly with the input, and that joint search often failed. With the label fixed by Equation 14.9, the search is over the input only.
Figure 14.2 shows both cases.






Figure 14.2: Labels from the last-layer bias gradient. Left: for one example, \(\nabla_{b_2}\ell = p - e_y\) has a single negative entry, at the true label (red). Right: for a batch of 16, the counts \(B(\bar p - \nabla_{b_2}\ell)\) with \(\bar p\) the model’s average prediction on the attacker’s own images (green) are close to the true counts (grey); with \(\bar p = 1/K\) (orange) they are off by up to about half an example.





14.4.5 Example: a batch of 16
A batch of 16 images has true counts \((4, 2, 4, 6)\) over the four shapes. Table 14.3 reads them off the bias gradient of the 32-unit ReLU network, with three different guesses for the total prediction \(\sum_ip_{ik}\) in Equation 14.10.

With the averaged guess every estimate is within \(\frac12\) of the truth (the largest miss is \(4.19 - 4 = 0.19\)), so rounding fixes it. With the uniform guess the first class is off by \(4 - 2.12 = 1.88\), and rounding cannot help.
Over 200 random batches and networks, the rounded counts are all correct in 1.000 of batches of 4, 0.975 of batches of 16 and 0.525 of batches of 64 with the averaged guess. With the uniform guess the rates are 0.925, 0.095 and 0.000. The reason for the decline is that the error of the estimate is a sum of \(B\) deviations, one per example, each the gap between that example’s prediction and the guess \(\bar p\). These do not cancel exactly, so the error of their sum grows with \(B\), and so does the chance that some class is off by more than \(\frac12\). Even when the counts are not all exact, they are close: Exercise 4 finds that at \(B = 16\) the largest error over the four classes, before rounding, has median 0.233 with the averaged guess and 1.102 with the uniform one.


14.4.6 Check yourself

Why must \(p_y - 1\) be negative, even for a model that is confidently right? (Softmax never outputs exactly 1, so \(p_y < 1\). A confident model gives a tiny negative entry, but its sign is still the only negative one. In floating point a \(p_y\) that rounds to 1 would hide it, which is one reason attacks are run on early-training models.)
The last layer has no bias and the hidden layer uses tanh. Which rule still works? (Neither as stated: there is no bias gradient, and tanh activations can be negative, so row \(y\) need not have a negative sum. But row \(y\) still has the opposite sign to all other rows, so for \(K \ge 3\) the odd one out is the label; see Exercise 3.)

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.5 Deep Leakage from Gradients

14.5.1 Context
The closed forms need a fully connected layer with a bias. Most image models start with convolutions, and many architectures have normalization layers, attention, or no biases at all. Zhu, Liu & Han (2019) gave a generic attack that needs none of these: guess an input, compute its gradient, and move the guess until the gradients match. If only the true input produces the observed gradient, a matching guess is the input.


14.5.2 Statement
To turn “move the guess until the gradients match” into something you can optimize, you need one number that says how badly a guess matches. DLG uses the squared distance between the gradient the guessed batch would produce and the observed gradient \(g\), summed over all the gradient’s entries. Call it the matching loss \(R\). It is zero for a perfect match and positive otherwise. Given \(\theta\), the observed gradient \(g\) and the labels \(y_1, \dots, y_B\) (from Section 14.4), DLG looks for the guesses \(x'_1, \dots, x'_B\) that make \(R\) smallest: \[\hat x_1, \dots, \hat x_B = \arg\min_{x_1', \dots, x_B'}R(x'), \qquad R(x') = \Big\|\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i) - g\Big\|^2, \tag{14.11}\] where \(\arg\min\) means “the inputs at which the minimum is reached”. It searches by a gradient method: start from random noise and repeatedly move the guess a little downhill on \(R\). The true batch has \(R = 0\), the smallest possible value.


14.5.3 Derivation

The true batch is a global minimizer of Equation 14.11. \(R\) is a squared length, so \(R \ge 0\) always. Plugging in the true \(x_i\) reproduces \(g\) exactly, so \(R = 0\) there, and nothing can do better.
The objective can be differentiated in \(x'\) if the network is twice differentiable. A gradient method needs the slope of \(R\) with respect to the guess. Write \(G(x') = \frac1B\sum_i\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; x_i', y_i)\), the function that takes a guessed batch to the gradient it would produce. Then \(R = \| G(x') - g\|^2\). The squared length \(\| u\|^2\) changes at the rate \(2u\), and the chain rule passes this back to \(x'\) through the Jacobian \(J_G\) of \(G\), the matrix of rates at which each gradient entry changes with each input pixel: \[\nabla_{x'}R = 2\,J_G(x')^\top\big(G(x') - g\big). \tag{14.12}\] \(G\) is already made of first derivatives of the network, so \(J_G\) is made of second derivatives. That is why Zhu et al. replaced ReLU by the sigmoid, and the experiments here do the same. The ReLU’s slope is 0 or 1, constant on each side of zero, so its second derivative is zero almost everywhere: the factor \(\sigma'(a)\) in Equation 14.6 is piecewise constant in \(a\), and the search gets no signal through it. The sigmoid’s slope varies smoothly, so it does.
Computing \(J_G^\top v\) without forming \(J_G\). \(J_G\) would have one row per parameter and one column per pixel, and no one builds it. Automatic-differentiation libraries instead run backpropagation through the backward pass itself, which is called double backpropagation. The script writes it out by hand for the one-hidden-layer network. The forward pass computes \(a, h, z, p\). The backward pass computes \(\gamma_2, \gamma_1\) and the four gradient blocks. A second backward pass then sends \(2(G - g)\) through every one of those steps back to \(x'\). To check it, the script also estimates the slope by finite differences (nudge one pixel slightly and see how much \(R\) changes), and the two agree to within \(1.2\times10^{-10}\).
Optimization finds a stationary point, not necessarily the minimizer. \(R\) is not convex in \(x'\): its surface can have dips and flat regions other than the true minimum. As the non-convex section of Optimization shows, for such a function a gradient method with a suitable step only guarantees that the slope \(\|\nabla R\|\) goes to zero. That gives a stationary point, where the surface is flat, which may or may not be the global minimum. So success is an empirical question. The value of \(R\) at the end tells you which case you are in: \(R = 0\) (up to rounding) means you found an exact match, while a value stuck well above zero means you got stuck.
Uniqueness is plausible when equations outnumber unknowns. Matching \(g\) imposes one equation per parameter: 2,212 here, against \(64B\) unknown pixels. That is not a proof that the minimizer is unique, but with a single example the closed form of Section 14.3 shows that it is: the input is determined by the gradient.



14.5.4 Interpretation
DLG is a general recipe. All it needs is the ability to differentiate the gradient with respect to the input, which any automatic-differentiation library provides. So it works for convolutional networks and on real images, where no closed form exists: Zhu et al. recover CIFAR-100 pictures and text tokens from single-example gradients.
When it fails, it fails first as an optimization, not for lack of information. If the run ends with \(R\) far from zero, the attacker knows it has not found the input, and better optimizers, restarts from new random guesses, and image priors help. Geiping et al. (2020) made two changes. They replaced the squared distance by a cosine distance between gradients, which compares only the directions of the two gradients and ignores their lengths. And they added a total-variation penalty, the sum of differences between neighbouring pixels, which is small for natural images made of smooth regions. (This penalty is a measure of image roughness, not the total variation distance between distributions.) With these they recover recognizable images from trained networks and from batches.
Note what the attack does not need. The label search is gone, thanks to iDLG. And the server need not be malicious: it only computes on what it legitimately received.
Figure 14.3 shows one run.






Figure 14.3: Deep Leakage from Gradients on one \(8\times8\) image, sigmoid network with 32 hidden units. Top: the reconstruction \(\hat x\) at selected iterations of Adam, starting from uniform noise, and the true input. Bottom: the matching loss \(R(\hat x)\) and the relative error, on a log scale. Both fall geometrically until they reach rounding error.





14.5.5 Example: one image
The script starts from uniform noise and runs 600 steps of the Adam optimizer, a variant of gradient descent that scales each pixel’s step by a running estimate of the size of that pixel’s gradient, with learning rate 0.05 decaying linearly to 0. The label comes from Equation 14.9.

By iteration 50 the image is visually correct (7.5% error); by iteration 600 it is exact to about 13 digits. The matching loss falls about as the square of the error, and that is what you should expect close to the answer. Near the true input \(x\), the gradient map \(G\) is nearly linear, so the mismatch is about the Jacobian times the error, \(G(x') - g \approx J_G(x)(x' - x)\), and its squared length is quadratic in the error: \(R \approx \| J_G(x)(x' - x)\|^2\). In the table, between iterations 50 and 100 the error shrinks by a factor \(0.075/0.0057 \approx 13\) and \(R\) by \(0.0025/0.000013 \approx 190\), close to \(13^2 \approx 170\).


14.5.6 Check yourself

The run ends with \(R = 10^{-5}\) and a reconstruction that looks like a shape. Has the attack succeeded? (Not certainly. At the true input \(R = 0\), and in Table 14.4 \(R = 1.3\times10^{-5}\) goes with an error below 1%, but a different input can also have small \(R\). A loss that has stopped falling well above rounding error signals a stationary point that is not the input; restart from a new random guess.)
Why does the attacker want the label before running DLG? (With the label fixed, \(R\) depends on the input only. Searching jointly over a soft label adds a variable that interacts with every gradient entry through \(p - e_y\), and Zhao et al. found that the joint search fails much more often.)

title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.6 Batches and averaging

14.6.1 Context
Clients rarely send the gradient of one example. They send the average over a batch, or the change in parameters after several local steps. Averaging is often said to protect the individual examples: the gradient now describes the batch, not anyone in it. This section measures that claim. Averaging does destroy the one-line formula of Equation 14.7, and it does make DLG harder, but three things survive: the span of the batch, every example that some unit “sees alone”, and a search that still works for small batches.


14.6.2 Statement
Take a batch of \(B\) examples and a fully connected first layer, and write \(\gamma_{1,i}\) for the backward signal of example \(i\) at that layer. Each claim below follows from the gradient being a sum of one outer product per example.
The gradient is a sum of \(B\) outer products, and its rows lie in the span of the batch. By Facts 1 and 3, averaging adds up the per-example outer products \(\gamma_{1,i}x_i^\top\). Each of those has rows that are multiples of its own \(x_i\), so every row of the sum is a weighted combination of the \(B\) inputs. It lies in their span, the set of all such combinations. And adding \(B\) rank-one matrices gives rank at most \(B\): \[\nabla_{W_1}\ell = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B\gamma_{1,i}\,x_i^\top, \qquad \operatorname{rank}\nabla_{W_1}\ell \le B, \qquad \text{every row} \in \operatorname{span}\{x_1, \dots, x_B\}. \tag{14.13}\]
Unit ratios are weighted averages. With one example, dividing row \(j\) by the bias entry cancelled a single scale. With a batch, row \(j\) is a sum of different inputs with different scales \(\gamma_{1,ij}\), and the bias entry is the sum of those scales. The division gives each input a weight equal to its share of the total, so the result is a weighted average of the inputs. For a unit \(j\) with \((\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j \ne 0\), \[\frac{(\nabla_{W_1}\ell)_{j,:}}{(\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j} = \sum_{i=1}^B\frac{\gamma_{1,ij}}{\sum_{i'}\gamma_{1,i'j}}\,x_i^\top, \tag{14.14}\] which equals \(x_i\) exactly when only example \(i\) contributes, that is when \(\gamma_{1,i'j} = 0\) for every \(i' \ne i\). For ReLU this happens when unit \(j\) is switched on for example \(i\) only: unit \(j\) isolates example \(i\).
How often an example is isolated. A unit isolates example \(i\) when it is on for \(i\) and off for every other example. Suppose each of the \(m\) ReLU units switches on for each example independently with probability \(\frac12\), like a fair coin. Then one unit isolates example \(i\) with probability \(2^{-B}\), the chance of one particular pattern of \(B\) coin flips. The example is missed only if all \(m\) units miss it, which has probability \((1 - 2^{-B})^m\). So each example of the batch is recovered exactly by some unit ratio with probability \[P_{\text{iso}}(B, m) = 1 - (1 - 2^{-B})^m. \tag{14.15}\]


14.6.3 Derivation

Sum of outer products. By Fact 3 the batch gradient is the average of the per-example gradients, and by Fact 1 each of those is \(\gamma_{1,i}x_i^\top\).
Rank and span. Stack the \(x_i^\top\) as the rows of a matrix \(X \in \mathbb R^{B\times d}\) and the \(\gamma_{1,i}^\top\) as the rows of \(\Gamma \in \mathbb R^{B\times m}\). Then the sum of outer products is a matrix product, \(\nabla_{W_1}\ell = \frac1B\Gamma^\top X\). A product has rank at most that of either factor, and \(X\) has only \(B\) rows, so the rank is at most \(B\). Row \(j\) is \(\frac1B\sum_i\Gamma_{ij}x_i^\top\), a combination of the \(x_i\), so it lies in their span.
Ratios. By step 1 and Fact 1, the bias gradient is \((\nabla_{b_1}\ell)_j = \frac1B\sum_i\gamma_{1,ij}\). Divide the \(j\)-th row by it. The factors \(\frac1B\) cancel, and the weights \(\gamma_{1,ij}/\sum_{i'}\gamma_{1,i'j}\) sum to 1 because they are each example’s share of the same total. If only \(\gamma_{1,ij}\) is nonzero, the weight on \(x_i\) is 1 and all the others are 0.
One unit. For ReLU, \(\gamma_{1,i'j} = 0\) whenever unit \(j\) is off on \(x_{i'}\), because the ReLU slope is 0 there (Fact 3). So unit \(j\) isolates example \(i\) if it is on for \(i\) (probability \(\frac12\)) and off for each of the other \(B - 1\) (probability \(\frac12\) each, independently). Multiplying the \(B\) independent probabilities gives \(2^{-B}\). (An active unit also needs \((W_2^\top\gamma_{2,i})_j \ne 0\), which holds with probability 1 for random weights.)
Many units. The units are independent by assumption, so the probability that none of the \(m\) units isolates example \(i\) is the product of \(m\) factors \(1 - 2^{-B}\), which is \((1 - 2^{-B})^m\). Subtracting from 1 gives Equation 14.15.
When the independence assumption holds. Suppose the first-layer bias is zero and the inputs are drawn from a distribution that is symmetric about zero, such as \(\mathcal N(0, I)\). Unit \(j\), whose weights are the row \((W_1)_{j,:}\), is on for \(x_i\) when \((W_1)_{j,:}\,x_i > 0\). Symmetry makes \((W_1)_{j,:}\,x_i\) equally likely to be positive or negative, and independent inputs make these signs independent across the batch. So each unit’s on/off pattern over the batch is exactly a sequence of fair coin flips, and step 4 is exact. Different units look at the same inputs, though, so their patterns are not fully independent of each other, and step 5 is only approximate. Real data are not symmetric: images of the same kind are positively correlated, and Table 14.5 shows that this changes the answer substantially.



14.6.4 Interpretation
The formula is exponential in \(B\) and linear in \(m\). A unit isolates a given example with probability \(2^{-B}\), so among \(m\) units the expected number that isolate it is \(m2^{-B}\). With \(m \gg 2^B\) almost every example is isolated; with \(m \ll 2^B\) almost none is. To find the width that gives an even chance, set the miss probability \((1 - 2^{-B})^m\) to at most \(\frac12\) and take logs: \(m\ln(1 - 2^{-B}) \le -\ln2\), so \(m \ge \ln2/(-\ln(1 - 2^{-B}))\). At \(B = 10\) this is \(\ln2/(-\ln(1 - 2^{-10})) = 0.6931/0.000977 \approx 709.4\), so you need \(m \ge 710\) units. Real first layers have thousands of units, so batches of 10 are not safe from this attack.
Correlated data are easier for the attacker, not harder. With images, a unit tends to fire on many examples of a batch or on few: the number of examples it fires for is more spread out than the coin-flip model predicts (statisticians call this overdispersion), instead of concentrating around \(B/2\). Units that fire on just one example are then much more common at large \(B\), and isolation decays much more slowly than \(2^{-B}\). Exercise 5 works out one extreme model, in which each unit has its own firing rate \(\rho\), drawn uniformly between 0 and 1, and fires on each example with that probability. Averaging the isolation probability \(\rho(1 - \rho)^{B-1}\) over \(\rho\) gives \(1/(B(B + 1))\) per unit, which shrinks only like \(1/B^2\) instead of halving with each extra example.
The span leaks even when nothing is isolated. By Equation 14.13, the server learns the \(B\)-dimensional subspace that contains the batch. For \(B \ll d\) that already rules out almost every input, since every example must be a combination of \(B\) known directions.
A malicious server does better still. The analysis above assumes random weights, as an honest server would send. A server that chooses \(\theta\) can plant first-layer units that fire on rare inputs only (“trap weights”, Boenisch et al. 2023), or that sort inputs into bins by a feature such as brightness (Fowl et al. 2022), so that most examples of even a large batch are isolated by construction.
DLG on batches has a harder search to do: it must untangle \(B\) inputs from one sum. In the experiments below it always recovers single examples, usually recovers pairs, and mostly fails beyond that, with the matching loss stuck well above zero. That is an optimization failure, not a shortage of information: at \(B = 4\) there are \(64\cdot4 = 256\) unknown pixels against 2,212 equations.
Finally, several local steps do not help either. If the client takes several SGD steps on its batch and sends the total change in parameters, every step’s first-layer gradient is made of outer products with the same inputs \(x_i\), and only the backward signals change from step to step. So for one example the change in \(W_1\) is still a multiple of \(x^\top\) in every row, still rank one, and Equation 14.7 still recovers \(x\) exactly (Exercise 6).






Figure 14.4: Fraction of a batch recovered exactly by first-layer unit ratios, for ReLU networks with \(m = 64\), 256 and 1024 hidden units. Lines: Equation 14.15. Filled circles: Gaussian inputs and zero first-layer bias, where each unit’s on/off pattern is a sequence of fair coin flips. Open squares: the \(8\times8\) images, which are correlated, so units fire on many or few of them and isolation decays much more slowly.









Figure 14.5: Deep Leakage from Gradients against batch size, sigmoid network with 32 hidden units. Left: relative error of the closest reconstruction for every example (dots) and the median (red), on a log scale; the dotted line marks an error of 0.05. Right: a batch of 4, true images (top) and their closest reconstructions (bottom). Some examples are recovered and others are blends.





14.6.5 Example: what a batch hides
Rank and isolation in one batch. A batch of 4 images through the 32-unit ReLU network gives a first-layer gradient whose singular values (the sizes of the matrix along its independent directions), relative to the largest, are \(1.0\), \(0.84\), \(0.69\), \(0.039\) and then \(1.5\times10^{-16}\). Four directions are nonzero and the rest are rounding error: rank 4, as Equation 14.13 says. Every row lies in the span of the four images to within \(4.6\times10^{-16}\). The unit ratios recover all 4 of the 4 images exactly. For comparison, Equation 14.15 with \(B = 4\) has \(1 - 2^{-4} = 15/16\) and predicts \(1 - (15/16)^{32} = 1 - e^{32\ln(15/16)} = 1 - e^{-2.065} = 0.873\) per example under independence.
Isolation against batch size. Table 14.5 compares Equation 14.15 with simulation, 20 random networks and batches per cell (see Figure 14.4 for the full range).

It usually overestimates slightly (in seven of the eight rows), because units share inputs and so their on/off patterns are not fully independent (step 6 of the derivation). For images the formula is far too reassuring about privacy. At \(B = 16\) it predicts that 1.6% of the batch is exposed in the 1024-unit network; 69.1% is.

14.6.6 Check yourself

A first layer has \(m = 4096\) ReLU units and the batch size is 8. Under the independence model, what fraction of the batch is exposed? (A unit isolates a given example with probability \(2^{-8} = 1/256\), so the expected number of isolating units per example is \(4096/256 = 16\), and \(P_{\text{iso}} = 1 - (1 - 1/256)^{4096} \approx 1 - e^{-16}\): essentially the whole batch.)
Why does the span of the batch, revealed by Equation 14.13, matter if the attacker cannot tell which direction is which example? (Each example is a combination of \(B\) known basis vectors, so any further search, such as DLG, has \(B\) unknowns per example instead of \(d\): 4 instead of 64 here, and 4 instead of hundreds of thousands for real images.)

title: 14  Gradient inversion
section: 14.7 Code: check every attack by computation
text:
14.7 Code: check every attack by computation
The script code/gradient_inversion.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. The network, its forward and backward passes and the hand-written double backpropagation for DLG are small typed functions; the attacks call them, and the figures loop over them. title: 14  Gradient inversion
text:
14.8 References

Zhu, Liu & Han, “Deep Leakage from Gradients” (NeurIPS 2019). The gradient-matching attack of Section 14.5, with reconstructions of images and text from single-example and small-batch gradients; replaces ReLU by the sigmoid to keep the objective twice differentiable.
Zhao, Mopuri & Bilen, “iDLG: Improved Deep Leakage from Gradients” (arXiv 2020). Label recovery from the sign of the last-layer gradient, and DLG with the label fixed.
Phong, Aono, Hayashi, Wang & Moriai, “Privacy-Preserving Deep Learning via Additively Homomorphic Encryption” (IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 2018). Points out that the input of a fully connected layer with a bias can be read off its gradient, Equation 14.7.
Geiping, Bauermeister, Dröge & Moeller, “Inverting Gradients — How easy is it to break privacy in federated learning?” (NeurIPS 2020). Cosine-similarity matching with a total-variation image prior; reconstructions from trained networks, from several local steps and from batches; the proof that fully connected layers leak their inputs in closed form.
Fowl, Geiping, Czaja, Goldblum & Goldstein, “Robbing the Fed: Directly Obtaining Private Data in Federated Learning with Modified Models” (ICLR 2022). A malicious server inserts a fully connected block whose units bin inputs by a feature, so that most examples of a large batch are isolated.
Boenisch, Dziedzic, Schuster, Shamsabadi, Shumailov & Papernot, “When the Curious Abandon Honesty: Federated Learning Is Not Private” (IEEE EuroS&P 2023). Trap weights that make first-layer units fire for single examples; exact recovery from large batches by a malicious server.
Wainakh et al., “User-Level Label Leakage from Gradients in Federated Learning” (PETS 2022). Label counts from batch gradients, as in Equation 14.10.
Huang, Gupta, Song, Li & Arora, “Evaluating Gradient Inversion Attacks and Defenses in Federated Learning” (NeurIPS 2021). How the strength of these attacks depends on assumptions such as known labels, batch normalization statistics and untrained models.
McMahan, Moore, Ramage, Hampson & Agüera y Arcas, “Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks from Decentralized Data” (AISTATS 2017). The federated averaging protocol, where clients send updates after several local steps.

Rules of thumb

A gradient is a sum of outer products of backward signals with forward inputs. Any layer whose input you can isolate, you can read.
One example, a fully connected layer with a bias: the input costs one division. The label costs one sign.
When there is no closed form, match gradients. The final matching loss tells you whether it worked.
Batching helps against search but not against structure. The label histogram and the span of the batch always leak, and examples isolated by a single unit leak exactly; with real data that is most of them for batches of 10 or more on wide layers.
An honest server can already do all of this. A malicious server that chooses the weights can do it for large batches by design.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1 Why this matters
A hospital wants to share its discharge records with researchers. It deletes the names, the addresses and the insurance numbers, and keeps what the research needs: postcode, date of birth, sex, diagnosis. Nobody’s name is in the file. Is anyone in it identifiable?
Usually, yes. Most people are the only person with their combination of postcode, birth date and sex. Anyone who holds a second table with names and those same three columns, such as a voter roll, can join the two tables and put a name back on most rows. This is a linkage attack, and putting a name back on a “de-identified” record is re-identification. It needs no model, no gradients and no queries: only a release and some auxiliary data about the people in it. The other chapters of this part attack trained models. This one attacks the data itself, and it explains why removing names was never the same as anonymizing.
Before those questions comes a shortcut that fails for a simpler reason: replacing each name by a code, or pseudonym, such as a hash of an identifier. The chapter shows that a hash of a guessable identifier can be undone by trying every value, and that even a code nobody can undo ties a person’s records together. The chapter then follows three questions, each building on the one before. The first is how many people are unique on a given set of attributes, and how you can predict that number without having the data. Once that is answered for tidy tables, the second question is what happens when the data are high-dimensional and sparse, like movie ratings or shopping baskets, so that no record matches the adversary’s information exactly. The third is whether releasing only a sample helps, since a record that is unique in the sample need not be unique in the population.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.1.1 The one idea: identifying information is measured in bits, and bits add up
Picking one person out of \(n\) takes \(\log_2 n\) bits of information, because each bit halves the number of candidates and you need to halve \(n\) down to 1. That is 27.9 bits for the 248.7 million people in the United States in 1990, and 32.9 bits for 8 billion people. Each attribute you learn about someone carries some bits too: an attribute with \(v\) equally likely values is worth \(\log_2 v\) bits. A sex is worth \(\log_2 2 = 1\) bit, a birth month \(\log_2 12 \approx 3.6\), and a birth date in a span of 80 years, one of \(365 \times 80 = 29{,}200\) days, about \(\log_2 29{,}200 = 14.8\). For independent attributes, the bits add: the chance of a given combination is the product of the chances of its values, and the logarithm turns that product into a sum. Once the bits of the attributes you know exceed \(\log_2 n\) by a few, almost everyone is unique. Every result in this chapter makes that sentence precise: the expected fraction of unique people as a function of the bits (Section 15.5), the score that adds up bits from rare movie ratings (Section 15.6), and the correction for a sample (Section 15.7).

What you need. Every outside fact this chapter uses is restated where it is used; these links are for more detail. Entropy, the chain rule and the conversion between probabilities and bits are in Information theory. The binomial and Poisson distributions, and Poisson thinning (Exercise 2 of that chapter), are in Probability distributions. McDiarmid’s inequality is in Concentration. The Neyman–Pearson lemma, the Bayesian view of a test, and why you should read a curve of true against false positive rates at small false positive rates are in Hypothesis testing. The birthday bound is in Cryptography basics. The vocabulary of adversaries, auxiliary knowledge and games is in Threat models.
Notation. A population has \(n\) people. Each person has a combination of attribute values, their cell. Under the model of the population, a person falls in cell \(c\) with probability \(p_c\), independently of everyone else. There are \(K\) cells. A person is unique when nobody else is in their cell. \(U\) is the number of unique people. Logarithms are base 2 when the unit is bits and natural otherwise.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
section: 15.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
15.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

15.2.1 Fact 1 — Counting with indicators
To find how many people are unique on average, you do not need the distribution of \(U\). Give each person a counter, an indicator, that is 1 if that person is unique and 0 otherwise. \(U\) is the sum of these counters, \(U = \sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf 1[\text{person } i \text{ is unique}]\). The average of a sum is the sum of the averages, and the average of a 0/1 counter is the probability that it is 1. So
\[\mathbb E U = \sum_{i=1}^n\Pr[\text{person } i \text{ is unique}]. \tag{15.1}\]
The rule “the average of a sum is the sum of the averages” is linearity of expectation, and it holds even when the terms depend on each other. Here they do: knowing that person 1 is unique changes the chance that person 2 is. Linearity does not care, because it only adds up how often each counter is 1, outcome by outcome. Walk through the smallest case to see it: \(n = 3\) people, \(K = 2\) equally likely cells A and B, so 8 equally likely outcomes (Table 15.2).

Directly, six of the eight outcomes have \(U = 1\), so \(\mathbb E U = 6/8 = 0.75\). Through the indicators, person 1 is unique when persons 2 and 3 are both in the other cell, which happens with probability \(\frac12 \times \frac12 = \frac14\); the same holds for each person, so \(\mathbb E U = 3 \times \frac14 = 0.75\). The two counts agree. This chapter uses the same move for the expected number of unique people, of sample uniques, and of false matches.


15.2.2 Fact 2 — \((1 - p)^k\) is \(e^{-pk}\), up to a factor you can bound
The question “does each of the other \(k\) people avoid my cell?” has the answer \((1 - p)^k\) when each avoids it with probability \(1 - p\). Powers like this are awkward, and an exponential is easier to read: \((1 - p)^k\) is close to \(e^{-pk}\) when \(p\) is small, because \(1 - p\) is close to \(e^{-p}\) for small \(p\). The fact pins down how close, with bounds on both sides. For \(0 \le p < 1\) and \(k \ge 0\),
\[e^{-pk/(1-p)} \le (1 - p)^k \le e^{-pk}. \tag{15.2}\]
To prove it, take logarithms, so that \((1 - p)^k\) becomes \(k\ln(1 - p)\) and the claim becomes \(-\frac{p}{1 - p} \le \ln(1 - p) \le -p\). Both sides come from one inequality, \(\ln x \le x - 1\) for all \(x > 0\), which holds because \(\ln\) is concave and \(x - 1\) is its tangent line at \(x = 1\), and a concave curve lies below its tangents. With \(x = 1 - p\) it gives the upper bound \(\ln(1 - p) \le -p\). With \(x = \frac1{1 - p}\) it gives \(\ln\frac1{1-p} \le \frac1{1-p} - 1 = \frac{p}{1-p}\), and flipping the sign gives the lower bound \(\ln(1 - p) \ge -\frac{p}{1-p}\). The two bounds differ only by the factor \(\frac1{1-p}\) in the exponent, which is close to 1 when \(p\) is small.
To see how tight this is, take \(p = 10^{-4}\) and \(k = 9999\). Then \(pk = 0.9999\) and \(pk/(1 - p) = 0.9999/0.9999 = 1\), and \((1-p)^k = 0.36790\) sits between the lower bound \(e^{-pk/(1-p)} = e^{-1} = 0.36788\) and the upper bound \(e^{-pk} = e^{-0.9999} = 0.36792\). This is how the chapter turns “every one of the other \(n - 1\) people avoids my cell” into \(e^{-np}\).


15.2.3 Fact 3 — Probabilities multiply, bits add
If attributes \(A_1, \dots, A_k\) are independent, the probability of a cell is the product of the probabilities of its values, \(p_c = \prod_j p_j(c_j)\), where \(p_j(c_j)\) is the probability that attribute \(j\) takes the value \(c_j\) that the cell has. Three quantities that this chapter uses follow from that one product.
The surprisal of a cell, \(\log_2(1/p_c)\), is the number of bits it takes to single out that cell: a cell with probability \(2^{-10}\) has a surprisal of 10 bits. Since the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms, surprisal adds up over attributes, \(\log_2(1/p_c) = \sum_j\log_2(1/p_j(c_j))\).
The entropy is the average surprisal, \(H = \sum_c p_c\log_2(1/p_c)\): how many bits a typical person’s cell carries. Averaging the sum above term by term, it adds up too, \(H(A_1, \dots, A_k) = \sum_jH(A_j)\). This is the chain rule of Information theory, which says that the entropy of a pair is the entropy of the first plus that of the second given the first, in the special case where knowing the first tells you nothing about the second.
The collision probability \(\sum_cp_c^2\) is the chance that two independent people land in the same cell: both land in cell \(c\) with probability \(p_c \cdot p_c\), and you add over cells. It multiplies over attributes, because two people share a cell exactly when they share the value of every attribute, and for independent attributes those agreements are independent events. In symbols, \(\sum_c\prod_jp_j(c_j)^2 = \prod_j\sum_vp_j(v)^2\), which you can check by expanding the product of sums on the right: each term of the expansion picks one value for each attribute, that is, one cell.
Real attributes are not independent (age and number of children, ZIP code and income), and then the pair carries fewer bits than the sum of their separate bits, because part of what the second attribute says was already said by the first. The sum is therefore an upper bound on the joint entropy, and adding up bits overstates how identifying correlated attributes are.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.3 Quasi-identifiers and the linkage attack

15.3.1 Context
Data protection practice sorts the columns of a table into three kinds. Direct identifiers name a person on their own: name, social security number, email address. Sensitive attributes are what the release is about and what must not be tied to a person: a diagnosis, a salary. Quasi-identifiers are everything in between: attributes that do not name anyone alone but that, combined, often single out one person, and that also appear in other datasets with names attached. ZIP code, birth date and sex are the classic example. Removing direct identifiers and keeping quasi-identifiers is the most common form of “de-identification”, and the linkage attack is what breaks it. This section asks how often the attack names the right record.


15.3.2 Statement
The linkage attack. The release \(R\) holds records (quasi-identifiers, sensitive attribute). The adversary holds an auxiliary table with (name, quasi-identifiers), for example a voter roll. For each name, it finds the records of \(R\) with the same quasi-identifiers and picks one of them uniformly at random.
The game. In the language of Threat models, an attack is scored by a game. A challenger draws a target uniformly from the \(n\) people in \(R\) and gives the adversary the target’s quasi-identifiers. The adversary wins if it outputs the target’s record. Group the records of \(R\) into equivalence classes, sets of records with identical quasi-identifiers, with sizes \(k_1, \dots, k_J\); there are \(J\) classes, one per distinct combination. A target alone in its class is found for sure, and a target in a class of \(k\) look-alikes is found one time in \(k\). A class of \(k\) records is therefore hit \(k\) times as often as a single record but won only a \(1/k\) share of those times, so each class contributes the same amount, one record’s worth, to the wins. Averaging over the target gives the success probability of the linkage attack,
\[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac1n\sum_{j=1}^J k_j\cdot\frac{1}{k_j} = \frac{J}{n}: \tag{15.3}\]
the number of distinct quasi-identifier combinations divided by the number of records. No adversary that sees only the quasi-identifiers can do better.
Sweeney’s measurement. Sweeney (2000) estimated from 1990 census tables that 87% of the US population, 216 of 248 million people, were likely unique on {5-digit ZIP code, date of birth, sex}. On {city, date of birth, sex} the figure was 53%, and on {county, date of birth, sex} 18%.


15.3.3 Derivation
The idea is to fix the class the target falls in, find the best guess within it, and then average over classes.

Condition on the target’s class. A target in a class of size \(k_j\) shares its quasi-identifiers with \(k_j - 1\) other records. To an adversary who sees only quasi-identifiers, those records look the same as the target’s. Picking one of the \(k_j\) at random wins with probability \(1/k_j\).
Show that nothing beats this. Within a class, the target is equally likely to be any of the \(k_j\) records, because it was drawn uniformly and the records differ only in their sensitive attribute, which the adversary does not know. So every guess within the class wins with probability exactly \(1/k_j\), and a guess outside the class never wins, since a record there has different quasi-identifiers from the target.
Average over the target. The target lands in class \(j\) with probability \(k_j/n\), the share of records in that class. Weighting each class’s win probability by how often the target lands in it gives \(\Pr[\text{win}] = \sum_j\frac{k_j}{n}\cdot\frac{1}{k_j} = \frac Jn\).



15.3.4 Interpretation
For this adversary, uniqueness is the whole story. A unique record is re-identified with certainty and a record in a class of 2 with probability \(\frac12\). Each unique record adds a full win and no class adds more, so the fraction of unique people is a lower bound on the success, and the success is at most 1. That is why the next section is about predicting uniqueness.
The game assumes the adversary knows the target is in the release, as a curious neighbour or an insurer with a list of patients might. Without that knowledge, a unique match in the release may belong to someone else who happens to share the quasi-identifiers but is not in \(R\). Whether that uncertainty protects anyone is the question of Section 15.7.
Re-identification is also not the only harm. If all records of a class share one diagnosis, the adversary learns the diagnosis without knowing which record is the target’s. In the other direction, Equation 15.3 shows that a release in which every class has at least \(k\) records keeps the linkage success at most \(1/k\): each class then contributes one win for at least \(k\) records, so \(J \le n/k\). That guarantee holds against this adversary only. Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks studies such releases and the attacks on the sensitive attribute that they leave open.

Joining on the three columns gives Ana’s asthma, Carla’s depression and Dan’s pneumonia with certainty, because each of them matches exactly one record. Ben matches two records, so the adversary gets diabetes or hypertension and is right with probability \(\frac12\). The release has classes of sizes 1, 1, 1, 2 and 3, so \(J = 5\) classes for \(n = 8\) records, and Equation 15.3 gives a success of \(5/8 = 0.625\) for a target drawn from the release.
This is, in miniature, how Sweeney re-identified the governor of Massachusetts in the late 1990s. The state’s Group Insurance Commission had released hospital records of about 135,000 state employees and their families without names. Sweeney bought the Cambridge voter roll for twenty dollars. Six people on it shared the governor’s birth date, three of them were men, and only one of those lived in his ZIP code. Barth-Jones (2012) later pointed out that the governor was an easy target in one respect: his hospital stay had been in the news, so the adversary knew he was in the release, the assumption of the game above. For an ordinary person, whom nobody knows to be in the data, a unique match is less certain, which is the question Section 15.7 takes up.
In bits (Figure 15.1). Now count the bits of Sweeney’s three attributes, treating each as uniform over its values, which gives an upper bound. There are about 40,000 ZIP codes, \(365 \times 80 = 29{,}200\) birthdays in about 80 birth years, and two sexes, so the three attributes carry at most \(\log_2 40{,}000 + \log_2 29{,}200 + 1 = 15.3 + 14.8 + 1.0 = 31.1\) bits, against \(\log_2(248.7\times10^6) = 27.9\) bits needed to single out one American. The same count in cells: there are \(K = 40{,}000 \times 29{,}200 \times 2 = 2.34\times10^9\) cells for \(n = 248.7\) million people, so \(n/K = 0.106\) people per cell. If everyone fell into a uniformly random cell, the next section shows that a fraction \(e^{-n/K} = e^{-0.106} = 0.899\) would be unique. Sweeney’s 87% is a little lower because people are not spread uniformly: ZIP codes range from a few residents to tens of thousands, and birth years are not equally common, so people crowd into the popular cells. Golle (2006) repeated the estimate with the 2000 census and found 63%. Both estimates have to model how birth dates spread within the age groups that census tables publish, and the answer is sensitive to that modelling.






Figure 15.1: The three classic quasi-identifiers, in bits, against the bits needed to single out one person in the US population of 1990 and in the world population. The bits are upper bounds that treat each attribute as uniform over its values.





15.3.6 Check yourself

A release of 1,000 records has 900 distinct quasi-identifier combinations. What is the linkage success for a target drawn from the release, and what is the smallest possible number of unique records? (0.9 by Equation 15.3. At least 800: with \(s\) singletons, the other \(900 - s\) classes hold at least 2 records each, so \(s + 2(900 - s) \le 1000\), that is \(s \ge 800\), attained with 100 pairs.)
Why does it not matter for Equation 15.3 what the sensitive attribute is? (The adversary chooses only from the quasi-identifiers. The sensitive attribute is what it learns after winning, not what it uses to win.)

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.4 Pseudonyms and hashed identifiers

15.4.1 Context
A common alternative to deleting an identifier is to replace it by a pseudonym, a code that stays the same for every record of one person. Analysts can then still follow that person through the data. A popular way to make the code is to apply a cryptographic hash function, such as the widely used MD5, to the identifier. A hash is easy to compute and hard to invert, and the same input always gives the same output. The hope is that the code hides who the person is while keeping their records together. This section shows that the code fails at the first goal, hiding who the person is, in two separate ways. A hash of an identifier drawn from a small set can be inverted by trying every member of the set. And even a pseudonym nobody can invert still ties all of a person’s records together, so linking one of them to the person links them all.


15.4.2 Statement
Inverting a hash by enumeration. Suppose the format of the identifiers is public, so that the adversary can list every possible value, say \(N\) of them, and suppose the release replaces each identifier by its hash under a public function with no secret key. The adversary computes the hash of all \(N\) values and keeps a table from each hash back to its identifier. It can then look up the identifier behind every pseudonym in the release. It needs \(N\) hash computations, done once for the whole release. So the attack costs \(N = 2^{\log_2N}\) hashes, whatever the hash function. Hashing protects the identifier only as well as its \(\log_2N\) bits of guessing work do.
Linking through one record. Suppose instead that each person gets a random pseudonym, or a keyed hash, which mixes a secret key into the hash so that only the key holder can compute it. Then nobody else can invert the pseudonym. The adversary may know enough about one of a person’s records to tie it to the person. It then learns that person’s pseudonym, and with it every record carrying that pseudonym. As Section 15.5 will count, one record is usually enough when its quasi-identifiers carry more bits than \(\log_2\) of the number of records in the release.


15.4.3 Derivation

The hash is a fixed function. With no secret key, the hash of an identifier \(x\) is \(h(x)\) for a public function \(h\) that anyone can compute. So the set of possible pseudonyms is \(\{h(x) : x \text{ in the set of identifiers}\}\), and the adversary can list it in full with \(N\) computations.
Distinct identifiers almost surely get distinct pseudonyms. A collision, two identifiers with the same hash, would make the lookup ambiguous. Suppose the hash behaves like a random function, which is what a cryptographic hash is designed for. Then, for a 128-bit hash such as MD5 and \(N\) in the millions, the birthday bound of Cryptography basics puts the chance of any collision below \(N^2/2^{129}\), which is negligible. So each pseudonym in the release maps back to exactly one identifier.
Being hard to invert does not help. A cryptographic hash is hard to invert only in the sense that no attack does better than guessing inputs. That protects an unpredictable input, such as a long random password, but here guessing costs only \(N\) evaluations.
A consistent pseudonym is a join key, a column on which records can be matched. A pseudonym that is the same on every record of one person groups those records exactly. Learning the pseudonym of any one record therefore identifies the whole group, and the cost of learning it is the cost of re-identifying one record, which the other sections of this chapter measure.



15.4.4 Interpretation
Hashing protects only identifiers that are already hard to guess. Phone numbers, licence numbers and national identity numbers all come from sets of a few million to about ten billion values, between about 20 and 33 bits. A laptop hashes millions of values per second, so it lists any of these sets in seconds to hours. A secret key turns the hash into a keyed hash, which closes the enumeration attack as long as the key stays secret, but it does nothing against the second failure.
The second failure is the one that matters for any pseudonymized release. A pseudonym keeps the rows of one person together, which is the reason to use it, and that makes each person’s set of rows one long record. As Section 15.6 will show for movie ratings, a long record of a person’s actions is identifying, and a single known action can be enough to find it.


15.4.5 Example: the New York City taxi release
In 2014 a freedom-of-information request obtained every New York City taxi trip of 2013, and the requester published them. That is about 173 million trips, with pickup and drop-off times and places, fares and tips. Each taxi’s medallion number, the permit that lets a cab operate, and each driver’s licence number had been replaced by its MD5 hash. Readers of the data soon found one hashed licence that seemed to earn thousands of dollars a day. The chapter’s script confirms that its code, cfcd208495d565ef66e7dff9f98764da, is the MD5 of the string “0”. That string was the placeholder for a missing licence, so the code pooled the trips of many drivers. That match also showed that the codes were plain MD5 hashes with no key.
Vijay Pandurangan then inverted all the pseudonyms. Licence numbers have six digits, or seven digits starting with 5, about 2 million possibilities or 20.9 bits. Medallion numbers follow a few fixed patterns, about 22 million possibilities or 24.4 bits. He hashed every possibility in minutes and looked up each pseudonym. Public lists of licence holders then put a name on every driver’s trips and income. The script repeats the attack in miniature. It hashes five secret six-digit identifiers, then hashes all \(10^6\) six-digit numbers, 19.9 bits’ worth, and recovers all five.
Passengers had no pseudonym at all, yet they were exposed too, because each trip is itself a sparse record of the kind Section 15.6 studies. Describe a trip by its pickup minute and pickup place. The minute is one of the 525,600 minutes of the year, worth 19.0 bits. The place, on a grid of 100-metre squares over the city’s roughly 780 km², is one of 78,000 squares, worth 16.3 bits. Call each pair of minute and square a cell. Together they carry at most 35.3 bits, more than the 27.4 bits that single out one trip among 173 million. So if trips spread evenly over the cells, a known pickup almost always picks out one trip, and busy times and places only add a few look-alikes (Exercise 8 works out how often under uniform cells). Anthony Tockar showed this in 2014 by matching photographs of celebrities getting into taxis to their trips, which revealed where they went and how much they tipped. With random driver pseudonyms, the same move works from the driver’s side. A passenger who knows who drove one trip finds that trip, learns the driver’s pseudonym, and with it every trip and the year’s income.


15.4.6 Check yourself

A company replaces customers’ 10-digit phone numbers by their SHA-256 hashes, without a key. How many hash computations does it take to invert them all? (At most \(10^{10}\), about 33.2 bits of work, done once for the whole table. A modern computer does this in hours. The strength of SHA-256 does not matter, because the inputs are guessable.)
The company switches to random pseudonyms. Is the release now anonymous? (No. Each customer’s records still share one pseudonym. Anyone who links one record to a customer, through a known purchase or visit, learns the pseudonym and every other record with it.)

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
section: 15.5 How many people are unique? A birthday calculation
text:
15.5 How many people are unique? A birthday calculation

15.5.1 Context
A data custodian who wants to know the re-identification risk of a release can count unique records in it. But counting needs the data, and it says nothing about a new release or a different set of columns. A model of the population answers both. If each person falls in cell \(c\) with probability \(p_c\), the expected fraction of unique people has a closed form. It is the birthday problem asked the other way round. The birthday problem, in Cryptography basics, asks whether any two of \(n\) people share a birthday; here you ask how many people share their cell with nobody.


15.5.2 Statement
Exact expected fraction. A person is unique when each of the other \(n - 1\) people lands outside their cell. If the person is in cell \(c\), each other person avoids it with probability \(1 - p_c\), independently, so all of them avoid it with probability \((1 - p_c)^{n-1}\). Averaging over the person’s own cell, which is \(c\) with probability \(p_c\), gives the expected fraction of unique people, for \(n\) people falling in cells independently with probabilities \((p_c)\):
\[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} = \sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}. \tag{15.4}\]
Uniform cells. If all \(K\) cells are equally likely, every term has \(p_c = 1/K\), and the formula becomes \((1 - 1/K)^{n-1} \approx e^{-n/K}\): the chance that nobody else lands in your cell when the average cell holds \(n/K\) people. Now count the cells in bits, \(b = \log_2K\), so that \(K = 2^b\) and \(n = 2^{\log_2 n}\). The average occupancy is \(n/K = 2^{\log_2n - b}\), and
\[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} \approx \exp\big(-2^{\log_2n - b}\big), \tag{15.5}\]
a single curve in \(b - \log_2n\), the bits beyond those needed to name one person. Solving \(e^{-n/K} = f\) for the bits says how many you need for a fraction \(f\) of people to be unique: \(b = \log_2n + \log_2\frac{1}{\ln(1/f)}\). That is half once \(b\) exceeds \(\log_2n\) by 0.53 bits, 90% at 3.25 bits more and 99% at 6.64 bits more.
A lower bound from the collision probability. The exact formula needs every \(p_c\), and there can be billions of cells. A cruder question needs much less: how likely is a random person to share a cell with one other random person? That is the collision probability \(\sum_cp_c^2\) of Fact 3. If you pretend every person’s cell is as crowded as average in this sense, you get a guaranteed floor on uniqueness. For any \((p_c)\),
\[\frac{\mathbb E U}{n} \ge \Big(1 - \sum_cp_c^2\Big)^{n-1}, \tag{15.6}\]
and for independent attributes \(\sum_cp_c^2 = \prod_j\sum_vp_j(v)^2\) by Fact 3, so the bound needs only the per-attribute frequencies (the marginals).
Concentration. The expectation is an average over many imagined populations, but you have only one. Moving a single person to another cell changes the number of unique people by at most 2, so in a large population no one person can move the fraction much, and the fraction in the population you have is close to its expectation: for every \(t > 0\),
\[\Pr\Big[\Big|\frac Un - \frac{\mathbb EU}{n}\Big| \ge t\Big] \le 2e^{-nt^2/2}. \tag{15.7}\]


15.5.3 Derivation
The exact formula (Equation 15.4).

Count with indicators. By Fact 1, \(\mathbb EU = \sum_i\Pr[\text{person } i \text{ is unique}]\). Every person draws their cell from the same probabilities \((p_c)\), independently of the others, so nothing distinguishes person \(i\) from person \(j\) and every term of the sum is the same. It is enough to find it for one person.
Condition on the person’s own cell. Call it \(c\); it has probability \(p_c\).
Ask the others to stay away. Given \(c\), person \(i\) is unique if each of the other \(n - 1\) people lands outside \(c\). They are independent and each avoids \(c\) with probability \(1 - p_c\), so this has probability \((1 - p_c)^{n-1}\).
Average over the cell. \(\Pr[\text{person } i \text{ is unique}] = \sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}\). Since all \(n\) terms are equal, \(\mathbb EU\) is \(n\) times this; divide by \(n\).

Uniform cells (Equation 15.5).

Put \(p_c = 1/K\) in Equation 15.4. There are \(K\) terms, each \(\frac1K(1 - \frac1K)^{n-1}\), so the sum is \((1 - \frac1K)^{n-1}\).
Replace the power by an exponential. Fact 2 with \(p = 1/K\) and \(k = n - 1\) squeezes \((1 - \frac1K)^{n-1}\) between \(e^{-(n-1)/K}\) and \(e^{-(n-1)/(K-1)}\). These exponents differ by \(\frac{n-1}{K(K-1)}\), of order \(n/K^2\), and replacing \(n - 1\) by \(n\) changes the exponent by only \(1/K\). So \((1 - \frac1K)^{n-1} \approx e^{-n/K}\) with relative error of order \(1/K + n/K^2\), negligible for \(K\) in the thousands or more.
Write the exponent in bits. \(n/K = 2^{\log_2n}/2^b = 2^{\log_2n - b}\).
Find the bits for a target fraction. Solve \(e^{-n/K} = f\) for \(K\): taking logarithms, \(n/K = \ln(1/f)\), so \(K = n/\ln(1/f)\) and \(b = \log_2n - \log_2\ln(1/f)\). At \(f = \frac12\), \(\ln 2 = 0.693\) and \(-\log_2 0.693 = 0.53\). At \(f = 0.9\), \(\ln\frac{1}{0.9} = 0.105\) and \(-\log_2 0.105 = 3.25\). At \(f = 0.99\), \(\ln\frac1{0.99} = 0.0101\) and \(-\log_2 0.0101 = 6.64\).

The collision lower bound (Equation 15.6). The idea is that Equation 15.4 is an average of the function \((1 - x)^{n-1}\) over the cell probabilities people find themselves in, and for a curve that bends upwards the average of the function is at least the function of the average.

Write Equation 15.4 as an average. Draw a person’s cell \(Y\), so \(Y = c\) with probability \(p_c\), and look at the probability \(p_Y\) of the cell they landed in. Then \(\frac{\mathbb EU}{n} = \mathbb E[g(p_Y)]\) with \(g(x) = (1 - x)^{n-1}\).
Check that \(g\) bends upwards. \(g\) is convex on \([0, 1]\), because its second derivative \(g''(x) = (n-1)(n-2)(1 - x)^{n-3}\) is never negative there.
Apply Jensen’s inequality. For a convex function, the average of the function is at least the function of the average, \(\mathbb E[g(X)] \ge g(\mathbb E X)\). The reason is that a convex curve lies above its tangent line at the point \(\mathbb E X\); averaging the curve gives at least the average of the tangent line, which is the tangent’s value at \(\mathbb E X\), which is \(g(\mathbb E X)\). So \(\mathbb E[g(p_Y)] \ge g(\mathbb E[p_Y])\).
Compute the inner average. \(\mathbb E[p_Y] = \sum_cp_c\cdot p_c = \sum_cp_c^2\), the collision probability. For independent attributes it factorizes by Fact 3.

Equality in step 3 holds when \(p_Y\) is constant, that is, when all cells with positive probability are equally likely, because then there is nothing to average. The bound is tight for uniform cells and loose when a few cells hold most of the people: those crowded cells push the collision probability up and the bound down, while the many people in rare cells are still unique.
Concentration (Equation 15.7). The tool is McDiarmid’s inequality (Concentration). It applies to any function \(f\) of \(n\) independent inputs such that changing input \(i\) alone, with the others fixed, moves \(f\) by at most \(c_i\). It says that \(f\) is unlikely to be far from its mean: \(\Pr[f - \mathbb Ef \ge t] \le \exp(-2t^2/\sum_ic_i^2)\), and the same for the lower tail. So the work is to find \(c_i\).

Change one input. \(U\) is a function of the \(n\) independent cells. Change one person’s cell from \(u\) to \(u'\); only cells \(u\) and \(u'\) change their counts, so only they can change \(U\).
Bound the change. A cell with count \(k\) contributes \(\mathbf 1[k = 1]\) to \(U\): it holds a unique person exactly when it holds one person. Cell \(u\)’s count drops by one and its contribution changes by \(\mathbf 1[k_u - 1 = 1] - \mathbf 1[k_u = 1] \in \{-1, 0, 1\}\). Cell \(u'\)’s count rises by one, and its contribution likewise changes by \(-1\), 0 or 1. So \(U\) changes by at most 2, and \(U/n\) by at most \(c_i = 2/n\). (It can change by exactly 2: move a person out of a pair and into an empty cell, and both the person and their former partner become unique.)
Apply McDiarmid. With \(c_i = 2/n\) for all \(n\) people, \(\sum_ic_i^2 = n \cdot 4/n^2 = 4/n\), so each tail is at most \(\exp(-2t^2/(4/n)) = e^{-nt^2/2}\). Adding the upper and lower tails gives the factor 2.



15.5.4 Interpretation
For uniform cells, the bits picture is exact. Equation 15.5 depends on \(n\) and \(K\) only through \(b - \log_2n\), so the curve is the same for a town and for the planet (Figure 15.2, right). The often-quoted “33 bits identify anyone” is the point \(b = \log_2 n\), where the average cell holds one person and the curve is at \(e^{-1}\). With \(2^{33}\) uniform cells for 8 billion people, \(n/K = 8\times10^9/2^{33} = 0.93\) and only a fraction \(e^{-0.93} = 0.394\) is unique. 33 bits are enough to give everyone a distinct label, but random labels of 33 bits collide often; you need \(32.9 + 6.64 = 39.5\) bits for 99% of the world to be unique.
Skew usually lowers uniqueness. When a few values are common (a big city, a common occupation), many people crowd into a few cells and are not unique, while many rare cells stay empty. In the census below, and for Sweeney’s attributes, the uniform model with the same number of cells overstates uniqueness for this reason. This is not a theorem, though: with far fewer cells than people, a uniform spread leaves nobody unique, while a few rare cells would hold some uniques.
The entropy \(H\) gives a rule of thumb, not a bound. The rule replaces the real cells by \(2^H\) equally likely cells, as if every cell carried the average surprisal, and gives \(e^{-n2^{-H}}\). The collision bound is always below it (up to replacing \(n\) by \(n - 1\)), because the collision probability is at least \(2^{-H}\). To see why, note that \(\log_2\sum_cp_c^2\) is the logarithm of an average of \(p_c\) (weighted by \(p_c\)), while \(-H = \sum_cp_c\log_2p_c\) is the average of the logarithm, and for the concave logarithm Jensen’s inequality runs the other way: the log of an average is at least the average of the log. So \(\log_2\sum_cp_c^2 \ge -H\). The exact value can sit on either side of the entropy rule: in Table 15.5 it is above it with three and four attributes and below it with five or more.
If attributes are independent, the prediction needs only the marginals. In practice they are not, and a model of the joint distribution is needed. That is what Rocher, Hendrickx & de Montjoye (2019) fit, a Gaussian copula: a model that keeps each attribute’s own frequencies and ties the attributes together through the correlations of a multivariate normal distribution. It is how Section 15.7 estimates risk from a sample.
Finally, one population is enough. Setting the right side of Equation 15.7 equal to a failure probability \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\) says that the fraction unique in the population you have is within \(\sqrt{2\ln(2/\beta)/n}\) of its expectation with probability \(1 - \beta\). For \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(\beta = 0.05\) that is \(\sqrt{2\ln 40/10^4} = 0.0272\). That is about five times the standard deviation of the fraction unique over the 20 simulated populations behind Table 15.5 (at most 0.0053, which the script prints next to each simulated mean), where a normal approximation would put 95% of populations within two standard deviations. McDiarmid is loose here because it charges every person the worst case, a change of 2 in \(U\), while most changes move it by 0 or 1.


15.5.5 Example: a synthetic census
The script builds a population of \(n = 10{,}000\) people with eight independent attributes, made up but shaped like real ones: sex (uniform), age in 16 five-year bands (flat, then thinning out), region (40 values with Zipf frequencies, so a few regions are large), birth month (uniform), marital status, number of children, occupation (20 values, Zipf) and blood group (real-world frequencies). It reveals them one at a time. Table 15.5 gives, for each step, the entropy \(H\) of the attributes known so far and the number of cells \(K\), then the exact expected fraction unique from Equation 15.4, the average over 20 simulated populations, the collision lower bound of Equation 15.6, the entropy rule \(e^{-n2^{-H}}\) and the uniform-cells value \(e^{-n/K}\) for the same number of cells.
