15.5.6 Check yourself

With \(n = 1000\) people and \(K = 1000\) equally likely cells, what fraction is unique, and how many bits beyond \(\log_2n\) is that? (\((1 - 0.001)^{999} = 0.368 \approx e^{-1}\), at zero bits beyond \(\log_2 n\), since \(K = n\).)
Why can the indicators “person \(i\) is unique” be dependent and still give \(\mathbb EU = n\Pr[\text{person 1 is unique}]\)? (Linearity of expectation holds for any random variables, dependent or not. Dependence matters for the variance, which is why the concentration step needs McDiarmid rather than a sum of independent terms.)

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
section: 15.6 Sparse, high-dimensional data: the Netflix attack
text:
15.6 Sparse, high-dimensional data: the Netflix attack

15.6.1 Context
In 2006 Netflix released about 100 million movie ratings by 480,189 subscribers for a public competition. Names were replaced by random numbers, and some ratings and dates were perturbed. The data look nothing like a census table: each record is a set of (movie, rating, date) triples, 209 on average out of 17,770 movies. There are no quasi-identifier columns to join on, and the adversary’s information about a person (“she watched these films around these dates and liked them”) is partial and noisy. Narayanan & Shmatikov (2008) showed that this does not help. In a sparse, high-dimensional dataset, a handful of approximate facts about a person typically matches one record far better than any other. They then matched a small sample of Netflix records to public reviews on the Internet Movie Database, which carry names or pseudonyms. The stakes were real. Viewing histories are protected by US law, the Video Privacy Protection Act of 1988, and Narayanan and Shmatikov pointed out that ratings of a few films can suggest a person’s political or religious views or sexual orientation. In 2009 a subscriber sued Netflix on these grounds in a class action that was later settled, and in 2010 Netflix cancelled a planned second competition after an inquiry by the Federal Trade Commission. This section explains why a scoring rule that favours rare items works, and when to trust its answer.


15.6.2 Statement
The scoring algorithm. The adversary has auxiliary information \(\mathrm{aux}\): a few items \(i\) (films) with approximate values \(\mathrm{aux}_i\) (ratings). Since no record will match exactly, it scores how well each record \(r\) of the release agrees, item by item, and adds up the agreements. An agreement on a film that half the subscribers rated says little, while an agreement on an obscure film says a lot, so each item gets a weight \(w_i\) that is larger for rarer items:
\[\mathrm{Score}(\mathrm{aux}, r) = \sum_{i \in \mathrm{aux}}w_i\,\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i), \tag{15.8}\]
where \(r_i\) is the record’s value for item \(i\) and \(\mathrm{Sim} \in [0, 1]\) measures agreement (here: 1 if \(r\) rated \(i\) within one star of \(\mathrm{aux}_i\), else 0). Narayanan and Shmatikov use \(w_i = 1/\ln\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert\), where \(\lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert\), the support of item \(i\), is the number of records that rated it.
The eccentricity test. The top-scoring record is the best guess, but the adversary also needs to know whether to trust it. A real match should stand out: its score should be well above the second-best one, measured against how spread out all the scores are. Let \(s_1 \ge s_2\) be the two largest scores and \(\sigma\) the standard deviation of all scores. The adversary declares a match only if the gap, in units of \(\sigma\), clears a threshold \(\tau\),
\[\frac{s_1 - s_2}{\sigma} \ge \tau, \tag{15.9}\]
and otherwise says “no match”. Narayanan and Shmatikov used \(\tau = 1.5\).
Their findings on Netflix. With 8 ratings, of which 2 may be completely wrong, and dates known to within 14 days, 99% of records are uniquely identified. With 2 ratings and dates within 3 days, 68% are.
The likelihood-ratio form of the score. The weighting can be derived rather than guessed. For each record, the adversary is weighing two explanations: “this record is the target” against “this record is someone unrelated”. The standard way to weigh two explanations of the same observations is the likelihood ratio, the probability of what you observed under the first explanation divided by its probability under the second. Its logarithm is a sum over items when items behave independently, so it has exactly the form of Equation 15.8. To make this precise, suppose an unrelated record agrees with the auxiliary value of item \(i\) with probability \(s_i\), independently across items, and the target’s record agrees with probability \(1 - \rho\), where \(\rho\) covers wrong or stale auxiliary information. Then ranking records by the likelihood ratio is ranking them by Equation 15.8 with
\[w_i = \ln\frac{1 - s_i}{s_i} + \ln\frac{1 - \rho}{\rho} \approx \ln\frac{1}{s_i} + \ln\frac{1 - \rho}{\rho}, \tag{15.10}\]
where the approximation uses \(1 - s_i \approx 1\) for rare items. The record with the highest score is the most likely to be the target.


15.6.3 Derivation
The weights. The plan is to write the probability of a record’s pattern of agreements under each explanation, take the log of the ratio, and collect the terms that differ from record to record.

Record the agreements. Write \(a_i(r) = \mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i) \in \{0, 1\}\): 1 if record \(r\) agrees with the auxiliary information on item \(i\).
Write the probability of the pattern under each explanation. If \(r\) is the target, each item agrees with probability \(1 - \rho\) and disagrees with probability \(\rho\), independently, so the pattern has probability \(\Pr[a(r)] = \prod_i(1 - \rho)^{a_i}\rho^{1 - a_i}\) (the exponents pick the right factor for each item). If \(r\) is unrelated, each item agrees with probability \(s_i\), so \(\Pr[a(r)] = \prod_is_i^{a_i}(1 - s_i)^{1 - a_i}\).
Take the log of the ratio. The logarithm turns the ratio of products into a sum over items: \(\sum_i\big[a_i\ln\frac{1 - \rho}{s_i} + (1 - a_i)\ln\frac{\rho}{1 - s_i}\big]\).
Keep only what depends on the record. Collect the terms with \(a_i\): \(\sum_ia_i\big[\ln\frac{1-\rho}{s_i} - \ln\frac{\rho}{1 - s_i}\big] + \sum_i\ln\frac{\rho}{1 - s_i}\). The last sum is the same for every record, so it does not change the ranking. The bracket, rearranged, is Equation 15.10: the log-likelihood ratio is the score with those weights, plus a constant.
Why the likelihood ratio is the right thing to threshold. For any single record, deciding between “target” and “unrelated” is a hypothesis test. The Neyman–Pearson lemma of Hypothesis testing says that, among all tests that wrongly accept an unrelated record with a given probability, the one that accepts when the likelihood ratio exceeds a threshold accepts the true target most often. The intuition: if you can afford only so many false accepts, spend them on the patterns that are most typical of the target relative to an unrelated record.

The best guess is the top score. Step 5 is about one record at a time. When the adversary knows the target is one of the \(n\) records and must pick one, Bayes’ rule gives the answer. Suppose each record is equally likely a priori to be the target, and records are independent given who the target is.

Write the probability of everything you see if \(t\) is the target. Record \(t\)’s pattern follows the target distribution and every other record’s follows the unrelated one, so all the agreement patterns together have probability \(P_1(a(t))\prod_{j \ne t}P_0(a(j))\), with \(P_1\) and \(P_0\) the two products of step 2 above.
Turn it into a posterior. Bayes’ rule says the posterior probability of \(t\) is proportional to its prior times this probability, and the prior is the same for every \(t\). Divide by \(\prod_jP_0(a(j))\), which does not depend on \(t\) either: what remains is \(P_1(a(t))/P_0(a(t)) = \mathrm{LR}(t)\), the likelihood ratio of record \(t\). Normalizing so the probabilities sum to 1, \[\Pr[\text{target} = t \mid \text{data}] = \frac{\mathrm{LR}(t)}{\sum_j\mathrm{LR}(j)}. \tag{15.11}\]
Pick the most probable record. The maximum a posteriori (MAP) guess is the record with the largest likelihood ratio, which is the top score.

Why rare items carry the attack. A false match is an unrelated record that happens to agree on every item the adversary knows. Take the clean case, \(\rho \to 0\) and exact agreement required. An unrelated record agrees on all of a set \(I\) of items with probability \(\prod_{i\in I}s_i\), and by Fact 1 the expected number of false matches among \(n\) records is \(n\) times that. Writing both factors as powers of 2 shows the bits:
\[n\prod_{i\in I}s_i = 2^{\log_2n - \sum_{i\in I}\log_2(1/s_i)}. \tag{15.12}\]
Each item contributes \(\log_2(1/s_i)\) bits, its surprisal, and the false matches vanish once the bits exceed \(\log_2n\): the same picture as in Section 15.5. A film that 1% of subscribers rated carries \(\log_2100 = 6.64\) bits; three of them carry \(3 \times 6.64 = 19.9\) bits, more than the \(\log_2480{,}189 = 18.9\) bits needed to single out one Netflix subscriber.


15.6.4 Interpretation
Sparsity is the vulnerability. In a sparse dataset most items are rated by few people, so each item a person rated is worth many bits, and nobody’s record is close to anyone else’s. Narayanan and Shmatikov formalize this as most records having no near neighbour. A census table has few columns with few values each; a ratings matrix has thousands of columns, and a person’s “row” is a long sequence of rare events.
Because the score adds up evidence rather than demanding a perfect match, noise in the auxiliary information costs little. With a wrong item, the target loses one term of the score, while unrelated records rarely gain one. The score needs a margin, not a perfect match.
The eccentricity test answers a different question from the score. The top score is the best guess if the target is in the release. If it may not be, the adversary also needs to decide whether to trust the guess, and the eccentricity asks whether the top score stands out from the crowd of scores. How often it stands out by chance depends on the shape of the score distribution, so \(\tau\) has to be calibrated on records known not to be the target. It should be read at a small false positive rate, as for any attack, because a match is only useful if the adversary can be confident in it (Hypothesis testing). Equation 15.11 gives the principled version. Add one more explanation, “the target is not in the release”, with prior \(1 - \pi\), and give each record prior \(\pi/n\). Under the new explanation every record is unrelated, so its likelihood, divided by \(\prod_jP_0(a(j))\) as before, is 1. Bayes’ rule then gives the posterior that record \(t\) is the target as \(\pi\,\mathrm{LR}(t)/\big(\pi\sum_j\mathrm{LR}(j) + (1 - \pi)n\big)\).
The weights matter less than the bits. Any weighting that favours rare items does about as well as any other; what decides success is whether the auxiliary information carries more bits than \(\log_2n\).


15.6.5 Example: a synthetic ratings matrix
The script draws a sparse matrix of 5,000 users and 4,000 items. Item popularity follows a Zipf law, the number of ratings per user is log-normal (median 30, mean 40.6), and ratings are 1 to 5 stars from a user bias, an item quality and noise. The result has 203,029 ratings and density 0.0102, close to Netflix’s 0.0118. An item drawn from a random user’s record carries a median of 5.83 bits, against \(\log_2 5000 = 12.29\) bits needed. The auxiliary information about a target is \(m\) items from their record, with the rating off by one star half the time; in the noisy setting, a quarter of the items are replaced by random items drawn by popularity, which the target has almost never rated. Table 15.6 gives the fraction of 400 targets whose record gets the top score (ties broken at random), for three weightings. The first is equal weights. The second is the Narayanan–Shmatikov weights. The third is the likelihood-ratio weights of Equation 15.10 in their approximate form \(\ln(1/s_i)\), which is close to the exact \(\ln\frac{1 - s_i}{s_i}\) because every item here is rated by a small fraction of users, with \(s_i = \lvert\mathrm{supp}(i)\rvert/n\), the fraction of users who rated the item, and \(\rho = \frac12\), which makes \(\ln\frac{1-\rho}{\rho} = \ln 1 = 0\) and so drops the constant term.

Read the table with the bits in mind. Two items carry about \(2 \times 5.83 = 11.7\) bits, a little under \(\log_2n\), and re-identify about 43% of targets. Four items carry about \(4 \times 5.83 = 23\) bits and re-identify 93%. With 8 items of which 2 are wrong, the rarity weightings re-identify 98–99% of targets, matching the 99% of Narayanan and Shmatikov for 8 ratings with 2 wrong. Equal weights fall to 94% because a wrong popular item helps many unrelated records. The two rarity weightings differ by less than two standard errors; the standard error of a rate near 0.98 over 400 targets is \(\sqrt{0.98 \times 0.02/400}\), which is 0.007 at these rates.
Figure 15.3 (left and centre) shows what the eccentricity measures. When the target is in the release, its record scores far above every other. When the target is not, the top score is just the high end of a long tail.






Figure 15.3: Left and centre: the scores of all 5,000 records for one target’s auxiliary information (8 items, 2 wrong), on a log scale. When the target is in the release its record stands far out; when it is not, the best score is the edge of the crowd. Right: re-identification rate against the number of auxiliary items, for three weightings, and for the likelihood-ratio weights when a quarter of the items, rounded down, are wrong.



To test the eccentricity rule, the script also scores 400 outsiders, people drawn from the same model who are not in the release, so that any match it declares for them is false. With 8 items, 2 of them wrong, and \(\tau = 1.5\), 94.8% of insiders are correctly re-identified, but 26.3% of outsiders are also “matched” to someone. The median eccentricity is 7.32 for insiders and 0.72 for outsiders, but the outsiders’ distribution has a long tail. Holding the false-match rate to 1% means raising \(\tau\) until only 1% of outsiders clear it, which happens at \(\tau = 4.83\), and that threshold still re-identifies 73.0% of insiders. Figure 15.4 shows the whole trade-off, the true positive rate (insiders matched) against the false positive rate (outsiders matched) as \(\tau\) varies, with false positives on a log axis.






Figure 15.4: True against false positive rates of the eccentricity test as the threshold \(\tau\) is swept, for 4, 6 and 8 auxiliary items with 1, 1 and 2 of them wrong. The dots mark \(\tau = 1.5\). A false positive rate of 0 is drawn at the left edge.





15.6.6 Check yourself

Why do the likelihood-ratio weights in Equation 15.10 contain a term in \(\rho\) that is the same for every item, and what does it do? (It is the evidence from agreeing at all, independent of rarity. When the auxiliary information is reliable (\(\rho\) small), every agreement counts a lot and a record that misses one item is heavily penalized relative to one that matches all of them.)
A record agrees with 3 auxiliary items, each rated by 1% of 480,189 users. How many unrelated records would you expect to agree with all three, if agreements were independent? (\(480{,}189 \times 10^{-6} = 0.48\), since each unrelated record agrees on all three with probability \(0.01^3 = 10^{-6}\): about half a false match, so three such items are close to, but not quite, enough.)

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.7 Does releasing a sample protect?

15.7.1 Context
Statistical agencies and companies often release a sample: 1% of a census, 5% of the patients. The argument is plausible deniability. A record that is unique in the sample need not be unique in the population: the person you have in mind may share their attributes with someone who was not sampled, so a match is not proof. Rocher, Hendrickx & de Montjoye (2019) measured how much this argument is worth. They fitted a Gaussian copula model (each attribute’s own frequencies, tied together by the correlations of a multivariate normal) to a sample and used it to estimate, for each record, how likely it is to be unique in the population and so how likely a match is to be correct. Their model predicted that 99.98% of Americans would be correctly re-identified in any dataset with 15 demographic attributes, and that releasing a sample does little to change that. This section derives the two probabilities that matter and checks them.


15.7.2 Statement
Each of \(n\) people is in the release independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate. Consider a cell with probability \(p\), and let \(\lambda = (n - 1)p\) be the expected number of other people in it. There are two ways to attack, depending on which side the adversary starts from.
From a person to the release. The adversary knows a target’s cell and finds exactly one record in that cell in the release. There are two ways that can happen. Either the target was sampled and none of the others in the cell were, and the match is right. Or the target was not sampled and exactly one of the others was, and the match is wrong. If the cell holds \(J\) others, the wrong story is \(J\) times as likely as the right one, because swapping who was sampled between the target and any one of the others leaves the probability unchanged. How many others should you expect? The release shows no second record in the cell, so the others who are there were all left out of the sample, and each of the \(n - 1\) others is in the cell and unsampled with probability about \(p(1 - q)\). So the cell is expected to hold about \(\lambda(1 - q)\) others, not \(\lambda\), and the wrong story is about \(\lambda(1 - q)\) times as likely as the right one. A match is correct with probability “right over right plus wrong”:
\[\kappa = \Pr[\text{correct} \mid \text{one match}] = \frac{1}{1 + \frac{(n-1)p(1 - q)}{1 - pq}} \approx \frac{1}{1 + \lambda(1 - q)}. \tag{15.13}\]
From a record to the population. The adversary takes a record that is alone in its cell in the release and looks the cell up in a register of the whole population, such as a voter roll. The record is identified if it is alone in its cell in the population too. Knowing the record is alone in the sample already tells you that nobody else in the cell was sampled. What remains is whether anyone in the cell was left out of the sample. Each of the \(n - 1\) others is in the cell but unsampled with probability about \(p(1 - q)\), so about \(\lambda(1 - q)\) people are expected to hide there, and the chance that nobody does is
\[\xi = \Pr[\text{population-unique} \mid \text{sample-unique}] = \left(\frac{1 - p}{1 - pq}\right)^{n-1} \approx e^{-\lambda(1 - q)}. \tag{15.14}\]
The whole release. Averaged over the release, the fraction of sample-unique records that are unique in the population is the expected number of records that are unique in both, divided by the expected number of sample-unique records:
\[\frac{\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}}{\sum_cp_c(1 - p_cq)^{n-1}}, \tag{15.15}\]
which equals the population uniqueness rate Equation 15.4 as \(q \to 0\) and rises to 1 at \(q = 1\).


15.7.3 Derivation
From a person (Equation 15.13). The plan is to compute the two stories, “right match” and “wrong match”, given the number of others in the cell, and then average over that number.

Name the crowd. Let \(J\) be the number of other people in the target’s cell. Each of the \(n - 1\) others is in it with probability \(p\), independently, so \(J \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, p)\).
The right match. Given \(J\), “exactly one match and it is the target” means the target is sampled and none of the \(J\) others are: probability \(q(1 - q)^J\).
The wrong match. Given \(J\), “exactly one match and it is someone else” means the target is not sampled and exactly one of the \(J\) others is. There are \(J\) choices of which other, each sampled with probability \(q\) while the remaining \(J - 1\) are not: probability \((1 - q)\cdot Jq(1 - q)^{J-1} = Jq(1 - q)^J\).
Form the conditional probability. The probability of a correct match given one match is the right story over the sum of both, each averaged over \(J\). The common factor \(q\) cancels, leaving \(\Pr[\text{correct} \mid \text{one match}] = \dfrac{\mathbb E[(1 - q)^J]}{\mathbb E[(1 + J)(1 - q)^J]}\).
Compute the first average. The probability generating function of \(J\) is \(\mathbb E[z^J]\). For a binomial it is \((1 - p + pz)^{n-1}\), because \(z^J\) is a product of one factor per other person, \(z\) if they are in the cell and 1 if not, and each factor averages to \(1 - p + pz\) independently. At \(z = 1 - q\): \(\mathbb E[(1 - q)^J] = (1 - pq)^{n-1}\).
Compute the second average. Differentiating \(z^J\) in \(z\) and multiplying by \(z\) gives \(Jz^J\), so \(\mathbb E[Jz^J] = z\frac{d}{dz}(1 - p + pz)^{n-1} = (n - 1)pz(1 - p + pz)^{n-2}\). At \(z = 1 - q\): \(\mathbb E[J(1 - q)^J] = (n-1)p(1 - q)(1 - pq)^{n-2}\).
Simplify. Divide numerator and denominator of step 4 by \((1 - pq)^{n-1}\) to get Equation 15.13. For small \(p\), \(1 - pq \approx 1\) and \((n-1)p = \lambda\), which gives the approximation.

From a record (Equation 15.14).

Sort the others into three groups. Each other person is, independently, in the cell and sampled (probability \(pq\)), in the cell and not sampled (\(p(1 - q)\)), or outside the cell (\(1 - p\)).
Condition on sample-uniqueness. “The record is sample-unique” says that no other person is in the first group. Because each person’s group is independent of the others’, this condition acts on each person separately: it rules out the first group and rescales the other two by \(1 - pq\), their total probability. So, given it, each other person is outside the cell with probability \(\frac{1 - p}{1 - pq}\), still independently.
Ask for population-uniqueness. Population-unique means all \(n - 1\) others are outside the cell: probability \(\big(\frac{1-p}{1-pq}\big)^{n-1}\). The ratio \(\frac{1 - p}{1 - pq}\) is \(1 - \frac{p(1 - q)}{1 - pq}\), close to \(1 - p(1 - q)\) for small \(p\), so by Fact 2 the whole power is about \(e^{-(n-1)(p - pq)} = e^{-\lambda(1 - q)}\).

The whole release (Equation 15.15).

Count the records unique in both. By Fact 1, the expected number of records that are sample-unique and population-unique is \(\sum_i\Pr[i \text{ sampled and population-unique}]\). Population-unique implies sample-unique, and sampling is independent of the cells, so each term is \(q\) times the probability of being population-unique, which is the per-person term of Equation 15.4. The total is \(nq\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}\).
Count the sample-unique records. Their expected number is \(nq\sum_cp_c(1 - p_cq)^{n-1}\): person \(i\) is sampled, and each other person is either outside \(i\)’s cell or not sampled, which fails only with probability \(p_cq\).
Divide. The factor \(nq\) cancels. Each cell’s term in the numerator is its term in the denominator times \(\big(\frac{1 - p_c}{1 - p_cq}\big)^{n-1}\), its \(\xi\) from Equation 15.14, so the ratio is an average of \(\xi\) over cells weighted by how often each is sample-unique. As \(q \to 0\) the denominator tends to \(\sum_cp_c = 1\), leaving the population uniqueness rate. At \(q = 1\) the two sums are equal and the ratio is 1.



15.7.4 Interpretation
Sampling only helps when the cell is crowded. In both formulas, sampling enters only through the factor \(1 - q\), which multiplies \(\lambda\). For rare combinations, \(\lambda \ll 1\), both are close to 1 whatever \(q\) is. Because \(1 - q \le 1\), both are at least their values at \(q = 0\): \(\kappa \ge 1/(1 + \lambda)\) and \(\xi \ge e^{-\lambda}\) for every sampling rate. Below a few percent, shrinking the sample further barely changes anything, because \(1 - q\) is already close to 1.
Matching from a person is more forgiving than matching from a record: \(\kappa \ge \xi\), since \(1/(1 + x) \ge e^{-x}\) (which is \(e^x \ge 1 + x\), the exponential lying above its tangent line at 0). A person-to-release match can be right even when the target is not unique in the population: the others in the cell may simply not have been sampled.
At small sampling rates, a sample unique is a population unique at the population rate. By Equation 15.15, a 1% sample gives plausible deniability exactly to the people who were not unique in the population anyway. With enough attributes, that is almost nobody.
Finally, the adversary can tell which matches to trust. \(\lambda\) depends on the cell, and the sample is a good sample of the population, so the adversary can estimate \(p\) from it and compute \(\kappa\) or \(\xi\) for each record. Rocher et al. showed this with a copula model; the script does it with the product of the marginals estimated from a 1% sample.


15.7.5 Example: a 1% sample of a synthetic census
For a single cell, Table 15.7 gives both probabilities in their Poisson forms, the approximations on the right of Equation 15.13 and Equation 15.14, for three values of \(\lambda\). For instance, with \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(q = 0.01\), \(\kappa = 1/(1 + 0.1 \times 0.99) = 1/1.099 = 0.910\).

Going from a 50% to a 1% sample lowers \(\kappa\) by \(0.952 - 0.910 = 0.04\) for a rare cell and by \(0.500 - 0.336 = 0.16\) for a crowded one.
The script then draws a population of \(n = 100{,}000\) with the first seven attributes of Table 15.5; 82.8% of its people are unique. Equation 15.15 gives 0.8301 of sample uniques being population-unique at \(q = 0.01\) (simulated: 0.8334 over 19,951 sample uniques in 20 samples), 0.8493 at \(q = 0.1\) and 0.9235 at \(q = 0.5\). As the formula predicts, the 1% value sits just above the population rate of 0.828. A 1% sample leaves 83% of its unique records identifiable against a population register.
The adversary’s own estimate works too. From one 1% sample with 993 sample-unique records, it estimates each attribute’s frequencies, multiplies them to get an estimate \(\hat p\) of each record’s cell probability, and computes \(\xi\) by Equation 15.14 with \(n\) and \(q\), which are public. Its mean prediction is 0.817 against an actual 0.824. The predictions also sort the records well. The 415 records it rates above 0.95 average a prediction of 0.980 and are population-unique 99.3% of the time; the 119 it rates below 0.5 average 0.284 and are unique 30.3% of the time. Figure 15.5 shows both experiments.






Figure 15.5: Left: the fraction of sample-unique records that are unique in a population of 100,000, against the sampling rate, for 5 to 8 attributes; lines are Equation 15.15, dots are simulations. As \(q \to 0\) each curve levels off at the population’s uniqueness rate. Right: the adversary’s predicted probability that a sample-unique record is unique in the population, estimated from a 1% sample, against the observed fraction, in bins of width 0.1.





15.7.6 Check yourself

A combination is expected to be shared by \(\lambda = 0.05\) other people. What is \(\kappa\) for a 1% sample, and for a full release? (\(1/(1 + 0.05 \times 0.99) = 0.953\) and \(1/(1 + 0) = 1\).)
Why does Equation 15.15 tend to the population uniqueness rate, not to 0, as \(q \to 0\)? (A tiny sample has almost no collisions, so nearly every sampled record is sample-unique. The fraction of them that are population-unique is then just the fraction of the population that is unique.)

15.8 Code: check every formula by simulation
The script code/linkage.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. The uniqueness formulas are computed by summing over all cells (grouped by probability, so even 59 million cells are summed quickly) and checked against simulated populations. The ratings experiment is a scaled-down Netflix: a NumPy matrix of 5,000 users, scored with Equation 15.8. From the repository root:

tests/test_linkage.py checks that the output still matches.
What to take from it. First, a hash of a guessable identifier is only a lookup table away from the identifier: one pass over a million hashes inverts every six-digit identifier. Second, the formulas are right: every simulated fraction agrees with its exact expectation to within 0.004. Third, the bits beyond \(\log_2n\) decide uniqueness. A few bits short, a minority is unique; seven bits beyond, almost everyone is, in a census table and in a ratings matrix alike. Fourth, the shortcuts err in known directions. For real, skewed attributes the uniform model usually overstates uniqueness (in the census, at every step from four attributes on) and the collision bound understates it, so compute the exact sum; it needs only a model of the population. Fifth, the decision rule needs calibration. Picking the top score is nearly always right when the target is in the data, but the popular threshold \(\tau = 1.5\) matches a quarter of outsiders in this toy, so choose \(\tau\) from the false positive rate you can accept. Last, sampling is not a defence. It protects the people in crowded cells, who were not at much risk, and the adversary can tell who they are.

title: 15  Linkage and re-identification
text:
15.9 References

Sweeney, “Simple Demographics Often Identify People Uniquely” (Carnegie Mellon University, Data Privacy Working Paper 3, 2000): the 87% estimate for {ZIP code, birth date, sex} and its variants with coarser geography. Sweeney, “k-Anonymity: A Model for Protecting Privacy” (International Journal of Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-Based Systems, 2002) tells the Massachusetts story in its introduction.
Golle, “Revisiting the Uniqueness of Simple Demographics in the US Population” (Workshop on Privacy in the Electronic Society, 2006): the same estimate from the 2000 census, and how it depends on the granularity of the attributes.
Narayanan & Shmatikov, “Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets” (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, 2008): the scoring algorithm, the eccentricity test, the formal notion of sparsity, and the Netflix Prize experiments.
Rocher, Hendrickx & de Montjoye, “Estimating the success of re-identifications in incomplete datasets using generative models” (Nature Communications, 2019): the Gaussian copula model, per-record correctness, and why sampling and incompleteness do not protect.
de Montjoye, Hidalgo, Verleysen & Blondel, “Unique in the Crowd: The privacy bounds of human mobility” (Scientific Reports, 2013): four spatio-temporal points identify 95% of 1.5 million mobile phone users, the same sparsity argument for location traces.
Pandurangan, “On Taxis and Rainbows” (blog post, 2014), and Tockar, “Riding with the Stars: Passenger Privacy in the NYC Taxicab Dataset” (Neustar Research blog, 2014): the inversion of the hashed taxi identifiers, and the re-identification of passengers’ trips from known pickups.
Barth-Jones, “The ‘Re-Identification’ of Governor William Weld’s Medical Information: A Critical Re-Examination of Health Data Identification Risks and Privacy Protections, Then and Now” (2012): what the Massachusetts story does and does not show about ordinary people.
Ohm, “Broken Promises of Privacy: Responding to the Surprising Failure of Anonymization” (UCLA Law Review, 2010): the legal side, with the Massachusetts, search-log and Netflix cases.
Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (2006): where the response to these attacks starts. The next part introduces differential privacy, a guarantee that holds whatever auxiliary information the adversary has. The next chapter first looks at the definitions that came before it.

\(\sum_{i\in\mathrm{aux}}w_i\,\mathrm{Sim}(\mathrm{aux}_i, r_i)\)
\(w_i \approx \ln(1/s_i) + \ln\frac{1-\rho}{\rho}\) is the log-likelihood ratio


Eccentricity
\((s_1 - s_2)/\sigma \ge \tau\)
Calibrate \(\tau\) on outsiders at a small false positive rate


Hashed identifier
\(N\) hash computations invert every pseudonym; a key stops this, not linkage
A consistent pseudonym is a join key


Expected false matches
\(n\prod_{i\in I}s_i = 2^{\log_2n - \sum_i\log_2(1/s_i)}\)
Each item is worth its surprisal in bits


Correct match, person to release
\(\kappa \approx 1/\big(1 + \lambda(1 - q)\big)\)
\(\ge 1/(1 + \lambda)\) for every \(q\)


Sample-unique is population-unique
\(\xi \approx e^{-\lambda(1 - q)}\)
\(\ge e^{-\lambda}\) for every \(q\)

\(\sum_cp_c(1 - p_c)^{n-1}/\sum_cp_c(1 - p_cq)^{n-1}\)

Rules of thumb

\(\log_2n\) bits name one person: 33 for the world, 28 for the US, 13 for a town of 10,000. About 7 bits more make 99% of people unique.
Add up the bits of the attributes an adversary might know. If the sum exceeds \(\log_2n\), assume most people are unique; if attributes are correlated, the true sum is lower.
In sparse data every rare item is worth \(\log_2(1/s_i)\) bits, so a handful of facts is enough, noise or not.
Hashing an identifier from a set of \(N\) values hides at most \(\log_2N\) bits, about 20 to 33 for licence, phone or identity numbers, which is at most \(2^{33}\) hash computations.
Removing names, replacing them by pseudonyms, releasing a sample, or perturbing a few values does not anonymize a dataset. The defence has to hold whatever auxiliary data exist. The next chapter tests the classic attempts, k-anonymity and its successors, against that requirement.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1 Why this matters
Linkage and re-identification showed that deleting names does not anonymize a table. The columns that remain, such as age, ZIP code and sex, are quasi-identifiers: none of them names anyone, but together they single out most people, and anyone who holds a list of names with the same columns (a voter roll, say) can join the two tables and put a name back on most rows. Between 1998 and 2008, data custodians and researchers answered with a family of definitions that constrain the released table itself. k-anonymity hides every record in a crowd of at least \(k\) that look alike. l-diversity asks each crowd to hold several different sensitive values. t-closeness asks each crowd to look like the whole table. They are called syntactic because each one is a property of the published table that you can check by reading it, with no reference to how the table was produced or to what else the adversary knows.
These definitions are not history. Statistics offices, hospital data-sharing agreements, regulators’ guidance and anonymization tools such as ARX still use them. You need to know what they promise and exactly where the promise ends, for two reasons. You will meet them in practice, and their failures are the specification of the definition the next part introduces.
The definitions form a chain, each proposed in answer to an attack on the one before it. Removing names falls to linkage, and k-anonymity caps linkage at \(1/k\) (Section 16.3). But k-anonymity only stops the adversary from picking out the target’s record; it does not stop the adversary from learning the target’s diagnosis. If every record in the target’s crowd has the same diagnosis (homogeneity), or if the adversary can rule out the other diagnoses from what it already knows about the target (background knowledge), the diagnosis leaks with no record picked out. l-diversity answers these two attacks (Section 16.4). A crowd can be diverse and still move the adversary’s belief a long way, though: half the crowd may have a disease that is rare in the population (skewness), or all its different diagnoses may be diseases of the same organ (similarity). t-closeness answers these (Section 16.5). Finally, composition defeats all three at once: two releases, each satisfying the definition, intersect to reveal what neither reveals alone (Section 16.6).

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.1.1 The one idea: a syntactic definition fixes the adversary’s knowledge
Each definition is a property of one table, and it protects against an adversary whose knowledge is fixed in advance. For k-anonymity the adversary knows the quasi-identifiers and nothing else. For l-diversity it knows the quasi-identifiers plus a few facts about the target. For t-closeness it knows the quasi-identifiers plus the table’s overall distribution. Each attack in this chapter gives the adversary one more piece of knowledge that the definition did not anticipate, and the guarantee then says nothing. A second release, the most ordinary auxiliary information there is, breaks all three definitions. A definition that survives has to hold whatever the adversary knows, and has to say what happens when releases are combined.
Table 16.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 16.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.

Recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diversity caps the posterior at \(c/(1 + c)\) after \(\ell - 2\) values are ruled out

What this chapter uses from elsewhere. Every idea below is restated where it is used, and these links are for more detail. The linkage game, Equation 15.3, and the uniform-cells model are in Linkage and re-identification. The imputation baseline, the best guess of a sensitive attribute from the population alone, is in Attribute inference and model inversion. Total variation is in Divergences, the Poisson approximation to the binomial in Probability distributions, and entropy in Information theory.
Notation. A table has \(n\) records. Each has quasi-identifiers and one sensitive attribute \(S\), such as a diagnosis, with \(m\) possible values. A generalization replaces each quasi-identifier by a coarser value: an age by a range, a ZIP code by a prefix. An equivalence class \(E\) is a set of records with the same generalized quasi-identifiers; \(\lvert E\rvert\) is its number of records. Within a class, \(n_E(v)\) is the number of records with \(S = v\), and \(P_E(v) = n_E(v)/\lvert E\rvert\) is the fraction of the class with that value, the class’s distribution. \(P(v)\) is the same fraction over the whole table. Suppression deletes records.

section: 16.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
16.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

16.2.1 Fact 1 — Within a class, the posterior is the frequency
The adversary’s posterior is its belief about the target’s sensitive value after it has seen the release. Here is the situation. The adversary knows the target’s quasi-identifiers and knows the target is in the release, so it can find the target’s class \(E\). But all records in \(E\) show the same generalized quasi-identifiers, so it cannot tell which one is the target’s. If it knows nothing else, it has no reason to favour any record, and each of the \(\lvert E\rvert\) records is equally likely to be the target’s. (This is step 2 of the derivation of Equation 15.3: the target was drawn at random, and the records of a class differ only in the sensitive attribute, which the adversary does not know.) The chance that the target has value \(v\) is then the number of records with \(v\) divided by the number of records: \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert} = P_E(v). \tag{16.1}\] Background knowledge works by elimination. If the adversary also knows that the target’s value is not in some set \(B\) of values, the records with values in \(B\) cannot be the target’s. It crosses them out and spreads its belief evenly over the records that are left. The number left is \(\lvert E\rvert\) minus the records with values in \(B\), so for a value \(v\) not in \(B\), \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}, S_{\text{target}} \notin B] = \frac{n_E(v)}{\lvert E\rvert - \sum_{u \in B}n_E(u)}. \tag{16.2}\]
For example, take a class of three records with the diagnoses cancer, cancer, flu. Two of the three records say cancer, so the adversary’s posterior is \(\frac23\) for cancer and \(\frac13\) for flu. If it knows that the target did not have flu, the flu record is crossed out, two records remain and both say cancer, so cancer has posterior \(\frac22 = 1\). Every attack on the sensitive attribute in this chapter is this calculation.


16.2.2 Fact 2 — Total variation bounds every event
To say that a class “looks like the whole table” you need a distance between two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) on the same values. The total variation (TV) distance is half the total absolute difference between the two probability tables, and it equals the largest difference in probability that any single question about the value can show: \[\mathrm{TV}(P, Q) = \frac12\sum_v\lvert P(v) - Q(v)\rvert = \max_A\,\lvert P(A) - Q(A)\rvert, \tag{16.3}\] where the maximum is over all sets of values \(A\), and \(P(A)\) is the probability that the value lands in \(A\) (Divergences).
The equality has a short reason. \(P(A) - Q(A) = \sum_{v \in A}(P(v) - Q(v))\), which is largest when \(A\) holds exactly the values where \(P(v) > Q(v)\), so the maximum is attained by \(A = \{v : P(v) > Q(v)\}\) and equals the total excess of \(P\) over \(Q\). Both distributions sum to 1, so the total excess of \(P\) over \(Q\) equals the total excess of \(Q\) over \(P\), and each is half the sum of all absolute differences. (Taking \(A\) to be the values where \(Q\) is larger gives the same number with the sign flipped, which is why the absolute value does no harm.) This is what t-closeness relies on: a bound on the distance is a bound on every question the adversary can ask.


16.2.3 Fact 3 — The number of others in your cell is nearly Poisson
Fact 3 is the tool for counting how many people share your quasi-identifiers. Model the generalized quasi-identifiers as \(K\) cells, and suppose the \(n\) people fall into them independently, each cell equally likely. Fix yourself. Each of the other \(n - 1\) people lands in your cell with probability \(1/K\), independently, so the number of other people in your cell is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n - 1, 1/K)\). When there are many trials, each with a small chance, the binomial is close to the Poisson distribution with the same mean, \(\Pr[N = j] \approx e^{-\lambda}\lambda^j/j!\) (Probability distributions). Here the mean is \(\lambda = (n-1)/K \approx n/K\), the average number of people per cell. Your class then has \(1 + \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda)\) members: you plus the others. This is how the chapter counts how many records violate k-anonymity at a given coarseness.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.3 k-anonymity

16.3.1 Context
Sweeney and Samarati proposed the first answer to the linkage attack in 1998: make sure that no combination of quasi-identifiers in the release singles out fewer than \(k\) people. A custodian gets there by generalizing (age 37 becomes 35–39, ZIP code 02139 becomes 021**) and by suppressing the few records that still stand out. The question is what this buys, and what it costs.


16.3.2 Statement
Definition. A release is k-anonymous if every equivalence class has at least \(k\) records.
What it guarantees. Recall the linkage game: a target is drawn uniformly from the release, the adversary is given the target’s quasi-identifiers, and it wins if it picks out the target’s record. Equation 15.3 says the best it can do is \(J/n\), where \(J\) is the number of classes. The reason is that in a class of size \(\lvert E\rvert\) the best guess is a random record of the class, right with probability \(1/\lvert E\rvert\), and the target lands in that class with probability \(\lvert E\rvert/n\), so each class contributes \(1/n\) and the \(J\) classes contribute \(J/n\). When every class has at least \(k\) records there cannot be many classes, and \[\Pr[\text{win}] = \frac{J}{n} \le \frac1k. \tag{16.4}\]
What it costs, for uniform cells. Coarse quasi-identifiers protect more but say less, so the question is how coarse they must be. Suppose the generalized quasi-identifiers split the population into \(K\) equally likely cells. A record violates k-anonymity when its cell holds fewer than \(k\) people, and by Fact 3 the expected fraction of such records is \[\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K) \le k - 2]. \tag{16.5}\] Keeping that fraction below a target \(\alpha\) needs enough people per cell, \(n/K \ge \lambda_k\), where \(\lambda_k\) is the mean at which the fraction is exactly \(\alpha\): \(\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_k) \le k - 2] = \alpha\). A quasi-identifier with \(K\) equally likely values carries \(\log_2 K\) bits of information about a person, so in bits the quasi-identifiers may carry at most \(b = \log_2 K = \log_2 n - \log_2\lambda_k\).


16.3.3 Derivation
The cap on linkage (Equation 16.4). The idea is that \(n\) records cannot fill more than \(n/k\) classes of at least \(k\) each.

Count records by class. The \(J\) classes split the \(n\) records between them, each record in exactly one class, so \(n = \sum_j\lvert E_j\rvert\).
Use the definition. Every class has at least \(k\) records, so the sum is at least \(Jk\): \(n \ge Jk\), that is \(J/n \le 1/k\).
Read off the linkage success. Equation 15.3 says the linkage success is \(J/n\), so it is at most \(1/k\).

The cost (Equation 16.5). The idea is to compute the chance that one person’s class is too small, then note that this chance is also the expected fraction of such people.

Size of a person’s class. A person’s class is their cell. By Fact 3 it holds the person plus \(N\) others, with \(N\) approximately \(\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K)\).
When it is too small. The class is smaller than \(k\) when \(1 + N \le k - 1\), that is \(N \le k - 2\), which has probability \(\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K) \le k - 2]\).
From one person to the fraction. The expected number of people in small classes is the sum, over people, of each one’s chance of being in one (linearity of expectation: the expected count of events is the sum of their probabilities). Every person has the same chance, so the sum is \(n\) times it, and the expected fraction is that chance.
Solve for the coarseness. As \(\lambda\) grows, the Poisson count moves up and the chance of a small count, the CDF (cumulative distribution function) at \(k - 2\), falls. So “at most \(\alpha\)” is the same as \(\lambda \ge \lambda_k\). Put \(K = n/\lambda\) and take \(\log_2\): \(\log_2 K = \log_2 n - \log_2 \lambda\), largest at \(\lambda = \lambda_k\).



16.3.4 Interpretation
The guarantee is about names only. Equation 16.4 bounds the chance of picking out the target’s record. It says nothing about the sensitive attribute, which is the whole point of the release, and the next two sections attack exactly that gap.
k-anonymity is the mirror image of uniqueness, and the bits make the comparison exact. In the same uniform-cells model, a person is unique when nobody else is in their cell, which by Fact 3 has probability \(\Pr[\mathrm{Poisson}(n/K) = 0] = e^{-n/K}\). For 99% of people to be unique you need \(e^{-n/K} = 0.99\), so \(n/K = \ln(1/0.99) \approx 0.01\) and \(K \approx 100n\), which is \(\log_2 n + \log_2 100 = \log_2n + 6.64\) bits (Section 15.5). At the other end, Table 16.2 shows that 2-anonymity for 99% of records needs the quasi-identifiers to carry at most \(\log_2n - 2.20\) bits. The window between “almost everyone is unique” and “almost everyone is hidden” is \(6.64 + 2.20 = 8.84\), about 9 bits wide, and every attribute you publish uses some of it.
k costs more than \(\log_2 k\) bits. You might expect that hiding everyone in a class of \(k\) needs \(k\) people per cell, that is \(\log_2 k\) bits fewer than \(\log_2 n\). But cells vary in size around their mean, and the unlucky small cells are the ones that violate the definition, so you need \(\lambda_k\) people per cell on average, and \(\lambda_k\) is larger than \(k\). The margin is largest for small \(k\). For \(k = 2\) a person violates the definition when \(N = 0\), which has probability \(e^{-\lambda}\); setting \(e^{-\lambda} = 0.01\) gives \(\lambda_2 = \ln 100 = 4.61\), more than twice \(k\).
Which columns are quasi-identifiers is a judgment, and in sparse data everything is one. Section 15.6 showed that a handful of rare movie ratings single out a subscriber. Making a ratings matrix k-anonymous means generalizing thousands of columns until little is left (Aggarwal, 2005).
Finally, the guarantee assumes the adversary knows no more than the quasi-identifiers. A neighbour who knows that the target’s record is the only one in the class with a given diagnosis needs no linkage at all.


16.3.5 Example: a k-anonymous hospital table
Table 16.2 applies Equation 16.5 to a population of \(n = 10{,}000\) (\(\log_2 n = 13.29\) bits) with \(\alpha = 1\%\). For each \(k\) it finds \(\lambda_k\), then subtracts \(\log_2 \lambda_k\) from \(\log_2 n\). For \(k = 2\), \(\lambda_2 = 4.61\) from the calculation above, \(\log_2 4.61 = 2.20\), and \(13.29 - 2.20 = 11.08\) bits are allowed.

The gap is about 1.2 bits at \(k = 2\) (\(2.20 - 1.00\)) and shrinks to about 0.4 bits at \(k = 50\) (\(6.06 - 5.64\)), because a Poisson count with a large mean varies little relative to its mean. Real tables are not uniform, so real anonymizers search for a generalization that works on the data. The script builds a synthetic hospital table of \(n = 10{,}000\) patients with three quasi-identifiers: age in years (0 to 89), a five-digit ZIP code (800 values, a few areas far more common than the rest) and sex. The sensitive attribute is one of eight diagnoses, and it depends on age: asthma peaks in childhood, fractures around 18, depression around 40, diabetes, hypertension and cancer later in life, while flu is equally common at every age and HIV is rare (1.0% of records). With exact quasi-identifiers, the linkage success is 0.933: by Equation 15.3, the 10,000 patients fall into \(0.933 \times 10{,}000 = 9{,}330\) distinct combinations of age, ZIP code and sex, so most of them are alone in theirs.
The script anonymizes the table with Mondrian (LeFevre, DeWitt & Ramakrishnan, 2006). Start with the whole table as one box. Split a box at the median of the quasi-identifier with the widest range (relative to its full range), as long as both halves still have at least \(k\) records. Stop when no split is allowed. Each final box is a class, published as a range per quasi-identifier. Mondrian recodes locally: a busy ZIP area gets narrow age ranges and a quiet one wide ranges. Because it keeps splitting until a split would leave fewer than \(k\) on one side, its classes stay close to size \(k\), much closer than those of a single global generalization of each column. 16.3.6 Check yourself

A k-anonymous release of 1,000 records has 120 classes. What is the largest \(k\) it can satisfy, and what is the linkage success? (At most \(\lfloor 1000/120\rfloor = 8\), since \(Jk \le n\). The success is \(120/1000 = 0.12\), below \(1/8 = 0.125\).)
Why does 2-anonymity need about 4.6 people per cell on average, not 2? (The number of others in your cell is roughly Poisson. With a mean of 1, a fraction \(e^{-1} = 0.37\) of people would have nobody else in their cell. To get that down to 1% you need \(e^{-\lambda} = 0.01\), that is \(\lambda = 4.61\).)

text:
16.4 Homogeneity, background knowledge and l-diversity

16.4.1 Context
Machanavajjhala, Kifer, Gehrke & Venkitasubramaniam (2006) pointed out that k-anonymity hides who a record belongs to but not what it says. Table 16.4 is a 3-anonymous release.



Table 16.4: A 3-anonymous release with three classes of three records.

Alice is 26 and lives in ZIP code 13053. Her class is the first, and every record in it says heart disease. By Fact 1 her posterior for heart disease is the fraction of her class that has it, \(\frac33 = 1\). This is the homogeneity attack: no re-identification, full disclosure. Bob is 35, lives in 13068, and is in the third class, where two of three records say cancer, so his posterior for cancer is \(\frac23\). His neighbour saw him at work through the whole flu season and rules out flu; crossing out the flu record leaves two cancer records, and cancer then has posterior 1. This is the background knowledge attack. The question is what condition on the classes stops both.


16.4.2 Statement
Both attacks work because one value dominates the class, either from the start or after a few values are ruled out. l-diversity asks for enough different values in each class, and its three versions differ in how they measure “enough”. Sort a class’s value counts from largest to smallest as \(r_1 \ge r_2 \ge \dots \ge r_m\), so \(r_1\) is the count of the most common value. A class is

distinct \(\ell\)-diverse if it holds at least \(\ell\) different values;
entropy \(\ell\)-diverse if the entropy of \(P_E\) is at least \(\log_2\ell\). The entropy \(H(P_E) = -\sum_v P_E(v)\log_2 P_E(v)\) measures in bits how spread out the values are; \(\ell\) equally common values have entropy exactly \(\log_2 \ell\), so the condition says the class is at least as spread out as \(\ell\) equal values;
recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diverse if \(r_1 < c\,(r_\ell + r_{\ell+1} + \dots + r_m)\): the most common value is less than \(c\) times the total of all but the \(\ell - 1\) most common. The right-hand side is the “tail” that is left after the \(\ell - 1\) biggest values are set aside, and the condition says the top value cannot swamp that tail.

A release is \(\ell\)-diverse if every class is.
What recursive diversity guarantees. The tail is what survives the background knowledge attack. An adversary who rules out \(\ell - 2\) values can at worst remove some of the big values, and the remaining ones still include a tail at least as large as the original one. Since the top value is less than \(c\) times that tail, it holds less than \(c\) parts out of \(c + 1\). Precisely: if a class is recursive \((c, \ell)\)-diverse, then after the adversary rules out any \(\ell - 2\) values that are not the target’s, every remaining value \(v\) has \[\Pr[S_{\text{target}} = v \mid \text{release}, \text{background}] < \frac{c}{1 + c}. \tag{16.6}\] For distinct \(\ell\)-diversity, the corresponding statement is weaker: the adversary needs to rule out \(\ell - 1\) values to be certain, but one value can still hold all but \(\ell - 1\) of the records.


16.4.3 Derivation
The plan is to compare the class after elimination with the original class: its top count cannot be larger, and its tail cannot be smaller, so the defining inequality survives.

What is left. Rule out a set \(B\) of \(\ell - 2\) values. The remaining \(m - \ell + 2\) values keep their original counts. Call the largest of them \(r'_1\), and the total of the other \(m - \ell + 1\) remaining values \(T'\).
The top does not grow. Ruling out values removes records but never adds any, so \(r'_1\) is one of the original counts, and no original count exceeds \(r_1\): \(r'_1 \le r_1\).
The tail does not shrink below the original tail. \(T'\) is a sum of \(m - \ell + 1\) of the original counts. The smallest such sum you could possibly get is that of the \(m - \ell + 1\) smallest counts, which is \(r_\ell + \dots + r_m\). So \(T' \ge r_\ell + \dots + r_m\).
Combine with the definition. Chain the three inequalities: \(r'_1 \le r_1 < c\,(r_\ell + \dots + r_m) \le c\,T'\).
Turn counts into a posterior. By Fact 1, after elimination the posterior of a remaining value is its count over the total count left, \(r'_1 + T'\), so it is at most \(r'_1/(r'_1 + T')\). The map \(x \mapsto x/(x + T')\) increases in \(x\) (a larger share of a pie whose other part is fixed), so with \(r'_1 < cT'\) this is below \(cT'/(cT' + T') = c/(1 + c)\).



16.4.4 Interpretation
l-diversity protects against certainty, not against likelihood. The bound \(c/(1 + c)\) is \(\frac12\) at \(c = 1\), \(\frac23\) at \(c = 2\) and \(\frac34\) at \(c = 3\), so even recursive diversity lets the adversary be fairly sure. Distinct and entropy \(\ell\)-diversity do not even give that, because neither limits the share of the top value directly: an entropy 3-diverse class over 8 values can have one value in 73% of its records, since the other 27% spread over seven values add enough entropy (Exercise 2).
The adversary’s knowledge is assumed, not bounded. The guarantee covers an adversary who rules out up to \(\ell - 2\) values. One who rules out more, or who knows something softer (“probably not flu”), is not covered.
A posterior also has to be read against what the adversary would believe with no release. A posterior of 0.6 for one diagnosis is not a leak if the population already gives 0.6 to people of the target’s age. The right comparison is the imputation baseline of Attribute inference and model inversion: the most likely value of the sensitive attribute given the target’s own quasi-identifiers, under the true population distribution, computed with no release at all. Whatever the release teaches beyond that is about the individual; up to it, it is about the population.
Some tables cannot be made diverse at all. The table’s distribution \(P\) is the average of its classes’ distributions \(P_E\), each weighted by the class’s share of the records. Entropy is concave: mixing distributions can only make the result more spread out, so the entropy of an average is at least the average of the entropies. If every class had entropy at least \(\log_2\ell\), the table would too. So a table dominated by one value, with entropy below \(\log_2\ell\), has no entropy \(\ell\)-diverse partition.


16.4.5 Example: homogeneity in the toy and in the hospital table
In Table 16.4 the three classes hold 1, 3 and 2 different values, so they are distinct 1-, 3- and 2-diverse. Their entropy versions are \(\ell = 2^{H(P_E)}\), the number of equally common values with the same entropy. The first class has one value, entropy 0 and \(\ell = 1.00\). The second has three equally common values and \(\ell = 3.00\). The third, \(\frac23\) cancer and \(\frac13\) flu, has entropy \(\frac23\log_2\frac32 + \frac13\log_2 3 = 0.918\) bits and \(\ell = 2^{0.918} = 1.89\): two values, but unevenly spread, so worth fewer than two. The release as a whole is only 1-diverse, because of Alice’s class.
In the hospital table, the “certain disclosure” column of Table 16.3 counts the patients in homogeneous classes. At \(k = 2\) it is 28.0% of all patients. At \(k = 5\) it is 2.3%, or 232 patients whose diagnosis the release states outright. The population never gives that certainty: at no age does the population law give any diagnosis more than 0.705.
The guess accuracy column needs the baselines of Figure 16.2 (right). Guessing the most common diagnosis of the whole table is right for 18.5% of patients. Imputation, which guesses the most likely diagnosis for each patient’s exact age under the population law, is right for 53.6%, with no release at all. A 5-anonymous release is right for 59.3%. So most of what the release teaches the adversary is the age–diagnosis pattern, which any useful study of this table would report. The excess over imputation, \(0.593 - 0.536 = 0.057\) at \(k = 5\), comes from the small classes, and it is down to \(0.540 - 0.536 = 0.004\) at \(k = 20\).

Is the class {cancer, cancer, cancer, flu, asthma} recursive \((2, 3)\)-diverse? (No. The sorted counts are \(r_1 = 3\), \(r_2 = 1\), \(r_3 = 1\), and the tail beyond the two most common values is \(r_3 = 1\), so the condition is \(3 < 2 \times 1\), which fails. It is distinct 3-diverse.)

(If the class has exactly \(\ell\) values, ruling out \(\ell - 1\) of them leaves one, with posterior 1, whatever \(c\) is. title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.5 Skewness, similarity and t-closeness

16.5.1 Context
Li, Li & Venkatasubramanian (2007) found two attacks that l-diversity does not see. In the skewness attack, 1% of the table has HIV, and a class that is half HIV, half not, is 2-diverse by every definition, yet by Fact 1 it raises the adversary’s belief that a member has HIV from 1% to 50%, fifty-fold. In the similarity attack, a class holds three different diagnoses, gastric ulcer, gastritis and stomach cancer, so it is 3-diverse, and the adversary still learns that the target has a stomach disease. Both say that diversity is the wrong yardstick: what matters is how far a class’s distribution is from what the adversary would believe anyway, which is the distribution of the whole table.


16.5.2 Statement
Definition. A release is t-close if every class’s distribution is within distance \(t\) of the whole table’s: \(d(P_E, P) \le t\), for a chosen distance \(d\) between distributions.
With total variation as the distance, the guarantee is that no question about the target’s value gets an answer more than \(t\) away from the answer the whole table gives. By Fact 2, the total variation is the largest such gap, so for every class and every set of values \(A\), \[\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert \le t. \tag{16.7}\] In particular, guessing the most common value of the target’s class is right with probability at most \(\max_vP(v) + t\): the best guess from the table alone, plus \(t\).
With the earth mover’s distance (EMD), the choice of Li et al., values that are similar are close, which is what the similarity attack needs. Think of each distribution as piles of sand on the values. The EMD is the least work needed to reshape one set of piles into the other, where moving a unit of sand between two values costs their distance apart. For \(m\) ordered values (salary bands, age groups), numbered \(1\) to \(m\) and placed at ground distance \(\lvert i - j\rvert/(m - 1)\) so that the two ends are distance 1 apart, the work comes out as a sum over the gaps between neighbouring values of how much sand must cross each one: \[\mathrm{EMD}(P_E, P) = \frac{1}{m - 1}\sum_{i=1}^{m-1}\Big\lvert\sum_{j \le i}\big(P_E(j) - P(j)\big)\Big\rvert. \tag{16.8}\]


16.5.3 Derivation
Total variation (Equation 16.7). The idea is that the adversary’s belief is the class distribution, so a bound on how far the class is from the table is a bound on how far the adversary’s belief moves.

A distance bound is an event bound. By Fact 2, \(\mathrm{TV}(P_E, P) = \max_A\lvert P_E(A) - P(A)\rvert\), so a bound \(t\) on the distance is a bound \(t\) on every event.
The adversary’s belief is the class distribution. By Fact 1, the adversary’s belief about a target in class \(E\) is \(P_E\). So every question it can ask about the target’s value, “is it in \(A\)?”, gets an answer within \(t\) of the answer from the table as a whole.
Apply it to the best guess. Take \(A = \{v\}\) for the class’s most common value: \(P_E(v) \le P(v) + t \le \max_uP(u) + t\).

Earth mover’s distance on ordered values (Equation 16.8). The idea is that on a line, sand can only get from one side of a gap to the other by crossing it, so you can count the work gap by gap.

What EMD is. EMD is the least total cost of moving the mass of \(P_E\) until it becomes \(P\), where moving mass \(f\) from value \(i\) to \(j\) costs \(f\lvert i - j\rvert/(m - 1)\). A move from \(i\) to \(j\) crosses each of the \(\lvert i - j\rvert\) gaps between them once, so its cost is \(1/(m - 1)\) per unit per gap crossed.
How much must cross each gap. Look at the gap between values \(i\) and \(i + 1\). The values up to \(i\) hold \(\sum_{j \le i}P_E(j)\) under the class and must end up holding \(\sum_{j \le i}P(j)\). The difference, \(\sum_{j \le i}(P_E(j) - P(j))\), is their excess (or shortfall), and that net mass has to cross the gap, rightwards if positive and leftwards if negative. Any plan moves at least this much across the gap.
A plan that does no more. A plan that only moves mass between neighbours and never in both directions across the same gap moves exactly the net amount across each gap. So the least cost is \(1/(m - 1)\) times the sum, over the \(m - 1\) gaps, of the absolute net mass crossing it, which is Equation 16.8.



16.5.4 Interpretation
The bound is additive, and rare values need a ratio. Equation 16.7 lets a 1% value rise to \(1\% + t\). At \(t = 0.15\) that is 16%, a sixteen-fold increase for the people who most need protection. A difference of 0.15 looks small next to a common value such as 40%, and enormous next to 1%. A guarantee for rare values has to bound the ratio of the adversary’s beliefs with and without the release, not their difference. That is the shape of the definition in the next part.
t-closeness also fights the purpose of the release. If age predicts diagnosis, a class of similar ages has a different diagnosis distribution from the whole table, so it is not t-close for small \(t\). Making every class t-close means mixing ages until the pattern is gone. But the pattern is a fact about the population, the kind of finding any study is published to report, not a secret about any one patient. Attribute inference and model inversion draws the same line between population inference and individual leakage.
The choice of distance is a choice of what is “similar”. EMD with a ground distance from a hierarchy of diagnoses treats gastritis and gastric ulcer as close, so a class full of stomach diseases is far from the table and fails. Total variation treats every pair of values as equally different, so it would not see the similarity attack.


16.5.5 Example: toy, skew and hospital
In Table 16.4, the table has four heart disease, three cancer and two flu records, so its distribution is \(\frac49\) heart disease, \(\frac39\) cancer, \(\frac29\) flu. Each class’s total variation from it is the total excess of the class over the table (Fact 2). Alice’s class is all heart disease, an excess of \(1 - \frac49 = \frac59 = 0.556\). The second class is \(\frac13 = \frac39\) of each, an excess of \(\frac39 - \frac29 = \frac19 = 0.111\) on flu only. Bob’s class, \(\frac69\) cancer and \(\frac39\) flu, has excesses \(\frac39\) and \(\frac19\), together \(\frac49 = 0.444\). So the release is \(t\)-close only for \(t \ge 0.556\).
For the skewness attack (Figure 16.3), the class that is 50% HIV is at total variation \(0.50 - 0.01 = 0.49\) from a table with 1% HIV (the excess on HIV). A class with 10% HIV is at \(0.10 - 0.01 = 0.09\), which passes \(t = 0.1\), and still makes HIV ten times as likely for its members.

title: 16  Syntactic anonymity and how it breaks
text:
16.6 The composition attack

16.6.1 Context
Every definition so far is about one release. Ganta, Kasiviswanathan & Smith (2008) asked what happens when there are two. Two hospitals in the same city publish their patient tables, each one properly k-anonymous, or \(\ell\)-diverse, with no coordination. A patient treated at both appears in a class of each. The adversary takes the diagnoses of the target’s class in one release, those of the class in the other, and intersects: the true diagnosis is in both. Neither hospital did anything wrong, and each release satisfies its definition, yet the combination can reveal the diagnosis outright.


16.6.2 Statement
The attack. For a target in both releases, with class \(E_A\) in release A and \(E_B\) in release B, the candidate values are those that appear in both classes, \[\{v : n_{E_A}(v) > 0\} \cap \{v : n_{E_B}(v) > 0\}, \tag{16.9}\] and the true value is always among them, because the target’s own record carries it in each class. The diagnosis is pinned down when one candidate is left.
How often, in a model. To see how often this happens, model the classes as random. Suppose the target’s class has \(k_A\) records in one release and \(k_B\) in the other, and the other members’ values are independent draws from the population distribution \(p\), with \(p_v\) the probability of value \(v\). Given that the target’s true value is \(v\), let \(A_v\) be the set of values other than \(v\) that appear among the \(k_A - 1\) other members of the class in release A, and \(B_v\) the same for the \(k_B - 1\) others in release B. These are the wrong values each release leaves open. The target is pinned exactly when no wrong value is left open by both, that is when \(A_v\) and \(B_v\) share nothing. So the probability is an average, over the true value \(v\) and over what release A leaves open, of the chance that every other member of the second class avoids those values. Writing \(p(S) = \sum_{u \in S}p_u\) for the probability of a set of values, \[\Pr[\text{pinned}] = \sum_vp_v\,\mathbb E\big[(1 - p(A_v))^{k_B - 1}\big],\qquad \Pr[A_v = S] = \sum_{T \subseteq S}(-1)^{\lvert S\rvert - \lvert T\rvert}\big(p_v + p(T)\big)^{k_A - 1}, \tag{16.10}\] where the expectation is over the random set \(A_v\), whose distribution is the second formula. A simpler lower bound counts, for each wrong value, the chance that both classes contain it, and subtracts the total from 1: \[\Pr[\text{pinned}] \ge 1 - \sum_vp_v\sum_{u \ne v}\big(1 - (1 - p_u)^{k_A - 1}\big)\big(1 - (1 - p_u)^{k_B - 1}\big). \tag{16.11}\]


16.6.3 Derivation
The exact probability (Equation 16.10). The idea is to fix the true value and what the first class contains, compute the chance that the second class avoids it, and then average.

Condition on the true value. The target’s true value is \(v\) with probability \(p_v\). Everything below is for a fixed \(v\), and the outer sum \(\sum_v p_v(\cdot)\) averages over it.
When the value is pinned. The candidates are \(v\) itself together with the wrong values that appear in both classes, \(\{v\} \cup (A_v \cap B_v)\). So the value is pinned exactly when \(A_v\) and \(B_v\) are disjoint.
Fix what the first class leaves open. Condition on \(A_v = S\) for a particular set \(S\). The \(k_B - 1\) others in the second class are independent draws, and each avoids \(S\) with probability \(1 - p(S)\). So \(\Pr[B_v \cap S = \emptyset] = (1 - p(S))^{k_B - 1}\). Averaging over the possible sets \(S\), weighted by \(\Pr[A_v = S]\), gives the expectation in Equation 16.10.
The distribution of the first class’s set. \(A_v = S\) means two things: every one of the \(k_A - 1\) draws lands in \(S \cup \{v\}\), and each value of \(S\) is hit at least once. The first part is easy: “all draws land in \(T \cup \{v\}\)” has probability \((p_v + p(T))^{k_A - 1}\) for any set \(T\). The second part is handled by inclusion–exclusion: start from “all draws land in \(S \cup \{v\}\)”, subtract the cases where some value of \(S\) is missed (all draws land in a smaller set), add back the cases subtracted twice, and so on. The sets \(T \subseteq S\) are the values not missed, and the sign \((-1)^{\lvert S\rvert - \lvert T\rvert}\) alternates with the number missed, which gives the alternating sum.

For a single wrong value, \(S = \{u\}\), the sum has two terms: \(\Pr[A_v = \{u\}] = (p_v + p_u)^{k_A - 1} - p_v^{k_A - 1}\), the probability that every draw is \(v\) or \(u\), minus the probability that every draw is \(v\) (in which case \(u\) was never hit).
The lower bound (Equation 16.11). The idea is that the target fails to be pinned only if some wrong value turns up in both classes, and the chance of “some” is at most the sum of the chances of each.

When it fails. Given \(v\), the value is not pinned when some \(u \ne v\) is in both \(A_v\) and \(B_v\).
The chance for one wrong value. \(u\) is missing from the first class when all \(k_A - 1\) others avoid it, which has probability \((1 - p_u)^{k_A - 1}\), so \(\Pr[u \in A_v] = 1 - (1 - p_u)^{k_A - 1}\), and likewise for \(B_v\). The two classes are drawn independently, so the probability that \(u\) is in both is the product.
Add over wrong values. The expected number of wrong values in both sets is the sum of these products, by linearity of expectation (the expected count of events is the sum of their probabilities; Fact 1 of Linkage and re-identification). The chance that there is at least one is at most this expected number, because a count that is at least 1 whenever the event happens has expectation at least the event’s probability (the union bound). Subtract from 1 and average over \(v\).



16.6.4 Interpretation
None of the three definitions composes. Each is a condition on one table, and the intersection of two tables is not a table that either custodian checked. Ganta et al. showed the attack on k-anonymous and on \(\ell\)-diverse releases. A custodian who checks only its own table cannot account for releases it does not know about.
That points to what is wanted instead. A definition that composes says: if release A leaks at most this much and release B at most that much, together they leak at most a known function of the two. It must also hold whatever the adversary knows, since another release is just auxiliary information. The next part starts from these two requirements.
The model understates the risk. It draws the other members of a class from the whole population. In real releases a class collects similar people (similar ages, here) who are more likely to share a diagnosis, so each class contains fewer distinct wrong values and the intersection is smaller than the model predicts.
The union bound is useful only for small classes. It charges every wrong value separately, so it is accurate when two wrong values rarely turn up in both classes at once. At \(k = 2\) each class has a single other member, so it holds at most one wrong value, two wrong values can never turn up together, and the bound is exact. At \(k = 5\) the expected number of shared wrong values exceeds 1, the bound is negative, and Equation 16.10 is needed.


16.6.5 Example: two hospitals
In the model, with \(p\) the population’s diagnosis distribution, from which the hospital table is drawn, the probability that two releases pin down the diagnosis is 0.8734 for classes of 2, 0.1615 for classes of 5, 0.0288 for classes of 7 and 0.0015 for classes of 10. It falls fast because a larger class contains more wrong values, and each one is another chance for the two classes to share one. Simulation agrees to within 0.001 (Figure 16.4, left). The union bound gives 0.8734 at \(k = 2\) and is negative from \(k = 5\) on.
The script then runs the attack. A city has 15,000 people drawn from the model of the hospital table. Two hospitals each treat a random 10,000 of them, so 6,649 people are treated at both. Each hospital publishes a 5-anonymous Mondrian release of its own patients. Table 16.7 gives what the adversary learns about the 6,649.

For comparison, in the single-table release of Table 16.3 at \(k = 5\) a patient’s class has 6.8 records on average over patients, and the model at \(k = 7\) predicts only 2.9%: real classes, which group patients of similar age, are more alike than random draws, as the interpretation above said. 16.6.6 Check yourself

Two releases are each 3-diverse in the distinct sense, over 8 possible values. If each class’s two other values were chosen uniformly at random from the 7 wrong ones, how likely is the intersection to pin down the truth? (\(\binom52/\binom72 = 10/21 = 0.476\): the second class must avoid both of the first class’s wrong values, so its two wrong values must come from the other 5. Exercise 4 derives it.)
Why can’t the second hospital prevent the attack by checking its own release more carefully? (The attack needs only that the two classes share no wrong value. The second hospital would need to know the first hospital’s classes, and every other release the patient appears in.)

16.7 Code: anonymize, then attack
The script code/syntactic_anonymity.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. It implements Mondrian with any criterion on a class (k-anonymity, distinct and recursive l-diversity, t-closeness in total variation), the uniform-cells calculation, the attacks on the sensitive attribute, and the composition attack, exactly by inclusion–exclusion, by simulation and on two synthetic hospital releases. uv run python code/part02-attacks/syntactic_anonymity.py

In practice, a census extract would be k-anonymized with ARX, a free anonymization tool that implements these criteria, and then linked back to a public table. The script’s Mondrian release plays the part of ARX, and its linkage column is that measurement: the re-identification rate against an adversary holding everyone’s quasi-identifiers, the strongest auxiliary table there can be.
What to take from it. k-anonymity does what it says: linkage success stays below \(1/k\), and Mondrian keeps it above \(1/(2k)\) at little cost in precision. But what it says is not enough, because small classes state diagnoses outright, for 2.3% of patients at \(k = 5\). Even where nothing is stated outright, most of what an anonymized table teaches is about the population, so measure attribute disclosure against imputation, not against guessing the most common value. Each fix costs utility: recursive diversity and t-closeness remove the certain disclosures by erasing the age–diagnosis pattern the data exist to show. And two releases are worse than one, under every definition here. The composition attack more than triples the pinned diagnoses, and it is the attack that a better definition has to survive.

text:
16.8 References

Samarati & Sweeney, “Protecting Privacy when Disclosing Information: k-Anonymity and Its Enforcement through Generalization and Suppression” (SRI technical report, 1998), and Sweeney, “k-Anonymity: A Model for Protecting Privacy” (International Journal of Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-Based Systems, 2002): the definition, generalization and suppression, and the linkage attack it answers.
LeFevre, DeWitt & Ramakrishnan, “Mondrian Multidimensional k-Anonymity” (ICDE, 2006): the median-split algorithm the script uses, and why multidimensional recoding loses less than one generalization per column.
Machanavajjhala, Kifer, Gehrke & Venkitasubramaniam, “l-Diversity: Privacy Beyond k-Anonymity” (ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data, 2007; ICDE 2006): the homogeneity and background knowledge attacks, and the three versions of l-diversity with their Bayesian justification.
Li, Li & Venkatasubramanian, “t-Closeness: Privacy Beyond k-Anonymity and l-Diversity” (ICDE, 2007): the skewness and similarity attacks, and the earth mover’s distance with ordered and hierarchical ground distances.
Ganta, Kasiviswanathan & Smith, “Composition Attacks and Auxiliary Information in Data Privacy” (KDD, 2008): the intersection attack on independent releases, experiments on public census data, and the argument that a definition must hold up against auxiliary information such as other releases.
Aggarwal, “On k-Anonymity and the Curse of Dimensionality” (VLDB, 2005): why high-dimensional data cannot be k-anonymized without destroying it.
Prasser, Kohlmayer and colleagues, the ARX data anonymization tool (arx.deidentifier.org): an open implementation of these criteria and many more, with risk models and utility measures.
Article 29 Working Party, “Opinion 05/2014 on Anonymisation Techniques”: how European regulators judge these techniques against singling out, linkability and inference, the three attacks of this chapter.

Rules of thumb

k-anonymity protects names, not attributes. Ask what a class’s sensitive values reveal, not just how big it is.
Measure attribute disclosure against imputation from the population, or you will count the study’s findings as leaks.
A rare sensitive value needs a bound on the ratio of beliefs, not on their difference.
