title: Differential privacy foundations
text:
How to read this part
Order. Chapters 18 to 21 are the core and should be read in order: the definition, the properties that make it usable, the two mechanisms everything else is built from, and advanced and optimal composition, which finishes the story of composition that chapter 19 starts and introduces the privacy loss random variable that the next part uses throughout. Chapter 22 adds mechanisms for selection, and chapter 23 builds on them to answer many queries at once, by releasing synthetic data with private multiplicative weights. Chapter 24 handles data whose worst case is far from typical. Chapter 25 is short and practical: read it before you implement any mechanism yourself. Chapter 26 changes who is trusted with the raw data. Chapter 27 is the most theoretical; it ties back to reconstruction and membership attacks and says what privacy must cost. Chapter 28 closes the part by putting these tools together on the most common statistical task, estimating a mean, and matches each of its error rates with a lower bound from chapter 27.
Structure of a chapter. Every chapter has the same shape as in the earlier parts: why it matters, a toolkit, one section per result with a statement, derivation, interpretation, worked example and two check yourself questions, then code, references and a cheat sheet. Exercises with worked solutions are collected in the exercise book, a companion website, with a link at the end of each chapter.
Proofs you can check by computer. Most privacy claims in this part are checked numerically as well as proved: the exact privacy profile of a mechanism is computed and compared with its bound, a composition formula is compared with brute-force enumeration, and a buggy mechanism is shown to leak by computing its privacy loss. Running the scripts is the fastest way to see how loose each bound is. From the repository root, for example,
uv run python code/part03-dp-foundations/laplace_gaussian.py

title: Differential privacy foundations
section: What you will be able to do

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.1 Neighbouring datasets
Each attack of Part 2 was a game in which the challenger ran an algorithm on one of two datasets that differ in one person, and the adversary guessed which (Threat models and privacy games). Each worked because a test could tell the two datasets apart from the output. Differential privacy (DP) forbids exactly that: for every pair of datasets that differ in one person, the distribution of the output barely changes. Then every attack of Part 2 fails at once, whatever the adversary knows and computes.
The one idea is the privacy loss. For one output of a randomized algorithm, it is the logarithm of how much more likely that output was under one dataset than under its neighbour, the log-likelihood ratio of Divergences. Differential privacy bounds it. Pure DP bounds it at every output, and approximate DP lets it exceed the bound on outputs of small total probability \(\delta\). Every later result is that bound read through a tool of Part 1.
The running example is a survey. Alice, Bob and Carol are asked whether they smoke, and each answers with two coins. On heads they tell the truth, and on tails they toss again and say “yes” on heads and “no” on tails. So each person tells the truth with probability \(\frac34\), and every “yes” has an excuse. This survey is \(\ln 3\)-DP, as Section 18.3 shows. A count released with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2 is the contrast case, because its privacy loss is unbounded and it needs a \(\delta\).
“Differ in one person” needs a precise meaning before anything can be proved. A dataset \(D\) is a multiset of records drawn from a universe \(\mathcal X\) of possible records. The neighbouring relation says which pairs of datasets the guarantee must protect, and so it fixes the unit of privacy, the thing whose presence or value the output must not reveal.
Add/remove protects participation, which is the question membership inference asks. Replace protects the value of your record and treats the dataset size as known. Separately, you choose what one record is. At example-level a record is one row, and at user-level it is all the data of one person, so example-level DP on 200 messages from one user protects each message, not the user. Neighbours also range over absurd records, such as a person aged 900, which is why mechanisms bound their inputs before adding noise.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
Definition 18.1 (Neighbouring datasets) Datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), in one of two senses, which every guarantee must name.

Add/remove (also called unbounded DP): \(D'\) is \(D\) with one record added or removed. The size \(n\) of the dataset is itself private.
Replace (also called bounded DP, or substitution): \(|D| = |D'|\), and they differ in the value of one record. The size \(n\) is public.

Both relations are symmetric: if \(D \sim D'\) then \(D' \sim D\).

crumbs: 18  The definition of differential privacy

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.2 Pure and approximate differential privacy
“The output distribution barely changes” needs a measure. An average such as the Kullback–Leibler divergence can hide one rare output with an enormous loss. A difference such as the total variation (TV) distance adds up along a chain of \(n\) replacements, so no single tolerance is both useful and private (Exercise 8). Differential privacy therefore bounds a ratio, in the worst case over every pair and every event, and allows a small difference only on top. Section A.1 in the appendices derives the definition’s forms from scratch.
Write \(M\) for a mechanism, a randomized algorithm that maps a dataset to a random output in a set \(\mathcal Y\). The probability that the output lands in an event \(S \subseteq \mathcal Y\) is taken over the mechanism’s own coins.

Definition 18.2 (Differential privacy) A mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private, for \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) and \(\delta \in [0, 1]\), if for every pair of neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and every event \(S \subseteq \mathcal Y\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{18.1}\] Because the neighbouring relation is symmetric, the inequality also holds with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped. The case \(\delta = 0\) is pure DP, written \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The case \(\delta > 0\) is approximate DP (Dwork, Kenthapadi, McSherry, Mironov & Naor, 2006).

The definition bounds events because an adversary’s decision rule, “say \(D'\) when the output is in \(S\)”, is an event. The dataset is fixed and the randomness is the mechanism’s own, so privacy comes only from added noise. A deterministic algorithm that is not constant fails the definition for every \(\delta < 1\) (Exercise 9), so rounding or suppressing small cells gives no guarantee by itself.
The privacy loss of the opening checks the definition output by output.

Definition 18.3 (Privacy loss) Write \(p_{M(D)}\) for the probability mass function or density of \(M(D)\). The privacy loss of an output \(y\) for the ordered pair \((D, D')\) is \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{18.2}\] It is 0 when \(y\) is equally likely in both worlds, large when \(y\) is strong evidence for \(D\), and infinite when \(y\) is impossible under \(D'\).

Pure DP can be checked one output at a time, because grouping outcomes into an event can only dilute the worst ratio. Approximate DP cannot, because the slack \(\delta\) is paid once per event, not once per outcome.

Proposition 18.1 (Pure DP is pointwise, approximate DP is not) Let \(M\) have a discrete output set. Then \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP if and only if \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) for every neighbouring pair and every output \(y\), and for densities the same holds at almost every \(y\). For \(\delta > 0\), \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP implies the pointwise bound \[p_{M(D)}(y) \le e^\varepsilon p_{M(D')}(y) + \delta \quad\text{for every } y, \tag{18.3}\] but the pointwise bound does not imply \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. The plan is to show that events and outcomes say the same thing when \(\delta = 0\), then to see the slack add up over the outcomes of an event when \(\delta > 0\).

Events imply outcomes. A single outcome is an event, so taking \(S = \{y\}\) in Equation 18.1 gives the pointwise bound. With \(\delta = 0\), together with the same bound for the swapped pair, this is \(|L_{D,D'}(y)| \le \varepsilon\).
Outcomes imply events when \(\delta = 0\). An event’s probability is the sum of the probabilities of its outcomes, so summing the pointwise bound over \(y \in S\) gives \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] = \sum_{y \in S}p_{M(D)}(y) \le e^\varepsilon\sum_{y \in S}p_{M(D')}(y) = e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S]. \tag{18.4}\] For densities, changing the density on a set of probability zero changes no event’s probability, which is why almost every \(y\) is enough.
Outcomes do not imply events when \(\delta > 0\). Each of the \(|S|\) outcomes of an event brings its own \(\delta\), so summing the pointwise bound over \(S\) gives only \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + |S|\,\delta. \tag{18.5}\]
A counterexample. Let \(M(D)\) be uniform on \(\{1, \dots, m\}\) and \(M(D')\) uniform on \(\{m + 1, \dots, 2m\}\). Every outcome has probability at most \(1/m\), so the pointwise bound holds with \(\delta = 1/m\). But the event \(\{1, \dots, m\}\) has probability 1 under \(M(D)\) and 0 under \(M(D')\), so Equation 18.1 needs \(\delta = 1\). With \(m = 1000\) the chapter’s script (Section 18.11) finds a pointwise \(\delta\) of 0.0010 and an event \(\delta\) of 1.0000.


For small \(\varepsilon\) the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) is about \(1 + \varepsilon\), so every event changes probability by at most about a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of itself. Along a chain of datasets or releases the factors multiply and the exponents add, which is how group privacy and composition work in Post-processing, group privacy and composition. At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), an event of probability 0.5 under \(M(D')\) has probability at most \(0.5e^{0.1} = 0.553\) under \(M(D)\), while at \(\varepsilon = 1\) the bound is 1.36 and says nothing.
In Figure 18.1, Laplace noise keeps the density on \(D\) inside the band that pure DP allows, while Gaussian noise leaves it in the tail, where \(\delta\) must pay.






Figure 18.1: The band from \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) to \(e^\varepsilon\) times the density on \(D'\) (orange), at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: Laplace noise keeps the density on \(D\) (blue) inside. Right: Gaussian noise (\(\sigma = 2\)) leaves it in the tail, and the red mass is what \(\delta\) covers.



The chain of factors also converts between the neighbouring relations, because a replace neighbour is two add/remove steps away.

Proposition 18.2 (From add/remove to replace) If \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove, then it is \(2\varepsilon\)-DP under replace: \[\varepsilon\text{-DP under add/remove} \implies 2\varepsilon\text{-DP under replace}. \tag{18.6}\] The converse fails: a mechanism can be \(0\)-DP under replace and not \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove for any \(\varepsilon\).


Proof. 

Build the two-step path. Let \(D \sim D'\) under replace, with \(D\) holding the record \(x\) where \(D'\) holds \(x'\), and let \(D_0 = D \setminus \{x\}\). Then \(D\) and \(D_0\) differ by one removal, and \(D_0\) and \(D'\) by one addition.
Chain the ratio bound along the path. Pure DP bounds each step by a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), so applying it to \((D, D_0)\) and then to \((D_0, D')\) gives, for every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D_0) \in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S]. \tag{18.7}\] Walking the path from \(D'\) back to \(D\) gives the other order.
The counterexample for the converse. Let \(M\) output the number of records. It is \(0\)-DP under replace, because datasets of the same size give the same output. Under add/remove, the event \(\{n + 1\}\) has probability 1 on a dataset of \(n + 1\) records and 0 on its neighbour, and no finite \(e^\varepsilon\) times 0 reaches 1.


The factor 2 is reached when one replacement changes two counts, as changing Alice’s answer does in the survey’s histogram (smokers, non-smokers). With Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) in each bin, the script finds largest losses of 1.0000 under add/remove and 2.0000 under replace at \(\varepsilon = 1\). For approximate DP the same path gives \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\) (Exercise 2).

Example 18.2 In the survey, take the true bits \((1, 0, 1)\) for Alice, Bob and Carol and the replace neighbour \((0, 0, 1)\). The script checks all 256 events of the 8 report vectors. The largest ratio over events is 3.0000, the same as over single outcomes, as Proposition 18.1 says. Every replace pair gives the same, so the survey is \(\ln 3\)-DP under replace and no better, and Theorem 18.1 shows why only Alice’s coins matter.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.3 Randomized response
You want the fraction of people who have done something embarrassing, but asked directly, people lie. Warner (1965) found the answer four decades before the definition. Each respondent tells the truth only with a known probability, so every “yes” has an excuse, yet the randomization averages out over the population. The two coins of the running example are the forced-response variant credited to Boruch (1971). Section A.4 in the appendices derives the mechanism from scratch.
The idea is to tell the truth with a probability \(t\) a little above \(\frac12\), so that the ratio \(t/(1 - t)\) of the chances of a report under the two true bits is \(e^\varepsilon\).

Definition 18.4 (Randomized response) Randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) reports a person’s bit \(x \in \{0, 1\}\) truthfully with probability \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flipped with probability \(1 - t\). On a dataset of \(n\) bits it is applied to each person independently, and the output is the vector of \(n\) reports.

With two coins, a respondent tells the truth on heads, or on tails when the second coin gives the true answer, so \(t = \frac34\), \(t/(1 - t) = 3\), and the survey is randomized response at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3 = 1.0986\) (Table 18.2).

Write \(\bar x\) for the true fraction of ones and \(\bar y\) for the mean of the reports. The coins push \(\bar y\) toward \(\frac12\) in a known way, and undoing the push scales up the noise by \(1/(2t - 1)\).

Theorem 18.1 (Privacy and accuracy of randomized response) Randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) on \(n\) people is \(\varepsilon\)-DP under replace. The estimate \[\hat{\bar x} = \frac{\bar y - (1 - t)}{2t - 1} \tag{18.8}\] of the true fraction is unbiased, and its standard deviation is \[\operatorname{sd}(\hat{\bar x}) = \frac{\sqrt{t(1 - t)}}{(2t - 1)\sqrt n} = \frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt n} \approx \frac{1}{\varepsilon\sqrt n}\quad\text{for small }\varepsilon. \tag{18.9}\]


Proof. The plan is to read one person’s privacy off Table 18.2, to show that the other people cancel out of the likelihood ratio, and then to compute the mean and the variance of the estimate.

One person. Every ratio between the two rows of Table 18.2 is \(e^\varepsilon\) or its inverse, so the privacy loss of each report is \(\pm\varepsilon\), and one report is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by Proposition 18.1.
The output distribution factors. People toss their own coins independently, so the probability of a report vector is a product of one factor per person, \(\prod_i p_i(y_i \mid x_i)\), where \(p_i(y_i \mid x_i)\) is the chance that person \(i\) reports \(y_i\) when their true bit is \(x_i\).
Neighbours differ in one factor. Under replace, \(D\) and \(D'\) differ only in person \(j\)’s bit, so every other factor cancels in the ratio. The loss is person \(j\)’s alone, so it is \(\pm\varepsilon\), and the vector is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by Proposition 18.1.
The mean of the reports. A report is 1 with probability \(t\) if the true bit is 1 and \(1 - t\) if it is 0. Averaging over a population in which a fraction \(\bar x\) have bit 1 gives \[\mathbb E[\bar y] = \bar x\,t + (1 - \bar x)(1 - t) = (1 - t) + \bar x(2t - 1). \tag{18.10}\] Solving for \(\bar x\) gives Equation 18.8, which is unbiased because it is a linear function of \(\bar y\).
The spread. Each report is a Bernoulli variable with variance \(t(1 - t)\), whatever its true bit, and the reports are independent, so \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar y) = \frac{t(1 - t)}{n}. \tag{18.11}\] Dividing \(\bar y\) by \(2t - 1\) divides the variance by \((2t - 1)^2\), which gives the first form. Substituting \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) gives the closed form, because \[t(1 - t) = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{(1 + e^\varepsilon)^2}, \qquad 2t - 1 = \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{18.12}\]


Deniability is the privacy, and the noise is added before the data leave each person, the local model of Local, shuffle and distributed trust models. Under add/remove the number of reports would reveal whether you took part, so the guarantee holds under replace only.
Privacy costs samples: halving \(\varepsilon\) doubles the error, so recovering the accuracy takes four times as many people, and much of that is the price of trusting nobody. A trusted curator can instead add Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) to the true count once, which is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. Its error on the fraction, \(\sqrt2/(\varepsilon n)\), falls like \(1/n\) rather than \(1/\sqrt n\).

Example 18.3 Of \(n = 1000\) respondents, a fraction \(\bar x = 0.3\) smoke, so the expected fraction of “yes” reports is \(0.3 \times 0.75 + 0.7 \times 0.25 = 0.4\), which Equation 18.8 turns back into 0.3. The formula gives \(\operatorname{sd}(\hat{\bar x}) = \sqrt{0.1875}/(0.5\sqrt{1000}) = 0.0274\), and ten thousand simulated surveys give a mean of 0.2996 and a standard deviation of 0.0278. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the formula gives 0.0626 (Figure 18.2). A trusted curator at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) would reach \(\sqrt2/(1000\ln 3) = 0.00129\), which is 21.3 times smaller.







Figure 18.2: Left: randomized response at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) as output probabilities. Right: estimates from 4000 simulated surveys of 1000 people with true fraction 0.3, at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) and 0.5, with the normal curves the formula predicts.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.4 Divergence forms and the privacy loss
text:
18.4 Divergence forms and the privacy loss
Equation 18.1 quantifies over all events, which is unusable for continuous outputs. A divergence turns “for all events” into one formula and shows what \(\delta\) measures. The two divergences are those of Divergences. The max-divergence \(D_\infty(P\|Q) = \ln\max_y p(y)/q(y)\) is the largest privacy loss (Section 3.4). The hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma(P\|Q) = \sum_y(p(y) - \gamma q(y))_+\) is the mass of \(P\) that sticks out above \(\gamma\) times \(Q\) (Section 3.8), where \((x)_+ = \max\{x, 0\}\).

Theorem 18.2 (Differential privacy as a divergence bound) For every pair of neighbours \(D \sim D'\) write \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), with probabilities \(p(y)\) and \(q(y)\) (densities when the output is continuous, with sums read as integrals), and \(L = L_{D,D'}\).

\(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP if and only if \(D_\infty(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon\) for every ordered pair of neighbours.
\(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if and only if, for every ordered pair of neighbours, \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+ = \mathbb E_{y \sim P}\Big[\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L(y)}\big)_+\Big] \le \delta. \tag{18.13}\]
If \(\Pr_{y \sim P}[L(y) > \varepsilon] \le \delta\) for every ordered pair, then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.



Proof. The plan is to find the worst event for the definition’s difference, to rewrite the resulting sum as an average under \(P\), and to bound that average by a tail probability.

Pure DP. By Proposition 18.1, \(\varepsilon\)-DP is \(|L(y)| \le \varepsilon\) at every output and in both orders of the pair, and the largest value of \(L\) is \(D_\infty(P\|Q)\) by definition.
The worst event for a difference. The definition asks \(\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S] \le \delta\) for every event. Each outcome in \(S\) adds \(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\) to the left side, which is positive exactly when \(L(y) > \varepsilon\). So the worst event takes every outcome with a positive contribution and no other, and the definition holds for every \(S\) exactly when it holds for this one: \[\max_S\big[\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S]\big] = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+ = E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q). \tag{18.14}\]
As an average under \(P\). Factor \(p(y)\) out of each term and use \(q/p = e^{-L}\) from Equation 18.2, so that each term becomes \(p\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\). A sum of \(p(y)\) times a function of \(y\) is the average of that function under \(P\), and outcomes with \(p(y) = 0\) contribute nothing.
The sufficient condition. The weight \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\) is 0 when \(L \le \varepsilon\) and less than 1 otherwise, so it is at most the indicator \(\mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon]\). Averaging both sides under \(P\) gives \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) \le \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta. \tag{18.15}\]


So the smallest valid \(\delta\) is not the probability that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), but an average that counts an output with loss just above \(\varepsilon\) for almost nothing and an infinite loss in full. What \(\delta\) bounds exactly is the chance of a total failure. The outputs that are impossible on \(D'\) have infinite loss, and Equation 18.1 applied to them says that their total probability on \(D\) is at most \(\delta\).
A mechanism has a curve, not a pair: it is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon\) (Figure 18.3). The curve reaches 0 only if the loss is bounded. The distribution of \(L\) with \(y\) drawn from \(M(D)\) is the privacy loss distribution, which the accountants of Numerical accounting work with directly.






Figure 18.3: The smallest \(\delta\) against \(\varepsilon\) for randomized response at \(\ln 3\), the Laplace count of scale 1 and the Gaussian count with \(\sigma = 2\). Only the Gaussian curve never reaches 0. Dashed: its loose tail \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon]\).




Example 18.4 For each mechanism, add up the excess mass where the likelihood ratio exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\). For the survey only the report with ratio 3 counts, which gives \(\delta(\varepsilon) = (3 - e^\varepsilon)_+/4\) (Exercise 3), so \(\delta(0.5) = 0.3378\) and \(\delta(1) = 0.0704\). For the Laplace count, the closed form of Section 3.8 gives \(\delta(0.5) = 0.2212\) and \(\delta(1) = 0\).
For the Gaussian count, whose true value moves by 1 between neighbours, write \(\mu = 1/\sigma = 0.5\) for that shift in units of the noise. The privacy loss is normal with variance \(\mu^2\) and mean \(\mu^2/2\) under \(M(D)\), \(-\mu^2/2\) under \(M(D')\) (Section 3.5). By step 2 of the proof, \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the \(P\)-probability of \(\{L > \varepsilon\}\) minus \(e^\varepsilon\) times its \(Q\)-probability, and standardizing the loss with the standard normal distribution function \(\Phi\) gives \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{18.16}\] Table 18.3 compares it with the tail, the first term alone.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.5 The hypothesis-testing interpretation
A membership attacker is a test that sees the output and decides between “the data were \(D\)” and “the data were \(D'\)”. Hypothesis testing described the best achievable pairs of error rates by the trade-off function. Differential privacy is exactly a lower bound on that function, uniform over all neighbours (Wasserman & Zhou, 2010; Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, 2015), and Section D.1 in the appendices derives it from scratch.
Let a test say “\(D'\)” on the event \(S\). Its false positive rate (FPR) is \(\alpha = \Pr[M(D) \in S]\), and its false negative rate (FNR) is \(\beta = \Pr[M(D') \notin S]\). A randomized test says “\(D'\)” with probability \(\phi(y) \in [0, 1]\) after seeing \(y\) (Section 4.3).

Theorem 18.3 (Differential privacy as a bound on every test) \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if and only if every test, randomized or not, for every pair of neighbours, satisfies \[\alpha + e^\varepsilon \beta \ge 1 - \delta \qquad\text{and}\qquad e^\varepsilon \alpha + \beta \ge 1 - \delta. \tag{18.17}\] Equivalently, the trade-off function of every pair of neighbours lies above \[f_{\varepsilon,\delta}(\alpha) = \max\big\{0,\ 1 - \delta - e^\varepsilon \alpha,\ e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \alpha)\big\}. \tag{18.18}\] In terms of the true positive rate (TPR) \(1 - \beta\), the second inequality reads \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon \alpha + \delta\).


Proof. The plan is to apply the definition to the complement of \(S\) and to the swapped pair, to extend both bounds to randomized tests, and to read them backwards for the converse.

The first inequality. Apply Equation 18.1 to the pair \((D, D')\) and the complement \(S^c\), on which the test says “\(D\)”. The left side is \(1 - \alpha\) and the probability on the right is \(\beta\), so \[1 - \alpha \le e^\varepsilon \beta + \delta. \tag{18.19}\]
The second inequality. Apply Equation 18.1 to the swapped pair \((D', D)\) and the event \(S\). The left side is then \(1 - \beta\) and the probability on the right is \(\alpha\).
Randomized tests. A test \(\phi\) is not an event, but the gap \(\mathbb E_{M(D)}[\phi] - e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_{M(D')}[\phi]\) is linear in each \(\phi(y)\), with coefficient \(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\). So it is largest at the worst event of Theorem 18.2, and at most \(\delta\), and steps 1 and 2 go through with \(\phi\) and \(1 - \phi\) in place of the events.
The converse. Every event is a test, so if Equation 18.17 holds for all tests, steps 1 and 2 read backwards give Equation 18.1.
The trade-off form. Solved for \(\beta\), the two inequalities give two lower bounds on \(\beta\), and \(\beta \ge 0\) is a third, so the smallest \(\beta\) at level \(\alpha\) is at least the largest of the three.


The result draws a forbidden region: every attack lies on or above the two lines of Equation 18.17 (Figure 18.4). Low FPR is where DP bites. Part 2 judged membership attacks by their TPR at a low FPR, which DP caps at \(e^\varepsilon \alpha + \delta\), and as \(\alpha \to 0\) the \(\delta\) term dominates.
Auditing runs this in reverse. Solving the cap for \(\varepsilon\) at an attack’s measured FPR and TPR gives the smallest \(\varepsilon\) consistent with the measurement. The neighbouring pair is a training set with and without a canary, a record planted to be easy to detect (Memorization and extraction). The bound is tight for randomized response and loose for most mechanisms, and keeping a mechanism’s whole trade-off curve is the idea of \(f\)-DP in Gaussian differential privacy.






Figure 18.4: Left: the region below \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) that no test can enter, for \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) and for \(\varepsilon = 1\) with \(\delta = 0\) and 0.05. Right: the largest TPR against FPR at \(\varepsilon = 1\), with the best TPR against the Gaussian count.




Example 18.5 In the survey, the best test says “\(D'\)” when Alice reports 0. Its FPR and FNR are both 0.25, so \(\alpha + 3\beta = 1\), the corner of the region.
The Gaussian count is \((1, 0.00683)\)-DP, so at FPR \(10^{-3}\) the bound allows TPR up to \(e \times 10^{-3} + 0.00683 = 0.0095\), against 0.002728 under \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The best test thresholds \(y\) (Neyman–Pearson), and the Gaussian trade-off curve of Section 4.6 gives its TPR as \(1 - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(0.999) - 0.5) = 0.0048\).

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.6 Bound on the membership advantage
Part 2 measured a membership attacker by its advantage. In the membership game the challenger flips a fair coin to pick \(D\) or \(D'\) and runs \(M\) on it, and the adversary guesses which. The advantage is \(2\Pr[\text{correct}] - 1\), which with a fair coin equals \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \alpha - \beta\) (Section 4.8). So the adversary wants the smallest sum of errors, and the lines of Equation 18.17 keep it away from the origin.

Corollary 18.1 (Membership advantage) If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, every adversary in the membership game between any two neighbours has \[\mathrm{Adv} = \mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}, \qquad \Pr[\text{correct}] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon + \delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{18.20}\] For \(\delta = 0\) the bound is \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), about \(\varepsilon/2\) for small \(\varepsilon\), and randomized response attains it. The bound also holds when the game draws the dataset at random before the coin flip.


Proof. The plan is to turn the advantage into a sum of error rates, to find the smallest sum over the region that Theorem 18.3 allows, and to check that randomized response sits at the corner.

Turn the advantage into a sum of errors. The advantage is \(1 - (\alpha + \beta)\), so the largest advantage comes from the smallest \(\alpha + \beta\) allowed by Equation 18.17 with \(\alpha, \beta \ge 0\).
Draw the feasible region. Its lower boundary has corners where the two lines meet the axes, at \((0, 1 - \delta)\) and \((1 - \delta, 0)\), and where they cross, at \(\alpha = \beta = (1 - \delta)/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).
Check the corners. A linear function such as \(\alpha + \beta\) changes at a constant rate along a straight edge, so its smallest value is at a corner. At the first two corners \(\alpha + \beta = 1 - \delta\), and the crossing point is smaller because \(e^\varepsilon \ge 1\): \[\alpha + \beta = \frac{2(1 - \delta)}{1 + e^\varepsilon} \le 1 - \delta. \tag{18.21}\]
Compute the advantage. One minus the smallest sum is \[1 - \frac{2(1 - \delta)}{1 + e^\varepsilon} = \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}, \tag{18.22}\] and \(\Pr[\text{correct}] = \frac12 + \frac12\mathrm{Adv}\) gives the second bound. Multiplying the top and bottom of the \(\delta = 0\) bound by \(e^{-\varepsilon/2}\) turns it into \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\).
Tightness and random datasets. Against randomized response, the test “say \(D'\) on report 0” has \(\alpha = \beta = 1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), the crossing point, so it attains the bound. A bound that holds for each fixed pair also holds for an average over random pairs.


Small \(\varepsilon\) is strong and large \(\varepsilon\) promises little. At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the best attacker is right with probability at most 0.525, while at \(\varepsilon = 5\) it may be right 99.3% of the time. The older bound \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) (Yeom et al., 2018) is about twice as large and says nothing once \(e^\varepsilon \ge 2\). A count with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) has best advantage \(1 - e^{-\varepsilon/2}\), from Section 3.8, which stays below \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) (Figure 18.5; Exercise 7 measures the gap).






Figure 18.5: The largest membership advantage under \(\varepsilon\)-DP (black), the looser bound \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) (dotted) and the exact best advantage against the Laplace count (orange). Markers: 100,000 simulated games with the likelihood-ratio adversary.

In 200,000 games with the likelihood-ratio adversary, which guesses \(D\) when the privacy loss is positive, the script measures 0.4624 against randomized response (exact 0.4621) and 0.3953 against the Laplace count (exact 0.3935) at \(\varepsilon = 1\).

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.7 The Bayesian interpretation
People often ask a different question: after seeing the output, how sure can someone be about me? Bayes’ rule in odds form (Section 4.10) says that the posterior odds are the prior odds times the likelihood ratio, which for an output \(y\) is \(e^{L_{D,D'}(y)}\). So a bound on the privacy loss is a bound on how far any belief can move, whatever the prior (Kasiviswanathan & Smith, 2014). Section D.2 in the appendices derives it with a two-hypothesis table.
Take an adversary who knows that the data are \(D\) or \(D'\) and gives \(D\) the prior probability \(\pi\). Under approximate DP, outputs whose loss exceeds a level \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\) are rare, because each adds a fixed fraction of its probability to the excess that \(\delta\) bounds.

Theorem 18.4 (What one output does to a belief) If \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then after any output \(y\), \[e^{-\varepsilon}\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi} \le \frac{\Pr[D \mid y]}{\Pr[D' \mid y]} \le e^\varepsilon\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}, \qquad \Pr[D \mid y] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon\pi}{e^\varepsilon\pi + 1 - \pi}. \tag{18.23}\] If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then for every \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\) the upper bounds hold with \(\varepsilon'\) in place of \(\varepsilon\) for every output except those in the set \(B = \{y : L_{D,D'}(y) > \varepsilon'\}\), which has \[\Pr_{y \sim M(D)}[y \in B] \le \frac{\delta}{1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}}. \tag{18.24}\]


Proof. The plan is to write the posterior odds as prior odds times \(e^L\), to bound \(e^L\) under pure DP, and then to show that the outputs where \(L\) is large are rare under approximate DP.

Odds. By Bayes’ rule, \(\Pr[D \mid y]\) is \(\pi\,p_{M(D)}(y)\) divided by the overall probability of \(y\), and the same holds for \(D'\) with the same denominator. The ratio cancels it and leaves the prior odds times \(e^{L_{D,D'}(y)}\).
Pure DP. By Proposition 18.1, \(e^{L}\) lies between \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) and \(e^\varepsilon\), and multiplying the prior odds by these extremes gives the odds bound.
From odds to a probability. Odds \(o\) convert to the probability \(o/(1 + o)\), which increases with \(o\). Taking \(o = e^\varepsilon\pi/(1 - \pi)\) and multiplying top and bottom by \(1 - \pi\) gives the bound on \(\Pr[D \mid y]\).
The bad set is rare. Write \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), and apply Equation 18.1 to \(B\): \[\Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B] \le \delta. \tag{18.25}\] On \(B\) the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon'\), so \(q < e^{-\varepsilon'}p\) and \(\Pr_Q[B] < e^{-\varepsilon'}\Pr_P[B]\). Putting this larger quantity in place of \(\Pr_Q[B]\) makes the left side smaller, which leaves \[\Pr_P[B]\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}\big) < \delta, \tag{18.26}\] and the factor is positive because \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\).
Outside the bad set. There the loss is at most \(\varepsilon'\), and steps 1 to 3 with \(\varepsilon'\) in place of \(\varepsilon\) give the upper bounds.


DP bounds the change in belief, not the belief, so an adversary who is already 99% sure stays about that sure. Against adversaries who do not know every other record, the same bound holds relative to the posterior computed without the person’s record (Kasiviswanathan & Smith, 2014).






Figure 18.6: The largest (solid) and smallest (dashed) posterior after one output of an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism, against the prior, for four values of \(\varepsilon\). Even at \(\varepsilon = 3\) a prior of 0.01 rises only to 0.169.




Example 18.7 In the survey, the interviewer knows every answer but Alice’s and gives a 50% chance that she smokes. Her “yes” is 3 times as likely from a true “yes”, so the posterior odds are at most 3 and the interviewer is at most 75% sure. From a prior of 1%, the posterior is at most 0.0294 (Table 18.5).

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.8 Why δ must be much smaller than 1/n
text:
18.8 Why δ must be much smaller than 1/n
How small must \(\delta\) be? The advantage bound barely notices a small \(\delta\), but a deliberately terrible mechanism shows the danger. It is DP with \(\varepsilon = 0\) and yet publishes records verbatim, because over a whole dataset its small chances add up.

Proposition 18.3 (Release each record with probability δ) The mechanism that publishes each record of the dataset, in full, independently with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP under add/remove. On a dataset of \(n\) records it publishes \(n\delta\) records on average, and at least one record with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}, \tag{18.27}\] so \(\delta = 1/n\) exposes someone with probability about \(1 - e^{-1} = 0.632\).


Proof. The plan is to run the mechanism on \(D\) and on \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\) with the same coins, so that the outputs differ only through one extra coin, and then to count the exposures.

Couple the two runs. Run the mechanism on \(D'\) by first running it on \(D\) and then tossing one more coin for \(x\). The two outputs are equal unless that coin publishes \(x\), which happens with probability \(\delta\).
Bound one direction. The output on \(D'\) lands in an event \(S\) either because the output on \(D\) did or because the extra coin changed it, so \[\Pr[M(D') \in S] \le \Pr[M(D) \in S] + \delta. \tag{18.28}\]
Bound the other direction. With probability \(1 - \delta\) the extra coin does nothing, and a probability is at most 1, so \[\Pr[M(D') \in S] \ge (1 - \delta)\Pr[M(D) \in S] \ge \Pr[M(D) \in S] - \delta. \tag{18.29}\] Both directions match Equation 18.1 with factor \(e^0 = 1\) and slack \(\delta\).
Count the exposures. The number of records published is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, \delta)\), with mean \(n\delta\), and none is published with probability \((1 - \delta)^n\). For small \(\delta\), \(\ln(1 - \delta) \approx -\delta\), which gives \[(1 - \delta)^n = e^{n\ln(1 - \delta)} \approx e^{-n\delta}. \tag{18.30}\]


So \(\delta\) is a per-person budget for catastrophe. Pick it well below \(1/n\), with \(n\) the number of people rather than records. A common choice is \(\delta = 1/n^{1.5}\), and fixed values need checking: Abadi et al. (2016) used \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for 60,000 training examples, so \(n\delta = 0.6\).
One pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) can describe mechanisms that fail in very different ways (Figure 18.7). The Gaussian count with \(\sigma = 2\) is \((1, 6.830\times10^{-3})\)-DP, and its loss exceeds 3 with probability \(4.462\times10^{-9}\). Publishing a person’s bit with probability \(6.830\times10^{-3}\), and otherwise running randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\), gives the same pair, with the whole \(\delta\) on outputs of infinite loss (Exercise 10). From the pair alone, Equation 18.24 at level 3 allows \[\Pr[L > 3] \le \frac{6.830\times10^{-3}}{1 - e^{1 - 3}} = 7.899\times10^{-3}, \tag{18.31}\] and the catastrophic mechanism comes close to it. So read a quoted pair pessimistically unless you know the whole curve \(\delta(\varepsilon)\).






Figure 18.7: The tail \(\Pr[L > c]\) of two \((1, 0.0068)\)-DP mechanisms on a log scale. Blue: the Gaussian count, whose tail falls fast. Red: publish the bit with probability \(\delta\), else randomized response; its tail stays at \(\delta\). Dotted: the largest tail the pair allows, from Equation 18.24.




Example 18.8 With \(n = 3\) and \(\delta = 0.1\) the script enumerates every output on \(D\) and on \(D \cup \{x\}\) and finds a largest gap over events of 0.1000, so the mechanism is \((0, 0.1)\)-DP and no better. title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
section: 18.9 What differential privacy does not protect
text:
18.9 What differential privacy does not protect
The definition compares two worlds that differ in one record, not the world before and after the release. Kifer & Machanavajjhala (2011) showed that no definition can block every inference without assumptions on how the data were generated. Four limits matter in practice.
Population inference. Suppose the cancer rate among smokers is 0.1 or 0.3, equally likely, so your belief that Alice, a smoker, will get cancer is 0.2. A study that excludes her reveals the rate 0.3, and your belief rises to 0.3. Yet the study never saw her record, so nothing happened to her because she took part.
Correlated records. If \(k\) records move together, as in a household, their joint privacy loss can reach \(k\varepsilon\), so the unit of privacy must match the unit of correlation.
Everything outside the mathematical mechanism. Floating-point leaks (Discrete and floating-point-safe mechanisms), timing side channels and other releases need separate care.
Tasks about one person. Contact tracing must find whom one infected person met, so its output must depend on that person, which DP forbids. DP protects your contribution, not secrets that other people’s data reveal.

Example 18.9 A count with Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) meets a household of \(k = 5\) people who always answer alike. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the script finds a largest privacy loss of 5.0000 for the household, which is protected only as if by a 5-DP mechanism. The exact best advantage against it is \(1 - e^{-5/2} = 0.9179\), under the bound 0.9866. An attacker who asks whether the household took part is right with probability up to 0.959, although each record is “protected at \(\varepsilon = 1\)”.

title: 18  The definition of differential privacy
text:
18.10 Is it a privacy violation?
Some reported privacy failures show that a release reveals something about the people whose data it used, and others that it reveals something true about the world, which then applies to particular people. DP is designed to stop only the first kind. Three questions, taught in Kamath’s course on private data analysis, sort a claim into one kind or the other.

Does it depend on this person’s record? DP bounds an inference’s probability by \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability without the record, plus \(\delta\), so it has nothing against an inference that is as likely without the record.
Does the inference succeed exactly when the model is accurate? Then it comes from patterns shared by many records, and blocking it is a decision not to learn.
When, and by whom, was the information given up? An inference from what the person disclosed elsewhere, such as her purchases, is the same whether or not her record was used.

The first question decides, and the other two explain a no. To measure a claimed attack, compare its success on members with its success on non-members, because only the excess can be a privacy loss (Attribute inference). An inference that is no violation can still be unacceptable, since norms of information flow (Nissenbaum, 2004) cover far more than DP.

Example 18.10 Train a regression model on points that all lie on the line \(y = x + 1\), among them \((2.7, 3.7)\). Asked about \(x = 2.7\) it answers the training label 3.7, which looks like a leak. But without that point the line and the answer stay the same, so the first question says no. Table 18.7 applies the test to four well-known cases.

18.13 References

Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (TCC 2006; journal version in the Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, 2016). The original definition of pure DP, with sensitivity and the Laplace mechanism.
Dwork, Kenthapadi, McSherry, Mironov & Naor, “Our Data, Ourselves: Privacy via Distributed Noise Generation” (EUROCRYPT 2006). Introduces approximate \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), ch. 2: the definition, randomized response, what DP promises and does not (§2.3), and the “release a random record” argument for small \(\delta\). The standard reference for this whole chapter.
Warner, “Randomized Response: A Survey Technique for Eliminating Evasive Answer Bias” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 1965). The original spinner design, which answers truthfully with a known probability, and its estimator.
Boruch, “Assuring Confidentiality of Responses in Social Research: A Note on Strategies” (The American Sociologist, 1971). The forced-response design, of which the two-coin protocol is an instance.
Vadhan, “The Complexity of Differential Privacy” (2017), §1.6. Why a purely additive (total variation) definition cannot be both useful and private.
Wasserman & Zhou, “A Statistical Framework for Differential Privacy” (Journal of the American Statistical Association, 2010). DP as a bound on the power of tests.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015). The hypothesis-testing characterization Equation 18.17 and its use for optimal composition (Advanced and optimal composition).
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (JRSS Series B, 2022). Trade-off functions as the privacy definition itself (\(f\)-DP); Equation 18.18 is their \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\).
Kasiviswanathan & Smith, “On the ‘Semantics’ of Differential Privacy: A Bayesian Formulation” (Journal of Privacy and Confidentiality, 2014). The posterior reading for arbitrary priors, and the bad-set argument for approximate DP.
Yeom, Giacomelli, Fredrikson & Jha, “Privacy Risk in Machine Learning: Analyzing the Connection to Overfitting” (CSF 2018). Membership advantage and the bound \(e^\varepsilon - 1\).
Kifer & Machanavajjhala, “No Free Lunch in Data Privacy” (SIGMOD 2011). Why DP cannot protect correlated data without assumptions on how it was generated.
Desfontaines & Pejó, “SoK: Differential Privacies” (PETS 2020). A map of the many variants of the definition, including the choice of neighbouring relation.
Abadi et al., “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy” (CCS 2016). Example-level DP for training neural networks, with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for 60,000 examples.
Kamath, “Algorithms for Private Data Analysis” (University of Waterloo, recorded lectures, 2020). The three-question test for privacy violations, and the catastrophic and graceful readings of \(\delta\).
Kosinski, Stillwell & Graepel, “Private Traits and Attributes Are Predictable from Digital Records of Human Behavior” (PNAS, 2013); Duhigg, “How Companies Learn Your Secrets” (New York Times Magazine, 2012). Inferences from public or volunteered data, the “not a violation” side of Table 18.7.
Narayanan & Shmatikov, “Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets” (IEEE S&P 2008); Carlini, Liu, Erlingsson, Kos & Song, “The Secret Sharer” (USENIX Security 2019). Two failures that depend on a person’s own record.
Nissenbaum, “Privacy as Contextual Integrity” (Washington Law Review, 2004). Norms of information flow, which cover far more than DP.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.1 Post-processing
You have proved that one mechanism satisfies differential privacy (DP), and now you use it: you round its output, you protect users who each contributed fifty records, and you answer a hundred queries rather than one. So three questions come up. Is a processed output still private? What does a guarantee about one record give for a group of \(k\) records? And what is the guarantee of many mechanisms run on the same data?
The answers are the three properties that make DP usable as an engineering tool. Two datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), when they differ by adding or removing one record, unless a section says otherwise. One idea organizes all three properties, the privacy loss of an output \(y\) from the definition of differential privacy, the log of how much more likely \(y\) is on \(D\) than on \(D'\): \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}. \tag{19.1}\] Here \(p_{M(D)}\) is the probability, or density, that the mechanism \(M\) gives to \(y\) on \(D\). Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the case \(\delta = 0\) of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, keeps this loss within \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\) for every output and every neighbouring pair. When you walk through several datasets, or run mechanisms whose coins (their internal randomness) are independent, likelihood ratios multiply, so privacy losses add, and that is what costs. Processing instead merges outputs and averages their likelihood ratios, which is free.
The running example is randomized response at level \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\): a person whose record is one private bit reports it truthfully with probability \(\frac34\) and flips it with probability \(\frac14\). If the bit is 1 the report 1 has probability \(\frac34\), and if it is 0 it has probability \(\frac14\), a ratio of 3, while the report 0 has the ratio \(\frac13\). So the privacy loss is \(\pm\ln 3\) on every output. The output distributions \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\) are written \(P\) and \(Q\), with mass functions or densities \(p\) and \(q\), and a sum over continuous outputs means an integral.
A private output is rarely published as is. You round a noisy count, fit a model to noisy marginals, or let an analyst decide what to do next, each time without looking at the data again. This section asks whether such processing can undo the protection. It cannot, because a processed output merges outputs, and its likelihood ratio is an average of theirs, which stays in the band \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\). For approximate DP the privacy loss is not bounded, so the proof works with events and needs one small lemma first.
In its event form, from the definition chapter, \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP says that \(\Pr_P[S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S] + \delta\) for every set \(S\) of outputs and every ordered neighbouring pair. Step 1 of the proof of post-processing turns an event about the processed output into a soft rule on the original output, one that accepts each output with some probability, and the lemma says that soft rules obey the same bound.
This is the randomized version of the worst-event argument of Divergences. The largest value of \(\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S]\) over events \(S\) is the hockey-stick divergence, \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+, \tag{19.3}\] where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\) keeps the positive parts. So \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when that divergence is at most \(\delta\) for every ordered neighbouring pair. The smallest such \(\delta\) at each \(\varepsilon\) is the privacy profile \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of \(M\), and the script computes it exactly for every mechanism in this chapter.
To cover randomized processing, describe it as a channel \(K\): \(K(z \mid y)\) is the probability that the processing outputs \(z\) when its input is \(y\). A deterministic function \(f\) is the case \(K(z \mid y) = \mathbf 1[z = f(y)]\), which is 1 when \(z = f(y)\) and 0 otherwise. The processed output on \(D\) has the distribution \(PK(z) = \sum_y p(y)K(z \mid y)\), which weights each \(y\) by how likely it is to become \(z\), and \(L^f_{D,D'}(z)\) is its privacy loss. The theorem says that processing never makes \(D\) and \(D'\) easier to tell apart.
So nothing downstream needs a new proof. A model trained on DP statistics, or a plot of them, never reads the data again and inherits the guarantee. Attackers are covered too: a membership-inference attacker of Part 2 applies a channel to \(y\), so the bounds of the definition chapter on its error rates hold for every attack. An analyst who picks the next question from earlier private answers is post-processing them, though answering that question is a new mechanism (Section 19.3; Adaptive data analysis).
Invertible processing, such as a change of units, keeps the privacy loss exactly, since nothing is averaged. Processing that merges outputs with different losses lowers it, though usually only a little. The one condition is that \(f\) must not read the data, because step 1 needed the same \(g\) under \(D\) and \(D'\). Looking up the exact count of the noisy winning category is therefore a second, non-private mechanism (Section 19.5).
crumbs: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
Lemma 19.1 (Soft tests obey the definition) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, fix a neighbouring pair with output distributions \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), and let \(g\) be any function of the output with values in \([0, 1]\). Then \[\mathbb E_P[g(Y)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_Q[g(Y)] + \delta. \tag{19.2}\]


Proof. 

Write the gap as a sum. The difference \(\mathbb E_P[g] - e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_Q[g]\) equals \(\sum_y g(y)\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)\), a sum in which each value \(g(y)\) multiplies a fixed bracket.
Push it to the extreme. The sum is largest when \(g(y) = 1\) wherever the bracket is positive and \(g(y) = 0\) wherever it is negative, because any value in between gives up part of a positive term or adds part of a negative one. That choice of \(g\) is the indicator of the event \(B = \{y : p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\}\), so the sum is at most \(\Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\).
Apply the definition to the event \(B\), which bounds \(\Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\) by \(\delta\).





Theorem 19.1 (Post-processing) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and let \(f\) be any randomized function of its output whose coins are independent of the data and of \(M\)’s coins. Then \(f \circ M\), the mechanism \(D \mapsto f(M(D))\), is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. In terms of the channel \(K\) of \(f\), for every neighbouring pair the hockey-stick divergence can only go down, and so can the largest privacy loss: \[E_{e^\varepsilon}\big(PK\,\|\,QK\big) \le E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q), \qquad \max_z\big|L^{f}_{D,D'}(z)\big| \le \max_y\big|L_{D,D'}(y)\big|. \tag{19.4}\]


Proof. The plan is to turn any event about the processed output into a soft test on the original output and apply Lemma 19.1, then to show the privacy-loss form by the averaging argument of the data processing inequality (DPI).

Fix an event \(S\) of processed outputs. Let \(g(y) = \sum_{z \in S}K(z \mid y)\), the probability that processing \(y\) lands in \(S\). It is a probability, so it takes values in \([0, 1]\), and it does not depend on the data, because \(f\) does not look at the data: the same \(g\) serves for \(D\) and for \(D'\).
Average over the output. To land in \(S\), the mechanism first produces some \(y\), and then processing sends it into \(S\) with probability \(g(y)\), so \(\Pr[f(M(D)) \in S] = \sum_y p(y)g(y) = \mathbb E_P[g(Y)]\), and the same with \(q\) for \(D'\).
Apply the lemma to \(g\). Lemma 19.1 gives \(\mathbb E_P[g] \le e^\varepsilon\mathbb E_Q[g] + \delta\), that is \(\Pr[f(M(D)) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[f(M(D')) \in S] + \delta\). This holds for every \(S\) and every ordered neighbouring pair, which is the event form of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for \(f \circ M\). The hockey-stick inequality of Equation 19.4 is the same statement for the worst event \(S\).
The privacy-loss form. The likelihood ratio of \(z\) is \(PK(z)/QK(z)\). In the numerator, for outputs with \(q(y) > 0\), write each \(p(y)\) as \(q(y)\) times its likelihood ratio \(e^{L(y)} = p(y)/q(y)\). That turns the ratio into a weighted average of the likelihood ratios of the \(y\) that can produce \(z\): \[e^{L^f(z)} = \frac{PK(z)}{QK(z)} = \sum_y\frac{q(y)K(z \mid y)}{QK(z)}\,e^{L(y)}. \tag{19.5}\] The weight of each \(y\) is the share of the \(D'\)-probability of \(z\) that comes through \(y\). The weights are non-negative and sum to 1, because \(\sum_y q(y)K(z \mid y) = QK(z)\). So \(e^{L^f(z)}\) lies between the smallest and the largest \(e^{L(y)}\), and \(|L^f(z)|\) is at most the largest \(|L(y)|\), which is the second inequality of Equation 19.4. This is step 1 of the DPI derivation in Divergences.





Example 19.1 Collect answers with randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) and then, before publishing, flip each answer with probability \(r = \frac14\) using a fresh coin. The published answer \(z = 1\) can be reached in two ways: the first answer was 1 and was kept, or it was 0 and was flipped. Each path’s probability is the product of its two steps, and Table 19.1 follows both paths.



Table 19.1: Randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), then a fresh coin that flips the answer with probability \(\frac14\). The published \(z = 1\) is reached by two paths.

\(\frac14 \cdot \frac34 = \frac3{16}\)

The likelihood ratio of \(z = 1\) is \(0.625/0.375 = \frac53\). Step 4 of the proof predicts it as the average of \(3\) and \(\frac13\), each weighted by its share \(\frac12\) of the \(D'\) column. The published \(z = 0\) has the ratio \(\frac35\), so the published answers are \(\ln\frac53 = 0.5108\)-DP, less than \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\). The right panel of Figure 19.1 shows \(\varepsilon\) for every flip probability: it falls to 0 at \(r = \frac12\), where the published bit is a fair coin.
A count with noise shows that processing can also lower \(\delta\) while keeping \(\varepsilon\). Add Laplace noise of scale 1 to a count whose neighbouring values are 0 and 1, so that the outputs are \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) and \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, 1)\), with densities \(\frac12e^{-|y|}\) and \(\frac12e^{-|y - 1|}\). Their privacy loss \(|y - 1| - |y|\) lies within \([-1, 1]\) by the triangle inequality, so the noisy count is 1-DP (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.2 Group privacy
The definition protects one record, but people are not rows. A user of a messaging app contributes hundreds of messages, and a household shares an address. To bound what an adversary learns about all \(k\) records of one user, you need a guarantee for datasets that differ in \(k\) records. Group privacy derives it from the one-record guarantee, at a price that is linear in \(k\) for \(\varepsilon\) and exponential in \(k\) for \(\delta\).
Say that \(D\) and \(D''\) are at distance \(k\) if a path \(D = D_0 \sim D_1 \sim \dots \sim D_k = D''\) joins them, changing one record per step. The idea is to apply the one-record guarantee once per step. Each step multiplies the bound by \(e^\varepsilon\) and adds a slack \(\delta\), which later steps multiply again, so the slacks pile up in a geometric sum.

Theorem 19.2 (Group privacy) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Then for every pair of datasets \(D\) and \(D''\) at distance \(k\) and every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D'') \in S] + \delta_k, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{19.6}\] In particular, pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP gives pure \(k\varepsilon\)-DP for groups of size \(k\).


Proof. The plan is to prove the pure case through the privacy loss, which adds along the path, and the approximate case through events, chaining the one-step bound \(k\) times.

Pure DP: telescope the likelihood ratio along the path. Multiply and divide by the densities at the intermediate datasets \(D_1, \dots, D_{k-1}\). Each appears once in a numerator and once in a denominator, so they cancel and only the two ends remain: \[\frac{p_{M(D_0)}(y)}{p_{M(D_k)}(y)} = \prod_{i=1}^k\frac{p_{M(D_{i-1})}(y)}{p_{M(D_i)}(y)}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad L_{D_0,D_k}(y) = \sum_{i=1}^k L_{D_{i-1},D_i}(y). \tag{19.7}\]
Bound each term. Each pair \(D_{i-1} \sim D_i\) is neighbouring, so \(|L_{D_{i-1},D_i}(y)| \le \varepsilon\) by pure DP.
Add. A sum of \(k\) terms, each between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\), lies between \(-k\varepsilon\) and \(k\varepsilon\), so \(|L_{D_0,D_k}(y)| \le k\varepsilon\) for every \(y\), which is pure \(k\varepsilon\)-DP.
Approximate DP: one step. With \(\delta > 0\) the privacy loss is no longer bounded, so there is nothing to add up, and the proof chains the event form instead. Fix an event \(S\) and write \(s_i\) for the probability \(\Pr[M(D_i) \in S]\). The definition applied to the neighbouring pair \(D_{i-1} \sim D_i\) gives \(s_{i-1} \le e^\varepsilon s_i + \delta\).
Substitute the next step into the right side. The bound on \(s_1\) goes in place of \(s_1\): \[s_0 \le e^\varepsilon s_1 + \delta \le e^\varepsilon\big(e^\varepsilon s_2 + \delta\big) + \delta = e^{2\varepsilon}s_2 + \delta(1 + e^\varepsilon). \tag{19.8}\]
Repeat \(k\) times. By induction, \(s_0 \le e^{k\varepsilon}s_k + \delta(1 + e^\varepsilon + \dots + e^{(k-1)\varepsilon})\). Each new \(\delta\) enters before \(k - 1, k - 2, \dots, 0\) more multiplications by \(e^\varepsilon\), which is where the geometric sum comes from.
Simplify. The geometric sum is \(\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\), because multiplying it by \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) cancels all terms but the first and last. Each of its \(k\) terms is at most the largest one, \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), which gives the simpler but looser \(k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta\).


No better bound holds for all \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanisms. The mechanism below shows it, because it has an event on which every one-step bound of steps 4 to 6 is an equality.

Proposition 19.1 (The alarm mechanism attains the bound) Fix \(\varepsilon > 0\), \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) and a cap \(K\) on the count of some kind of record. On a count \(c \le K\) the alarm mechanism outputs “alarm” with probability \[a_c = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{K-c-1}e^{j\varepsilon} \tag{19.9}\] and “quiet” otherwise, and on a count above \(K\) it always outputs “quiet”. If \(a_0 \le (e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for neighbouring counts, which differ by 1, and for the counts \(0\) and \(k \le K\) it meets Equation 19.6 with equality on the event “alarm”.


Proof. 

One step is tight. Pulling the first term \(\delta\) out of the sum and a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) out of the rest shows that \(a_c = e^\varepsilon a_{c+1} + \delta\) for \(c < K\). So each neighbouring pair meets the event form with equality on “alarm”.
The mechanism is private. The other three checks, “alarm” in the reverse order and “quiet” in both orders, hold exactly when \(a_0 \le (e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). Section J.7 in the appendices proves it, and Exercise 2 proves the simpler sufficient condition \(a_0 \le 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\). For \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the condition allows \(K \le 21\).
The chain is tight. Along the path of counts \(0, 1, \dots, k\), step 5 of the proof of Theorem 19.2 substitutes equalities into equalities, so \(a_0 - e^{k\varepsilon}a_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta_k\).


Pure DP degrades linearly. A \(0.1\)-DP guarantee per record is \(10\)-DP for a user with 100 records, which is almost nothing, since a likelihood ratio of up to \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\) lets an adversary be nearly certain. This is the formal version of the “correlated records” caveat of the definition chapter. For approximate DP the \(\delta\) term grows exponentially: with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(k = 10\) it is \(\delta_k = \frac{e^{10} - 1}{e - 1}\,\delta = 12818.3\,\delta\). Since \(\delta\) must already be much smaller than \(1/n\) for \(n\) records (the definition chapter), group privacy for large groups is often vacuous.
A specific mechanism can do much better than the generic bound. With Gaussian noise on a count, a group of \(k\) records shifts the count by \(k\), so its exact group profile is that of a Gaussian pair with a larger shift (Part 4). The better fix is often to define neighbours as datasets that differ in one user’s records, bound each user’s contribution, and prove DP at that level.

Example 19.2 For randomized response a group of \(k\) records is \(k\) people, and the reports in which all \(k\) favour the same side have privacy loss exactly \(k\ln 3\), so the pure bound is exact. A noisy count shows the telescoping of step 1 at work. Take \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise and the path of counts \(0, 1, 2, 3\), so \(k = 3\). With density \(\frac12e^{-|y - c|}\) at true count \(c\), the privacy loss between counts \(c\) and \(c + 1\) is \(L_{c,c+1}(y) = |y - c - 1| - |y - c|\), how much farther \(y\) is from \(c + 1\) than from \(c\). title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.3 Basic sequential composition
An analyst asks \(k\) queries of the same dataset, each with fresh noise. Each output alone is private, but an adversary sees all of them. This section asks what guarantee holds for the whole transcript \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\), even when each mechanism is chosen after seeing the previous outputs. For pure DP the answer rests on one fact about independent coins, which step 2 of the proof needs and parallel composition reuses: probabilities multiply, so privacy losses add.

Lemma 19.2 (Privacy losses of independent outputs add) Let \(Y = (Y_1, Y_2)\), where \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are produced with independent coins, so that \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)p_2(y_2)\) on \(D\) and likewise \(q(y_1, y_2) = q_1(y_1)q_2(y_2)\) on \(D'\). Then the privacy loss of the pair is the sum of the privacy losses of its parts, \[L(y_1, y_2) = \ln\frac{p_1(y_1)p_2(y_2)}{q_1(y_1)q_2(y_2)} = L_1(y_1) + L_2(y_2). \tag{19.10}\] The same holds when the second output depends on the first, with the conditional probabilities \(p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\) and \(q_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\) in place of \(p_2(y_2)\) and \(q_2(y_2)\).


Proof. 

Independent outputs. The probability of seeing both outputs is the product of their probabilities, and the logarithm of a product of two ratios is the sum of the two logarithms.
Dependent outputs. The chain rule of probability writes any joint probability as “first, times second given first”, \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)\,p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\), and the same on \(D'\). The same logarithm then gives the same sum, with the conditional loss \(\ln\frac{p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)}{q_2(y_2 \mid y_1)}\) as its second term.


In the theorem below, each mechanism \(M_i\) may also read the previous outputs, the way an analyst picks the next query after reading the last answer. This is adaptive composition, and non-adaptive composition is the case where \(M_i\) ignores them. The condition is that each step is private however the earlier outputs turned out. Section B.1 in the appendices derives the theorem from scratch, with worked numbers.

Theorem 19.3 (Basic composition) Let \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) run on the same dataset with independent coins, where \(M_i\) may read the previous outputs \(y_1, \dots, y_{i-1}\). If, for every fixed value of the previous outputs, \(D \mapsto M_i(D; y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP, then the mechanism that releases \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\) is \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{19.11}\] For pure DP the bound \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) is the exact worst-case privacy loss whenever each \(M_i\) attains its own worst case at outputs that can occur together.


Proof. The plan is to prove the pure case by adding privacy losses with Lemma 19.2. The approximate case takes two mechanisms, since induction on \(k\) does the rest. That case splits an event over the first output, applies the second mechanism’s guarantee for each value of it, and applies the first mechanism’s guarantee to what is left, a soft test of the first output.

Pure DP: factor the probability of a transcript. By the chain rule, the probability of \((y_1, \dots, y_k)\) is the probability of \(y_1\), times that of \(y_2\) given \(y_1\), and so on. On \(D\), \[p_D(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \prod_{i=1}^k p_{M_i(D;\,y_{<i})}(y_i), \tag{19.12}\] where \(y_{<i} = (y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\) and each factor uses fresh coins. The same holds on \(D'\), with the same previous outputs plugged in.
Take the log-ratio. By Lemma 19.2, applied \(k - 1\) times in its dependent form, \(L_{D,D'}(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \sum_{i=1}^k L^{(i)}(y_i;\,y_{<i})\), where \(L^{(i)}\) is the privacy loss of \(M_i\) with its previous outputs fixed.
Bound each term and add. For the fixed \(y_{<i}\), \(M_i\) is \(\varepsilon_i\)-DP by assumption, so \(|L^{(i)}| \le \varepsilon_i\), and the sum is at most \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) at every transcript, which is pure \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\)-DP. When every \(M_i\) attains \(\varepsilon_i\) at outputs that can occur together, the sum is attained, which is the exactness claim.
Approximate DP: split an event over the first output. Take \(k = 2\), and write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the distribution of the transcript \((Y_1, Y_2)\) on \(D\) and on \(D'\). For a set \(S\) of transcripts, let \(S_{y_1} = \{y_2 : (y_1, y_2) \in S\}\), the second outputs that complete \(y_1\) into \(S\). The transcript lands in \(S\) when the first output is some \(y_1\) and the second lands in \(S_{y_1}\), so \[P(S) = \sum_{y_1}p_1(y_1)\,P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}), \tag{19.13}\] where \(p_1\) is the mass function of \(M_1(D)\) and \(P_2^{y_1}\) the distribution of \(M_2(D; y_1)\). Write \(q_1\) and \(Q_2^{y_1}\) for the same objects on \(D'\).
Apply the second mechanism’s guarantee inside the sum. For each \(y_1\), \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) + \delta_2\), and also \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le 1\) because it is a probability. So \(P_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1}) \le g(y_1) + \delta_2\) with \[g(y_1) = \min\big(1,\ e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\big) \in [0, 1]. \tag{19.14}\]
Sum over \(y_1\). The weights \(p_1(y_1)\) add up to 1, so \(\delta_2\) comes out once: \(P(S) \le \mathbb E_{p_1}[g] + \delta_2\).
Apply the first mechanism’s guarantee to \(g\). The function \(g\) takes values in \([0, 1]\), which is why it was capped at 1, so Lemma 19.1 gives \(\mathbb E_{p_1}[g] \le e^{\varepsilon_1}\mathbb E_{q_1}[g] + \delta_1\).
Undo the cap. Since \(g(y_1) \le e^{\varepsilon_2}Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\), the average \(\mathbb E_{q_1}[g]\) is at most \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\sum_{y_1}q_1(y_1)Q_2^{y_1}(S_{y_1})\), which by step 4 on \(D'\) is \(e^{\varepsilon_2}Q(S)\).
Combine. Steps 6 to 8 give \(P(S) \le e^{\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2}Q(S) + \delta_1 + \delta_2\). Nothing used that \(M_2\) ignores \(y_1\), so this covers adaptive composition.


Basic composition is exact for the worst case, and the worst case is rare. For \(k\) randomized-response answers about the same bit, “every answer is true” has loss \(k\ln 3\) but probability \((\frac34)^k\). Typical transcripts mix truths with lies, whose losses cancel. Under \(D\), each answer contributes \(+\varepsilon_0\) when it tells the truth, with probability \(t = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), and \(-\varepsilon_0\) otherwise. Its mean is therefore \(\varepsilon_0(2t - 1) = \varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\), which is \(\varepsilon_0/2\) for \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\). A sum of \(k\) such independent terms stays within a spread of order \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt k\) of its mean (Concentration). An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee may ignore losses above \(\varepsilon\) that occur with probability at most \(\delta\), so a small \(\delta\) writes off the unlikely tail, and the \(\varepsilon\) you need grows like \(\sqrt k\) rather than \(k\), which is the advanced composition of Advanced and optimal composition, previewed by Exercise 6.
The \(\delta\)s add without the inflation of group privacy, because each mechanism compares the same pair \(D, D'\), and step 6 of the proof just averages the second slack. Adaptivity is free, but only with budgets fixed in advance. Choosing the budgets from the outputs (“stop when the answer is good enough”) needs the privacy filters of Advanced and optimal composition.

Example 19.3 Start with an adaptive survey. Ask a person for a randomized-response answer with \(\varepsilon_1 = \ln 3\), then ask again with \(\ln 3\) if the answer was 1 and with \(0.5\) if it was 0. Level \(0.5\) tells the truth with probability \(e^{0.5}/(1 + e^{0.5}) = 0.6225\). So the second step depends on \(y_1\), but it is at most \(\ln 3\)-DP for each value of \(y_1\). In Table 19.5 each probability is the product of the two steps. For example, \((0, 1)\) under bit 1 is a lie and then the truth, \(\frac14 \times 0.6225 = 0.1556\).

One record shifts each noisy count by 1, and \(k\) independent Gaussians shifted by 1 carry the same evidence as one shifted by \(\sqrt k\) (Section B.3 in the appendices derives this). By Table 19.7, basic composition overstates \(\varepsilon\) for ten queries by a factor of \(5/1.504 = 3.3\).

title: 19  Post-processing, group privacy and composition
text:
19.4 Parallel composition
A histogram counts people in disjoint bins. Sequential composition would charge \(d\varepsilon\) for \(d\) bins, which is far too pessimistic, because one person’s record lands in one bin only. Parallel composition makes that precise, with care about the two common neighbouring relations. Under add/remove, neighbours differ by adding or removing one record. Under replace, neighbours have the same size and differ in the content of one record, which is a removal followed by an addition.
Split the data universe into disjoint parts \(U_1, \dots, U_d\) by a rule that may depend on a record’s content but not on the rest of the dataset, and run \(M_i\) on \(D \cap U_i\), the records in part \(i\). A changed record touches only its own part, so you pay only that part’s budget.

Theorem 19.4 (Parallel composition) Let \(U_1, \dots, U_d\) be a partition of the data universe fixed in advance, and let \(M_i\) run on \(D \cap U_i\) with independent coins, each \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP under add/remove. Then the release \((M_1(D \cap U_1), \dots, M_d(D \cap U_d))\) is \[\big(\max_i\varepsilon_i,\ \max_i\delta_i\big)\text{-DP under add/remove}. \tag{19.15}\] Under replace, a record that moves from part \(a\) to part \(b \ne a\) costs \((\varepsilon_a + \varepsilon_b, \delta_a + \delta_b)\), and one replaced within part \(a\) costs that part’s guarantee for two add/remove steps, at most group privacy with \(k = 2\); for pure DP with equal budgets both cases give \(2\varepsilon\). If the parts are fixed slots, so that record \(i\) always goes to part \(i\), a replacement changes one part only and the cost is \((\max_i\varepsilon_i, \max_i\delta_i)\) again.


Proof. 

Add/remove changes one part. If \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\), then \(x\) lies in exactly one part \(U_j\), because the parts are disjoint and cover the universe. For \(i \ne j\), \(D \cap U_i = D' \cap U_i\), so \(M_i\) gets the same input and has the same output distribution on both.
Pure DP: the other losses are zero. By Lemma 19.2 the privacy loss of the whole release is \(\sum_iL^{(i)}\), and \(L^{(i)} \equiv 0\) for \(i \ne j\) because the two distributions are equal and their ratio is 1. So \(|L| = |L^{(j)}| \le \varepsilon_j \le \max_i\varepsilon_i\).
Approximate DP: condition on the unchanged parts. Let \(W\) be the outputs of the parts \(i \ne j\), which have the same distribution on \(D\) and \(D'\) and are independent of \(Y_j\). Given \(W\), the release lands in an event \(S\) when \(Y_j\) falls in \(S_W\), the set of \(y_j\) completing \(W\) into \(S\). So the probability of \(S\) is the average over \(W\) of \(\Pr[Y_j \in S_W]\). Inside that average, \(M_j\)’s guarantee bounds the probability on \(D\) by \(e^{\varepsilon_j}\) times that on \(D'\), plus \(\delta_j\), and averaging over the same \(W\) carries the bound to \(S\).
Replace changes up to two parts. If \(D'\) replaces a record \(x \in U_a\) by \(x' \in U_b\), then \(D \cap U_a\) loses a record and \(D \cap U_b\) gains one: two add/remove steps on two independent mechanisms, which is a composition of two mechanisms (Theorem 19.3, with the other parts handled as in step 3), giving \((\varepsilon_a + \varepsilon_b, \delta_a + \delta_b)\). If \(a = b\), part \(a\) sees a removal and an addition, two neighbouring steps, which is Theorem 19.2 with \(k = 2\) inside one part. In fixed slots a replacement changes only slot \(i\), and steps 1 to 3 apply again.


So a histogram costs one \(\varepsilon\), not \(d\). Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) on each of \(d\) bins is \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove, because adding a record changes one bin by 1. Under replace it is \(2\varepsilon\)-DP, since moving a record changes two bins, which is why a histogram’s sensitivity is quoted as 2 under replace (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms).
The partition must not depend on the data. “Split the data at its median” changes when one record changes, which can move many records between parts, and then step 1 of the proof fails. Use fixed bins, or account for the data-dependent split as a mechanism of its own.

Example 19.4 Local randomized response composes in parallel. Each of \(n\) people reports their own bit at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), and each person is one slot, so the whole vector of \(n\) reports is \(\ln 3\)-DP for any \(n\), not \(n\ln 3\), under either neighbouring relation.
A two-bin histogram shows the factor of 2. Give each bin rounded \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise, and let the script compute the exact pure \(\varepsilon\) of the pair under each relation. Adding or removing a record changes one bin by 1, so only that bin contributes privacy loss, and \(\varepsilon = 1.0000\). Replacing a record in bin 1 by one in bin 2 moves bin 1 up by 1 and bin 2 down by 1. The worst output then has both noisy counts far out on the side that favours \(D\), where both step losses equal 1 at once, so \(\varepsilon = 2.0000\). Exercise 4 works out the losses by hand.

19.5 What composes and what doesn’t
The three properties hold under weak assumptions, which makes it tempting to apply them where even those fail. Each assumption appeared in a proof. Post-processing needs \(f\) not to read the data, composition needs independent coins and one neighbouring relation, and group privacy and composition need budgets fixed in advance. Table 19.8 collects the ways these break in practice, and the section then proves that the commonest break, two releases sharing one noise draw, is a total failure.
