When two releases share one noise draw, the noise can be subtracted away, and privacy fails completely.

Proposition 19.2 (Shared noise is not private) Release two counts with the same Laplace draw \(Z\) of scale \(b\): \(c_1(D) + Z\) and \(c_2(D) + Z\), where removing some record lowers \(c_1\) by 1 and leaves \(c_2\) unchanged. Each count alone is \(1/b\)-DP, but the pair is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\) and any \(\delta < 1\).


Proof. 

The difference is noise-free. \((c_1 + Z) - (c_2 + Z) = c_1(D) - c_2(D)\), a deterministic function of the data.
It changes between neighbours. If the difference is \(c\) on \(D\), it is \(c - 1\) on the neighbour \(D'\) without that record, since removing the record lowers \(c_1\) by 1 and leaves \(c_2\).
One event separates the two. The event “the difference equals \(c\)” has probability 1 on \(D\) and 0 on \(D'\), so the event form \(1 \le e^\varepsilon \cdot 0 + \delta\) fails for every \(\varepsilon\) unless \(\delta \ge 1\).


What broke is step 1 of the proof of Theorem 19.3: the transcript’s probability is no longer a product of the two mechanisms’ probabilities. So fresh randomness is part of the mechanism. Seeding two mechanisms with the same seed, re-adding a cached noise draw to a related query, or reusing noise across shards are all the shared-noise bug. An exact total published elsewhere can be differenced against a DP release in the same way.
The neighbouring relation is part of the budget too. A guarantee proved under add/remove and reported under replace can be off by a factor of 2, and mixing the two inside one accountant, the code that totals the budget, is a bug that comes back in Subsampling.

Example 19.5 Randomized response does not have this failure: if two answers reuse one coin, the second repeats the first, which is post-processing, but additive noise does have it. The script simulates the differencing attack of Proposition 19.2 on two Laplace counts, the number of smokers and the number of smokers aged 40 or over. Alice is a smoker aged 30, so she counts only in the first. She is in the data with probability \(\frac12\), and the attacker guesses “in” when the difference of the two counts exceeds the midpoint of its two possible true values. Over 200,000 runs with \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) noise, the attack with shared noise has accuracy \(1.0000\), because the difference is exact.
With fresh noise the same attack has accuracy \(0.6206\). The second count no longer depends on Alice, so the best any attack can reach is that of the first count alone, \(\frac12\) plus half the total variation distance between what it sees in the two cases (Divergences). For \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, 1)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(1, 1)\) the best event is “the output is above \(\frac12\)”, whose probabilities differ by \(1 - e^{-1/2}\), so the best accuracy is \(\frac12 + \frac12(1 - e^{-1/2}) = 0.6967\). The difference attack falls short of it because it adds the noise of the second count.

19.8 References

Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014): Proposition 2.1 (post-processing), Theorem 2.2 (group privacy, pure), Theorem 3.16 (basic composition, with the proof for approximate DP in Appendix B), and §3.5 for composition in general. The standard reference for every statement here.
Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (TCC 2006): the paper that defined DP, where the guarantee for groups of records first appears.
McSherry, “Privacy Integrated Queries” (SIGMOD 2009): parallel composition, and a system built on post-processing and composition as its only rules.
Vadhan, “The Complexity of Differential Privacy” (2017), the opening sections: the basic properties of DP (post-processing, group privacy, composition) with careful proofs, at a more theoretical level than Dwork & Roth.
Near & Abuah, Programming Differential Privacy, chapters on the properties of DP: sequential and parallel composition and post-processing, with code.
Kifer & Machanavajjhala, “No Free Lunch in Data Privacy” (SIGMOD 2011): why correlated records defeat a per-record guarantee, the problem group privacy addresses.
Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan, “Boosting and Differential Privacy” (FOCS 2010), and Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015): advanced and optimal composition, the subject of Advanced and optimal composition.
Rogers, Roth, Ullman & Vadhan, “Privacy Odometers and Filters: Pay-as-you-Go Composition” (NeurIPS 2016): what changes when the budgets themselves are chosen adaptively.

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.1 Sensitivity
You run a hospital database and want to publish how many patients have diabetes, with a differential privacy (DP) guarantee. The definition of differential privacy says what the release must satisfy: changing one person’s record must barely change the distribution of what you publish. It does not say how to build such a release. The two mechanisms of this chapter are the answer used almost everywhere. Both compute the exact answer, call it \(f(D)\) for the dataset \(D\), and blur it with random noise \(Z\) drawn fresh each time, so that what you publish is \[M(D) = f(D) + Z. \tag{20.1}\] If the noise is wide compared with how far one person can move the answer, an observer cannot tell from the output whether that person was there.
Three questions decide everything. The first is how much one record can move the answer. That is the sensitivity of \(f\), and it sets the scale of the noise. The second is which noise distribution to use. Laplace noise gives pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, while Gaussian noise gives only \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP but scales better when many numbers are released at once. The third is how much noise exactly. For Laplace noise the answer is a one-line formula. For Gaussian noise the textbook formula is loose, and the exact answer comes from solving one equation numerically.
The running example is the hospital’s count: 1,234 of its \(n = 10{,}000\) patients have diabetes, and the count must be released under add/remove neighbours. Every later mechanism that adds noise, from the private mean to the noisy gradients of private model training in a later part, is calibrated with the tools of this chapter.
To hide one record, the noise has to cover the largest change one record can make to the answer. That change is the sensitivity, and it is the first thing to compute for any release. It depends on the query, on the norm you measure the change in, and on the neighbouring relation of the definition of differential privacy: under add/remove a neighbour has one record more or less, so the dataset size changes, and under replace one record is swapped for another, so the size \(n\) is fixed and public.
For a vector answer you need a way to measure a change, and two are used. The \(\ell_1\) norm \(\|v\|_1 = \sum_i|v_i|\) is the total change summed over coordinates, and Laplace noise is calibrated to it. The \(\ell_2\) norm \(\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{\sum_iv_i^2}\) is the straight-line length, and Gaussian noise is calibrated to it.
The two sensitivities are never far apart, and how far depends on how one record’s change spreads over the coordinates. The next result says exactly how far, and Section 20.5 turns it into the rule for choosing between the two mechanisms.
The sensitivities of the standard queries follow by asking what the single worst record can do. Table 20.1 collects them; records take values in a domain \(\mathcal X\), and \(B\) bounds a numerical record.
Sensitivity is a worst case over datasets. It does not depend on the data you hold, only on what the domain allows, which is why it can be computed before looking at the data. It is also why the sum of arbitrary real numbers has infinite sensitivity, since one record can be as large as it likes; clipping, in Beyond global sensitivity, forces a finite \(B\). The neighbouring relation changes the answer by up to a factor of 2, because replacing is removing one record and adding another, so a guarantee stated without its neighbouring relation is ambiguous by that factor in \(\varepsilon\).

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
Definition 20.1 (Sensitivity) Let \(f\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^d\) be a query with values in \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(p \in \{1, 2\}\), the \(\ell_p\) sensitivity of \(f\) is the largest distance between its answers on two neighbouring datasets, \[\Delta_pf = \max_{D \sim D'}\big\|f(D) - f(D')\big\|_p. \tag{20.2}\]



Proposition 20.1 (The two sensitivities) For every query \(f\) with values in \(\mathbb R^d\), \[\Delta_2f \le \Delta_1f \le \sqrt d\,\Delta_2f. \tag{20.3}\] The left bound is reached when one record moves a single coordinate, the right one when it moves all \(d\) coordinates equally.


Proof. 

Fix a vector \(v \in \mathbb R^d\). Squaring the sum \(\sum_i|v_i|\) gives every \(v_i^2\) plus cross terms that are never negative, so \(\|v\|_2^2 \le \|v\|_1^2\), that is \(\|v\|_2 \le \|v\|_1\).
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to the sum \(\sum_i 1\cdot|v_i|\) gives \(\|v\|_1 \le \sqrt d\,\|v\|_2\).
Both inequalities hold for the change \(v = f(D) - f(D')\) of every neighbouring pair, so they hold for the maximum over pairs. If only one coordinate of \(v\) is non-zero, both norms equal its absolute value; if all \(d\) coordinates equal \(c\), then \(\|v\|_1 = dc\) and \(\|v\|_2 = \sqrt d\,c\).

Proposition 20.2 (Sensitivities of the standard queries) The sensitivities in Table 20.1 hold, and each is reached by some neighbouring pair.


Proof. 

Count. Adding or removing a record changes \(|D|\) by exactly 1. Replacing a record leaves it unchanged, which is why under replace the size is not private and a count of all records needs no noise.
Sum. Adding a record \(x \in [0, B]\) changes the sum by \(x \le B\), and replacing \(x\) by \(x'\) changes it by \(|x - x'| \le B\). Both bounds are reached with \(x = B\) and \(x' = 0\).
Mean with public \(n\). Under replace the mean is the sum divided by the fixed \(n\), so its sensitivity is the sum’s divided by \(n\), which is \(B/n\). Under add/remove the denominator moves too, so there is no such simple bound; Exercise 1 releases a noisy sum and a noisy count instead.
Histogram. Under add/remove the record lands in one bin, so that bin changes by 1 and the others not at all. The change vector is \(\pm e_j\), where \(e_j\) has a 1 in bin \(j\) and 0 elsewhere, and both of its norms are 1. Under replace one bin loses 1 and another gains 1, so the change is \(e_{j'} - e_j\), with \(\ell_1\) norm \(1 + 1 = 2\) and \(\ell_2\) norm \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt2\).
Threshold counts. The count for threshold \(j\) is the number of records with \(x \ge j\), so a record \(x\) adds 1 to every count with \(j \le x\). A record with \(x \ge d\) moves all \(d\) counts by 1, so the change vector is \((1, \dots, 1)\), with \(\ell_1\) norm \(d\) and \(\ell_2\) norm \(\sqrt d\). Under replace, changing \(x\) to \(x'\) moves only the counts with \(j\) between the two values, at most \(d\) of them, by 1 each, so the same bounds hold.




Example 20.1 The hospital also releases the mean age of its \(n = 10{,}000\) patients, with ages clipped to \([0, 100]\), under replace neighbours. By row 3 of Table 20.1 the sensitivity is \(B/n = 100/10{,}000 = 0.01\) year, so one patient can move the mean by at most a hundredth of a year, however old they are. For the diabetes count under add/remove, row 1 gives a sensitivity of 1.

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.2 The Laplace mechanism
The Laplace mechanism is the first mechanism to try (Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith 2006). It adds independent Laplace noise to each coordinate, with scale proportional to the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity. Section A.3 in the appendices derives the same result from scratch for a single count, with every number shown.
Everything rests on the privacy loss of the definition of differential privacy. For an output \(y\), it is the log of how much more likely \(y\) is when the data are \(D\) than when they are \(D'\), \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}, \tag{20.4}\] where \(p_{M(D)}\) is the density of the published output on dataset \(D\). Write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the two output distributions \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\). That chapter proved that a mechanism whose loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) at every output, for every neighbouring pair, is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, in its section on pure DP being pointwise. The Laplace mechanism is proved private exactly this way.
For additive noise the loss has a simple shape. On neighbouring datasets the mechanism outputs \(f(D) + Z\) and \(f(D') + Z\), the same noise placed around two different centres, so the density of \(Q\) is the density of \(P\) slid over by the shift \(f(D') - f(D)\). How far apart two distributions are, at a factor \(\gamma \ge 1\), is measured by the hockey-stick divergence of Divergences, \(E_\gamma(P\|Q)\), the largest value of \(\Pr_P[S] - \gamma\Pr_Q[S]\) over events \(S\). At \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\) it is the smallest \(\delta\) that works for the pair. The first result says that under this measure the true answer drops out, and only the shift matters.

Lemma 20.1 (Additive noise reduces to one shifted pair) Let \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\), where \(Z\) has a density on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let \(v = f(D') - f(D)\) be the shift between the two answers on a neighbouring pair. Then for every \(\gamma \ge 1\), \[E_\gamma\big(M(D)\|M(D')\big) = E_\gamma\big(Z\|Z + v\big). \tag{20.5}\]


Proof. 

The map \(y \mapsto y - f(D)\) sends \(M(D)\) to \(Z\) and \(M(D')\) to \(Z + v\), and it is a bijection: every output corresponds to exactly one relabelled output, and back.
So an event \(S\) about \(M\)’s output is the same as the event \(S - f(D)\) about the relabelled output, with the same probability under each dataset. The hockey-stick divergence is a maximum of \(\Pr_P[S] - \gamma\Pr_Q[S]\) over events, and both sides range over the same values, so they are equal.


For the hospital’s count, the true value 1234 drops out and only the shift \(v = 1\) remains. Privacy is a property of the noise and of the set of shifts that neighbouring datasets can produce, which Section 20.1 bounded. The Laplace mechanism chooses its scale so that the largest shift one record can cause, divided by the scale, is exactly \(\varepsilon\).

Theorem 20.1 (The Laplace mechanism) The Laplace distribution \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) with scale \(b > 0\) has density \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\), a two-sided exponential peaked at 0. Let \(f\colon \mathcal X^n \to \mathbb R^d\) have \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1f\) and let \(\varepsilon > 0\). The Laplace mechanism \[M(D) = f(D) + (Z_1, \dots, Z_d), \qquad Z_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Lap}(b), \quad b = \frac{\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}, \tag{20.6}\] is \(\varepsilon\)-DP (i.i.d. means independent and identically distributed). Its error per coordinate is about \(b\), and for every failure probability \(\beta \in (0, 1)\) the largest error over the \(d\) coordinates obeys \[\mathbb E[|Z_i|] = b, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Z_i) = 2b^2, \qquad \Pr\Big[\max_i|Z_i| > b\ln\frac d\beta\Big] \le \beta. \tag{20.7}\] The scale is the smallest that works in general: for a count, \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise with \(b < 1/\varepsilon\) is not \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. The plan is to write the privacy loss down and bound it at every output by the triangle inequality, then to read the error off the Laplace distribution, and finally to exhibit an event on which the privacy bound is reached.

Write the two densities. Fix \(D \sim D'\) and write \(a = f(D)\) and \(a' = f(D')\) for the two true answers. The coordinates of the noise are independent, so the density of \(M(D)\) at \(y\) is the product \(\prod_i\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|y_i - a_i|/b}\), and that of \(M(D')\) is the same with \(a'\) in place of \(a\).
Take the log-ratio. The constants \(\frac1{2b}\) cancel, and the log of a product of exponentials is the sum of the exponents, so \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \frac1b\sum_{i=1}^d\big(|y_i - a'_i| - |y_i - a_i|\big). \tag{20.8}\]
Bound each term. The distance from \(y_i\) to \(a'_i\) is at most the distance from \(y_i\) to \(a_i\) plus the distance from \(a_i\) to \(a'_i\), by the triangle inequality \(|y_i - a'_i| \le |y_i - a_i| + |a_i - a'_i|\). So each term of the sum is at most \(|a_i - a'_i|\), whatever \(y\) is.
Add the terms. Summing over \(i\) gives the \(\ell_1\) norm of the shift, which is at most the sensitivity, so for every \(y\) \[L_{D,D'}(y) \le \frac{\|a - a'\|_1}{b} \le \frac{\Delta_1f}{b} = \varepsilon. \tag{20.9}\] The privacy loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) at every output, so the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by the pointwise criterion recalled above.
Accuracy. The absolute value \(|Z_i|\) has density \(\frac1be^{-z/b}\) on \(z \ge 0\), an exponential distribution with mean \(b\) and second moment \(2b^2\); since \(Z_i\) has mean 0, that gives \(\mathbb E[|Z_i|] = b\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Z_i) = 2b^2\). Integrating the same density from \(t\) to infinity gives the tail \(\Pr[|Z_i| > t] = e^{-t/b}\).
All coordinates at once. Give each coordinate a share \(\beta/d\) of the failure probability: setting \(e^{-t/b} = \beta/d\) gives \(t = b\ln(d/\beta)\). The probability that at least one of the \(d\) coordinates fails is at most the sum of their failure probabilities, by the union bound, which is \(d\cdot\beta/d = \beta\).
Tightness. The outputs where the loss is largest are those left of both answers, so take a count with \(f(D) = 0\) and \(f(D') = 1\) and the event \(S = \{y \le 0\}\). Under \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise, \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] = \Pr[Z \le 0] = \frac12\) by the symmetry of the noise about 0, and \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] = \Pr[Z \le -1] = \frac12e^{-1/b}\) from the tail of step 5. So the ratio of the two probabilities is exactly \(e^{1/b}\), and on \(S\) the bound of step 4 holds with equality at every point. If \(b < 1/\varepsilon\), the ratio exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) and the definition fails on this event.


The noise does not depend on \(n\). A count gets noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\) whether the database has a hundred records or a hundred million, because one record moves a count by 1 either way. The relative error of a count of size \(n\) is therefore about \(1/(n\varepsilon)\), so large populations are cheap to protect and small subgroups are expensive. The worst case is not rare, either: the privacy loss equals \(\varepsilon\) on the event \(S\) of step 7, which has probability \(\frac12\) (Figure 20.1, left), so the guarantee is tight in the strongest sense and not just at some unlikely output.






Figure 20.1: Left column: a count released with \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) noise on neighbouring datasets with true counts 0 and 1, and the privacy loss \(L(y)\). It equals \(+\varepsilon\) for every \(y \le 0\) and \(-\varepsilon\) for every \(y \ge 1\), never more. Right column: the same count with \(\mathcal N(0, 2^2)\) noise. The privacy loss is a straight line, and exceeds \(\varepsilon = 1\) on the shaded tail, which has probability 0.0401 under \(M(D)\). The exact \(\delta(1) = 0.0068\) is smaller, because the hockey-stick subtracts \(e^\varepsilon\) times the mass of \(M(D')\) on the same tail.



Two more facts about the Laplace mechanism matter later, and the exercise book derives both. Drawn as a random number, the privacy loss of an output from \(M(D)\) never leaves \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\). It has an atom of probability \(\frac12\) at \(+\varepsilon\), an atom of probability \(\frac12e^{-\varepsilon}\) at \(-\varepsilon\), and a continuous ramp between them (Figure 20.2, left, and Exercise 7), and Part 4’s accountants track exactly this distribution. The mechanism also satisfies a whole curve of weaker guarantees. For every \(\varepsilon' < \varepsilon\) it is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP with \(\delta = 1 - e^{-(\varepsilon - \varepsilon')/2}\), the dashed curve of Figure 20.3 (Exercise 2). As for the shape of the noise, the proof used only that the log-density changes by at most \(\varepsilon/\Delta_1f\) per unit of shift, and the Laplace log-density \(-|z|/b\) has exactly that slope everywhere. Other shapes are slightly better for large \(\varepsilon\) (Geng & Viswanath’s staircase mechanism), but the Laplace is within a small factor and is the standard choice.






Figure 20.2: The privacy loss distribution under \(M(D)\) for a count, with \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: Laplace noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\). The loss never leaves \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\); it has an atom of probability 0.5000 at \(+\varepsilon\), an atom of 0.1839 at \(-\varepsilon\), and a continuous ramp of total probability 0.3161 in between (density shown). Right: Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2. The loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\), here \(\mu = 0.5\), and exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability 0.0401 (shaded).




Example 20.2 Release the diabetes count, 1,234 of \(n = 10{,}000\) patients, with \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) under add/remove. The sensitivity is 1, so the noise is \(\mathrm{Lap}(10)\) and the expected absolute error is \(b = 10\) (simulated over a million releases: 9.978). For a 95% guarantee take \(d = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\) in the accuracy bound. With probability 0.95 the error is then below \(b\ln20 = 29.96\) (simulated 95th percentile: 29.85), a relative error of \(29.96/1234 = 0.0243\).
To see the privacy loss itself, take a count with \(b = 1\), so \(\varepsilon = 1\), and true answers 0 and 1. Table 20.2 evaluates the two densities and the loss at a few outputs. Left of both true answers the ratio of the densities is stuck at \(e\), right of them at \(e^{-1}\), and in between the loss falls linearly from 1 to \(-1\). Once \(y\) is past both centres, moving it further away multiplies both densities by the same factor, so however far out an output lands, it never favours one dataset by more than a factor of \(e\). A million simulated draws reproduce the tight event’s probabilities to three decimals (Table 20.7).

title: 20  The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms
text:
20.3 The Gaussian mechanism: classic calibration
Gaussian noise is the other natural choice. It has lighter tails than Laplace noise, a sum of independent Gaussians is again Gaussian, and it is calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which can be much smaller than the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity. The price is that its privacy loss is a straight line in the output and so is unbounded (Figure 20.1, right), so the pointwise criterion never applies and Gaussian noise cannot give pure DP. Instead you accept a small probability \(\delta\) that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\). This section derives the calibration found in the textbook of Dwork & Roth and in many papers and libraries, and shows where it is loose; Section A.6 in the appendices derives the same formula from scratch, with worked numbers.
The smallest \(\delta\) that works for one pair is its hockey-stick divergence at \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\), and the largest of these over all pairs, as a function of \(\varepsilon\), is the privacy profile \(\delta_M(\varepsilon)\) of \(M\). The first tool says which event is the worst one: the set of outputs where the loss is too large.

Lemma 20.2 (The bad event and the exact δ) Fix a neighbouring pair, write \(P\) and \(Q\) for the distributions of \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\), with densities \(p\) and \(q\), and let \(L\) be the privacy loss. Call \(B = \{y : L(y) > \varepsilon\}\) the bad event, the outputs that favour \(D\) over \(D'\) by more than a factor \(e^\varepsilon\). Then \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B] \le \Pr_P[B] = \Pr_{y \sim P}[L(y) > \varepsilon]. \tag{20.10}\] Equivalently, writing \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\) for the positive part, \[E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_Q[(e^L - e^\varepsilon)_+] = \mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]. \tag{20.11}\]


Proof. 

The quantity \(\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S]\) is the integral over \(S\) of \(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\). To make the integral as large as possible, include every output where the integrand is positive and no other. The integrand is positive exactly where \(p > e^\varepsilon q\), that is where \(L > \varepsilon\), which is \(B\). This is the argument of Divergences for the worst event of a hockey-stick divergence, and it gives the equality.
The inequality drops the term \(e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\), which is never negative.
For the expectation forms, the hockey-stick is the integral of \((p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\). Factoring out \(q\) gives \(q\,(e^L - e^\varepsilon)_+\), and factoring out \(p\) gives \(p\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\); integrating each against its density is the stated expectation.


So the bad event’s probability is always a valid \(\delta\), though usually a loose one, and the last form needs only the distribution of the loss under \(P\), the starting point of Numerical accounting. For Gaussian noise that distribution is itself normal.

Lemma 20.3 (The privacy loss of Gaussian noise) Let \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\), that is \(d\) independent normal coordinates with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\), and let \(v = f(D') - f(D)\) be the shift of a neighbouring pair. Write \(\mu = \|v\|_2/\sigma\) for the shift measured in standard deviations of the noise. Under \(M(D)\) the privacy loss is normal, \[L \sim \mathcal N\Big(\frac{\mu^2}2, \mu^2\Big), \tag{20.12}\] and under \(M(D')\) it is \(\mathcal N(-\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\).


Proof. 

Under \(M(D)\), write the output as \(y = f(D) + z\), where \(z\) is the noise. The density of \(M(D)\) at \(y\) is proportional to \(e^{-\|z\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), and that of \(M(D')\) to \(e^{-\|z - v\|^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), since \(y\) sits at distance \(z - v\) from \(f(D')\). The log of their ratio is the difference of the exponents, and expanding \(\|z - v\|^2 = \|z\|^2 - 2\langle z, v\rangle + \|v\|^2\) gives \[L(y) = \frac{\|v\|^2 - 2\langle z, v\rangle}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{20.13}\]
The loss depends on \(z\) only through the inner product \(\langle z, v\rangle = \sum_iz_iv_i\), the component of the noise along the shift. That is a sum of independent normals, so it is normal, with mean 0 and variance \(\sum_i\sigma^2v_i^2 = \sigma^2\|v\|^2\).
A constant minus a multiple of a normal is normal, so \(L\) is normal with mean \(\|v\|^2/(2\sigma^2) = \mu^2/2\) and variance \(4\sigma^2\|v\|^2/(4\sigma^4) = \mu^2\). The other \(d - 1\) directions of \(z\), perpendicular to \(v\), do not enter.
Under \(M(D')\) the noise is centred one shift further along \(v\), which lowers \(\langle z, v\rangle\) by \(\|v\|^2\) on average and so lowers the loss by \(\mu^2\); the variance is unchanged.


Unlike the Laplace loss, the Gaussian loss has no atoms and no largest value (Figure 20.2, right). The classic calibration bounds \(\delta\) by the probability that it exceeds \(\varepsilon\) and chooses \(\sigma\) to make that tail small.

Theorem 20.2 (Classic Gaussian calibration) Let \(f\) have \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2f\), and let \(\varepsilon \in (0, 1)\) and \(\delta \in (0, 1)\). The Gaussian mechanism \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\) and \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon} \tag{20.14}\] is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP (Dwork & Roth 2014, Theorem A.1).


Proof. The plan is to bound \(\delta\) by the bad-event probability of Lemma 20.2, which by Lemma 20.3 is a normal tail, and to show with a standard tail bound that this tail is below \(\delta\) for the \(\sigma\) above. The route is Dwork & Roth’s, in a one-sided form that is a little shorter. Write \(c = \sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\), so \(\sigma = c\,\Delta_2f/\varepsilon\).

Bound \(\delta\) by the bad event. By Lemma 20.2, \(\delta \le \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\). By Lemma 20.3 the loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\), so \(L > \varepsilon\) exactly when a standard normal exceeds \((\varepsilon - \mu^2/2)/\mu = \frac\varepsilon\mu - \frac\mu2\). Writing \(\Phi\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF), and using its symmetry \(\Phi(-t) = 1 - \Phi(t)\), \[\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(-t), \qquad t = \frac\varepsilon\mu - \frac\mu2. \tag{20.15}\]
Take the worst shift. A larger shift makes the bad event more likely, because \(t\) decreases as \(\mu\) grows. So the worst neighbouring pair has the largest shift, \(\|v\|_2 = \Delta_2f\), that is \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma = \varepsilon/c\), and then \(t = c - \frac{\varepsilon}{2c}\).
Bound the normal tail. The Mills-ratio bound of Concentration inequalities says \(\Phi(-t) \le \varphi(t)/t\) for \(t > 0\), where \(\varphi(t) = e^{-t^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\) is the standard normal density. The reason is that beyond \(t\) every point \(z\) has \(z/t \ge 1\), so \(\int_t^\infty\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz \le \int_t^\infty\frac zt\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz\), and since the derivative of \(\varphi\) is \(-z\varphi(z)\) the right side integrates to \(\varphi(t)/t\).
Expand \(t^2\). Squaring \(t = c - \varepsilon/(2c)\) gives \(t^2 = c^2 - \varepsilon + \frac{\varepsilon^2}{4c^2} \ge c^2 - \varepsilon\), dropping the last term because it is positive. By the definition of \(c\), \(e^{-c^2/2} = \delta/1.25\), so \[e^{-t^2/2} \le \frac{\delta}{1.25}\,e^{\varepsilon/2}. \tag{20.16}\]
Combine. Steps 3 and 4 give \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta\,e^{\varepsilon/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi}\,t)\), which is at most \(\delta\) when \(t \ge e^{\varepsilon/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi})\). For \(\varepsilon \le 1\) the right side is at most \(e^{1/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi}) = 0.5262\).
Check that \(t\) is large enough. For \(\varepsilon \le 1\), \(t = c - \varepsilon/(2c) \ge c - 1/(2c)\), and this lower bound grows with \(c\). It equals 0.5262 at the positive root of \(c^2 - 0.5262c - \frac12 = 0\), which is where \(\delta = 0.7448\); since \(c\) grows as \(\delta\) shrinks, \(t \ge 0.5262\) for every \(\delta \le 0.7448\), and every \(\delta\) of practical interest qualifies.


The constant 1.25 absorbs \(e^{\varepsilon/2} \le e^{1/2}\) and the \(1/(t\sqrt{2\pi})\) factor of step 5, and the condition \(\varepsilon < 1\) keeps \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) under control. The proof made three approximations in a row, the bad-event bound, the Mills ratio and the constants, and the example follows the chain to see what each one costs.

Example 20.3 Release the diabetes count with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The sensitivity is 1, so \(c = \sqrt{2\ln(1.25\times10^5)}\) gives \(\sigma = 4.8448\) and \(t = c - 1/(2c) = 4.7416\). Table 20.3 follows the proof step by step.

The classic \(\sigma\) delivers a \(\delta\) about 240 times smaller than asked for, since \(10^{-5}/(4.11\times10^{-8}) \approx 243\). Most of the slack is in two places. The bad-event bound throws away the \(e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B]\) correction, a factor of \(1.06\times10^{-6}/(4.11\times10^{-8}) \approx 26\) here, and the constants of steps 4 and 5 lose another factor of \(10^{-5}/(1.10\times10^{-6}) \approx 9\). The Mills ratio itself costs almost nothing.

Equivalently, you could use less noise for the same \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), and Section 20.4 finds exactly how much less. The classic theorem is stated for \(\varepsilon < 1\), and its constants are designed for that range. The formula does not fail immediately above 1: at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the classic \(\sigma\) still gives a valid guarantee up to \(\varepsilon = 8.42\) and violates it beyond (Figure 20.4, right), because the classic \(\sigma\) shrinks like \(1/\varepsilon\) while the exact one shrinks more slowly. Nothing in the classic proof tells you that, so for \(\varepsilon \ge 1\) you need the exact curve.

section: 20.4 The exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism
text:
20.4 The exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism
Lemma 20.2 says that the smallest valid \(\delta\) is the bad-event probability minus the correction \(e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B]\), and Lemma 20.3 says that for Gaussian noise both terms are normal tail probabilities. So the exact \(\delta\) has a closed form, the one Divergences computed for two Gaussians with the same variance. Balle & Wang (2018) turned that observation into a calibration: instead of bounding \(\delta\), compute it exactly, and pick the smallest \(\sigma\) for which it is below the target. Section A.7 in the appendices derives the formula from scratch, with worked numbers.

Theorem 20.3 (Exact privacy profile of the Gaussian mechanism) Let \(f\) have \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2f\), reached by some neighbouring pair, and let \(M(D) = f(D) + Z\) with \(Z \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\). Write \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\). Then \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if and only if \(\delta \ge \delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\), where \[\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{20.17}\] The function \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) is strictly decreasing in \(\varepsilon\) and strictly increasing in \(\mu\). At \(\varepsilon = 0\) it is the total variation (TV) distance \(2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\) between the two output distributions, and it tends to 0 as \(\varepsilon \to \infty\).


Proof. The plan is to reduce the worst pair to one dimension, apply the two lemmas there, and show that the largest shift is the worst one; the monotonicity claims then follow from the formula.

Reduce to a shifted pair. By Lemma 20.1, for a neighbouring pair with shift \(v\) the smallest \(\delta\) at this \(\varepsilon\) is \(E_{e^\varepsilon}\big(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I_d)\|\mathcal N(v, \sigma^2I_d)\big)\).
Reduce to one dimension. Rotate coordinates so that \(v\) points along the first axis. A rotation is a bijection, so as in Lemma 20.1 it changes no divergence, and the normal distribution with independent equal-variance coordinates looks the same after any rotation (Section E.1 in the appendices proves it). Now both distributions are products: the first coordinate is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) or \(\mathcal N(\|v\|_2, \sigma^2)\), and the other \(d - 1\) coordinates have the same density \(h\) under both. The hockey-stick is the integral of \((p - \gamma q)_+\), and \((p_1h - \gamma q_1h)_+ = h\,(p_1 - \gamma q_1)_+\) because \(h \ge 0\), so integrating out the last \(d - 1\) coordinates leaves \(E_\gamma\) of the first coordinate alone. Coordinates that are identical under both hypotheses carry no evidence.
Use the two lemmas. By Lemma 20.2, \(E_{e^\varepsilon} = \Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[B]\) with \(B = \{L > \varepsilon\}\). By Lemma 20.3 with \(\mu_v = \|v\|_2/\sigma\), the loss is \(\mathcal N(\mu_v^2/2, \mu_v^2)\) under \(P\) and \(\mathcal N(-\mu_v^2/2, \mu_v^2)\) under \(Q\), so standardizing each tail gives \[\Pr_P[B] = \Phi\Big(\frac{\mu_v}2 - \frac\varepsilon{\mu_v}\Big), \qquad \Pr_Q[B] = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\mu_v}2 - \frac\varepsilon{\mu_v}\Big). \tag{20.18}\] This is Equation 20.17 with \(\mu_v\) in place of \(\mu\).
The worst pair has the largest shift. A smaller shift is harder to detect, and the proof shows that the pair with a smaller shift is a post-processing of the pair with a larger one, which cannot help anyone tell them apart. Let \(\mu' < \mu_v\), take \(Y\) from the unit-variance pair with shift \(\mu_v\), and output \(Y' = \frac{\mu'}{\mu_v}Y + W\) with independent \(W \sim \mathcal N(0, 1 - \mu'^2/\mu_v^2)\). If \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, 1)\) then \(Y'\) has mean 0 and variance \(\mu'^2/\mu_v^2 + (1 - \mu'^2/\mu_v^2) = 1\); if \(Y \sim \mathcal N(\mu_v, 1)\) the mean becomes \(\mu'\) and the variance is still 1. By the data-processing inequality of Divergences, the hockey-stick of the post-processed pair is no larger, so \(\delta_{\mu_v}(\varepsilon)\) is non-decreasing in \(\mu_v\) and the maximum over neighbours is at \(\|v\|_2 = \Delta_2f\), that is at \(\mu\).
If and only if. The hockey-stick at \(\gamma = e^\varepsilon\) is the smallest \(\delta\) that works for one pair, and steps 1 to 4 show that the pair at shift \(\Delta_2f\) is the worst. So \(\delta \ge \delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) is sufficient, since it covers the worst pair and hence all, and necessary, since any smaller \(\delta\) fails on that pair.
Monotone in \(\varepsilon\) and in \(\mu\). Exercise 3 differentiates Equation 20.17 and finds \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\varepsilon}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = -e^\varepsilon\Phi(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) < 0\) and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\mu}\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \varphi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu) > 0\).
The two ends. At \(\varepsilon = 0\) the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) is 1 and Equation 20.17 reads \(\Phi(\frac\mu2) - \Phi(-\frac\mu2) = 2\Phi(\mu/2) - 1\), which is the TV distance because the TV distance is the hockey-stick with \(\gamma = 1\). As \(\varepsilon \to \infty\) the first term \(\Phi(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu)\) goes to 0 and the second is non-negative, so \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) \to 0\).


Because \(\delta_\mu\) grows with \(\mu\), less noise always means a larger \(\delta\), and there is a single noise level that hits the target exactly.

Corollary 20.1 (Analytic calibration) For \(0 < \delta < 1\) the equation \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \delta\) has exactly one root \(\mu^*\) in \(\mu\), and \[\sigma^*(\varepsilon, \delta) = \frac{\Delta_2f}{\mu^*} \tag{20.19}\] is the smallest \(\sigma\) for which the Gaussian mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

As a function of \(\mu\), \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) is continuous, tends to 0 as \(\mu \to 0\) (both arguments of \(\Phi\) go to \(-\infty\), since there is no signal) and to 1 as \(\mu \to \infty\) (the first \(\Phi\) goes to 1 and the second to 0), and is strictly increasing by Theorem 20.3. So it crosses every \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) exactly once.
By Theorem 20.3, a noise level \(\sigma\) works exactly when \(\delta_{\Delta_2f/\sigma}(\varepsilon) \le \delta\), that is when \(\Delta_2f/\sigma \le \mu^*\), so the smallest such \(\sigma\) is \(\Delta_2f/\mu^*\).


The root is found by bisection: start with an interval of \(\mu\) whose ends put \(\delta_\mu(\varepsilon)\) on either side of \(\delta\), evaluate at the midpoint, and keep the half where the sign changes. Monotonicity is what makes this safe, since there is exactly one crossing to find. The script halves in \(\ln\mu\), because \(\mu^*\) ranges over several orders of magnitude, and 60 halvings pin it to machine precision; Exercise 4 runs it by hand.

Example 20.4 Release the diabetes count at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) with Gaussian noise. The sensitivity is 1, so the analytic calibration gives \(\sigma^* = 30.75\), the row \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) of Table 20.5. A normal variable stays within 1.96 standard deviations of its mean with probability 0.95, so the 95% error is \(1.96\sigma^* = 60.27\), against 29.96 for Laplace noise with \(\delta = 0\): for a single count, Laplace noise is better on both error and guarantee, and Section 20.5 says when the Gaussian earns its place.
To see the two terms of Equation 20.10 at work, take \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\) and measure the noise \(z\) in units of \(\sigma\). With \(\mu = 1\) the loss is \(L = \frac12 - z\), so the bad event \(B = \{L > 1\}\) is \(\{z < -\frac12\}\). Under \(M(D)\) the noise is standard normal, so \(\Pr_P[B] = \Phi(-0.5)\); under \(M(D')\) the output is centred one unit higher, so in the same coordinates \(z\) is \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\) and \(\Pr_Q[B] = \Phi(-1.5)\). text:
20.5 Laplace against Gaussian in many dimensions
Real releases are vectors: a histogram over many bins, all the marginals of a table, a gradient with millions of coordinates. The Laplace mechanism scales with \(\Delta_1f\) and the Gaussian mechanism with \(\Delta_2f\), and by Proposition 20.1 these can differ by a factor of up to \(\sqrt d\). Which noise is better depends on how one record spreads across the coordinates, and the comparison is made at the same \(\varepsilon\) by the typical error in each released number, the root-mean-square error per coordinate.

Proposition 20.3 (Laplace against Gaussian per coordinate) Let \(\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\) be the analytic \(\sigma^*\) of Corollary 20.1 for unit \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, so that \(\sigma^* = \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\) for any \(f\). At the same \(\varepsilon\), the root-mean-square errors per coordinate of the two mechanisms are \[\text{Laplace: } \frac{\sqrt2\,\Delta_1f}{\varepsilon}, \qquad \text{Gaussian: } \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta). \tag{20.20}\] For a sparse query, where one record moves one coordinate, \(\Delta_1f = \Delta_2f\), and Laplace noise is more accurate whenever \(\sqrt2 < \varepsilon\,\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\), whatever \(d\) is. For a dense query, where one record moves every coordinate by 1, \(\Delta_1f = d\) and \(\Delta_2f = \sqrt d\), and Laplace noise is more accurate only while \[d < \frac{\big(\varepsilon\,\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\big)^2}2. \tag{20.21}\]


Proof. 

Laplace error. A \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) coordinate has mean 0 and variance \(2b^2\) by Theorem 20.1, so its root-mean-square error is \(\sqrt2\,b\), which with \(b = \Delta_1f/\varepsilon\) is \(\sqrt2\,\Delta_1f/\varepsilon\).
Gaussian error. A Gaussian coordinate has variance \(\sigma^2\), so its root-mean-square error is \(\sigma\). The analytic calibration gives \(\sigma^* = \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1(\varepsilon, \delta)\), because only \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) enters Equation 20.17, so scaling the sensitivity scales the solution by the same factor.
Sparse queries. With \(\Delta_1f = \Delta_2f\), Laplace is better when \(\sqrt2\,\Delta_2f/\varepsilon < \Delta_2f\,\sigma_1\); dividing by \(\Delta_2f\) and multiplying by \(\varepsilon\) leaves \(\sqrt2 < \varepsilon\sigma_1\), with no \(d\).
Dense queries. Substituting \(\Delta_1f = d\) and \(\Delta_2f = \sqrt d\), Laplace is better when \(\sqrt2\,d/\varepsilon < \sqrt d\,\sigma_1\). Dividing both sides by \(\sqrt d\) and rearranging gives \(\sqrt d < \varepsilon\sigma_1/\sqrt2\), and squaring both sides gives the bound on \(d\).


So use Laplace noise for sparse queries and Gaussian noise for dense ones. When a record touches one coordinate, the two sensitivities agree, and the stronger guarantee of Laplace, with \(\delta = 0\), comes with less noise too. When a record touches all coordinates, \(\Delta_1f\) pays \(d\) while \(\Delta_2f\) pays \(\sqrt d\), and the Gaussian wins by a factor that grows like \(\sqrt d\) (Figure 20.5). This is why private training of neural networks uses Gaussian noise: one example’s gradient moves every coordinate of a model with millions of parameters, the densest query there is, and clipping bounds its \(\ell_2\) norm, which is exactly what the Gaussian mechanism is calibrated to.
Keep in mind that the comparison is at equal \(\varepsilon\) but unequal guarantees, since the Laplace release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP and the Gaussian release has an extra \(\delta\). The Gaussian mechanism also has a second advantage that the comparison does not show: many Gaussian releases compose into another Gaussian mechanism, exactly, because stacking independent Gaussian answers gives one Gaussian answer whose \(\ell_2\) sensitivity is the root-sum-of-squares of theirs (Exercise 5).






Figure 20.5: Root-mean-square error per count at \(\varepsilon = 1\) for the Laplace mechanism (calibrated to \(\Delta_1\)) and the Gaussian mechanism (analytic calibration to \(\Delta_2\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), as the number of released counts \(d\) grows; dots are simulations. Left: a histogram, where each record falls in one bin, so neither error depends on \(d\) and Laplace noise is smaller. Right: threshold counts, where a record can move all \(d\) counts; the Laplace error grows like \(d\), the Gaussian like \(\sqrt d\), and they cross near \(d = 7\).




Example 20.5 The hospital releases the empirical cumulative distribution function (CDF) of its patients’ ages, read off at \(d\) thresholds, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). There \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\), the value found by bisection in Section 20.4. For one count, Laplace noise has root-mean-square error \(\sqrt2 = 1.4142\) against 3.7306 for Gaussian noise, so Laplace wins. For threshold counts the crossover is at \(d = (3.7306)^2/2 = 6.96\). 20.8 References

Dwork, McSherry, Nissim & Smith, “Calibrating Noise to Sensitivity in Private Data Analysis” (TCC 2006): the paper that introduced global sensitivity and the Laplace mechanism.
Dwork, Kenthapadi, McSherry, Mironov & Naor, “Our Data, Ourselves: Privacy via Distributed Noise Generation” (EUROCRYPT 2006): approximate \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and Gaussian noise.
Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), §3.3 for the Laplace mechanism and its accuracy, and Appendix A for the classic Gaussian calibration (Theorem A.1) with its two-sided proof.
Balle & Wang, “Improving the Gaussian Mechanism for Differential Privacy: Analytical Calibration and Optimal Denoising” (ICML 2018): the exact privacy profile Equation 20.17, the bisection calibration, and why the classic formula fails for large \(\varepsilon\).
Near & Abuah, Programming Differential Privacy, the chapters on sensitivity and on the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms: the same material with code, and the practical pitfalls of computing sensitivity.
Geng & Viswanath, “The Optimal Noise-Adding Mechanism in Differential Privacy” (IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2016): the staircase mechanism, optimal for pure DP, and how close the Laplace mechanism comes to it.
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (JRSS-B 2022): the Gaussian mechanism as a trade-off curve, which is where Gaussian differential privacy takes \(\mu = \Delta_2f/\sigma\) next.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.1 The privacy loss of a composition
A differentially private system rarely answers one query: a dashboard refreshes a hundred counts, and a training run takes thousands of noisy gradient steps. Each step satisfies \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy (DP) on its own, and you need a guarantee for the whole run. Post-processing, group privacy and composition gave the first answer, basic composition: \(k\) mechanisms that are each \(\varepsilon\)-DP are together \(k\varepsilon\)-DP. For large \(k\) that answer is far too pessimistic. A hundred queries at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) give \(k\varepsilon = 10\), which lets an observer multiply its odds between two neighbouring datasets by up to \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\). Yet at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the same hundred queries are \((4.31, 10^{-5})\)-DP, and no analysis that knows only each query’s \(\varepsilon\) can say less.
The one idea behind the gap is that the privacy loss of a composition is a sum. Each output is evidence for one dataset or the other, measured by the logarithm of how much likelier the output is under \(D\) than under its neighbour \(D'\), and the evidence of \(k\) outputs adds up. Basic composition charges the largest value that sum can take, as if every step produced its worst output. But a sum of \(k\) bounded random terms rarely strays from its mean by more than a multiple of \(\sqrt k\). Allowing a small \(\delta\) lets you ignore the rare extreme sums and charge for the typical one, and that is advanced composition. The best bound of this kind, optimal composition, can be computed exactly, because randomized response is the mechanism whose composition is hardest to protect. Both survive an analyst who chooses each query after seeing the earlier answers, which is adaptive composition.
The running example is the dashboard: \(k = 100\) counts, each released by a mechanism that is \(0.1\)-DP, under add/remove neighbours. Basic composition charges \(\varepsilon = 10\), advanced composition 5.85 at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), and optimal composition 4.31, and the chapter derives all three from the distribution of the total privacy loss.
Every bound in this chapter is a statement about one random variable, the total privacy loss of the run. This section defines it, shows that it is a sum over the steps, and works out its distribution for composed randomized response, which Section 21.3 proves is the worst case.
The evidence an output carries is the logarithm of how much likelier it is under \(D\) than under \(D'\): positive when it favours \(D\), negative when it favours \(D'\), zero when it says nothing.
\((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP asks that \(\Pr_P[S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S] + \delta\) for every set of outputs \(S\); with \(\delta = 0\) this says \(|L| \le \varepsilon\) for every output (The definition of differential privacy). For one ordered pair of datasets, the smallest \(\delta\) that works at a given \(\varepsilon\) is the largest gap \(\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_Q[S]\), which Divergences shows is reached on the outputs with \(p(y) > e^\varepsilon q(y)\). That largest gap is the hockey-stick divergence, \[\delta(\varepsilon) = E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+, \qquad (x)_+ = \max\{x, 0\}, \tag{21.2}\] and as a function of \(\varepsilon\) it is the privacy profile of the pair in one direction. DP asks for it in both directions, for every pair of neighbours.
The smallest case is randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) (The definition of differential privacy), which reports a person’s bit truthfully with probability \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flips it otherwise. For a person whose bit is 0 in \(D\) and 1 in \(D'\), at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), a report of 0 has probability \(\frac34\) under \(D\) and \(\frac14\) under \(D'\), so its loss is \(\ln 3\), and a report of 1 has loss \(-\ln 3\). The first lemma says that the profile is an average of a function of the loss, so a composition theorem only has to control the distribution of the total loss.
An output whose loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) contributes nothing to \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and an output that is impossible under \(D'\) contributes its whole probability. For randomized response at \(\ln 3\), the lemma at \(\varepsilon = 0\) gives \(\delta(0) = \frac34(1 - \frac13) = \frac12\), the total variation distance \(\frac34 - \frac14\), as it should. Advanced composition uses the tail bound of the lemma, and optimal composition uses the equality.
Now run \(k\) mechanisms. The probability of a whole sequence of outputs is built one step at a time, and the logarithm turns that product into a sum.
Table 21.1 shows the sum for two independent rounds of randomized response at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\): the output \((0, 1)\) has loss 0 because one report favours \(D\) as much as the other favours \(D'\).
For randomized response the sum is a random walk with steps \(\pm\varepsilon\), and its whole distribution can be written down. A report of 0 is the truth under \(D\), so it points to \(D\); under \(D\) a report points to \(D'\) only when it is a lie.
For small \(\varepsilon\), \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2) \approx \varepsilon/2\), so the mean is about \(k\varepsilon^2/2\) and the standard deviation about \(\sqrt k\,\varepsilon\), both far below the worst case \(k\varepsilon\), which needs all \(k\) reports to be truthful. Basic composition guards against an event that will never happen.
By the central limit theorem the total loss is nearly normal (Figure 21.1), the starting point of the Gaussian view of privacy in Privacy accounting. Advanced composition bounds its tail, and optimal composition evaluates Equation 21.3 on the binomial exactly.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
Definition 21.1 (The privacy loss random variable) Let \(M\) be a mechanism and \(D \sim D'\) two neighbouring datasets. Write \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) for the two output distributions, with mass functions or densities \(p\) and \(q\). The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the log-ratio \(L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\big(p(y)/q(y)\big)\), which is \(+\infty\) where \(q(y) = 0 < p(y)\), and the privacy loss random variable is the loss of a random output drawn under \(D\), \[L = L_{D,D'}(Y) = \ln\frac{p(Y)}{q(Y)}, \qquad Y \sim P. \tag{21.1}\] Its distribution is the privacy loss distribution of the pair. Once the pair is fixed, \(L(y)\) is short for \(L_{D,D'}(y)\).




Lemma 21.1 (The privacy profile is an average of the privacy loss) For every pair \((P, Q)\) and every \(\varepsilon \ge 0\), \[\delta(\varepsilon) = E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \sum_y\big(p(y) - e^\varepsilon q(y)\big)_+ = \mathbb E\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] \le \Pr[L > \varepsilon], \tag{21.3}\] where the expectation and the probability are over \(Y \sim P\). In particular, \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) depends on the pair only through the distribution of \(L\) under \(P\).


Proof. 

Factor out \(p\). Each term of the hockey-stick sum is \((p - e^\varepsilon q)_+ = p\,(1 - e^\varepsilon q/p)_+\), and the ratio in the bracket is \(e^\varepsilon q/p = e^{\varepsilon - \ln(p/q)} = e^{\varepsilon - L(y)}\). A sum of \(p(y)\) times a function of \(y\) is the expectation of that function when \(Y \sim P\), which gives the equality with the expectation. An output with \(q = 0\) has \(L = +\infty\) and bracket 1, as it should.
Bound the bracket. When \(L \le \varepsilon\) the exponent \(\varepsilon - L\) is non-negative, so \(e^{\varepsilon - L} \ge 1\) and the bracket is 0. When \(L > \varepsilon\) the bracket is \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\), which lies strictly between 0 and 1. So the bracket is at most the indicator \(\mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon]\), and its average is at most \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon]\).





Lemma 21.2 (The privacy loss of a composition is a sum) Run \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) in sequence, where \(M_i\) may depend on the earlier outputs \(y_{<i} = (y_1, \dots, y_{i-1})\). Write \(p_i(y_i \mid y_{<i})\) for the probability that step \(i\) outputs \(y_i\) on \(D\) after the history \(y_{<i}\), and \(q_i(y_i \mid y_{<i})\) for the same on \(D'\). Then the privacy loss of the whole sequence is the sum of the per-step losses, \[L(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \sum_{i=1}^k L_i(y_i \mid y_{<i}), \qquad L_i(y_i \mid y_{<i}) = \ln\frac{p_i(y_i \mid y_{<i})}{q_i(y_i \mid y_{<i})}, \tag{21.4}\] where \(L_i\) is the privacy loss of step \(i\) alone, for the mechanism that was run after that history. If step \(i\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every history, then \(|L_i| \le \varepsilon\), and so \(|L| \le k\varepsilon\).


Proof. 

Chain rule. The probability of a sequence of outputs is the probability of \(y_1\), times the probability of \(y_2\) given \(y_1\), and so on. So the joint output has probability \(p(y_1, \dots, y_k) = \prod_i p_i(y_i \mid y_{<i})\) on \(D\), and likewise with \(q_i\) on \(D'\).
Log of a ratio of products. The ratio of the two products is the product of the step-by-step ratios, and the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms, which is Equation 21.4.
Basic composition. If step \(i\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP whatever the history, each term lies in \([-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\), and adding \(k\) such bounds gives \(|L| \le k\varepsilon\).

Proposition 21.1 (The loss of composed randomized response) Compose \(k\) independent rounds of randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\), on a person whose bit is 0 in \(D\) and 1 in \(D'\), and let \(J\) be the number of rounds whose report points to \(D'\). Under \(D\), \[J \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, 1 - t), \qquad L = (k - 2J)\varepsilon, \tag{21.5}\] and the loss has mean, variance and worst-case probability \[\mathbb E[L] = k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2), \qquad \operatorname{Var}(L) = k\varepsilon^2\big(1 - \tanh^2(\varepsilon/2)\big), \qquad \Pr[L = k\varepsilon] = t^k. \tag{21.6}\]


Proof. The plan is to find the loss of one round, add \(k\) of them, and then compute the mean and variance of one round and multiply by \(k\).

One round. A truthful report has probability \(t\) under \(D\) and \(1 - t\) under \(D'\), so its loss is \(\ln\frac{t}{1 - t} = \ln e^\varepsilon = \varepsilon\), because \(t/(1 - t) = e^\varepsilon\) by the definition of \(t\). A lie has the two probabilities swapped and loss \(-\varepsilon\).
\(k\) rounds. By Lemma 21.2 the total is the sum of the \(k\) per-round losses. The \(J\) rounds that point to \(D'\) contribute \(-\varepsilon\) each and the other \(k - J\) contribute \(+\varepsilon\), so \(L = (k - J)\varepsilon - J\varepsilon = (k - 2J)\varepsilon\). Each round points to \(D'\) exactly when it lies, independently with probability \(1 - t\), so \(J\) counts the successes in \(k\) independent trials and is binomial.
Mean. One round has mean \(\varepsilon t - \varepsilon(1 - t) = \varepsilon(2t - 1)\). Substituting \(t\) gives \(2t - 1 = \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1}{e^\varepsilon + 1}\), and this is \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), because \(\tanh x = \frac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^{2x} + 1}\). The mean of a sum is the sum of the means, so multiply by \(k\).
Variance. One round takes the two values \(\pm\varepsilon\), so its square is always \(\varepsilon^2\) and its variance is \(\varepsilon^2 - (\text{mean})^2 = \varepsilon^2(1 - \tanh^2(\varepsilon/2))\). Variances of independent terms add, so the total variance is \(k\) times this.
The worst case. The value \(L = k\varepsilon\) needs \(J = 0\), every report truthful, which has probability \(t^k\).










Figure 21.1: The total privacy loss of 100 rounds of randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), under \(D\), with its mean, the optimal and advanced \(\varepsilon'\) at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), and basic composition’s \(k\varepsilon = 10\).




Example 21.1 Release each of the dashboard’s \(k = 100\) counts by randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the worst \(0.1\)-DP mechanism by Section 21.3. Each round is truthful with probability \(t = e^{0.1}/(1 + e^{0.1}) = 0.5250\). By Proposition 21.1 the total loss has mean \(100 \times 0.1\tanh(0.05) = 0.4996\) and standard deviation 0.9988. Basic composition’s \(k\varepsilon = 10\) sits \((10 - 0.50)/1.00 = 9.5\) standard deviations above the mean, and it needs all 100 reports to be truthful, which has probability \(t^{100} = 1.0\times10^{-28}\). The loss \((100 - 2J) \times 0.1\) exceeds 4 only when \(J < 30\), about 3.5 standard deviations of \(J\) (which are 5) below its mean \(100(1 - t) = 47.5\). The optimal \(\varepsilon'\) at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) that Section 21.4 computes, 4.3068, sits \((4.3068 - 0.4996)/0.9988 = 3.8\) standard deviations above the mean of the loss.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.2 Advanced composition
Advanced composition, due to Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan (2010), charges for the typical value of the sum rather than its largest: it needs only each step’s \(\varepsilon\), holds for mechanisms chosen in any adaptive way, and grows like \(\sqrt k\). Its tool is Azuma’s inequality, a version of Hoeffding’s inequality for sums whose terms may depend on the earlier terms. Azuma controls how far the sum strays from its mean, so the theorem also needs a bound on the mean of each term, the drift of the sum, and that bound comes first.
The loss can be as large as \(\varepsilon\), but on average it is much smaller: when \(\varepsilon\) is small, positive and negative losses nearly cancel, and what is left is of order \(\varepsilon^2\). The average loss under \(P\) is \(\sum_y p(y)\ln(p(y)/q(y))\), the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) of Divergences.

Lemma 21.3 (The mean privacy loss of an ε-DP pair is second order in ε) If \(|L| \le \varepsilon\) for every output, then \[\mathbb E[L] = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{21.7}\]


Proof. 

Symmetrize. The KL divergence is never negative (Divergences): by Jensen’s inequality for the concave logarithm, \(-D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P) = \sum_y q\ln(p/q) \le \ln\sum_y q\,(p/q) = \ln 1 = 0\). So adding \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P) \ge 0\) to \(\mathbb E[L]\) can only increase it, and the two sums combine term by term: \[\mathbb E[L] \le \sum_y p\ln\frac pq + \sum_y q\ln\frac qp = \sum_y (p - q)\ln\frac pq. \tag{21.8}\]
Use the bound on the loss. Each \(|\ln(p/q)|\) is at most \(\varepsilon\), so the sum is at most \(\varepsilon\sum_y|p - q|\), and the total difference \(\sum_y|p - q|\) is itself small when \(P\) and \(Q\) are close.
Bound the total difference. Write \(\sum_y|p - q| = \sum_y q\,|p/q - 1|\). The ratio \(p/q\) lies in \([e^{-\varepsilon}, e^\varepsilon]\), and on that interval \(|p/q - 1|\) is largest at the upper end, where it is \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) (at the lower end it is \(1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\), which is smaller). Since the \(q(y)\) sum to 1, \(\sum_y|p - q| \le e^\varepsilon - 1\), and the bound follows.


So the mean is of order \(\varepsilon^2\): at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) the bound is \(0.1(e^{0.1} - 1) = 0.0105\), but it is not tight: Theorem 21.3 in Section 21.3 gives the best bound, \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), which is 0.0050 at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and 0.4621 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), where the lemma gives 1.7183. Section B.2 in the appendices derives the same bound from scratch for a single count, with every number shown.

Theorem 21.1 (Advanced composition (Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan 2010)) Fix \(k\) and \(\varepsilon > 0\) in advance, and let \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) be mechanisms, each chosen after seeing the earlier outputs, such that every \(M_i\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every history. Then for every \(\delta' > 0\) the composition is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{21.9}\]


Proof. The plan is to write the loss as a sum, centre each term by its conditional mean to get a martingale, bound the fluctuation of the martingale by Azuma’s inequality and the drift by Lemma 21.3, and convert the tail bound into a \(\delta\) by Lemma 21.1.

The loss is a sum. By Lemma 21.2, \(L = \sum_i L_i\), where \(L_i\) is the loss of step \(i\) given the history \(y_{<i}\).
Each term is bounded, given the past. For every fixed history, step \(i\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, so \(L_i \in [-\varepsilon, \varepsilon]\).
Each term has a small conditional mean. Given the history, the average of \(L_i\) over step \(i\)’s output is \(m_i = \mathbb E[L_i \mid y_{<i}] = \sum_{y_i}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i)\), the KL divergence of step \(i\)’s pair. So \(m_i \le \varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) by Lemma 21.3.
Centre the terms to get a martingale. A martingale is a running sum whose next increment has mean zero given everything that happened before. Subtracting each term’s conditional mean makes one: \(W_k = \sum_i(L_i - m_i)\) has increments with conditional mean zero. Given the past, \(L_i - m_i\) lies in \([-\varepsilon - m_i, \varepsilon - m_i]\), an interval of length \(c_i = 2\varepsilon\), whose position depends on the past but whose length does not.
Azuma. The Azuma–Hoeffding inequality of Concentration inequalities says that if each increment of a martingale has conditional mean zero and lies, given the past, in an interval of length \(c_i\) fixed in advance, then the sum exceeds \(s\) with probability at most \(\exp(-2s^2/\sum_i c_i^2)\). It holds because Hoeffding’s lemma bounds each increment’s conditional moment generating function using only its mean and the length of its range, and these bounds multiply one step at a time. With \(c_i = 2\varepsilon\), so that \(\sum_i c_i^2 = 4k\varepsilon^2\), \[\Pr[W_k \ge s] \le \exp\left(-\frac{2s^2}{4k\varepsilon^2}\right) = \exp\left(-\frac{s^2}{2k\varepsilon^2}\right). \tag{21.10}\]
Choose the level. Setting the right side to \(\delta'\) and solving, \(s^2 = 2k\varepsilon^2\ln(1/\delta')\), gives \(s = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\). The loss is the fluctuation plus the drift, \(L = W_k + \sum_i m_i \le W_k + k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\). So if \(L\) exceeds \(\varepsilon' = s + k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), then \(W_k\) must exceed \(s\), and \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon'] \le \delta'\).
Convert. By Lemma 21.1, \(\delta(\varepsilon') \le \Pr[L > \varepsilon'] \le \delta'\). The same argument with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped gives the other direction, so the composition is \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP.


The gain is \(\sqrt k\) instead of \(k\). The price is \(\delta'\) and the factor \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta')}\), which is \(\sqrt{2 \times 11.51} = 4.80\) at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), so the theorem beats basic composition only once \(k\) is large. Dividing both bounds by \(\varepsilon\) and squaring, which needs \(\varepsilon < \ln 2\) so that \(2 - e^\varepsilon > 0\), gives the crossover (Exercise 2): \[k > \frac{2\ln(1/\delta')}{(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2}. \tag{21.11}\] Setting the leading term equal to a target \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}\) gives each step \(\varepsilon \approx \varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}/\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}\), where basic composition would allow only \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}/k\). Corollary 21.1 in Section 21.4 extends the theorem to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP steps at a cost of \(k\delta\), with the sharper drift \(k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\).
The bound is loose in three places: Azuma assumes each increment has the largest variance its range allows, the mean bound of Lemma 21.3 is a factor 2 too large for small \(\varepsilon\), and the tail bound of Lemma 21.1 counts every output above \(\varepsilon'\) in full. At \(k = 100\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the exact \(\delta\) at the advanced \(\varepsilon' = 5.85\) is \(1.96\times10^{-9}\), not \(10^{-5}\).

Example 21.2 Take the dashboard’s \(k = 100\) counts at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\). The Azuma term is \(0.1\sqrt{200\ln10^5} = 0.1\sqrt{2302.6} = 4.7985\), and the mean term is \(100 \times 0.1(e^{0.1} - 1) = 1.0517\), so \(\varepsilon' = 5.8502\), against 10 for basic composition. The crossover is \(23.03/0.8948^2 = 28.8\), so advanced composition wins from \(k = 29\) on (Figure 21.2, and Table 21.4 in Section 21.4). At \(k = 10{,}000\) the mean term dominates: it costs 105 of the total 153, against 48 for the Azuma term, and the sharper drift of Corollary 21.1 costs 50 instead.
Laplace noise in many dimensions. The same arithmetic explains why the Gaussian mechanism wins in high dimension. Take \(d\) dense counts, where one record can move every count by 1, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Laplace noise of scale \(b\) has root-mean-square error \(\sqrt2\,b\), and on the whole vector it must use the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(d\), so \(b = d/\varepsilon\). Composing \(d\) separate Laplace mechanisms instead, at the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) whose composition stays at 1, gives error \(\sqrt2/\varepsilon_0\): for \(d = 1000\), \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.00645\) by Equation 21.9, or \(0.00849\) by the optimal composition of Section 21.4. Table 21.2 adds the Gaussian mechanism of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. Composed Laplace noise grows like \(\sqrt d\) and stays within a factor of 1.9 of the Gaussian, while pure-DP Laplace noise falls behind by a factor of 38 at \(d = 10{,}000\). So the \(\sqrt d\) gain comes from allowing \(\delta > 0\), not from the Gaussian density.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.3 The worst mechanism
Advanced composition is one bound among many, and the question is which is best. Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath (2015) answered it with post-processing: every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is a post-processing of one version of randomized response, so no composition of such mechanisms can be worse than composed randomized response. This section builds that mechanism and proves the reduction, and Section 21.4 composes it.
A channel \(K\) is a table of probabilities \(K(y \mid z)\): given an input \(z\), it draws an output \(y\) without looking at the data, and feeding a distribution \(P^\star\) through it gives \(P^\star K(y) = \sum_z P^\star(z)K(y \mid z)\). The data-processing inequality of Divergences says that a channel never increases the hockey-stick divergence or the KL divergence. For the hockey-stick the reason is short: the gap \(P^\star K(S) - e^{\varepsilon'}Q^\star K(S)\) on a set \(S\) is \(\sum_z K(S \mid z)\big(P^\star(z) - e^{\varepsilon'}Q^\star(z)\big)\) with weights in \([0, 1]\), so it is at most the sum of the positive brackets, which is the hockey-stick before the channel.
The worst mechanism must spend both parameters. It spends \(\delta\) by announcing, with probability \(\delta\), which dataset it ran on, and \(\varepsilon\) by otherwise running randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\).

Definition 21.2 (The four-point randomized response) The four-point pair \((P^\star, Q^\star)\) at level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is the pair of output distributions in Table 21.3: with probability \(\delta\) the mechanism announces its dataset outright, and otherwise it reports the person’s bit through randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\), with \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).
