Every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP pair can be produced from the four-point pair by one channel, and for \(\delta = 0\) the channel has a closed form.

Theorem 21.2 (Randomized response is the worst (ε, δ)-DP mechanism) Let \((P, Q)\) be a pair of distributions on a common set of outputs that satisfies \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP in both directions. Then there is a channel \(K\) with \(P = P^\star K\) and \(Q = Q^\star K\), where \((P^\star, Q^\star)\) is the four-point pair of Definition 21.2. For \(\delta = 0\) the channel is \[K(y \mid 0) = \frac{e^\varepsilon p(y) - q(y)}{e^\varepsilon - 1}, \qquad K(y \mid 1) = \frac{e^\varepsilon q(y) - p(y)}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{21.12}\]


Proof. For \(\delta = 0\), solve for the channel and check that it reproduces the pair; for \(\delta > 0\), the last step says why the channel exists and where it is built.

Solve for the channel. Plain randomized response outputs 0, the report that points to \(D\), with probability \(t\) on \(D\) and \(1 - t\) on \(D'\). So the channel must satisfy, for every output \(y\) of the target pair, \(p(y) = tK(y \mid 0) + (1 - t)K(y \mid 1)\) and \(q(y) = (1 - t)K(y \mid 0) + tK(y \mid 1)\). These are two linear equations in the two unknowns \(K(y \mid 0)\) and \(K(y \mid 1)\), and solving them with \(t/(1 - t) = e^\varepsilon\) gives Equation 21.12.
The rows are distributions. A channel’s rows must be non-negative and sum to 1. \(K(y \mid 0) \ge 0\) exactly when \(e^\varepsilon p(y) \ge q(y)\), and \(K(y \mid 1) \ge 0\) exactly when \(e^\varepsilon q(y) \ge p(y)\). Both hold for every \(y\) because the pair is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Since \(p\) and \(q\) each sum to 1, each row sums to \((e^\varepsilon - 1)/(e^\varepsilon - 1) = 1\).
They reproduce \(P\). Mixing the rows with randomized response’s probabilities on \(D\) gives \[t\,K(y \mid 0) + (1 - t)K(y \mid 1) = \frac{\big(te^\varepsilon - (1 - t)\big)p(y) + \big((1 - t)e^\varepsilon - t\big)q(y)}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{21.13}\] With \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), \((1 - t)e^\varepsilon = t\), so the coefficient of \(q\) is 0. The coefficient of \(p\) is \(\frac{te^\varepsilon - (1 - t)}{e^\varepsilon - 1} = \frac{(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1)/(1 + e^\varepsilon)}{e^\varepsilon - 1} = 1\), since \(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1 = (e^\varepsilon - 1)(e^\varepsilon + 1)\).
They reproduce \(Q\). The same computation with \(t\) and \(1 - t\) swapped.
The case \(\delta > 0\), cited. The trade-off function of a pair gives, for each false positive rate, the smallest false negative rate any test between \(P\) and \(Q\) can reach. The definition of differential privacy shows that a pair is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when its trade-off function lies above a boundary \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) made of two straight lines, on which the four-point pair sits (Figure 21.3, left). So every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP pair is at least as hard to test as \((P^\star, Q^\star)\), at every level. Blackwell’s theorem (1953) says that a pair is at least as hard to test as another at every level exactly when it is a post-processing of the other. Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath (2015) construct the channel, and Section J.1 in the appendices derives it step by step, by splitting each distribution into an \(\varepsilon\)-DP part of mass \(1 - \delta\) and a leftover of mass \(\delta\).








Figure 21.3: Left: the boundaries \(f_{\varepsilon,\delta}\) at \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) with \(\delta = 0\) and \(0.1\), attained by randomized response, and a Laplace mechanism’s trade-off curve inside the allowed region. Right: the pair of Example 21.3 and the two rows of its channel.



The same reduction sharpens the drift term of advanced composition, because the KL divergence, like the hockey-stick, can only shrink under a channel.

Theorem 21.3 (The sharp mean loss) If the pair \((P, Q)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP in both directions, then \[\mathbb E[L] = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2), \tag{21.14}\] with equality for randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\).


Proof. 

Reduce to randomized response. By Theorem 21.2 with \(\delta = 0\), the pair is a post-processing of randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) through the channel Equation 21.12. Passing two distributions through the same channel can only make them more alike, which is the data-processing inequality for the KL divergence, so \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) is at most the KL divergence of randomized response.
The KL divergence of randomized response. Its mean loss is \(\varepsilon t - \varepsilon(1 - t) = \varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), by step 3 of the proof of Proposition 21.1 with \(k = 1\), and randomized response itself reaches it.



Example 21.3 The dashboard’s randomized-response steps need no channel, so take another pair: \(P = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\) and \(Q = (0.2, 0.3, 0.5)\) have largest loss \(\ln(0.5/0.2) = \ln 2.5 = 0.9163\), below \(\ln 3 = 1.0986\), so the pair is \(\ln 3\)-DP. With \(e^\varepsilon = 3\), Equation 21.12 gives \(K(\cdot \mid 0) = (3P - Q)/2 = (0.65, 0.30, 0.05)\) and \(K(\cdot \mid 1) = (3Q - P)/2 = (0.05, 0.30, 0.65)\) (Figure 21.3, right). Randomized response at \(\ln 3\) has \(t = \frac34\), and the first output comes back as \(\frac34 \times 0.65 + \frac14 \times 0.05 = 0.5\). As Theorem 21.3 requires, the pair’s KL divergence, \(0.5\ln 2.5 + 0.3\ln 1 + 0.2\ln 0.4 = 0.2749\), is below randomized response’s \(\ln 3 \times \frac12 = 0.5493\), and its \(\delta(0)\), the total variation \(0.5 - 0.2 = 0.3\), is below 0.5.

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.4 Optimal composition
With the worst mechanism in hand, the best bound for \(k\) mechanisms known only by their \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is the exact profile of \(k\) copies of the four-point pair. Either some step raises a flag, and the output counts in full, or none does, and the loss is binomial by Equation 21.5. Lemma 21.1 turns that binomial loss into a \(\delta\), written \(\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon')\).

Theorem 21.4 (Optimal composition (Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath 2015)) For every composition of \(k\) mechanisms that are each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, adaptive or not, and every \(\varepsilon' \ge 0\), \[\delta(\varepsilon') \le 1 - (1 - \delta)^k\big(1 - \delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon')\big), \qquad \delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon') = \sum_{j=0}^k\binom kj t^{k-j}(1 - t)^j\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon' - (k - 2j)\varepsilon}\big)_+, \tag{21.15}\] with equality for \(k\) independent copies of the four-point pair. The binomial weight \(\binom kj t^{k-j}(1 - t)^j\) is the probability that exactly \(j\) of the \(k\) reports point to \(D'\). At the points where \(\varepsilon'\) equals one of the values the loss can take, \(\varepsilon' = (k - 2i)\varepsilon\) for \(i = 0, \dots, \lfloor k/2\rfloor\), the positive part can be dropped and the sum becomes a ratio of exponentials, \[\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}\big((k - 2i)\varepsilon\big) = \frac{\sum_{\ell=0}^{i-1}\binom k\ell\big(e^{(k-\ell)\varepsilon} - e^{(k - 2i + \ell)\varepsilon}\big)}{(1 + e^\varepsilon)^k}, \tag{21.16}\] which is the formula of Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath’s main theorem.


Proof. The plan is to show that a composition, adaptive or not, is a post-processing of \(k\) independent four-point pairs, so that the data-processing inequality reduces the bound to the four-point product, and then to evaluate Lemma 21.1 on that product.

Non-adaptive. If step \(i\) is \(P_i = P^\star K_i\) and \(Q_i = Q^\star K_i\) by Theorem 21.2, then the product \(P_1 \times \dots \times P_k\) is \((P^\star)^k\) followed by the channel that applies \(K_i\) to coordinate \(i\), independently. So \(\delta(\varepsilon')\) of the composition is at most that of \((P^\star)^k\) against \((Q^\star)^k\), by the data-processing inequality.
Adaptive. Now the mechanism of step \(i\), and so its channel \(K_i^{y_{<i}}\), may depend on the earlier outputs. The trick is to draw all the four-point outputs \(z_i\) first and apply the channels afterwards. Draw \(z_1, \dots, z_k\) from \((P^\star)^k\), then \(y_1 \sim K_1(\cdot \mid z_1)\), then \(y_2 \sim K_2^{y_1}(\cdot \mid z_2)\), and so on. Given \(y_{<i}\), \(z_i\) is still a fresh draw from \(P^\star\), because it was drawn independently of \(z_{<i}\) and \(y_{<i}\) depends only on those. So \(y_i\) has law \(P^\star K_i^{y_{<i}} = P_i(\cdot \mid y_{<i})\), and the sequence has exactly the law of the adaptive run on \(D\). The same sampler fed with \((Q^\star)^k\) produces the run on \(D'\), so the adaptive run is still one post-processing of \((P^\star)^k\) against \((Q^\star)^k\).
The four-point product. With probability \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k\) some coordinate of \((P^\star)^k\) shows “flag \(D\)”, which \((Q^\star)^k\) never produces, so there \(L = +\infty\), the bracket \((1 - e^{\varepsilon' - L})_+\) is 1, and the output contributes its full probability to Equation 21.3. Outputs with “flag \(D'\)” have probability 0 under \((P^\star)^k\). Otherwise, with probability \((1 - \delta)^k\), all coordinates are plain randomized response; the factor \((1 - \delta)\) per coordinate cancels in the ratio, so \(L = (k - 2J)\varepsilon\) by Equation 21.5, and Lemma 21.1 on this part gives \((1 - \delta)^k\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon')\). Adding the two parts gives \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k + (1 - \delta)^k\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}(\varepsilon')\), which is Equation 21.15.
Equality. The four-point pair is itself a mechanism, on a dataset of one bit, and it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Composing \(k\) independent copies of it gives equality, so no better bound can hold for the whole class.
The grid formula. At \(\varepsilon' = (k - 2i)\varepsilon\), the terms of \(\delta_{\mathrm{RR}}\) with \(j \ge i\) vanish, because their loss \((k - 2j)\varepsilon\) is at most \(\varepsilon'\) and the bracket is 0. For \(j = \ell < i\) the bracket is positive and the positive part can be dropped. Since \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and \(1 - t = 1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), the weight is \(\binom k\ell t^{k-\ell}(1-t)^\ell = \binom k\ell e^{(k-\ell)\varepsilon}/(1 + e^\varepsilon)^k\). Multiplying it by \(e^{\varepsilon' - (k - 2\ell)\varepsilon} = e^{(2\ell - 2i)\varepsilon}\) turns \(e^{(k-\ell)\varepsilon}\) into \(e^{(k - 2i + \ell)\varepsilon}\), which is Equation 21.16.


“Optimal” means optimal for the class: Equation 21.15 is the best you can say about \(k\) mechanisms if all you know about each is its \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). A Laplace mechanism with the same \(\varepsilon\) does a little better, because its loss often lies strictly inside \((-\varepsilon, \varepsilon)\): its mean loss at \(\varepsilon = 1\) is 0.3679, against 0.4621 for randomized response.
A single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) also throws information away. The privacy loss of a Gaussian step is normal (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms), so \(k\) steps with noise \(\sigma\) on a sensitivity-1 query have exactly the loss of one step with noise \(\sigma/\sqrt k\) (Exercise 6). Figure 21.4 shows what a point summary costs: with \(\sigma = 20\), \(k = 1{,}000\) steps are exactly \((7.51, 10^{-5})\)-DP, but the best per-step split of \(\delta\) followed by optimal composition gives 62.7. Composing the curves themselves is the subject of Privacy accounting.






Figure 21.4: Total \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) after \(k\) Gaussian steps with \(\sigma = 20\) on a sensitivity-1 query. Three curves summarize each step by one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) point and compose it with basic, advanced or optimal composition; the dashed curve is the exact composition, one Gaussian step with noise \(\sigma/\sqrt k\).



The four-point product also extends advanced composition to steps with \(\delta > 0\), and with the sharper drift: the flags cost their probability, and the rest is randomized response.

Corollary 21.1 (Advanced composition for (ε, δ)-DP steps, with the sharp drift) Fix \(k\), \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \ge 0\) in advance, and let \(M_1, \dots, M_k\) be mechanisms, each chosen after seeing the earlier outputs, such that every \(M_i\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for every history. Then for every \(\delta' > 0\) the composition is \((\varepsilon', k\delta + \delta')\)-DP with \(\varepsilon'\) from Equation 21.9, and also with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2). \tag{21.17}\]


Proof. 

Reduce to the four-point product. By step 2 of the proof of Theorem 21.4, the adaptive run is a post-processing of \(k\) independent copies of the four-point pair, and a channel never increases \(\delta(\varepsilon')\), so it suffices to bound the \(k\)-fold four-point product.
The flags. Some coordinate shows “flag \(D\)” with probability \(1 - (1 - \delta)^k\), which is at most \(k\delta\) because the chance that at least one of \(k\) events happens is at most the sum of their chances (Exercise 4 proves the inequality). Those outputs are impossible under \(D'\) and contribute their whole probability to \(\delta(\varepsilon')\), so the flags cost at most \(k\delta\).
The rest. Otherwise all \(k\) coordinates are plain randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\), which are \(k\) independent \(\varepsilon\)-DP steps, so Theorem 21.1 bounds their contribution at the \(\varepsilon'\) of Equation 21.9 by \(\delta'\). Their drift is exactly \(k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\) by Proposition 21.1, so step 6 of that proof with this drift in place of \(k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) gives the same \(\delta'\) at the \(\varepsilon'\) of Equation 21.17. Adding the two parts gives \(k\delta + \delta'\).



Example 21.4 For the dashboard’s \(k = 100\) steps at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) is 4.3068, and the sharper advanced bound of Equation 21.17 is \(4.7985 + 0.4996 = 5.2981\). The optimal value is 19% below it (\(4.3068/5.2981 = 0.81\)), 26% below the original advanced bound (\(4.3068/5.8502 = 0.74\)) and 57% below basic composition’s 10. Table 21.4 compares the four bounds over \(k\); at \(k = 10\), below the crossover, both advanced bounds are worse than basic composition, while the optimal bound is slightly better, 0.994 against 1. If each step also has \(\delta = 5\times10^{-8}\), the flags use up \(1 - (1 - \delta)^{100} = 5.0\times10^{-6}\) of a total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and the optimal \(\varepsilon'\) rises to 4.4469; advanced composition with the remaining \(\delta' = 5\times10^{-6}\) gives 5.9926.

With a different \(\varepsilon_i\) per step the loss depends on which steps lied, not just how many, and the exact bound is #P-complete to compute (Murtagh & Vadhan, 2016); for a few steps you can still enumerate (Exercise 7).

title: 21  Advanced and optimal composition
text:
21.5 Adaptive composition
In practice the next query depends on the last answer: an analyst zooms into the largest bin of a noisy histogram, and a training loop computes each gradient at parameters that came from earlier noisy gradients. The proofs above were written to cover this; this section makes the model explicit, collects the guarantees in one statement, and says where adaptivity does break things.

Definition 21.3 (The k-fold adaptive composition experiment) An adversary plays \(k\) rounds against a hidden bit \(b \in \{0, 1\}\), fixed for the whole run (Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan 2010). In round \(i\) it looks at the outputs \(y_1, \dots, y_{i-1}\) so far and, as any function of them, chooses a pair of neighbouring datasets \(D_i^0 \sim D_i^1\) and a mechanism \(M_i\) from a class of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanisms; it then receives \(y_i \sim M_i(D_i^b)\). Everything the adversary sees, its view, is the sequence \(V = (y_1, \dots, y_k)\). A composition theorem holds for the experiment when, for every adversary, the distributions of the view under \(b = 0\) and under \(b = 1\) satisfy its guarantee in both directions.

The claim is that every bound of this chapter holds in the experiment.

Theorem 21.5 (Every composition bound holds under adaptive choice) In the experiment of Definition 21.3, with \(k\), \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) fixed before the interaction starts, the views under \(b = 0\) and \(b = 1\) satisfy basic composition, \((k\varepsilon, k\delta)\)-DP; advanced composition, \((\varepsilon', k\delta + \delta')\)-DP with \(\varepsilon'\) from Equation 21.9 or Equation 21.17; and optimal composition, Equation 21.15.


Proof. Every argument above looked at one step at a time, given the history so far, and once the history is fixed, so is the adversary’s choice.

The loss of the view is a sum. Lemma 21.2 applies with each term \(L_i(y_i \mid y_{<i})\) computed for the mechanism and the pair of datasets chosen after \(y_{<i}\). Nothing in Lemma 21.1, Lemma 21.2 or Lemma 21.3 needs the pair to be the same in every round; each step only needs its own pair to be neighbours.
Basic composition. For \(\delta = 0\), \(|L_i| \le \varepsilon\) for every history, so \(|L| \le k\varepsilon\) by Lemma 21.2. For \(\delta > 0\), step 1 of the proof of Corollary 21.1 reduces the run to \(k\) independent four-point pairs: a flag shows with probability at most \(k\delta\), and otherwise \(|L| \le k\varepsilon\), so \(\delta(k\varepsilon) \le k\delta\).
Advanced composition. Azuma’s inequality needs only conditional statements, given the past: a conditional mean of zero and a range of fixed length. That is the setting of steps 2 to 5 of the proof of Theorem 21.1, and the \(\delta > 0\) extension goes through the same reduction as step 2.
Optimal composition. Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 21.4 builds the adaptive run from the four-point product with history-dependent channels.


Adaptivity does not allow choosing the privacy parameters on the fly. If the analyst picks \(\varepsilon_i\) after seeing earlier outputs, the range length \(c_i = 2\varepsilon_i\) in the proof of Theorem 21.1 depends on the history, and Azuma’s inequality needs it fixed in advance. A rule such as “keep querying until the budget is spent” needs its own theorem, a privacy filter (Rogers, Roth, Ullman & Vadhan, 2016), and reporting the privacy spent so far at every moment needs a privacy odometer; both are treated in Adaptive composition. For pure DP with basic composition the naive rule is fine, because \(|L| \le \sum_i\varepsilon_i\) holds pointwise whatever order the \(\varepsilon_i\) came in.
Nor does adaptivity allow choices that depend on the data rather than the outputs. A system that answers private counts until the true count of some group crosses a threshold reveals that count through the number of answers it gives, so every answer can be \(\varepsilon\)-DP and the whole run still not be DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\). A rule that stops early within a fixed \(k\), looking only at the noisy answers, is covered, because the stopping time is then a post-processing of the outputs.

Example 21.5 The script simulates an analyst who, at each of the dashboard’s \(k = 100\) steps, chooses the next mechanism from the last output. If the previous output pointed to \(D\), meaning its privacy loss was positive, the analyst asks a Laplace query at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\); otherwise a randomized-response query at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). Over 100,000 simulated runs on \(D\), Table 21.5 estimates \(\delta(2)\) through Equation 21.3, by averaging \((1 - e^{2 - L})_+\) over the simulated total losses \(L\). The exact Laplace mean is 100 times the per-step KL divergence of two Laplace densities whose centres are \(\varepsilon\) scale units apart, \(e^{-\varepsilon} + \varepsilon - 1\).

21.8 References

Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan, “Boosting and Differential Privacy” (FOCS 2010). Introduces the adaptive composition experiment and advanced composition, Equation 21.9, with the bound \(\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) on the mean loss.
Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), §3.5: basic and advanced composition with full proofs (Theorem 3.20), including the \(\delta > 0\) case through a decomposition of approximate DP pairs.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015; IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2017). The hypothesis-testing view, the four-point randomized response, the optimal composition formula Equation 21.16, and improved closed-form bounds of the advanced kind.
Blackwell, “Equivalent Comparisons of Experiments” (Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 1953). The theorem that one experiment is uniformly harder to test than another exactly when it is a post-processing of it.
Murtagh & Vadhan, “The Complexity of Computing the Optimal Composition of Differential Privacy” (TCC 2016). Optimal composition with different \(\varepsilon_i\) is #P-complete, with an efficient approximation.
Vadhan, “The Complexity of Differential Privacy” (2017): composition theorems in the order used here, with the privacy loss as the central object.
Rogers, Roth, Ullman & Vadhan, “Privacy Odometers and Filters: Pay-as-you-Go Composition” (NeurIPS 2016). Why adaptively chosen privacy parameters need new theorems, and the first filters and odometers.
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (JRSS Series B, 2022). Composition of whole trade-off curves, and the central limit theorem for composition that the loss distribution of Section 21.1 foreshadows.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.1 The exponential mechanism
Many questions ask you to pick something rather than to compute a number, such as the best of 50 trained models or the first statistic to cross an alarm level. The answer is a name from a list, and adding noise to a name makes no sense. The Laplace mechanism of differential privacy (DP) could release a noisy score for every candidate. But if one record can move each of the \(|\mathcal R|\) candidates’ scores by 1, it moves the vector by \(|\mathcal R|\) in the \(\ell_1\) norm, so the noise would grow with the number of candidates.
This chapter shows that you never have to pay for the losers. The one idea is to release the position, not the values. Each mechanism adds noise to scores that are never published and reports only which candidate came out on top. The privacy proof asks how far one record can move the bar that the chosen candidate must clear. That bar is a maximum over the other candidates, and a maximum of numbers that each move by at most some amount moves by at most that amount, however many there are. So the number of candidates never enters the privacy cost, and enters the accuracy only through its logarithm.
The exponential mechanism samples a candidate with probability exponential in its score. Report-noisy-max adds noise to every score and names the winner. The sparse vector technique reports the first query of a stream above a threshold. The running example is model selection. Fifty models are scored on a private validation set of 1,000 examples, and model \(r\) gets \(900 - r\) right. A vote of six people checks the exponential mechanism by hand, and the sparse vector technique watches 1,000 counts for an alarm. Neighbours differ by adding or removing one record.
You want to output a good candidate, where “good” is measured by a score that one record can move only a little. The natural private answer is a random candidate tilted toward high scores, and this section finds how much tilting a budget of \(\varepsilon\) allows.
A selection problem has a finite set \(\mathcal R\) of candidates, fixed before the data are seen, and a score function \(u(D, r)\) saying how good candidate \(r\) is on the dataset \(D\). Its sensitivity is the largest change of any one score between two neighbours, \[\Delta u = \max_{r \in \mathcal R}\ \max_{D \sim D'}\big|u(D, r) - u(D', r)\big|, \tag{22.1}\] written \(\Delta\) when the score is clear. McSherry and Talwar (2007) weighted each candidate exponentially in its score, at a rate that lets one record change every weight by at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\). Section A.5 in the appendices derives the mechanism and its utility from scratch.
Counts under add/remove are monotone, because adding a record can only raise each count. A candidate’s probability is a weight divided by a total, and one record can change both, so the proof bounds each part. With monotone scores the two parts cannot both grow, which lets the 2 go.
The 2 pays for two effects that can act together. One record can raise the score of \(r\) and lower its competitors’, so \(r\)’s weight grows while the normalizer shrinks. Exercise 1 builds neighbours on which the ratio approaches \(e^{2\varepsilon}\) without the 2. The mechanism is a softmax of the scores with temperature \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\), uniform as \(\varepsilon \to 0\) and the argmax as \(\varepsilon \to \infty\) (Figure 22.1).
The candidate set must not depend on the data, because the proof compares the same list on \(D\) and \(D'\). It may be infinite, though. On a continuous range the sum becomes an integral against a fixed base measure, such as length, and the two factors bound the ratio of densities at every point. Nothing else uses the structure of \(\mathcal R\), so the candidates can be models, split points, strings or graphs.

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
Definition 22.1 (The exponential mechanism) For \(\varepsilon > 0\), the exponential mechanism \(M_E\) outputs candidate \(r\) with probability proportional to \(\exp\big(\varepsilon u(D, r)/(2\Delta)\big)\). The total weight \(Z(D)\) is the normalizer: \[\Pr[M_E(D) = r] = \frac{\exp\big(\frac{\varepsilon\,u(D, r)}{2\Delta}\big)}{Z(D)}, \qquad Z(D) = \sum_{s \in \mathcal R}\exp\Big(\frac{\varepsilon\,u(D, s)}{2\Delta}\Big). \tag{22.2}\] The scores are monotone if, for every pair of neighbours, either every score goes up from \(D\) to \(D'\) or every score goes down.



Theorem 22.1 (Privacy of the exponential mechanism) The exponential mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. If the scores are monotone, the mechanism with weights \(\exp\big(\varepsilon u(D, r)/\Delta\big)\), without the 2, is also \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. The plan is to split the ratio of the probabilities of one candidate into its own weight and the normalizer, and bound each factor by sensitivity.

Reduce to single outputs. The output set is finite, so by Proposition 18.1 it is enough that every single output’s probability changes by at most \(e^\varepsilon\) between neighbours. Fix \(D \sim D'\) and a candidate \(r\). Dividing the two probabilities of Equation 22.2 separates the two effects of one record: \[\frac{\Pr[M_E(D) = r]}{\Pr[M_E(D') = r]} = \exp\Big(\frac{\varepsilon\big(u(D, r) - u(D', r)\big)}{2\Delta}\Big)\cdot\frac{Z(D')}{Z(D)}. \tag{22.3}\]
The candidate’s own weight. By sensitivity, \(u(D, r) - u(D', r) \le \Delta\), so the first factor is at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\).
The normalizer. For every candidate \(s\), sensitivity gives \(u(D', s) \le u(D, s) + \Delta\), so each term of \(Z(D')\) is at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) times the matching term of \(Z(D)\). Adding the terms gives \(Z(D') \le e^{\varepsilon/2}Z(D)\), and the product is at most \(e^\varepsilon\).
Monotone scores. With weights \(e^{\varepsilon u/\Delta}\), each factor alone could reach \(e^\varepsilon\). If every score goes up from \(D\) to \(D'\), the first factor is at most 1 and the normalizer ratio at most \(e^\varepsilon\), by step 3 with \(\Delta\) for \(2\Delta\). If every score goes down, the first factor is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) and the normalizer ratio at most 1. Either way the product is at most \(e^\varepsilon\).










Figure 22.1: Left: the scores of 50 models, model \(r\) getting \(900 - r\) of 1,000 validation examples right. Right: the probability that the exponential mechanism selects each model, for four values of \(\varepsilon\). Small \(\varepsilon\) spreads the probability toward uniform; large \(\varepsilon\) concentrates it on the best model.




Example 22.1 Six people vote among options A, B, C and X, with counts \((3, 2, 1, 0)\) on the dataset \(D\). The neighbour \(D'\) has one more vote, for B, so \(\Delta = 1\). With \(\varepsilon = 1\) the weights are \(e^{u/2}\), and Table 22.1 shows the output of the chapter’s script (Section 22.8).

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.2 Utility of the exponential mechanism
Privacy came for free in the number of candidates, but accuracy does not, because more candidates means more bad ones to pick by accident. This section bounds how far below the best score the choice can fall. The idea is that a bad candidate weighs little next to the best one, whose weight is part of the normalizer.
Write \(\mathrm{OPT}(D) = \max_r u(D, r)\) for the best score, and call the gap the difference between it and the score of the chosen candidate.

Theorem 22.2 (Utility of the exponential mechanism) For every dataset \(D\) and every \(t > 0\), \[\Pr\Big[u(D, M_E(D)) \le \mathrm{OPT}(D) - \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}(\ln |\mathcal R| + t)\Big] \le e^{-t}, \tag{22.4}\] and the expected gap is at most \(\frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}(\ln |\mathcal R| + 1)\). With monotone scores and weights \(e^{\varepsilon u/\Delta}\), \(2\Delta\) can be replaced by \(\Delta\).


Proof. The plan is to bound the bad candidates’ weight from above and the normalizer from below, solve for the gap, and integrate the tail. Write \(G\) for the gap. It is at least \(a\) exactly when the mechanism picks a candidate at least \(a\) below the best.

Bad candidates are light. The weight grows with the score, so each such candidate weighs at most \(e^{\varepsilon(\mathrm{OPT} - a)/(2\Delta)}\).
The normalizer is heavy. It includes the weight of an optimal candidate, so \(Z(D) \ge e^{\varepsilon\,\mathrm{OPT}/(2\Delta)}\).
Divide. There are at most \(|\mathcal R|\) bad candidates, so dividing their total weight by the normalizer gives \[\Pr[G \ge a] \le |\mathcal R|\,e^{-\varepsilon a/(2\Delta)}. \tag{22.5}\]
Solve for the gap. Setting the right side to \(e^{-t}\) and taking logarithms gives \(a = \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}(\ln |\mathcal R| + t)\), which is Equation 22.4.
Expectation. The mean of a non-negative quantity is the integral of its tail. Bound the tail by 1 up to \(a_0 = \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\ln |\mathcal R|\), where step 3 reaches 1, and by step 3 beyond. The second piece is an exponential integral equal to \(\frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\), so \(\mathbb E[G] \le a_0 + \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\). With monotone weights the same steps run with \(\Delta\) for \(2\Delta\).


Doubling the candidates adds only \(\frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}\ln 2\) to the gap, and a lower bound shows that no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism avoids the \(\ln|\mathcal R|\). The proof counted every candidate as bad at the largest bad weight and kept one term of the normalizer. Both are nearly exact when one best candidate faces 49 runners-up all exactly \(a\) below it (Figure 22.2, right). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(a = 20\) the bound is 0.0023 and the truth 0.0022.
When scores are spread out, most bad candidates sit far below the best and are much lighter than the bound assumes. Figure 22.2 (left) shows the bound orders of magnitude above the truth for the 50 models.






Figure 22.2: Probability that the exponential mechanism’s choice is at least \(a\) below the best score, exact against the bound \(|\mathcal R| e^{-\varepsilon a/2\Delta}\). Left: the 50 models with scores \(900 - r\), for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 1; the bound is loose because the scores are spread out. Right: one best model and 49 runners-up all the same distance below it, with \(\varepsilon = 1\); the bound is tight.




Example 22.2 Release the best of the 50 models. The score counts correct predictions, so one validation example changes each score by at most 1 and \(\Delta = 1\). Table 22.2 shows the script’s output.

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.3 Applications of the exponential mechanism
To use the exponential mechanism, you choose a fixed candidate set, a score and its sensitivity. This section makes those choices three times. The first recovers the Laplace mechanism and shows a second way to drop the 2. The second picks a classifier from a finite class, and the third finds a median over an interval, which private training in Part 5 uses to set its clipping norm.

22.3.1 The Laplace mechanism
Take a query \(f\) of sensitivity \(\Delta\), let every real number \(h\) be a candidate, and score it by \(u(D, h) = -|f(D) - h|\). With length as the base measure, the density is proportional to \(e^{-\varepsilon|f(D) - h|/(2\Delta)}\), a Laplace density of scale \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\) centred at \(f(D)\). Changing the data only slides it along the line, so the normalizer cannot change and cannot work against any candidate.

Proposition 22.1 (A data-independent normalizer allows the full rate) If \(Z(D) = Z(D')\) for every pair of neighbours, the exponential mechanism with weights \(e^{\varepsilon u(D, h)/\Delta}\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. For the score \(-|f(D) - h|\) on the real line, the normalizer does not depend on the data, and the mechanism outputs \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon)\).


Proof. 

General claim. When \(Z(D) = Z(D')\), the ratio of the densities at \(h\) is the own factor of Theorem 22.1, now at most \(e^\varepsilon\), and integrating bounds every event.
Sensitivity. By the triangle inequality, \(\big||f(D) - h| - |f(D') - h|\big| \le |f(D) - f(D')| \le \Delta\).
The normalizer. Shifting the variable of integration by \(f(D)\) removes the data: \[Z(D) = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\varepsilon|f(D) - h|/\Delta}\,\mathrm dh = \int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-\varepsilon|h|/\Delta}\,\mathrm dh = \frac{2\Delta}{\varepsilon}. \tag{22.6}\]
It is the Laplace mechanism. A density proportional to \(e^{-\varepsilon|h - f(D)|/\Delta}\) is the \(\mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon)\) density shifted to \(f(D)\).


So monotone scores keep the two factors from both being large, and a data-independent normalizer makes the second one 1. A constant normalizer needs candidates that look the same after a shift and data that only shift the scores, which is why the Laplace mechanism needs only half the scale \(2\Delta/\varepsilon\) of the exponential mechanism (Exercise 7).


22.3.2 A private learner
A learning problem has a finite class \(\mathcal H\) of classifiers and \(n\) labelled examples drawn independently from one unknown distribution. The training error \(\mathrm{err}_D(h)\) is the fraction of training examples that \(h\) gets wrong, and the population error \(\mathrm{err}(h)\) is its error probability on a fresh example. The learner of Kasiviswanathan, Lee, Nissim, Raskhodnikova and Smith (2008) is the exponential mechanism over \(\mathcal H\) with score \(-n\,\mathrm{err}_D(h)\), minus the number of mistakes. Its excess error over the best classifier has a sampling term, paid without privacy too, and a privacy term.

Theorem 22.3 (A private learner for a finite class) The learner is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. For a failure probability \(\beta\), with probability at least \(1 - 2\beta\) its choice \(\hat h\) satisfies \[\mathrm{err}(\hat h) \le \min_{h \in \mathcal H}\mathrm{err}(h) + 2\sqrt{\frac{\ln(2|\mathcal H|/\beta)}{2n}} + \frac{2\ln(|\mathcal H|/\beta)}{\varepsilon n}. \tag{22.7}\]


Proof. The plan is to get privacy from Theorem 22.1, then chain two bounds: the choice is nearly the best on the training set, and training errors are close to population errors.

Privacy. One example changes every classifier’s number of mistakes by at most 1, so \(\Delta = 1\). This holds for any example, so privacy does not assume independence.
Nearly the best on the training set. Equation 22.4 with \(t = \ln(1/\beta)\), divided by \(n\), gives \(\mathrm{err}_D(\hat h) \le \min_h\mathrm{err}_D(h) + c_E\) with \(c_E = 2\ln(|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(\varepsilon n)\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).
Close to the population. A training error is an average of \(n\) independent indicators, so Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration inequalities) bounds the chance that it strays by more than \(s\) by \(2e^{-2ns^2}\). A union bound over the class and setting the total to \(\beta\) give \(s = \sqrt{\ln(2|\mathcal H|/\beta)/(2n)}\) for all classifiers at once.
Chain. Let \(h^\star\) have the smallest population error. On both events, step 3 moves to the training set, step 2 compares with \(h^\star\), and step 3 moves back: \[\mathrm{err}(\hat h) \le \mathrm{err}_D(\hat h) + s \le \mathrm{err}_D(h^\star) + c_E + s \le \mathrm{err}(h^\star) + c_E + 2s. \tag{22.8}\]


The sampling term falls like \(1/\sqrt n\) and the privacy term like \(1/n\), so for fine accuracy privacy costs little (Exercise 8 finds the records each needs). The class must be finite. Alon, Livni, Malliaris and Moran (2019) showed that thresholds at every real number cannot be learned privately in the probably approximately correct (PAC) sense.


22.3.3 A private median
Take records \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) in an interval \([0, B]\) fixed before looking at the data, and score every point \(r\) by \(-\big|\#\{i : x_i < r\} - \#\{i : x_i > r\}\big|\). The absolute value is the imbalance of \(r\). Here the 2 stays, because a new record raises the scores on one side of the median and lowers them on the other. Assume no two records are equal, and write \(x_{(1)} < \dots < x_{(n)}\) for them in increasing order. They cut the interval into \(n + 1\) pieces, with \(x_{(0)} = 0\) and \(x_{(n+1)} = B\) as end points. Write \(\ell_j\) for the length of the piece from \(x_{(j)}\) to \(x_{(j+1)}\), and \(\ell^\star\) for the total length of the best pieces.

Proposition 22.2 (The private median) Under add/remove the score has sensitivity 1, and the exponential mechanism with length as base measure is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. It picks piece \(j\) with probability proportional to \(\ell_je^{-\varepsilon|2j - n|/2}\), then a uniform point inside it. For even \(n\) and any \(t > 0\), with probability at least \(1 - e^{-t}\) its output \(r\) satisfies \[\big|\#\{i : x_i < r\} - \#\{i : x_i > r\}\big| \le \frac2\varepsilon\Big(\ln\frac{B}{\ell^\star} + t\Big). \tag{22.9}\] For odd \(n\) the right side gains 1, because no point splits the data evenly.


Proof. 

Sensitivity. One record changes the count below \(r\) or the count above it by 1, or neither, so the imbalance moves by at most 1. Theorem 22.1 gives privacy.
Sampling. Inside piece \(j\), exactly \(j\) records lie below \(r\) and \(n - j\) above, so the score is \(-|2j - n|\) and the density is flat. The piece’s probability is its length times its weight, over \(Z\).
Utility. Repeat Theorem 22.2 with lengths for counts. The points at least \(a\) below the best have total length at most \(B\), so they weigh at most \(Be^{\varepsilon(\mathrm{OPT} - a)/2}\), while the best pieces weigh \(\ell^\star e^{\varepsilon\,\mathrm{OPT}/2}\). Their ratio \((B/\ell^\star)e^{-\varepsilon a/2}\), set to \(e^{-t}\), bounds the imbalance by the best imbalance plus \(\frac2\varepsilon(\ln(B/\ell^\star) + t)\). The best imbalance is 0 for even \(n\) and 1 for odd \(n\).


The range enters only through \(\ln(B/\ell^\star)\), so a generous range is cheap, but it must be fixed without looking at the data, as a clamping range must be in Sensitivity. The guarantee controls the output’s rank, not its value. For the quantile \(q\), the score \(-\big|(1 - q)\#\{x_i < r\} - q\,\#\{x_i > r\}\big|\) works the same way.






Figure 22.3: Left: excess population error of the learner that picks one of 1,001 threshold classifiers with the exponential mechanism, against the non-private learner that picks the fewest training mistakes, averaged over 100 datasets per point (the text’s numbers use 200); the non-private learner finds the best threshold exactly at \(n = 10{,}000\), which a log axis cannot show. Right: 1,000 lognormal gradient norms (histogram) and the density of the private median over \([0, 10]\) for \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), zoomed in around the true median.




Example 22.3 A threshold classifier. The data are \(x\) uniform on \([0, 1]\), labelled 1 when \(x \ge 0.3\), with each label flipped with probability 0.1. The class holds the 1,001 thresholds \(0, 0.001, \dots, 1\). Over 200 datasets of \(n = 1{,}000\), the private learner’s average excess error is 0.0024 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.0206 at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), against 0.0008 without privacy (Figure 22.3, left). At \(\beta = 0.05\), Equation 22.7 has a sampling term of 0.1456 and a privacy term of 0.0198, both far above the observed errors, because the union bound guards against all 1,001 classifiers at once.
A clipping norm. Take 1,000 gradient norms drawn from a lognormal distribution with median 1, capped at \(B = 10\). Their median is 0.9804. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the private median is on average 0.0013 from it, and 0.0157 at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) (Figure 22.3, right). With \(t = \ln 20\), Equation 22.9 allows an imbalance of 26.4 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 264.5 at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\).

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.4 Report-noisy-max
The obvious way to select privately is to add independent noise to every score and report only the index of the largest. This section proves that counts then need noise of scale \(1/\varepsilon\), for any number of candidates, with the bar argument of the opening. Its three tools, used again for the sparse vector technique, come first as lemmas.
The proof looks at one candidate \(i\) and freezes the noise of all the others. The first lemma says that freezing is allowed when the frozen noise is drawn the same way on both datasets.

Lemma 22.1 (Fix the data-independent randomness) Let \(W\) be randomness inside a mechanism whose distribution does not depend on the data, and \(A\) an event. If \(\Pr[A \mid D, W = w] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[A \mid D', W = w]\) for every \(w\), then \(\Pr[A \mid D] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[A \mid D']\).


Proof. Both probabilities average the conditional ones (a sum, or an integral for continuous noise) with the same weights \(\Pr[W = w]\), because \(W\) does not depend on the data. Bounding each term of the first average by \(e^\varepsilon\) times the matching term of the second bounds the averages.

Once the other noise is frozen, candidate \(i\) wins when its own noise clears a bar built from a maximum over the others. The second lemma bounds how far one record moves that maximum.

Lemma 22.2 (A maximum moves no more than its terms) If \(|v'_j - v_j| \le \Delta\) for every \(j\), then \(|\max_jv'_j - \max_jv_j| \le \Delta\), for any number of terms. If every \(v'_j - v_j\) lies in \([0, \Delta]\), so does \(\max_jv'_j - \max_jv_j\).


Proof. Raising every term to its highest value gives \(\max_jv'_j \le \max_jv_j + \Delta\), and swapping \(v\) and \(v'\) gives the other side. When every term moves up, the maximum cannot fall.

The third lemma pays for the move. The Laplace density falls by \(e^{-1/b}\) per unit of distance from 0, so sliding it by \(s\) changes its height anywhere by at most \(e^{|s|/b}\).

Lemma 22.3 (Moving a Laplace threshold) For \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\) and all real \(t\) and \(s\), \[\Pr[Z > t - s] \le e^{|s|/b}\,\Pr[Z > t]. \tag{22.10}\]


Proof. 

Compare densities. With \(p(z) = \frac1{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\), the ratio \(p(z - s)/p(z)\) is \(e^{(|z| - |z - s|)/b}\). Two points \(s\) apart differ in distance from 0 by at most \(|s|\), so \(p(z - s) \le e^{|s|/b}p(z)\).
Change variables. Substituting \(z \mapsto z - s\) writes \(\Pr[Z > t - s]\) as \(\int_t^\infty p(z - s)\,\mathrm dz\), which step 1 bounds by \(e^{|s|/b}\Pr[Z > t]\).


With \(b = s = 1\), the ratio of the two tails is 1.6321 at \(t = 0\) and exactly \(e = 2.7183\) at \(t = 2\), where \(t\) and \(t - s\) both lie above 0 and each tail is \(\frac12e^{-x/b}\).

Theorem 22.4 (Report-noisy-max) Report-noisy-max adds independent \(Z_r \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b)\) to every score and outputs \(M_N(D) = \arg\max_r\big(u(D, r) + Z_r\big)\). With \(b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\) it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and with monotone scores \(b = \Delta/\varepsilon\) suffices (Dwork and Roth, Claim 3.9). With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), its gap is at most \(2b\ln(|\mathcal R|/\beta)\).


Proof. The plan is to freeze the other noise, write the output as one Laplace noise clearing a bar, bound how far the bar moves, and pay for the move.

Freeze the others. Fix \(D \sim D'\), a candidate \(i\) and the noise \(z_{-i}\) of the others. By Lemma 22.1 it is enough to bound the conditional probability that \(i\) wins.
A bar. Candidate \(i\) wins on \(D\) exactly when \(Z_i > t(D)\), with \[t(D) = \max_{j \ne i}\big(u(D, j) + z_j\big) - u(D, i). \tag{22.11}\]
The bar moves by at most \(2\Delta\). Each term \(u(\cdot, j) + z_j\) moves by at most \(\Delta\), so the maximum does too by Lemma 22.2, however many terms it has. The score \(u(\cdot, i)\) adds another \(\Delta\).
Monotone scores. If every score goes up by an amount in \([0, \Delta]\), then by Lemma 22.2 so does the maximum, and their difference lies in \([-\Delta, \Delta]\). The same holds when every score goes down.
Pay. Lemma 22.3 with \(s = t(D) - t(D')\) gives a factor at most \(e^{2\Delta/b} = e^\varepsilon\) in general and \(e^{\Delta/b} = e^\varepsilon\) for monotone scores. Lemma 22.1 removes the conditioning, and Proposition 18.1 gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Accuracy. By the accuracy bound of Theorem 20.1, a union bound over the candidates’ Laplace tails, every \(|Z_r|\) is below \(x = b\ln(|\mathcal R|/\beta)\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). Then the winner’s noisy score beat that of a best candidate, so \(u(D, i) + x > \mathrm{OPT} - x\), and the gap is below \(2x\).


Figure 22.4 draws steps 2 to 5 with \(b = 1\) and a bar lowered from 0.7 by 1. The winning probability rises from 0.2483 to 0.6296, a ratio of 2.5357, below \(e\) because the lowered bar left the tail where Lemma 22.3 is exact.






Figure 22.4: The proof of report-noisy-max in one picture. With the other candidates’ noise fixed, candidate \(i\) wins when its own noise \(Z_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1)\) exceeds a bar \(t\). Moving to a neighbouring dataset moves the bar by at most \(s\), and the winning probability changes by at most a factor \(e^{s/b}\).



The losers enter only through one maximum in step 3, which is why they cost nothing. The 2 is needed in general because competitors can rise while \(i\) falls. A histogram under replace neighbours, where one record is swapped for another, does exactly that, so it is not monotone.
Release only the index, because the winning noisy score would publish \(Z_i\), the noise the proof averages over. Neither Laplace report-noisy-max nor the exponential mechanism always selects better (Exercise 6).

Example 22.4 On the vote of Table 22.1 the counts are monotone, so \(b = 1\) is allowed at \(\varepsilon = 1\). The script’s exact winning probabilities give a largest privacy loss of 0.6674, and 0.3626 with \(b = 2\). On the 50 models at \(\varepsilon = 1\), the general mechanism (\(b = 2\)) picks the best with probability 0.4241, against 0.3935 for the exponential mechanism, and has expected gap 1.40 against 1.54. The monotone one (\(b = 1\)) has expected gap 0.54. The accuracy bound at \(\beta = 0.05\), 27.63 for \(b = 2\), is loose for spread-out scores.

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
section: 22.5 Gumbel noise: report-noisy-max is the exponential mechanism
text:
22.5 Gumbel noise: report-noisy-max is the exponential mechanism
Report-noisy-max with Laplace noise is close to the exponential mechanism but not equal to it. This section shows that Gumbel noise makes the noisy argmax give exactly the probabilities of Equation 22.2. This is the Gumbel-max trick. The Gumbel distribution with scale \(\kappa\), \(\mathrm{Gumbel}(\kappa)\), has cumulative distribution function (CDF) \(\Pr[G \le g] = \exp(-e^{-g/\kappa})\), and NumPy’s rng.gumbel(0, kappa) samples it.

Theorem 22.5 (The Gumbel-max trick) For scores \(u_r\) and independent \(G_r \sim \mathrm{Gumbel}(\kappa)\), \[\Pr\Big[\arg\max_r\big(u_r + G_r\big) = i\Big] = \frac{e^{u_i/\kappa}}{\sum_r e^{u_r/\kappa}}. \tag{22.12}\] With \(\kappa = 2\Delta/\varepsilon\) this is the exponential mechanism.


Proof. Conditioning on the winner’s noise lets you multiply the chances that each other candidate falls short, and the integral can then be done exactly. Dividing everything by \(\kappa\) keeps the argmax, so take \(\kappa = 1\), with CDF \(H(g) = \exp(-e^{-g})\) and density \(H'(g) = e^{-g}H(g)\).

Condition. If \(G_i = g\), candidate \(i\) wins when every other \(G_j < g + u_i - u_j\). These events are independent, so \[\Pr[i \text{ wins}] = \int_{-\infty}^\infty H'(g)\prod_{j \ne i}H(g + u_i - u_j)\,\mathrm dg. \tag{22.13}\]
Collect. Each factor is \(\exp(-e^{-g}e^{u_j - u_i})\), and the \(H(g)\) inside \(H'(g)\) is the factor for \(j = i\). The product is \(\exp(-e^{-g}A)\), with \(A = e^{-u_i}\sum_je^{u_j}\).
Substitute \(w = e^{-g}\). The factor \(e^{-g}\) and \(\mathrm dg\) together are \(-\mathrm dw\), and the minus sign flips the limits, so \[\Pr[i \text{ wins}] = \int_0^\infty e^{-wA}\,\mathrm dw = \frac1A = \frac{e^{u_i}}{\sum_je^{u_j}}. \tag{22.14}\]


So the Gumbel noisy max inherits the privacy of Theorem 22.1. It works in score units, while \(e^{\varepsilon u/(2\Delta)}\) overflows for scores in the thousands. Taking the \(c\) largest of \(u_r + G_r\) at once has the distribution of \(c\) exponential mechanisms run in turn without replacement, at \(c\varepsilon\) (Durfee and Rogers 2019; Section J.6 derives it).

title: 22  Selection: exponential mechanism, report-noisy-max, sparse vector
text:
22.6 The sparse vector technique
Now the queries arrive one at a time, and you care only about the first one above a threshold, such as the first statistic to cross an alarm level. Answering each with the Laplace mechanism would cost \(\varepsilon\) per query. Report-noisy-max needs the whole list in advance, but here each query must be answered before the next is seen. The sparse vector technique (Dwork, Naor, Reingold, Rothblum and Vadhan 2009) compares each query with one noisy threshold and pays only for the one above it. Its basic form is Algorithm 1 of Dwork and Roth (2014).

Definition 22.2 (AboveThreshold) The input is a dataset \(D\), a stream of \(k\) queries \(f_i\) of sensitivity \(\Delta\), possibly adaptive, a threshold \(\tau\) and budgets \(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 > 0\). Draw \(\rho \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_1)\) once. For each query, draw fresh \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\). If \(f_i(D) + \nu_i \ge \tau + \rho\), output \(\top\) (“above”) and halt; otherwise output \(\bot\) (“below”). The output \(\bot^{j-1}\top\) stops at query \(j\).

The output “stop at query \(j\)” says that the noisy threshold is above every earlier noisy answer and at or below the \(j\)-th. The proof slides \(\rho\) by however much the largest earlier answer moved, which costs at most \(\Delta\) by Lemma 22.2, and slides \(\nu_j\) to keep query \(j\) in place, which costs at most \(2\Delta\).

Theorem 22.6 (AboveThreshold) AboveThreshold is \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP for any number of queries (Dwork and Roth, Theorem 3.23; Lyu, Su and Li 2017). For monotone queries, which all move the same way between neighbours as counts under add/remove do, \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\) suffices. With \(\varepsilon_1 = \varepsilon_2 = \varepsilon/2\) and \(k\) fixed before the run, with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) every \(\bot\) query has \(f_i(D) < \tau + \alpha\) and the \(\top\) query has \(f_j(D) > \tau - \alpha\), where \[\alpha = \frac{8\Delta\big(\ln k + \ln(2/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{22.15}\]


Proof. The plan is to freeze the earlier noise, write the output as two conditions on \((\rho, \nu_j)\), shift both noises to turn the conditions for \(D\) into those for \(D'\), and pay with the Laplace density; accuracy then comes from Laplace tails. Fix \(D \sim D'\) and write \(g(D) = \max_{i < j}\big(f_i(D) + \nu_i\big)\).

Freeze. Fix \(\nu_1, \dots, \nu_{j-1}\), which do not depend on the data, and use Lemma 22.1. Adaptive queries are then fixed too, since they depend only on earlier answers, all \(\bot\).
Two conditions. The earlier queries say \(\bot\) exactly when \(g(D) < \tau + \rho\), and query \(j\) says \(\top\) when \(f_j(D) + \nu_j \ge \tau + \rho\). With noise densities \(p_\rho\) and \(p_\nu\), the output has probability \[\iint p_\rho(\rho)\,p_\nu(\nu)\,\mathbf 1\big[g(D) < \tau + \rho\big]\,\mathbf 1\big[f_j(D) + \nu \ge \tau + \rho\big]\,\mathrm d\rho\,\mathrm d\nu. \tag{22.16}\]
Shift both noises. Substitute \(\rho = \rho' + g(D) - g(D')\) and \(\nu = \nu' + \big(g(D) - g(D')\big) - \big(f_j(D) - f_j(D')\big)\). After cancelling, the indicators are those for \(D'\), and a translation leaves \(\mathrm d\rho\,\mathrm d\nu\) unchanged, so only the densities are evaluated at shifted points.
Size of the shifts. Each term of \(g\) moves by at most \(\Delta\), so \(|g(D) - g(D')| \le \Delta\) by Lemma 22.2, whatever \(j\) is. The shift of \(\nu\) is a difference of two such terms, at most \(2\Delta\).
Pay. By step 1 of the proof of Lemma 22.3, a Laplace density of scale \(b\) changes by at most \(e^{|x|/b}\) when its argument moves by \(x\). That is \(e^{\varepsilon_1}\) for \(\rho\) and \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\) for \(\nu\). The output \(\bot^k\) has only the first indicator and costs \(e^{\varepsilon_1}\). Lemma 22.1 and Proposition 18.1 conclude.
Monotone queries. If all queries move the same way, \(g\) and \(f_j\) move the same way by Lemma 22.2, so the shift of \(\nu\) is at most \(\Delta\).
Accuracy. With the equal split, the Laplace tail of Theorem 20.1 gives \(\Pr[|\rho| \ge \alpha/2] = e^{-\alpha\varepsilon/(4\Delta)}\), and a union bound over the \(k\) query noises gives \(k\,e^{-\alpha\varepsilon/(8\Delta)}\). Setting the second to \(\beta/2\) gives Equation 22.15, and the first is then smaller. The union bound needs \(k\) fixed in advance, because the index where the run stops depends on the noise.
Read off. If all noises are below \(\alpha/2\), a \(\bot\) means \(f_i < \tau + \rho - \nu_i < \tau + \alpha\), and the \(\top\) means \(f_j \ge \tau + \rho - \nu_j > \tau - \alpha\).


To find \(c\) queries above the threshold, the algorithm Sparse of Dwork and Roth restarts AboveThreshold with fresh threshold noise after each \(\top\) and halts after the \(c\)-th. Each run gets a share of the budget and of the failure probability.

Corollary 22.1 (Sparse: c answers above) With \(c\) runs at budget \(\varepsilon/c\) each, Sparse is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and with probability \(1 - \beta\) all its answers are accurate to within \[\alpha_c = \frac{8c\Delta\big(\ln k + \ln(2c/\beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{22.17}\] With runs at the largest \(\varepsilon_0\) whose \(c\)-fold advanced composition (Advanced and optimal composition) is at most \(\varepsilon\) at slack \(\delta\), it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, with margin Equation 22.15 at \(\varepsilon_0\) and \(\beta/c\).


Proof. 

Privacy. The runs form an adaptive composition of \(c\) AboveThresholds, so basic composition at \(\varepsilon/c\) gives \(\varepsilon\), and advanced composition at \(\varepsilon_0\) gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).
Accuracy. Apply Theorem 22.6 to each run at its budget and failure probability \(\beta/c\), and take a union bound over the runs.


The advanced margin grows like \(\sqrt c\) instead of \(c\), and Exercise 9 finds where it starts to win.
The \(\bot\) answers are free because step 4 pays for all of them through one maximum, whether there are 3 or 3 million. The run must halt because that payment covers one \(\top\), and each further \(\top\) against the same \(\rho\) needs its own shift. Query noise \(\mathrm{Lap}(2c\Delta/\varepsilon_2)\) pays for \(c\) shifts at once (Section J.5). The split of \(\varepsilon\) matters only for accuracy (Exercise 4). The proof is tight in the limit. On the pair of \(2m\) queries built in Section 22.7, the largest privacy loss is 0.994011, 0.999981 and 1.000000 at \(m = 10\), 20 and 40. Figure 22.6 shows one run.






Figure 22.6: One run of AboveThreshold with \(\varepsilon = 1\) on 30 queries whose true answers rise from 8 to 22.5, with threshold \(\tau = 20\). Each query’s noisy answer is compared with the same noisy threshold. The first one above it is reported and the run halts; later queries are never looked at.




Example 22.6 You monitor \(k = 1000\) counts (\(\Delta = 1\)) with threshold \(\tau = 500\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\). With \(\beta = 0.05\), Equation 22.15 gives \(\alpha = 8(\ln 1000 + \ln 40) = 84.77\). In the script’s stream every count is 400, below \(500 - \alpha\), except query 700, at 600, above \(500 + \alpha\). So with probability at least 0.95 the output is query 700. In 10,000 simulated runs it always was, and the margin the noises needed had a 95% quantile of 78.59, so the union bound is nearly tight. For the first \(c\) alarms, Equation 22.17 gives a margin of 1,032 at \(c = 10\). Advanced composition at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) gives the worse 1,746 there, and wins only at \(c = 100\), with 6,506 against 12,161.

22.7 When the sparse vector technique goes wrong
The sparse vector technique is easy to break. Lyu, Su and Li (2017) found several published variants, each a harmless-looking optimization of AboveThreshold, that were not private at all (Table 22.4). Each removes an ingredient that one step of the proof of Theorem 22.6 needs, and finding that step is how to review an implementation.



Table 22.4: Variants of the sparse vector technique and their actual privacy, from Lyu, Su & Li (2017).










Variant (as numbered by Lyu, Su & Li)
What it changes
Privacy shown by Lyu, Su & Li




Algorithm 1 (theirs); Algorithm 2 (Dwork & Roth)
Correct, with \(c\) answers above
\(\varepsilon\)


Algorithm 3 (Roth’s 2011 lecture notes)
Outputs the noisy value \(f_i + \nu_i\) for each \(\top\)
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 4 (Lee & Clifton 2014)
Query noise does not grow with \(c\)
\(\frac{1 + 6c}{4}\varepsilon\)


Algorithm 5 (Stoddard et al. 2014)
No noise on the queries
\(\infty\)


Algorithm 6 (Chen et al. 2015)
Never halts
\(\infty\)






The no-halt variant keeps the noise of AboveThreshold at the equal split but answers every query. One pair of neighbours and one output with too large a ratio suffice to break it. The pair below makes each answer of \(\bot^m\top^m\) a little more likely under \(D\), and without a halt the \(2m\) factors multiply. Take \(\Delta = 1\) and \[f(D) = (\underbrace{0, \dots, 0}_m, \underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_m), \qquad f(D') = (\underbrace{1, \dots, 1}_m, \underbrace{0, \dots, 0}_m). \tag{22.18}\]

Proposition 22.3 (Without the halt, the loss is unbounded) On this pair, the no-halt variant has \[\ln\frac{\Pr[\bot^m\top^m \mid D]}{\Pr[\bot^m\top^m \mid D']} \ge \frac{m\varepsilon}{4}, \tag{22.19}\] so it is not \(\varepsilon'\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon'\).


Proof. Once the shared threshold is fixed the answers are independent, so the plan is to fix it, multiply, bound the ratio at every threshold, and average. Let \(b = 4/\varepsilon\) be the query-noise scale \(2\Delta/\varepsilon_2\) at the equal split, \(F\) its Laplace CDF and \(\bar F = 1 - F\).

Fix the threshold. Given \(\tau + \rho = t\), a query of value \(f\) says \(\bot\) with probability \(F(t - f)\) and \(\top\) with probability \(\bar F(t - f)\).
Multiply. Under \(D\) the output needs \(m\) zeros below and \(m\) ones above, and under \(D'\) the values swap: \[a_D(t) = F(t)^m\,\bar F(t - 1)^m, \qquad a_{D'}(t) = F(t - 1)^m\,\bar F(t)^m. \tag{22.20}\]
A power. Their ratio is \(\omega(t)^m\), with \(\omega(t) = \frac{F(t)}{F(t - 1)}\cdot\frac{\bar F(t - 1)}{\bar F(t)}\), and both factors are at least 1.
Bound \(\omega\). The CDF is \(\frac12e^{x/b}\) for \(x \le 0\) and the survival function \(\frac12e^{-x/b}\) for \(x \ge 0\). So the first factor is \(e^{1/b}\) when \(t \le 0\), and the second is \(e^{1/b}\) when \(t \ge 1\). For \(0 < t < 1\), \(F(t) \ge \frac12\) makes the first factor at least \(e^{(1 - t)/b}\), and likewise the second is at least \(e^{t/b}\). So \(\omega(t) \ge e^{1/b}\) at every threshold.
Average. The threshold has the same distribution under both datasets, so averaging \(a_D \ge e^{m/b}a_{D'}\) gives Equation 22.19. The pair exists for every \(m\), so the loss is unbounded.


AboveThreshold’s proof fails here because each \(\top\) after the first needs its own shift, and the halt is what limits them to one. Without query noise (Algorithm 5), even the halting version fails, because two queries can give an output that is impossible on \(D'\) (Exercise 5). Publishing \(f_j + \nu_j\) (Algorithm 3) releases the noise the proof integrates over. The no-halt variant adds as much noise per query as AboveThreshold, so a reviewer who checks only noise scales will not find the bug. An audit will find it. Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP every test, a rule that says “\(D\)” or “\(D'\)” from the output, fires at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times as often under \(D\) as under \(D'\), by the definition, and a simple sign test breaks that (Figure 22.7, right).






Figure 22.7: Left: privacy loss on the neighbouring pair \(f(D) = (0^m, 1^m)\), \(f(D') = (1^m, 0^m)\) with \(\varepsilon = 1\), computed exactly by integrating over the threshold noise. For the no-halt variant, the loss of the output \(\bot^m\top^m\) grows linearly in \(m\), above the lower bound \(m\varepsilon/4\). For AboveThreshold, the largest loss over all outputs levels off at \(\varepsilon\). Right: the no-halt variant under a simple test, the probability that the second half has more \(\top\) answers than the first. Once the probability under \(D\) exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times the probability under \(D'\) (dotted), no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism could produce it.




Example 22.7 Table 22.5 gives the script’s exact values for \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\tau = 0\): the largest loss over all outputs for AboveThreshold, and the loss of \(\bot^m\top^m\) for the no-halt variant.

22.10 References

Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), §3.3 (report-noisy-max, Claim 3.9), §3.4 (the exponential mechanism, Theorems 3.10 and 3.11) and §3.6 (the sparse vector technique: AboveThreshold, Theorems 3.23 and 3.24, and the algorithms Sparse and NumericSparse, with Theorem 3.26 for their accuracy). The proofs above follow theirs. Their version of Sparse with \(\delta > 0\) uses a closed-form per-run budget where this chapter solves for the largest one.
McSherry & Talwar, “Mechanism Design via Differential Privacy” (FOCS 2007). The exponential mechanism, with the continuous version and its use in auctions.
Lyu, Su & Li, “Understanding the Sparse Vector Technique for Differential Privacy” (Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, 2017). The general algorithm with \(c\) answers above and a budget split, the monotone improvement, the survey of incorrect variants in Table 22.4, and the optimal split. The best single source on the technique.
Dwork, Naor, Reingold, Rothblum & Vadhan, “On the Complexity of Differentially Private Data Release” (STOC 2009). Where the sparse vector idea first appears.
Kasiviswanathan, Lee, Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith, “What Can We Learn Privately?” (FOCS 2008; SIAM Journal on Computing 2011). The private learner of Equation 22.7: any finite class is learnable privately with \(O(\ln|\mathcal H|)\) records.
Alon, Livni, Malliaris & Moran, “Private PAC Learning Implies Finite Littlestone Dimension” (STOC 2019). Why the class must be finite: thresholds over an infinite domain cannot be learned privately.
Smith, “Privacy-Preserving Statistical Estimation with Optimal Convergence Rates” (STOC 2011), and Gillenwater, Joseph & Kulesza, “Differentially Private Quantiles” (ICML 2021). The exponential mechanism for medians and quantiles over an interval, sampled exactly piece by piece.
Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold & Roth, “The Reusable Holdout: Preserving Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis” (Science 2015). Thresholdout, an application of the sparse vector technique to validation sets reused across many experiments, treated in Adaptive data analysis.
Durfee & Rogers, “Practical Differentially Private Top-k Selection with Pay-what-you-get Composition” (NeurIPS 2019). The one-shot Gumbel top-\(c\) and its equivalence to repeated exponential mechanisms.
McKenna & Sheldon, “Permute-and-Flip: A New Mechanism for Differentially Private Selection” (NeurIPS 2020), and Ding et al., “The Permute-and-Flip Mechanism is Identical to Report-Noisy-Max with Exponential Noise” (2021).
Maddison, Tarlow & Minka, “A* Sampling” (NeurIPS 2014): the Gumbel-max trick in machine learning, with its history going back to Gumbel and to Yellott (1977).
Near & Abuah, Programming Differential Privacy, the chapters on the exponential mechanism and the sparse vector technique: short implementations alongside Dwork & Roth.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 23  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
23.1 Linear queries as inner products
Many private releases are a large batch of simple statistics: every cross-tabulation of a census file, or the hundreds of counts on a dashboard. Each is a linear query, the average over the records of a function that gives each record a value between 0 and 1. Adding noise to every answer makes the noise grow with the number of queries, in proportion to it under pure differential privacy (DP) and like its square root under approximate DP (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). With millions of queries, either is useless. Yet the reconstruction attack breaks privacy only when the answers are within about \(1/\sqrt n\) of the truth, for \(n\) records. This chapter fills the gap with an error that grows only with the logarithms of the number of queries and of the number of possible records.
The one idea is to learn the data from its mistakes. Keep a public guess of the data, a histogram that starts out uniform, find a query that the guess gets badly wrong, measure that one query privately, and nudge the guess toward the answer. Each nudge is a step of the multiplicative weights method from online learning, and its guarantee says that about \(\ln N/\alpha^2\) nudges suffice for error \(\alpha\) on every query, where \(N\) is the number of possible records. The number of queries does not appear, so the privacy budget is spent on corrections instead of on queries, and the final guess can be published as a synthetic dataset.
The running example is a table of \(n = 10{,}000\) records with eight yes/no attributes, drawn from a mixture of three groups, so there are \(N = 2^8 = 256\) possible records. The queries are every cell of every marginal table: for each set of attributes and each combination of their values, the fraction of records with those values. That gives \(2^8 - 1 = 255\) tables, and a cell fixes each attribute to 0 or 1 or leaves it out, which gives \(3^8 - 1 = 6560\) cells. The uniform histogram, which uses no data, has a largest error of 0.232 over these queries.
Every algorithm in this chapter treats a dataset as a histogram and a query as a vector, so that answering a query is an inner product. This section fixes that view first, because it lets a guessed histogram answer every query.
The answer depends on the records only through how many of them take each value, which is what the histogram records.
Two consequences carry the chapter. Any distribution \(\hat p\) over the universe, not only the histogram of a real dataset, gives an answer \(\langle q, \hat p\rangle\) to every query, so a histogram is a synthetic dataset. And the error of \(\hat p\) on \(q\), the distance between its answer and the true one, is \(|\langle q, \hat p - p\rangle|\), which is linear in the difference of the two histograms. The target throughout is an error of at most \(\alpha\) on every query of the workload, except with a small failure probability \(\beta\), and all logarithms are natural.

title: 23  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
Definition 23.1 (Universe, histogram and linear query) The universe \(\mathcal X\) is the set of all possible records, and \(N = |\mathcal X|\) is its size. A dataset \(D = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\) holds \(n\) records from the universe. Its histogram \(p\) gives, for each element \(x\) of the universe, the fraction \(p(x)\) of the records that equal \(x\). A linear query is a function \(q\colon \mathcal X \to [0, 1]\), and its answer on \(D\) is the average of its values over the records, \[q(D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nq(x_i). \tag{23.1}\] The set of queries to answer is the workload \(\mathcal Q\), with \(|\mathcal Q|\) queries. Neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) differ by replacing one record, so \(n\) is public.



Proposition 23.1 (A linear query is an inner product with the histogram) For every linear query \(q\) and dataset \(D\) with histogram \(p\), \[q(D) = \sum_{x \in \mathcal X}q(x)\,p(x) = \langle q, p\rangle, \tag{23.2}\] the inner product of two vectors indexed by the universe. Replacing one record moves the answer by at most \(1/n\), so \(q\) has sensitivity \(1/n\).


Proof. 

Group the records by value. Each element \(x\) of the universe contributes \(q(x)\) once for every record equal to it, and there are \(np(x)\) such records, so \(\sum_iq(x_i) = \sum_xnp(x)q(x)\). Dividing by \(n\) gives Equation 23.2.
Replacing one record \(x_i\) by \(x_i'\) changes the sum by \(q(x_i') - q(x_i)\), which lies in \([-1, 1]\) because \(q\) takes values in \([0, 1]\). Divided by \(n\), the answer moves by at most \(1/n\).




Example 23.1 Take two yes/no attributes, so the universe is \(\{00, 01, 10, 11\}\), and four records \(01, 11, 11, 10\). Table 23.1 lists the histogram and the query “the first attribute is 1”. The inner product is \(0 + 0 + \frac14 + \frac12 = \frac34\), and indeed three of the four records have a first attribute of 1. The running example is the same picture with 256 elements, where each marginal cell is a query with a 1 on the elements that match it, so the script answers all 6,560 queries at once with one matrix product.

title: 23  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
23.2 Noise on every answer
The direct way to release a workload is to add noise to each answer. Before improving on it, it helps to know what it costs, because the two sample sizes of this section are the targets that the rest of the chapter beats.
Write \(f(D)\) for the vector of the \(|\mathcal Q|\) answers. By Proposition 23.1, replacing one record moves each coordinate by at most \(1/n\), so the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity of \(f\) is at most \(|\mathcal Q|/n\) and its \(\ell_2\) sensitivity at most \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}/n\). The square root comes from the norm: the \(\ell_1\) norm adds the moves, while the \(\ell_2\) norm adds their squares and takes a square root. The Laplace mechanism adds noise of scale \(b = \Delta_1f/\varepsilon\) to every coordinate, and each noise exceeds \(t\) in absolute value with probability \(e^{-t/b}\) (Theorem 20.1). The Gaussian mechanism is calibrated through \(\mu = \mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\), the largest ratio of sensitivity to noise standard deviation that the exact calibration allows (Corollary 20.1).

Proposition 23.2 (Records needed with noise on every answer) Let the workload have \(|\mathcal Q|\) queries, and let \(z\) be the number that a standard normal variable exceeds with probability \(\beta/(2|\mathcal Q|)\). The Laplace mechanism on the answer vector, with scale \(|\mathcal Q|/(n\varepsilon)\), is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) its largest error is at most \(\alpha\) once \[n \ge \frac{|\mathcal Q|\ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta)}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{23.3}\] The Gaussian mechanism with standard deviation \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}/(n\mu)\) on every answer is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, and with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) its largest error is at most \(\alpha\) once \[n \ge \frac{\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}\,z}{\mu\alpha}. \tag{23.4}\]


Proof. 

Laplace. Each answer gets noise of scale \(b = |\mathcal Q|/(n\varepsilon)\), which exceeds \(b\ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta)\) in absolute value with probability \(\beta/|\mathcal Q|\). The union bound, which says that the probability that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities, gives probability at most \(\beta\) that some answer’s noise exceeds that level. Setting \(b\ln(|\mathcal Q|/\beta) = \alpha\) and solving for \(n\) gives Equation 23.3.
Gaussian. A normal variable exceeds \(z\) standard deviations in absolute value with probability \(2\Phi(-z)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, and the one-sided tail \(\beta/(2|\mathcal Q|)\) that defines \(z\) makes this \(\beta/|\mathcal Q|\). By the union bound, some answer’s noise exceeds \(\sigma z\) with probability at most \(\beta\), where \(\sigma = \sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}/(n\mu)\) is the standard deviation. Setting \(\sigma z = \alpha\) and solving for \(n\) gives Equation 23.4.


The records needed grow like \(|\mathcal Q|\) under pure DP and like \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}\), times a slowly growing \(z\), under approximate DP. For a few hundred queries on a large dataset that is fine, and nothing in this chapter beats it there. But a table with 30 yes/no attributes has \(3^{30} - 1 \approx 2\times10^{14}\) marginal cells, too many for independent noise.
A workload with structure does better. Replacing one record lowers one cell of a marginal table by \(1/n\) and raises another by \(1/n\), so each table contributes only \(2/n\) to the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity, whatever its number of cells, and \(2/n^2\) to the squared \(\ell_2\) sensitivity.

Example 23.2 With \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), the 255 marginal tables give an \(\ell_1\) sensitivity of \(2 \times 255/n = 0.0510\), so the Laplace mechanism adds noise of scale 0.0510 to each of the 6,560 cells. Its largest error, averaged over 20 runs, is 0.497, worse than the 0.232 of the uniform histogram, which uses no data. The Gaussian mechanism at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt{2 \times 255}/n = 0.00226\). With \(\mu = 0.2367\) its noise has standard deviation 0.0095, and its average largest error is 0.037. Both use the structure of the marginals: treated as 6,560 unrelated queries, the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity would be \(|\mathcal Q|/n = 0.656\), about 13 times larger.

section: 23.3 Multiplicative weights and its regret bound
