23.3 Multiplicative weights and its regret bound
Forget privacy for two sections. The method behind this chapter comes from a prediction game, and the question is how well a learner can do against any sequence of outcomes when all it may do is reweight a fixed set of advisers. The answer is a regret bound that depends on the number of advisers only through a logarithm, and it drives every algorithm that follows.
Each day, \(N\) experts predict a yes/no outcome, and you must decide whom to follow before you see it. If one expert is always right, the halving algorithm follows the majority of the experts who have never erred and drops each one that errs. Each of your mistakes drops at least half of them, so you err at most \(\log_2N\) times (Exercise 1). In 20 simulated runs with 1,024 experts it never made more than 6 mistakes, against the bound \(\log_2 1024 = 10\). Real experts are never perfect, so multiplicative weights keeps every expert but shrinks its weight each time it does badly.

Definition 23.2 (The experts game and multiplicative weights) The game has \(T\) rounds. In round \(t\) the learner chooses a probability distribution \(p_t\) over the \(N\) experts. Then a loss vector \(\ell_t\) is revealed, which gives each expert \(x\) a loss \(\ell_t(x)\) in \([-1, 1]\), and the learner pays the average loss under its distribution, \(\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle\). The losses may be chosen by an adversary who knows the learner’s rule. Multiplicative weights keeps a positive weight \(w_t(x)\) on each expert, starting from \(w_1(x) = 1\), and has a learning rate (step size) \(\eta \le \frac12\). In round \(t\) it plays \(p_t(x) = w_t(x)/W_t\), where \(W_t = \sum_xw_t(x)\) is the total weight, and after the losses are revealed it updates each weight by \[w_{t+1}(x) = w_t(x)\big(1 - \eta\ell_t(x)\big). \tag{23.5}\] The learner’s regret against a distribution \(\pi\) over the experts, fixed in hindsight, is its total loss minus the total loss of \(\pi\), that is \(\sum_t\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle - \sum_t\langle\ell_t, \pi\rangle\).

An expert with a positive loss loses weight, and one with a negative loss gains it. The proof of the regret bound takes the logarithm of factors \(1 - x\) twice: from above, when it turns the total weight into the learner’s loss, and from below, when it turns one expert’s weight into that expert’s loss. The next lemma supplies both bounds, and its range \(|x| \le \frac12\) is why the learning rate is at most \(\frac12\).

Lemma 23.1 (Two bounds on the logarithm) For every \(x < 1\), \(\ln(1 - x) \le -x\). For \(|x| \le \frac12\), \[\ln(1 - x) \ge -x - x^2. \tag{23.6}\]


Proof. 

Upper bound. The logarithm is concave, so it lies below its tangent line at any point. The tangent of \(\ln(1 - x)\) at \(x = 0\) is \(-x\), which gives \(\ln(1 - x) \le -x\).
Lower bound. Let \(g(x) = \ln(1 - x) + x + x^2\), so that \(g(0) = 0\) and the claim is that \(g\) is never negative on the range. Its derivative is \[g'(x) = -\frac1{1 - x} + 1 + 2x = \frac{x(1 - 2x)}{1 - x}. \tag{23.7}\] On \([0, \frac12]\) every factor is non-negative, so \(g\) rises from 0 and stays non-negative. On \([-\frac12, 0]\) the numerator is at most 0 and the denominator positive, so \(g\) falls toward \(g(0) = 0\) and is non-negative there too.


At the end of the range the bound is close, since \(\ln\frac12 = -0.6931\) lies just above \(-0.75\). Outside the range it can fail, and at \(x = 0.9\) it does, because \(\ln 0.1 = -2.30\) lies below \(-1.71\). A loss outside \([-1, 1]\) pushes \(\eta\ell_t(x)\) out of the range in the same way, and at \(\eta\ell_t(x) \ge 1\) a weight can even become zero or negative, so losses are rescaled into \([-1, 1]\) first.

Theorem 23.1 (The regret bound of multiplicative weights) Run multiplicative weights with learning rate \(\eta \le \frac12\) for \(T\) rounds against any sequence of loss vectors with entries in \([-1, 1]\). Then for every distribution \(\pi\) over the experts, \[\sum_{t=1}^T\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle - \sum_{t=1}^T\langle\ell_t, \pi\rangle \le \eta T + \frac{\ln N}{\eta}. \tag{23.8}\] When \(T \ge 4\ln N\), the learning rate \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln N/T}\) is allowed and gives regret at most \(2\sqrt{T\ln N}\).


Proof. The plan is to bound \(\ln W_{T+1}\) from above by the learner’s total loss and from below by any one expert’s total loss, to compare the two bounds, and then to average the comparison over the experts.

The total weight shrinks with the learner’s loss. Summing Equation 23.5 over the experts gives \(W_{t+1} = \sum_xw_t(x) - \eta\sum_xw_t(x)\ell_t(x)\). Factoring out \(W_t\) turns each weight into \(p_t(x)\), so \[W_{t+1} = W_t\big(1 - \eta\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle\big). \tag{23.9}\]
Upper bound. Unrolling step 1 from \(W_1 = N\) makes \(W_{T+1}\) equal to \(N\) times the product of the factors. Each \(\eta\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle\) is below 1, so the upper bound of Lemma 23.1 applies to every factor: \[\ln W_{T+1} = \ln N + \sum_{t=1}^T\ln\big(1 - \eta\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle\big) \le \ln N - \eta\sum_{t=1}^T\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle. \tag{23.10}\]
Lower bound from one expert. The total weight is at least the weight of any single expert \(x\), and that weight is the product of its own factors. Each \(\eta\ell_t(x)\) lies in \([-\frac12, \frac12]\), so the lower bound of Lemma 23.1 applies, and \(\ell_t(x)^2 \le 1\) bounds each squared term: \[\ln W_{T+1} \ge \ln w_{T+1}(x) = \sum_{t=1}^T\ln\big(1 - \eta\ell_t(x)\big) \ge -\eta\sum_{t=1}^T\ell_t(x) - \eta^2T. \tag{23.11}\]
Compare. The upper bound of step 2 is at least the lower bound of step 3, so \(\eta\sum_t\langle\ell_t, p_t\rangle \le \ln N + \eta\sum_t\ell_t(x) + \eta^2T\). Dividing by \(\eta\) gives Equation 23.8 for the comparison with the single expert \(x\).
Any distribution. The inequality of step 4 holds for every expert \(x\), and its left side does not depend on \(x\). Multiply it by \(\pi(x)\) and add over the experts. The \(\pi(x)\) sum to 1, so the left side and the constant terms are unchanged, and \(\sum_x\pi(x)\ell_t(x) = \langle\ell_t, \pi\rangle\), which is Equation 23.8.
Choose the learning rate. A larger \(\eta\) raises \(\eta T\) and lowers \(\ln N/\eta\), so the bound is smallest where the two terms are equal, at \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln N/T}\), where it equals \(2\sqrt{T\ln N}\). The lemma needs \(\eta \le \frac12\), that is \(T \ge 4\ln N\).


The average regret per round, \(2\sqrt{\ln N/T}\), goes to zero, so over many rounds the learner does as well as the best fixed distribution. Nothing in the proof assumed that the losses were random or independent of the weights, so an adversary who knows the rule gains nothing, and the number of experts enters only through \(\ln N\). The sequences met in practice are rarely as hostile as the worst case, as Section 23.4 shows.
The weights also look familiar. Each factor \(1 - \eta\ell\) is close to \(e^{-\eta\ell}\) when \(\eta\) is small, so the distribution is close to a softmax of minus the cumulative losses, the shape of the exponential mechanism. The version with the factor \(e^{-\eta\ell}\) exactly is called Hedge, and online learning also views it as follow the regularized leader (FTRL) with an entropy penalty; DP-FTRL uses a squared-norm penalty to train models privately.

Example 23.3 The smallest case shows the mechanics. Take \(N = 2\) experts and \(\eta = \frac12\) over \(T = 3\) rounds, with losses \(\ell_1 = (1, 0)\), \(\ell_2 = (0, 1)\) and \(\ell_3 = (1, 0)\). Table 23.2 follows the weights. The learner pays \(\frac12 + \frac23 + \frac12 = \frac53\) in total. Expert 2 lost only 1, so the regret against it is \(\frac23\), and the bound Equation 23.8 is \(\frac12 \times 3 + \ln 2/\frac12 = 1.5 + 1.386 = 2.886\). The running example enters in the next section, where the experts are the 256 elements of the universe.

23.4 From regret to a mistake bound
Now turn the game into an algorithm for releasing answers, still without privacy. The question is how many corrections a guessed histogram needs before it answers every query to within \(\alpha\), and the answer must not depend on the number of queries. Let the experts be the elements of the universe, so that \(p_t\) is a guessed histogram, and compare it with the true histogram \(p\), one particular distribution \(\pi\). If each round’s regret against \(p\) is the guess’s error on one query, the regret bound limits the number of large errors.

Theorem 23.2 (The mistake bound) Run multiplicative weights over the universe, starting from the uniform histogram, with learning rate \(\eta = \alpha/2\). In each round, look for a query \(q_t \in \mathcal Q\) on which the current guess has error more than \(\alpha\). If there is none, stop: the guess is within \(\alpha\) on every query. Otherwise let \(s_t\) be \(+1\) if the guess’s answer is too high and \(-1\) if it is too low, and use the loss \(\ell_t = s_tq_t\). The number \(U\) of rounds before the algorithm stops satisfies \[U < \frac{4\ln N}{\alpha^2}, \tag{23.12}\] whatever the workload and however the queries are chosen.


Proof. The plan is to show that the regret against the true histogram grows by more than \(\alpha\) in every round, to bound the same regret by Equation 23.8, and to compare the two.

Each round’s regret is the error. The regret bound holds for every distribution \(\pi\), and the loss of \(p\) is the true answer times \(s_t\), so by Equation 23.2 \(\langle\ell_t, p_t - p\rangle = s_t\big(\langle q_t, p_t\rangle - \langle q_t, p\rangle\big)\). The sign \(s_t\) makes the bracket positive, so this is the error of \(p_t\) on \(q_t\), more than \(\alpha\).
Total regret is large. Adding over the \(U\) rounds, the regret against \(p\) is more than \(\alpha U\).
Total regret is small. The losses \(s_tq_t\) have entries in \([-1, 1]\), and \(\eta = \alpha/2 \le \frac12\), so Theorem 23.1 with \(\pi = p\) and \(T = U\) bounds the same regret by \(\eta U + \ln N/\eta = \alpha U/2 + 2\ln N/\alpha\).
Combine. The regret is more than \(\alpha U\) by step 2 and at most \(\alpha U/2 + 2\ln N/\alpha\) by step 3, so \[\alpha U < \frac{\alpha U}{2} + \frac{2\ln N}{\alpha}. \tag{23.13}\] Subtracting \(\alpha U/2\) from both sides and dividing by \(\alpha/2\) gives Equation 23.12.


If the guess’s answer is too high, the loss is \(+q_t\), and the weights of the records that the query counts shrink, which lowers the answer. A few such corrections fix every query at once because each one moves the guess closer to the true histogram in relative entropy, a distance that starts at no more than \(\ln N\). The algorithm never looks at the queries it gets right, so their number never enters, and doubling the universe adds only \(4\ln2/\alpha^2\) corrections. Exercise 3 shows that \(\alpha/2\) is the best learning rate.
The choice of query and its sign are the only places where the algorithm touches the data, and both use only answers of sensitivity \(1/n\), which makes it easy to privatize. The bound is very loose, because in practice the first corrections fix errors several times larger than \(\alpha\), and many queries at once.






Figure 23.1: Non-private multiplicative weights on the running example, \(\alpha = 0.05\), \(\eta = \alpha/2\). Left: the largest error over the 6,560 queries before each update. Right: the regret against the true histogram and its bound \(\eta t + \ln N/\eta\).




Example 23.4 With \(\alpha = 0.05\) the bound Equation 23.12 allows \(4\ln 256/0.05^2 = 8872\) corrections. The algorithm needs 148 (Figure 23.1). The first three queries it corrects have errors 0.232, 0.228 and 0.226, more than four times \(\alpha\). After 148 rounds the regret is 16.70, against a bound of 225.5.

23.5 Private multiplicative weights
The algorithm of Section 23.4 touches the data in two places, the choice of a badly answered query and the sign of its error. This section makes both private, which gives an error that grows only with the logarithms of \(|\mathcal Q|\) and \(N\). The exponential mechanism picks a query whose error is close to the largest, and the Laplace mechanism measures its answer, which gives the sign. Both can miss, so the algorithm cannot tell when to stop. Instead it runs a fixed number of rounds \(T\) and releases the average of its guesses. This is the multiplicative weights exponential mechanism (MWEM) of Hardt, Ligett & McSherry (2012), the practical form of private multiplicative weights (Hardt & Rothblum 2010).

Definition 23.3 (Private multiplicative weights, offline) Input: the dataset \(D\), the workload \(\mathcal Q\), a number of rounds \(T \ge 4\ln N\) and a per-step budget \(\varepsilon_0\). Start from the uniform histogram \(p_1\) and set \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln N/T}\). For \(t = 1, \dots, T\):

Select. Run the exponential mechanism over \(\mathcal Q\) with budget \(\varepsilon_0\) and score \(|\langle q, p_t\rangle - q(D)|\), the error of the current guess on \(q\). Call the chosen query \(q_t\).
Measure. Release \(m_t = q_t(D) + \mathrm{Lap}\big(1/(n\varepsilon_0)\big)\).
Update. Let \(s_t = +1\) if \(\langle q_t, p_t\rangle > m_t\) and \(-1\) otherwise, and apply Equation 23.5 with the loss \(s_tq_t\) to get \(p_{t+1}\).

Output the average histogram \(\bar p = \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^Tp_t\).

The measurement needs its own budget, because the exponential mechanism releases only the index of the chosen query, never its exact score.
Three earlier results do the private work. The exponential mechanism over the \(|\mathcal Q|\) queries, with a score of sensitivity \(1/n\), is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, and except with probability \(\beta'\) the chosen score is within \(\frac{2}{n\varepsilon_0}\big(\ln|\mathcal Q| + \ln(1/\beta')\big)\) of the best (Selection). The Laplace mechanism with scale \(b = 1/(n\varepsilon_0)\) is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, and its noise exceeds \(b\ln(1/\beta')\) in absolute value with probability \(\beta'\) (Theorem 20.1). Advanced composition (Advanced and optimal composition) makes \(k\) adaptive \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP steps \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)} + k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). The privacy step below needs a closed-form per-step budget from it.

Lemma 23.2 (A closed-form per-step budget) Let \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0, 1)\) satisfy \(\varepsilon \le 8\ln(1/\delta)\). If each of \(k\) adaptively chosen steps is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP with \[\varepsilon_0 = \frac{\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}}, \tag{23.14}\] then the whole is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

Substitute \(\varepsilon_0\) into the advanced composition bound. The first term, \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}\), is exactly \(\varepsilon/2\).
The second term, \(k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\), is at most \(k\varepsilon_0^2/2\), because \(\tanh\) never exceeds its argument. Substituting \(\varepsilon_0\) turns \(k\varepsilon_0^2/2\) into \(\varepsilon^2/(16\ln(1/\delta))\), and the condition \(\varepsilon \le 8\ln(1/\delta)\) makes this at most \(\varepsilon/2\).
The two terms add to at most \(\varepsilon\), so the composition is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


The condition is mild, since at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) it allows any \(\varepsilon\) up to 110. When \(\varepsilon_0\) is small the second term is far below \(\varepsilon/2\), so the closed form leaves up to half the budget unspent (Example 23.5).

Theorem 23.3 (Privacy and accuracy of private multiplicative weights) The algorithm of Definition 23.3 is \(2T\varepsilon_0\)-DP. So \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(2T)\) makes it \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and \(\varepsilon_0\) from Equation 23.14 with \(k = 2T\) makes it \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when \(\varepsilon \le 8\ln(1/\delta)\). With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), the largest error of the average histogram over the workload is at most \[\max_{q \in \mathcal Q}\big|\langle q, \bar p\rangle - q(D)\big| \le 2\sqrt{\frac{\ln N}{T}} + \frac{2}{n\varepsilon_0}\Big(\ln|\mathcal Q| + 2\ln\frac{2T}\beta\Big). \tag{23.15}\]


Proof. The plan is to check that each private step is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, to define the event on which every selection and every measurement works as intended, and on that event to run the regret argument of Theorem 23.2 with a deficit per round for the two private steps.

Privacy. Given the history, the guess \(p_t\) is a fixed histogram, so the score moves by at most \(1/n\) between neighbours (Proposition 23.1) and the selection is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP. The measurement is a Laplace mechanism of scale \(1/(n\varepsilon_0)\) on an answer of sensitivity \(1/n\), so it is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP too. The update and the average are post-processing, and composition allows the \(2T\) steps to be adaptive (Advanced and optimal composition).
The good event. Write \(\mathrm{err}_t(q) = |\langle q, p_t\rangle - q(D)|\) for the error of round \(t\)’s guess on query \(q\). Give each of the \(2T\) private steps the failure probability \(\beta' = \beta/(2T)\). The utility bound of the exponential mechanism then says that the selection picks a query whose error is within \[c_E = \frac{2}{n\varepsilon_0}\Big(\ln|\mathcal Q| + \ln\frac{2T}\beta\Big) \tag{23.16}\] of the largest, except with probability \(\beta/(2T)\). The Laplace tail says that the measurement’s noise is below \[c_L = \frac{1}{n\varepsilon_0}\ln\frac{2T}\beta, \tag{23.17}\] also except with probability \(\beta/(2T)\). The union bound over the \(2T\) steps makes all of this hold at once except with probability \(\beta\).
Each round’s regret is nearly the largest error. If the sign \(s_t\) is right, then the round’s regret \(\langle s_tq_t, p_t - p\rangle\) is \(\mathrm{err}_t(q_t)\), as in step 1 of Theorem 23.2. If it is wrong, the guess’s answer lies between the measured and the true answers, which are at most \(c_L\) apart, so \(\mathrm{err}_t(q_t) \le c_L\), and the regret \(-\mathrm{err}_t(q_t)\) falls short of \(\mathrm{err}_t(q_t)\) by at most \(2c_L\). Either way the loss is at least \(\mathrm{err}_t(q_t) - 2c_L\), and by step 2 the chosen query’s error is within \(c_E\) of the largest, so \[\langle s_tq_t, p_t - p\rangle \ge \max_q\mathrm{err}_t(q) - c_E - 2c_L. \tag{23.18}\]
Sum and use the regret bound. Adding over the \(T\) rounds, the regret against the true histogram is at least \(\sum_t\max_q\mathrm{err}_t(q) - T(c_E + 2c_L)\). By Theorem 23.1 with \(\eta = \sqrt{\ln N/T}\) it is at most \(2\sqrt{T\ln N}\). Comparing the two and dividing by \(T\), \[\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\max_q\mathrm{err}_t(q) \le 2\sqrt{\frac{\ln N}{T}} + c_E + 2c_L. \tag{23.19}\]
The average histogram. For any query \(q\), the error of the average is the average of the errors by Equation 23.2, \(\langle q, \bar p\rangle - q(D) = \frac1T\sum_t\langle q, p_t - p\rangle\). Its absolute value is at most \(\frac1T\sum_t\mathrm{err}_t(q)\), which is at most the left side of step 4. Finally \(c_E + 2c_L = \frac{2}{n\varepsilon_0}\big(\ln|\mathcal Q| + 2\ln\frac{2T}\beta\big)\), which gives Equation 23.15.


The algorithm releases the average guess because the regret bound controls the sum of the rounds’ largest errors, and says nothing about any single round. The constants are poor: on the running example the bound is above 1, while the real error is far smaller (Example 23.5).
The first term of Equation 23.15 falls with more rounds, and the second grows, because each round gets less budget. Balancing the two turns the bound into a sample size.

Corollary 23.1 (Records needed by private multiplicative weights) Write \(L = \ln|\mathcal Q| + 2\ln(2T/\beta)\) for the logarithmic term of Equation 23.15, treated as a constant because it depends on \(T\) only through a logarithm. Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with the budget of Equation 23.14 for \(2T\) steps, there is a number of rounds \(T\) at which the error bound is at most \(\alpha\) once \[n \ge \frac{64\sqrt{\ln N\,\ln(1/\delta)}\,L}{\alpha^2\varepsilon}. \tag{23.20}\]


Proof. 

The shape of the bound. With \(k = 2T\) steps, Equation 23.14 gives \(\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon/(4\sqrt{T\ln(1/\delta)})\), so the second term of Equation 23.15 is \(8\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\,L\sqrt T/(n\varepsilon)\). The bound therefore has the shape \(A/\sqrt T + B\sqrt T\), with \(A = 2\sqrt{\ln N}\) from the regret and \(B = 8\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\,L/(n\varepsilon)\) from the noise.
Balance. A sum of this shape is smallest where its two terms are equal, at \(T = A/B\), and there it equals \(2\sqrt{AB}\). Substituting \(A\) and \(B\), \[2\sqrt{AB} = 8\big(\ln N\ln(1/\delta)\big)^{1/4}\sqrt{\frac{L}{n\varepsilon}}. \tag{23.21}\]
Solve for \(n\). Setting this to \(\alpha\) and squaring gives \(64\sqrt{\ln N\ln(1/\delta)}\,L/(n\varepsilon) = \alpha^2\), which rearranges to Equation 23.20.


Under pure DP the second term grows linearly in \(T\), and the same balancing gives \(n \ge 108\,L\ln N/(\alpha^3\varepsilon)\) (Exercise 4). The queries enter only through \(L\), which grows like \(\ln|\mathcal Q|\), where the baseline paid \(|\mathcal Q|\) or \(\sqrt{|\mathcal Q|}\). The price is accuracy, because at a fixed \(n\) the error falls like \(n^{-1/2}\), or \(n^{-1/3}\) under pure DP, against \(1/n\) for independent noise, so the method wins only when the queries far outnumber the records. No method can do much better on every workload, since errors below about \(1/\sqrt n\) on many queries let the reconstruction attack recover the data. Up to constants it is close to optimal, by the packing and fingerprinting arguments of Lower bounds (Bun, Ullman & Vadhan 2014).
The running time is proportional to \(N\), which is \(2^{50}\) for 50 attributes. Some such cost is unavoidable, since Ullman & Vadhan (2011) showed that under standard cryptographic assumptions no efficient algorithm releases private synthetic data accurate for every two-way marginal, with probabilistically checkable proof (PCP) techniques. Practical methods keep the select–measure–update loop with a compact model in place of the histogram (McKenna, Mullins, Sheldon & Miklau 2022).

The dotted line is the uniform histogram.

The bound picks a good \(T\), although its values are useless as numbers. With 38 rounds the largest error is 0.078, against 0.497 for Laplace noise and 0.037 for Gaussian noise, so here the Gaussian mechanism wins. Figure 23.2 shows that Gaussian noise wins above a few thousand records, because 6,560 queries are not many enough.
With \(\delta > 0\), advanced composition gives each step more budget once \(T\) is large. At \(T = 100\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), pure DP gives each step \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.00500\). The closed form Equation 23.14 gives 0.00673, although in total that budget spends only \(0.505\varepsilon\), while solving the advanced composition bound exactly for \(\varepsilon_0\) gives 0.01322. At \(T = 1000\) the same three budgets are 0.00050, 0.00213 and 0.00418.
The guarantees separate only at a much larger scale. Table 23.4 gives the records needed for error 0.05 on every query with probability 0.95, over a universe of \(N = 2^{20}\) and a workload with no structure. The Laplace and SmallDB columns are pure DP, and the other two are \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. For private multiplicative weights the table solves Equation 23.15 for \(n\) after a search over \(T\). At \(10^6\) queries the search finds \(T = 81{,}552\) and \(L = 43.81\), and needs \(1.56\times10^7\) records, while the closed form Equation 23.20 gives \(1.55\times10^7\). That bound hardly moves as the queries grow a millionfold, and it crosses the Gaussian column near \(10^9\) queries (Figure 23.3).

title: 23  Query release and private multiplicative weights
text:
23.6 Online private multiplicative weights
The offline algorithm needs the whole workload in advance, but an interactive query server receives queries one at a time, each perhaps chosen after the earlier answers. The question is how to pay only for the queries the guess gets wrong without searching for them. The sparse vector technique of Selection waits for a bad query to arrive instead, which is the original form of private multiplicative weights (Hardt & Rothblum 2010).
Its basic form, AboveThreshold, compares each query’s noisy value with a noisy threshold, answers \(\bot\) (“below”) or \(\top\) (“above”), and halts at the first \(\top\), while the \(\bot\) answers cost nothing. With probability \(1 - \beta\), every \(\bot\) lies below the threshold plus a margin and every \(\top\) above it minus the margin, which for \(K\) queries of sensitivity \(\Delta\) at budget \(\varepsilon\) is \(8\Delta(\ln K + \ln(2/\beta))/\varepsilon\) (Equation 22.15). The variant Sparse restarts it after each \(\top\). Here the question asked is whether the guess’s error is large, so only the few queries it gets wrong cost privacy.

Definition 23.4 (Online private multiplicative weights) Input: the dataset, a target error \(\alpha\), privacy parameters \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), and a stream of at most \(K\) queries, with \(K\) fixed in advance. Set the budget of updates to \(c = \lceil16\ln N/\alpha^2\rceil\), the learning rate to \(\eta = \alpha/4\), and the guess \(\hat p\) to the uniform histogram. Give each of the at most \(c\) runs of AboveThreshold inside Sparse, and each of the at most \(c\) measurements, the budget \(\varepsilon_0\) of Equation 23.14 with \(k = 2c\) steps. For each incoming query \(f_i\) (the letter \(f\) marks queries of the stream), the score is the current guess’s error on it, \(g_i = |\langle f_i, \hat p\rangle - f_i(D)|\). Run Sparse on these scores with threshold \(3\alpha/4\), allowing up to \(c\) answers \(\top\), and act on its answer:

If Sparse answers \(\bot\), answer \(\langle f_i, \hat p\rangle\) from the guess.
If it answers \(\top\), measure \(m_i = f_i(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(1/(n\varepsilon_0))\), answer \(m_i\), and update \(\hat p\) by Equation 23.5 with the loss \(s_if_i\), where \(s_i\) is the sign of \(\langle f_i, \hat p\rangle - m_i\).
After the \(c\)-th \(\top\), halt.


The threshold sits at \(3\alpha/4\) because a \(\top\) must certify an error of at least \(\alpha/2\), twice the learning rate, so that each update gains regret faster than Theorem 23.1 allows, while a \(\bot\) must certify an error below \(\alpha\). A margin of \(\alpha/4\) gives both, so accuracy needs enough records to keep every margin and every measurement’s noise at most \(\alpha/4\).

Theorem 23.4 (Privacy and accuracy of the online algorithm) The algorithm of Definition 23.4 is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when \(\varepsilon \le 8\ln(1/\delta)\). If \[n \ge \frac{32\big(\ln K + \ln(4c/\beta)\big)}{\alpha\varepsilon_0}, \qquad \varepsilon_0 = \frac{\varepsilon}{2\sqrt{4c\ln(1/\delta)}}, \tag{23.22}\] then with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) every answer is within \(\alpha\) of the truth, and the algorithm answers the whole stream without using up its \(c\) answers \(\top\).


Proof. The plan is to check the scores’ sensitivity, compose the steps, and, on the event where every margin and noise is at most \(\alpha/4\), show that every answer is accurate and every update is a real correction, so that the mistake bound limits their number.

Sensitivity. Between two updates the guess \(\hat p\) is fixed, because it changes only after a measurement, which is a released output. Given the history, each score \(g_i\) is the distance between a fixed number and an answer of sensitivity \(1/n\), so it has sensitivity \(1/n\).
Privacy. The runs of AboveThreshold and the measurements alternate: a run ends with its \(\top\), that query is measured, then the next run starts with the updated guess. So the algorithm is a sequence of at most \(2c\) steps, each \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP and each chosen as a function of the earlier outputs, and by Lemma 23.2 with \(k = 2c\) it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
The good event. Half of the failure probability goes to the \(c\) runs, \(\beta/(2c)\) each, and half to the \(c\) measurements. With budget \(\varepsilon_0\), sensitivity \(1/n\) and failure probability \(\beta/(2c)\), the margin of one run is \(8(\ln K + \ln(4c/\beta))/(n\varepsilon_0)\) by Equation 22.15, and Equation 23.22 says exactly that this is at most \(\alpha/4\). A measurement’s noise exceeds \(\ln(2c/\beta)/(n\varepsilon_0)\) with probability \(\beta/(2c)\) by the Laplace tail, and that level is below the margin of a run, so it is at most \(\alpha/4\) too. The union bound over the \(c\) runs and the \(c\) measurements gives total failure probability \(\beta\).
Answers. On the good event, a \(\bot\) means \(g_i < 3\alpha/4 + \alpha/4 = \alpha\), so the guess’s answer is within \(\alpha\). A \(\top\) is answered by the measurement, which is within \(\alpha/4\).
Updates are real corrections. A \(\top\) means \(g_i \ge 3\alpha/4 - \alpha/4 = \alpha/2\). The measurement’s noise is at most \(\alpha/4\), less than the error, so the measured answer lies on the same side of the guess’s answer as the true one, and the sign \(s_i\) is right. As in step 1 of Theorem 23.2, the update’s regret against the true histogram is \(g_i \ge \alpha/2\).
Few updates. After \(U\) updates the regret is at least \(\alpha U/2\), and by Equation 23.8 with \(\eta = \alpha/4\) it is at most \(\alpha U/4 + 4\ln N/\alpha\). So \(\alpha U/4 \le 4\ln N/\alpha\), which is \(U \le 16\ln N/\alpha^2 \le c\), and the budget of \(c\) answers \(\top\) is never used up.


Because \(\sqrt c\) is about \(4\sqrt{\ln N}/\alpha\), the records needed grow like \(\sqrt{\ln N\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha^2\varepsilon)\) times a logarithm, as offline, but the logarithm is of the stream length \(K\) instead of \(|\mathcal Q|\). A \(\top\) query must be measured, because the guess is off by at least \(\alpha/2\) there and the measurement gives the sign.
The guarantee holds even when the analyst chooses each query after the earlier answers, because every step of the proof conditions on the history, which is the setting of Adaptive data analysis. The budget \(c\) is set by the worst case, so it is far larger than a real stream needs.

Example 23.6 On the running example, with \(\alpha = 0.05\), the budget is \(c = 35{,}490\) corrections, against the 148 of Example 23.4. For a query server over a universe of \(N = 2^{20}\) records, the budget is \(c = 88{,}723\). A stream of \(K = 10^6\) queries at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), with probability 0.95, needs \(8.39\times10^7\) records by Equation 23.22. That is about five times the offline bound in Table 23.4, the price of the worst-case budget and the wider margin.

section: 23.7 SmallDB: the exponential mechanism over small datasets
text:
23.7 SmallDB: the exponential mechanism over small datasets
Blum, Ligett & Roth (2008) were the first to answer many linear queries with error that grows only with \(\ln|\mathcal Q|\), and their algorithm answers a different question: what can the exponential mechanism achieve in a single choice, when running time is ignored? SmallDB makes that choice among whole small datasets, like the classifier selection of Selection with datasets in place of classifiers.
The proof first needs some small dataset that answers every query well, so that the exponential mechanism has a good candidate. The next lemma shows that a random sample of the data is one with positive probability, and Exercise 5 checks it on the running example.

Lemma 23.3 (A small dataset with small error exists) Let \(m > 2\ln(2|\mathcal Q|)/\alpha^2\). Then some dataset of \(m\) records from the universe has error at most \(\alpha/2\) on every query of \(\mathcal Q\).


Proof. 

Draw \(m\) records independently from the true histogram \(p\) and call the result \(\hat D\). For one query \(q\), the answer \(q(\hat D)\) is an average of \(m\) independent values in \([0, 1]\) with mean \(q(D)\).
Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration inequalities) says that such an average is more than \(s\) away from its mean with probability at most \(2e^{-2ms^2}\), which at \(s = \alpha/2\) is \(2e^{-m\alpha^2/2}\).
By the union bound, some query is more than \(\alpha/2\) off with probability at most \(2|\mathcal Q|e^{-m\alpha^2/2}\), and with \(m > 2\ln(2|\mathcal Q|)/\alpha^2\) this is below 1. So with positive probability no query is off by more than \(\alpha/2\), and a dataset with that property exists.



Theorem 23.5 (SmallDB) Let \(m = \lceil2\ln(2|\mathcal Q|)/\alpha^2\rceil\) (or \(2\ln(2|\mathcal Q|)/\alpha^2 + 1\) if that ratio is an integer), and run the exponential mechanism with budget \(\varepsilon\) over every dataset \(\hat D\) of \(m\) records from the universe, with the score \(-\max_{q \in \mathcal Q}|q(\hat D) - q(D)|\), minus the candidate’s largest error. The mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and the chosen dataset has error at most \(\alpha\) on every query with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) once \[n \ge \frac{4\big(m\ln N + \ln(1/\beta)\big)}{\alpha\varepsilon} \approx \frac{8\ln(2|\mathcal Q|)\ln N}{\alpha^3\varepsilon}. \tag{23.23}\]


Proof. The plan is to show that the best candidate scores at least \(-\alpha/2\), to count the candidates, and to apply the utility bound of the exponential mechanism.

Privacy. Each \(q(D)\) has sensitivity \(1/n\) by Proposition 23.1, so a candidate’s largest error moves by at most \(1/n\) between neighbours, the score has sensitivity \(1/n\), and the exponential mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
A good candidate exists. By Lemma 23.3, some candidate has error at most \(\alpha/2\) on every query, so the best score is at least \(-\alpha/2\).
Count the candidates. A dataset of \(m\) records is a list of \(m\) elements of the universe, so there are at most \(N^m\) candidates, and \(\ln N^m = m\ln N\).
The selection is nearly the best. The utility bound of the exponential mechanism, with \(N^m\) candidates, sensitivity \(1/n\) and failure probability \(\beta\), says that the chosen dataset’s score is within \(\frac{2}{n\varepsilon}\big(m\ln N + \ln(1/\beta)\big)\) of the best, except with probability \(\beta\). Its error is therefore at most \(\alpha/2\) plus that amount.
Records. Asking that the amount be at most \(\alpha/2\) gives the first form of Equation 23.23. Substituting \(m \approx 2\ln(2|\mathcal Q|)/\alpha^2\) and dropping the smaller term \(\ln(1/\beta)\) gives the approximate form.


SmallDB has the same logarithm of \(|\mathcal Q|\) as private multiplicative weights, and under pure DP the same \(\alpha^{-3}\), which comes from \(m\), growing like \(1/\alpha^2\), times the \(1/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) of the exponential mechanism’s error. It is simpler to analyse, because it makes one choice instead of \(T\), but hopeless to run, because the exponential mechanism must weigh \(N^m\) candidates.

Example 23.7 For the 6,560 marginal queries at \(\alpha = 0.1\), a dataset of \(m = 1897\) records suffices, and there are \(256^{1897} \approx 10^{4568}\) candidates. Equation 23.23 asks for \(4.21\times10^5\) records at \(\varepsilon = 1\). For a universe of \(2^{20}\) and \(\alpha = 0.05\), the last column of Table 23.4 shows that SmallDB’s bound is close to that of private multiplicative weights.

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.1 Local sensitivity, and why it leaks
The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms add noise scaled to the global sensitivity of a query \(f\), the most that changing one record can move \(f\) over every pair of neighbouring datasets that could exist (Definition 20.1). For counts that is the right scale, but the median of ages in \([0, 100]\) has global sensitivity 100. On a dataset with half its people at 0 and half at 100, one person moves the median from one end to the other. Yet on the dataset you actually hold, the median of 1,001 ages moves by about a tenth of a year when one person changes. This chapter asks whether you can add noise on the scale of the data you have and still satisfy differential privacy (DP).
The answer is yes, and one idea organizes every method: the noise scale is itself a function of the data, so it must be private too. Smooth sensitivity, propose-test-release and inverse sensitivity repair the leak for a statistic like the median. Stability-based release handles discrete answers, subsample-and-aggregate handles black-box estimators, and clipping handles unbounded data, at the price of a bias.
The running example is the median of \(n = 1{,}001\) synthetic ages, drawn from a normal distribution with mean 38 and standard deviation 14 and clipped to \([0, 100]\), released with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and, where needed, \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Its median is 36.96, and one changed age moves it by at most 0.1386 years. Values lie in a range \([0, \Lambda]\), with \(\Lambda = 100\) for the ages, and are sorted as \(x_1 \le \dots \le x_n\). Datasets have a fixed size \(n\), and their neighbours \(D \sim D'\) differ by one replaced record (The definition of differential privacy), so the Hamming distance \(d(D, D'')\) to any third dataset counts the records in which they differ. Every proof bounds the privacy loss of an output \(y\), how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\), \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \ln\frac{p_{M(D)}(y)}{p_{M(D')}(y)}, \tag{24.1}\] and pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP holds exactly when it never exceeds \(\varepsilon\) for any neighbours in either order.
Global sensitivity takes a maximum over all pairs of neighbours, including pathological ones. The natural fix is to take the maximum only over the neighbours of the dataset you hold. This section computes that quantity for the median and shows why noise proportional to it is not private.
For the median, and for its smooth sensitivity in Section 24.2, you need to know how far an order statistic can travel when \(k\) records change.
Now add Laplace noise scaled to the local sensitivity, \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}(D) = f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)/\varepsilon)\). The proof of Theorem 20.1 needs the same scale on both sides of the pair, but by Equation 24.4 one record can change this scale from 0 to \(\Lambda\), and then no \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee survives.

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
Definition 24.1 (Local sensitivity) The local sensitivity of a real-valued query \(f\) at a dataset \(D\) is the most that one record can move \(f\) starting from \(D\) itself, \[\mathrm{LS}_f(D) = \max_{D' \sim D}|f(D) - f(D')|. \tag{24.2}\] The global sensitivity is its worst case over all datasets, \(\Delta f = \max_D\mathrm{LS}_f(D)\), so \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le \Delta f\) always.



Lemma 24.1 (Changing k records moves each order statistic by at most k places) Sort the values of \(D\) as \(x_1 \le \dots \le x_n\), all in \([0, \Lambda]\), and pad with \(x_i = 0\) for \(i \le 0\) and \(x_i = \Lambda\) for \(i > n\). If \(D''\) differs from \(D\) in at most \(k\) records and has sorted values \(x''_1 \le \dots \le x''_n\), then for every rank \(j\), \[x_{j-k} \le x''_j \le x_{j+k}. \tag{24.3}\]


Proof. 

Upper bound. At least \(j + k\) values of \(D\) are at most \(x_{j+k}\), and the padding makes this true when \(j + k > n\). Changing \(k\) records removes at most \(k\) of them, so at least \(j\) values of \(D''\) are still at most \(x_{j+k}\), which says that \(x''_j \le x_{j+k}\).
Lower bound. At least \(n - j + k + 1\) values of \(D\) are at least \(x_{j-k}\), and at least \(n - j + 1\) of them survive \(k\) changes, so \(x''_j \ge x_{j-k}\).



Proposition 24.1 (Local and global sensitivity of the median) Let \(n\) be odd and \(m = (n + 1)/2\), so that the median of \(D\) is \(x_m\). Then \[\mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{med}}(D) = \max\big(x_m - x_{m-1},\ x_{m+1} - x_m\big), \qquad \Delta\,\mathrm{med} = \Lambda. \tag{24.4}\]


Proof. 

The median of a neighbour lies between \(x_{m-1}\) and \(x_{m+1}\). This is Lemma 24.1 with \(k = 1\) and \(j = m\).
Both ends are reached. Replacing \(x_m\) by \(\Lambda\) makes \(x_{m+1}\) the \(m\)-th smallest value. Replacing it by 0 puts the new 0 first, and \(x_{m-1}\) becomes the \(m\)-th smallest.
The global sensitivity. With \(m\) values at 0 and \(m - 1\) at \(\Lambda\), the gap above the median is \(\Lambda\), and no gap can exceed \(\Lambda\).




Proposition 24.2 (Noise scaled to the local sensitivity is not private) For the median with \(n = 5\) and \(\Lambda = 100\), there is a neighbouring pair on which \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}\) is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any finite \(\varepsilon\) and any \(\delta < 1\) (Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith 2007, Example 1).


Proof. 

A dataset that gets no noise. \(D = (0, 0, 0, 0, 100)\) has median 0 and both gaps next to it are 0, so \(\mathrm{LS}_{\mathrm{med}}(D) = 0\), the noise has scale 0, and \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}(D) = 0\) exactly.
Its neighbour gets wide noise. \(D' = (0, 0, 0, 100, 100)\) also has median 0, but the gap above it is 100. So \(M_{\mathrm{LS}}(D')\) has a continuous distribution, which equals 0 with probability 0.
The inequality fails. The output 0 has probability 1 under \(D\) and 0 under \(D'\), so DP would need \(1 \le e^\varepsilon\cdot 0 + \delta\), which no \(\delta < 1\) satisfies.



Example 24.1 The leak needs neither a degenerate dataset nor different answers. Take \(\Lambda = 100\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the neighbours of Table 24.1, which have the same median but local sensitivities six times apart.



Table 24.1: Two neighbouring datasets with the same median and very different local sensitivities.











Dataset
Values
Median
\(\mathrm{LS}\)




\(D\)
10, 20, 30, 31, 90
30
\(\max(30 - 20, 31 - 30) = 10\)


\(D'\) (31 replaced by 90)

The releases are \(30 + \mathrm{Lap}(10)\) and \(30 + \mathrm{Lap}(60)\). The narrow density decays six times faster, so the log-ratio of the two Laplace densities grows with the distance from the centre: \[L_{D',D}(y) = \ln\frac{20}{120} + |y - 30|\Big(\frac1{10} - \frac1{60}\Big) = -1.792 + \frac{|y - 30|}{12}. \tag{24.5}\] No pure \(\varepsilon\) holds (Figure 24.1). The loss exceeds 1 once \(|y - 30| > 33.50\), which happens with probability 0.572 under \(D'\) and 0.0351 under \(D\). The smallest \(\delta\) for which the pair is \((1, \delta)\)-DP, its privacy profile of Divergences, is \(0.572 - e\times0.0351 = 0.477\) with \(D'\) in the numerator, and the script finds 0.215 with the roles swapped. An adversary tells the two apart by the width of the noise, not its centre.







Figure 24.1: Left: the two releases of Example 24.1, with Laplace noise of scales 10 and 60. Right: their privacy loss, which crosses \(\varepsilon = 1\) at distance 33.5.

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.2 Smooth sensitivity
The leak came from a noise scale that jumps between neighbours. So use a scale that cannot jump: an upper bound on the local sensitivity that changes by at most a factor \(e^\beta\) between neighbours, since stretching noise by \(e^\beta\) moves its log-density by about \(\beta\). This section finds the smallest such bound (Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith 2007) and computes it for the median; Section 24.3 says which noise it can be used with.

Definition 24.2 (Smooth upper bound and smooth sensitivity) Let \(\beta > 0\). A function \(S\) of the dataset is a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound on \(\mathrm{LS}_f\) if \[S(D) \ge \mathrm{LS}_f(D) \quad\text{and}\quad S(D) \le e^\beta S(D') \quad\text{for all } D \sim D'. \tag{24.6}\] A dataset \(D''\) at distance \(k\) with a large local sensitivity forces such a bound up at \(D\) too, discounted by a factor \(e^{-\beta}\) per step. So the \(\beta\)-smooth sensitivity of \(f\) takes the maximum over every dataset \(D''\) of size \(n\), \[S^*_{f,\beta}(D) = \max_{D''}\ \mathrm{LS}_f(D'')\,e^{-\beta\,d(D, D'')}. \tag{24.7}\]


Proposition 24.3 (The smooth sensitivity is the smallest smooth upper bound) \(S^*_{f,\beta}\) is a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound on \(\mathrm{LS}_f\), and every \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound \(S\) satisfies \(S(D) \ge S^*_{f,\beta}(D)\) for every \(D\).


Proof. 

Upper bound. The term \(D'' = D\) of Equation 24.7, at distance 0, contributes \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D)\), and a maximum is at least each of its terms.
Smooth. A path from \(D'\) to \(D''\) can go through \(D\) first, so \(d(D', D'') \le 1 + d(D, D'')\). Each term of \(S^*_{f,\beta}(D')\) is then at least \(e^{-\beta}\) times the term for the same \(D''\) in \(S^*_{f,\beta}(D)\). Maximizing over \(D''\) gives \(S^*_{f,\beta}(D') \ge e^{-\beta}S^*_{f,\beta}(D)\), and exchanging the two neighbours gives the other direction.
Smallest. Let \(S\) be any \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound and \(D''\) a dataset at distance \(k\) from \(D\). Walking from \(D''\) to \(D\) in \(k\) steps, \(S\) falls by at most a factor \(e^{-\beta}\) per step, so \(S(D) \ge e^{-\beta k}S(D'') \ge e^{-\beta k}\mathrm{LS}_f(D'')\). Maximizing over \(D''\) gives \(S(D) \ge S^*_{f,\beta}(D)\).


The smooth sensitivity is positive even where the local sensitivity is 0. On the degenerate pair of Proposition 24.2 it is already \(100e^{-\beta}\) at \(D\), the discounted local sensitivity of its neighbour \(D'\) (Exercise 7).
You cannot enumerate all datasets, but all those at distance \(k\) get the same discount, so you need only the largest local sensitivity within each distance (a closer dataset counted again gets a smaller weight, which changes nothing): \[S^*_{f,\beta}(D) = \max_{k = 0, \dots, n} e^{-k\beta}A^{(k)}(D), \qquad A^{(k)}(D) = \max_{D'':\ d(D, D'') \le k}\mathrm{LS}_f(D''). \tag{24.8}\] For the median, \(A^{(k)}\) is the widest gap that \(k\) changes can open next to the median. You open one by moving the \(k\) values between two order statistics \(k + 1\) ranks apart out to 0 or \(\Lambda\), so that the emptied window ends up next to the median.

Proposition 24.4 (The smooth sensitivity of the median) For the median, with the sorting and padding of Lemma 24.1, the largest local sensitivity within \(k\) changes is the widest of \(k + 2\) windows of the sorted data, \[A^{(k)}(D) = \max_{0 \le t \le k+1}\big(x_{m+t} - x_{m+t-k-1}\big), \qquad k = 0, \dots, n, \tag{24.9}\] where the window with index \(t\) runs from rank \(m + t - k - 1\) to rank \(m + t\) (Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith 2007, Proposition 3.4). Since \(A^{(n)} = \Lambda\) and each \(A^{(k)}\) costs one subtraction per window, \(S^*_{\mathrm{med},\beta}\) takes \(O(n^2)\) operations.


Proof. Steps 1 to 4 show that no dataset within distance \(k\) has a gap next to its median wider than the widest window, and step 5 shows that every window is reached.

What the gap looks like. Let \(D''\) be within distance \(k\) of \(D\), with sorted values \(x''_1 \le \dots \le x''_n\). By Equation 24.4 its local sensitivity is one of its two gaps next to the median. Take the upper one, \((x''_m, x''_{m+1})\), since the reflection \(x \mapsto \Lambda - x\) turns lower gaps into upper ones and maps the windows of Equation 24.9 to themselves.
The gap contains at most \(k\) original values. Assume the gap is positive, and let \(x_\ell\) be the largest value of \(D\) at or below \(x''_m\). No value of \(D''\) lies strictly inside the gap, so the values of \(D\) inside it, say \(x_{\ell+1}, \dots, x_{\ell+j}\), were all changed, and \(j \le k\). The next value \(x_{\ell+j+1}\) is then at or above \(x''_{m+1}\), so the gap is at most \(x_{\ell+j+1} - x_\ell\).
The gap sits near rank \(m\). Exactly \(m\) values of \(D''\) are at or below \(x''_m\). Each is an unchanged value among \(x_1, \dots, x_\ell\) or one of at most \(k\) new values, so \(m \le \ell + k\). And at least \(\ell - (k - j)\) of \(x_1, \dots, x_\ell\) are unchanged, because \(j\) of the \(k\) changes were used inside the gap, and these unchanged values are among the \(m\), so \(\ell - (k - j) \le m\).
Fit it in a window. If \(\ell \le m\), the window from rank \(\ell\) to rank \(\ell + k + 1\) has \(t = \ell + k + 1 - m\) in \([0, k + 1]\) by step 3, and it contains the span of step 2 because \(j \le k\). If \(\ell > m\), the window with \(t = k + 1\) runs from rank \(m\) to rank \(m + k + 1\), which is at least \(\ell + j + 1\) by the second inequality of step 3, and contains it.
Every window is reached. The window with index \(t\) has \(k\) values strictly between its ends, at ranks \(\ell = m + t - k - 1\) and \(u = m + t\). Moving \(k + 1 - t\) of them to 0 and the rest to \(\Lambda\) gives \(x_\ell\) rank \(m\) (or \(m - 1\) when \(t = 0\)), so the median sits at one end of an empty interval of length \(x_u - x_\ell\). With \(k = n\) and \(t = m\) the window runs from the padded \(x_0 = 0\) to \(x_{n+1} = \Lambda\), so \(A^{(n)} = \Lambda\) and no larger \(k\) is needed.



Example 24.2 Take \(D = (1, 3, 4, 6, 9)\) on \([0, 10]\), with median 4. Table 24.2 evaluates Equation 24.9 with \(\beta = 0.5\) and checks it against brute force over all \(11^5 = 161{,}051\) datasets with values in \(\{0, \dots, 10\}\).

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.3 Admissible noise for smooth sensitivity
A smooth bound still changes by up to a factor \(e^\beta\). This section asks which noise tolerates that, in the mechanism \[M(D) = f(D) + \frac{S(D)}{\alpha}\,Z, \tag{24.10}\] where \(Z\) has a fixed density \(h\) and the constant \(\alpha > 0\) sets how many noise scales one record’s shift of \(f\) is worth. The answer depends on the tail of \(h\), because a light-tailed density and a stretched copy of it have a log-ratio that grows without bound, as in Example 24.1.

Theorem 24.1 (Pure DP with Cauchy-like noise) Let \(h_\gamma(z) \propto 1/(1 + |z|^\gamma)\) with \(\gamma > 1\), a density whose tails decay like \(|z|^{-\gamma}\); \(\gamma = 2\) is the standard Cauchy. Let \(S\) be a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound on \(\mathrm{LS}_f\), and let \[\gamma\alpha + (\gamma + 1)\beta \le \varepsilon. \tag{24.11}\] Then Equation 24.10 with \(Z \sim h_\gamma\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. The plan is to split the privacy loss at an output \(y\) into three pieces, for the scales, the centres and the stretch of the noise draw, and to bound each.

Write out the privacy loss. The density of \(M(D)\) at \(y\) is \(\frac{\alpha}{S(D)}h(z)\), where \(z = \alpha\frac{y - f(D)}{S(D)}\) is the draw that produces \(y\) from \(D\), and likewise for \(D'\) with \(z'\). Substituting \(y\) in terms of \(z\) shows that \(z'\) is \(z\) shifted, then stretched: \[z' = e^{\kappa}(z + v), \qquad e^\kappa = \frac{S(D)}{S(D')},\quad v = \alpha\,\frac{f(D) - f(D')}{S(D)}. \tag{24.12}\] Inserting \(h(z + v)\) in the middle of the ratio splits the log-ratio of the densities into three terms: \[L_{D,D'}(y) = \underbrace{\ln\frac{S(D')}{S(D)}}_{\text{scale}} + \underbrace{\ln\frac{h(z)}{h(z + v)}}_{\text{sliding}} + \underbrace{\ln\frac{h(z + v)}{h(e^\kappa(z + v))}}_{\text{dilation}}. \tag{24.13}\]
Size of the shift and the stretch. Smoothness gives \(|\kappa| \le \beta\). One record moves \(f\) by at most \(\mathrm{LS}_f(D) \le S(D)\), so \(|v| \le \alpha\), the only use of the upper-bound property.
Scale term. It is at most \(\beta\), by smoothness.
Sliding term. Write \(\psi(u) = \ln(1 + u^\gamma)\), so that \(-\ln h_\gamma(z) = \psi(|z|)\) plus a constant. Its slope \(\gamma u^{\gamma-1}/(1 + u^\gamma)\) is at most \(\gamma\), because \(u^{\gamma-1} \le 1 + u^\gamma\) both for \(u \le 1\) and for \(u > 1\). The arguments \(|z|\) and \(|z + v|\) differ by at most \(|v|\), so by the mean value theorem the term is at most \(\gamma|v| \le \gamma\alpha\).
Dilation term. With \(w = |z + v|\) and \(\kappa \ge 0\), the inequality \((1 + ca)/(1 + a) \le c\) for \(c \ge 1\) gives \[\frac{h(w)}{h(e^\kappa w)} = \frac{1 + e^{\kappa\gamma}w^\gamma}{1 + w^\gamma} \le e^{\kappa\gamma} \tag{24.14}\] for every \(w\), however far in the tail; that is what the power-law tail buys. For \(\kappa < 0\) the argument moves towards 0, where \(h\) is larger, and the ratio is at most 1. So the term is at most \(\gamma\beta\).
Add up. The loss is at most \(\beta + \gamma\alpha + \gamma\beta \le \varepsilon\) at every \(y\), which is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith (2007, Lemma 2.7) take \(\alpha = \beta = \varepsilon/(2(\gamma + 1))\), which for the Cauchy gives the release \(f(D) + \frac{6}{\varepsilon}S^*_{f,\varepsilon/6}(D)\,Z\) with loss bound \(0.8333\,\varepsilon\); Exercise 2 sharpens the sliding constant and divides the noise scale by three. For Laplace noise the dilation term grows with the draw, so the condition gains a term that charges for draws above \(\ln(1/\delta)\).

Theorem 24.2 (Approximate DP with Laplace noise) Let \(Z \sim \mathrm{Lap}(1)\), with density \(\frac12e^{-|z|}\), let \(S\) be a \(\beta\)-smooth upper bound on \(\mathrm{LS}_f\), let \(\delta \in (0, 1)\), and let \[\beta + e^\beta\alpha + (e^\beta - 1)\ln(1/\delta) \le \varepsilon. \tag{24.15}\] Then Equation 24.10 is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Proof. 

Reuse the split. Steps 1 to 3 of the proof of Theorem 24.1 did not use the shape of \(h\). So the loss is the scale term, at most \(\beta\), plus \(\ln(h(z)/h(z'))\) with \(z' = e^\kappa(z + v)\), \(|\kappa| \le \beta\) and \(|v| \le \alpha\).
Bound the shape term by the draw. For the Laplace density that log-ratio is \(|z'| - |z|\). The triangle inequality and the bounds on \(\kappa\) and \(v\) give \[\ln\frac{h(z)}{h(z')} \le e^\beta(|z| + \alpha) - |z| = (e^\beta - 1)|z| + e^\beta\alpha. \tag{24.16}\]
The rare draws pay \(\delta\). A \(\mathrm{Lap}(1)\) variable exceeds \(\ln(1/\delta)\) in absolute value with probability exactly \(\delta\). Outside that event the loss is at most the left side of Equation 24.15, hence at most \(\varepsilon\). By Lemma 20.2 the smallest \(\delta\) that works for a pair is at most the probability that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), so the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.


Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith (2007, Lemma 2.9) split the budget as \(\alpha = \varepsilon/2\) and \(\beta = \varepsilon/(2\ln(2/\delta))\). With either split \(\beta\) must shrink like \(1/\ln(1/\delta)\), because Laplace noise cannot give pure DP. Pure DP needs \(h\) at a point and at a stretched point to stay within a bounded ratio however far out the point is, and applying that repeatedly shows that \(h\) can decay at most like a power. A density that tolerates the shift and the rescaling is called admissible.
Heavy tails have a price. A standard Cauchy variable has \(\Pr[|Z| \le t] = \frac2\pi\arctan t\), so \(|Z|\) has median 1, but about one release in 16 is off by more than ten times that (\(\Pr[|Z| > 10] = 0.0635\), against \(e^{-10} \approx 4.5\times10^{-5}\) for Laplace noise).

Example 24.3 Release the median of the 1,001 ages with \(\varepsilon = 1\), and compare the options by their median absolute error, which for noise \(bZ\) is \(b\) for the Cauchy and \(b\ln 2\) for the Laplace. With global sensitivity it is \(100\ln 2 = 69.31\) years. Cauchy noise with \(\alpha = \beta = 1/6\) uses \(S^*_{\mathrm{med},1/6} = 0.1632\), barely above the local sensitivity, so its error is \(6\times0.1632 = 0.979\) (simulated: 0.980). Laplace noise with \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) and \(\alpha = 1/2\) allows \(\beta = 0.0322\) by Equation 24.15, close to the \(0.0345\) of Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith. Then \(S^*_{\mathrm{med},0.0322} = 0.5144\), the noise scale is 1.029 and the error is 0.713.
Both smooth releases are 70 to 100 times more accurate than the global one, and the gain grows with \(n\) (Figure 24.3). Below about 20 points the smooth noise is worse, because a handful of changes can then open a gap of nearly the whole range.

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.4 Propose-test-release
Smooth sensitivity needs a formula like Equation 24.9, and those are known for only a few functions. Dwork & Lei (2009) take a cruder route. Propose a bound \(b\) on the local sensitivity, check privately that the data are far from any dataset where it fails, and only then release with noise of scale \(b/\varepsilon\). The check counts how many changes it takes before something bad happens, and the proof needs such a count to have sensitivity 1.

Lemma 24.2 (Distances to a set have sensitivity 1) For any set \(\mathcal B\) of datasets, let \(\operatorname{dist}(D, \mathcal B) = \min_{D'' \in \mathcal B}d(D, D'')\) be the number of changes needed to reach the nearest of them. Then \(|\operatorname{dist}(D, \mathcal B) - \operatorname{dist}(D', \mathcal B)| \le 1\) for all \(D \sim D'\).


Proof. 

One direction. A path from \(D'\) into \(\mathcal B\) can go through \(D\) first, so \(d(D', D'') \le 1 + d(D, D'')\) for every \(D''\). Minimizing over \(D'' \in \mathcal B\) gives \(\operatorname{dist}(D', \mathcal B) \le 1 + \operatorname{dist}(D, \mathcal B)\).
The other. Exchange \(D\) and \(D'\).


So a distance to a set can be released with \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) noise, and propose-test-release compares it with a threshold that noise alone lifts a distance of 0 above only with probability \(\delta/2\).

Theorem 24.3 (Propose-test-release) Fix a proposed bound \(b > 0\), \(\varepsilon > 0\) and \(\delta \in (0, 1)\). Let \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = \min\{d(D, D'') : \mathrm{LS}_f(D'') > b\}\) be the number of records that must change before the local sensitivity can exceed \(b\). Propose-test-release outputs

\(\bot\) if \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) \le \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\);
\(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(b/\varepsilon)\) otherwise.

It is \((2\varepsilon, \delta/2)\)-DP. For the median, \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = \min\{k : A^{(k)}(D) > b\}\) with \(A^{(k)}\) from Equation 24.9.


Proof. The plan is to split neighbouring pairs into two cases. If the proposal is right for the pair, the release is an ordinary Laplace mechanism. If it is wrong, both datasets sit at an unstable point and the test almost always refuses.

The test is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. \(\operatorname{dist}_b\) is a distance to a set, so it has sensitivity 1 by Lemma 24.2, and adding \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) is the Laplace mechanism. Whether the test passes is post-processing of that noisy value.
Case 1: \(|f(D) - f(D')| \le b\). The release \(f(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(b/\varepsilon)\) has privacy loss at most \(\varepsilon\) by Theorem 20.1. The output is a function of two independent draws, each with loss at most \(\varepsilon\), so by basic composition the mechanism is \(2\varepsilon\)-DP on this pair.
Case 2: \(|f(D) - f(D')| > b\). Then both local sensitivities exceed \(b\), because each neighbour is in the other’s maximum, so \(\operatorname{dist}_b(D) = 0\). The test passes only if \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) exceeds \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), which has probability \(\frac12e^{-\ln(1/\delta)} = \delta/2\).
Bound case 2. For any set \(S\) of outputs, \(M(D)\) lands in \(S\) by refusing, if \(\bot \in S\), or by releasing, with probability at most \(\delta/2\). The refusal is post-processing of the \(\varepsilon\)-DP test, so its probability is at most \(e^\varepsilon \le e^{2\varepsilon}\) times that under \(D'\), and \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{2\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta/2. \tag{24.17}\]
Combine. Case 1 satisfies the same inequality, so every pair does.


When the data are stable the noise scale is set by the proposal, so it reveals nothing, and otherwise \(\bot\) says only that the data were probably near an unstable dataset. The threshold is large, \(\ln(10^6) = 13.82\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), so the data must be stable against more than a dozen changes. The method needs only the distance to instability, which is often easier to bound than \(S^*_{f,\beta}\), but it pays \(2\varepsilon\) and can refuse.
The proposal must not depend on the data. Setting \(b\) to twice the observed local sensitivity makes the noise scale a function of the data again, and the leak of Section 24.1 returns.

Example 24.4 On the 1,001 ages, propose \(b = 1\) year. The first \(k\) with \(A^{(k)} > 1\) is 21, so \(\operatorname{dist}_1(D) = 21\), and the test passes with probability \(1 - \frac12e^{-(21 - 13.82)} = 0.999621\). The release then has median absolute error \(\ln 2 = 0.693\) years, at a total budget of 2. On 101 ages \(\operatorname{dist}_1 = 1\), and the pass probability is \(\frac12e^{-(13.82 - 1)} = 1.36\times10^{-6}\). Figure 24.3 (right) shows it switching from 0 to 1 between \(n = 500\) and \(n = 1000\); Exercise 4 sizes the proposal for a given pass probability.







Figure 24.3: Left: median absolute noise of each release of the median age with \(\varepsilon = 1\), averaged over 10 synthetic datasets per \(n\); the dotted line is the local sensitivity. Right: the probability that propose-test-release with \(b = 1\) answers.

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.5 Inverse sensitivity
Smooth sensitivity and propose-test-release spend their effort on choosing a noise scale safely. Inverse sensitivity (Asi & Duchi 2020) has no noise scale. It samples each candidate output with a probability that falls exponentially in the number of records you would have to change to make it the true answer. That count is a distance to a set, so by Lemma 24.2 no smooth bound, test or refusal is needed.

Definition 24.3 (Inverse sensitivity and its mechanism) The inverse sensitivity of \(f\) at \(D\) toward an output \(y\) is the number of records you must change to make \(f\) equal to \(y\), \[\mathrm{len}_f(D, y) = \min\{d(D, D'') : f(D'') = y\}. \tag{24.18}\] The inverse-sensitivity mechanism samples \(y\) from \([0, \Lambda]\) with the density \[p_D(y) = \frac{e^{-\varepsilon\,\mathrm{len}_f(D, y)/2}}{\int_0^\Lambda e^{-\varepsilon\,\mathrm{len}_f(D, y')/2}\,\mathrm dy'}. \tag{24.19}\]

This is the exponential mechanism with the score \(-\mathrm{len}_f(D, y)\), and its proof is the exponential mechanism’s.

Theorem 24.4 (The inverse-sensitivity mechanism is pure DP) If every output in \([0, \Lambda]\) is the value of \(f\) on some dataset of size \(n\), so that every count \(\mathrm{len}_f(D, y)\) is finite, then the mechanism of Equation 24.19 is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.


Proof. 

The penalty has sensitivity 1. For each \(y\), \(\mathrm{len}_f(D, y)\) is the distance from \(D\) to the non-empty set of datasets on which \(f\) equals \(y\), so by Lemma 24.2 it changes by at most 1 between neighbours.
Each weight moves by at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\). So the weight of each output changes by a factor between \(e^{-\varepsilon/2}\) and \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), and so does the normalizer, an integral of such weights.
Pointwise, hence pure DP. The density is a weight over the normalizer, so \(p_D(y)/p_{D'}(y) \le e^{\varepsilon/2}\cdot e^{\varepsilon/2} = e^\varepsilon\) at every \(y\).


The factor 2 is needed because a weight and the normalizer can move in opposite directions. For the median the count has a closed form, and the density is a staircase, flat on each gap between sorted values.

Proposition 24.5 (The count for the median) Let \(n\) be odd, so that the median has rank \(m = (n + 1)/2\), with the sorting and padding of Lemma 24.1. For a candidate \(y\) in the open gap \((x_i, x_{i+1})\), \[\mathrm{len}_{\mathrm{med}}(D, y) = \begin{cases} m - i & \text{if } i < m,\\ i - m + 1 & \text{if } i \ge m.\end{cases} \tag{24.20}\]


Proof. 

Above the median. Take \(i \ge m\), so \(i\) values of \(D\) lie below \(y\). A dataset with median \(y\) has at most \(m - 1\) values below \(y\), and each change removes at most one, so at least \(i - m + 1\) changes are needed. That many suffice: move one value from below \(y\) to \(y\) and \(i - m\) others to \(\Lambda\).
Below the median. The reflection \(x \mapsto \Lambda - x\) turns the gap with index \(i < m\) into the gap with index \(n - i \ge m\), and step 1 gives \((n - i) - m + 1 = m - i\), since \(n + 1 = 2m\).


There is no noise scale to leak. Where the data are dense, the outputs a few steps from the median are also a short distance from it, so the error is a few gaps times a factor that grows with \(1/\varepsilon\). Asi & Duchi (2020) show that, up to logarithmic factors, no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism does much better on a dataset and its close neighbours, so the method is near-optimal dataset by dataset.
It has two limits. The outer gaps \((0, x_1)\) and \((x_n, \Lambda)\) can be long and are \(m\) steps away, which is negligible for a thousand points but not for eleven. And the count must be computed: closed forms like Equation 24.20 are known for medians, quantiles and a few other statistics, and Exercise 8 extends it to any quantile.

Example 24.5 Take the walkthrough dataset \(D = (1, 3, 4, 6, 9)\) on \([0, 10]\) with \(\varepsilon = 1\). Table 24.3 lists its six gaps, their counts from Equation 24.20, and their probabilities, each its length times \(e^{-\mathrm{len}/2}\) over the total. The two gaps next to the median are one change away and together get probability \(0.1477 + 0.2955 = 0.4432\).

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.6 Stability-based release
Some statistics take discrete values, such as the most common diagnosis or the model a selection procedure picks. On most datasets one record cannot change them, so their local sensitivity is 0. Propose-test-release with \(b = 0\) then gives the stability-based release: test privately that the data are far from any dataset where one change flips the answer, and if so release the answer exactly (Dwork & Roth 2014, ch. 7; Thakurta & Smith 2013).

Theorem 24.5 (Stability-based release) Let \(f\) be a discrete statistic, and let \(s\) be a stability score: a function of the data with sensitivity 1 that equals 0 on every dataset that has a neighbour where \(f\) gives a different answer. The stability-based release outputs \[M(D) = \begin{cases}\bot & \text{if } s(D) + \mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon) \le \ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon,\\ f(D) & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases} \tag{24.21}\] and it is \((\varepsilon, \delta/2)\)-DP. By Lemma 24.2, the distance to the set of datasets that have a neighbour with a different answer is one such score.


Proof. The proof is that of Theorem 24.3, except that nothing but the test depends on the data when the answers agree.

The test is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, as in step 1 of the proof of Theorem 24.3.
Neighbours with the same answer. The release is the same function of the test’s outcome on both, so it is post-processing of an \(\varepsilon\)-DP output. The second \(\varepsilon\) that propose-test-release paid for its noisy answer is not needed.
Neighbours with different answers. Then \(s(D) = s(D') = 0\), and the test passes with probability \(\delta/2\). Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 24.3, with \(e^\varepsilon\) in place of \(e^{2\varepsilon}\), gives \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta/2\) for every set \(S\).


For the mode of a categorical dataset, the most frequent value with ties broken by a fixed order, a score can be read off the lead of the winner.

Proposition 24.6 (A stability score for the mode) Let the lead \(g\) be the top count minus the second-highest count. Under replacement, \[s(D) = \max\big(0,\ \lceil g/2\rceil - 1\big) \tag{24.22}\] is a stability score for the mode.


Proof. 

Sensitivity 1. One replacement lowers one count by at most 1 and raises another by at most 1, so the lead moves by at most 2. Halving and rounding up turns that into a move of at most 1, since \(\lceil (g + 2)/2\rceil = \lceil g/2\rceil + 1\).
Zero where the answer can flip. If \(g \ge 3\), after one change the mode keeps at least \(c_1 - 1\) records, where \(c_1\) is its count, and every other value has at most \(c_2 + 1 \le c_1 - 2\), where \(c_2\) is the second-highest count. So a dataset whose neighbour has a different mode has \(g \le 2\), and then \(s = 0\).


The release is exact, and the cost of privacy is the chance of a refusal, which depends on the lead and not on the number of possible values. The mode must lead by about \(2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, whether there are ten categories or a billion. Under pure DP, the packing lower bound of Lower bounds needs a lead of about \(\ln N/\varepsilon\) to choose among \(N\) values, so this is how approximate DP gets around it. An exact release next to a flip happens with probability \(\delta/2\), and that is what \(\delta\) pays for.

Example 24.6 The median is not discrete, so take a mode, with \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) (threshold 13.82). Leads of 10, 30 and 40 records give scores 4, 14 and 19, and the release answers with probability \(2.73\times10^{-5}\), 0.5842 and 0.9972. So a lead of 35 is needed for probability 0.95, whatever the number of categories. When a neighbour adds or removes a record instead, the lead needed halves (Exercise 9).

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.7 Subsample-and-aggregate
Sometimes you cannot analyse \(f\) at all, because it is a trained model or a pipeline you did not write. Subsample-and-aggregate (Nissim, Raskhodnikova & Smith 2007; Smith 2011) runs \(f\) as a black box on disjoint pieces of the data and privately combines the answers. One record can change only one answer, so the aggregator needs to be private only with respect to one input.

Theorem 24.6 (Subsample-and-aggregate) Split the \(n\) records into \(B\) disjoint blocks of \(n/B\) records by a partition fixed in advance. Compute the block answers \(a_j = f(\text{block } j)\), clamp each to \([0, R]\), and release \[M(D) = \frac1B\sum_{j=1}^B \operatorname{clip}_{[0,R]}(a_j) + \mathrm{Lap}\Big(\frac{R}{B\varepsilon}\Big). \tag{24.23}\] This is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(f\). When the clipping is inactive and the blocks are independent samples, its mean squared error as an estimate of a target \(\theta\) is, with \(a\) the output of \(f\) on one block, \[\underbrace{\big(\mathbb E[a] - \theta\big)^2}_{\text{bias of } f \text{ on } n/B \text{ records}} + \underbrace{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(a)}{B}}_{\text{sampling}} + \underbrace{2\Big(\frac{R}{B\varepsilon}\Big)^2}_{\text{noise}}. \tag{24.24}\]


Proof. The privacy part bounds the sensitivity of the average; the error comes from squaring a sum of three independent pieces.

One record touches one block. The partition does not depend on the values, so replacing a record changes at most one block answer.
The aggregate has sensitivity \(R/B\). After clamping, that answer moves by at most \(R\), and the average divides by \(B\).
Privacy. Laplace noise of scale \(R/(B\varepsilon)\) on a quantity of sensitivity \(R/B\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by Theorem 20.1.
Error. The released value minus \(\theta\) is the bias \(\mathbb E[a] - \theta\), plus the mean-zero average of the \(a_j - \mathbb E[a]\), with variance \(\operatorname{Var}(a)/B\), plus the Laplace noise, with variance \(2(R/(B\varepsilon))^2\). The cross terms of the square each contain an independent mean-zero factor and average to zero, which leaves Equation 24.24.


The noise falls like \(1/B\), while the sampling term hardly moves, because a block estimate has about \(B\) times the variance of \(f\) on all records and averaging divides by \(B\) again. The bias of \(f\) on small blocks grows with \(B\), so the best \(B\) balances bias and noise (Exercise 5 finds it in closed form). The partition must not depend on the values, or one record could reshuffle many records between blocks.
The proof never looks inside \(f\), so the method suits trained models, as in private aggregation of teacher ensembles (Papernot et al. 2017). But the range \(R\) is still a global bound, and a loose \(R\) means large noise. Smith (2011) shows that for asymptotically normal estimators a version of the method loses nothing in the leading-order error.

Example 24.7 The running example has no black-box statistic, so take one: estimate the rate \(\lambda = 1\) of \(n = 10{,}000\) independent exponential inter-arrival times with \(\varepsilon = 1\). The estimate \(1/\bar x\), one over the sample mean, has infinite global sensitivity, because tiny times make it huge.
On a block of \(n_b = n/B\) records the block sum \(G\) is gamma with shape \(n_b\) and rate \(\lambda\), and the block estimate is \(a = n_b/G\). Integrating \(1/g\) and \(1/g^2\) against the gamma density leaves gamma densities with shapes \(n_b - 1\) and \(n_b - 2\), which gives \[\mathbb E[a] = \frac{n_b\lambda}{n_b - 1}, \qquad \text{bias } \frac{\lambda}{n_b - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(a) = \frac{n_b^2\lambda^2}{(n_b - 1)^2(n_b - 2)}. \tag{24.25}\] With \(R = 5\), Table 24.4 and Figure 24.4 show the trade-off; at \(B = 10\) the noise standard deviation is \(\sqrt2\times0.5 = 0.7071\).

title: 24  Beyond global sensitivity
text:
24.8 Clipping
The mean is the most common statistic of all, and on unbounded data its global sensitivity is infinite. Clipping replaces each value \(x\) by \(\min(x, C)\) before averaging, so the sensitivity becomes \(C/n\). But clipping changes the quantity you estimate, and the choice of \(C\) trades that bias against the noise. Applied to per-example gradients, the same move drives private model training in later parts.

Theorem 24.7 (The clipped mean and its best clipping norm) Take non-negative data \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) drawn independently from a distribution with mean \(\mu\), and write \((x - C)_+ = \max(x - C, 0)\) for the part of a value above \(C\). The clipped mean \[M(D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min(X_i, C) + \mathrm{Lap}\Big(\frac{C}{n\varepsilon}\Big) \tag{24.26}\] is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and its mean squared error as an estimate of \(\mu\) is \[\operatorname{err}(C)^2 = \underbrace{\mathbb E[(X - C)_+]^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\min(X, C))}{n}}_{\text{sampling}} + \underbrace{\frac{2C^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}_{\text{noise}}. \tag{24.27}\] The clipping norm that minimizes it solves \[\Pr[X > C]\Big(\mathbb E[(X - C)_+] - \frac{C - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)]}{n}\Big) = \frac{2C}{n^2\varepsilon^2}. \tag{24.28}\]


Proof. The privacy part is one line, the error splits as in Equation 24.24, and the best \(C\) is where the derivative of the error vanishes.

Sensitivity. Each clipped value lies in \([0, C]\), so one replacement moves the mean by at most \(C/n\), and the noise makes it \(\varepsilon\)-DP by Theorem 20.1.
The bias. Clipping removes exactly the excess, \(x - \min(x, C) = (x - C)_+\), so \(\mu - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)] = \mathbb E[(X - C)_+]\).
Error decomposition. As in step 4 of the proof of Theorem 24.6, the error is the bias, a mean-zero sampling term with variance \(\operatorname{Var}(\min(X, C))/n\) and independent noise with variance \(2(C/(n\varepsilon))^2\), which gives Equation 24.27.
Derivatives in \(C\). Raising \(C\) slightly raises \(\min(X, C)\) by that amount exactly when \(X > C\), so \(\mathbb E[\min(X, C)]\) has derivative \(\Pr[X > C]\) and \(\mathbb E[\min(X, C)^2]\) has derivative \(2C\Pr[X > C]\). By the chain rule the three terms have derivatives \(-2\,\mathbb E[(X - C)_+]\Pr[X > C]\), then \(\frac2n\Pr[X > C]\big(C - \mathbb E[\min(X, C)]\big)\), then \(4C/(n^2\varepsilon^2)\).
Set the sum to zero and divide by 2, which is Equation 24.28.


The bias does not shrink with \(n\), but the noise does, so the best \(C\) grows with \(n\) and moves into the tail (Exercise 6 solves Equation 24.28 for an exponential tail). Clipping from above always underestimates. Clipping to an interval around a centre cuts both sides, and the two cuts cancel for a symmetric distribution, which is why Private mean estimation first estimates the centre privately.
Choosing \(C\) is itself a data-dependent decision. Setting it to the observed maximum or the empirical 99th percentile brings back the leak of Section 24.1. Choose \(C\) from domain knowledge, or spend part of the budget on a private quantile by inverse sensitivity (Section 24.5).

Example 24.8 The ages are already bounded, so take incomes, in thousands, with \(\ln X \sim \mathcal N(\ln 40, 0.8^2)\). The median is 40 and the mean is \(e^{\ln 40 + 0.64/2} = 55.085\), pulled up by the heavy right tail. The averages of \(X\) and \(X^2\) below \(C\) that Equation 24.27 needs have a closed form in the normal distribution function (Probability distributions), and Table 24.5 uses it with \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\).
