title: 26  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.4 Large and unknown domains
A unary report carries one bit per possible value, which is absurd for all web addresses. And an oracle answers only for values the analyst names in advance, while a keyboard app wants words nobody listed. This section removes both limits. Hashing makes reports short, and growing prefixes finds the frequent values without a dictionary, the heavy hitters problem.
In local hashing each person draws a hash function \(h\) from a public family that maps the domain to \(w\) buckets, so that two values collide with probability \(1/w\). They send the index of \(h\) and a \(w\)-ary randomized response of \(h(x)\), with the \(p\) and \(q\) of Proposition 26.4 at \(w\) in place of \(k\). A report supports \(v\) if its bucket equals \(h(v)\).

Proposition 26.5 (Local hashing) Let \(\hat g_v\) be the estimate of Equation 26.11 applied to the supports of \(v\), which estimates the share of people whose own bucket is \(h(v)\). Then the estimate below is unbiased for \(f_v\), with the stated variance at \(f_v = 0\): \[\hat f_v = \frac{w\,\hat g_v - 1}{w - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat f_v)\big|_{f_v = 0} = \frac{(e^{\varepsilon_0} + w - 1)^2}{n\,(w - 1)\,(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)^2}. \tag{26.14}\] It is smallest at \(w = e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1\), where it equals optimized unary encoding’s \(4e^{\varepsilon_0}/(n(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)^2)\).


Proof. The plan is to undo two shrinkings with Lemma 26.1, the randomized response and then the collisions, and then to minimize the rare-value variance.

The own bucket. A holder of \(v\) lands in \(h(v)\), and anyone else does with probability \(1/w\). So a person’s bucket is \(h(v)\) with probability \(g_v = \frac1w + f_v\frac{w - 1}{w}\).
The randomized response. A report equals \(h(v)\) with probability \(p\) if the bucket is \(h(v)\) and \(q\) otherwise, so Lemma 26.1 makes \(\hat g_v\) unbiased for \(g_v\).
The collisions. Step 1 has offset \(1/w\) and slope \((w - 1)/w\), so Lemma 26.1 gives \(\hat f_v\), with \((w/(w - 1))^2\) times the variance of \(\hat g_v\).
A rare value. At \(f_v = 0\) a report supports \(v\) with probability exactly \(1/w\), so each support has variance \((w - 1)/w^2\). Dividing by \(n\) and \((p - q)^2\) and multiplying by \(w^2/(w - 1)^2\) leaves \(1/(n(w - 1)(p - q)^2)\), and \(p - q = (e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + w - 1)\).
The best width. With \(u = w - 1\), the part that depends on \(w\) is \(e^{2\varepsilon_0}/u + 2e^{\varepsilon_0} + u\). Two positive terms with a fixed product have the smallest sum when equal, at \(u = e^{\varepsilon_0}\).


Too few buckets waste the signal on collisions, and too many spread it thin (Figure 26.4). At \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\), with \(w = 56\), a report needs about 6 bits. The price is the server’s work, which Hadamard response (Acharya, Sun & Zhang 2019) makes fast at a constant factor in variance.






Figure 26.4: \(n\) times the rare-value variance of local hashing against \(w\), at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) and 4. Dots mark \(w = e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1\); dotted lines are optimized unary encoding.



To find unlisted values, write each as a string of \(L\) symbols from an alphabet of \(A\) symbols, and split the people at random into \(L\) groups. Group \(\ell\) reports its first \(\ell\) symbols, its prefix, by local hashing. The analyst keeps the prefixes whose estimate passes a threshold, extends each by every symbol, and moves to the next group. Write \(s\) for the standard deviation of an absent value’s estimate, and \(\Phi\) for the standard normal distribution function.

Proposition 26.6 (Heavy hitters by growing prefixes) If \(c_\ell\) candidates are tested at level \(\ell\), then under the normal approximation the threshold \[\tau_\ell = z_\ell\,s, \qquad\text{where}\quad c_\ell\,\big(1 - \Phi(z_\ell)\big) = \beta, \tag{26.15}\] admits on average \(\beta\) false candidates. Every prefix of a string is at least as frequent as the string, and each level tests only \(A\) extensions of each kept prefix.


Proof. 

The threshold. An absent value’s estimate averages many independent reports, so it is close to normal with mean 0, and exceeds \(z\,s\) with probability about \(1 - \Phi(z)\). Linearity of expectation sums this over the \(c_\ell\) candidates.
Prefixes. Each holder of a string holds all its prefixes, so a prefix is at least as frequent as every string that starts with it.


The search is the TreeHist protocol of Bassily et al. (2017), and Bassily & Smith (2015) show that no local protocol finds values rarer than order \(\sqrt{\ln k/n}/\varepsilon_0\).

Example 26.4 A million users each type one of 200 six-letter words with Zipf frequencies, at \(\varepsilon_0 = 4\). The domain has \(26^6 = 308{,}915{,}776\) strings. Local hashing uses \(w = 56\), the integer nearest \(e^4 + 1 = 55.60\), from 16,384 hash functions, so that collisions average out. Each of the six levels sees about 166,666 people, giving \(s = 6.75\times10^{-4}\), and no level tests more than 2,054 candidates. At the last level, \(\beta = 0.1\) puts the threshold at 3.80 standard deviations, a frequency of 0.0026.
The search returns 50 strings, all real words (Figure 26.5). The rarest word found has frequency 0.0033, and the most frequent word missed has 0.0035, lost to noise at one level. Testing all \(26^6\) strings would need 6.18 standard deviations, and at 3.80 it would raise about 22,418 false alarms.







Figure 26.5: The 200 words by rank: true frequency (circles, filled when found) and the estimate for each word found (crosses). The dashed line is the last level’s threshold.
crumbs: 26  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 26  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.5 Estimating a mean
Telemetry also collects numbers, such as minutes in the app. Each person holds \(x_i\) between 0 and a known bound \(m\), and the analyst wants the mean \(\mu = \frac1n\sum_ix_i\). The questions are how accurate a local mean can be, and how few bits each phone must send.
Adding Laplace noise to each value is the obvious randomizer. Ding, Kulkarni & Yekhanin (2017) send one bit instead, whose probability of a 1 rises linearly from randomized response’s lie probability at \(x = 0\) to its truth probability at \(x = m\).

Proposition 26.7 (Local means) Reports \(x_i + \mathrm{Lap}(m/\varepsilon_0)\) are \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, and their average is unbiased with standard deviation \(\sqrt2\,m/(\varepsilon_0\sqrt n)\). A bit \(Y_i\) with \[\Pr[Y_i = 1] = \frac{1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} + \frac{x_i}{m}\cdot\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} \tag{26.16}\] is also \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, and the estimate below is unbiased with the stated bound for all data: \[\hat\mu = \frac mn\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)Y_i - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(\hat\mu) \le \frac{m}{2\sqrt n}\cdot\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}. \tag{26.17}\]


Proof. The plan is to handle the Laplace reports in one step, then show that the bit is private, unbiased and of bounded variance.

Laplace reports. One value moves by at most \(m\), so Theorem 20.1 applies, and the average of \(n\) variances \(2m^2/\varepsilon_0^2\) has variance \(2m^2/(n\varepsilon_0^2)\).
Private. For every value, both outcome probabilities of the bit lie between \(1/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)\) and \(e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)\), whose ratio is \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\).
Unbiased. The mean of \(Y_i\) is linear in \(x_i\), so Lemma 26.1 makes each summand of \(\hat\mu\) unbiased for \(x_i\).
Variance. A 0/1 variable has variance at most \(1/4\), the summand scales it by \((m(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)/(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1))^2\), and the average divides by \(n\).


Both errors are of order \(m/(\varepsilon_0\sqrt n)\), against \(m/(\varepsilon_0n)\) centrally, and Duchi, Jordan & Wainwright (2018) show that no local protocol beats this order. The bit wins on communication, since a Laplace report needs about \(\log_2 m\) bits. Its bound is 0.765 times the Laplace standard deviation at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), and the two are equal at \(\varepsilon_0 = 2.324\).
The bound \(m\) must be fixed before collection, because every randomizer uses it. A device whose value exceeds \(m\) clips it, which biases the mean down, so a bound set too low trades noise for bias.

Example 26.5 A million users spend between 0 and \(m = 1{,}440\) minutes a day in the app, with a mean of 82.74. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) the one-bit estimate has standard deviation 1.420 minutes, within the bound 1.558 of Equation 26.17. In 200 simulated collections the estimates average 82.61, with standard deviation 1.415. Laplace reports would give 2.036 minutes, at about 11 bits each.
crumbs: 26  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models

title: 26  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.6 Collecting every day
Telemetry asks the same question every day, and basic composition (Post-processing, group privacy and composition) prices \(T\) reports of one record at \(T\varepsilon_0\). This section shows that the price is real, then gives the two fixes deployments use, memoization and α-point rounding.

Proposition 26.8 (Fresh reports leak) Suppose a person reports the same bit every day by randomized response at level \(\varepsilon_0\), with fresh randomness. After \(T\) days with \(k\) ones, the likelihood ratio between bit 1 and bit 0 is \(e^{\varepsilon_0(2k - T)}\), and the majority of the reports is wrong with a probability that falls exponentially in \(T\).


Proof. 

The ratio. A sequence with \(k\) ones has probability \(t^k(1 - t)^{T - k}\) under bit 1 and \((1 - t)^kt^{T - k}\) under bit 0, and \(t/(1 - t) = e^{\varepsilon_0}\).
The majority. It errs when more than half the reports flip, a binomial tail with flip probability below \(\frac12\), which falls exponentially by the Chernoff bound of Concentration inequalities.


The fix is to randomize once. In memoization the person draws one permanent randomized response per value and reuses it. RAPPOR encodes the value as a Bloom filter, a bit vector in which \(H\) hash functions each set one bit, and the permanent response replaces each bit by a fair coin with probability \(\phi\).

Proposition 26.9 (Memoization) All reports of an unchanged value, however many, are together as private as its permanent response. For RAPPOR that level, written \(\varepsilon_\infty\) because it covers unboundedly many reports, is \[\varepsilon_\infty = 2H\ln\frac{1 - \phi/2}{\phi/2}. \tag{26.18}\]


Proof. 

Post-processing. The reports are a function of the permanent response and of randomness independent of the data.
RAPPOR. A 1 is reported as 1 with probability \(1 - \phi/2\) and a 0 with probability \(\phi/2\). Two values’ filters differ in at most \(2H\) bits, and the others cancel.


Each new value costs another \(\varepsilon_\infty\). RAPPOR’s homepage collection used \(H = 2\) and \(\phi = 0.75\), giving \(\varepsilon_\infty = 4\ln(5/3) = 2.043\). A fixed response would let the collector link a sender’s reports across days, like a cookie, so RAPPOR re-randomizes it before each report, and one report is then \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP with \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.5343\) (Exercise 9).
A value that drifts, such as minutes, would need a new response every day. Ding, Kulkarni & Yekhanin (2017) instead draw, once, a bit \(b_0\) by Equation 26.16 at \(x = 0\), a bit \(b_m\) at \(x = m\) and an offset \(\alpha\) uniform on \([0, m)\). In round \(t\) the person sends \(b_m\) if \(x_t + \alpha \ge m\) and \(b_0\) otherwise, so that the random offset picks \(b_m\) with probability \(x_t/m\). Output perturbation then flips each sent bit with a small probability \(\kappa\), to blur the days on which the sent bit switches.

Proposition 26.10 (α-point rounding) With values in \([0, m]\), and \(b_0\), \(b_m\) and \(\alpha\) drawn once, independently of the data:

Each report has the distribution of Equation 26.16, so each round’s \(\hat\mu\) satisfies Equation 26.17.
The reports depend on the data only through the days with \(x_t + \alpha \ge m\), and with probability \(2e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)^2\) the kept bits agree, so every report is the same.
Values that stay in a band of width \(d\) change the report only if \(m - \alpha\) falls in the band, which has probability \(d/m\).
With output perturbation one round is \(\varepsilon_0'\)-DP, with \[\varepsilon_0' = \ln\frac{(1 - 2\kappa)\frac{e^{\varepsilon_0}}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} + \kappa}{(1 - 2\kappa)\frac{1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1} + \kappa}, \tag{26.19}\] and if, for every offset, two sequences of values select different kept bits on at most \(r\) days, their transcripts have likelihood ratio at most \(((1 - \kappa)/\kappa)^r\).



Proof. The plan is to average over the offset for item 1, read items 2 and 3 off the construction, and multiply daily ratios for item 4.

Unbiased. For a value \(x\), \(b_m\) is sent with probability \(\Pr[\alpha \ge m - x] = x/m\), so the report is 1 with probability \((1 - x/m)/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1) + (x/m)\,e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)\).
Dependence. Each report is \(b_0\) or \(b_m\), chosen by \(x_t + \alpha \ge m\). Both kept bits are 1 with probability \(e^{\varepsilon_0}/(e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1)^2\), and both 0 with the same probability. The choice switches only if \(m - \alpha\), uniform on \((0, m]\), lies in the band.
One round. The flip maps a probability \(\pi\) of a 1 to \(\kappa + (1 - 2\kappa)\pi\), still linear, so the worst ratio is between the ends of Equation 26.16.
Transcripts. Fix the kept bits and offset. A day sending the same kept bit under both sequences cancels, and a differing day has ratio at most \((1 - \kappa)/\kappa\). The flips are independent, so the ratios multiply, for every offset.


So the collector learns nothing about people whose kept bits agree, and about the others only when their value crosses a secret threshold. So the guarantee protects steady behaviour, while a person whose behaviour changes reveals roughly when. Microsoft deployed the protocol in Windows 10 at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) every six hours with \(\kappa = 0.2\), where Equation 26.19 gives 0.569 per round, while the paper reports a more conservative 0.686.

Example 26.6 Fresh reports at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) leak fast. After 100 days with 75 ones the likelihood ratio is \(3^{50}\), about \(7.18\times10^{23}\), while a memoized report leaves the majority wrong with probability \(1 - t = 0.25\) (Figure 26.6).
For the app’s minutes, with \(m = 1{,}440\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), the kept bits agree with probability \(2e/(e + 1)^2 = 0.3932\). Let each person’s minutes wobble by up to 15 either side of their level for 30 days. By item 3, the fraction whose report ever changes is \((1 - 0.3932)\) times the expected range of their values over \(m\), which is 0.0118. A simulation of 100,000 people gives 0.0119, against 1.0000 with fresh one-bit reports. On one freshly simulated day the α-point estimate is 82.17 minutes against that day’s true mean of 82.68, within the standard deviation of 1.42. With \(\kappa = 0.2\), each change costs \(\ln(0.8/0.2) = 1.386\).







Figure 26.6: Left: how often the majority of \(T\) daily reports is wrong, fresh or memoized. Right: the fraction of reports that ever change in 30 days, α-point or fresh.

title: 26  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.7 The shuffle model
The local model loses \(\sqrt n\) because the analyst knows whose report is whose. In the shuffle model (Bittau et al. 2017; Cheu et al. 2019) each person sends a randomized report to a shuffler, which strips identifiers and forwards a random permutation. The shuffler is trusted only to unlink, since the reports it sees are \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP. This section asks how far the central \(\varepsilon\) then falls.
Call the person whose privacy is at stake the target. The more reports the target’s report is mixed with, the less the multiset reveals. The bound to compute with is Theorem 3.1 of Feldman, McMillan & Talwar (2021), in this book’s notation and for replace neighbours. Its randomizers may depend on earlier outputs, which covers adaptive protocols.

Theorem 26.2 (Amplification by shuffling) Let \(R_i(z_{1:i-1}, \cdot)\), for \(i = 1, \dots, n\), be an \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizer for every value of the earlier outputs \(z_{1:i-1}\). Let \(M_{\mathrm{sh}}\) draw a uniform random permutation \(\Pi\), compute \(z_i = R_i(z_{1:i-1}, x_{\Pi(i)})\) in turn and output \(z_{1:n}\). For any \(\delta \in [0, 1]\) with \(\varepsilon_0 \le \ln\big(\frac{n}{16\ln(2/\delta)}\big)\), \(M_{\mathrm{sh}}\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon \le \ln\left(1 + \frac{e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1}{e^{\varepsilon_0} + 1}\left(\frac{8\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(4/\delta)}}{\sqrt n} + \frac{8e^{\varepsilon_0}}{n}\right)\right). \tag{26.20}\]


The proof is in Amplification by shuffling and by iteration, which bounds the hockey-stick divergence of two binomial counts. Its first step, the lemma below, carries the intuition that other people’s reports can look exactly like the target’s.

Lemma 26.4 (Clones) Let \(R\) be an \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP local randomizer and \(x^0, x^1\) the two values the target might hold. Then for every other value \(x\) there is a distribution \(\mathrm{LO}(x)\), the leftover, with \[R(x) = \frac{e^{-\varepsilon_0}}{2}R(x^0) + \frac{e^{-\varepsilon_0}}{2}R(x^1) + (1 - e^{-\varepsilon_0})\,\mathrm{LO}(x). \tag{26.21}\]


Proof. 

A floor. By Equation 26.1, \(p_R(y \mid x)\) is at least \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}p_R(y \mid x^0)\) and at least \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}p_R(y \mid x^1)\), so it is at least half their sum.
The leftover. Subtracting the two pieces leaves a non-negative mass of total \(1 - e^{-\varepsilon_0}\), which rescales to \(\mathrm{LO}(x)\).


So with probability \(e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) each other person sends a clone, a report distributed like one of \(x^0\) or \(x^1\). About \((n - 1)e^{-\varepsilon_0}\) clones, split at random between the two values, hide the target after shuffling. The theorem’s condition, \(ne^{-\varepsilon_0} \ge 16\ln(2/\delta)\), asks for enough expected clones.

Example 26.7 For 4-ary randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\) (Figure 26.7), \(p = \frac12\) and \(q = \frac16\). Take a target with \(x^0 = 1\) or \(x^1 = 2\). Another person with value 3 reports \((\frac16, \frac16, \frac12, \frac16)\), the clone part is \(\frac16\big(R(1) + R(2)\big) = (0.1111, 0.1111, 0.0556, 0.0556)\), and the leftover has mass \(0.6667 = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon_0}\).
For central \((1, 10^{-6})\), bisection on Equation 26.20 allows each user \(\varepsilon_0 = 3.504\) at \(n = 10^4\), \(5.701\) at \(10^5\) and \(7.992\) at \(10^6\). At 7.992, 8-ary randomized response keeps the truth with probability 0.998. For adding up bits as in Cheu et al. (2019), only about 676 of a million people then send a random bit, and the count has standard deviation 18.4, against 960 for local randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\).







Figure 26.7: The report distribution of value 3 under 4-ary randomized response at \(\varepsilon_0 = \ln 3\), split into clones of value 1 (blue) and value 2 (orange) and a leftover (grey).



The factor before the bracket of Equation 26.20 is \(\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). For large \(n\) the \(1/n\) term is negligible and \(\ln(1 + u) \approx u\), so the bound is about \(8\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\sqrt{e^{\varepsilon_0}\ln(4/\delta)/n}\) (Figure 26.8). So a target \(\varepsilon\) allows \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) of order \(\varepsilon^2n/\ln(1/\delta)\), and binary randomized response at that level has error about \(1/\sqrt{ne^{\varepsilon_0}} = \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/(\varepsilon n)\) on a fraction. Times \(n\), that is the shuffle row of Table 26.2. The constants are loose (Table 26.4). The numeric column computes the paper’s clone-count comparison exactly, and the exact column is shuffled binary randomized response, below which no general bound can go. Reason with the closed form, but deploy with a numerical accountant.

title: 26  Local, shuffle and distributed trust models
text:
26.8 Distributed noise
The shuffle model still adds noise to every report. In the distributed model each client adds a small share of the central noise, and a secure aggregation protocol reveals only the sum. The question is what that costs, and what dishonest clients do to it.
Secure aggregation is built from the additive secret sharing of Cryptography basics, with a practical version by Bonawitz et al. (2017). The one property used is simulation: everything the server sees could be generated from the sum alone. The noise works because independent Gaussian shares add to a Gaussian whose variance is the sum of theirs.

Proposition 26.11 (Distributed Gaussian noise) Let \(n\) clients hold vectors \(x_i\) whose sum \(f(D)\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\), and let each send \(x_i + Z_i\) through secure aggregation, with independent \(Z_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}I)\). The server’s view is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP whenever the Gaussian mechanism with noise \(\sigma\) on \(f\) is. If an adversary knows the noise of \(t\) clients, the guarantee is that of noise \(\sigma\sqrt{(n - t)/n}\).


Proof. 

The shares add up. Independent normals add their variances, so \(\sum_iZ_i \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I)\).
Only the sum is revealed. By simulation the view is a function of the sum and independent randomness, so post-processing applies.
Colluders. Removing what they know leaves \(n - t\) shares of variance \(\sigma^2/n\), whose privacy is the exact curve of Theorem 20.3.


Secure aggregation adds integers modulo a large number, because only on a finite set can shares be uniformly random. Skellam noise (Agarwal, Kairouz & Liu 2021) fits. \(\mathrm{Sk}(\mu)\) is the difference of two independent \(\mathrm{Poisson}(\mu)\) variables, with variance \(2\mu\). Sums of independent Poisson variables are Poisson, because their moment generating functions multiply (Distributions), so \(n\) shares \(\mathrm{Sk}(\mu/n)\) add to exactly \(\mathrm{Sk}(\mu)\). Its privacy is close to a Gaussian’s of the same variance, which this chapter uses as the approximation. The distributed discrete Gaussian (Kairouz, Liu & Steinke 2021) is the alternative.
Distributed noise gives central Gaussian accuracy without a curator, as long as enough clients are honest (Figure 26.9). If at most a fraction \(\rho\) may collude or drop out, each client adds variance \(\sigma^2/(n(1 - \rho))\), so the honest ones alone supply \(\sigma^2\) (Exercise 7). Malicious inputs are another problem, since secure aggregation does not check them.

Example 26.8 A server aggregates the app’s histogram through 100 clients at \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-6})\). A user who changes value moves one count down and another up, so \(\Delta_2 f = \sqrt2\). The analytic calibration of Corollary 20.1 gives total noise \(\sigma = 5.975\), so each client adds standard deviation \(5.975/\sqrt{100} = 0.597\). With 80%, 50% or 10% of the clients honest, \(\varepsilon\) rises to 1.128, 1.455 or 3.525. The script also checks that 100 Skellam shares of total variance 25 sum to mean 0.004 and variance 25.15, and that sharing \((3, -2)\), \((5, 7)\) and \((0, 1)\) modulo \(2^{20}\) reveals \((8, 6)\).







Figure 26.9: The actual \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) against the fraction of the noise the adversary does not know.

title: 27  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
27.1 Packing: pure DP pays the logarithm of the number of candidates
The earlier chapters of this part built mechanisms and measured their error. The Laplace mechanism releases a histogram over \(N\) bins with error about \(\ln N/\varepsilon\) per bin, and the Gaussian mechanism releases \(d\) attribute means with error about \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(n\varepsilon)\) each. These upper bounds leave a question open: is that error the price of privacy, or of a clumsy mechanism? A lower bound answers it, because it says that no mechanism satisfying differential privacy (DP) can be more accurate.
One idea proves every lower bound here: accuracy is an attack. An accurate output tells an attacker which of many datasets was used, whether a person is in it, or what a secret bit was. DP limits every such attack, because no test can tell the outputs on two neighbouring datasets apart much better than chance. So if the attack built from an accurate mechanism would beat that limit, the mechanism cannot be both accurate and private, and solving the inequality for the error or for the number of records \(n\) gives the bound.
The running example is a survey in which each of \(n\) people answers \(d\) yes/no questions, and the release is the vector of the \(d\) attribute means, under replace neighbours. One question with \(N = 10^6\) possible answers, a ZIP code, gives a histogram under add/remove neighbours. The examples use \(\varepsilon = 1\), a failure probability \(\beta = 0.05\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\). Packing shows that under pure DP the histogram’s error grows like \(\ln N/\varepsilon\). Fingerprinting shows that under approximate DP the \(d\) means need \(n\) growing like \(\sqrt d\), through a membership inference attack that you will run. The Dinur–Nissim attack of Reconstruction attacks shows that about \(n\) counting queries need error of order \(\sqrt n\). Table 27.1 lists the symbols.
Suppose the output of a mechanism must point to one of \(m\) candidates, such as the most common ZIP code. For each candidate \(i\) you can build a dataset \(D_i\) on which an accurate mechanism lands in a region \(G_i\) of outputs almost always. Run the mechanism on one reference dataset \(D_0\) instead, and on average each region gets at most a share \(1/m\) of its probability. But DP says the output on \(D_0\) cannot look very different from the output on a nearby \(D_i\). For large \(m\) the two clash, and the clash is packing, the private version of Fano’s method in Information theory.
Every bound in this chapter starts from an accuracy guarantee.
The packing lemma compares \(D_0\) with datasets \(k\) records away, so it uses group privacy, proved in Post-processing, group privacy and composition. Each of the \(k\) steps multiplies the bound by \(e^\varepsilon\) and adds a slack \(\delta\), which later steps multiply again. If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and \(D\), \(D''\) differ in \(k\) records, then for every set of outputs \(S\) \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D'') \in S] + \delta_k, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} \le k\,e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\delta. \tag{27.1}\] The slack grows geometrically: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), \(\delta_5 = 8.6\times10^{-5}\) is small, while \(\delta_{20} = 282\) bounds a probability by more than 1. So the lemma is stated for pure DP, where it says that \(m\) demands of size \((1 - \beta)e^{-k\varepsilon}\) must fit into a total of 1.
Two consequences follow by choosing the datasets. The mode is the most frequent element of the data. A histogram is the vector of counts of \(N\) elements, and its \(\ell_\infty\) error is its largest error over the bins. A histogram accurate to within \(\alpha\) finds a spike of height above \(2\alpha\), so it inherits the mode’s bound, halved.
Both bounds are matched, up to constants, by mechanisms you already have. The Laplace mechanism adds independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) noise to every count, since one record moves one count by 1. Report-noisy-max adds the same noise and returns the bin with the largest noisy count (Selection).
Both the lower bound and the Laplace error grow like \(\ln N/\varepsilon\) (Figure 27.2), with slopes \(1/(2\varepsilon)\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), so Laplace is optimal up to a factor of about 2. The lemma loses that factor in step 2, which counts only the mass inside the good regions, while the Laplace output on \(\emptyset\) falls almost entirely outside every ball \(G_x\). Under replace neighbours the Laplace error doubles while the lower bound barely moves (Exercise 1).
The lemma needs \(\delta = 0\), because with slack the share in step 1 turns negative once \(e^{-k\varepsilon}\) falls below about \(k\delta\). What survives is a capped bound.
The cap is real, because a mechanism reaches it. The stability-based histogram (Vadhan 2017) noises only the non-empty bins and releases those above a threshold of order \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\), so its error does not grow with \(N\) (Section J.3). On the mode’s packing datasets, the stability-based release reports the mode once it leads by about \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) replacements, however many values there are (Exercise 2 computes the cap).

title: 27  Lower bounds: what privacy costs
text:
Definition 27.1 ((α, β)-accuracy) A mechanism \(M\) is \((\alpha, \beta)\)-accurate for a quantity if, on every dataset, its output is within the error \(\alpha\) of that quantity with probability at least \(1 - \beta\), where \(\beta\) is the failure probability. These are not the error rates of a test, which other chapters write \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).



Lemma 27.1 (Packing lemma) Let \(D_0, D_1, \dots, D_m\) be datasets with \(D_0\) within \(k\) records of every \(D_i\), and let \(G_1, \dots, G_m\) be disjoint sets of outputs. If \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP and \(\Pr[M(D_i) \in G_i] \ge 1 - \beta\) for every \(i\), then \[m(1 - \beta)e^{-k\varepsilon} \le 1, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad k \ge \frac{\ln\big(m(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{27.2}\]


Proof. 

Each region gets a share of \(M(D_0)\). Accuracy says that \(G_i\) is likely under \(D_i\), and group privacy Equation 27.1 with \(\delta = 0\) says that it cannot be much less likely under \(D_0\): \[1 - \beta \le \Pr[M(D_i) \in G_i] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_i]. \tag{27.3}\] So \(M(D_0)\) puts probability at least \((1 - \beta)e^{-k\varepsilon}\) on each \(G_i\).
The shares fit into one distribution. The regions are disjoint, so no output is counted twice and the \(m\) shares add up to at most 1. Overlapping regions would let one output serve several candidates.
Combine. Adding the \(m\) bounds of step 1 and using step 2 gives the first form, and taking logarithms gives the second. Figure 27.1 draws this step.








Figure 27.1: The packing argument at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\beta = 0.05\). Black: the share \((1 - \beta)e^{-k\varepsilon}\) that \(M(D_0)\) must put on each good region. Dashed: the average share available with \(m\) regions. Accuracy at group distance \(k\) is impossible left of each dot.





Theorem 27.1 (Mode and histogram lower bounds) Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon\)-DP under add/remove neighbours, over a universe of \(N\) elements. If \(M\) returns the most frequent element with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) whenever that element appears \(k\) times and every other element appears 0 times, then \[k \ge \frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{27.4}\] If \(M\) releases a histogram over the \(N\) bins that is \((\alpha, \beta)\)-accurate in \(\ell_\infty\) error, then \[\alpha \ge \frac12\left(\frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} - 1\right). \tag{27.5}\]


Proof. The plan is to build the candidates once, apply the lemma to the mode, and then show that an accurate histogram separates the same candidates.

The candidates. Take \(D_0 = \emptyset\), the empty dataset, and for each element \(x\) let \(D_x\) be \(k\) copies of \(x\). Each \(D_x\) is \(k\) additions from \(D_0\), and there are \(m = N\) of them.
The mode. On \(D_x\) a correct answer lands in \(G_x = \{x\}\), and these regions are disjoint, so Lemma 27.1 gives Equation 27.4.
Disjoint regions for the histogram. The true histogram of \(D_x\) is \(k\,e_x\), with \(k\) in bin \(x\) and 0 elsewhere, and a correct answer lies in the ball \(G_x\) of \(\ell_\infty\) radius \(\alpha\) around it. Two centres differ by \(k\). A point in both balls would put the centres within \(2\alpha\) of each other, by the triangle inequality, so the balls are disjoint when \(k > 2\alpha\).
Pick the smallest such \(k\). The lemma’s bound is strongest for the closest datasets, so take \(k = \lfloor2\alpha\rfloor + 1 \le 2\alpha + 1\).
Apply the lemma. With step 4 it gives \[2\alpha + 1 \ge \frac{\ln(N(1 - \beta))}{\varepsilon}, \tag{27.6}\] and subtracting 1 and halving gives Equation 27.5.




Proposition 27.1 (Laplace histograms and report-noisy-max match packing) Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP with add/remove neighbours, the Laplace histogram over \(N\) bins has \(\ell_\infty\) error, at failure probability \(\beta\), of exactly \(-\ln\big(1 - (1 - \beta)^{1/N}\big)/\varepsilon\), which is at most \(\ln(N/\beta)/\varepsilon\). When one element leads by \(k\) records and every other count is 0, report-noisy-max returns the mode except with probability at most \((N - 1)e^{-k\varepsilon}(2 + k\varepsilon)/4\).


Proof. 

One Laplace coordinate. A \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) variable, with density \(\frac1{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\), exceeds \(\alpha\) in absolute value with probability \(e^{-\alpha/b}\), here \(e^{-\alpha\varepsilon}\).
All \(N\) bins at once. The noises are independent, so all stay within \(\alpha\) with probability \((1 - e^{-\alpha\varepsilon})^N\), and setting this to \(1 - \beta\) gives the exact error. A union bound over the bins puts the failure probability at most \(Ne^{-\alpha\varepsilon}\), and setting that to \(\beta\) gives \(\ln(N/\beta)/\varepsilon\).
Report-noisy-max. It fails only if some other bin’s noise exceeds bin \(x\)’s noise by \(k\) or more. The difference of two independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) variables has density \(\frac\varepsilon4(1 + \varepsilon|z|)e^{-\varepsilon|z|}\), a convolution that Section E.5 works out. Substituting \(u = \varepsilon z\), its tail beyond \(k\) is \[\frac14\int_{k\varepsilon}^\infty(1 + u)e^{-u}\,\mathrm du = \frac{e^{-k\varepsilon}(2 + k\varepsilon)}4. \tag{27.7}\] A union bound over the \(N - 1\) other bins gives the claim.









Figure 27.2: \(\ell_\infty\) error of \(\varepsilon\)-DP histograms over \(N\) bins at \(\varepsilon = 1\), failure probability 0.05. Orange: the Laplace mechanism, exact (line), union bound (dotted) and simulated (dots). Blue: the packing lower bound, with no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism in the shaded region.





Proposition 27.2 (Packing under approximate DP) Let \(D_0, \dots, D_m\) and the disjoint sets \(G_1, \dots, G_m\) be as in Lemma 27.1, with \(\Pr[M(D_i) \in G_i] \ge 1 - \beta\) for every \(i\), but let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Then at least one of \[e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) \le 2k\delta \qquad\text{or}\qquad m\,e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) \le 2 \tag{27.8}\] holds. In words, the group distance \(k\) must be at least about \(\min\big(\ln m, \ln(1/\delta)\big)/\varepsilon\).


Proof. 

The share with slack. Group privacy Equation 27.1 applied to \(D_i\), \(D_0\) and \(G_i\) gives \[\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_i] \ge e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - e^{-k\varepsilon}\delta_k. \tag{27.9}\] The subtracted part is a sum of \(k\) terms \(\delta e^{(j - k)\varepsilon}\), each at most \(\delta e^{-\varepsilon} \le \delta\), so the share is at least \(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta) - k\delta\).
Two cases. If the first condition fails, \(k\delta\) is less than half of \(e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta)\), so each share is more than \(\frac12e^{-k\varepsilon}(1 - \beta)\).
Fit into 1. The \(m\) shares add up to at most 1, as in the lemma, which is the second condition.




Example 27.1 Table 27.2 compares the bounds at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\). For \(N = 10^6\) locations, the most common one must lead by at least \(\ln(10^6\times0.95)/1 = 13.76\) records before an \(\varepsilon\)-DP release can report it reliably, and report-noisy-max needs 18.44. Every \(\varepsilon\)-DP histogram has, at the 95% level, an error of at least \(\frac12(13.76 - 1) = 6.38\) in some bin, and Laplace has 16.79. Simulated at \(N = 1000\), the Laplace error is 9.84 against the exact 9.88, and report-noisy-max at the lead 11.09 fails 2.28% of the time against the union bound’s 5%.

text:
27.2 Sample complexity: how many records privacy costs
An error of 6 records is large in a dataset of 50 and negligible in one of a million, so a lower bound on error is a lower bound on the number of records. This section translates the packing bounds into records, where privacy can be compared with sampling error, a cost you pay anyway. It is also where pure and approximate DP part ways once the output has many dimensions.
For the histogram, an error of \(\alpha\) in each frequency is an error of \(\alpha n\) in each count.

Proposition 27.3 (Records for a private histogram) An \(\varepsilon\)-DP histogram over \(N\) bins whose \(\ell_\infty\) error is at most \(\alpha n\) with probability \(1 - \beta\), on every dataset of up to \(n\) records, needs \[n \ge \frac{\ln\big(N(1 - \beta)\big) - \varepsilon}{2\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{27.10}\] Without privacy, estimating all \(N\) frequencies to within \(\alpha\) with probability \(1 - \beta\) takes at most \(n = \ln(2N/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\) samples.


Proof. 

The private bound. The packing datasets have \(k \le n\) records, so the guarantee covers them, and Equation 27.5 with the error \(\alpha n\) gives \[\alpha n \ge \frac12\left(\frac{\ln(N(1 - \beta))}{\varepsilon} - 1\right). \tag{27.11}\] Multiplying by \(2\varepsilon\) and dividing by \(2\alpha\varepsilon\) gives Equation 27.10.
The sampling bound. By Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration inequalities), an average of \(n\) independent variables in \([0, 1]\) is more than \(\alpha\) from its mean with probability at most \(2e^{-2n\alpha^2}\). Each frequency is such an average, so a union bound over the \(N\) bins gives a failure probability of at most \(2Ne^{-2n\alpha^2}\). Setting this to \(\beta\) and solving for \(n\) gives the claim.


So privacy adds a term of order \(\ln N/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) to a statistical cost of order \(\ln N/\alpha^2\), which Fano’s method shows is really needed. Their ratio is about \(\alpha/\varepsilon\), so privacy dominates only for coarse answers at strong privacy.
The survey’s \(d\) means make the candidates multiply. Records are \(x \in \{-1, +1\}^d\), a person’s \(d\) yes/no answers, and the release is the vector of means \(\bar x \in [-1, 1]^d\). Datasets made of copies of one corner of the cube \(\{\pm1\}^d\) give \(2^d\) candidates, so packing charges \(\ln 2^d = d\ln 2\).

Theorem 27.2 (Records for d marginals under pure DP) Any \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism under replace neighbours that releases the \(d\) attribute means with \(\ell_\infty\) error at most \(\alpha\) with probability \(1 - \beta\) needs \[n \ge \frac1\alpha\left(\frac{\ln\big((2^d - 1)(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon} - 1\right) \approx \frac{d\ln 2}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{27.12}\] The approximation holds for large \(d\).


Proof. This is packing at a fixed size \(n\), so the candidates replace records rather than add them.

Candidates. Fix a corner \(u_0 \in \{\pm1\}^d\) and let \(D_0\) be \(n\) copies of it. For each of the \(m = 2^d - 1\) other corners \(u\), let \(D_u\) be \(D_0\) with \(k\) records replaced by \(u\).
Disjoint regions. The mean of \(D_u\) is \(u_0 + \frac kn(u - u_0)\). Two corners differ in some coordinate by 2, so their means differ there by \(2k/n\). As in step 3 of the proof of Theorem 27.1, the balls of radius \(\alpha\) around the means are disjoint when \(k > \alpha n\).
Apply the lemma with \(k = \lfloor\alpha n\rfloor + 1 \le \alpha n + 1\): \[\alpha n + 1 \ge \frac{\ln\big((2^d - 1)(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}. \tag{27.13}\] Subtracting 1 and dividing by \(\alpha\) gives Equation 27.12.


Two mechanisms come close. By Theorem 20.3 of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) on a query with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\Delta_2/\sigma\) is at most the root \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) of Equation 20.17, which is \(0.2367\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\).

Proposition 27.4 (Laplace and Gaussian upper bounds for d marginals) Under replace neighbours, the Laplace mechanism releases the \(d\) means with \(\ell_\infty\) error at most \(\alpha\) with probability \(1 - \beta\), at \(\varepsilon\)-DP, once \[n = \frac{2d\ln(d/\beta)}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{27.14}\] The Gaussian mechanism does so at \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP once \(n = 2\sqrt d\,z/(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\,\alpha)\), where \(z\) is the number with \(\Phi(-z) = \beta/(2d)\) and \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function.


Proof. 

Sensitivities. Replacing one record moves each of the \(d\) means by at most \(2/n\), so the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity is \(\Delta_1 = 2d/n\) and the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity is \(\Delta_2 = 2\sqrt d/n\).
Laplace. The noise \(\xi_j\) in coordinate \(j\) is \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) with \(b = \Delta_1/\varepsilon = 2d/(n\varepsilon)\), and it exceeds \(\alpha\) with probability \(e^{-\alpha/b}\). A union bound over the coordinates gives \[\Pr\Big[\max_j|\xi_j| > \alpha\Big] \le de^{-\alpha/b}. \tag{27.15}\] Setting this to \(\beta\) gives \(\alpha n\varepsilon/(2d) = \ln(d/\beta)\), and solving for \(n\) gives the claim.
Gaussian. The noise has standard deviation \(\sigma = \Delta_2/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). A normal variable exceeds \(z\) standard deviations in absolute value with probability \(2\Phi(-z)\), so a union bound gives \[\Pr\Big[\max_j|\xi_j| > \sigma z\Big] \le 2d\,\Phi(-z) = \beta. \tag{27.16}\] Setting \(\sigma z = \alpha\), that is \(2\sqrt d\,z/(n\mu) = \alpha\), and solving for \(n\) gives the claim.


Pure DP pays linearly in the dimension, and Laplace matches it up to the factor \(2\ln(d/\beta)/\ln 2\). The Gaussian requirement grows only like \(\sqrt{d\ln d}\), because its noise follows \(\Delta_2\) rather than \(\Delta_1\), so for large \(d\) it beats every pure-DP mechanism. That is no contradiction, because under approximate DP (Proposition 27.2) the corners force only \(k \ge 13\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), against \(\ln(2^{1000}\times0.95) = 693.10\) for pure DP at \(d = 1000\). Approximate DP needs the idea of Section 27.3.
Packing also prices a question every analyst meets: what does it cost not to know where the data lie? Write the unknown mean as \(c\), because \(\mu\) is the Gaussian ratio here.

Proposition 27.5 (A mean known to lie in a range) Let the records be drawn from a normal distribution with unknown mean \(c\) and variance 1, and let \(|c| \le R\) be all that is known. An \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism under replace neighbours that returns an estimate closer than \(\alpha\) to \(c\), with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) whatever \(c\) is, needs \[n \ge \frac{\ln\big(\lfloor R/\alpha\rfloor(1 - \beta)\big)}{\varepsilon}, \tag{27.17}\] where \(\lfloor R/\alpha\rfloor\) is \(R/\alpha\) rounded down.


Proof. This is the packing lemma with random datasets.

Candidates. Place \(m = \lfloor R/\alpha\rfloor\) means \(c_1, \dots, c_m\) in \([-R, R]\), spaced at least \(2\alpha\) apart, and let \(G_j\) be the open interval of radius \(\alpha\) around \(c_j\). These intervals are disjoint.
Every dataset is close to a reference. Fix a reference dataset \(D_0\) of size \(n\). Any dataset \(D\) of size \(n\) is at most \(n\) replacements away, so group privacy with \(\delta = 0\) gives \[\Pr[M(D) \in G_j] \le e^{n\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_j]. \tag{27.18}\]
Average over the data. Draw the records of \(D\) from the normal distribution with mean \(c_j\). Averaged over \(D\), the left side is at least \(1 - \beta\) by accuracy, while the right side does not depend on \(D\). So \(\Pr[M(D_0) \in G_j] \ge (1 - \beta)e^{-n\varepsilon}\).
Combine as in the lemma: the \(m\) shares fit into a total of 1, which is Equation 27.17.


At \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\beta = 0.05\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), the bound is \(n \ge 4.55\) for \(R = 10\), \(9.16\) for \(R = 10^3\) and \(16.07\) for \(R = 10^6\). Clipping to \([-R, R]\) needs records linear in \(R\), and Private mean estimation closes the gap by first locating the data with a histogram. In \(d\) dimensions the cost is about \(d\ln(R/\alpha)/\varepsilon\) (Exercise 8).

Example 27.2 Table 27.3 gives the numbers for the survey at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\). A histogram over \(N = 10^6\) cells to within \(\alpha = 0.1\) needs at least \((13.76 - 1)/(2\times0.1\times1) = 63.8\), so 64 records under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and at most 875 for sampling error. At \(\alpha = 0.01\) the numbers are 638 and 87,522, so privacy is the smaller cost in both cases.

text:
27.3 Fingerprinting: the √d lower bound for approximate DP
Packing fails under approximate DP because group privacy breaks down at large distances. Fingerprinting compares only neighbours, so \(\delta\) never blows up. It asks whether an accurate release of one random dataset’s \(d\) means agrees with a member’s record more than with a stranger’s. The fingerprinting lemma shows that accuracy forces agreement of order \(d\) in total, and DP caps each record’s share, so \(n\) must be large. The idea comes from fingerprinting codes in cryptography, which Bun, Ullman & Vadhan (2014) brought to DP; this version follows Steinke & Ullman (2016).

Definition 27.2 (The random survey) Draw attribute means \(p_1, \dots, p_d\) independently and uniformly from \([-1, 1]\). Given \(p\), draw \(n\) records independently, each coordinate \(x_{ij} \in \{\pm1\}\) independently with mean \(p_j\), that is, \(+1\) with probability \((1 + p_j)/2\) and \(-1\) otherwise.

The means are random because, for a fixed \(p\), a mechanism that ignores the data and outputs \(p\) would be accurate up to sampling error yet tell nothing about any record. A mechanism that must be accurate for every \(p\) has to learn \(p\) from the records, and so must correlate with them.
The lemma is about one attribute, so drop the index \(j\) and write \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\) for its column. It says that an estimate’s correlation with the records’ deviations \(x_i - p\) cannot be small unless the estimate is inaccurate.

Lemma 27.2 (Fingerprinting lemma) For the column \(x\) of one attribute of Definition 27.2, with mean \(\bar x\), and any estimate \(f\colon \{\pm1\}^n \to \mathbb R\) of \(p\) computed from it, \[\mathbb E\Big[f(x)\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i - p)\Big] = 2\,\mathbb E\big[p\,f(x)\big] \ge \frac23 - 2\,\mathbb E[|f(x) - \bar x|], \tag{27.19}\] where the expectations are over \(p\) and the column.


Proof. The plan is to show that the correlation is the slope of the average estimate \(g(p) = \mathbb E[f(x) \mid p]\), weighted by \(1 - p^2\), and then to average that slope by integrating by parts. An accurate estimate rises from about \(-1\) to about \(+1\), so its slope cannot be small on average.

How the data respond to \(p\). The column has probability \(\prod_i\frac{1 + x_ip}2\). Its log-derivative in \(p\), the score of statistics, is \(\sum_i\frac{x_i}{1 + x_ip}\). Each term equals \(\frac{x_i - p}{1 - p^2}\), as you can check for \(x_i = 1\) and for \(x_i = -1\).
Differentiate the average estimate. Since \(g(p) = \sum_xf(x)\Pr[x \mid p]\) and the derivative of \(\Pr[x \mid p]\) is \(\Pr[x \mid p]\) times its log-derivative, \(g'\) is the average of \(f\) times the score. Inserting step 1 and multiplying by \(1 - p^2\) gives \[(1 - p^2)\,g'(p) = \mathbb E\Big[f(x)\sum_i(x_i - p)\ \Big|\ p\Big]. \tag{27.20}\]
Average over \(p\) and integrate by parts. The density of \(p\) is \(\frac12\) on \([-1, 1]\). Integration by parts moves the derivative from \(g\) onto \(1 - p^2\), whose derivative is \(-2p\): \[\frac12\int_{-1}^1(1 - p^2)g'(p)\,\mathrm dp = \frac12\Big[(1 - p^2)g(p)\Big]_{-1}^1 + \int_{-1}^1p\,g(p)\,\mathrm dp. \tag{27.21}\] The boundary term vanishes because \(1 - p^2 = 0\) at \(\pm1\) and \(g\), a polynomial, is finite there. The remaining integral is \(2\,\mathbb E[p\,g(p)]\), which equals \(2\,\mathbb E[p\,f(x)]\) because \(g\) is the average of \(f\) given \(p\). This is the equality.
Compare with the sample mean. The sample mean has average \(p\) given \(p\), so \(\mathbb E[p\,\bar x] = \mathbb E[p^2] = \frac13\). Any other estimate differs from it by \(f - \bar x\), and \(|p| \le 1\), so \[\mathbb E[p\,f] = \tfrac13 + \mathbb E[p(f - \bar x)] \ge \tfrac13 - \mathbb E[|f - \bar x|]. \tag{27.22}\] Multiplying by 2 gives the inequality.








Figure 27.3: The fingerprinting lemma for one attribute and \(n = 5\) records. Left: the average estimate \(g(p)\) for the sample mean, half the sample mean, and the constant 0. Right: each estimate’s correlation with the records’ deviations, \((1 - p^2)g'(p)\).



The lower bound below needs DP to bound the average of a score, while the definition bounds the probability of each event. The bridge is that an average is an integral of tail probabilities, and DP bounds each tail.

Lemma 27.3 (DP bounds the average of a bounded score) If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, \(D \sim D'\), and \(h\) is a function of the output with \(|h| \le B\), then \[\mathbb E[h(M(D))] \le \mathbb E[h(M(D'))] + (e^\varepsilon - 1)\,\mathbb E[|h(M(D'))|] + 2\delta B. \tag{27.23}\]


Proof. The plan is to write the mean as an integral of tails, bound each tail by the definition, and integrate back.

The mean as an integral of tails. A variable \(Y\) with \(0 \le Y \le B\) has \(\mathbb E[Y] = \int_0^B\Pr[Y > t]\,\mathrm dt\), because each value \(y\) is counted once for every level \(t\) below it. For \(Y\) equal to 1, 2 or 3 with probability \(\frac13\) each, the integral is \(1 + \frac23 + \frac13 = 2\). Splitting \(h\) into its positive part \(h_+\) and negative part \(h_-\) gives \[\mathbb E[h] = \int_0^B\Pr[h > t]\,\mathrm dt - \int_0^B\Pr[h < -t]\,\mathrm dt. \tag{27.24}\]
Bound the positive part from above. The definition applied to the event \(\{h > t\}\) gives \[\Pr[h(M(D)) > t] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[h(M(D')) > t] + \delta. \tag{27.25}\]
Bound the negative part from below, since it is subtracted. The definition with \(D'\) on the left and the event \(\{h < -t\}\), solved for the term on \(D\), gives \[\Pr[h(M(D)) < -t] \ge e^{-\varepsilon}\big(\Pr[h(M(D')) < -t] - \delta\big). \tag{27.26}\]
Integrate over \(t \in [0, B]\). Write \(h' = h(M(D'))\). By step 1 the integrated tails are means again, and each \(\delta\) integrates to \(\delta B\): \[\mathbb E[h(M(D))] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[h_+'] - e^{-\varepsilon}\,\mathbb E[h_-'] + (1 + e^{-\varepsilon})\delta B. \tag{27.27}\]
Pull out the mean on \(D'\). Since \(\mathbb E[h'] = \mathbb E[h_+'] - \mathbb E[h_-']\), the first two terms equal \[\mathbb E[h'] + (e^\varepsilon - 1)\mathbb E[h_+'] + (1 - e^{-\varepsilon})\mathbb E[h_-']. \tag{27.28}\] The coefficient \(1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\) is at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1\), because their difference is \(e^\varepsilon + e^{-\varepsilon} - 2 \ge 0\), so the middle terms are at most \((e^\varepsilon - 1)\mathbb E[|h'|]\). Finally \(1 + e^{-\varepsilon} \le 2\).


So a score centred on \(D'\), with mean absolute value 1, has mean at most \(e - 1 = 1.72\) on \(D\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), plus \(2\delta B\). The lower bound plays the two lemmas against each other through an attack that scores each record \(x_i\) by its correlation with the release: \[Z_i = \big\langle M(D),\ x_i - p\big\rangle = \sum_{j=1}^dM(D)_j\,(x_{ij} - p_j). \tag{27.29}\] A member should score high, because the release follows the data, and a stranger should score around 0.

Theorem 27.3 (The fingerprinting lower bound) Let \(M\) be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP under replace neighbours, with outputs in \([-1, 1]^d\), and let its average error on the random survey of Definition 27.2 be \(\mathbb E[\|M(D) - \bar x\|_1] \le \alpha'd\), where \(\alpha'\) is the average error per attribute. Then \[n \ge \frac{(2/3 - 2\alpha')\,d}{(e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d}. \tag{27.30}\]


Proof. The plan is that accuracy makes the members’ scores total order \(d\), while DP keeps each within a multiple of a stranger’s spread \(\sqrt d\), so the \(n\) members must carry the total.

Accuracy makes the scores large on average. Fix an attribute \(j\) and condition on the other columns, which leaves column \(j\) and \(p_j\) distributed as in the lemma. Apply Lemma 27.2 to \(f\), the average of \(M(D)_j\) over the mechanism’s coins. That averaging leaves the correlation unchanged and cannot increase the error. Summing over \(j\) and swapping the sums over \(j\) and \(i\) gives \[\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E[Z_i] \ge \frac23d - 2\,\mathbb E[\|M(D) - \bar x\|_1] \ge \Big(\frac23 - 2\alpha'\Big)d. \tag{27.31}\]
A stranger’s score is small. Let \(D^{(i)}\) be \(D\) with record \(i\) replaced by a fresh one, and let \(Z_i' = \langle M(D^{(i)}), x_i - p\rangle\) score \(x_i\) against a release that never saw it. Given \(p\), the deviations \(x_{ij} - p_j\) are independent of that release, with mean 0 and variance at most 1. So \(\mathbb E[Z_i'] = 0\), the cross terms of \(Z_i'^2\) average to 0, and \(\mathbb E[Z_i'^2] \le d\) because each output coordinate lies in \([-1, 1]\). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, \(\mathbb E[|Z_i'|] \le \sqrt d\).
DP keeps a member’s score close to a stranger’s. \(D\) and \(D^{(i)}\) differ only in record \(i\), so they are neighbours under replace. The score \(h(y) = \langle y, x_i - p\rangle\) has \(|h| \le 2d\), so Lemma 27.3 with \(B = 2d\), averaged over the data and combined with step 2, gives \[\mathbb E[Z_i] \le (e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d. \tag{27.32}\]
Combine. Summing step 3 over the \(n\) records bounds the total from above, and step 1 bounds it from below: \[\Big(\frac23 - 2\alpha'\Big)d \le n\big((e^\varepsilon - 1)\sqrt d + 4\delta d\big), \tag{27.33}\] which rearranges to Equation 27.30.


An \((\alpha, \beta)\)-accurate mechanism in \(\ell_\infty\), clipped to \([-1, 1]^d\), has \(\alpha' \le \alpha + 2\beta\), since a coordinate off by more than \(\alpha\) is off by at most 2. The \(\sqrt d\) is the gap between signal and noise: a member scores of order \(d/n\), and DP lets that exceed a stranger’s spread \(\sqrt d\) only by a constant factor. So \(\delta\) must stay far below \(1/\sqrt d\), and the term \(4\delta d\) cannot be removed, because a mechanism that publishes each record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP (The definition of differential privacy).
The rate matches the Gaussian mechanism, but the constants are poor. At \(\alpha = 0.1\), \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) the bound gives \(n \ge 5.0\) for \(d = 1000\) and \(n \ge 15.8\) for \(d = 10{,}000\), against the Gaussian mechanism’s 10,836 and 38,570 (Figure 27.4). The lower bounds already gain a factor \(1/\alpha\) by padding the dataset with fixed records (Exercise 4). Drawing \(p\) from a sharper distribution gains a further \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\) (Steinke & Ullman 2016). The last gap, \(\sqrt{\ln d}\), comes from the union bound in the Gaussian upper bound, not from privacy.






Figure 27.4: Records needed to release \(d\) attribute means to \(\ell_\infty\) error 0.1 with probability 0.95, at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), on log–log axes. Orange: pure DP (Laplace upper bound, packing lower bound), slope 1. Blue: approximate DP (Gaussian upper bound, fingerprinting lower bound), slope ½.




Example 27.3 For \(n = 5\) the script sums over all \(2^5 = 32\) columns and integrates over \(p\) exactly, for the three estimates of Figure 27.3. For the sample mean, both sides of Equation 27.19 are 0.6667. For half the sample mean, the correlation is 0.3333 and the error is \(\frac12\mathbb E[|\bar x|] = 0.3000\), so the bound is \(\frac23 - 0.6 = 0.0667\). For \(f = 0\) the bound, \(\frac23 - 1.2 = -0.5333\), is vacuous. So the lemma is tight for unbiased estimators and loose for shrunk ones (Exercise 3).

section: 27.4 Tracing attacks: the lower bound is a membership inference attack
text:
27.4 Tracing attacks: the lower bound is a membership inference attack
In 2008 Homer et al. showed that the published allele frequencies of a genetic study revealed whether a given person’s DNA was in it, and the US National Institutes of Health withdrew such summaries that year. Their test is, up to details, the score \(Z_i\) of Theorem 27.3. This section runs it on the random survey and compares its power with what DP allows. Dwork et al. (2015) proved it robust: it works on noisy means and with only a small reference sample (Exercise 6).
The attacker sees \(\hat p = \bar x + \xi\), the true means with Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) per coordinate, a target record \(x^*\) and the population means \(p\). It scores \(Z(x^*) = \langle\hat p, x^* - p\rangle\) and says “member” when the score is large. Each member pulls the release toward its own record by \(1/n\) of its deviation, which shifts its score up. The attack’s advantage is its true positive rate (TPR), how often it says “member” for a member, minus its false positive rate (FPR), how often it does so for a non-member.

Proposition 27.6 (Mean gap and spread of the tracing score) On the random survey of Definition 27.2, with the release \(\hat p = \bar x + \xi\), \[\mathbb E[Z \mid \text{member}] - \mathbb E[Z \mid \text{non-member}] = \frac{2d}{3n}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(Z \mid \text{non-member}) = d\left(\frac2{15} + \frac{8}{15n} + \frac{2\sigma^2}3\right). \tag{27.34}\] If the score is approximately normal with this mean gap \(\kappa\) and standard deviation \(s\) under both hypotheses, the best threshold has advantage \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} = 2\Phi\big(\kappa/(2s)\big) - 1\).


Proof. For \(p\) uniform on \([-1, 1]\), \(\mathbb E[p^2] = \frac13\), \(\mathbb E[p^4] = \frac15\) and \(\mathbb E[(1 - p^2)^2] = \frac8{15}\). A \(\pm1\) variable with mean \(p\) has square 1 and variance \(1 - p^2\).

Non-member mean. A fresh \(x^*\) is independent of \(\hat p\) given \(p\), with deviations of mean 0, so \(\mathbb E[Z] = 0\).
Member mean. For \(x^* = x_i\), coordinate \(j\) contributes \(\mathbb E[\bar x_j(x_{ij} - p_j)]\). In \(\bar x_j\), other people’s records are independent of \(x_{ij}\) and contribute 0. The member’s own term contributes \(\frac1n\mathbb E[x_{ij}(x_{ij} - p_j)] = \frac1n(1 - p_j^2)\). Averaging over \(p_j\) and summing over the \(d\) coordinates gives \(\frac{2d}{3n}\).
Non-member variance. The deviations \(x^*_j - p_j\) are independent of each other and of \(\hat p\), so the cross terms of \(Z^2\) vanish and \[\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \sum_j\mathbb E\big[\hat p_j^2(1 - p_j^2)\big]. \tag{27.35}\] Given \(p\), the mean square of \(\hat p_j\) is its squared mean plus the sampling and noise variances, \(p_j^2 + \frac{1 - p_j^2}n + \sigma^2\). Multiplying by \(1 - p_j^2\) and averaging gives, per coordinate, \[\mathbb E[p^2 - p^4] + \frac1n\mathbb E[(1 - p^2)^2] + \sigma^2\,\mathbb E[1 - p^2] = \frac2{15} + \frac8{15n} + \frac{2\sigma^2}3. \tag{27.36}\]
Advantage of a threshold. For \(\mathcal N(0, s^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(\kappa, s^2)\), the Neyman–Pearson lemma says that the best test thresholds the density ratio, which grows with the score, at the crossing point \(\kappa/2\). A member exceeds it with probability \(\Phi(\frac\kappa{2s})\) and a non-member with probability \(\Phi(-\frac\kappa{2s}) = 1 - \Phi(\frac\kappa{2s})\), so the advantage is \(2\Phi(\frac\kappa{2s}) - 1\). This is the total variation (TV) distance of the two normals, which Hypothesis testing shows to be the best advantage of any test.


Without noise, the signal-to-noise ratio \(\kappa/s \approx \frac{2d}{3n}\big/\sqrt{2d/15}\) is of order \(\sqrt d/n\), so tracing reaches advantage 0.5 once \(d \approx 0.56\,n^2\) (Exercise 5). Noise adds \(2\sigma^2/3\) per coordinate, so the attack fails when \(\sigma \gg \sqrt d/n\), the order of the Gaussian mechanism’s \(\sigma = 2\sqrt d/(n\mu)\). Aggregates are not safe because they are aggregates; what protects members is the ratio of \(n\) to \(\sqrt d\), or noise.
DP bounds the attack for each target, because the game is a test between the neighbours \(M(D)\) and \(M(D^{(i)})\). By Corollary 18.1 of the definition of differential privacy, its advantage is at most \((e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\) (Equation 18.20), which is 0.4621 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 0\). For the Gaussian mechanism, step 4 with \(\kappa = \Delta_2\) and \(s = \sigma\) bounds the TV distance of the two outputs by \(2\Phi\big(\Delta_2/(2\sigma)\big) - 1\).

Example 27.4 The script draws 200 datasets of \(n = 50\) records with \(d = 2000\) attributes and scores the 50 members and 50 fresh non-members of each. Without noise, Equation 27.34 predicts a mean gap of \(2\times2000/(3\times50) = 26.67\) and a spread of \(\sqrt{2000(\frac2{15} + \frac8{750})} = 16.97\); the simulation gives 26.70 and 16.92. The normal approximation gives the advantage \(2\Phi(0.786) - 1 = 0.568\). Table 27.4 shows three noise levels, the last being the \(\sigma = 6.67\) of the \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP Gaussian mechanism.

title: 27  Lower bounds: what privacy costs

27.5 Dinur–Nissim as a lower bound
Reconstruction attacks showed that \(n\) secret bits can be almost entirely reconstructed from about \(n\) random subset sums answered with error \(o(\sqrt n)\), error that grows more slowly than \(\sqrt n\). Each query counts the 1s in a random subset of people, and the attacker fits the bits to the answers by least squares. Combined with DP’s limit on guessing any single bit, it becomes a lower bound: a release that reveals most bits cannot be private.
The limit on guessing is Corollary 18.1 of the definition of differential privacy. If \(D\) and \(D'\) differ only in one uniformly random secret bit, every guess of that bit from the output of an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism is right with probability at most \((e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), which is \(e/(e + 1) = 0.7311\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 0\). Read the other way, recovering a fraction \(r\) of the bits proves a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\).

Theorem 27.4 (Reconstruction bounds ε from below) Let the database be \(n\) independent uniform bits, and call two databases neighbours when they differ in one bit. If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then the expected fraction \(r\) of bits that any reconstruction procedure recovers from \(M\)’s output satisfies \[r \le \frac{e^\varepsilon + \delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{r - \delta}{1 - r}. \tag{27.37}\] In particular, a mechanism that answers \(Q = O(n)\) random subset-sum queries with error \(o(\sqrt n)\) is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any fixed \(\varepsilon\) and any \(\delta < \frac12\). Error \(\Omega(\sqrt n)\), at least a constant times \(\sqrt n\), is necessary.


Proof. 

One bit at a time. Fix \(i\) and every bit but \(x_i\), which stays uniform because the bits are independent. Its two values give neighbouring databases, and the guess of \(x_i\) is a post-processing of \(M\)’s output, so it is a test between them, right with probability at most \((e^\varepsilon + \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). The uniform prior matters, because with a biased one guessing the likelier value already beats \(\frac12\).
Average over the bits. The expected fraction recovered is the average over \(i\) of the probability that bit \(i\) is guessed right, so it obeys step 1. Multiplying by \(e^\varepsilon + 1\) gives \(e^\varepsilon(1 - r) \ge r - \delta\), and dividing by \(1 - r\) and taking logarithms gives the second form.
Insert the attack. By the Dinur–Nissim theorem, in the sharper form of Dwork, McSherry and Talwar (2007) that needs only \(O(n)\) queries, errors of \(o(\sqrt n)\) let the decoder miss only \(o(n)\) bits. So \(r \to 1\), and the bound forces \(\varepsilon \to \infty\).


The Gaussian mechanism matches it. Changing one bit changes by 1 the answer of every query whose subset contains that person, so the answers move by at most \(\sqrt Q\) in \(\ell_2\), and \(\sigma\) proportional to \(\sqrt Q/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) suffices, of order \(\sqrt n\) for \(Q = 4n\). So independent noise costs error of order \(\sqrt Q\) per query under approximate DP, and of order \(Q\) under pure DP. For many more than \(n\) queries, private multiplicative weights (Query release) answers every query from a small private synthetic dataset, with error that grows only like a small power of \(\ln Q\).
The bound is crude, because least squares is not the best attack, so the \(\varepsilon\) it proves is far below the one the Gaussian mechanism guarantees. The true privacy loss lies between them. A lower bound from one attack is never a guarantee, and auditing, in a later part, narrows the gap with stronger attacks.

Example 27.5 The script answers \(Q = 800\) random subset sums of \(n = 200\) uniform bits with Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\), decodes by least squares and rounds at \(\frac12\), over 40 databases. Table 27.5 gives the fraction recovered, the \(\varepsilon\) it implies by Equation 27.37 at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), and the \(\varepsilon\) the Gaussian mechanism guarantees with \(\mu = \sqrt{800}/\sigma\). For instance, recovering 0.9607 of the bits proves \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\big((0.9607 - 10^{-6})/(1 - 0.9607)\big) = 3.20\).
