title: 28  Private mean estimation
text:
28.1 Bounded data
The mean is the statistic that private machine learning computes most often. Every step of private gradient descent clips per-example gradients, averages them and adds noise, and a survey that reports the share of people with some property releases a mean of yes/no answers. Earlier chapters released the mean of the dataset in hand. An analyst usually wants something else: the mean of the population the data were drawn from. So this chapter asks how many records a private estimate of a population mean needs, and what each thing you do not know about the data costs.
Two guarantees with different shapes meet here. Privacy must hold for every dataset, including ones that your assumptions say cannot happen, because a guarantee that fails when an assumption fails protects nobody. Accuracy, on the other hand, is a statement about data drawn from a distribution, such as “the records are normal with variance 1”. So an assumption about the data may make a mechanism more accurate, but it may never enter the privacy proof. Every mechanism below respects that split: it clips the data to a range, which makes it private whatever the data are, and the assumption only says how often the clipping changes nothing. One idea then organizes the chapter: spend a small part of the budget to learn where the data are, then clip there and spend the rest on the mean. The noise of a clipped mean is proportional to the width of the clipping range, so a range set by your prior ignorance makes the noise pay for that ignorance in full. Finding the data privately first costs a number of records that grows only like the logarithm of the range, and the final step can then clip to a narrow window and add little noise.
The running example is a survey of \(n = 1000\) people at \(\varepsilon = 1\), and each section changes what is known about the records: yes/no answers first, then normal measurements whose mean could be anywhere up to a bound \(R\), then vectors, then incomes with a heavy tail. Throughout, datasets have a fixed size \(n\), and two datasets \(D \sim D'\) are neighbours when they differ in one replaced record, as in Beyond global sensitivity. The records \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) are drawn independently from a distribution whose mean \(\mu\) is the target, and every statement of the form “the data lie in this range” is allowed to fail with probability \(\beta = 0.05\). An estimate \(\hat\mu\) is judged by its root-mean-square error (RMSE), the square root of the average of \((\hat\mu - \mu)^2\) over the data and the mechanism’s noise. The guarantees are those of the definition of differential privacy (DP): a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when changing one record changes the probability of any set of outputs by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) plus \(\delta\), and pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP when \(\delta = 0\). Table 28.1 lists the symbols the chapter uses.
Start where nothing is unknown except the mean. The records lie in a known interval, such as yes/no answers coded 0 and 1, so no clipping is needed and no assumption about the data enters at all. The question is how many more records a private estimate needs than a non-private one. The answer is the best case of the chapter, and every later section tries to recover it when the data are not bounded.
Every estimator in this chapter has the same form: clip each record to an interval, average, and add Laplace noise. The lemma below says what such an estimator costs in privacy and in error, and every later proof starts from it. Its privacy part is the Laplace mechanism of the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms applied to a mean. Its error part is the three-way split of the clipping section of Beyond global sensitivity: the clipped average varies from sample to sample, clipping shifts its expected value away from \(\mu\), and the noise adds its own spread.
With the lemma in hand, the bounded case is a matter of reading off the error and solving for \(n\). Bounded records need no clipping, so the bias is zero, and the only question is how the sampling term and the noise term add up.
The second form of Equation 28.4 reads as two costs added together. Sampling needs about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2\) records whatever you do, and privacy adds about \(w/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) more. The ratio of the privacy term to the sampling term is \(\sqrt2\,w\alpha/(\varepsilon\sigma^2)\), so for a small target error \(\alpha\) privacy costs a lower-order number of records. Halving \(\varepsilon\) doubles the privacy term and leaves the sampling term alone.
The privacy term grows with the width \(w\) and not with the variance \(\sigma^2\), because the noise is set by the worst change one record can make, which is the width, whatever the data look like. The variance describes typical data, and typical data enter only the sampling term. That split between worst-case noise and typical-case sampling is the pattern of every section below.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
text:
Lemma 28.1 (A clipped mean with Laplace noise) Let each record \(X_i\) be replaced by a clipped value \(Y_i\) that depends on \(X_i\) alone and lies in an interval of width \(w\), and release the average of the clipped values plus Laplace noise \(\xi\), \[\hat\mu = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i + \xi, \qquad \xi \sim \mathrm{Lap}\Big(\frac{w}{n\varepsilon}\Big). \tag{28.1}\] The release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every dataset. When the records are independent draws from a distribution with mean \(\mu\), the mean squared error of the release splits into three parts, \[\mathbb E\big[(\hat\mu - \mu)^2\big] = \underbrace{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}{n}}_{\text{sampling}} + \underbrace{\big(\mathbb E[Y] - \mu\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{\operatorname{Var}(\xi)}_{\text{noise}}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\xi) = \frac{2w^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}. \tag{28.2}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the sensitivity of the clipped average, calibrate the Laplace noise to it, then square the error and watch the cross terms vanish.

Sensitivity. Replacing one record changes one clipped value \(Y_i\), by at most \(w\) since both values lie in the interval, and the other values stay put because each depends on its own record alone. So the sum moves by at most \(w\) and the average by at most \(w/n\), which is its sensitivity under replace neighbours, as for the mean with public \(n\) in Proposition 20.2.
Privacy. By Theorem 20.1, Laplace noise with scale equal to the sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\), here \(w/(n\varepsilon)\), makes the release \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Nothing in steps 1 and 2 assumed anything about the data, because the clipping, not an assumption, keeps every \(Y_i\) in the interval.
The three parts. Write \(\hat\mu - \mu\) as a sum of three pieces: the average of \(Y_i - \mathbb E[Y]\) over the records, the constant \(\mathbb E[Y] - \mu\), and the noise \(\xi\). The first and the last have mean 0 and are independent of each other, so when the sum is squared and averaged, every cross term contains a mean-zero factor and vanishes. The average of \(n\) independent copies has \(1/n\) times the variance of one, which gives the sampling part.
The noise. By Theorem 20.1 a Laplace variable with scale \(s\) has variance \(2s^2\), which with \(s = w/(n\varepsilon)\) is \(2w^2/(n^2\varepsilon^2)\).




Theorem 28.1 (Private mean of bounded data) Let the records be independent draws from a distribution on an interval of width \(w\) with variance \(\sigma^2\), and release their average plus \(\mathrm{Lap}(w/(n\varepsilon))\) noise. The release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and its RMSE is \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma^2}{n} + \frac{2w^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}. \tag{28.3}\] The RMSE is at most \(\alpha\) once \[n \ge \frac{\sigma^2 + \sqrt{\sigma^4 + 8w^2\alpha^2/\varepsilon^2}}{2\alpha^2}, \qquad\text{which is at most}\qquad \frac{\sigma^2}{\alpha^2} + \frac{\sqrt2\,w}{\alpha\varepsilon}. \tag{28.4}\]


Proof. 

Privacy and error. The records already lie in the interval, so Lemma 28.1 applies with \(Y_i = X_i\) and width \(w\), and the release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. In Equation 28.2 the bias is 0, the sampling term is \(\sigma^2/n\) and the noise term is \(2w^2/(n\varepsilon)^2\), and their sum is the square of Equation 28.3.
Solve for \(n\). Setting the square of Equation 28.3 equal to \(\alpha^2\) and multiplying by \(n^2\) gives the quadratic \(\alpha^2n^2 - \sigma^2n - 2w^2/\varepsilon^2 = 0\), whose positive root is the first form of Equation 28.4. The RMSE falls as \(n\) grows, so every \(n\) above the root reaches \(\alpha\).
The simpler bound. The square root of a sum is at most the sum of the square roots, so \(\sqrt{\sigma^4 + 8w^2\alpha^2/\varepsilon^2} \le \sigma^2 + 2\sqrt2\,w\alpha/\varepsilon\). Inserting this and dividing by \(2\alpha^2\) gives the second form.





Example 28.1 Take yes/no answers, so \(w = 1\), and the worst case for sampling, a population that is half yes, so \(\sigma = 0.5\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the private RMSE is 0.0520 for 100 people, against 0.0500 without privacy. For 1,000 people it is 0.0159 against 0.0158, and at 10,000 both are 0.0050. To reach \(\alpha = 0.05\) you need 108 people instead of 100, and to reach \(\alpha = 0.01\) you need 2,508 instead of 2,500. Privacy costs eight people at a sample size where sampling already needs 2,500. Exercise 1 redoes the count at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), where the privacy term is no longer small.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
section: 28.2 Gaussian data with a known range
text:
28.2 Gaussian data with a known range
Now let the records be unbounded, but drawn from a normal distribution with unknown mean \(\mu\) and variance 1, and suppose all you know about the mean is that \(|\mu| \le R\). The bound \(R\) measures your ignorance. A height in centimetres might have \(R\) of a few hundred, while a feature of a model you have never looked at might need \(R = 10^6\). Unbounded records have no finite sensitivity, so the estimator must clip, and the obvious choice is to clip to the whole range where the data could possibly be. This section works out what that costs, and the answer is the baseline that the next section improves on.
Clipping changes a record only if the record lies outside the range. To show that this is rare, the proof needs to know how far \(n\) normal draws can stray from their mean, which is the lemma below.

Lemma 28.2 (Normal draws stay close to their mean) Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent draws from a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance 1, and let \(\beta \in (0, 1)\). With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), every draw lies within \[\tau_1 = \sqrt{2\ln(2n/\beta)} \tag{28.5}\] of \(\mu\).


Proof. 

One draw. A standard normal variable exceeds a level \(t\) in absolute value with probability at most \(2e^{-t^2/2}\), which is the Chernoff bound of Concentration inequalities applied to each of its two tails. Each \(X_i - \mu\) is standard normal.
All draws. The probability that at least one of the \(n\) draws lies further than \(t\) from \(\mu\) is at most the sum of their \(n\) probabilities, by the union bound, which is \(2ne^{-t^2/2}\). Setting this equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(t\) gives \(\tau_1\).


The bound is loose. Concentration inequalities proves a tail bound half as large for one draw, but the factor 2 changes \(\tau_1\) only slightly, so the chapter keeps the simpler form. For \(n = 1000\) and \(\beta = 0.05\) it gives \(\tau_1 = 4.604\), and in 20,000 simulated datasets the largest distance exceeded \(\tau_1\) in a fraction 0.0039 of them, not 0.05.
The naive estimator widens the range \([-R, R]\) by \(\tau_1\) on each side and clips there, so that with high probability it clips nothing.

Proposition 28.1 (The naive estimator) Let the records be independent draws from a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\), where \(|\mu| \le R\), and variance 1, and let \(\tau_1\) be as in Equation 28.5. Clip every record to \([-R - \tau_1, R + \tau_1]\), average, and add \(\mathrm{Lap}\big(2(R + \tau_1)/(n\varepsilon)\big)\) noise. The release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every dataset. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\) the clipping changes no record. On that event the estimate is the plain average plus noise, and, ignoring the rare event where it fails, the error has no bias and \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac1n + \frac{8(R + \tau_1)^2}{n^2\varepsilon^2}}. \tag{28.6}\]


Proof. 

Privacy. The clipping interval has width \(w = 2(R + \tau_1)\), so Lemma 28.1 gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every dataset.
Clipping changes nothing, usually. By Lemma 28.2, with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) every record lies within \(\tau_1\) of \(\mu\). Since \(|\mu| \le R\), every record then lies in \([-R - \tau_1, R + \tau_1]\), where clipping leaves it alone. This is why the interval is widened by \(\tau_1\): a mean near \(R\) has half its records above \(R\), and clipping them would bias the estimate toward 0.
Error. On that event the clipped average is the plain average, so Equation 28.2 has no bias, a sampling term \(1/n\), and the noise term \(2w^2/(n^2\varepsilon^2)\) with \(w = 2(R + \tau_1)\), which is \(8(R + \tau_1)^2/(n^2\varepsilon^2)\). Their sum is the square of Equation 28.6.


The noise grows linearly in \(R\), so reaching an error \(\alpha\) takes about \(1/\alpha^2 + R/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) records. The estimator pays for \(R\) in full: doubling your uncertainty about where the data are doubles the noise, even though the data themselves have not changed. Normality entered only in step 2, to show that the clipping usually changes nothing, while the privacy of step 1 holds for every dataset.
The lower-bounds chapter shows that paying for \(R\) in full is not the price of privacy. Its packing argument gives a lower bound of only \(\ln(R/\alpha)/\varepsilon\) records, so a cleverer mechanism should pay logarithmically, not linearly, for the range.

Example 28.2 Take \(n = 1000\) records at \(\varepsilon = 1\), with \(\beta = 0.05\) so that \(\tau_1 = 4.604\), and put the true mean at \(\mu = R/2\). For \(R = 10\), the noise standard deviation is 0.0413 and the RMSE is 0.0520, against 0.0316 without privacy. The error grows with the range, to 2.8416 for \(R = 10^3\) and to 2828.44 for \(R = 10^6\). That last estimate is useless, although the 1,000 records pin the mean down to within about 0.03. The script also computes the exact error, without conditioning on the event of Lemma 28.2, from the mean and variance of a clipped normal variable, and the two agree to the digits quoted.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
text:
28.3 Coarse then fine
The naive estimator wastes its noise on the empty parts of \([-R, R]\). Karwa & Vadhan (2018) split the work in two. A coarse step spends a small part of the budget to find, privately, a short interval that holds the data. A fine step then clips to that interval and spends the rest of the budget on the mean. The coarse step is a selection problem among about \(R\) candidate intervals, and selection costs only the logarithm of the number of candidates, which is how the range drops out of the noise.
Two earlier results carry the proof. The first is the utility bound of the exponential mechanism (Selection). When the mechanism chooses among \(m\) candidates with a score of sensitivity 1 at budget \(\varepsilon_1\), it picks a candidate whose score is at least \(g\) below the best with probability at most \(m\,e^{-\varepsilon_1 g/2}\), which is Equation 22.4 with \(t = \varepsilon_1 g/2 - \ln m\). The second is adaptive basic composition (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). If a first step is \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP and a second step, which may use the first step’s output, is \(\varepsilon_2\)-DP for each value of that output, then together they are \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP. That is what allows the coarse step to choose the clipping window of the fine step.

Theorem 28.2 (Coarse then fine) Let the records be independent draws from a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\), where \(|\mu| \le R\), and variance 1, let \(\tau_1\) be as in Equation 28.5, and split the budget as \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2\). Cut \([-R - b, R + b]\) into \(m = \lceil 2(R + b)/b\rceil\) bins of width \(b = 2\tau_1\), where \(\lceil\cdot\rceil\) rounds up.

Coarse step. Choose a bin \(J\) with the exponential mechanism at \(\varepsilon_1\), with the number of records in the bin as its score.
Fine step. Clip every record to the window made of bin \(J\) and its two neighbours, an interval of width \(3b\). Average, and add \(\mathrm{Lap}(3b/(n\varepsilon_2))\) noise.

The mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every dataset. With probability at least \(1 - \beta - m e^{-\varepsilon_1 n/4}\), no record is clipped. On that event the estimate is the plain average plus noise, and, ignoring the rare event where it fails, \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac1n + \frac{18b^2}{n^2\varepsilon_2^2}}, \tag{28.7}\] which does not depend on \(R\). The coarse step fails with probability at most \(\beta\) once \[n \ge \frac{4\ln(m/\beta)}{\varepsilon_1}. \tag{28.8}\]


Proof. The plan is to show that the two steps are private by composition, that the data fill at most two bins, that the coarse step therefore picks a non-empty bin, that the window around a non-empty bin holds every record, and finally to read the error off Equation 28.2.

Privacy. Replacing one record takes it out of one bin and puts it into another, so every count changes by at most 1, and the coarse step is the exponential mechanism with a score of sensitivity 1, which is \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP. For each value of \(J\), the fine step is a clipped mean over a window of width \(3b\), which is \(\varepsilon_2\)-DP by Lemma 28.1. By adaptive basic composition the two steps together are \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The window depends on the data only through \(J\), which was chosen privately, so no leak of the kind seen in Beyond global sensitivity arises.
The data fill at most two bins. By Lemma 28.2, with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) every record lies within \(\tau_1 = b/2\) of \(\mu\). Then the records span an interval of length at most \(b\), which meets at most two neighbouring bins. So the fullest bin holds at least \(n/2\) records, and every other bin except one is empty.
The coarse step picks a non-empty bin. An empty bin has score 0, at least \(n/2\) below the best. The utility bound with the \(m\) bins as candidates and the gap \(g = n/2\) bounds the chance of picking one by \(m e^{-\varepsilon_1 n/4}\). Setting this equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(n\) gives Equation 28.8.
The window holds every record. A non-empty bin \(J\) contains a record within \(b/2\) of \(\mu\), so \(\mu\) lies within \(b/2\) of the bin. Every record lies within \(b/2\) of \(\mu\), hence within \(b\) of the bin, which is inside the window. Clipping to bin \(J\) alone would not do, because the data can straddle two bins and \(J\) may be the less full one.
Error. On the events of steps 2 and 3, the fine step clips nothing, so Equation 28.2 has no bias, a sampling term \(1/n\), and the noise term with \(w = 3b\) and budget \(\varepsilon_2\), which is \(18b^2/(n^2\varepsilon_2^2)\). That is Equation 28.7.


The range \(R\) now enters only through the number of bins \(m\), and only inside a logarithm in Equation 28.8. So an error \(\alpha\) needs about \(1/\alpha^2 + 1/(\alpha\varepsilon) + \ln R/\varepsilon\) records in total, up to factors of \(\sqrt{\ln n}\) hidden in \(b\). The packing bound Equation 27.17 of the lower-bounds chapter says a pure-DP mechanism must pay that logarithm, so the coarse step is optimal up to constants. The fine step pays for a window of width \(3b = 6\sqrt{2\ln(2n/\beta)}\), a few standard deviations, which is where the \(\ln n\) factors come from. The bins cannot be much narrower, because step 2 needs the data to fill at most two of them, so that the fullest bin leads every empty one by \(n/2\).
The split has a cost when you already know a lot. The fine step gets only \(\varepsilon_2\) and clips to a window wider than the spread of the data, so for small \(R\) the naive estimator wins. With \(n = 1000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and a quarter of the budget for the coarse step, the crossover is at \(R = 13.81\) (Figure 28.2). The quarter is a simple default rather than the best split, and Exercise 2 sizes the coarse budget from Equation 28.8 instead.

Example 28.3 Take \(n = 1000\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\beta = 0.05\) again, with \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.25\) and \(\varepsilon_2 = 0.75\). The bins have width \(b = 9.207\) and the window \(27.62\). Table 28.2 compares the two estimators. The fine step’s noise has standard deviation 0.0521 and the RMSE is 0.0609 for every \(R\), while the naive estimator’s error grows with \(R\). The number of records the coarse step needs, by Equation 28.8, grows from 74 to 245 as \(R\) grows by a factor of \(10^5\). The bound on its failure probability is below \(10^{-21}\) in all three cases, because 1,000 records is far more than it needs.

Figure 28.1 shows the coarse step on one dataset with \(R = 100\) and \(\mu = 37\), which has 24 bins. On the script’s own draw of such a dataset, 876 and 124 records fall into the two non-empty bins. The exponential mechanism picks the fuller one with a probability that prints as 1 to twelve digits, and any given empty bin with probability about \(2.8\times10^{-48}\).







Figure 28.1: Top: the coarse histogram of 1,000 normal records with mean 37, in 24 bins of width 9.2 covering a range with \(R = 100\) (a fresh draw). Bottom: the probability that the exponential mechanism with \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.25\) picks each bin, on a log scale.









Figure 28.2: Root-mean-square error of the naive estimator and of coarse then fine, against the bound \(R\) on the mean, for \(n = 1000\) normal records and \(\varepsilon = 1\). The dots are simulations of coarse then fine; the dotted line is the non-private error \(1/\sqrt n\).



Under approximate DP the range can go altogether. The stability-based release reports the fullest bin exactly, with high probability, once it leads the others by about \(2\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) records, whatever the number of bins. Its test is noisy, so a smaller lead gives a refusal rather than a wrong bin. Karwa & Vadhan use a stability-based histogram of this kind, so their \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP coarse step needs a number of records of order \(\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon\) and works even with no bound \(R\) at all, which matches the packing bound under approximate DP, Equation 27.8. Section J.3 in the appendices proves the histogram’s guarantee for added or removed records; under this chapter’s replaced records two bins change, so the histogram is run at \(\varepsilon/2\) and \(\delta/2\), which changes only the constant.
The same trick handles an unknown variance. Differences of pairs of records, \(X_2 - X_1\) and so on, have mean 0 and a spread set by the variance alone. Put the sizes \(|X_2 - X_1|, |X_4 - X_3|, \dots\) into bins whose edges double, from \([1, 2)\) to \([2, 4)\) and so on, scaled to the possible range of the standard deviation \(\sigma\). Most sizes fall within a factor of a few of \(\sigma\), so the fullest bins locate \(\sigma\) within a constant factor. With \(\sigma\) known to lie between \(\sigma_{\min}\) and \(\sigma_{\max}\) there are about \(\log_2(\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min})\) bins, and choosing a full one with the exponential mechanism costs, by the same utility bound, records of order the logarithm of that number divided by \(\varepsilon\) (Karwa & Vadhan 2018 give the details).

title: 28  Private mean estimation
text:
28.4 Many dimensions: shrinking balls
Now each record is a vector in \(d\) dimensions, drawn from a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and identity covariance, and all you know is that the length of \(\mu\), \(\|\mu\|\), is at most \(R\). Error is measured by the length of \(\hat\mu - \mu\). The coarse step of Section 28.3 does not carry over cheaply, because a histogram over cells of a grid would need about \((R/b)^d\) cells, and the logarithm of that is \(d\ln(R/b)\), a cost linear in \(d\). Biswas, Dong, Kamath & Ullman (2020) shrink a ball instead. Keep a ball that contains \(\mu\), clip the data to a slightly larger ball, take a noisy mean, and use it to draw a smaller ball. A few rounds take the ball from radius \(R\) down to the spread of the data.
Two tools replace the one-dimensional ones. The noise is Gaussian rather than Laplace, because one record moves a vector average in every coordinate at once, and Gaussian noise is calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, the most one record can move the answer in length (Proposition 20.3). Write \(\kappa(\varepsilon, \delta)\) for the largest ratio of \(\ell_2\) sensitivity to noise standard deviation at which Gaussian noise is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, the root that Corollary 20.1 finds by bisection and calls \(\mu^*\); this page writes it \(\kappa\) because \(\mu\) is the mean here. Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\Delta_2/\kappa(\varepsilon, \delta)\) on a query of \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2\) is then \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, and so is any larger noise. The second tool is the \(d\)-dimensional version of Lemma 28.2, which the proof needs twice: once to say how far records stray from \(\mu\), and once to bound the length of a round’s noise.

Lemma 28.3 (Normal vectors stay close to their mean) Let \(Z\) be a standard normal vector in \(d\) dimensions, that is, a vector of \(d\) independent standard normal coordinates. For every \(t \ge 0\), \[\Pr\big[\|Z\| > \sqrt d + t\big] \le e^{-t^2/2}. \tag{28.9}\] So \(k\) independent such vectors all have length at most \(\sqrt d + \sqrt{2\ln(k/\beta)}\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\).


Proof. 

One vector. The length \(\|Z\|\) changes by at most the length of the move when \(Z\) moves, and such functions of a normal vector concentrate around their average. That average is at most \(\sqrt d\), because the mean of a length is at most the square root of its mean square, which is \(d\). The tail bound is Boucheron, Lugosi & Massart (2013, ch. 5), and Section E.4 in the appendices proves the same bound with the Chernoff method alone.
Several vectors. Give each of the \(k\) vectors a share \(\beta/k\) of the failure probability. Setting \(e^{-t^2/2} = \beta/k\) gives \(t = \sqrt{2\ln(k/\beta)}\), and the probability that at least one vector is longer is at most the sum of the \(k\) shares, by the union bound, which is \(\beta\).


The mechanism below keeps two lengths fixed before it sees the data: a radius \(\tau_d\) that every record stays within, from the lemma with \(k = n\), and a margin \(u\) that bounds the sampling error and the noise of each step, from the lemma with \(k = 1\).

Theorem 28.3 (Shrinking balls) Let the records be independent draws from a normal distribution in \(d\) dimensions with mean \(\mu\), where \(\|\mu\| \le R\), and identity covariance, and let \(T \ge 0\) be a number of rounds. Two lengths set the scale. The first bounds how far records lie from the mean, \[\tau_d = \sqrt d + \sqrt{2\ln(2n/\beta)}, \tag{28.10}\] and the second, \(u\), is a margin for the \(T + 1\) steps of the mechanism, \(T\) rounds and a final step: \[u = \sqrt{2\ln(4(T + 1)/\beta)}. \tag{28.11}\] Give each step a budget \((\varepsilon_t, \delta_t)\) such that all the steps add up to \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). Start from the ball of radius \(r_0 = R\) around the centre \(c_0 = 0\). In round \(t = 0, \dots, T - 1\):

Move every record that lies outside the ball of radius \(r_t + \tau_d\) around \(c_t\) onto its surface.
Release the average plus Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(s_t = 2(r_t + \tau_d)/(n\,\kappa(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t))\) in each coordinate, and call the result \(c_{t+1}\).
Set the next radius to \[r_{t+1} = \frac{\sqrt d + u}{\sqrt n} + s_t\big(\sqrt d + u\big). \tag{28.12}\]

A final step does steps 1 and 2 once more, with the rest of the budget and noise \(s_T\), and releases the noisy average. The mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for every dataset. With probability at least \(1 - \beta\), every ball contains \(\mu\) and no record is ever moved. On that event the final release is the plain average plus noise, and, ignoring the rare event where it fails, \[\mathrm{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac dn + d\,s_T^2}. \tag{28.13}\]


Proof. The plan is to show that each step is a Gaussian mechanism and compose them, then that, as long as the current ball holds \(\mu\), nothing is clipped and the next ball holds \(\mu\) too, and finally to read the error off the last step.

Privacy of one step. After the move of step 1 every record lies in a ball of radius \(r_t + \tau_d\), whose diameter is \(2(r_t + \tau_d)\). Replacing one record therefore moves the sum by a vector of length at most \(2(r_t + \tau_d)\), and the average by that divided by \(n\), which is the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. The noise \(s_t\) is this sensitivity divided by \(\kappa(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t)\), so the step is \((\varepsilon_t, \delta_t)\)-DP for each value of the centre, which was chosen privately. Adaptive basic composition (Post-processing, group privacy and composition) adds the budgets of the \(T + 1\) steps.
Records stay within \(\tau_d\) of the mean. Each \(X_i - \mu\) is a standard normal vector, so Lemma 28.3 with \(k = n\) vectors and failure probability \(\beta/2\) says that, with probability at least \(1 - \beta/2\), every record lies within \(\sqrt d + \sqrt{2\ln(2n/\beta)} = \tau_d\) of \(\mu\).
The balls keep the mean. Suppose \(\mu\) lies in the ball of round \(t\) and the event of step 2 holds. Then every record lies within \(\tau_d\) of \(\mu\), hence inside the clipping ball, and nothing moves. So \(c_{t+1} - \mu\) is the sampling error \(\bar X - \mu\) plus the noise. The sampling error is a normal vector with variance \(1/n\) in each coordinate, so \(\sqrt n\) times it is a standard normal vector, and the noise divided by \(s_t\) is one too. By Lemma 28.3 with \(k = 1\) and failure probability \(\beta/(4(T + 1))\) for each of the two, the sampling error has length at most \((\sqrt d + u)/\sqrt n\) and the noise has length at most \(s_t(\sqrt d + u)\), so \(\mu\) lies in the next ball, of radius Equation 28.12. The \(2(T + 1)\) shares of \(\beta/(4(T + 1))\) and the \(\beta/2\) of step 2 add up to \(\beta\), which is the total failure probability.
Final error. On that event the final release is \(\bar X\) plus independent noise. The expected squared length of \(\bar X - \mu\) is \(d/n\), the sum of \(d\) variances of \(1/n\), and that of the noise is \(d\,s_T^2\), and the cross term has mean 0 as in Lemma 28.1. That gives Equation 28.13.


In a round, the radius drops from \(r_t\) to about \(2(r_t + \tau_d)\sqrt d/(n\,\kappa(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t))\). When \(n\) is larger than a constant times \(\sqrt d/\kappa(\varepsilon_t, \delta_t)\), which is of order \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/\varepsilon_t\), that is a reduction by a constant factor, and about \(\ln R\) rounds bring the radius down to the order of \(\tau_d \approx \sqrt d\). Below that the ball cannot shrink, because the records themselves are spread about \(\sqrt d\) around \(\mu\) and the clipping ball must leave them alone; Exercise 4 computes the \(n\) a round needs to halve the radius. In the final step the sensitivity is then about \(2\sqrt d/n\), so \(d\,s_T^2\) is about \(4d^2/(n\kappa)^2\), and an error \(\alpha\) needs \(n\) of order \(d/(\alpha\kappa)\), that is, \(d\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha\varepsilon)\). Reaching an error \(\alpha\) therefore takes about \(d/\alpha^2 + d\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}/(\alpha\varepsilon) + \sqrt d\ln R/\varepsilon\) records, up to logarithmic factors.
Without privacy the error is \(\sqrt{d/n}\). The privacy noise is about \(d/(n\varepsilon)\) up to logarithmic factors, so it grows like \(d\) instead of \(\sqrt d\), and it is larger than the sampling error unless \(n\) is above about \(d/\varepsilon^2\). That is not a weakness of the method. The fingerprinting lower bound says that releasing \(d\) means with an error \(\alpha'\) in each coordinate needs about \(\sqrt d/(\alpha'\varepsilon)\) records. An \(\ell_2\) error \(\alpha\) spread over \(d\) coordinates is an error of about \(\alpha/\sqrt d\) in each, so substituting \(\alpha' = \alpha/\sqrt d\) gives \(d/(\alpha\varepsilon)\). Exercise 5 does the substitution with the constants, and Kamath, Li, Singhal & Ullman (2019) prove the matching lower bound directly for normal data.
The range costs \(\sqrt d\ln R/\varepsilon\), which is less than the \(d\ln R/\varepsilon\) of a grid histogram, because each round makes progress in all \(d\) directions at once. The rounds compose here by basic composition, which adds the budgets; the tighter accountants of Part 4 make several rounds cheaper, and the original method uses one of them. This is the shape of every private average of vectors, including the average of clipped gradients in private training. There the clipping norm is a fixed number rather than a shrinking ball, and choosing it is the clipping trade-off of Beyond global sensitivity in many dimensions.

Example 28.4 The running example needs more records here, because an error below 1 in \(d = 1000\) dimensions is out of reach for 1,000 records even without privacy, where the sampling error alone is \(\sqrt{d/n} = 1\). Take \(n = 100{,}000\) records with \(\|\mu\| \le 1000\), at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-6}\), with \(\beta = 0.05\) and a quarter of the budget for the rounds. Here \(\kappa(1, 10^{-6}) = 0.2367\). Table 28.3 compares the naive estimator, which clips to the ball of radius \(R + \tau_d\), with shrinking balls. The script tries every number of rounds up to 29 and keeps the best, which is two for each \(d\). For \(d = 100\) the radius falls from 1000 to 8.54 after one round and to 0.243 after the second. The ratio of the privacy noise to \(d/(n\varepsilon)\) falls from 32.2 at \(d = 10\) to 14.2 at \(d = 1000\), as the terms in \(\sqrt d\) give way to the term in \(d\). A simulation at \(d = 100\) with 40 datasets gives an RMSE of 0.0363 against the formula’s 0.0366, and every ball contained \(\mu\) in all 40.

title: 28  Private mean estimation
section: 28.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
text:
28.5 Heavy tails: clip into the data
Normal data rarely stray far, so every estimator so far could clip without touching a record. Many real quantities have heavy tails: incomes, session lengths, the norms of per-example gradients. Suppose all you know is that the variance is at most \(\sigma^2\). Chebyshev’s inequality then only says that a record is more than \(\sigma\sqrt{n/\beta}\) from the mean with probability at most \(\beta/n\), so a clipping range wide enough to touch no record has half-width \(\sigma\sqrt{n/\beta}\), and its noise is enormous. The way out is to clip into the data on purpose and accept a bias, and the question is how wide to clip.
The estimator clips around a centre that a coarse step has placed near the mean; to keep the formulas clean, the theorem takes the centre to be \(\mu\) itself, and writes \(\tau\) for the clipping half-width. The bias of clipping is the average amount by which records stick out of the window, and a variance bound controls that amount: a record that sticks out contributes to the variance a squared distance at least \(\tau\) times its distance, so the excess of all such records together is at most \(\sigma^2/\tau\).

Theorem 28.4 (Clipping into heavy-tailed data) Let the records be independent draws from any distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance at most \(\sigma^2\). Clip every record to \([\mu - \tau, \mu + \tau]\) for a half-width \(\tau > 0\), average, and add \(\mathrm{Lap}(2\tau/(n\varepsilon))\) noise. The release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every \(\tau\) and every dataset, and \[\mathrm{RMSE} \le \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\tau} + \frac{2\sqrt2\,\tau}{n\varepsilon}. \tag{28.14}\] The right side is smallest at \[\tau_b = \sigma\sqrt{\frac{n\varepsilon}{2\sqrt2}}, \qquad\text{where it equals}\qquad \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n} + 2\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2\sqrt2}{n\varepsilon}}. \tag{28.15}\]


Proof. The plan is to bound the three parts of Equation 28.2 one at a time, add them, and minimize over \(\tau\).

Privacy. The clipping interval has width \(2\tau\), so Lemma 28.1 gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP for every dataset, whatever \(\tau\) is.
Bias. Clipping moves a record \(X\) toward \(\mu\) by \((|X - \mu| - \tau)_+\), the amount by which its distance from \(\mu\) exceeds \(\tau\), or 0. So the bias is at most the average of that amount. The amount is positive only where \(|X - \mu| > \tau\), and there it is at most \(|X - \mu| \le (X - \mu)^2/\tau\), because dividing \(|X - \mu|\) by \(\tau\) gives a number above 1. Averaging, the bias is at most \(\mathbb E[(X - \mu)^2]/\tau \le \sigma^2/\tau\).
Sampling. A variance is half the average squared difference between two independent copies of a variable. Clipping to an interval never moves two values further apart, so the clipped record varies at most as much as the record itself, and its variance is at most \(\sigma^2\). The sampling term of Equation 28.2 is at most \(\sigma^2/n\).
Noise. The clipping interval has width \(2\tau\), so by Equation 28.2 the noise standard deviation is \(\sqrt2\cdot2\tau/(n\varepsilon)\).
Add. By Equation 28.2, the RMSE is the length of a vector with these three components, and a length is at most the sum of its components. That gives Equation 28.14.
Minimize. The two terms that depend on \(\tau\) are \(\sigma^2/\tau\), falling, and \(2\sqrt2\,\tau/(n\varepsilon)\), rising. The derivative of their sum, \(-\sigma^2/\tau^2 + 2\sqrt2/(n\varepsilon)\), is zero at \(\tau_b\), and there the two terms are equal, each \(\sigma\sqrt{2\sqrt2/(n\varepsilon)}\). That gives Equation 28.15.


Requiring the second term of Equation 28.15 to be at most \(\alpha\) and squaring shows that an error \(\alpha\) needs about \(\sigma^2/\alpha^2 + 8\sqrt2\,\sigma^2/(\alpha^2\varepsilon)\) records, of order \(1/(\alpha^2\varepsilon)\). Without clipping into the data, at \(\tau = \sigma\sqrt{n/\beta}\), it would need of order \(1/(\beta\alpha^2\varepsilon^2)\). With heavy tails, then, privacy stops being a lower-order cost. For bounded data the privacy term in Equation 28.4 had a single \(1/\alpha\), while here it has \(1/\alpha^2\), the same power as sampling, divided by \(\varepsilon\). Kamath, Singhal & Ullman (2020) show that this is unavoidable: no \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism does better for every distribution with bounded variance. Section J.4 in the appendices derives this lower bound, and its \(k\)-th moment version, from a two-point distribution and group privacy. They also show what more knowledge buys. If the \(k\)-th moment \(\mathbb E[|X - \mu|^k]\) is bounded for some \(k > 2\), the cost falls to about \(1/(\varepsilon\,\alpha^{k/(k-1)})\) records, and as \(k\) grows it approaches the \(1/(\alpha\varepsilon)\) of bounded data.
The bound Equation 28.14 is a worst case, and it is tight up to a constant factor. A sharper version of step 2 gives \(\sigma^2/(4\tau)\), because \((|y| - \tau)_+ \le y^2/(4\tau)\) for every \(y\), and a distribution that puts a little mass at distance \(2\tau\) on one side of the mean attains that. So the worst case hides its variance in a few far-out records on one side. For an ordinary heavy-tailed distribution the bias falls faster than \(\sigma^2/\tau\), the best \(\tau\) is smaller than \(\tau_b\), and the error is lower. But \(\tau_b\) uses only \(n\), \(\varepsilon\) and the variance bound, so it can be set without looking at the data; if the variance bound is four times too large, \(\tau_b\) doubles, the release stays private and only the accuracy suffers. Setting \(\tau\) from the data, such as to the observed maximum, would bring back the leak of Beyond global sensitivity.

Example 28.5 Take a Pareto distribution with shape 3, the law of \(x_m U^{-1/3}\) for a uniform \(U\) on \((0, 1)\), scaled so that its variance is 1. Its smallest value is \(x_m = 1.1547\) and its mean is 1.7321, and its third moment is infinite. With \(n = 1000\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\), Table 28.4 compares three choices of \(\tau\). Clipping wide enough to touch nothing costs an RMSE of 0.4012. The worst-case choice \(\tau_b = 18.80\) gives 0.0607, and the best \(\tau\) for this particular distribution, 5.36, gives 0.0329, close to the non-private 0.0316. The bound Equation 28.15 promises 0.1380, which is loose for this distribution, as predicted: for this law the average excess beyond a point falls like the inverse square of the point rather than its inverse, and Exercise 3 computes the exact bias. At \(n = 100{,}000\) the pattern repeats, with RMSE 0.0401, 0.0062 and 0.0032 for the three choices.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
Who this part is for
The previous part defined differential privacy (DP), built the basic mechanisms and proved how \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees compose. This part answers the question that decides whether a trained model’s privacy claim means anything: after thousands of noisy steps, each on a random subset of the data, how large is \(\varepsilon\), really? The answer is never read off a single theorem. It comes from an accountant, a procedure that tracks some summary of each step’s privacy loss, combines the summaries, and converts the result into the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) you report. The running case throughout is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD, and the workhorse summary is Rényi differential privacy (RDP). Two accountants given the same training run can report values of \(\varepsilon\) that differ by a large factor. Both can be correct upper bounds, but only the tighter one tells you what the noise actually bought.
You are expected to have read the prerequisites and the part on DP foundations. From Divergences you need the Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha\), the hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma\) and the data-processing inequality. From Hypothesis testing you need trade-off functions \(T(P, Q)\) and the Gaussian trade-off curve. From Concentration inequalities you need Hoeffding’s lemma, and from Optimization the contraction of a gradient step. From the DP foundations you need randomized response and the hypothesis-testing reading of DP, basic composition, the privacy loss random variable with advanced and optimal composition from Composition, the Gaussian mechanism and its exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) from the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, and the local and shuffle models from Trust models. Each chapter restates the facts it uses in one line and links to them.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
The common thread
Composition is easy for the privacy loss itself. If you run \(k\) mechanisms, the privacy loss of the whole run is the sum of the \(k\) per-step losses, and its distribution is a convolution. Composition is hard for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), because a pair of numbers forgets almost everything about that distribution. Advanced composition recovers part of what is lost. The rest of the field rests on one move: track a richer summary of the privacy loss, one that composes simply, and convert to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) only once, at the end.
The summaries differ in how much they keep, and Table 1 lists them.

Read the table from top to bottom as a ladder. An RDP curve is a lossy summary of the trade-off function, a zero-concentrated DP (zCDP) parameter \(\rho\) is a lossy summary of the RDP curve, and \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is a lossy summary of all three. Numerical accounting keeps the whole privacy loss distribution and loses only discretization error, which it bounds. Amplification (chapters 33 and 35) is a separate axis. It is about which pair of distributions you account for in the first place, and every accountant above must use the pair that matches the sampling scheme the training code actually runs.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
The running example
Every chapter that can compute it reports the same number: the \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of DP-SGD with Poisson sampling rate \(q = 0.01\), noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\) and up to \(T = 10{,}000\) steps. That is about one hundred epochs at a typical setting. A single Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = 1\) serves as the small example. Watching the same number move from chapter to chapter shows what each tool gains. Choosing an accountant puts all the values side by side.

title: Privacy accounting
text:
How to read this part
Order. Read chapters 29 and 30 first: every later chapter uses the RDP curve and its conversion. Chapter 30 ends by reading the curve as a constraint on tests, and chapter 32 develops that trade-off view in full, so read it next. Chapters 33 and 34 form the practical core and should be read in order. Chapter 31 can be read any time after chapter 30, except its section on subsampling, which uses one formula from chapter 33; read it before chapter 36, which uses its conversion. Chapter 35 needs chapter 33. Chapter 36 needs chapters 31 and 33. Chapter 37 closes the part and uses all the others, so read it last.
Structure. The chapters follow the shape of the earlier parts: why the topic matters, a toolkit, one section per result with a derivation, interpretation, worked example and two check-yourself questions, then code, references and a cheat sheet. Exercises with worked solutions are collected in the exercise book, a companion website, with a link at the end of each chapter.
Run the code. Each chapter has a script in code/ that prints every number its text quotes, except values attributed to an external library or paper, and regenerates its figures, for example
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/renyi_dp.py
None of the scripts uses an accounting library. Each accountant is implemented from its definition in a few dozen lines of NumPy, so you can read exactly what it computes. As an exercise, compare them with Google’s dp_accounting or Opacus.

title: Privacy accounting
section: What you will be able to do

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.1 Why this matters
You train a model with 1000 steps of full-batch noisy gradient descent. Each step computes a quantity whose sensitivity is 1, meaning that changing one person’s record moves it by at most 1, and releases it with Gaussian noise whose standard deviation is \(\sigma = 20\) times that sensitivity; \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier. What is the total differential privacy (DP) guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)? Recall what such a guarantee says: a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if, for any two neighbouring datasets (datasets that differ in one person’s record) and any set of outputs, the probability of that set under one dataset is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability under the other, plus a small slack \(\delta\).
Part 3 gives one answer. Turn each step into a single guarantee \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\), then apply advanced composition (Composition), the theorem that says \(k\) such steps cost roughly \(\varepsilon_0\sqrt{k}\) rather than \(k\varepsilon_0\). With the best split of \(\delta\) between the steps and the final tail, over the grid of splits Part 3 searches, that gives \(\varepsilon = 68.01\). The true answer is \(\varepsilon = 7.51\). You can compute it exactly because 1000 Gaussian steps behave like one Gaussian mechanism with noise \(\sigma/\sqrt{1000}\): the 1000 shifts of 1 form a vector of Euclidean length \(\sqrt{1000}\), and a Gaussian with shift \(\sqrt{1000}\) and noise \(\sigma\) is the same as one with shift 1 and noise \(\sigma/\sqrt{1000}\). The bound is nine times too large (\(68.01/7.51 \approx 9\)).
The loss comes from the very first move. A Gaussian step does not have one \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\). For each \(\varepsilon_0\) there is a smallest \(\delta_0\) that works, so it has a whole curve of valid pairs, its privacy curve. Collapsing the curve to a single point throws away the information about how the step behaves at every other point, and that is exactly the information composition needs. After that, no composition theorem can recover it.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.1.1 The one idea: track a curve that adds
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) keeps a whole curve instead of a point, and it chooses a curve that is easy to compose. For each mechanism and each pair of neighbouring datasets, consider how much more likely an output is under one dataset than under the other. RDP summarizes that likelihood ratio by its moments: for each order \(\alpha > 1\) it records the Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha\) between the two output distributions, which is, up to a logarithm and a factor \(1/(\alpha - 1)\), the average of the likelihood ratio raised to the power \(\alpha\) (the Toolkit below restates it). Taking the worst pair of neighbours at each order gives a function \(\alpha \mapsto \varepsilon(\alpha)\), the RDP curve.
Two facts make this curve the workhorse of privacy accounting. First, curves add under composition. When you run several mechanisms in sequence, even when each is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs, the curve of the whole run is at most the pointwise sum of their curves, with equality for independent steps. The reason is that a moment of a product of independent likelihood ratios is a product of moments, and the logarithm turns that product into a sum. No \(\delta\) is spent along the way. Second, any point of the curve converts to an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee at the end. The conversion is a Chernoff bound, Markov’s inequality applied to an exponential, which turns a bound on a moment of the privacy loss into a bound on how often the loss is large. So you compose curves, and choose the best order once, after composing.
For the 1000 Gaussian steps, adding curves and converting once gives \(\varepsilon = 8.84\), 18% above the exact 7.51 (\(8.84/7.51 = 1.177\)). The same bookkeeping, under the name moments accountant, is what made differentially private deep learning practical.
Table 29.1 lists the results of this chapter and where each is used.

What you need. The Rényi divergence, its limits, its monotonicity in \(\alpha\) and the data-processing inequality are in Divergences (Section 3.4, Section 3.10). The Chernoff method is in Concentration. From Part 3 you need the definition of DP (Definition), the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms (Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms), randomized response (Definition, Section 18.3) and the privacy loss random variable (Composition). The Toolkit restates the facts this chapter uses, and each mechanism is restated where it first appears.
Notation. \(M\) is a mechanism and \(D \sim D'\) are neighbouring datasets. \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) are the output distributions, with densities (or probability mass functions) \(p\) and \(q\). The privacy loss at output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\), the log of how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\): positive when \(y\) points to \(D\), negative when it points to \(D'\). The privacy loss random variable is \(L(Y)\) with \(Y \sim P\), the loss of an output actually drawn from the mechanism on \(D\). The Gaussian mechanism adds \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2\Delta_2^2)\) noise to a query \(f\) of \(\ell_2\)-sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\) (the largest Euclidean distance between the query’s answers on neighbours), so \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier. Logarithms are natural. Whenever this part optimizes over the order, it uses the same grid of orders: 99 orders from 1.1 to 10.9 in steps of 0.1, the 52 integers from 12 to 63, and 128, 256 and 512, which is \(99 + 52 + 3 = 154\) orders from 1.1 to 512:
ORDERS = [1 + x / 10 for x in range(1, 100)] + list(range(12, 64)) + [128, 256, 512]

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.2 Toolkit: four facts from Part 1
Every derivation below reuses four facts about the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\). They are proved in Divergences and Concentration; each is restated here with the short reason it holds. Throughout, \(r = p/q\) is the likelihood ratio, how many times more likely an output is under \(P\) than under \(Q\), and \(L = \ln r\) is the privacy loss.

29.2.1 Fact 1 — A moment of the likelihood ratio
The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is defined as \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,dy. \tag{29.1}\] The integral inside is an average of a power of the likelihood ratio, and you can take that average under either distribution. Multiply both sides of the definition by \(\alpha - 1\) and exponentiate: \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,dy = \mathbb E_Q\big[r^\alpha\big] = \mathbb E_P\big[r^{\alpha - 1}\big] = \mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]. \tag{29.2}\] The first equality after the integral holds because \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha} = q\,(p/q)^\alpha\), and integrating \(q\) times something is averaging that something under \(Q\). The next one is the change of measure \(\mathbb E_P[g] = \mathbb E_Q[r g]\), which holds because \(\int p\,g = \int q\,(p/q)\,g\): an average under \(P\) is an average under \(Q\) with each output reweighted by its likelihood ratio. Applied with \(g = r^{\alpha - 1}\), it turns \(\mathbb E_Q[r \cdot r^{\alpha-1}]\) into \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha-1}]\). The last form uses \(r^{\alpha - 1} = e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\). It says that \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha\) is the logarithm of the moment generating function (MGF) of \(L\) under \(P\), the function \(\lambda \mapsto \mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}]\), evaluated at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\) (Equation 3.12). That is why a Rényi divergence is a statement about the exponential moments of the privacy loss.


29.2.2 Fact 2 — Limits and monotonicity
\(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\). As \(\alpha \to 1\) it tends to the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence \(\mathbb E_P[L]\), the average privacy loss, and as \(\alpha \to \infty\) it tends to the max-divergence \(D_\infty = \sup_y L(y)\), the largest privacy loss of any output.
The reason is a picture. Write \(\psi(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}]\), the log-MGF of Fact 1. It passes through the origin, since \(\psi(0) = \ln 1 = 0\), and it is convex, as every log-MGF is. By Fact 1, \(D_\alpha = \psi(\alpha - 1)/(\alpha - 1)\), the slope of the chord of \(\psi\) from the origin to the point at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\). Chords of a convex function from a fixed point get steeper as their far end moves right, so \(D_\alpha\) grows with \(\alpha\). As \(\alpha \to 1\) the chord shrinks to the tangent at 0, whose slope is \(\psi'(0) = \mathbb E_P[L]\), the KL divergence. As \(\alpha \to \infty\), \(D_\alpha\) is the log of \(\big(\mathbb E_P[r^{\alpha - 1}]\big)^{1/(\alpha-1)}\), a power mean of \(r\) with a growing exponent, and such a mean is pulled toward the largest value of \(r\); its logarithm tends to \(\sup_y L(y)\).


29.2.3 Fact 3 — Data processing
Processing the output cannot make two distributions easier to tell apart. For any channel \(K\), a randomized map applied to the output that does not depend on which distribution produced it, \(D_\alpha(PK\|QK) \le D_\alpha(P\|Q)\), for every \(\alpha\) including \(\infty\) (Section 3.10). Here \(PK\) is the distribution of the processed output when the input is drawn from \(P\). The idea is that the likelihood ratio of a processed output is an average of the ratios of the original outputs that could have produced it, and averaging pulls ratios toward each other. Since \(x \mapsto x^\alpha\) is convex for \(\alpha > 1\), Jensen’s inequality (the power of an average is at most the average of the powers) says that averaging can only lower the moment \(\mathbb E_Q[r^\alpha]\), and with it \(D_\alpha\).


29.2.4 Fact 4 — Markov on an exponential (the Chernoff method)
For any random variable \(X\), any \(c\) and any \(\lambda > 0\), \[\Pr[X \ge c] \le e^{-\lambda c}\,\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda X}\big]. \tag{29.3}\] The reason is one line. On the event \(X \ge c\) the non-negative quantity \(e^{\lambda X}\) is at least \(e^{\lambda c}\), so its average is at least \(e^{\lambda c}\Pr[X \ge c]\); divide by \(e^{\lambda c}\). This is how an exponential moment, which is what a Rényi divergence controls, becomes a bound on a tail probability.

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.3 Rényi differential privacy

29.3.1 Context
\(\varepsilon\)-DP bounds the privacy loss \(L(y)\) at every output. That is a statement about the maximum of \(L\), which is the max-divergence. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP allows the bound to be exceeded on outputs carrying a small amount of probability mass, measured by \(\delta\). Both summarize the distribution of the privacy loss by one point of its upper tail. The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) summarizes it differently, by an exponential moment \(\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\) (Fact 1). An exponential moment weights large losses more heavily than small ones, and the larger the order, the more heavily. So small orders look at the typical loss and large orders at the worst case (Fact 2). Requiring a bound at every order describes the whole upper tail of the loss, not one point of it.


29.3.2 Statement
The definition asks for the same bound on the Rényi divergence for every pair of neighbours. A mechanism \(M\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP, for an order \(\alpha > 1\), if for all neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) \le \varepsilon. \tag{29.4}\] The RDP curve of \(M\) records, at each order, the smallest \(\varepsilon\) that works, which is the divergence of the worst pair of neighbours: \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) = \sup_{D \sim D'} D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big). \tag{29.5}\] The curve has three properties, which tie its two ends to familiar quantities.

\(\alpha = \infty\) is pure DP. \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP if and only if \(\varepsilon_M(\infty) \le \varepsilon\).
Monotone. \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha)\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\). So an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP at every order.
\(\alpha \to 1\) is KL. As \(\alpha \to 1\), \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha)\) tends to a limit at least the largest KL divergence between neighbours, with equality for every mechanism in this chapter.



29.3.3 Derivation

Pure DP is the max-divergence. \(\varepsilon\)-DP says \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) for every event \(S\), that is, \(\ln\frac{P(S)}{Q(S)} \le \varepsilon\). The largest value of that log ratio over events equals the largest privacy loss of a single output, which is the event form of the max-divergence (Section 3.4). The reason: \(\frac{P(S)}{Q(S)} = \frac{\int_S q\,r}{\int_S q}\) is an average of the likelihood ratio \(r\) over the outputs in \(S\), weighted by \(q\), so it can never exceed the largest \(r\), and an event concentrated on the outputs where \(r\) is largest comes as close to it as you like. So \(\sup_S \ln\frac{P(S)}{Q(S)} = D_\infty(P\|Q)\), and \(\varepsilon\)-DP holds exactly when \(D_\infty(M(D)\|M(D')) \le \varepsilon\) for all neighbours, that is, when \(\varepsilon_M(\infty) \le \varepsilon\).
Monotonicity passes through the supremum. For each pair, \(D_\alpha\) is non-decreasing in \(\alpha\) (Fact 2). A supremum of non-decreasing functions is non-decreasing, because if every function in the family is larger at \(\alpha'\) than at \(\alpha\), so is the largest of them. Combined with step 1, \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_M(\infty) \le \varepsilon\) for an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism.
The KL limit. For each pair, \(D_\alpha \ge D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) and \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) as \(\alpha \to 1\) (Fact 2). So \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \ge \sup_{D \sim D'}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(M(D)\|M(D')\big)\) at every order, and the limit is at least the largest KL. Equality would need the limit and the supremum to commute, which can fail in general: each pair’s divergence could approach its KL at a different speed. For the mechanisms below the curves are explicit, and you can check the limit directly.



29.3.4 Interpretation
An RDP guarantee is a curve, not a number. “Randomized response with \(p = 0.75\) is \((2, 0.8473)\)-RDP” (from the example below) is one point of it. What accountants store is the curve on a grid of orders. Each point is a valid guarantee, and different orders serve different purposes: composition works at every order at once, and the conversion to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) picks the best order at the end.
The curve sits between the average case and the worst case. As \(\alpha \to 1\) it sees only the average loss, the KL divergence. A mechanism whose loss is usually small but occasionally large has a small KL divergence, because the rare large losses barely move the average, but large high-order divergences, because a high exponential moment is dominated by those rare large losses. So it is caught at large orders. Pure DP, at \(\alpha = \infty\), is the most demanding point of the curve.
Why only \(\alpha > 1\)? Orders below 1 exist as divergences, but they are not used for privacy. The conversion to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) applies the Chernoff method to the loss, which needs an exponential moment \(\mathbb E_P[e^{\lambda L}]\) with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1 > 0\), and only orders above 1 provide one (Section 29.8).


29.3.5 Example: randomized response, outcome by outcome
Randomized response reports one person’s bit truthfully with probability \(p > \frac12\), the keep-probability, and flips it otherwise. The two neighbouring inputs are the two values of the bit. Take \(p = 0.75\). The likelihood ratio of any output is \(0.75/0.25 = 3\) or its inverse, so the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = \ln\frac{p}{1-p} = \ln 3\). Table 29.2 lists the outputs when the true bit is 1 (\(P\)) and 0 (\(Q\)).

The same recipe works at any order: sum \(p(y)^\alpha q(y)^{1-\alpha}\) over the two outputs, take the logarithm, and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). The output 1 contributes \(p^\alpha(1-p)^{1-\alpha}\) and the output 0 contributes \((1-p)^\alpha p^{1-\alpha}\), so \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big(p^\alpha(1-p)^{1-\alpha} + (1-p)^\alpha p^{1-\alpha}\Big). \tag{29.6}\] Swapping the roles of the bits swaps the two rows of the table and gives the same sum, so both directions of the pair have the same curve. The KL value is the average loss under \(P\): the loss is \(\ln 3\) with probability 0.75 and \(-\ln 3\) with probability 0.25, so \(\mathbb E_P[L] = (0.75 - 0.25)\ln 3 = 0.5\ln 3 = 0.5493\). 29.3.6 Check yourself

A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP. Is it \((\alpha', \varepsilon)\)-RDP for \(\alpha' < \alpha\)? For \(\alpha' > \alpha\)? (For \(\alpha' < \alpha\) yes, by monotonicity: the curve at \(\alpha'\) is at most the curve at \(\alpha\). For \(\alpha' > \alpha\) not in general: the curve can keep rising, as the Gaussian’s does.)
Why is \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) for randomized response the same in both directions of the pair? (Swapping the bit swaps \(p(y)\) and \(q(y)\) between the two outputs, and the sum \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) over both outputs is unchanged.)

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
section: 29.4 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms
text:
29.4 RDP curves of the basic mechanisms

29.4.1 Context
To account for a mechanism you need its curve. For a mechanism that adds noise to a query’s answer, the two outputs on neighbours are the same noise distribution centred at two different answers. So the curve comes from the Rényi divergence between the noise distribution and a shifted copy of itself, which Part 1 computed for the normal and the Laplace distributions. The only new step is the supremum over neighbours: you need to know which pair of neighbouring inputs is the worst, and for these mechanisms it is the pair whose answers are furthest apart.


29.4.2 Statement
With sensitivity 1, the three curves are as follows. The Gaussian mechanism adds normal noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\) (the noise multiplier). The Laplace mechanism adds noise from the Laplace distribution with scale \(b\), whose density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|y|/b}\) falls off exponentially on both sides. Randomized response has keep-probability \(p\). The Gaussian curve is a straight line in \(\alpha\), the Laplace curve is the Part 1 formula for a shift of one scale unit \(1/b\), and the randomized response curve is the sum over two outputs from the previous section: \[\text{Gaussian:}\quad \varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{29.7}\] \[\text{Laplace:}\quad \varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)/b} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha/b}\right), \tag{29.8}\] \[\text{randomized response:}\quad \varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big(p^\alpha(1-p)^{1-\alpha} + (1-p)^\alpha p^{1-\alpha}\Big). \tag{29.9}\] These are Corollaries 3 and 2 and the randomized response entry of Table 2 in Mironov (2017). The Laplace formula is for a real-valued query. Section B.4 in the appendices derives the Gaussian curve by completing the square.


29.4.3 Derivation
Gaussian. The plan is to reduce any pair of neighbours to two one-dimensional normals a distance \(s\) apart, use the Part 1 formula, and then take the largest \(s\).

One pair. With \(\Delta_2 f = 1\) the noise is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2 I)\). On neighbours with answers \(f(D)\) and \(f(D')\), the outputs are \(\mathcal N(f(D), \sigma^2 I)\) and \(\mathcal N(f(D'), \sigma^2 I)\).
Divergence of the pair. Translating and rotating the output space is a bijection, a relabelling of the outputs that can be undone, so it changes no divergence (apply Fact 3 in both directions). So you can move \(f(D)\) to 0 and \(f(D') - f(D)\) onto the first axis. The noise is the same in every direction, so after the rotation the two distributions differ only in the first coordinate; the other coordinates are identical, independent normals under both. Rényi divergence is additive over independent coordinates (Section 3.4), because the moment of Fact 1 factorizes into a product over coordinates, and identical coordinates contribute 0. What remains is the one-dimensional divergence \(D_\alpha(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\|\mathcal N(s, \sigma^2)) = \alpha s^2/(2\sigma^2)\) (Equation 3.15), with \(s = \|f(D) - f(D')\|_2\). Part 1 derives it by noting that the privacy loss of a normal pair is itself normal, with mean \(s^2/(2\sigma^2)\) and variance \(s^2/\sigma^2\), and a normal variable’s log-MGF is known in closed form.
Supremum. The divergence grows with \(s\), and \(s \le \Delta_2 f = 1\) for neighbours. So the worst pair has \(s = 1\) and gives Equation 29.7. The script also integrates \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) numerically and gets 1.0000 at \(\alpha = 2\) and 5.0000 at \(\alpha = 10\) for \(\sigma = 1\), matching \(2/2\) and \(10/2\).

Laplace. The plan is the same: reduce to a shift, use Part 1’s closed form, and show the worst shift is the largest.

One pair. The outputs are \(\mathrm{Lap}(f(D), b)\) and \(\mathrm{Lap}(f(D'), b)\). After a translation, this is \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\) with \(s = |f(D) - f(D')| \le 1\).
Divergence of the pair. Part 1 computes it by splitting the integral \(\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) at the two kinks of the densities, 0 and \(s\), where the absolute values change sign; on each of the three pieces the integrand is a plain exponential (Equation 3.19). With \(t = s/b\), the shift in units of the scale, the result is the formula above with \(1/b\) replaced by \(t\).
Supremum. You need the divergence to grow with the shift, so that the largest shift is the worst. Write the argument of the logarithm as \(g(t) = \frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}e^{(\alpha - 1)t} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{2\alpha - 1}e^{-\alpha t}\). Its derivative is \(g'(t) = \frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}{2\alpha - 1}\big(e^{(\alpha - 1)t} - e^{-\alpha t}\big)\), which is positive for \(t > 0\) because the first exponent is positive and the second negative. So \(\ln g(t)/(\alpha - 1)\) increases with \(t\). The reverse direction, \(\mathrm{Lap}(s, b)\) against \(\mathrm{Lap}(0, b)\), gives the same value, because the reflection \(y \mapsto s - y\) swaps the two distributions and changes no divergence. So the worst pair has \(s = 1\), \(t = 1/b\), and gives Equation 29.8.
Numerical check. The script integrates \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) on a grid of step \(10^{-4}\), with both kinks as grid points. For \(b \in \{0.5, 1, 4\}\) and \(\alpha \in \{1.5, 2, 10, 64\}\), the largest difference from Equation 29.8 is \(1.3 \times 10^{-8}\).

Randomized response. There is only one pair of inputs, the two values of the bit, so no supremum is needed, and Table 29.2 is its distribution. Fact 1 sums \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) over the two outputs, as in the previous section.


29.4.4 Interpretation
Figure 29.2 draws the three curves. Two shapes appear, and which one you get depends on whether the privacy loss is bounded.
When the privacy loss is bounded, the curve levels off. For randomized response the loss is \(\pm\ln 3\). For Laplace the loss at \(y\) is \((|y - 1| - |y|)/b\), and by the triangle inequality \(\big||y - 1| - |y|\big| \le 1\), so \(|L| \le 1/b\). Since every \(D_\alpha\) is at most \(D_\infty\), the largest loss (Fact 2), the curves rise towards \(1/b\) and \(\ln 3\) and stay below them. For large \(\alpha\) you can see the approach. The first term of Equation 29.8 dominates, because \(e^{(\alpha - 1)/b}\) grows while \(e^{-\alpha/b}\) shrinks. Keeping only it, the logarithm splits as \(\ln\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1} + \frac{\alpha - 1}{b}\), and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac1b + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}\). As \(\alpha\) grows, \(\frac{\alpha}{2\alpha - 1}\) tends to \(\frac12\), so \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \approx \frac1b - \frac{\ln 2}{\alpha - 1}\): the curve approaches \(1/b\) from below at rate \(1/(\alpha - 1)\). At \(\alpha = 512\) and \(b = 1\), both the formula and this approximation give 0.9986.
When the privacy loss is unbounded, the curve grows linearly. The Gaussian privacy loss is a straight line in the output \(y\) (the squares in the two exponents cancel, leaving a linear term), so it has no maximum, and the curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) grows without bound. The Gaussian mechanism is therefore not \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\). It is still \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP at every finite order, and that is all composition and conversion need.
The straight-line shape of the Gaussian curve has a meaning of its own. For a single pair, a curve of the form \(\rho\alpha\) means the privacy loss is exactly normal, \(\mathcal N(\rho, 2\rho)\). The reason is Fact 1: \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is the log-MGF of the loss at \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), and with \(\varepsilon = \rho\alpha = \rho(\lambda + 1)\) it is \(\rho\lambda + \rho\lambda^2\). The log-MGF of a normal variable with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\) is \(m\lambda + v\lambda^2/2\), so this one has \(m = \rho\) and \(v = 2\rho\). Concentrated DP builds a definition on it.

The Laplace and randomized response curves level off at their pure DP levels \(1/b\) and \(\ln 3\) (dotted). The Gaussian curve \(\alpha/2\) grows linearly.

For the Gaussian mechanism on a vector query, why does only the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity matter, and not the \(\ell_1\)? (The divergence between two isotropic normals depends only on the Euclidean distance between their means, by rotation invariance.)

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.5 Composition adds curves

29.5.1 Context
Training a model runs thousands of mechanisms, each chosen after seeing the outputs of the earlier ones. You need the curve of the whole run. For a product of independent distributions, Part 1 showed that Rényi divergences add: the moment of Fact 1 is an integral of a product, which splits into a product of integrals, and the logarithm turns the product into a sum. Adaptive composition is not a product of independent distributions, because the second mechanism depends on the first output. The chain rule below shows that the curves still add, as long as each step’s curve is bounded whatever the earlier outputs were.


29.5.2 Statement
Let \(M_1\) have RDP curve \(\varepsilon_1\). Let \(M_2(\cdot\,; y_1)\) be a mechanism chosen using the first output \(y_1\), whose RDP curve is at most \(\varepsilon_2\) for every \(y_1\). The adaptive composition releases both outputs, \(M(D) = (y_1, y_2)\), with \(y_1 \sim M_1(D)\) and \(y_2 \sim M_2(D; y_1)\). Its curve is at most the sum of the two curves: \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_1(\alpha) + \varepsilon_2(\alpha) \qquad\text{for every } \alpha > 1. \tag{29.10}\] By induction, treating the first \(k - 1\) steps as one mechanism, \(k\) adaptively chosen mechanisms have curve at most \(\sum_{i=1}^k \varepsilon_i(\alpha)\). This is Mironov (2017), Proposition 1. Section B.4 in the appendices derives it from scratch, and Section B.5 compares it with the other accountants on one mechanism.


29.5.3 Derivation
The idea is to write the order-\(\alpha\) moment of the pair of outputs as a double integral, bound the inner integral (over \(y_2\)) by the worst case of the second step, and recognise what is left as the moment of the first step. Fix neighbours \(D \sim D'\) and an order \(\alpha > 1\). Write \(p_1, q_1\) for the densities of \(y_1\) under \(D\) and \(D'\), and \(p_2(\cdot \mid y_1), q_2(\cdot \mid y_1)\) for those of \(y_2\) given \(y_1\).

Factor the joint densities. By the definition of the adaptive composition, \(y_1\) is drawn first and \(y_2\) is drawn given \(y_1\), so \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)\,p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\), and the same for \(q\).
Write the order-\(\alpha\) moment as a double integral (Fact 1): \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \int\!\!\int p_1^\alpha q_1^{1-\alpha}\;p_2(y_2\mid y_1)^\alpha q_2(y_2\mid y_1)^{1-\alpha}\,dy_2\,dy_1. \tag{29.11}\] The integrand splits into a factor for \(y_1\) and a factor for \(y_2\) given \(y_1\), because a power of a product is the product of the powers.
Do the inner integral first, with \(y_1\) fixed. It is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P_2(\cdot\mid y_1)\|Q_2(\cdot\mid y_1))}\), by Fact 1 again. For fixed \(y_1\), \(P_2(\cdot\mid y_1)\) and \(Q_2(\cdot\mid y_1)\) are the outputs of the mechanism \(M_2(\cdot\,; y_1)\) on \(D\) and \(D'\), so the divergence is at most \(\varepsilon_2(\alpha)\). Since \(\alpha - 1 > 0\), the exponential is increasing, and the inner integral is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_2(\alpha)}\), whatever \(y_1\) is.
The outer integral. Pull that constant out. What is left is \(\int p_1^\alpha q_1^{1-\alpha}\,dy_1\), which by Fact 1 is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P_1\|Q_1)} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_1(\alpha)}\). So the double integral is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_2(\alpha)}e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_1(\alpha)}\).
Take logarithms and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). This gives \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon_1(\alpha) + \varepsilon_2(\alpha)\) for this pair. The right side does not depend on the pair, so the supremum over neighbours satisfies the same bound.

To see the steps on numbers, take an adaptive pair of randomized responses. The first step reports the bit with keep-probability 0.75. The second reports it again, with keep-probability 0.75 if the first output was 1 and 0.6 if it was 0. Table 29.5 lists the four joint outcomes when the true bit is 1 (\(P\)) and 0 (\(Q\)). Each joint probability is the first step’s probability times the second’s, as in step 1.
