The terms sum to 5.3472, so \(D_2 = \ln 5.3472 = 1.6766\). The bound adds the first step’s curve to the worst curve the second step can have. At order 2 the second step’s curve is \(\varepsilon_{0.75}(2) = 0.8473\) on the branch \(y_1 = 1\) and \(\varepsilon_{0.6}(2) = 0.1542\) on the branch \(y_1 = 0\), writing \(\varepsilon_p\) for the curve of randomized response with keep-probability \(p\). So the bound is \(\varepsilon_1(2) + \max\big(\varepsilon_{0.75}(2), \varepsilon_{0.6}(2)\big) = 0.8473 + \max(0.8473, 0.1542) = 1.6946\). The bound holds, and it is not tight here, because step 3 replaced the inner divergence by its worst case, 0.8473, on the branch \(y_1 = 0\) where it is really 0.1542. When the second step does not adapt (keep-probability 0.75 on both branches), the joint distribution is a product and \(D_2 = 1.6946\) exactly.


29.5.4 Interpretation
The bound is tight for products and exact for the Gaussian. When the mechanisms are independent, the inner divergence in step 3 is the same for every \(y_1\), so replacing it by its worst case loses nothing and the curves add exactly (additivity, Section 3.4). A sum of independent Gaussian steps is again Gaussian, so for Gaussian steps the composed curve is exactly the curve of a single mechanism.
This is why composition works for RDP and not for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) directly. The order-\(\alpha\) moment is an integral of a product, so it factorizes over the steps, as step 2 used. The smallest \(\delta\) that works for a given \(\varepsilon\) is the hockey-stick divergence \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \int(p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\), the total probability by which \(P\) exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times \(Q\), where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\). A positive part of a difference does not factorize over the steps. That is why composing \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) points needs a separate theorem with its own slack.
One condition remains. The mechanisms can be chosen adaptively, but each step’s curve bound \(\varepsilon_i\) must be fixed in advance; it must not depend on the data. When the budget itself is chosen on the fly, you need the filters and odometers of Adaptive composition.


29.5.5 Example: \(k\) Gaussian steps
With \(\sigma = 20\), each step has \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/(2 \cdot 20^2) = \alpha/800\). After \(k\) steps, the curve is \(k\alpha/800\). Setting \(k\alpha/800 = \alpha/(2\sigma'^2)\) shows that this is the curve of one Gaussian step with noise multiplier \(\sigma' = 20/\sqrt k\):

\(k = 10\): \(0.0125\,\alpha\), the curve of one Gaussian with \(\sigma = 6.3246\);
\(k = 100\): \(0.1250\,\alpha\), one Gaussian with \(\sigma = 2.0000\);
\(k = 1000\): \(1.2500\,\alpha\), one Gaussian with \(\sigma = 0.6325\).

In general, \(k\) Gaussian steps with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) have the curve of one Gaussian with noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt k\). The function compose_rdp adds 1000 copies of the curve on the grid of orders and returns 2.5000 at \(\alpha = 2\), which is \(1000 \times 2/800\).
Different mechanisms compose just as easily, because their curves are added order by order. A Laplace step with \(b = 1\) followed by a Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 1\) has \(\varepsilon(2) = 0.6191 + 1 = 1.6191\) and \(\varepsilon(10) = 0.9287 + 5 = 5.9287\), reading both terms from Table 29.4.
Full-batch DP-SGD. The part’s running example runs 10,000 steps of DP-SGD with \(\sigma = 1\). If each step used the whole dataset, each would have the curve \(\alpha/2\), and the composed curve would be \(10{,}000\,\alpha/2 = 5000\,\alpha\). The converted guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) would be \(\varepsilon = 5425.5\) even when computed exactly. That is no guarantee at all. With the conversion of Section 29.8, which adds a tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) with \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\), RDP on ORDERS gives \(5000 \times 1.1 + 11.5129/0.1 = 5615.1\) at \(\alpha = 1.1\), the lowest order of the grid. The continuous optimum (Equation 29.18 with the composed noise multiplier \(1/\sqrt{10{,}000} = 0.01\)) is \(\alpha^* = 1 + 0.01 \times 4.7985 = 1.048\), with \(5000 + 4.7985/0.01 = 5479.9\). A curve this steep needs orders just above 1. DP-SGD is private only because each step touches a random 1% of the data. Amplification by subsampling computes the curve of a subsampled step.


29.5.6 Check yourself

Two mechanisms with curves \(\alpha/8\) and \(\alpha/2\) are composed. Which single Gaussian mechanism has the same curve? (The sum is \(5\alpha/8 = \alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2 = 0.8\), so \(\sigma = 0.8944\).)
In Table 29.5, where does the derivation lose \(1.6946 - 1.6766 = 0.0180\) nats? (In step 3, which bounds the inner divergence on the branch \(y_1 = 0\) by the worst case 0.8473, while the keep-probability 0.6 gives only 0.1542.)

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.6 Post-processing and group privacy

29.6.1 Context
Two properties of DP carry over to RDP. Post-processing matters because a released model or its predictions must not leak more than the training procedure that produced them. Group privacy matters because records are correlated: a family shares a household, and a user contributes many rows. For \(\varepsilon\)-DP, a group of \(k\) records gets \(k\varepsilon\) (Properties of DP), because the likelihood ratios along a chain of \(k\) neighbours multiply. For RDP the answer is weaker: the Rényi divergence does not satisfy a plain triangle inequality, so going through an intermediate dataset costs a higher order, and the order of the group guarantee must shrink as the group grows.


29.6.2 Statement
Post-processing. Applying any randomized map \(g\) that does not look at the data to the output cannot raise the curve: \(\varepsilon_{g\circ M}(\alpha) \le \varepsilon_M(\alpha)\) for every \(\alpha\).
Weak triangle inequality (Mironov 2017, Proposition 11). To bound the divergence from \(P\) to \(Q\) through an intermediate distribution \(R\), you pay with higher orders on the two legs, and the exponents \(u\) and \(v\) choose how the cost is split between them. For distributions \(P, R, Q\), an order \(\alpha > 1\) and exponents \(u, v > 1\) with \(\frac1u + \frac1v = 1\), \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{\alpha - 1/u}{\alpha - 1}D_{u\alpha}(P\|R) + D_{v(\alpha - 1) + 1}(R\|Q). \tag{29.12}\] The even split \(u = v = 2\) (Corollary 4 there) doubles the order on the first leg and nearly doubles it on the second: \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{\alpha - 1/2}{\alpha - 1}D_{2\alpha}(P\|R) + D_{2\alpha - 1}(R\|Q). \tag{29.13}\]
Group privacy (Mironov 2017, Proposition 2). If \(M\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP and \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\), then on inputs that differ in \(2^c\) records \(M\) satisfies the RDP bound of order \(\alpha/2^c\) with \(\varepsilon\) replaced by \(3^c\varepsilon\).


29.6.3 Derivation
Post-processing. \(g \circ M(D)\) is \(M(D)\) passed through the channel \(g\), the same channel whichever dataset was used, so \(D_\alpha\) can only decrease (Fact 3). Take the supremum over neighbours. For a concrete case, pass the output of randomized response (\(p = 0.75\)) through a channel that flips it with probability 0.2. When the bit is 1, the final output is 1 if the first output was 1 and was kept, or was 0 and was flipped: \(0.75 \times 0.8 + 0.25 \times 0.2 = 0.65\). When the bit is 0, it is \(0.25 \times 0.8 + 0.75 \times 0.2 = 0.35\). The two outputs are now closer in probability, and \(D_2\) drops from 0.8473 to \(\ln\big(0.65^2/0.35 + 0.35^2/0.65\big) = 0.3333\), while \(D_\infty\) drops from 1.0986 to \(\ln(0.65/0.35) = 0.6190\).
Weak triangle inequality. The idea is to write the moment for \(P\) against \(Q\) as an average under \(R\) of a product of two likelihood ratios, \(p/r\) and \(r/q\), and then separate the two factors with Hölder’s inequality. Write \(p, r, q\) for the densities of \(P, R, Q\).

Insert the middle distribution. Multiply and divide by powers of \(r\): since \((p/r)^\alpha (r/q)^{\alpha-1} r = p^\alpha r^{-\alpha + \alpha - 1 + 1} q^{1-\alpha} = p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\), Fact 1 gives \[e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = \int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha} = \mathbb E_R\Big[\Big(\frac pr\Big)^\alpha\Big(\frac rq\Big)^{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{29.14}\]
Separate the two ratios with Hölder’s inequality. Hölder’s inequality bounds the average of a product of two non-negative quantities by a product of their higher moments: for \(u, v > 1\) with \(\frac1u + \frac1v = 1\), \(\mathbb E_R[XY] \le \big(\mathbb E_R X^u\big)^{1/u}\big(\mathbb E_R Y^v\big)^{1/v}\). (With \(u = v = 2\) it is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.) Apply it with \(X = (p/r)^\alpha\) and \(Y = (r/q)^{\alpha-1}\).
The first factor is \(\mathbb E_R[(p/r)^{u\alpha}]\), the moment of the ratio \(p/r\) at order \(u\alpha\) under \(R\). By Fact 1 at order \(u\alpha\), it equals \(e^{(u\alpha - 1)D_{u\alpha}(P\|R)}\).
The second factor is \(\mathbb E_R[(r/q)^{v(\alpha-1)}]\). By the change of measure (\(\mathbb E_R[g] = \mathbb E_Q[(r/q)g]\)) it equals \(\mathbb E_Q[(r/q)^{v(\alpha - 1) + 1}]\), and by Fact 1 at order \(v(\alpha - 1) + 1\) that is \(e^{v(\alpha - 1)D_{v(\alpha-1)+1}(R\|Q)}\).
Combine. Raise the two factors to the powers \(1/u\) and \(1/v\) and take logarithms: \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \frac{u\alpha - 1}{u}D_{u\alpha}(P\|R) + (\alpha - 1)D_{v(\alpha-1)+1}(R\|Q)\). Divide by \(\alpha - 1\) to get Equation 29.12, since \(\frac{u\alpha - 1}{u} = \alpha - \frac1u\). With \(u = v = 2\), \(v(\alpha - 1) + 1 = 2\alpha - 1\), which gives Equation 29.13.

Group privacy, two records (\(c = 1\)). The idea is to walk from \(D\) to \(D'\) through a dataset that differs from each in one record, and apply the weak triangle inequality to the two neighbouring steps. Let \(D\) and \(D'\) differ in two records, and let \(D_1\) be the dataset in between, a neighbour of both. Put \(P = M(D)\), \(R = M(D_1)\), \(Q = M(D')\) and let \(\beta = \alpha/2 \ge 2\) be the order of the group guarantee.

Apply Equation 29.13 at order \(\beta\). Its orders become \(2\beta = \alpha\) and \(2\beta - 1 = \alpha - 1\): \(D_\beta(P\|Q) \le \frac{\beta - 1/2}{\beta - 1}D_{\alpha}(P\|R) + D_{\alpha - 1}(R\|Q)\).
Both pairs are neighbours, so \(D_\alpha(P\|R) \le \varepsilon\), and \(D_{\alpha-1}(R\|Q) \le D_\alpha(R\|Q) \le \varepsilon\) by monotonicity (Fact 2).
Bound the factor. The factor \(\frac{\beta - 1/2}{\beta - 1} = 1 + \frac{1/2}{\beta - 1}\) decreases in \(\beta\) and equals \(\frac{1.5}{1} = \frac32\) at \(\beta = 2\), so it is at most \(\frac32\) for \(\beta \ge 2\). So \(D_\beta(P\|Q) \le \frac32\varepsilon + \varepsilon = \frac52\varepsilon \le 3\varepsilon\). Mironov states the bound with the constant 3; the argument gives \(\frac52\).

For \(c > 1\), repeat: a group of \(2^c\) records is two groups of \(2^{c-1}\), so each round halves the order and multiplies \(\varepsilon\) by 3. After \(c\) rounds the order is \(\alpha/2^c\) and the bound is \(3^c\varepsilon\); the condition \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\) keeps the order of the last round at least 2.


29.6.4 Interpretation
Each doubling of the group costs half the order as well as a factor in \(\varepsilon\). The reason is step 2 of the Hölder argument: the divergence across two steps involves the product of two likelihood ratios, and to control the average of a product you need higher moments of each factor. A bound at order \(\alpha\) for one record therefore buys a bound at only about order \(\alpha/2\) for two.
How loose is this? Test it on the Gaussian, where the exact answer is known. A group of \(2^c\) records shifts a Gaussian query of sensitivity 1 by up to \(2^c\), so the exact group curve is Equation 29.7 with the shift \(2^c\) in place of 1, \(\alpha(2^c)^2/(2\sigma^2)\). Table 29.6 compares it with the bounds at \(\sigma = 1\). For two records, the weak triangle inequality loses little once \(\beta \ge 4\), and Proposition 2’s constant 3 costs a factor 1.5, because the exact value is \(2\varepsilon(2\beta)\) (\(4\beta/2 = 2 \cdot 2\beta/2\)) and Proposition 2 gives \(3\varepsilon(2\beta)\). The loss compounds with \(c\): \(3^c\) against \(2^c\) gives a factor \(1.5^c\).
So use the mechanism when you can. For the Gaussian, the exact group curve is just the curve with sensitivity \(2^c\). The generic bound matters for mechanisms whose curve on far-apart inputs you cannot compute.

29.6.5 Example: two records under Gaussian and Laplace noise
Figure 29.3 draws the two-record case for the Gaussian with \(\sigma = 1\). The weak-triangle bound hugs the exact line \(2\beta\) for \(\beta \ge 3\) and blows up near \(\beta = 1\), where its factor \(\frac{\beta - 1/2}{\beta - 1}\) does. Proposition 2 applies only from \(\beta = 2\), and its line has slope 3 instead of 2.
For the Laplace mechanism with \(b = 1\) at order 2, two records apart, the exact value is the Laplace curve with shift 2, that is Equation 29.8 with \(1/b\) replaced by 2: 1.5958. The weak triangle gives 1.9674 and Proposition 2 gives 2.4411. The pure DP group bound, \(2/b = 2\), is better than Proposition 2 here. Because the Laplace mechanism is \(1/b\)-DP, a group of two is \(2/b\)-DP, and by monotonicity that bound holds at every order. In general, for a mechanism that is already \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the group bound \(k\varepsilon\) of pure DP holds at every order, and it can beat the RDP route.

Dashed: the weak triangle inequality with \(u = v = 2\). Dotted: Proposition 2’s bound \(3\varepsilon(2\beta)\), drawn from \(\beta = 2\), where its condition \(\alpha = 2\beta \ge 4\) starts to hold.





29.6.6 Check yourself

A mechanism is \((8, 1)\)-RDP. What does Proposition 2 give for groups of two and of four records? (Two records: order \(8/2 = 4\) and \(\varepsilon = 3\). Four records: order \(8/4 = 2\) and \(\varepsilon = 3^2 = 9\).)
Why does post-processing need \(g\) to ignore the data? (If \(g\) reads the data, \(g \circ M\) is not a channel applied to \(M\)’s output, and Fact 3 does not apply: \(g\) could simply print a record.)

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
section: 29.7 The moments accountant is RDP in disguise
text:
29.7 The moments accountant is RDP in disguise

29.7.1 Context
Abadi et al. (2016) introduced the moments accountant to train neural networks with DP. For each \(\lambda > 0\) (in practice, the integers up to 32), it tracks the logarithm of the moment generating function (MGF) of the privacy loss, \(\ln\mathbb E[e^{\lambda L}]\). It adds these numbers over the training steps and converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) with a tail bound. Their paper predates RDP and is written in different notation. But Fact 1 already says that the log-MGF of the privacy loss at \(\lambda\) is \((\alpha - 1)D_\alpha\) at \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\). This section makes that precise: the moments accountant tracks the same object as the RDP curve, so everything in this chapter applies to it.


29.7.2 Statement
Abadi et al. define the log-moment \(\alpha_M(\lambda) = \sup_{D \sim D'}\ln\mathbb E_{Y \sim M(D)}\big[e^{\lambda L(Y)}\big]\), the log-MGF of the privacy loss for the worst pair of neighbours. Their letter \(\alpha\) clashes with our order, so write it \(K_M(\lambda)\). It is the RDP curve one order up, multiplied by \(\lambda\): \[K_M(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon_M(\lambda + 1), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \varepsilon_M(\alpha) = \frac{K_M(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{29.15}\] The two parts of their Theorem 2 (Abadi et al. 2016) then become the two results of this chapter that RDP needs.

Composability: \(K_M(\lambda) \le \sum_i K_{M_i}(\lambda)\). This is Equation 29.10 at order \(\lambda + 1\), multiplied by \(\lambda\).
Tail bound: \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\delta = \min_\lambda\exp\big(K_M(\lambda) - \lambda\varepsilon\big)\). This is the conversion of Section 29.8, read in the other direction: it fixes \(\varepsilon\) and solves for \(\delta\) instead of fixing \(\delta\) and solving for \(\varepsilon\) (Exercise 3).



29.7.3 Derivation
The identity is Fact 1 written out, with one change of measure.

Write the moment as a sum over outputs (for densities, an integral). Since \(e^{\lambda L} = (p/q)^\lambda\), \(\mathbb E_P\big[e^{\lambda L}\big] = \sum_y p(y)\Big(\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}\Big)^\lambda\).
Change of measure. Move one factor of \(p/q\) onto the weight: \(p\,(p/q)^\lambda = q\,(p/q)^{\lambda + 1}\). So the sum is an average under \(Q\), \(\mathbb E_Q\big[r^{\lambda + 1}\big]\).
Fact 1 at order \(\alpha = \lambda + 1\): \(\mathbb E_Q[r^{\alpha}] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} = e^{\lambda D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\).
Take logarithms and the supremum over neighbours. The factor \(\lambda > 0\) does not change which pair is worst, so \(K_M(\lambda) = \lambda\,\varepsilon_M(\lambda + 1)\).

As a concrete check, take randomized response with \(p = 0.75\) at \(\lambda = 1\), using Table 29.2. The output 1 has \(p(1) = 0.75\) and \(e^{L} = 3\), the output 0 has \(p(0) = 0.25\) and \(e^{L} = 1/3\). So \(\mathbb E_P[e^L] = 0.75 \times 3 + 0.25 \times \frac13 = 2.2500 + 0.0833 = 2.3333\), the same two terms as in the order-2 column of Table 29.2. Its logarithm, 0.8473, is \(1 \cdot \varepsilon(2)\). At \(\lambda = 2\), the direct sum and \(2\varepsilon(3)\) both give 1.9136.


29.7.4 Interpretation
The two accountants give the same numbers with different bookkeeping. The moments accountant stores \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)\) where RDP stores \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), and both add over steps. Libraries that say “moments accountant” and libraries that say “RDP accountant” compute the same thing.
The identity itself is simple, so what was new in 2016? The contribution of Abadi et al. was a bound on \(K(\lambda)\) for the subsampled Gaussian step of DP-SGD, where each step uses a random fraction of the data. Amplification by subsampling derives it in RDP form.
There is also a statistical reading. The log of a moment generating function is called the cumulant generating function: its derivatives at 0 are the mean, the variance and the higher cumulants of the variable. So \(K_M(\lambda)\) is the cumulant generating function of the privacy loss of the worst pair (more precisely, the supremum over neighbours of their cumulant generating functions). If the loss is normal, all cumulants beyond the variance vanish, \(K\) is a quadratic in \(\lambda\), and the RDP curve is linear in \(\alpha\), as for the Gaussian.


29.7.5 Example: the Gaussian privacy loss
Take the Gaussian pair \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The log-ratio of the two densities is \(-\frac{y^2}{2} + \frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2} = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu y\), so the privacy loss \(L(Y) = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu Y\) with \(Y \sim P\) is a linear function of a standard normal. It is therefore normal, with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\) (Divergences). The log-MGF of a normal variable with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\) is \(m\lambda + v\lambda^2/2\), so \[K(\lambda) = \lambda\frac{\mu^2}{2} + \frac{\lambda^2\mu^2}{2} = \lambda\cdot\frac{(\lambda + 1)\mu^2}{2} = \lambda\,\varepsilon(\lambda + 1), \tag{29.16}\] with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\), as Equation 29.15 says. At \(\mu = 1\), the formula gives \(K(1) = \frac12 + \frac12 = 1.0000\) and \(K(2) = 1 + 2 = 3.0000\). Averaging \(e^{\lambda L}\) over a million draws of \(Y\) gives 1.0000 and 3.0003.


29.7.6 Check yourself

A mechanism has \(K_M(\lambda) = \lambda(\lambda + 1)/8\). What is its RDP curve? (\(\varepsilon(\alpha) = K(\alpha - 1)/(\alpha - 1) = (\alpha - 1)\alpha/(8(\alpha - 1)) = \alpha/8\), a Gaussian with \(\sigma = 2\).)
Why does Abadi et al.’s composability theorem need no new proof once you know Equation 29.10? (Multiplying Equation 29.10 at order \(\lambda + 1\) by \(\lambda > 0\) gives it.)

title: 29  Rényi differential privacy
text:
29.8 From RDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)

29.8.1 Context
After composing, you hold a curve. What you report is an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair, because that is the guarantee with a direct meaning for an event: no set of outputs becomes more than \(e^\varepsilon\) times likelier, up to an additive \(\delta\) (Definition). The conversion rests on one observation. Outputs whose privacy loss is at most some threshold \(c\) already satisfy the \(e^c\) bound, so only the outputs with loss above \(c\) can break it, and their total probability can be charged to \(\delta\). That probability is a tail of the privacy loss, and a Chernoff bound controls a tail with an exponential moment, which is exactly what each point of the RDP curve provides. Every order gives a valid \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), and you pick the best one.


29.8.2 Statement
Mironov’s conversion (Mironov 2017, Proposition 3). The converted \(\varepsilon\) is the RDP value plus a tail term, which pays for \(\delta\) and shrinks as the order grows. If \(M\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP, then for every \(0 < \delta < 1\) it is \((\varepsilon_\delta, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon_\delta = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{29.17}\] If you hold the whole curve, take the best order: \(\varepsilon_\delta = \min_\alpha\big[\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\big]\). For the Gaussian curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\), the first term grows with \(\alpha\) and the second falls, and over all real \(\alpha > 1\) the minimum is where they balance: \[\alpha^* = 1 + \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}, \qquad \varepsilon_\delta = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}}{\sigma}. \tag{29.18}\]


29.8.3 Derivation
The conversion. The plan is to split every event into outputs with small loss, which satisfy the \(e^c\) bound, and outputs with large loss, whose probability is the tail, then bound the tail with Chernoff. Fix neighbours, with privacy loss \(L\), and a threshold \(c\) to be chosen.

Split any event \(S\) by the size of the loss: \(P(S) = P(S \cap \{L \le c\}) + P(S \cap \{L > c\})\).
Bound each part. On \(\{L \le c\}\), \(\ln(p/q) \le c\), so \(p \le e^c q\) by the definition of \(L\). Integrating over \(S \cap \{L \le c\}\), the first term is at most \(e^cQ(S)\). The second term is at most \(\Pr_P[L > c]\), since \(S \cap \{L > c\}\) is a subset of \(\{L > c\}\).
Chernoff on the loss. Apply Fact 4 with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\) and then Fact 1, which says \(\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}\): \(\Pr_P[L > c] \le e^{-(\alpha-1)c}\,\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] = e^{(\alpha - 1)(D_\alpha(P\|Q) - c)} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - c)}\).
Choose \(c\) to make the tail \(\delta\). Setting \((\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - c) = \ln\delta\) gives \(c = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\). Then \(P(S) \le e^cQ(S) + \delta\) for every \(S\) and every pair of neighbours, which is \((c, \delta)\)-DP.

Mironov proves the same bound by a different route, through Hölder’s inequality (“probability preservation”).
The Gaussian optimum. The plan is to minimize the converted \(\varepsilon\) over the order with calculus. Write \(a = \alpha - 1 > 0\) and \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\). Substituting the Gaussian curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2) = (a + 1)/(2\sigma^2)\) into Equation 29.17 gives \(\varepsilon_\delta(a) = \frac{a + 1}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\ell}{a}\).

Set the derivative to zero: \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2} - \frac{\ell}{a^2} = 0\), so \(a^2 = 2\sigma^2\ell\) and \(a = \sigma\sqrt{2\ell}\). The function is convex in \(a > 0\) (a line plus \(\ell/a\), whose second derivative \(2\ell/a^3\) is positive), so this is the minimum.
Substitute: \(\frac{a}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{\sqrt{2\ell}}{2\sigma}\) and \(\frac{\ell}{a} = \frac{\ell}{\sigma\sqrt{2\ell}} = \frac{\sqrt{2\ell}}{2\sigma}\). The two terms that depend on \(a\) are equal at the optimum, and they add to \(\sqrt{2\ell}/\sigma\). With the constant \(\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\), this is Equation 29.18.



29.8.4 Interpretation
The conversion gives something away in two places. Step 2 charges the whole tail \(\Pr_P[L > c]\) to \(\delta\). The exact smallest \(\delta\) at level \(c\) is the hockey-stick divergence, which can be written as an average over outputs, \(\delta(c) = \mathbb E_P\big[(1 - e^{c - L})_+\big]\): factoring \(p\) out of \((p - e^cq)_+\) leaves \((1 - e^{c - L})_+\). So the exact \(\delta\) charges an output with loss \(L > c\) only the fraction \(1 - e^{c - L}\) of its probability, not all of it. Step 3 then bounds the tail with a Chernoff bound, which overestimates it. From RDP to (ε, δ) and to tests removes much of both losses with sharper conversions.
The order trades two terms against each other. Small orders make the curve small but the tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) large; large orders do the opposite (Figure 29.4, left). The optimum moves to smaller orders as the composed curve grows, because a steeper curve makes large orders more expensive. By Equation 29.18 with \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} = 4.7985\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one Gaussian step with \(\sigma = 20\) wants \(\alpha \approx 1 + 20 \times 4.7985 \approx 97\), while 1000 steps, with composed noise multiplier \(20/\sqrt{1000} = 0.6325\), want \(\alpha \approx 1 + 0.6325 \times 4.7985 \approx 4\). That is why the grid runs from 1.1 to 512.
For many Gaussian steps the conversion reproduces the square-root growth of advanced composition. For \(k\) steps, Equation 29.18 with \(\sigma/\sqrt k\) in place of \(\sigma\) gives \(\varepsilon_\delta = \frac{k}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}}{\sigma}\). The second term grows like \(\sqrt k\), the same shape as advanced composition, but with constants derived from the Gaussian curve instead of from a worst-case \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) point.


29.8.5 Example: one Gaussian step, and many
One step, \(\sigma = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Here \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\) and \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} = \sqrt{23.0259} = 4.7985\). The curve is \(\alpha/2\), and Equation 29.17 adds \(11.5129/(\alpha - 1)\). Three orders show the trade-off:

\(\alpha = 2\): \(1.0000 + 11.5129 = 12.5129\);
\(\alpha = 5.8\): \(2.9000 + 2.3985 = 5.2985\);
\(\alpha = 20\): \(10.0000 + 0.6059 = 10.6059\).

At the small order the tail term dominates, at the large order the curve does, and in between they nearly balance. The grid’s best order is 5.8, next to the continuous optimum \(\alpha^* = 1 + 4.7985 = 5.7985\), and both give \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\).
To see how good this is, compare it with the exact \(\varepsilon\) of the Gaussian mechanism at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The exact privacy curve of a Gaussian pair whose means are \(\mu = 1/\sigma\) standard deviations apart is \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) \tag{29.19}\] (Balle & Wang 2018; Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function, \(\Phi(t)\) being the probability that a standard normal variable is below \(t\). It is the hockey-stick divergence \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) evaluated on the set \(S\) of outputs whose privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\): since the loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\) under \(P\) (and mean \(-\mu^2/2\) under \(Q\)), each of \(P(S)\) and \(Q(S)\) is a normal tail, which gives the two \(\Phi\) terms. Solving \(\delta(\varepsilon) = 10^{-5}\) for \(\varepsilon\) by bisection gives 4.3772. The conversion is 21% too large (\(5.2985/4.3772 = 1.21\)). Read the other way, the mechanism at \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\) actually has \(\delta = 1.300 \times 10^{-7}\), 76.9 times smaller than the conversion promises (\(10^{-5}/(1.300 \times 10^{-7}) = 76.9\)).
\(k\) steps, \(\sigma = 20\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Table 29.7 compares four ways to account for \(k\) Gaussian steps. The exact value is available because \(k\) steps are one Gaussian with \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\). The two generic routes from Part 3 first turn each step into one \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) point of its exact curve, then compose the points. Basic composition adds the per-step guarantees, both the \(\varepsilon\)s and the \(\delta\)s, so it spends \(\delta/k\) per step and reports \(k\varepsilon_0\). Advanced composition treats the total privacy loss as a sum of \(k\) independent bounded terms and bounds its tail. It spends a fraction \(s\) of \(\delta\) on the \(k\) per-step slacks, \(\delta_0 = s\delta/k\) each, and the rest, \(\delta' = (1 - s)\delta\), on the tail of the sum, and it gives \[\varepsilon_0\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2). \tag{29.20}\] The first term is the size of a fluctuation of the summed loss that is exceeded with probability at most \(\delta'\), from Azuma’s inequality for a sum of \(k\) terms each between \(-\varepsilon_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0\). The second term is a bound on the mean of the summed loss: \(k\) times the largest mean loss of one step, \(\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\). The script picks the best \(s\) on the grid Part 3 uses, the powers \(10^{-1/4}, 10^{-2/4}, \dots, 10^{-10}\); at every \(k\) in Table 29.7 it lands on \(s = 10^{-1/4} \approx 0.56\).
The second term is the sharper form from Part 3. The textbook form, \(k\varepsilon_0(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\) (Dwork & Roth 2014, Theorem 3.20), would give 105.86 at \(k = 1000\) instead of 68.01.

Advanced composition is loose, and it gets looser as \(k\) grows: it is 5 to 9 times the exact value, because each step’s curve was collapsed to one point before composing. For one step it is even worse than basic composition, since the factor \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta')}\) is paid even when \(k = 1\), when there is no sum to concentrate.
RDP is 18% to 57% above exact in this table, and it gets tighter as \(k\) grows. At \(k = 1\) the best order on the continuous scale would be 97.0 (giving 0.241), but the grid jumps from 63 to 128, so the grid’s answer 0.251 is a little worse. For \(k \ge 10\) the grid optimum agrees with Equation 29.18 to within 0.001 (0.771 at 31.3, 2.524 at 10.6, and 8.838 on the grid against 8.837 at \(\alpha^* = 4.03\)). The remaining gap to the exact value is the conversion’s slack, which the next chapter reduces.
That slack depends on the composed \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\), the distance between the two composed Gaussians in standard deviations. At the continuous optimum, Mironov’s conversion is 1.07 times exact at \(\mu = 10\), 1.21 at \(\mu = 1\), 1.42 at \(\mu = 0.1\) and 1.76 at \(\mu = 0.01\). Weak composed mechanisms pay the most, because as \(\mu \to 0\) the exact \(\varepsilon\) falls faster than the Chernoff bound does.
Figure 29.4 shows both halves: the trade-off over orders for \(k = 1000\), and the three methods as \(k\) grows.

The converted \(\varepsilon\) (black) is the sum of the RDP curve (dashed) and the tail term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) (dotted). Its minimum over the grid, 8.84 at \(\alpha = 4\), sits above the exact value 7.51 (green). Right: total \(\varepsilon\) against the number of steps \(k\) on log axes, for advanced composition, RDP with Mironov’s conversion, and the exact value.





29.8.6 Check yourself

A mechanism is \((10, 0.5)\)-RDP. What \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP does Equation 29.17 give at that order? (\(0.5 + 11.5129/9 = 1.7792\).)
In Table 29.7, why is the best order 4 for \(k = 1000\) steps but 128 for one step? (The composed curve is 1000 times steeper, so large orders cost more. In Equation 29.18, replacing \(\sigma\) by \(\sigma/\sqrt k\) shrinks \(\alpha^* - 1\) by \(\sqrt k\).)

29.9 Code: check every curve and every conversion
The script code/renyi_dp.py computes every number in this chapter and draws every figure. The curves are small typed functions (gaussian_rdp, laplace_rdp, randomized_response_rdp). Composition is compose_rdp, a pointwise sum on the grid ORDERS. The conversion is rdp_to_dp_mironov, which returns the best \(\varepsilon\) and the order that attains it. The exact Gaussian privacy curve is gaussian_delta_exact, and gaussian_eps_exact inverts it by bisection. Later chapters import these functions. From the repository root:

What to take from it. First, the closed forms are right. The Laplace and Gaussian curves agree with direct numerical integration, and the moments accountant’s log-moments agree with the RDP curve and with simulation. Second, composition is exact where it should be. Non-adaptive randomized responses and Gaussian steps compose with equality, because their outputs are independent and the moments factorize; the adaptive example shows where the bound gives something away, on the branch where the second step is less revealing than its worst case. Third, the conversion costs 18% to 57% in Table 29.7, while advanced composition costs 5 to 9 times. Most of the gain of RDP comes from composing curves rather than points, so even a loose conversion done once at the end beats a good theorem applied to points.

29.10 References

Mironov, “Rényi Differential Privacy” (IEEE Computer Security Foundations Symposium, CSF 2017; arXiv:1702.07476). The source of this chapter: the definition (Definition 4), adaptive composition (Proposition 1), weak group privacy (Proposition 2), the conversion (Proposition 3), the curves of randomized response, Laplace and Gaussian (Table 2, Corollaries 2 and 3) and the weak triangle inequality (Proposition 11, Corollary 4). Short and readable.
Abadi, Chu, Goodfellow, McMahan, Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Deep Learning with Differential Privacy” (CCS 2016). DP-SGD and the moments accountant; Theorem 2 is composability and the tail bound. Read it for the subsampled Gaussian bound and the experiments.
van Erven & Harremoës, “Rényi Divergence and Kullback–Leibler Divergence” (IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 2014). The properties of \(D_\alpha\) that RDP inherits, proved for general measures.
Balle & Wang, “Improving the Gaussian Mechanism for Differential Privacy: Analytical Calibration and Optimal Denoising” (ICML 2018). The exact privacy curve of the Gaussian mechanism used here as the ground truth (Theorem 8).
Dwork & Roth, The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy (2014), ch. 3. Basic composition (Theorem 3.16) and advanced composition (Theorem 3.20), the baseline that RDP improves.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (arXiv 2019). The curves that make DP-SGD accounting work, and the reference implementation behind most RDP accountants; used in Amplification by subsampling.

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.1 Why this matters
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) is the quantity accountants track, because it composes by adding curves (previous chapter). Recall what the curve is. For two neighbouring datasets, which differ in one person’s record, a mechanism produces two output distributions, \(P\) on the dataset without your record and \(Q\) on the one with it. For each order \(\alpha > 1\), the Rényi divergence \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) measures how far apart they are: it is a logarithmic average of the likelihood ratio \(P/Q\) raised to the power \(\alpha - 1\), so larger orders weigh the outputs where \(P\) is much more likely than \(Q\) more heavily. The RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) bounds that divergence, over all neighbouring pairs, at every order. When mechanisms run one after another, their curves add.
The curve is not the quantity anyone reports. A paper, a model card or a regulator asks for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differential privacy (DP), or for a statement about attacks: how much better than guessing can a test tell whether your record was used? So every RDP analysis ends with a conversion, and the conversion decides the number you publish. This chapter answers three questions: how much the standard conversion loses, and where; what the best \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is that you can claim from an RDP curve, and which order to use for it; and what an RDP curve says about tests, and what it can never say.
One idea organizes all three answers: an RDP curve is a summary of the privacy loss distribution, and converting it asks for the largest \(\delta\) consistent with that summary. The privacy loss of an output is the logarithm of how much more likely that output is under \(P\) than under \(Q\). Drawn at random from the mechanism, it is the privacy loss random variable (PRV), and \(\delta\) is a particular average over it. The RDP curve records the moment generating function (MGF) of the PRV, the average of \(e^{\lambda L}\) for a loss \(L\), at the points \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), and nothing else. A conversion has to bound the average that defines \(\delta\) using only those MGF values. Mironov’s conversion does this with Markov’s inequality and throws away most of what the summary says. The improved conversion, and the hypothesis-testing view behind it, recover almost all of it: for the Gaussian mechanism the improved conversion agrees to three decimals with the best any method could do with the curve alone. What remains, 5 to 10% of \(\varepsilon\), is not a defect of any formula. A two-outcome mechanism has an RDP curve no larger than the Gaussian’s and a larger \(\delta\), so no conversion that sees only the curve can do better. Table 30.1 lists the results.
Conventions. \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\) are the output distributions of the mechanism \(M\) on neighbouring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\). The same letters name their densities at an output \(y\), \(P(y)\) and \(Q(y)\), because \(q\) is the sampling rate. As in Part 3, \(D'\) is the dataset that holds your record and \(D\) the one without it. A guarantee must hold for every ordered pair of neighbours, so every bound below holds just as well with the roles of \(P\) and \(Q\) swapped. The privacy loss at an output \(y\) is \(L(y) = \ln(P(y)/Q(y))\): positive when \(y\) is more likely under \(D\) than under \(D'\), negative when it is less likely. With \(Y \sim P\), the random number \(L(Y)\) is the PRV (composition). Throughout, \(\alpha\) is the Rényi order and never an error rate. A test of “the output came from \(P\)” against “it came from \(Q\)”, that is, of “your record was not used” against “it was”, looks at the output and either accepts or rejects. It has type I error \(\mathrm{FPR}\), its false positive rate, the probability that it rejects although the output came from \(P\) (for a membership test, saying \(D'\) when the data were \(D\)), and type II error \(\mathrm{FNR}\), its false negative rate, the probability that it accepts although the output came from \(Q\), as in hypothesis testing. Its power \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\) is the probability that it correctly rejects when the output came from \(Q\).
The running example is the Gaussian mechanism. One step adds noise \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) to a query of sensitivity 1, where \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier. After dividing the output by \(\sigma\), the two worlds are \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(1/\sigma, 1)\). With \(k\) independent steps the outputs form a vector, and only its component along the direction of the shift differs between the worlds; that shift has length \(\sqrt{k}/\sigma\). So every quantity in this chapter depends only on \(\mu = \sqrt k/\sigma\), and the composed mechanism is the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). Its RDP curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\): one step has curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) (previous chapter), and \(k\) steps add \(k\) copies, \(k\alpha/(2\sigma^2) = \alpha\mu^2/2\). All numbers use \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and the part’s grid of 154 orders: 1.1 to 10.9 in steps of 0.1, every integer from 12 to 63, and then 128, 256 and 512.

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
section: 30.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
30.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

30.2.1 Fact 1 — δ is an expectation over the privacy loss
\((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for the ordered pair \((P, Q)\) says \(P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S) + \delta\) for every event \(S\) (definition): any set of outputs is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times more likely under \(D\) than under \(D'\), up to an additive slack \(\delta\). The smallest \(\delta\) that works is therefore the largest value of \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) over all events. That largest value is reached by putting into \(S\) exactly the outputs with \(P > e^\varepsilon Q\), because each such output adds a positive amount \(P - e^\varepsilon Q\) and every other output would subtract. The result, \(\int (P - e^\varepsilon Q)_+\), where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\), is the hockey-stick divergence \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q)\) of divergences. Written in terms of the privacy loss, it is an average over the PRV: \[\delta(\varepsilon) = E_{e^\varepsilon}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big] = \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[L > \varepsilon]. \tag{30.1}\]
The second form comes from factoring \(P\) out of the integrand. Where \(P > 0\), \((P - e^\varepsilon Q)_+ = P\,(1 - e^\varepsilon Q/P)_+\), and \(Q/P = e^{-L}\), so this is \(P\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\); integrating \(P\) times a function of the output is taking its average under \(P\). The integrand is positive exactly where \(L > \varepsilon\), and integrating \(P - e^\varepsilon Q\) over that set gives the last form.
The second form is the one to remember. Each output contributes to \(\delta\) only if its privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and then only the fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of its probability. An output with loss \(L = \varepsilon + \ln 2\) contributes half its probability, since \(1 - e^{-\ln 2} = 1 - \frac12\). An output with loss just above \(\varepsilon\) contributes almost nothing, and only an output with infinite loss contributes all of its probability.


30.2.2 Fact 2 — RDP is the MGF of the privacy loss
The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is defined by \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha}\). Write \(P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha} = P\,(P/Q)^{\alpha - 1}\) and \((P/Q)^{\alpha - 1} = e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\): the integral is the average under \(P\) of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), which is the MGF of the PRV at the point \(\alpha - 1\). An RDP bound \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) is therefore a bound on that MGF value: \[\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{30.2}\] This is Equation 3.12 of divergences, with the exponent multiplied out.
So knowing the RDP curve at the orders \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \dots\) is knowing (an upper bound on) the MGF of the PRV at \(\alpha_1 - 1, \alpha_2 - 1, \dots\). That is the whole summary. Every conversion is a way of bounding the average in Equation 30.1 using only the averages in Equation 30.2.


30.2.3 Fact 3 — Data processing on a test
A test \(\phi\) maps the output to “reject” or “accept”, so its outcome is a coin. Under \(P\) the coin shows “reject” with probability \(\mathrm{FPR}\); under \(Q\) it shows “reject” with probability \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\). Turning the output into this coin is post-processing, and post-processing cannot increase a Rényi divergence: this is the data processing inequality of divergences. The short reason is that merging outputs can only shrink the sum \(\int P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha}\). The function \(x^\alpha y^{1 - \alpha}\) is convex for \(\alpha > 1\) and scales linearly when \(x\) and \(y\) are both multiplied by the same factor, and such a function satisfies \(g(x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2) \le g(x_1, y_1) + g(x_2, y_2)\); merging two outputs replaces the right side by the left (Section F.5 in the appendices proves this). (A test that randomizes its decision is handled the same way; divergences gives the general proof.) So, writing \(\mathrm{Bern}(x)\) for “reject with probability \(x\)”, \[D_\alpha\big(\mathrm{Bern}(\mathrm{FPR})\,\|\,\mathrm{Bern}(1 - \mathrm{FNR})\big) \le D_\alpha(P\|Q). \tag{30.3}\] In words: a test cannot tell the two worlds apart better, in Rényi divergence, than the full output does.


30.2.4 Fact 4 — The Gaussian pair, exactly
For the running example everything can be computed in closed form, which is what lets this chapter measure each conversion against the truth. Take \(P = \mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The privacy loss is the difference of the two log densities, \(L(y) = -\frac{y^2}{2} + \frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2} = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu y\). It is a linear function of \(y\), so under \(P\), where \(y\) is standard normal, the PRV is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\): \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\).
Now evaluate the last form of Equation 30.1. Write \(\Phi(x) = \Pr[Z \le x]\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function. Under \(P\), \(L > \varepsilon\) means \(y < \mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\), which has probability \(\Phi(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu)\). Under \(Q\), write \(y = \mu + z\) with \(z\) standard normal; then \(L = -\mu^2/2 - \mu z\), and \(L > \varepsilon\) means \(z < -\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\). So \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big), \tag{30.4}\] the closed form already derived in divergences. It falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows, because the integrand \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\) does, so inverting it by bisection gives the exact \(\varepsilon\) at any \(\delta\). The script evaluates the second term in logarithms so that it stays accurate when \(e^\varepsilon\) overflows. As a check, at \(\mu = 1\) a Riemann sum of \(\mathbb E_P[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\) over the normal density gives \(1.2694\times10^{-1}\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(1.5372\times10^{-3}\) at \(\varepsilon = 3\), the same as the closed form to all printed digits.

30.3 Where Mironov’s conversion loses

30.3.1 Context
Rényi DP derived Mironov’s conversion: an \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP mechanism, one whose Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), is \((\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1), \delta)\)-DP. It is easy to remember and easy to compute, and Section D.3 in the appendices derives it from scratch, with the Gaussian’s best order in closed form. This section rewrites that proof as two inequalities on the privacy loss and measures what each one costs on the Gaussian, so that you can see where the excess comes from.


30.3.2 Statement
The proof first replaces \(\delta\) by the probability that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), and then bounds that probability with the MGF. For every order \(\alpha > 1\) and every \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta(\varepsilon) \;\overset{(1)}{\le}\; \Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \;\overset{(2)}{\le}\; e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}, \tag{30.5}\] and setting the right side equal to \(\delta\) gives Mironov’s conversion \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.6}\]


30.3.3 Derivation
The proof in Rényi DP has exactly these two steps. Written with Fact 1 and Fact 2:

Drop the fraction. Fact 1 says each output with \(L > \varepsilon\) contributes the fraction \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\) of its probability. Step 1 rounds that fraction up to 1: \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+ \le \mathbf 1[L > \varepsilon]\), because the left side is 0 when \(L \le \varepsilon\) and below 1 otherwise. Averaging under \(P\) gives inequality (1). This is the step that charges the whole tail \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon]\) to \(\delta\).
Bound the tail by the MGF (Chernoff). Markov’s inequality says a nonnegative random variable exceeds a level \(t\) with probability at most its average divided by \(t\). Apply it to \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), which exceeds \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\) exactly when \(L > \varepsilon\): \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\,e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\). Fact 2 bounds the average by \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\), which gives inequality (2).
Solve for \(\varepsilon\). Setting \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)} = \delta\) and taking logarithms gives \((\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon) = -\ln(1/\delta)\), which is Equation 30.6. DP also needs the inequality with the roles of the two datasets swapped, the pair \((Q, P)\). RDP bounds \(D_\alpha(Q\|P)\) by the same curve, because swapping two neighbours gives two neighbours, so the same argument applies.



30.3.4 Interpretation
The two steps lose in different places. Table 30.2 measures them on the Gaussian, converting each inequality of Equation 30.5 into an \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The first row is the exact \(\varepsilon\) from Equation 30.4. The second is the \(\varepsilon\) at which the tail \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu)\) equals \(\delta\). Since \(\Phi(x) = 10^{-5}\) at \(x = -\Phi^{-1}(1 - 10^{-5}) = -4.2649\), where \(\Phi^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(\Phi\), this is \(\varepsilon = \mu^2/2 + 4.2649\,\mu\): \(0.5 + 4.2649 \approx 4.765\) at \(\mu = 1\) and \(50 + 42.649 = 92.649\) at \(\mu = 10\). The third row is Mironov’s \(\varepsilon'\) minimized over the grid.

Step 1 ignores how far past \(\varepsilon\) the loss goes. An output with \(L\) slightly above \(\varepsilon\) counts fully toward the tail but almost nothing toward \(\delta\). The density of the Gaussian PRV is falling steeply at \(\varepsilon\), which sits several standard deviations above its mean, so most of the tail sits just above \(\varepsilon\), and step 1 overcounts it.
Step 2 replaces a tail by an MGF, and that costs more. Markov’s inequality is tight only for a variable that puts all its mass on 0 and on the level \(t\); the Gaussian PRV is nothing like that, so the bound is far above the true tail at 4.765. At \(\mu = 10\) this step costs 5.377 of the \(98.026 - 91.817 = 6.209\) total excess (Table 30.2). Of that, 0.041 is the grid’s: over all real orders Mironov’s conversion gives 97.985 at \(\alpha = 1.480\), against 98.026 at the grid’s 1.5.
On the \(\delta\) side the losses are multiplicative. At Mironov’s \(\varepsilon = 5.299\) for \(\mu = 1\), the exact \(\delta\) is \(1.300\times10^{-7}\). The tail is \(7.992\times10^{-7}\), 6.1 times larger, and Mironov’s bound is \(1.000\times10^{-5}\), 12.5 times larger again. You pay for \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and get \(1.3\times10^{-7}\).


30.3.5 Example: one release of a mean
You release the mean of a bounded statistic with the Gaussian mechanism at noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\), so \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\). Mironov’s conversion gives \(\alpha/2 + \ln(10^5)/(\alpha - 1)\) at each order. The first term grows with the order and the second shrinks, so there is a best order in between. Over the continuous range of orders the sum is smallest at \(\alpha = 5.799\), with \(\varepsilon' = 5.299\) (Section 30.6 derives both); the grid’s best order, 5.8, gives the same 5.299. The exact answer is 4.377. Reporting Mironov’s number overstates \(\varepsilon\) by 0.921, which means \(e^{0.921}\) more “allowed” likelihood ratio for every output.


30.3.6 Check yourself

Why does step 2 lose about ten times more at \(\mu = 10\) than at \(\mu = 1\)? (The PRV has mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\). At the best order, Mironov’s \(\varepsilon^* = \mu^2/2 + 2\sqrt{(\mu^2/2)\ln(1/\delta)} = \mu^2/2 + \mu\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\) sits \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)} \approx 4.799\) standard deviations above the mean, while the true tail point sits \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \delta) = 4.2649\) standard deviations above it. The gap is a fixed number of standard deviations, about 0.534, so in \(\varepsilon\) it grows like \(\mu\): 0.534 at \(\mu = 1\), about ten times that at \(\mu = 10\).)
Is step 1 ever tight? (Only when every output with \(L > \varepsilon\) has \(L = \infty\), where \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L} = 1\), such as a mechanism that sometimes reveals the record outright, with the pair ordered so that \(P\) is the output on the dataset that holds the record.)

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.4 The improved conversion

30.4.1 Context
Both of Mironov’s steps together replace the integrand \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\) of Equation 30.1, as a function of the loss value \(z\), by an exponential \(c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\) that lies above it. An exponential is used because it is the only kind of function whose average Fact 2 tells you. Mironov’s choice is \(c = e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\), the exponential that equals 1 at \(z = \varepsilon\) and so passes through the corner of the indicator. That is not the smallest exponential above the integrand, because the integrand is well below 1 near \(z = \varepsilon\). Using the smallest one is the whole improvement.


30.4.2 Statement
An \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon', \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{30.7}\] or equivalently, at a given \(\varepsilon\), \[\delta = \frac{e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}}{\alpha}\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big)^{\alpha - 1}. \tag{30.8}\] This is Theorem 21 of Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu & Sato (2020) and Proposition 12 of Canonne, Kamath & Steinke (2020), who also give the \(\delta\) form; Asoodeh, Liao, Calmon, Kosut & Sankar proved it independently (2020, Lemma 1, Eq. 20). We call it the improved conversion. Compared with Equation 30.6, its \(\delta\) is Mironov’s \(e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}\) multiplied by the factor \(\frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\), which is below 1.


30.4.3 Derivation
The plan: find the smallest constant \(c\) for which \(c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\) stays above the integrand, then average.

Bound the integrand by an exponential. If \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+ \le c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\) for every real \(z\), then the same holds with \(z\) replaced by the random loss \(L\), and averaging under \(P\) keeps the inequality. By Fact 1 the left side averages to \(\delta(\varepsilon)\), and by Fact 2 the right side averages to at most \(c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\). So \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le c\,\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}] \le c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\).
The smallest \(c\). The condition of step 1 says \(c \ge (1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\,e^{-(\alpha - 1)z}\) for every \(z\), so the smallest valid \(c\) is \(c^* = \sup_z (1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\,e^{-(\alpha - 1)z}\). For \(z \le \varepsilon\) the expression is 0, so only \(z > \varepsilon\) matters. There it is \(g(z) = e^{-(\alpha - 1)z} - e^{\varepsilon - \alpha z}\).
Find the maximum. Differentiate: \(g'(z) = -(\alpha - 1)e^{-(\alpha - 1)z} + \alpha e^{\varepsilon - \alpha z} = e^{-\alpha z}\big(\alpha e^\varepsilon - (\alpha - 1)e^z\big)\). The bracket equals \(e^\varepsilon > 0\) at \(z = \varepsilon\) and decreases as \(z\) grows, so \(g\) first rises and then falls. Its maximum is where the bracket vanishes, at \(e^{z^*} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}e^\varepsilon\), that is, \(z^* = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\).
Evaluate it. Factor \(g(z^*) = e^{-\alpha z^*}(e^{z^*} - e^\varepsilon)\). At \(z^*\), \(e^{z^*} - e^\varepsilon = e^\varepsilon\big(\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1} - 1\big) = e^\varepsilon\cdot\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\), and \(e^{-\alpha z^*} = e^{-\alpha\varepsilon}(1 - 1/\alpha)^\alpha\). Multiplying, \[c^* = \frac{e^{-(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}}{\alpha - 1}\Big(1 - \frac1\alpha\Big)^\alpha. \tag{30.9}\]
Collect. Step 1 gives \(\delta \le c^* e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\). Since \((1 - 1/\alpha)/(\alpha - 1) = 1/\alpha\), the constant in front simplifies to \(\frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\), and this is Equation 30.8.
Solve for \(\varepsilon\). Set the bound equal to \(\delta\) and take logarithms: \(\ln\delta = (\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon) - \ln\alpha + (\alpha - 1)\ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\). Divide by \(\alpha - 1\) and solve for \(\varepsilon\), using \(\ln(1 - 1/\alpha) = \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha}\), to get Equation 30.7. As before, the reverse pair \((Q, P)\) follows because RDP bounds \(D_\alpha(Q\|P)\) by the same curve.

The script checks step 4 by brute force: at \(\alpha = 6\) and \(\varepsilon = 4\) the formula gives \(c^* = 1.380552\times10^{-10}\) at \(z^* = 4 - \ln(5/6) = 4.1823\), and the maximum of \(g\) over a grid of two million points is the same to all seven digits.
Figure 30.1 draws the two exponentials. Mironov’s passes through the corner of the indicator at \(z = \varepsilon\); the smallest one sits lower and touches the integrand at \(z^*\), slightly to the right of \(\varepsilon\).






Figure 30.1: The hockey-stick integrand \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - z})_+\) (black) at \(\varepsilon = 3\), the indicator \(\mathbf 1[z > \varepsilon]\) that Mironov’s step 1 replaces it with (dashed), and the two exponentials of order \(\alpha = 6\) that bound it: Mironov’s, through the corner of the indicator (red), and the smallest one, which touches the integrand at \(z^* = \varepsilon - \ln(1 - 1/\alpha)\) (blue). The shaded curve is the density of the Gaussian privacy loss at \(\mu = 1\): the conversions average the exponentials against it.





30.4.4 Interpretation
The gain depends only on the order. Both conversions add something to the same \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), so when you subtract Equation 30.7 from Equation 30.6 at the same \(\alpha\), the \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) terms cancel, and so do the \(\ln(1/\delta)\) terms. What is left is how much smaller the improved \(\varepsilon'\) is: \[\Delta(\alpha) = \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{30.10}\] whatever the mechanism and whatever \(\delta\). On the \(\delta\) side, the improved \(\delta\) is Mironov’s times \(\frac1\alpha(1 - \frac1\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}\). Because \((1 - 1/\alpha)^{\alpha - 1} \to 1/e\), that factor behaves like \(1/(e\alpha)\) for large \(\alpha\). Table 30.3 gives values; at \(\alpha = 2\), for instance, the factor is \(\frac12\cdot\frac12 = 0.25\) and the saving is \(\ln 2 + \ln 2 = 1.3863\).

Over a grid, the saving is at least \(\Delta(\alpha_M)\), where \(\alpha_M\) is the order Mironov’s conversion picks, for any RDP curve. The reason is that the improved conversion takes its own best order, so its minimum is at most its value at \(\alpha_M\), and that value is Mironov’s minimum minus \(\Delta(\alpha_M)\) by Equation 30.10. So you can read the saving of any accountant off Table 30.3 from its best order: about 1.39 at order 2, 0.36 at order 10, 0.06 at order 100. For the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\), Mironov picks order 5.8, \(\Delta(5.8) = \frac{\ln 5.8}{4.8} + \ln\frac{5.8}{4.8} = 0.555\), and the actual saving is 0.570, a little more because the improved conversion moves to a better order. If two accountants report \(\varepsilon\) about 0.4 apart from the same curve at a best order near 10, one of them is using Mironov’s conversion. Opacus and dp_accounting both use the improved one.
The improved conversion also beats both of Mironov’s steps, not only the second. For the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\) it gives 4.729 (at \(\alpha = 5.4\)), below even the 4.765 of the tail \(\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] = \delta\) after step 1 in Table 30.2. That is possible because it never replaces the integrand by an indicator: its exponential is allowed to dip below 1 just above \(\varepsilon\), where the integrand is small. At \(\mu = 10\) it gives 96.116 against Mironov’s 98.026 and the exact 91.817. At \(\varepsilon = 4.729\) the exact Gaussian \(\delta\) is \(2.097\times10^{-6}\), so the guarantee still holds with room to spare.
For one order, it is close to optimal. The next section computes the best possible conversion from the RDP values on a whole grid, and a single order is the special case of a grid with one point. Take only the forward constraint \(D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) at one order, as the improved conversion does, at \(\mu = 1\). At order 2, where \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\), Mironov gives \(1 + \ln(10^5) = 12.513\), the improved conversion \(1 + \ln\frac12 + \ln(10^5) - \ln 2 = 11.127\), and the optimum 10.668. At orders 8 and 32 the improved conversion and the optimum agree to three decimals (5.214 and 16.228). Exercise 6 explains why the gap appears only at small orders.
Balle et al. derive the same formula geometrically, as a tangent line. In the plane of test errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\), the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) constraint \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FNR} + \delta\) is a straight line, and the best line that keeps a relaxed version of the region RDP allows (Section 30.5) on its feasible side touches the region’s boundary. Figure 30.1 shows the same tangency in the privacy-loss variable: the blue exponential touches the integrand at \(z^*\).


30.4.5 Example: the same release, converted better
For the mean released with \(\sigma = 1\), the improved conversion over the grid gives \((4.729, 10^{-5})\)-DP at order 5.4. Mironov’s gave 5.299 at order 5.8, and the exact value is 4.377. The improved conversion removes 0.570 of the 0.921 excess, at no cost: it uses the same RDP curve and one extra line of code.


30.4.6 Check yourself

Why must the bounding function be an exponential in \(z\), rather than, say, a polynomial that hugs the integrand more closely? (Fact 2 only tells you \(\mathbb E_P[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}]\). To bound \(\mathbb E_P[g(L)]\) you need \(g \le c\,e^{(\alpha - 1)z}\); any other \(g\) has an expectation the RDP curve does not determine.)
The improved conversion can return a negative \(\varepsilon'\) when \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is tiny. What should you report? (\(\varepsilon' = 0\). \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) can only fall as \(\varepsilon\) grows, so a bound at some \(\varepsilon' < 0\) also holds at 0. The script clips at 0, as Canonne et al. do.)

section: 30.5 RDP as a constraint on tests
text:
30.5 RDP as a constraint on tests

30.5.1 Context
An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) statement is one straight line in the plane of test errors: every test has \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FNR} + \delta\). An RDP curve says more. By Fact 3, each order constrains the pair \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) of every test, and the constraints for different orders bend differently. This section draws the region an RDP curve allows, following Balle et al. (2020), compares it with the Gaussian’s true trade-off curve, and uses it to compute the best possible conversion. The trade-off function \(T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR})\) of hypothesis testing is the smallest type II error any test can have at type I error \(\mathrm{FPR}\); it describes the most powerful possible attack at each false-positive rate.


30.5.2 Statement
The statement turns Fact 3 into an explicit inequality on \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) for each order, in both directions. Let \(M\) have RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\cdot)\) at the orders of a grid. Every test between \(P = M(D)\) and \(Q = M(D')\), with type I error \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and type II error \(\mathrm{FNR}\), satisfies for every order \(\alpha\) in the grid \[\mathrm{FPR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FNR})^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR})^\alpha \mathrm{FNR}^{1 - \alpha} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}, \qquad (1 - \mathrm{FNR})^\alpha \mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha} + \mathrm{FNR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{1 - \alpha} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{30.11}\] Call the set of \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) satisfying all of these the RDP privacy region, and let \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) be the smallest \(\mathrm{FNR}\) in it at type I error \(\mathrm{FPR}\). Two claims follow.

Trade-off bound. \(T(P, Q)(\mathrm{FPR}) \ge f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) for every \(\mathrm{FPR}\): no test is more powerful than the region allows.
Optimal conversion. Every pair consistent with the curve has \[\delta(\varepsilon) \le \delta_{\mathrm{opt}}(\varepsilon) = \max_{\mathrm{FPR}}\big[1 - \mathrm{FPR} - e^\varepsilon f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\big], \tag{30.12}\] and some two-outcome pair consistent with the curve attains it. So \(\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}\) is the best \(\delta\) that any conversion using only these RDP values can certify.



30.5.3 Derivation
The first three steps compute the Rényi divergence of a test’s outcome and apply the RDP curve to it. The last two rewrite \(\delta\) as a statement about tests, so that the region bounds it.

The outcome of a test is a coin (Fact 3). Table 30.4 lists the outcome’s distribution under each hypothesis.




Table 30.4: The outcome of a test with errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\), as a two-point distribution under each hypothesis.





Outcome
Probability under \(P\)
Probability under \(Q\)




reject
\(\mathrm{FPR}\)
\(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\)


accept
\(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\)
\(\mathrm{FNR}\)







Compute its Rényi divergence. The definition \(D_\alpha = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum P^\alpha Q^{1 - \alpha}\) for a two-point distribution is a sum of two terms, one per row of Table 30.4: \(D_\alpha(\text{outcome under } P\,\|\,\text{outcome under } Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big[\mathrm{FPR}^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FNR})^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR})^\alpha \mathrm{FNR}^{1 - \alpha}\big]\).
Apply the RDP curve. Data processing (Fact 3) gives this divergence \(\le D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\). Multiply by \(\alpha - 1 > 0\) and exponentiate to get the first inequality of Equation 30.11. The second comes the same way from \(D_\alpha(Q\|P) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\), which RDP also guarantees because swapping two neighbours gives two neighbours; it is the same sum with the columns of the table swapped. Since every test’s \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) lies in the region, its \(\mathrm{FNR}\) is at least the smallest \(\mathrm{FNR}\) the region allows at its \(\mathrm{FPR}\). This proves claim 1.
Write \(\delta\) as a best test. Let \(S\) be the acceptance region of a test, the outputs on which it accepts \(P\), so \(P(S) = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) and \(Q(S) = \mathrm{FNR}\). Fact 1 says \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the largest \(P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)\) over all events, so \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \max_S[P(S) - e^\varepsilon Q(S)] = \max_\phi[1 - \mathrm{FPR} - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FNR}]\). Every test’s \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) is in the region, so \(\mathrm{FNR} \ge f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\), and replacing \(\mathrm{FNR}\) by \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) can only increase the expression. That gives the bound in Equation 30.12.
Show that the bound is attained. Let \((\mathrm{FPR}^*, \mathrm{FNR}^*)\) maximize Equation 30.12, with \(\mathrm{FNR}^* = f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR}^*)\). Build a mechanism whose output is just the coin of Table 30.4 with these errors: \(M(D) = \mathrm{Bern}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}^*)\) and \(M(D') = \mathrm{Bern}(\mathrm{FNR}^*)\), where the outcome 1 is “accept”. By step 2 its Rényi divergences in both directions are exactly the left sides of Equation 30.11 at \((\mathrm{FPR}^*, \mathrm{FNR}^*)\), which lie in the region, so the mechanism satisfies the curve. The test “accept on outcome 1” has errors \((\mathrm{FPR}^*, \mathrm{FNR}^*)\), so this mechanism’s \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is at least \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}^* - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FNR}^*\), which is \(\delta_{\mathrm{opt}}(\varepsilon)\).

Computing it. For fixed \(\mathrm{FPR}\), both left sides of Equation 30.11 equal 1 at \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\): the first becomes \(\mathrm{FPR}^\alpha \mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR})^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{1 - \alpha} = \mathrm{FPR} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR})\), the second likewise. That is where the test ignores the output and the two coins are identical. Both are convex in \(\mathrm{FNR}\) (each term has the form \(x^\alpha y^{1 - \alpha}\), which is jointly convex in \((x, y)\) for \(\alpha > 1\), by Section F.5), and their smallest value is at \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\), so they decrease on \([0, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}]\). The constraints therefore hold for \(\mathrm{FNR}\) above some cut-off and fail below it, and \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) is that cut-off, found by bisection. The script works with logarithms of \(\mathrm{FPR}\), \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\), \(\mathrm{FNR}\) and \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\), because the interesting tests have errors like \(10^{-6}\). The objective in Equation 30.12 is concave in \(\mathrm{FPR}\), because \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is convex: the region is an intersection of convex sets, one per constraint, and the lower boundary of a convex set is a convex function. So a grid search refined by a one-dimensional bracketing search finds the maximum. The \(\varepsilon\) at a given \(\delta\) is the maximum over \(\mathrm{FPR}\) of \(\ln\big((1 - \mathrm{FPR} - \delta)/f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\big)\), the \(\varepsilon\) at which the line through the point \((\mathrm{FPR}, f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR}))\) just reaches \(\delta\).


30.5.4 Interpretation
To see how loose the region is, compare it with the truth for the Gaussian. The best test between \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) and \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\) rejects when the output exceeds a threshold \(\tau\) (the Neyman–Pearson lemma: the best test thresholds the likelihood ratio, which here increases with the output). Its type I error is \(\mathrm{FPR} = 1 - \Phi(\tau)\), so \(\tau = \Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\), and its type II error is the probability that an output from \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\) falls below \(\tau\), which is \(G_1(\mathrm{FPR}) = \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - 1)\). At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\), \(\Phi^{-1}(0.9) = 1.2816\), so \(G_1 = \Phi(0.2816) = 0.6109\) and the true power is \(0.3891\). Figure 30.2 plots, for the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\), the largest power \(1 - f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) that its RDP curve allows, against this true power \(1 - G_1(\mathrm{FPR})\).






Figure 30.2: Largest power \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\) at type I error \(\mathrm{FPR}\) allowed by the Gaussian’s RDP curve at \(\mu = 1\) (red, all orders of the grid together), by the single orders 2 and 8 (blue), and achieved by the Gaussian itself (black). Left: linear axes. Right: log axes, with the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) line \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} \le e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) from the improved conversion (grey), which touches the red curve.



Each order guards a different range of \(\mathrm{FPR}\). For small \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\) near 1, the term \((1 - \mathrm{FNR})^\alpha \mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha}\) of the second inequality of Equation 30.11 is by far the larger, because \(\mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha}\) blows up as \(\mathrm{FPR} \to 0\). Keeping only that term and solving for \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\) gives \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} \lesssim e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha}\,\mathrm{FPR}^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\). On log axes this is a line of slope \((\alpha - 1)/\alpha\), with intercept \((\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha = (\alpha - 1)/2\) when \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\). Order 2 has slope \(\frac12\) and is weak at small \(\mathrm{FPR}\): at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-6}\) it allows power \(1.3118\times10^{-3}\), while order 8 (slope \(\frac78\)) allows \(1.8622\times10^{-4}\). In the bulk the roles swap: at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\), order 2 allows \(0.4932\) and order 8 allows \(0.9838\). The two lines meet where \(\frac12 + \frac12\ln \mathrm{FPR} = \frac72 + \frac78\ln \mathrm{FPR}\), that is \(-3 = \frac38\ln \mathrm{FPR}\), at \(\mathrm{FPR} = e^{-8} \approx 3.35\times10^{-4}\). The lines are bounds on the boundaries, not the boundaries themselves, because they drop a term. Order 8’s line is exact at small \(\mathrm{FPR}\), but order 2’s overstates its power: at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-6}\) it gives \(e^{1/2}\cdot 10^{-3} \approx 1.6487\times10^{-3}\) against the exact \(1.3118\times10^{-3}\). So the exact boundaries of the two orders cross a little lower, at \(\mathrm{FPR} \approx 1.87\times10^{-4}\), the value the script finds by solving for equal power. At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-3}\) neither is binding: the binding order is 3.7, which alone allows \(2.4910\times10^{-2}\), the grid’s value. Large orders guard small \(\mathrm{FPR}\), small orders the bulk.
The RDP region is a good but loose summary of the trade-off curve. Table 30.5 compares powers. The curve allows 1.24 to 1.36 times the power the Gaussian has, at every \(\mathrm{FPR}\) shown; at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\), for instance, \(0.48376/0.38914 = 1.24\).



Table 30.5: Power of the best test against the Gaussian mechanism at \(\mu = 1\), true and allowed by its RDP curve.

The RDP region is not an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) region. The grey line in Figure 30.2 is the improved conversion’s guarantee. It touches the red curve at one small \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and lies far above it elsewhere, because an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair is a single straight line, and the best it can do is be tangent to the curved region at one point. A whole trade-off curve is the envelope of such lines, one for each \(\varepsilon\), which is the duality that Gaussian DP develops.
Nor does the region characterize RDP. A test squeezes the output into a single bit, and the Rényi divergence of a pair is in general larger than the largest Rényi divergence of any single test’s outcome: information spread over many outputs is lost when they are merged into “accept” and “reject”. So a pair can have every test inside the region and still violate the RDP curve. The region is what RDP implies about tests, not an equivalent definition.


30.5.5 Example: a membership test against a released statistic
An auditor runs a membership test against the mean released with \(\sigma = 1\) and wants a false-positive rate of \(\mathrm{FPR} = 10^{-3}\). The RDP curve alone guarantees that no test detects membership with probability above \(2.4910\times10^{-2}\). The Gaussian’s exact trade-off curve says the best test reaches \(1.8298\times10^{-2}\). The \((4.729, 10^{-5})\) guarantee from the improved conversion only says power \(\le e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta\), which is \(e^{4.729}\times10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.1131\), more than four times the region’s bound. Reading an RDP result through one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair throws away most of what it says about low false-positive rates.


30.5.6 Check yourself

Why are there two inequalities per order in Equation 30.11? (One for \(D_\alpha(P\|Q)\) and one for \(D_\alpha(Q\|P)\). RDP bounds both, because the neighbouring relation is symmetric; the first matters for tests with \(\mathrm{FPR}\) near 1, the second for \(\mathrm{FPR}\) near 0.)
Why is the optimum in Equation 30.12 attained by a two-outcome mechanism, rather than needing a richer one? (Any mechanism’s \(\delta\) is the best value of \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FNR}\) over its tests, and each test only sees a coin. The coin with the extreme errors is itself a mechanism with the same constraints.)

title: 30  From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests
text:
30.6 Choosing the order

30.6.1 Context
Both conversions hold at every order, so you take the best one. Each converted \(\varepsilon'\) is the RDP curve, which grows with the order, plus a term in \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), which shrinks with it, so the best order balances the two. For the Gaussian the curve is linear in \(\alpha\), and the best order has a closed form or nearly so. The formulas show how the best order moves with the number of steps and with \(\delta\), and that tells you what an accountant’s grid of orders must contain.


30.6.2 Statement
Let \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), with slope \(\rho = \mu^2/2 = k/(2\sigma^2)\) for the composed Gaussian. Over continuous \(\alpha > 1\), the best orders are as follows. For Mironov’s conversion, the best order is \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho}\), and \(\varepsilon^* = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\). For the improved conversion, the best order solves \[\rho(\alpha - 1)^2 = \ln\frac{1}{\alpha\delta}, \tag{30.13}\] which the script solves by iterating \(\alpha \leftarrow 1 + \sqrt{\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))/\rho}\) from Mironov’s \(\alpha^*\). The only difference from Mironov’s condition is the extra \(\alpha\) inside the logarithm, which pulls the best order slightly lower.


30.6.3 Derivation
Each step sets a derivative to zero, as for any smooth minimum.

Mironov. The derivative of \(\rho\alpha + \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) is \(\rho - \ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)^2\). Setting it to zero gives \((\alpha - 1)^2 = \ln(1/\delta)/\rho\), which is \(\alpha^*\). Substitute back: \(\rho\alpha^* = \rho + \rho\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho} = \rho + \sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\), and the second term is \(\ln(1/\delta)/\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho} = \sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}\) too. At the optimum the two terms contribute equally beyond \(\rho\).
Improved, derivative. Write Equation 30.7 as \(\rho\alpha + \ln(1 - \frac1\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta) - \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\) and differentiate term by term: \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\alpha}\ln(1 - \frac1\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}\), and \(\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d\alpha}\frac{\ln(1/\delta) - \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} = -\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)} - \frac{\ln(1/\delta) - \ln\alpha}{(\alpha - 1)^2}\) by the quotient rule. The \(\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}\) terms cancel, leaving \(\rho - \frac{\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))}{(\alpha - 1)^2}\). Setting it to zero gives Equation 30.13.
It is a minimum. The derivative of that expression is \(\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha - 1)^2} + \frac{2\ln(1/(\alpha\delta))}{(\alpha - 1)^3}\), which is positive whenever \(\alpha < 1/\delta\), so the objective is convex there and the stationary point is its minimum.
Scaling. Ignoring the slowly varying \(\ln\alpha\), \(\alpha^* - 1 \approx \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)/\rho} = \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)/k}\). More steps or less noise push the best order toward 1; smaller \(\delta\) pushes it up, but only through \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\).



30.6.4 Interpretation
Figure 30.3 shows the two converted \(\varepsilon'(\alpha)\) for \(\mu = 1\). Both are U-shaped: at small \(\alpha\) the \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) term explodes, at large \(\alpha\) the curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) itself does. The improved curve sits below Mironov’s everywhere by \(\Delta(\alpha)\) of Equation 30.10, and its minimum is at a slightly smaller order.






Figure 30.3: Converted \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for each order of the grid, for the Gaussian at \(\mu = 1\), with Mironov’s conversion (red) and the improved one (blue). Dots mark the best order of each. The dashed line is the exact \(\varepsilon\), and the grey curve is the RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\) that both conversions add to.



Table 30.6 shows how the best order moves over four settings. In the first row, for instance, \(\rho = 1/(2\cdot 100) = 0.005\), and Mironov’s best order is \(1 + \sqrt{\ln(10^5)/0.005} = 1 + \sqrt{2302.6} = 48.985\); the improved conversion’s extra \(\ln\alpha\) brings it down to 40.525.
