title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.2 Every accountant on one run

37.2.1 Context
This is the question the part has built up to: for DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and up to \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, compute \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) with every accountant, and see what choosing a loose one costs. Amplification by subsampling and Numerical accounting each computed some of these numbers. This section puts them in one table, adds the optimal conversion of an RDP curve, and says for each accountant what it assumes and whether it is a bound.


37.2.2 Statement
All accountants start from the same object: what one step of DP-SGD reveals about one record. Look at the noisy gradient sum along the direction of that record’s clipped gradient, and measure it in units of the clipping norm \(C\). Without the record, the output is pure noise, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\). With the record, the record is in the batch with probability \(q\), and then its gradient shifts the output by 1; otherwise it is absent and the output is the same noise. So the output is the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The accountants differ in what they keep of this pair and how they combine \(T\) copies of it. Here they are, each with where it was derived:

Per step, then composition (Amplification by subsampling, Section 33.7). First find an \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) guarantee for one Gaussian step on its own. Then use subsampling: because the record is missing from the batch with probability \(1 - q\), the factor \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) by which it can change a probability is diluted to \(1 + q(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1)\), which is Equation 33.5, \(\varepsilon_1 = \ln(1 + q(e^{\varepsilon_0} - 1))\). Finally compose \(T\) steps, either by basic composition, where the \(\varepsilon\)’s simply add to \(T\varepsilon_1\), or by advanced composition, which grows like \(\sqrt T\) at the price of an extra \(\delta'\).
RDP, Mironov’s conversion (Rényi DP). RDP describes one step by a curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) between the two output distributions; for the subsampled Gaussian it is Equation 33.9. Its appeal is that curves of composed steps simply add, so \(T\) steps have curve \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\). To get back to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), Mironov’s conversion uses the fact that \(\delta\) is at most the chance that the privacy loss \(L\) (defined in item 6) exceeds \(\varepsilon\). The curve fixes the moment \(\mathbb E[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}] = e^{(\alpha - 1)T\varepsilon(\alpha)}\), so Markov’s inequality gives \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le e^{(\alpha - 1)(T\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}\). Setting the right side equal to \(\delta\) and solving gives, at each order, \(\varepsilon = T\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\), and the conversion takes the best order: \(\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\big[T\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\big]\).
RDP, improved conversion (From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) and to tests, Equation 30.7). The same curve, converted with a sharper analysis of the same tail (Balle et al. 2020) that saves a fixed amount at each order: \(\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\big[T\,\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}\alpha - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\big]\).
RDP, optimal conversion (Section 30.5). The best any conversion of the curve can do: the smallest \(\varepsilon\) that every pair of distributions with the curve \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\) satisfies at \(\delta\).
GDP central-limit approximation (f-DP and Gaussian DP, Equation 32.17). A mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP if telling its two output distributions apart is no easier than telling \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The privacy loss of \(T\) steps is a sum of \(T\) small losses, so by the central limit theorem it is close to Gaussian, and the approximation treats the run as \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\). It then reads \(\varepsilon\) off the exact \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) curve of a \(\mu\)-GDP mechanism, Equation 32.10.
PLD, pessimistic and optimistic (Numerical accounting, Equation 34.6). The privacy loss at an output \(y\) is the log of how much more likely \(y\) is on one of the two neighbouring datasets than on the other, and its distribution over outputs is the PLD. Each order of the pair gives its own PLD: the remove direction puts the dataset with the record first, so the loss measures how much more likely \(y\) is with the record than without it, and the add direction puts it second. Under composition the losses add, so the PLD of \(T\) steps is the \(T\)-fold convolution of one step’s PLD, which a computer does quickly with the fast Fourier transform (FFT). The convolution needs the loss on a grid, here of width \(h = 10^{-5}\). Rounding every loss up gives the pessimistic PLD, rounding it down the optimistic one. Solve each for \(\varepsilon\), and take the larger of the add and remove directions, since the guarantee must hold whichever of the two datasets has the record (each direction’s pair dominates its case, as Section L.2 in the appendices proves).

37.2.3 Derivation: what each accountant assumes, and why it is a bound
Every row of Table 37.2 assumes the same model of the training run: Poisson sampling at rate \(q\), add/remove neighbours (the two datasets differ by one record being present or absent), per-example clipping to norm \(C\) and Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) on the summed gradients, and every intermediate noisy gradient released. Under that model, one step is the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian pair of the statement, \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), in units of \(C\) (Amplification by subsampling). The accountants differ only in what they keep of this pair, and each step below says whether what is kept still gives a proof.

Per step, then composition: an upper bound. One step is \((\varepsilon_1, q\delta_0)\)-DP by the amplification theorem (Section 33.3), and basic and advanced composition hold even when each step is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs, which is how SGD works (Composition). So the result is a proof. It is very loose because each step’s whole privacy loss distribution is replaced by just two numbers, \(\varepsilon_1\) and \(q\delta_0\), and composition has to assume the worst distribution consistent with them at every step.
RDP with Mironov’s or the improved conversion: an upper bound. Three facts make this a proof. The subsampled curve Equation 33.9 is the exact Rényi divergence of the pair, not an estimate. RDP curves add under adaptive composition (Equation 29.10), because the Rényi divergence is the log of a moment of the likelihood ratio, and the moment of a product of independent factors is the product of their moments. And both conversions are proved for every pair with the curve (Section 30.3, Section 30.4). The accountant evaluates the curve only on a grid of orders, and minimizing over fewer orders can only give a larger \(\varepsilon\), so the grid costs tightness, never validity.
RDP with the optimal conversion: an upper bound. It computes the largest \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) over all pairs of distributions with the given RDP curve. The real pair has that curve, so it is in the set, and its \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is no larger than the maximum (Section 30.5). The same argument shows it is the tightest bound any accountant that sees only the curve can give: some pair in the set attains the maximum, and such an accountant cannot tell that pair from the real one.
The GDP central-limit approximation: not a bound. Equation 32.17 comes from two approximations (Section 32.8). It is a limit as \(T \to \infty\) with \(q\sqrt T\) held fixed, and it uses a second-order expansion of the per-step loss, keeping its mean and variance and dropping the rest. Neither step comes with an error bound in the tail of the loss distribution, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is read exactly there: it asks about the chance of a rare, large loss, which is where a Gaussian approximation is least reliable.
The pessimistic PLD: an upper bound; the optimistic PLD: a lower bound. Rounding every loss up describes a pair that leaks at least as much as the real one (a dominating pair), and composing two dominating pairs gives a dominating pair, so the rounding error keeps its sign through all \(T\) convolutions. Rounding down does the same in the other direction. So \(\delta^\downarrow(\varepsilon) \le \delta(\varepsilon) \le \delta^\uparrow(\varepsilon)\) for every \(\varepsilon\) (Equation 34.6). The upper bound holds under adaptive composition of the fixed per-step pair (Section K.3 in the appendices proves it). How far apart are the two? Each step’s loss moves by less than one grid width \(h\) between rounding down and rounding up, so after \(T\) steps the two composed losses differ by at most \(Th\), and so do the \(\varepsilon\)’s they give, as long as no tail is truncated (Section 34.5). Here \(Th = 10{,}000 \times 10^{-5} = 0.1\).

Steps 2, 3 and 5 put the bounds in two orders, which together read \[\varepsilon_{\text{RDP, Mironov}} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{RDP, improved}} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{RDP, optimal}} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{true}}, \qquad \varepsilon_{\text{PLD}}^{\uparrow} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{true}} \;\ge\; \varepsilon_{\text{PLD}}^{\downarrow}. \tag{37.1}\] The second chain is the sandwich of step 5. In the first chain, the last inequality is step 3. Mironov’s conversion is above the improved one because at every order the improved one is smaller by \(\Delta(\alpha) = \frac{\ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1} + \ln\frac{\alpha}{\alpha - 1} > 0\) (Equation 30.10); both terms are positive for \(\alpha > 1\), and if one expression is above another at every order, its minimum over the grid is above too. The improved conversion is above the optimal one because the optimal one is, by definition, the smallest \(\varepsilon\) valid for every pair with the curve, and the improved one is one such valid \(\varepsilon\).
The theory does not order the two chains against each other. You might expect the RDP bounds to always sit above the PLD upper bound, because RDP throws away information. But the pessimistic PLD describes a rounded-up pair, not the real one, and its \(\varepsilon\) may exceed the truth by up to \(Th\). A bound from the curve alone that came very close to the truth could therefore fall below it. Without truncation, all that follows is \(\varepsilon_{\text{RDP, optimal}} \ge \varepsilon_{\text{true}} \ge \varepsilon^\uparrow_{\text{PLD}} - Th\). On the running example the script checks both chains at all nine values of \(T\) from 1 to 10,000. It also finds RDP optimal \(\ge\) PLD upper at every one of them, because the curve slack (at least 0.2677, from Table 37.4 below) is far larger than \(Th\) (at most 0.1000). That is an observation about this example, not a theorem. The script also checks that the CLT value is below the PLD lower bound at every \(T\).


37.2.4 Interpretation
Figure 37.1 plots the table on a log scale, with each accountant’s ratio to the PLD upper bound beside it. Table 37.3 lists the ratios. Since the PLD upper bound is within \(Th\) of the truth, a ratio well above 1 measures how much an accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\), and a ratio below the PLD lower column means the number is not a valid guarantee.

Per-step composition is useless beyond a handful of steps. It is the right answer only at \(T = 1\), where there is nothing to compose and basic composition is just the amplified one-step guarantee. At \(T = 10{,}000\) it is off by a factor of over a thousand, because adding \(\varepsilon\)’s assumes every step leaks its worst case, while in reality the losses of different steps mostly cancel. Advanced composition is worse than basic here, for the reason given in Section 33.7. Its bound is \(\varepsilon_1\sqrt{2T\ln(1/\delta')} + T\varepsilon_1(e^{\varepsilon_1} - 1)\): a \(\sqrt T\) term with a large constant (at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), \(\sqrt{2\ln(10^5)} \approx 4.80\)), plus a term that still grows like \(T\). The \(\sqrt T\) only wins when \(\varepsilon_1\) is so small that the second term is negligible, and the amplified per-step \(\varepsilon_1\) is too large for that.
RDP is a safe bound, and its slack has two sources. RDP with the improved conversion exceeds the PLD upper bound for two separate reasons, and Table 37.4 splits the excess accordingly. The first is the conversion: turning the curve into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair with the improved formula loses against the best possible conversion of the same curve, and that loss is improved minus optimal. The second is the curve itself: even the best conversion of the curve is above the PLD, because the curve keeps only a family of moments of the privacy loss, not its whole distribution, and that loss is optimal minus PLD upper.
Conversion slack dominates short runs. At \(T = 1\) the conversion loses 0.4656 of the 0.7561 excess. The reason is the term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) in the conversion (about \(11.5/(\alpha - 1)\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), which you pay however small the curve is. When the curve is tiny, as after one step, this fixed toll is most of the answer.
Curve slack dominates long runs. After many steps the curve \(T\,\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is large, the best order moves up, and the fixed toll shrinks in comparison. From \(T = 1000\) on, the conversion slack is negligible (0.0005 at \(T = 1000\), zero to four decimals at \(T = 10{,}000\)), and almost all the slack is in the curve. That last 7.6% at \(T = 10{,}000\) is what only a numerical accountant removes, because only it keeps the whole distribution.
The CLT under-reports here. It is below the certified lower bound at every \(T\): at \(T = 10{,}000\), 6.0071 against 6.1377. Its ratio climbs toward 1 as \(T\) grows, as a central limit theorem should, since a sum of more terms is closer to Gaussian. But at no \(T\) in the table is it a valid guarantee.
The PLD bracket is the truth, to within \(Th\). At \(T = 10{,}000\) the width is \(6.2377 - 6.1377 = 0.1000\) on this grid, exactly \(Th\). If that is too wide, refine \(h\). Its only other error, truncating the far tails of the loss, is pushed in the safe direction on each side (mass is moved so that the upper bound only rises and the lower bound only falls), so \(h\) is the one knob to turn.

37.2.5 Example: the number you would have reported
Suppose you ran 1,000 steps. Depending on the accountant, your paper says \(\varepsilon = 2.54\) (RDP with Mironov’s conversion, as in older code), 2.10 (RDP with the improved conversion, as in Opacus’s RDP accountant), 1.83 (a PLD accountant), or 1.62 (the CLT). The first three are true statements about the run, because each is an upper bound; the third is the most informative, because it is the smallest. The fourth is false: the optimistic PLD proves \(\varepsilon \ge 1.8232\), so the true \(\varepsilon\) is larger than 1.62 and the run is not \((1.62, 10^{-5})\)-DP.


37.2.6 Check yourself

At \(T = 1\), per-step basic composition gives 0.20 and RDP gives 0.9555. Does that make the RDP accountant wrong? (No. Both are upper bounds, and the basic one happens to be tighter for a single step, because RDP’s conversion pays \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) even when the curve is tiny. RDP wins as soon as there is something to compose.)
Why can the optimal conversion of an RDP curve never beat the pessimistic PLD by more than \(Th\)? (It must cover every pair with the same RDP curve, and the real pair is one of them, so it is at least the true \(\varepsilon\). The pessimistic PLD is at most \(Th\) above the true \(\varepsilon\). So the optimal conversion can fall below the PLD upper bound, but by at most \(Th\) (without truncation). Here the curve slack is much larger than \(Th\), and the script finds optimal \(\ge\) PLD upper at every \(T\).)

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
section: 37.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε
text:
37.3 The inverse problem: noise for a target ε

37.3.1 Context
Practitioners rarely compute \(\varepsilon\) after the fact. They fix a budget, say \(\varepsilon = 3\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), fix the number of steps and the batch size, and ask how much noise they must add. The noise multiplier is then the knob that sets utility. The noise added to the gradient sum has standard deviation \(\sigma C\), and the sum is divided by the expected batch size \(qn\) for \(n\) records, so the noise in the averaged gradient has standard deviation \(\sigma C/(qn)\). A loose accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\) at every \(\sigma\), so it asks for a larger \(\sigma\) to meet the same budget: its slack turns directly into extra noise.


37.3.2 Statement
For each accountant \(A\), write \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma)\) for the \(\varepsilon\) it reports at \(\delta\) for the run with noise multiplier \(\sigma\). The noise it requires for a target \(\varepsilon^*\) is the smallest \(\sigma\) at which its reported \(\varepsilon\) meets the target: \[\sigma_A(\varepsilon^*) = \min\{\sigma > 0 : \varepsilon_A(\sigma) \le \varepsilon^*\}. \tag{37.2}\] Table 37.5 gives it for \(T = 10{,}000\), \(q = 0.01\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and three targets.



Table 37.5: The noise multiplier \(\sigma\) each accountant requires for a target \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), with \(T = 10{,}000\) steps at \(q = 0.01\). PLD on the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\); the PLD lower column is the \(\sigma\) at which the optimistic bound reaches the target.














Target \(\varepsilon\)
Advanced
RDP, Mironov
RDP, improved

37.3.3 Derivation
The plan is to show that more noise never raises any accountant’s \(\varepsilon\), so that Equation 37.2 asks for the point where a decreasing function crosses a level, and then to find that point numerically.

Every bound decreases in \(\sigma\). The idea is that a noisier run can be produced from a less noisy one without touching the data, and that cannot reveal more. Fix \(\sigma < \sigma'\). (a) Post-processing: the variances of independent Gaussians add, so adding independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma'^2 - \sigma^2)\) noise to the output of the step with noise \(\sigma\) gives exactly the step with noise \(\sigma'\), in both runs and in every step. That map does not look at the data. (b) Data processing: the data-processing inequality (Divergences) says that passing two distributions through the same data-independent map can only make them harder to tell apart, so every divergence between them can only fall. That applies to the per-step and the composed pair, and to both the Rényi divergences and the hockey-stick divergence that defines \(\delta(\varepsilon)\). Every accountant is built from those divergences, so its \(\varepsilon\) falls too. For the discretized PLD this holds only up to grid effects of order \(Th\), since rounding can move a value by up to that much. The CLT’s \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) falls in \(\sigma\) directly, because \(e^{1/\sigma^2}\) does.
So Equation 37.2 is a root of a decreasing function, \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma) - \varepsilon^*\), and any bracketing method finds it: start from a low \(\sigma\) where the function is positive and a high one where it is negative, and shrink the interval while keeping the sign change inside. The script uses false position with the Illinois modification. False position places each new guess where the straight line through the two ends crosses zero, rather than at the midpoint as bisection does. The Illinois modification halves the function value kept at an end that has not moved for two rounds, which stops one end from getting stuck. It needs only a handful of evaluations. That matters for the PLD, where each evaluation is two FFT compositions of 10,000 steps. The script stops when the bracket is narrower than \(10^{-4}\) and returns the upper end, where \(\varepsilon_A \le \varepsilon^*\). The method does not need exact monotonicity for this. Up to discretization, the returned \(\sigma\) may not be the minimum in Equation 37.2, but it was checked to satisfy \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma) \le \varepsilon^*\), which is all safety needs. For an upper-bound accountant the returned \(\sigma\) is therefore safe.
The bracket for the PLD comes from the other accountants. The RDP value serves as the upper end: RDP was above the PLD upper bound at every \(T\) in Table 37.2, so it should need more noise, though the theory does not guarantee it (Equation 37.1). Ninety percent of the smaller of the RDP and CLT values serves as the lower end. Because neither end is guaranteed, the solver checks that the two ends really bracket the root, with the function positive at one end and negative at the other, and stops with an error if they do not.
The CLT has a closed form. First find the \(\mu^*\) whose GDP curve Equation 32.10 gives \(\varepsilon^*\) at \(\delta\). Then solve \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) for \(\sigma\): squaring gives \(q^2T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1) = \mu^{*2}\), so \(e^{1/\sigma^2} = 1 + \mu^{*2}/(q^2T)\), and taking logs and square roots, \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{\ln(1 + \mu^{*2}/(q^2T))}\).

As a check, the RDP column reproduces \(\sigma = 4.126\) for \(\varepsilon = 1\) from Exercise 4 of Amplification by subsampling, and the PLD upper bound at \(\sigma = 3.9884\) is 1.0000, as the solution of \(\varepsilon_A(\sigma) = 1\) should give.


37.3.4 Interpretation
Figure 37.2 shows each accountant’s \(\sigma\) relative to the PLD upper bound’s, the tightest certified one.
Advanced composition needs six times the noise. It asks for 6.19 to 6.63 times the \(\sigma\) of the PLD (\(24.682/3.988 \approx 6.19\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(10.505/1.584 \approx 6.63\) at \(\varepsilon = 3\)), a noise level at which DP-SGD rarely trains a useful model.
The RDP conversions cost a few percent of noise. Mironov’s conversion costs 8.6 to 24.7% more noise, most at the strictest target, where its fixed \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) toll is the largest share of a small \(\varepsilon\). RDP with the improved conversion costs 3.4 to 4.9% more noise. This is the \(\sigma\)-side image of the 7.6% \(\varepsilon\)-excess in Table 37.4, and it is smaller because \(\varepsilon\) falls faster than \(\sigma\) rises: in this range a small relative increase in \(\sigma\) buys a larger relative decrease in \(\varepsilon\), so closing a gap in \(\varepsilon\) costs a smaller gap in \(\sigma\). Seen from the other side, at \(\sigma = 0.8851\), where the PLD certifies \(\varepsilon = 8\), the RDP accountant reports 8.6330.
The CLT asks for less noise than the certified bound needs, 2.0 to 4.8% less. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) this is provably too little: at the CLT’s \(\sigma = 0.8676\) the optimistic PLD, a lower bound on the true \(\varepsilon\), already gives 8.2594, so the run is not \((8, 10^{-5})\)-DP. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 3 the grid is too coarse to tell. At the CLT’s \(\sigma\) the PLD bracket is \([0.9550, 1.0550]\) and \([2.9938, 3.0938]\), and both contain the target, so the truth could be on either side.
The sandwich width matters most at small targets. The width \(Th = 0.1\) is a fixed amount of \(\varepsilon\), and it is 10% of \(\varepsilon = 1\), so the PLD brackets \(\sigma\) only to \([3.654, 3.988]\). For a tight \(\sigma\) at a small target, refine \(h\).






Figure 37.2: For each target \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) (\(T = 10{,}000\), \(q = 0.01\)), the noise multiplier each accountant requires, divided by the one the PLD upper bound requires. RDP with Mironov’s conversion asks for up to 25% more noise and RDP with the improved conversion about 4% more. The CLT and the PLD lower bound fall in the shaded region: they ask for less noise than any certified accountant can justify. Advanced composition (6.19 to 6.63) is off the chart.





37.3.5 Example: what 4% of noise is worth
With \(n = 50{,}000\) records and \(q = 0.01\), the expected batch holds \(0.01 \times 50{,}000 = 500\) records. At \(\varepsilon = 8\), the RDP accountant sets \(\sigma = 0.917\), so the averaged gradient carries noise of standard deviation \(0.917C/500\). The PLD accountant sets \(\sigma = 0.885\): the RDP accountant asks for 3.6% more noise for the same certified budget (the ratio 1.036 in Figure 37.2). The same budget, with a tighter accountant, buys a less noisy model. In the other direction, the PLD lets you keep \(\sigma\) and train longer; the exercises quantify that.


37.3.6 Check yourself

Why does the script return the upper end of the final bracket rather than its midpoint? (The upper end is a \(\sigma\) at which the accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) was checked to be at most the target. For an upper-bound accountant that \(\sigma\) certifiably meets the budget; the midpoint might not.)
A colleague calibrates \(\sigma\) with the CLT and then reports the \(\varepsilon\) of the PLD upper bound at that \(\sigma\). Is their report valid? (Yes. The reported number comes from a bound, so it is valid. It is just above the target they meant to meet: 8.3594 instead of 8 at the \(\varepsilon = 8\) target.)

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.4 Where each accountant is tight

37.4.1 Context
DP-SGD is one mechanism. You will also release statistics with the Gaussian mechanism, answer queries with pure-DP mechanisms (those with \(\delta = 0\)), shuffle locally randomized reports, or stop training adaptively. The ranking of accountants changes with the mechanism, because what makes an accountant tight is whether the summary it keeps describes that mechanism’s privacy loss exactly. This section collects, from the earlier chapters of this part, which accountant is tight for which mechanism, and puts numbers on three of the rows.


37.4.2 Statement
Table 37.6 is the decision table.



Table 37.6: Which accountant to use for which mechanism, with the chapter or section that establishes it.





Mechanism
Use
Why, and how tight
Avoid




Gaussian, no subsampling (any number of steps, any sensitivity mix)
GDP or zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP), converted exactly with Equation 32.10
\(\mu^2\) adds and the Gaussian profile is exact (f-DP and Gaussian DP). RDP and zCDP keep the curve exactly but the conversion loses 5 to 10% (Section 30.7)
Per-step \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) composition


Poisson-subsampled Gaussian (DP-SGD)
PLD, pessimistic, with the optimistic value as error bar
Certified bracket of width \(Th\) (Numerical accounting). RDP with the improved conversion is 7.6 to 69% above it on the running example for \(T \ge 100\)
zCDP, which cannot express amplification (Section 31.8); the CLT as a guarantee


Pure-DP steps (randomized response, Laplace, exponential mechanism)
PLD (exact for finite outputs), or RDP with the mechanism’s own curve
The privacy loss takes few values, so the PLD is exact or nearly so. zCDP with \(\rho = \varepsilon^2/2\) is convenient but loose for large \(\varepsilon\) (Section 31.4)
Advanced composition when a tighter accountant is available


Adaptive choice of noise, stopping or per-record budgets
RDP filter at a fixed order (Adaptive composition)
Free at a fixed order (Section 36.5); an odometer costs a union bound over orders
Plugging realized \(\varepsilon_t\) into a fixed-parameter theorem

The closed-form clone bound is 4.47 to 7.55 times the exact value there
The Poisson-subsampling accountant

Amplification by iteration (Amplification by shuffling and by iteration)
Needs a convex, smooth loss, contractive steps and no released checkpoints; rarely applies to deep learning
Any hidden-state claim for non-convex training








37.4.3 Derivation: three rows with numbers
The script computes three rows at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one where the composed loss is exactly Gaussian, one where it takes only a few values, and the DP-SGD case where it is neither.

Gaussian without subsampling. A Gaussian step with sensitivity 1 and noise multiplier \(\sigma\) is exactly \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = 1/\sigma\), and under composition the squares of \(\mu\) add, just as variances of independent Gaussians do (f-DP and Gaussian DP). So one hundred steps with \(\sigma = 10\) compose to \(\mu = \sqrt{100 \times (1/10)^2} = \sqrt{100}/10 = 1\). The exact \(\varepsilon\) from Equation 32.10 is 4.3772. RDP’s curve for this run, \(\alpha\mu^2/2\), is also exact, but converting it costs: it gives 4.7285 with the improved conversion, 8.0% above, and 5.2985 with Mironov’s. Here zCDP, which describes the curve by a line \(\rho\alpha\), is the same as RDP, because the curve already is a line.
Pure DP: one hundred steps of randomized response with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\). In randomized response each output is \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\) times more likely under one dataset than the other, in one direction or the other, so its privacy loss is \(\pm\varepsilon_0\). The composed loss is \(\varepsilon_0\) times (number of \(+\) steps minus number of \(-\) steps), so the composed PLD is a binomial and the exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is a finite sum (Numerical accounting). The exact \(\varepsilon\) is 4.3068. RDP with the exact randomized-response curve gives 4.6154. zCDP needs a \(\rho\) with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\); the smallest that works for randomized response is \(\varepsilon_0\tanh(\varepsilon_0/2)\) per step, which is also the sharp charge every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP mechanism satisfies (Equation 31.7 in Concentrated DP), and it gives 4.7263. Advanced composition with \(\delta' = \delta\) gives 5.8502, and basic composition \(100 \times 0.1 = 10.0000\).
The subsampled Gaussian at \(T = 10{,}000\). From Table 37.2, the PLD brackets \(\varepsilon\) in \([6.1377, 6.2377]\), RDP (improved) gives 6.7127, 7.6% above the upper bound, and the CLT gives 6.0071, below the bracket.



37.4.4 Interpretation
The more structure the accountant keeps, the tighter it is. The ranking in each row follows the ladder of the part’s introduction. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair keeps two numbers, zCDP one line, RDP a whole curve, GDP the whole trade-off function (the best type II error of any test at each type I error) when that function is Gaussian, and the PLD the entire distribution of the privacy loss. Each rung loses information the next one keeps, and lost information has to be filled in with a worst case.
The right tool depends on what is Gaussian. When the composed pair is exactly Gaussian, as in the first row, GDP is exact and costs nothing. When subsampling makes it a mixture, as in DP-SGD, no closed form is exact, and only the PLD is both certified and tight.
Adaptivity is the one place where RDP is the natural tool. If the noise or the stopping time is chosen while training runs, based on what has been released, the per-step pair is not fixed in advance. The Rényi filter of Section 36.5 handles that and loses nothing at a fixed order, whereas the PLD accountant above assumes the per-step pair is fixed in advance. The references of Adaptive composition include filters built on GDP and PLDs (Koskela, Tobaben & Honkela 2023) for when the RDP slack matters.


37.4.5 Example: an analytics pipeline
A team releases 100 noisy counts with the Gaussian mechanism at \(\sigma = 10\) and reports \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\), from an old RDP accountant with Mironov’s conversion. The same release is exactly \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP, as GDP shows. The reported number is 21.0% above the truth (\(5.2985/4.3772 \approx 1.210\)): the team could have answered more queries, or added less noise, at no cost in privacy.


37.4.6 Check yourself

For the randomized-response row, why is the PLD exact rather than a bracket? (The privacy loss takes only the values \(\pm\varepsilon_0\), so the composed loss lies on the lattice \(\{(2j - k)\varepsilon_0\}\), where \(j\) is the number of \(+\) steps, and no rounding is needed; \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is a finite binomial sum.)
Why is zCDP the wrong accountant for DP-SGD even though it is exact for the Gaussian? (The ratio \(\varepsilon(\alpha)/\alpha\) of the subsampled curve tends to \(1/(2\sigma^2)\) as \(\alpha\) grows, so the smallest \(\rho\) with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for all \(\alpha\) is the unsubsampled \(1/(2\sigma^2)\), even though the curve is far below that line at small orders. zCDP cannot express the amplification. See Section 31.8.)

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
section: 37.5 Matching the accountant to the code
text:
37.5 Matching the accountant to the code

37.5.1 Context
Every number in Table 37.2 assumes a model of the training run. The accountant cannot check that model against your code: it takes \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) and trusts that the code does what the theorem assumes. Ponomareva et al. (2023, Section 5.3.1) put the point in one heading: “privacy accounting assumptions should match training reality”. They note that many papers have reported the Poisson-sampling number while training with shuffled fixed-size batches, going back to Abadi et al. (2016). A mismatch does not make the number a little loose. It makes it a statement about a different algorithm.


37.5.2 Statement
Before reporting \(\varepsilon\), check each item of Table 37.7 against the code.



Table 37.7: A checklist for matching the accountant to the training code.











Item
What the accountant assumes
What to check in the code
If it does not match




Sampling scheme
Poisson sampling at rate \(q\)
Is each record included independently with probability \(q\), giving variable batch sizes?
Fixed-size random batches: account the Poisson pair with \(\sigma/2\) (Table 33.4). Shuffle and partition: no amplification theorem applies; report the guarantee without amplification, for zero-out neighbours


Neighbouring relation
Add/remove one record
Is the guarantee stated for add/remove, replace-one or zero-out?
Replace-one under Poisson sampling costs more per step: the group-privacy bound is about \(e^\varepsilon + 1\) times the add/remove value, and the exact pure-DP cost is about twice it for small \(\varepsilon\) (Section 33.4, Equation 33.8)


Privacy unit
One example
Can one person contribute several examples?
Account for users: clip and sample per user, or pay group privacy


Released outputs
Every noisy gradient
Are checkpoints, logs or gradients exposed?
Nothing to fix: the guarantee covers them all. Claiming less leakage needs Section 35.6 and its conditions


Hyperparameter tuning
Not counted
Were learning rate, clipping norm or \(\sigma\) chosen by looking at results on the private data?
Account for the tuning runs too, or tune on public data


Adaptive parameters
\(\sigma\), \(q\) and \(T\) fixed in advance
Early stopping, noise schedules, per-record budgets?
Use a filter (Section 36.5)


Implementation
Exact real-valued Gaussian noise, exact clipping
Floating-point noise sampling, gradient accumulation across devices, clipping applied before or after accumulation
Out of scope of the accountant: a question for the implementation and its verification, not for this part








37.5.3 Derivation: the price of three mismatches

Fixed-size batches accounted as Poisson. Suppose each step draws a fresh random batch of exactly \(qn\) records. With a fixed batch size, adding a record has to push another one out, so in effect one record is swapped for another, and the batch sum can move by up to \(2C\) instead of \(C\). Lebeda et al. (2024, Proposition 9; Table 33.4) show that such a run is covered by the Poisson pair with noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\): the same noise, measured against a shift twice as large. At \(T = 10{,}000\) the RDP accountant then gives 47.42 instead of 6.71, as in Amplification by subsampling, and the PLD upper bound gives 43.42 instead of 6.24.
Shuffle and partition. Here each epoch shuffles the data once and cuts it into consecutive batches, so the record is used exactly once per epoch, and there is no amplification theorem that holds for every dataset (Section 33.4). What remains certain is the composition of the record’s own steps, one per epoch, for zero-out neighbours, the relation of Table 33.4 for this sampler: the two datasets differ in that the record’s gradient is replaced by zero, so the batch that holds it moves by at most \(C\) in each epoch. With noise \(\sigma C\), that is a Gaussian mechanism with \(\mu = 1/\sigma\). Then 100 epochs at \(\sigma = 1\) are 100 Gaussian mechanisms with \(\mu = 1\), whose squares add to \(\mu = \sqrt{100} = 10\) (Section 32.6), so Equation 32.10 gives \(\varepsilon = 91.8173\). This needs the zero-out relation. Under add/remove there is no clean bound at all, because inserting a record shifts the fixed partition into batches and changes every batch after it. Under replace-one, the batch sum moves by up to \(2C\), so \(\mu = 2\) per epoch, \(\mu = \sqrt{100} \times 2 = 20\) in total, and \(\varepsilon = 284.39\). Ponomareva et al. recommend reporting such a guarantee without amplification whenever the sampling assumption does not hold.
Tuning on the private data. If you train 10 configurations on the private data and release the best, which one is best depends on all 10 runs, so the release is a post-processing of all 10 of them, and its privacy cost is that of the 10 runs composed, ten times the run. With RDP, ten times the curve converts to \(\varepsilon = 27.23\); for 100 configurations, 145.17. Papernot & Steinke (2022) give much better bounds for tuning procedures that try a random number of configurations. NIST SP 800-226 (Section 4.3) recommends tuning on non-sensitive data, or with a differentially private algorithm.



37.5.4 Interpretation
The sampling scheme is the largest single risk. A factor of 6.96 in \(\varepsilon\) (\(43.42/6.24 \approx 6.96\)) from a one-line change in the data loader is more than the choice between the RDP and PLD accountants (at most 1.19 here, from Table 37.3). Opacus, for one, uses Poisson sampling by default when you make a model private.
The privacy unit decides what is protected. The guarantee is about datasets that differ in one unit, so it protects one unit. NIST SP 800-226 (Section 2.4) calls a guarantee whose unit is one event, when a person contributes many, a privacy hazard. Example-level DP-SGD on a dataset with many examples per user protects each example, not each user.
The accountant does not see the implementation. The theorems assume exact real-valued Gaussian noise. Floating-point sampling of noise can break the guarantee of a mechanism that is correct on paper (NIST SP 800-226, Section 4.3). That is a question for formal methods and careful implementation, not for an accountant.


37.5.5 Example: a code review
A training script uses a DataLoader with shuffle=True and batch_size=500 on 50,000 records for 100 epochs, and calls an RDP accountant with sample_rate=0.01. The checklist flags the first row. The sampler is shuffle and partition, so the Poisson accountant’s 6.71 does not apply. The certified guarantee is the unamplified 91.8173, for zero-out neighbours. Switching the loader to Poisson sampling, a change of a few lines, makes the accountant’s assumptions true and the guarantee 6.24 with a PLD accountant.


37.5.6 Check yourself

Your code draws fixed-size random batches, and you want the Poisson accountant’s 6.24 to be honest. What noise multiplier must you train with? (Twice the one in the accountant: \(\sigma = 2\), since fixed-size batches are dominated by the Poisson pair with \(\sigma/2\), and \(2/2 = 1\) is the \(\sigma\) the accountant used.)
Does releasing every checkpoint of a DP-SGD run cost extra privacy? (No. The accountant already assumes every noisy gradient is released, and checkpoints are a post-processing of them.)

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.6 What to report

37.6.1 Context
An \(\varepsilon\) without its assumptions cannot be checked, compared or even read: the same number means different things for one example or one user, with or without tuning, at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) or \(10^{-10}\). Two guidance documents say what a statement should contain. NIST SP 800-226, “Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees” (Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth, March 2025), is written for anyone evaluating a DP claim. Ponomareva et al., “How to DP-fy ML” (JAIR 2023), Section 5.3.3, is written for machine learning.


37.6.2 Statement
From Ponomareva et al. (2023, Section 5.3.3), a report should give:

The DP setting: central or local, and who is trusted.
The instantiated definition: which data accesses are covered (one training run, or tuning too), what the mechanism’s output is, the unit of privacy, and the neighbouring relation.
Accounting details: the type of accounting (RDP, PLD, …), its assumptions and whether they hold, and the formal statement, such as the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) or \(\rho\) values, for the final model and for the tuning.
Transparency: code, when possible, using standard libraries for the mechanism and the accountant.

On \(\delta\), both documents want it small compared with \(1/n\) for \(n\) units of privacy. The reason is that \(\delta\) is the probability with which the promise may fail. A mechanism that publishes one randomly chosen record in full changes its output distribution by only about \(1/n\) when one record changes, so it meets a \(\delta\) of about \(1/n\) with \(\varepsilon = 0\), and yet it exposes someone completely. A \(\delta\) near \(1/n\) therefore allows guarantees that protect nobody. Ponomareva et al. (Section 5.3.2) give the convention \(\delta \ll 1/n\), for example \(\delta = n^{-1.1}\), with \(n\) counted in units of privacy. NIST SP 800-226 (Section 2.3) gives \(\delta \le 1/n^2\) as a common recommendation, calls values above \(10^{-5}\) suspicious, and asks you to report the original parameters of an RDP, zCDP or GDP guarantee alongside any \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) conversion, so that others can interpret it more precisely.
For DP-SGD, add what the accountant needs to recompute \(\varepsilon\): the sampling scheme, \(q\) (or batch size and \(n\)), \(T\) (or epochs), \(\sigma\), and the accountant’s version and discretization. Report the clipping norm \(C\) too, although \(\varepsilon\) does not depend on it.


37.6.3 Derivation: the numbers in the statement
Take the running example with \(n = 50{,}000\) records. Then the expected batch is \(qn = 500\), \(T = 10{,}000\) steps are \(Tq = 100\) epochs (each step touches a fraction \(q\) of the data), and the conventions give \(1/n = 2.0\times10^{-5}\), \(n^{-1.1} = 6.8\times10^{-6}\) and \(1/n^2 = 4.0\times10^{-10}\). The pessimistic PLD composed for \(T = 10{,}000\) is computed once. Solving it at several \(\delta\) is cheap, because it only means evaluating \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) on the same composed distribution, and Table 37.8 gives the result.



Table 37.8: The running example’s privacy profile: \(\varepsilon\) at several \(\delta\) for \(T = 10{,}000\), \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\).

\(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is half of \(1/n = 2.0\times10^{-5}\) for this dataset, so it does not meet Ponomareva et al.’s “much smaller than \(1/n\)”. At \(1/n^2\), as NIST suggests, the certified \(\varepsilon\) rises to 9.0502.
The PLD bracket has width 0.1000, the \(Th = 10{,}000 \times 10^{-5}\) of Numerical accounting, at every \(\delta\) down to \(10^{-6}\), and \(9.0502 - 8.9378 = 0.1124\) at \(1/n^2\), slightly more. Without truncation the width is at most \(Th\) (Section 34.5), so the excess comes from the tails the accountant truncates. Each step’s PLD moves up to \(10^{-15}\) of tail mass on each side, in the safe direction. Over \(10^4\) steps that is of order \(10^4 \times 10^{-15} = 10^{-11}\), a few percent of \(\delta = 4\times10^{-10}\), so it starts to matter only at such a small \(\delta\).
The RDP accountant’s original parameter, the thing NIST asks you to report, is its curve. At the best order \(\alpha = 4.1\) the composed curve is \(\varepsilon(4.1) = 3.7336\), which the improved conversion turns into 6.7127.


37.6.4 Interpretation
Report the profile, not a point. A single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair cannot be converted to a smaller \(\delta\) (Exercise 3), because many different mechanisms share that one pair and they behave differently at smaller \(\delta\). So a reader who wants \(\delta = 1/n^2\) needs either the PLD or the RDP curve, or your table. Table 37.8 costs one line.
Report the accountant’s error bar. For a PLD accountant, the optimistic value says how much the number could still fall. For RDP, nothing does: it has no matching lower bound. That is one more reason to prefer the PLD.
State the fallback. If any item of Table 37.7 is in doubt, give the guarantee that does not rely on it, as Ponomareva et al. recommend for amplification. A reader can then see what holds even in the worst case.


37.6.5 Example: a filled-in privacy statement

Privacy guarantee. The model was trained with DP-SGD in the central model: the training server is trusted to run the code below, and the guarantee covers every intermediate noisy gradient, hence every checkpoint and the final model. Unit of privacy: one training example; each person contributes at most one example. Neighbouring relation: add or remove one example. Training: Poisson sampling with rate \(q = 0.01\) (\(n = 50{,}000\) examples, expected batch size 500), \(T = 10{,}000\) steps (100 epochs), per-example clipping norm \(C = 1\), Gaussian noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\). Accountant: privacy loss distributions, pessimistic discretization on the grid \(h = 10^{-5}\), both add and remove directions (this book’s numerical_accounting.py). Guarantee: \((6.24, 10^{-5})\)-DP and \((9.06, 4.0\times10^{-10})\)-DP. The optimistic discretization gives 6.1377 and 8.9378, so the accountant’s own error is at most 0.1000 and 0.1124. For comparison, the RDP accountant with the improved conversion gives 6.7127 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Not covered: hyperparameters were tuned on a public proxy dataset; no tuning on the private data was performed. If the sampling assumption failed (for example, shuffled fixed-size batches), the guarantee without amplification is \((91.82, 10^{-5})\)-DP for zero-out neighbours (one example’s gradient replaced by zero).

Each number in the statement is in Table 37.8 or Section 37.5. Upper bounds are rounded up, never to the nearest value: 9.0502 becomes 9.06, because 9.05 would be a claim the accountant has not certified.


37.6.6 Check yourself

Why does the statement give the clipping norm even though \(\varepsilon\) does not depend on it? (The noise added is \(\sigma C\), so \(C\) with \(\sigma\) tells a reader the actual noise level and lets them check the implementation. Ponomareva et al. (Section 4.2) note that the common convention is to report \(\sigma\) and \(C\) separately, so that the noise reads as a fraction of the clipping norm and transfers between models.)
A paper reports “\(\varepsilon = 3\)” and nothing else. Name two items without which you cannot interpret it. (Any two of: \(\delta\), the unit of privacy, the neighbouring relation, the sampling scheme, the accountant.)

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.7 Checking your accountant

37.7.1 Context
An accountant is code, and code has bugs. Before you trust a number, whether from your own accountant or a library’s, run checks whose answers you know. A good check is a case where the truth is known exactly, or a property every correct accountant must have.


37.7.2 Statement
Four checks, each run by the script:

Set \(q = 1\) and compare with the closed form. A bound must lie above the exact \(\varepsilon\) of \(T\) full-batch Gaussian steps.
Run the PLD machinery on a pair with a closed form. The PLD bracket for the plain Gaussian must contain the exact \(\varepsilon\).
Check both chains of Equation 37.1 at every \(T\), and that no upper bound falls below the optimistic PLD.
Round-trip \(\delta\). The composed pessimistic PLD, evaluated at its own \(\varepsilon\), must give back the \(\delta\) it was solved at, and its \(\varepsilon\) must increase with \(T\).



37.7.3 Derivation: why each answer is known

\(q = 1\). Without subsampling every record is in every batch, so each step is the plain Gaussian mechanism. That mechanism is exactly \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = 1/\sigma\), and since squares of \(\mu\) add under composition, \(T\) of them are exactly \(\sqrt{T \times (1/\sigma)^2} = \sqrt T/\sigma\)-GDP (Section 32.6). Equation 32.10 then gives the exact \(\varepsilon\), and every upper bound must be at least this.
The plain Gaussian PLD. The same closed form is the truth for the composed Gaussian pair. The pessimistic and optimistic discretizations bracket the truth, and without truncation they are within \(Th\) of each other (Equation 34.6), so the bracket must contain the closed form.
The chains. They were proved above for every correct implementation, so a violation is a bug, not slack.
The round trip. Solving \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \delta\) for \(\varepsilon\) and evaluating \(\delta\) at the solution are inverse operations on the same decreasing profile, so they must give back \(\delta\). For the growth in \(T\): whatever the first \(T\) steps release is part of what the first \(T + 1\) steps release, so the \(T\)-step transcript is obtained from the \((T + 1)\)-step one by dropping the last output. Dropping an output is a data-independent map, so by the data-processing inequality the \(T\)-step pair is no easier to tell apart, and no correct accountant can decrease in \(T\).



37.7.4 Example: the checks on this book’s accountants

For \(\sigma = 1\), \(T = 10\), \(q = 1\): the exact \(\mu\) is \(\sqrt{10}/1 = 3.1623\), and the exact \(\varepsilon\) is 17.8566. The RDP accountant gives 19.0536, above it as a bound must be. The CLT formula, with \(q = 1\), gives \(\mu = \sqrt{10(e - 1)} = 4.1452\) instead of \(3.1623\) and \(\varepsilon = 25.5853\): it fails the check, because its derivation assumes small \(q\) (Section 32.8).
On the plain Gaussian with \(\mu = 1\) and \(T = 10\) at \(h = 10^{-3}\), the PLD bracket \([17.8516, 17.8616]\) contains the closed form 17.8566. Its width is \(10 \times 10^{-3} = 0.01\), which is \(Th\).
Both chains hold on the running example at all nine values of \(T\), and the CLT lies below the PLD lower bound at every one.
Evaluating the composed pessimistic PLD at its own \(\varepsilon\) gives back \(\delta = 1.000\times10^{-5}\), and the PLD upper bound increases with \(T\).



37.7.5 Interpretation: comparing with independent libraries
This book’s accountants use no library, so that every line can be read. Production code should use a maintained one and compare against a second. Three are widely used: Google’s dp_accounting (RDP and PLD accountants), Opacus (RDP, privacy loss random variable (PRV) and GDP accountants; its default is the PRV accountant), and Microsoft’s prv_accountant (Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz 2021), which returns a lower bound, an estimate and an upper bound for \(\varepsilon\). What agreement should you expect?
RDP accountants agree when the grid and the conversion agree. Two RDP accountants differ only in the orders they try and the formula they convert with. Opacus’s default orders are this part’s grid without 128, 256 and 512, and its conversion is the improved one (Balle et al. 2020, Theorem 21). On the running example the best orders lie between 4.1 and 9.9, inside both grids, so the results should agree to the precision of the fractional-order computation. If they differ by about \(\Delta(\alpha)\) of Equation 30.10, the fixed amount by which the improved conversion beats Mironov’s at order \(\alpha\), one of them uses Mironov’s conversion. At order 10 that gap is \(\frac{\ln 10}{9} + \ln\frac{10}{9} = 0.3612\) (Table 30.3).
Fractional orders are a known weak spot. At an integer order the subsampled Gaussian’s RDP is a finite sum, but at a fractional order it needs an infinite series with terms of both signs. dp_accounting 0.6.0 computes it with a series whose negative terms it counts as positive, so it returns a loose upper bound there, not the exact value. Opacus keeps the signs and is exact. Checking the fixed-size-batch value 47.42 of Section 37.5 with dp_accounting 0.6.0 gives 49.43 (computed with that library, not by this book’s scripts). Compare at integer orders, or against Opacus.
PLD and PRV accountants agree within their error bars. Different discretizations give different numbers, but every certified upper bound must lie above the truth and every certified lower bound below it, so every upper bound must lie above every lower bound. If two libraries’ brackets do not overlap, one of them has a bug.
No accountant may fall below a certified lower bound. The optimistic PLD is the referee: any reported upper bound below it, like the CLT’s, is wrong.
A cross-check against the libraries, run outside this book’s scripts, gives a clean result. The RDP and PLD numbers of this chapter agree with Opacus 1.6.0, dp_accounting 0.6.0 and prv_accountant 0.2.0 to the printed precision, and the libraries’ tight PLD estimate at \(T = 10{,}000\) is about 6.19, inside the bracket \([6.1377, 6.2377]\). These library values (and the 49.43 above) are quoted from the libraries; the book’s scripts do not import them and cannot print them.


37.7.6 Check yourself

Your RDP accountant reports 7.43 for the running example at \(T = 10{,}000\) and a colleague’s reports 6.71. Which conversion does each use? (7.43 is Mironov’s, 6.71 the improved one; see Table 37.2.)
Why is \(q = 1\) a good test case for a DP-SGD accountant? (The composed pair is exactly Gaussian, so the true \(\varepsilon\) has a closed form. A bound must lie above it, and an approximation that misses it is caught at once.)

title: 37  Choosing an accountant
text:
37.8 Code
The script code/choosing_an_accountant.py imports every accountant from the chapter that derived it and implements nothing new except the comparison, the inverse problem and the checks. Its public functions are accountant_table(q, sigma, delta, ks), which returns one AccountantRow per \(T\) with every accountant’s \(\varepsilon\), and sigma_for_target(eps_target, q, steps, delta, accountant), which solves Equation 37.2 for any accountant named in ACCOUNTANTS. From the repository root:
uv run python code/part04-privacy-accounting/choosing_an_accountant.py

What to take from it. First, the accountants of the part agree where they must. Every number shared with Amplification by subsampling and Numerical accounting is reproduced to the printed digits, and the bounds satisfy both proved chains of Equation 37.1. Second, the gaps between them are the cost of the choice: per-step composition is off by orders of magnitude, RDP by 7.6% at 10,000 steps and much more for short runs, and the CLT is invalid on this example. Third, mismatched assumptions cost more than the choice between RDP and PLD: a factor of 6.96 over the Poisson PLD bound for fixed-size batches, and 14.72 without amplification (\(91.8173/6.2377\)).

text:
37.9 References

Ponomareva, Hazimeh, Kurakin, Xu, Denison, McMahan, Vassilvitskii, Chien & Thakurta, “How to DP-fy ML: A Practical Guide to Machine Learning with Differential Privacy” (Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 77, 2023; arXiv:2303.00654). Section 5.3.1 on matching accounting to data processing (Table 3), Section 5.3.2 on setting \(\delta\), Section 5.3.3 on what to report, Section 5.2.1 on target \(\varepsilon\) tiers. The practical companion to this chapter.
Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth, “Guidelines for Evaluating Differential Privacy Guarantees” (NIST Special Publication 800-226, March 2025). The unit of privacy (Section 2.4), the choice of \(\delta\) and reporting original parameters of RDP, zCDP and GDP guarantees (Section 2.3), floating-point and hyperparameter-tuning hazards (Section 4.3). Read it for what an evaluator will ask.
Gopi, Lee & Wutschitz, “Numerical Composition of Differential Privacy” (NeurIPS 2021). The PRV accountant with certified error bounds, and examples where the CLT under-reports; the basis of prv_accountant and Opacus’s default accountant.
Doroshenko, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar & Manurangsi, “Connect the Dots: Tighter Discrete Approximations of Privacy Loss Distributions” (PoPETs 2022). The pessimistic PLD discretization used in Google’s dp_accounting.
Mironov, Talwar & Zhang, “Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism” (arXiv 2019). The RDP of the subsampled Gaussian, computed exactly; the core of every RDP accountant for DP-SGD.
Balle, Barthe, Gaboardi, Hsu & Sato, “Hypothesis Testing Interpretations and Rényi Differential Privacy” (AISTATS 2020). Theorem 21 is the improved conversion that Opacus and dp_accounting use.
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B, 2022), and Bu, Dong, Long & Su, “Deep Learning with Gaussian Differential Privacy” (Harvard Data Science Review, 2020). The GDP CLT for DP-SGD; read with this chapter’s warning that it is not a bound.
Lebeda, Regehr, Kamath & Steinke, “Avoiding Pitfalls for Privacy Accounting of Subsampled Mechanisms under Composition” (arXiv:2405.20769, 2024; IEEE SaTML 2025). Fixed-size batches versus Poisson sampling, and the factor that the wrong accountant costs.
Chua, Ghazi, Kamath, Kumar, Manurangsi, Sinha & Zhang, “How Private are DP-SGD Implementations?” (ICML 2024). Shuffled batches can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports.
Papernot & Steinke, “Hyperparameter Tuning with Renyi Differential Privacy” (ICLR 2022). Privacy cost of tuning with a random number of trials, far below naive composition.
Google, dp_accounting library; Meta, Opacus; Microsoft, prv_accountant. Documentation of the production RDP, PLD and PRV accountants to check this book’s numbers against.

Rules of thumb

Report the pessimistic PLD, with the optimistic value beside it. Use RDP with the improved conversion when you need adaptivity or a quick bound, and expect it to overstate \(\varepsilon\) by 5 to 10% for long runs and by far more for short ones.
Never report a CLT number as a guarantee. Check any reported number against the PLD lower bound.
Calibrate \(\sigma\) with the accountant you will report: a looser accountant costs noise, an approximation can cost the guarantee.
Check the sampling scheme first. Fixed-size or shuffled batches accounted as Poisson is the most expensive error in practice.
Report the privacy unit, the neighbouring relation, \(q\), \(T\), \(\sigma\), \(C\), the accountant and its discretization, \(\varepsilon\) at several \(\delta\) including one well below \(1/n\), and what was not accounted for.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
Who this part is for
The previous parts built the guarantee and the tools to account for it. This part trains models with it. It asks the questions that decide whether a private model is worth deploying: how do you train with differential privacy (DP), how much accuracy does it cost, which knobs move that cost, and how do you check that the trained model is as private as the accountant claims? The answers are mostly about one algorithm, stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD, and about everything around it: how its hyperparameters are chosen, what replaces it when its assumptions fail, how public data and the choice of privacy unit change it, who pays for its noise, which \(\varepsilon\) to target, and how to audit the result. The last chapter turns the guarantee to a different use: the same noise that protects people also keeps a reused validation or test set honest.
You are expected to have read the earlier parts. From Optimization you need SGD, strong convexity and the sensitivity of regularized empirical risk minimization (ERM). From Membership inference you need the likelihood-ratio attack (LiRA) and the true and false positive rates of an attack. From the DP foundations you need the Gaussian mechanism (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms), clipping (Beyond global sensitivity), the exponential mechanism and report-noisy-max (Selection) and the lower bounds of Lower bounds. From the accounting part you need Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) and trade-off functions (f-DP and Gaussian DP), amplification by subsampling and the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant for DP-SGD (Amplification by subsampling), and what to report (Choosing an accountant). The last chapter also uses the replace-one argument of Algorithmic stability and generalization and the sparse vector technique of Selection. Each chapter restates the facts it uses and links to them.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
text:
The common thread
A private training algorithm has two halves. The privacy half says which quantity has bounded sensitivity and how much noise covers it; it is a theorem, and the accountants of the previous part turn it into a number. The utility half says how much the noise and the bounding cost; it is mostly measured, rarely proved. Every chapter of this part moves one of the two.
The first two chapters build the algorithm: Private ERM compares three places to inject noise into training and shows why, in practice, only noise on the gradients survives non-convex models, and DP-SGD adds clipping, minibatches and accounting. The next three ask what else spends the budget or could spend it better: hyperparameter search; mechanisms that do not rely on random batches, such as the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) algorithm run on noisy gradient sums, DP-FTRL; and private prediction instead of private training, such as private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE). The next three change the setting: public data, a different privacy unit, and the effect on under-represented groups. The next two close the loop between theory and practice: which \(\varepsilon\) to choose, and how to test a claim empirically. The last chapter uses the privacy half for a different purpose. A mechanism that reveals little about any one record cannot be overfitted, so DP also lets one holdout set answer many adaptively chosen questions, the situation of every hyperparameter search and leaderboard. The running examples
Two models recur. The first is regularized logistic regression in \(d = 10\) dimensions on synthetic data, where the exact minimizer can be computed and every method can be compared with the non-private optimum; Private ERM introduces it. The second is a small neural network trained with DP-SGD on synthetic data, small enough that every experiment of the part runs on a laptop in seconds, yet non-convex, so that clipping and noise behave as they do in deep learning; DP-SGD introduces it. The full-scale experiment, DP-SGD on CIFAR-10 audited with LiRA, needs a GPU and PyTorch, which are not dependencies of the repository; the chapters scale it down and say how.

Order. Read chapters 38 and 39 first, in order: every later chapter uses DP-SGD. Chapters 40 and 41 change how the algorithm is run, and can be read in either order. The chapters follow the shape of the earlier parts: why the topic matters, a toolkit, one section per result with a derivation, interpretation, worked example and two check-yourself questions, then code, references and a cheat sheet. Exercises with worked solutions are in the exercise book, a companion website, with a link at the end of each chapter.

title: Differential privacy in machine learning
section: What you will be able to do

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.1 Why this matters
Most of machine learning is empirical risk minimization (ERM): choose the parameters \(\theta\) that minimize the average loss on the training data, usually plus a penalty on the size of \(\theta\). The trained weights are a function of every training record, and Membership inference showed that they give some of those records away. Differential privacy (DP) promises the opposite: the distribution of whatever you release changes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), plus a slack \(\delta\), when one record is replaced. To keep that promise for a trained model, randomness has to enter somewhere between the data and the released weights. This chapter asks where.
Two familiar examples show how directly an exact minimizer can expose a record. The median of an odd number of values minimizes the average absolute loss, and it is one of the values, the middle one, released exactly. A hard-margin support vector machine (SVM) maximizes the margin between the classes, and its weight vector is a weighted sum of a few training records, the support vectors that sit closest to the boundary. Add one record just inside the margin and it becomes a support vector, so the hyperplane swings toward it, by an amount that does not shrink as the dataset grows. Neither model leaks by accident: an exact minimizer is a function of the records, and nothing stops a single record from moving it.
There are three natural places, and each gives a classic algorithm. Output perturbation trains as usual and adds noise to the final weights. Objective perturbation adds a random linear term to the objective, then minimizes it exactly. Gradient perturbation adds noise to every gradient during training. All three were analysed for convex losses between 2008 and 2014, by Chaudhuri, Monteleoni and Sarwate, by Kifer, Smith and Thakurta, and by Bassily, Smith and Thakurta, and the third is the ancestor of the algorithm almost every private deep-learning system runs today: stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, the subject of the next chapter. A fourth place, the data themselves, is not on the list. Adding noise to each record before training is the local model of Trust models, in which every record must hide itself from everyone. That model needs far more data for the same accuracy than adding the noise once, inside the computation.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.1.1 The one idea: privacy needs a bound on how far one record can move what you release
Every DP mechanism in this book works the same way. Find a quantity whose change, when one record is replaced, is bounded by a known number, its sensitivity. Then add noise large enough to hide a change of that size. The three methods differ only in which quantity they bound.
Output perturbation bounds the minimizer itself. Strong convexity, the curvature a ridge penalty \(\frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2\) adds, guarantees that replacing one of \(n\) records moves the minimizer by at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\), where \(L\) bounds the length of each record’s loss gradient (Optimization). Objective perturbation bounds the gradient of the objective at every point, which also moves by at most \(2L/n\), and turns that into a bound on the output’s density through a change of variables. Gradient perturbation bounds the gradient at the points the algorithm actually visits, one step at a time, and composes the steps.
The order matters because each step back toward the data needs fewer assumptions. Output perturbation needs an exact, unique minimizer of a strongly convex objective. Objective perturbation needs that and a loss with bounded curvature. Gradient perturbation, for its privacy, needs only that each record’s gradient is bounded: no convexity, no exact solution. That is why it is the one that survives in deep learning.
