Notation. A training set \(D = (z_1, \dots, z_n)\) holds \(n\) records \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\) with features \(x_i \in \mathbb R^d\) and labels \(y_i \in \{-1, +1\}\). The loss of parameters \(\theta\) on a record is \(\ell(\theta; z)\), and the objective is the empirical risk, which in this chapter includes the ridge penalty, \[\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(\theta; z_i) + \frac\lambda2\|\theta\|^2, \tag{38.1}\] with minimizer \(\theta^*(D)\). Neighbouring datasets \(D \sim D'\) differ by replacing one record, \(z\) in \(D\) by \(z'\) in \(D'\), so both have size \(n\); the next chapter switches to adding or removing one, and says why. \(L\) bounds the length of every gradient \(\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; z)\), \(\|\cdot\|\) is the Euclidean norm, and a released, private version of the parameters is written \(\tilde\theta\). The excess risk of a release is \(\mathcal L(\tilde\theta; D) - \mathcal L(\theta^*; D)\), how much worse it fits the training objective than the exact minimizer.
The running example. Regularized logistic regression, with loss \(\ell(\theta; (x, y)) = \ln(1 + e^{-y\langle \theta, x\rangle})\), in \(d = 10\) dimensions with ridge \(\lambda = 0.01\). The features are uniform on the unit sphere, \(\|x\| = 1\), and the labels come from a logistic model whose true weights have length 5. The derivative of \(\ln(1 + e^{-m})\) in the margin \(m = y\langle \theta, x\rangle\) lies in \((-1, 0)\), so each gradient has length at most \(\|x\| = 1\) and \(L = 1\). Every method targets \(\varepsilon = 1\), with \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for those that need a \(\delta\), on \(n\) from 1,000 to 100,000 records.
How to read this chapter. Read the toolkit, then Section 38.3, which sets the pattern. Section 38.4 has the chapter’s one long derivation; its one-dimensional example shows each step on numbers. Section 38.5 is the one to know well, because the next chapter builds on it. Section 38.6 drops the ridge and derives the rate for convex Lipschitz losses. Section 38.7 and Section 38.8 say which method to use when.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.2 Toolkit: six facts every derivation uses
text:
38.2 Toolkit: six facts every derivation uses

38.2.1 Fact 1 — The Gaussian mechanism, calibrated exactly
To release a vector-valued function \(f(D)\) whose value moves by at most \(\Delta_2 f\) in Euclidean length between neighbours (its \(\ell_2\) sensitivity), add independent normal noise \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) to each coordinate. What matters for privacy is only the ratio \(\mu = \Delta_2 f/\sigma\), the shift measured in noise standard deviations: rotate so the shift lies along one axis, and the other coordinates have the same distribution under both datasets. The mechanism is then \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \[\delta \ge \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big), \tag{38.2}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms, Balle & Wang 2018). The right side increases with \(\mu\), so for each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) there is a largest admissible ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\), and the smallest noise is \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). For \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\mu = 0.2681\), so \(\sigma = 3.7306\,\Delta_2 f\). The classic formula \(\sigma = \Delta_2 f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\) gives \(4.8448\,\Delta_2 f\), 30% more noise for the same guarantee; this chapter always uses the exact calibration.


38.2.2 Fact 2 — The regularized minimizer moves by at most \(2L/(\lambda n)\)
The ridge is the same device that stops a model from overfitting, and for the same reason. Fit a polynomial of high degree to a handful of points without a penalty and it passes through every point, so it swings wildly between them, and it swings again if you delete one point. A penalty on the size of the weights makes the fit prefer smooth curves, which change little when one point goes. Generalization and privacy both ask for that stability, and the ridge supplies a guaranteed amount of it.
Optimization proves the bound, and the argument is short enough to restate. Replacing \(z\) by \(z'\) changes \(\mathcal L\) by \(h(v) = \frac1n(\ell(v; z') - \ell(v; z))\), whose gradient has length at most \(2L/n\): one gradient leaves, another arrives. At the new minimizer \(\theta' = \theta^*(D')\), the old objective’s gradient is therefore \(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta'; D) = -\nabla h(\theta')\), of length at most \(2L/n\). The ridge makes \(\mathcal L(\cdot; D)\) \(\lambda\)-strongly convex: its gradient grows by at least \(\lambda\) per unit of distance in every direction, so a point where the gradient has length \(g\) is within \(g/\lambda\) of the minimizer. Hence \[\|\theta^*(D) - \theta^*(D')\| \le \frac{2L}{\lambda n}. \tag{38.3}\] The same argument gives a bound for any point, not only the exact minimizer: if \(\|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta; D)\| \le g\), then \(\|\theta - \theta^*(D)\| \le g/\lambda\).


38.2.3 Fact 3 — Noise with density proportional to \(e^{-\|b\|/s}\)
Pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, with \(\delta = 0\), needs noise whose density falls off no faster than exponentially in every direction. The standard choice in \(d\) dimensions has density \(\nu(b) \propto e^{-\|b\|/s}\): it depends on \(b\) only through its length. If \(f\) has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\) and \(s = \Delta_2 f/\varepsilon\), then \(f(D) + b\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. At any output \(y\), the ratio of the two output densities is \(e^{(\|y - f(D')\| - \|y - f(D)\|)/s}\). By the triangle inequality the exponent is at most \(\|f(D) - f(D')\|/s \le \Delta_2 f/s = \varepsilon\).
To sample it, split \(b\) into a direction and a length. The density depends only on the length \(r\), and the sphere of radius \(r\) has surface area proportional to \(r^{d - 1}\), so the length has density proportional to \(r^{d-1}e^{-r/s}\). That is a gamma distribution with shape \(d\) and scale \(s\), and the direction is uniform on the sphere. Its moments are \(\mathbb E\|b\| = ds\) and \(\mathbb E\|b\|^2 = d(d + 1)s^2\). Compare the Gaussian, whose squared length has mean \(d\sigma^2\): the pure-DP noise is longer by a factor that grows with \(d\).


38.2.4 Fact 4 — Change of variables for densities
If a random vector \(b\) has density \(\nu\) and \(\theta\) is obtained from \(b\) by a smooth invertible map, write the inverse as \(b = \phi(\theta)\). Then \(\theta\) has density \[p(\theta) = \nu\big(\phi(\theta)\big)\,\big|\det\nabla\phi(\theta)\big|. \tag{38.4}\] The determinant corrects for stretching: if \(\phi\) squeezes a small box around \(\theta\) into a box of half the volume around \(b\), the probability of that box is the same, so the density at \(\theta\) is half the density at \(b\). In one dimension this is the familiar \(p(\theta) = \nu(\phi(\theta))|\phi'(\theta)|\).


38.2.5 Fact 5 — Adaptive Gaussian steps compose into one Gaussian
Run \(T\) Gaussian mechanisms in sequence, each allowed to depend on the outputs of the earlier ones, with sensitivity-to-noise ratios \(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_T\). The whole sequence is exactly as private as a single Gaussian mechanism with ratio \[\mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_T^2}. \tag{38.5}\] This is composition of Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) from f-DP and Gaussian differential privacy. The reason is that the privacy loss of each step is a normal random variable with variance \(\mu_t^2\) and mean \(\mu_t^2/2\), given the past. Their sum is normal with variance \(\sum_t\mu_t^2\) and half that as its mean, which is the privacy loss of one Gaussian with ratio \(\mu\). So \(T\) equal steps with ratio \(\mu_{\text{step}}\) give \(\mu = \sqrt T\,\mu_{\text{step}}\), and Equation 38.2 converts the total to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) with no slack.


38.2.6 Fact 6 — Projected SGD needs only unbiased gradients of bounded second moment
Sometimes the weights must stay inside a closed convex set fixed in advance, written \(\mathcal W\), such as the ball of all weights with length at most a radius \(R\). After each step, the optimizer replaces its point by the closest point of the set, which is called projecting onto it. For the ball, that shrinks a point that left the ball back to the sphere of radius \(R\).
Projected stochastic gradient descent steps along a random vector \(g_t\) instead of the true gradient of the objective \(\mathcal L\). Optimization proves that only two properties of \(g_t\) matter. Given the points visited so far, it must be right on average, \[\mathbb E[g_t \mid \theta_1, \dots, \theta_t] = \nabla\mathcal L(\theta_t), \tag{38.6}\] and its squared length must be bounded on average by a number written \(G^2\), \[\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2 \le G^2. \tag{38.7}\] Suppose \(\mathcal L\) is convex, and its minimizer \(\theta^*\) over \(\mathcal W\) is within distance \(R\) of the starting point. Run \(T\) steps with the learning rate \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\) (also called the step size), and average the points visited into \(\bar\theta_T = \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\theta_t\). Then \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta_T)\big] - \mathcal L(\theta^*) \le \frac{RG}{\sqrt T}. \tag{38.8}\] The proof follows the squared distance to \(\theta^*\). Each step shrinks it by an amount that convexity ties to the current error, and grows it by at most \(\eta^2\|g_t\|^2\). So the randomness of \(g_t\) enters only through that second term, that is through \(G^2\), and neither smoothness nor strong convexity is needed.

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.3 Output perturbation

38.3.1 Context
The simplest private trainer treats training as a black box: compute the exact minimizer \(\theta^*(D)\), then add noise. Fact 2 says the minimizer is a function with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(2L/(\lambda n)\), so this is just the Gaussian mechanism (or Fact 3’s mechanism) applied to it. Chaudhuri & Monteleoni (2008) introduced it for logistic regression. Two questions remain: how much accuracy does it cost, and what happens when, as always in practice, the minimizer is only computed approximately?


38.3.2 Statement
Release \[\tilde\theta = \theta^*(D) + Z, \qquad Z \sim \mathcal N\big(0, \sigma^2I\big), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{\lambda n\,\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}. \tag{38.9}\] This is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for replace-one neighbours. Replacing \(Z\) by noise with density \(\propto e^{-\|b\|/s}\) and \(s = 2L/(\lambda n\varepsilon)\) gives pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. If the objective has Hessian \(H\) at \(\theta^*\), the excess risk is, to second order, \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\tilde\theta) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big] \approx \frac12\,\mathbb E\big[Z^\top HZ\big] = \frac{\mathbb E\|Z\|^2}{2d}\operatorname{tr}H, \tag{38.10}\] for any noise whose direction is uniform, so \(\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\operatorname{tr}H\) for the Gaussian. Without the second-order approximation, Section M.1 in the appendices brackets the excess risk exactly between \(\frac\lambda2\mathbb E\|Z\|^2\) and \(\frac\beta2\mathbb E\|Z\|^2\), where \(\lambda\) and \(\beta\) are the smallest and largest curvature of \(\mathcal L\). An approximate minimizer \(\theta\) with \(\|\nabla \mathcal L(\theta; D)\| \le g\) has sensitivity at most \[\frac{2L}{\lambda n} + \frac{2g}{\lambda}. \tag{38.11}\]


38.3.3 Derivation

Privacy. By Fact 2, \(\theta^*\) moves by at most \(\Delta_2\theta^* = 2L/(\lambda n)\) between neighbours. Adding Gaussian noise with \(\sigma = \Delta_2\theta^*/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP by Fact 1, and adding noise \(\propto e^{-\|b\|/s}\) with \(s = \Delta_2\theta^*/\varepsilon\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP by Fact 3. Nothing else about the data reaches the output.
Expand the objective around its minimizer. The gradient vanishes at \(\theta^*\), so a second-order Taylor expansion gives \(\mathcal L(\theta^* + Z) - \mathcal L(\theta^*) \approx \frac12Z^\top HZ\), with \(H = \nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta^*)\). The noise is small next to the scale on which the curvature changes in the cases of interest; Section 38.7 checks the approximation against simulation.
Average over the direction. Write \(Z = \|Z\|u\) with \(u\) a unit vector. For a uniformly random direction, \(\mathbb E[u_iu_j]\) is \(1/d\) when \(i = j\), because the \(d\) squared coordinates of a unit vector add up to 1 and are exchangeable, and 0 otherwise, by symmetry under flipping one coordinate’s sign. So \(\mathbb E[u^\top Hu] = \sum_iH_{ii}/d = \operatorname{tr}H/d\), and if the length is independent of the direction, as for both noises here, \(\mathbb E[Z^\top HZ] = \mathbb E\|Z\|^2\operatorname{tr}H/d\). For the Gaussian, \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2 = d\sigma^2\). This is Equation 38.10.
Approximate minimizers. Let \(\theta\) and \(\theta'\) be the outputs of the optimizer on \(D\) and \(D'\), with gradients of length at most \(g\). By the last line of Fact 2, each is within \(g/\lambda\) of its exact minimizer. The triangle inequality along the path \(\theta \to \theta^*(D) \to \theta^*(D') \to \theta'\) gives \(\|\theta - \theta'\| \le g/\lambda + 2L/(\lambda n) + g/\lambda\), which is Equation 38.11. The stopping rule must be a gradient check, not a step count: only the gradient bound is guaranteed on every dataset.



38.3.4 Interpretation
The noise is calibrated to the worst case, the damage to the actual case. The sensitivity \(2L/(\lambda n)\) uses only the curvature \(\lambda\) that the ridge guarantees. The damage, Equation 38.10, is measured by the actual curvature \(H\), which includes the data’s own. Put the two together for the Gaussian: the excess risk is about \(\frac{\operatorname{tr}H}{2}\cdot\frac{4L^2}{\lambda^2n^2\mu^2}\). If every eigenvalue of \(H\) is close to some \(h\), this is \(\frac{2dL^2}{\mu^2n^2}\cdot\frac{h}{\lambda^2}\). The factor \(h/\lambda^2\) grows as the ridge shrinks, whatever the data look like. A small ridge buys a better non-private fit and costs a lot of noise.
It falls like \(1/n^2\). The noise standard deviation falls like \(1/n\), so its square, and the excess risk with it, falls like \(1/n^2\). The statistical error of the non-private minimizer falls only like \(1/n\), so for large \(n\) privacy eventually costs less than sampling does, in this convex, low-dimensional setting.
It needs the exact solution. Equation 38.11 adds \(2g/\lambda\) to the sensitivity. To keep that below the exact term, the optimizer must reach a gradient of length \(g \le L/n\), which shrinks with the dataset. An optimizer stopped after a fixed number of steps has no such guarantee on every dataset, and then the sensitivity bound, and the privacy proof, do not apply. Wu et al. (2017) analyse output perturbation of SGD run for a fixed number of passes directly, with a different sensitivity bound.






Figure 38.1: Left: two neighbouring regularized logistic objectives in one dimension (\(n = 20\), \(\lambda = 0.5\)), their minimizers (vertical lines) 0.083 apart, below the bound \(2L/(\lambda n) = 0.2\). Right: the released weight’s density under each dataset with Gaussian noise for \(\varepsilon = 1\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); the noise must hide a shift as large as the bound, not the actual shift.





38.3.5 Example: one dimension, then the running example
Take one feature, \(n = 20\) records and \(\lambda = 0.5\) (Figure 38.1). Replacing the last record, which has \(x = 1\), by the same feature with the opposite label moves the minimizer from 0.2128 to 0.1296, by 0.0832. The bound is \(2/(0.5 \times 20) = 0.2\), and that is what the noise is calibrated to: \(\sigma = 3.7306 \times 0.2 = 0.7461\). The two output densities overlap almost completely, as they must.
In the running example (\(d = 10\), \(\lambda = 0.01\)), \(n = 10{,}000\) gives sensitivity \(2/(0.01 \times 10{,}000) = 0.02\) and \(\sigma = 0.07461\) per coordinate, next to a minimizer of length 2.886. The Hessian at \(\theta^*\) has eigenvalues between 0.0263 and 0.0330, and trace 0.3129. Equation 38.10 predicts \(\frac12 \times 0.07461^2 \times 0.3129 = 8.711 \times 10^{-4}\), and 20 simulated releases average \(9.274 \times 10^{-4}\). The pure-DP version, with noise \(\propto e^{-\|b\|/s}\) and \(s = 0.02\), has \(\mathbb E\|b\|^2 = 110 \times 0.02^2\); the prediction \(6.885 \times 10^{-4}\) and the simulated \(8.321 \times 10^{-4}\) differ by more, because the squared length of gamma noise varies a lot from draw to draw and 20 draws average it only roughly.
Stopping early is costly. With a gradient tolerance of \(g = 10^{-6}\) the sensitivity is 0.0202, essentially exact. With \(g = 10^{-4}\) it doubles to 0.04, and with \(g = 10^{-3}\) it is 0.22, eleven times the exact value. A tolerance that looks tight, \(10^{-3}\), multiplies the noise by eleven and the excess risk by about 121.


38.3.6 Check yourself

You halve the ridge \(\lambda\). By what factor does the Gaussian noise grow, and roughly by what factor does the excess risk grow if the data’s curvature dominates \(H\)? (The noise doubles, since \(\sigma \propto 1/\lambda\). With \(H\) unchanged the excess risk, proportional to \(\sigma^2\operatorname{tr}H\), grows fourfold.)
Why must the stopping rule be “stop when \(\|\nabla \mathcal L\| \le g\)” rather than “stop after 50 Newton steps”? (The privacy proof needs the sensitivity bound on every pair of neighbouring datasets. A gradient check guarantees it everywhere; a step count only guarantees it on datasets where 50 steps happen to be enough.)

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.4 Objective perturbation

38.4.1 Context
Output perturbation wastes the data’s curvature: it pays for the worst case \(\lambda\) and is judged on the actual \(H\). Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate (2011) put the noise inside the optimization instead. Add a random linear term \(\frac1n\langle b, \theta\rangle\) to the objective and minimize exactly. A linear term is a constant force; the objective’s curvature, all of it, resists that force. Where the data add curvature, the minimizer moves less. The price is a subtler privacy proof, because the output is no longer “something fixed plus noise”.


38.4.2 Statement
Let the loss have the form \(\ell(\theta; (x, y)) = g(y\langle \theta, x\rangle)\) with \(g\) convex and twice differentiable, \(|g'| \le 1\) and \(0 \le g'' \le c\), and let \(\|x\| \le 1\); so the gradients have length at most \(L = 1\). Logistic regression qualifies with \(c = \frac14\). Set \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon - 2\ln\Big(1 + \frac{c}{n\lambda}\Big), \tag{38.12}\] draw \(b\) with density \(\nu(b) \propto e^{-\varepsilon'\|b\|/2}\) (Fact 3 with \(s = 2/\varepsilon'\)), and release \[\tilde\theta = \arg\min_\theta\Big[\mathcal L(\theta; D) + \frac1n\langle b, \theta\rangle\Big]. \tag{38.13}\] If \(\varepsilon' > 0\), this is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for replace-one neighbours (Chaudhuri, Monteleoni & Sarwate 2011, Algorithm 2). If not, increase the ridge to \(\lambda + \lambda_+\) with \(\lambda_+ = \frac{c}{n(e^{\varepsilon/4} - 1)} - \lambda\), which makes the logarithm \(\varepsilon/4\) and lets \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon/2\).
The minimizer moves, to first order, by \(-H^{-1}b/n\), so the excess risk is about \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\tilde\theta) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big] \approx \frac{1}{2n^2}\mathbb E\big[b^\top H^{-1}b\big] = \frac{\mathbb E\|b\|^2}{2dn^2}\operatorname{tr}H^{-1}. \tag{38.14}\] Without the approximation, Section M.1 in the appendices brackets it between \(\lambda\mathbb E\|b\|^2/(2\beta^2n^2)\) and \(\mathbb E\|b\|^2/(2\lambda n^2)\).


38.4.3 Derivation
The plan is to write the density of \(\tilde\theta\) explicitly with Fact 4, then bound the ratio of the two densities, for \(D\) and \(D'\), at every point. The ratio splits into a noise factor and a stretching factor, and each consumes part of \(\varepsilon\).

From the output back to the noise. The perturbed objective is \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, so it has exactly one minimizer, where its gradient is zero: \(\nabla \mathcal L(\tilde\theta; D) + b/n = 0\). Solving for \(b\), \[b = \phi_D(\tilde\theta) = -n\nabla \mathcal L(\tilde\theta; D) = -\sum_{i=1}^n\nabla\ell(\tilde\theta; z_i) - n\lambda\tilde\theta. \tag{38.15}\] Every \(\theta\) is the output for exactly one \(b\), namely \(\phi_D(\theta)\), so the map from noise to output is invertible and \(\phi_D\) is its inverse.
The density of the output. By Fact 4, \(p_D(\theta) = \nu(\phi_D(\theta))\,|\det\nabla\phi_D(\theta)|\), and the same for \(D'\) with \(\phi_{D'}\). The ratio at any \(\theta\) is \[\frac{p_D(\theta)}{p_{D'}(\theta)} = \underbrace{\frac{\nu(\phi_D(\theta))}{\nu(\phi_{D'}(\theta))}}_{\text{noise}}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{|\det\nabla\phi_D(\theta)|}{|\det\nabla\phi_{D'}(\theta)|}}_{\text{Jacobian}}. \tag{38.16}\]
The noise factor is at most \(e^{\varepsilon'}\). The sums in \(\phi_D\) and \(\phi_{D'}\) share every term except the replaced record’s, so \(\phi_{D'}(\theta) - \phi_D(\theta) = \nabla\ell(\theta; z) - \nabla\ell(\theta; z')\), of length at most \(2\). The noise factor is \(e^{\varepsilon'(\|\phi_{D'}(\theta)\| - \|\phi_D(\theta)\|)/2}\), and by the triangle inequality the exponent is at most \(\varepsilon'\cdot 2/2 = \varepsilon'\).
The Jacobian is the Hessian. \(\nabla\phi_D(\theta) = -n\nabla^2\mathcal L(\theta; D) = -A\), with \(A = \sum_ig''(m_i)x_ix_i^\top + n\lambda I\), where \(m_i = y_i\langle \theta, x_i\rangle\) is the margin; the chain rule gives each loss’s Hessian as \(g''(m_i)\) times \(y_i^2x_ix_i^\top = x_ix_i^\top\). Every term is positive semi-definite and \(n\lambda I\) is added, so all eigenvalues of \(A\) are at least \(n\lambda\). For \(D'\) the matrix is \(A' = A + E\) with \(E = g''(m')x'x'^\top - g''(m)xx^\top\): one rank-one term in, one out.
The Jacobian factor is at most \((1 + c/(n\lambda))^2\). The ratio of determinants is \(\det(A')/\det(A) = \det(I + A^{-1}E) = \det(I + K)\) with \(K = A^{-1/2}EA^{-1/2}\), since \(A^{-1}E\) and \(K\) are similar matrices. \(K\) is symmetric and is the difference of two rank-one positive semi-definite matrices, \(g''(m')\tilde x'\tilde x'^\top - g''(m)\tilde x\tilde x^\top\) with \(\tilde x = A^{-1/2}x\). A rank-one matrix \(vv^\top\) has one nonzero eigenvalue, \(\|v\|^2\), and here \(\|\tilde x\|^2 = x^\top A^{-1}x \le \|x\|^2/(n\lambda) \le 1/(n\lambda)\). So \(K\) has at most two nonzero eigenvalues, which we call \(\kappa_1\) and \(\kappa_2\), each between \(-a\) and \(a\) with \(a = c/(n\lambda)\), and \(\det(I + K) = (1 + \kappa_1)(1 + \kappa_2) \le (1 + a)^2\). Exchanging the roles of \(D\) and \(D'\) gives the same bound for the inverse ratio, because \(A'\) also has all eigenvalues at least \(n\lambda\).
Add the two budgets. The log of the density ratio is at most \(\varepsilon' + 2\ln(1 + c/(n\lambda)) = \varepsilon\) by Equation 38.12, at every \(\theta\) and in both directions. A bound on the density ratio everywhere is pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
When \(\varepsilon' \le 0\). The Jacobian factor alone would exceed \(\varepsilon\). A larger ridge shrinks \(a\): with \(\lambda + \lambda_+\) in place of \(\lambda\), \(c/(n(\lambda + \lambda_+)) = e^{\varepsilon/4} - 1\), so \(2\ln(1 + a) = \varepsilon/2\), and the noise gets the other half.
Excess risk. To first order in \(b\), the perturbed minimizer solves \(H(\tilde\theta - \theta^*) + b/n = 0\), so \(\tilde\theta - \theta^* = -H^{-1}b/n\). Substituting this into the second-order expansion \(\mathcal L(\tilde\theta) - \mathcal L(\theta^*) \approx \frac12(\tilde\theta - \theta^*)^\top H(\tilde\theta - \theta^*)\) of step 2 of Section 38.3 gives \(\frac{1}{2n^2}b^\top H^{-1}HH^{-1}b = \frac{1}{2n^2}b^\top H^{-1}b\). Averaging over the uniform direction, as in step 3 there, replaces \(b^\top H^{-1}b\) by \(\mathbb E\|b\|^2\operatorname{tr}H^{-1}/d\), which is Equation 38.14.

Walk-through in one dimension. With \(d = 1\) everything in steps 1–5 is a number, and the script computes both densities exactly on a grid of outputs. Take \(n = 5\) records with features in \([-1, 1]\), \(\lambda = 0.1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\). Then \(c/(n\lambda) = 0.25/0.5 = 0.5\), the Jacobian budget is \(2\ln 1.5 = 0.8109\), and the noise gets \(\varepsilon' = 0.1891\). Figure 38.2 shows one dataset: the two densities, and their log ratio, which stays inside \(\pm\varepsilon\). Over 500 random datasets and replacements, the largest log ratio anywhere on the grid is 0.3779. Its noise part never exceeds 0.0992, about half its budget of 0.1891, and its Jacobian part never exceeds 0.3395, well under its budget of 0.8109, and under even \(\ln 1.5 = 0.4055\), half of it.






Figure 38.2: Objective perturbation in one dimension, \(n = 5\), \(\lambda = 0.1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: the exact densities of the released weight under a dataset and its neighbour, computed by change of variables. Right: their log ratio, the privacy loss, which stays well inside \(\pm\varepsilon\).





38.4.4 Interpretation
Where the slack is. Both factors in step 2 are bounded by worst cases that cannot happen together, and mostly cannot happen at all for logistic regression. The noise factor reaches \(e^{\varepsilon'}\) only if the old and new record have full-length gradients pointing in opposite directions. A logistic gradient has full length only when its margin is very negative, and two records whose gradients point in opposite directions have opposite margins, so at most one of them can be saturated: the difference has length at most about 1, not 2, which is why the noise part stops at half its budget. The Jacobian bound charges both the record that leaves and the one that arrives the full curvature \(c\), while their eigenvalues \(\kappa_1 \ge 0 \ge \kappa_2\) have opposite signs, so the product \((1 + \kappa_1)(1 + \kappa_2)\) is at most \(1 + a\): the Jacobian needs only half its budget (Exercise 6). The analysis is safe, not tight.
Curvature helps. Compare Equation 38.14 with Equation 38.10. In output perturbation the noise has length about \(1/(\lambda n)\) and the damage is weighted by \(H\); in objective perturbation the noise has length about 1, is divided by \(n\), and the damage is weighted by \(H^{-1}\). If every eigenvalue of \(H\) is close to \(h\), the ratio of the two excess risks is about \((h/\lambda)^2\) (with \(\varepsilon' \approx \varepsilon\)). When the ridge supplies all the curvature, \(h = \lambda\) and the two are equivalent. When the data supply more, objective perturbation wins quadratically.
What it needs. It needs exact minimization, which no computer delivers. An iterative solver stops early, and floating-point arithmetic rounds every number. Rounding can itself leak, as Mironov (2012) showed for a textbook implementation of Laplace noise (Discrete mechanisms). Beyond that, it needs twice-differentiable losses (the hinge loss of a support vector machine must be smoothed first), a bound \(c\) on the curvature, and a loss that depends on \(\theta\) through one inner product, which makes each record’s Hessian rank one. Kifer, Smith & Thakurta (2012) extend it to Gaussian noise with \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP and to constrained problems, and Iyengar et al. (2019) give a version that tolerates approximate minimization by adding a little output noise on top.


38.4.5 Example: the running example at \(n = 10{,}000\)
At \(n = 10{,}000\) the Jacobian budget is \(2\ln(1 + 0.25/100) = 0.0050\), so \(\varepsilon' = 0.9950\): almost all of \(\varepsilon\) goes to the noise. (At \(n = 100\) the split would be \(\varepsilon' = 0.5537\), and the Jacobian would take almost half.) The noise has \(\mathbb E\|b\|^2 = d(d+1)(2/\varepsilon')^2\), and \(\operatorname{tr}H^{-1} = 320.7\), so Equation 38.14 predicts an excess risk of \(7.127 \times 10^{-5}\); 20 simulated releases average \(8.156 \times 10^{-5}\). The pure-DP output perturbation of Section 38.3, with the same \(\varepsilon\), had \(8.321 \times 10^{-4}\): objective perturbation is ten times better. The rule of thumb \((h/\lambda)^2\) predicts this: the objective’s curvature, ridge included, lies between 0.0263 and 0.0330, about three times the ridge’s 0.01, and \(3^2 = 9\).


38.4.6 Check yourself

Why does the proof need the minimizer to be unique? (Step 1 inverts the map from noise to output. If two weights both minimized the perturbed objective, the output would not be a function of \(b\), and Fact 4 would not apply.)
If you double \(n\), what happens to the share of \(\varepsilon\) that the Jacobian consumes? (It roughly halves: \(2\ln(1 + c/(n\lambda)) \approx 2c/(n\lambda)\) for large \(n\).)

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.5 Gradient perturbation: noisy gradient descent

38.5.1 Context
The first two methods release one point and need the exact minimizer. Real training is iterative and stops early. Gradient perturbation, proposed by Williams & McSherry (2010) and analysed by Song, Chaudhuri & Sarwate (2013) and Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014), makes each step of the optimizer private and composes the steps. Here is its simplest form, full-batch gradient descent with Gaussian noise. Its privacy argument uses nothing about convexity; convexity enters only when you ask how accurate it is.


38.5.2 Statement
Start from \(\theta_0 = 0\) and run \(T\) steps of \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\big(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I)\ \text{independent}, \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\sqrt T}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}. \tag{38.17}\] Releasing all the iterates \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for replace-one neighbours, for any loss whose per-record gradients have length at most \(L\), convex or not.
For a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, \(\beta\)-smooth objective (curvature between \(\lambda\) and \(\beta\) everywhere) and learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\), the excess risk of the last iterate is approximately \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\theta_T) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big] \approx \Big(1 - \frac\lambda\beta\Big)^T\big(\mathcal L(\theta_0) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\big) + \frac{d\sigma^2}{4\beta}, \tag{38.18}\] an optimization error that shrinks with \(T\) plus a noise floor that grows with \(T\), because \(\sigma^2 \propto T\).


38.5.3 Derivation

One step is a Gaussian mechanism. Given \(\theta_t\), the step releases \(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\). The ridge term \(\lambda \theta_t\) is the same on both datasets, and the averages differ only in the replaced record, so the gradient moves by \(\frac1n\|\nabla\ell(\theta_t; z) - \nabla\ell(\theta_t; z')\| \le 2L/n\). Its ratio is \(\mu_{\text{step}} = 2L/(n\sigma)\). The point \(\theta_t\) was itself computed from earlier noisy gradients, but it is public at that moment, which is what adaptive composition allows.
Compose. By Fact 5, \(T\) such steps are exactly as private as one Gaussian with \(\mu = \sqrt T\cdot 2L/(n\sigma)\). Setting this to \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) gives the \(\sigma\) of Equation 38.17. The iterates are computed from the noisy gradients and \(\theta_0\) alone, so releasing them is post-processing.
Where convexity was not used. Steps 1 and 2 bounded the gradient’s change by \(2L/n\) at the point \(\theta_t\), whatever \(\theta_t\) is. Nothing required a minimizer, convexity or smoothness.
Optimization error. Without noise, gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\) on a \(\lambda\)-strongly convex, \(\beta\)-smooth function shrinks \(\mathcal L(\theta_t) - \mathcal L(\theta^*)\) by at least a factor \(1 - \lambda/\beta\) per step (Optimization), which gives the first term.
The noise floor. Near the minimizer, the gradient is about \(H(\theta_t - \theta^*)\), so the error \(e_t = \theta_t - \theta^*\) evolves as \(e_{t+1} \approx (I - \eta H)e_t - \eta\xi_t\). Along an eigenvector of \(H\) with curvature \(h\), the error’s variance \(v\) settles where one step leaves it unchanged: \(v = (1 - \eta h)^2v + \eta^2\sigma^2\), so \(v = \eta^2\sigma^2/(1 - (1 - \eta h)^2) = \eta\sigma^2/(h(2 - \eta h))\). Its cost is \(\frac12hv = \eta\sigma^2/(2(2 - \eta h))\), about \(\eta\sigma^2/4\) when \(\eta h\) is small. Summing over the \(d\) directions with \(\eta = 1/\beta\) gives \(d\sigma^2/(4\beta)\), and the curvature \(h\) has cancelled: directions with little curvature wander farther but cost less per unit of wandering.



38.5.4 Interpretation
The step count is a privacy parameter. Every step spends budget, so the noise per step grows like \(\sqrt T\) and the noise floor like \(T\). Too few steps leave optimization error, too many drown the solution in noise. Figure 38.3 shows the trade-off on the running example. And you cannot pick the best \(T\) by trying several and keeping the one with the best validation score without paying for it: that selection is itself a computation on the data, the subject of Hyperparameter tuning.
A public rule for \(T\). Equation 38.18 can be evaluated without looking at the data, using only public quantities: \(\lambda\), the curvature bound \(\beta = \frac14 + \lambda\) for logistic loss with unit features, \(\mathcal L(\theta_0) = \ln 2\) for \(\theta_0 = 0\) (each loss is \(\ln 2\) at \(\theta = 0\), and \(\mathcal L(\theta^*) \ge 0\)), \(d\), \(n\) and the budget. The rule picks the \(T\) that minimizes it. It is pessimistic, because it only knows that the curvature is at least \(\lambda\).
Why it is the one that generalizes. Gradient perturbation needs a gradient bound, not a minimizer. For a neural network no such bound holds, because gradients can be arbitrarily long, but you can force one by clipping: rescale each record’s gradient to length at most \(C\) before averaging, exactly as Beyond global sensitivity clips a value before averaging it. That, with minibatches instead of full batches, is DP-SGD.






Figure 38.3: Excess risk of noisy gradient descent at \(n = 10{,}000\), \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (1, 10^{-5})\), against the number of steps \(T\), averaged over datasets, with the same steps without noise (dashed). The noiseless error falls geometrically and reaches machine precision; the noisy run is limited by noise that grows with \(T\), so its error is smallest near \(T = 50\).





38.5.5 Example: choosing \(T\) for the running example
For \(n = 10{,}000\), the public rule picks \(T = 218\), which gives per-step noise \(\sigma = 0.01102\) on the mean gradient and an estimated excess risk of \(1.301 \times 10^{-3}\). Simulated runs average \(1.384 \times 10^{-3}\), close to the estimate.
Figure 38.3 shows that the rule overshoots. With the actual curvature of the data, between 0.0263 and 0.0330 rather than the 0.01 the rule assumes, noiseless gradient descent is already within \(2.679 \times 10^{-11}\) of the minimum after 100 steps. Measured over 10 datasets, the excess risk is \(1.027 \times 10^{-3}\) at \(T = 20\), \(2.875 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(T = 50\), \(7.137 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(T = 100\) and \(6.018 \times 10^{-3}\) at \(T = 1{,}000\). The best \(T\) is near 50, four times smaller than the rule’s, and gives five times less excess risk. You may only use that knowledge if you obtained it privately, or from public data that resembles yours.

The step count grows slowly with \(n\), like \(\ln n\), because the optimization error shrinks geometrically while the target, the noise floor, shrinks like \(1/n^2\) (Table 38.2).


38.5.6 Check yourself

Noisy gradient descent with \(T = 100\) steps is \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP. You run it for \(T = 400\) steps with the same per-step noise. What is \(\mu\) now? (Twice as large: \(\mu = \sqrt T\,\mu_{\text{step}}\), and \(\sqrt{400/100} = 2\). So \(\mu = 2 \times 0.2681 = 0.5362\), a weaker guarantee.)
In step 1 of the derivation, why is it allowed that the point \(\theta_t\) at which the gradient is evaluated depends on the data? (Because \(\theta_t\) is computed from earlier released outputs only. Adaptive composition covers mechanisms chosen based on earlier outputs, so the bound holds conditionally on the past, at whatever \(\theta_t\) it produced.)

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.6 Noisy projected gradient descent without a ridge
text:
38.6 Noisy projected gradient descent without a ridge

38.6.1 Context
Every method so far leaned on the ridge. Output and objective perturbation need it for their privacy, and the noise floor of Equation 38.18 needs it for its accuracy. Many models have no ridge, though, or one so small that a bound in \(1/\lambda\) says nothing. A linear classifier trained with the hinge or logistic loss inside a fixed ball of weights is convex and has bounded gradients, but it is not strongly convex. How accurate can a private trainer be on such a model, and where does the dimension enter? Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014) answer with noisy gradient descent and the convergence guarantee of projected SGD, and get a rate of order \(RL\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\) for gradients of length at most \(L\) in a ball of radius \(R\). The derivation also shows that privacy noise acts on the optimizer exactly like any other gradient noise.


38.6.2 Statement
Keep the weights in the ball \(\mathcal W = \{\|\theta\| \le R\}\), fixed in advance. Let the loss be convex in \(\theta\) with per-record gradients of length at most \(L\), and minimize the plain average \(\mathcal L(\theta; D) = \frac1n\sum_i\ell(\theta; z_i)\), with no ridge. Start from \(\theta_1 = 0\) and run \(T\) steps of \[\theta_{t+1} = \Pi_{\mathcal W}\Big(\theta_t - \eta\big(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\big)\Big), \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2I), \qquad \sigma = \frac{2L}{n}\cdot\frac{\sqrt T}{\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)}, \tag{38.19}\] where \(\Pi_{\mathcal W}\) is the projection onto the ball and \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) is, as in Fact 1, the largest ratio of sensitivity to noise at which one Gaussian release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Use the learning rate \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\) with \(G^2 = L^2 + d\sigma^2\), and release the average of the iterates, \(\bar\theta = \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\theta_t\). The release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for replace-one neighbours, and its excess risk over the best weights in the ball is at most \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta; D)\big] - \min_{\theta\in\mathcal W}\mathcal L(\theta; D) \le RL\sqrt{\frac1T + \frac{4d}{n^2\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)^2}}. \tag{38.20}\] Once \(T \ge n^2\mu^2/(4d)\), this is at most \(2\sqrt2\,RL\sqrt d/(n\mu)\). For \(\varepsilon < 1\) the exact ratio is at least the classic one, \(\mu \ge \varepsilon/\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\), so \[\mathbb E\big[\mathcal L(\bar\theta; D)\big] - \min_{\theta\in\mathcal W}\mathcal L(\theta; D) \le \frac{4RL\sqrt{d\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}. \tag{38.21}\]


38.6.3 Derivation

Privacy. Each step releases the noisy gradient \(\nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\), whose noiseless part moves by at most \(2L/n\) when one record is replaced, as in step 1 of Section 38.5. Fact 5 composes the \(T\) steps into one Gaussian with ratio \(\sqrt T\cdot 2L/(n\sigma) = \mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). The projection uses only the public ball, and the average uses only the iterates, so both are post-processing.
The noisy gradient is unbiased. Write \(g_t = \nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D) + \xi_t\). Given the past, \(\xi_t\) is fresh noise with mean zero, so \(\mathbb E[g_t] = \nabla \mathcal L(\theta_t; D)\), the first condition of Fact 6.
Its second moment is \(L^2 + d\sigma^2\). Expand the square: \(\mathbb E\|g_t\|^2 = \|\nabla \mathcal L\|^2 + 2\,\mathbb E\langle\nabla \mathcal L, \xi_t\rangle + \mathbb E\|\xi_t\|^2\). The gradient of \(\mathcal L\) is an average of vectors of length at most \(L\), so its length is at most \(L\). The cross term is zero, because \(\xi_t\) has mean zero and is independent of \(\theta_t\). The last term is \(d\sigma^2\), one \(\sigma^2\) per coordinate. So \(G^2 = L^2 + d\sigma^2\) satisfies the second condition of Fact 6.
Apply Fact 6. The minimizer over the ball and the start \(\theta_1 = 0\) both lie in the ball, so they are at most \(R\) apart. With the learning rate \(\eta = R/(G\sqrt T)\), Equation 38.8 bounds the excess risk of \(\bar\theta\) by \(RG/\sqrt T = R\sqrt{(L^2 + d\sigma^2)/T}\).
The step count cancels from the noise term. By Equation 38.19, \(\sigma^2 = 4L^2T/(n^2\mu^2)\), so \(d\sigma^2/T = 4L^2d/(n^2\mu^2)\), whatever \(T\) is. Factoring out \(L^2\) gives Equation 38.20.
Choose \(T\). The first term under the root falls with \(T\) and the second does not. When \(T \ge n^2\mu^2/(4d)\), the first is at most the second, and the root is at most \(\sqrt{8d/(n^2\mu^2)} = 2\sqrt2\,\sqrt d/(n\mu)\).
In terms of \(\varepsilon\). The classic calibration of Fact 1 adds noise \(\Delta_2 f\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\), and it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for \(\varepsilon < 1\). The exact calibration uses the least noise that is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, so it adds no more noise than the classic one, and its ratio \(\mu\) is at least the classic ratio, \[\frac1\mu \le \frac{\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon}. \tag{38.22}\] Substituting this into step 6 gives \(2\sqrt2 \cdot \sqrt2 = 4\) in front, which is Equation 38.21.



38.6.4 Interpretation
Privacy noise is just more gradient variance. The convergence guarantee of Fact 6 does not care where the randomness of \(g_t\) comes from, only how large its second moment is. Sampling one record instead of averaging all of them raises \(G^2\), and so does Gaussian noise for privacy, by \(d\sigma^2\). That is where the dimension enters the cost of privacy: one \(\sigma^2\) for every coordinate the optimizer moves. Public data and private fine-tuning builds on this, by training fewer coordinates.
More steps never hurt here. In Section 38.5 the noise floor grew with \(T\), because the learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\) was fixed while the noise per step grew like \(\sqrt T\). Here the learning rate shrinks like \(1/\sqrt T\) and the iterates are averaged, and step 5 shows the two effects cancel exactly. The noise term is fixed by \(n\), \(d\) and the budget, and extra steps only remove optimization error. So the step count needs no tuning. It only has to reach the public threshold \(n^2\mu^2/(4d)\).
The rate cannot be beaten. For convex losses with \(L\)-bounded gradients over a ball of radius \(R\), Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014) prove that, as long as \(\sqrt d \le n\varepsilon\), every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm has excess risk of order \(RL\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\) on some dataset, by the fingerprinting argument of Lower bounds. Section M.1 in the appendices derives this lower bound step by step, with explicit but loose constants. Equation 38.21 matches it up to the factor \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\) and constants. Compare the strongly convex rate Equation 38.23 of Section 38.7, which is of order \(d/(\lambda n^2\varepsilon^2)\): a guaranteed curvature \(\lambda\) turns \(\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\) into its square, divided by \(\lambda\).
The cost is computation. Full-batch steps touch all \(n\) records, so \(T \approx n^2\mu^2/(4d)\) steps cost about \(n^3\mu^2/(4d)\) gradient evaluations. Bassily, Smith & Thakurta use one random record per step instead, about \(n^2\) steps. Sampling makes each step cheaper, and by Amplification by subsampling also more private, so the noise per step can be smaller. The rate is the same up to logarithms. Random batches, clipping and an accountant for many such steps are the ingredients of DP-SGD in the next chapter.
It is a worst case. The bound uses only convexity and the gradient bound, and the worst case is a loss that is nearly linear around its minimizer. The logistic loss is curved there, so the measured excess risk falls faster than \(1/n\), as the example shows.






Figure 38.4: Noisy projected gradient descent on unregularized logistic regression in the ball of radius 5, \(d = 10\), \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP, with \(T = \lceil n^2\mu^2/(4d)\rceil\) steps: the measured excess risk over the best weights in the ball (circles) against the bound Equation 38.20 (squares), averaged over 3 datasets drawn separately from those of the table. The bound falls like \(1/n\); the measured excess risk falls faster.





38.6.5 Example: logistic regression in a ball
Take the running example’s data, with \(d = 10\) features and gradients of length at most \(L = 1\), drop the ridge, and keep the weights in the ball of radius \(R = 5\). The budget is \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), for which the exact ratio is \(\mu = 0.2681\). The classic ratio \(\varepsilon/\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\) is smaller, 0.2064, as step 7 requires. With a thousand records the rule \(T = \lceil n^2\mu^2/(4d)\rceil\) gives 1,797 steps, and the noise on the mean gradient is \(\sigma = 0.3163\). The noise adds \(d\sigma^2 = 10 \times 0.3163^2\) to the second moment, so \(G^2 = 2.0004\), about twice the noiseless \(L^2 = 1\). The learning rate is then 0.0834, and Equation 38.20 evaluates to 0.1668.
The bound falls with the number of steps but levels off at its limit, \(2RL\sqrt d/(n\mu) = 0.1180\). It is 0.5137 after 100 steps and 0.1973 after 1,000. After 10,000 steps it is 0.1281, and after 100,000 it is 0.1190, within 1% of the limit.

Noisy gradient descent with a ridge has a noise floor that grows with the number of steps, but here extra steps never raise the bound. What is different? With a fixed learning rate \(\eta = 1/\beta\) and the last iterate, the floor is \(d\sigma^2/(4\beta)\), which grows with \(\sigma^2 \propto T\).)

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
text:
38.7 How the three compare

38.7.1 Context
Each method is private by its own argument. Which should you use? Theory answers by rates, how the excess risk falls with \(n\), \(d\) and \(\varepsilon\), and by lower bounds that no method can beat. Simulation answers for the running example. They agree on the rate and disagree on the constant, and the constant is what you choose by.


38.7.2 Statement
For \(\lambda\)-strongly convex objectives with \(L\)-Lipschitz losses, Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014) show that the best achievable expected excess risk under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is of order \[\frac{L^2\,d}{\lambda\,n^2\varepsilon^2}, \tag{38.23}\] up to logarithmic factors in \(n\) and \(1/\delta\). Their upper bound, attained by noisy stochastic gradient descent, carries such factors. Their lower bound, which holds for every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm, does not, so the two match only up to those logarithms. Section M.1 in the appendices proves both sides with explicit constants; with full gradients and a weighted average of the iterates, the upper bound needs no logarithm of \(n\). For convex objectives over a ball of radius \(R\), without strong convexity, the rate is of order \(LR\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\) up to logarithms, and Section 38.6 derives the upper bound. The lower bounds come from the fingerprinting codes of Lower bounds: a private algorithm whose output is too accurate would let an adversary trace which records were used.

38.7.3 Derivation
The upper bounds for output and objective perturbation are Equation 38.10 and Equation 38.14 with the noise of each method substituted. Both have \(\mathbb E\|\text{noise}\|^2 \propto 1/n^2\) (the output noise has scale \(1/(\lambda n)\); the objective noise has scale 1 and is divided by \(n\)), which gives the \(1/n^2\). For noisy gradient descent, the noise floor \(d\sigma^2/(4\beta)\) has \(\sigma^2 \propto T/n^2\), and the optimization error must be pushed below it, which takes \(T \propto \frac\beta\lambda\ln n\) steps; this gives \(1/n^2\) times a logarithm. Bassily, Smith & Thakurta (2014) give both proofs. Section M.1 in the appendices derives an upper bound of this order, with explicit constants, for noisy projected gradient descent, and the lower bound by a reduction to the fingerprinting bound.


38.7.4 Interpretation
The rate is the same; the constants are not. All three methods fall like \(1/n^2\), and noisy gradient descent a little slower, \(-1.79\), because its step count grows with \(\ln n\). On this problem objective perturbation is about ten times better than output perturbation at every \(n\), the \((h/\lambda)^2\) of Section 38.4, and noisy gradient descent with the public step rule is the worst of the three for \(n \ge 10{,}000\). Tuned privately to \(T \approx 50\), it would sit between the two perturbation methods.
Pure against approximate DP. At \(d = 10\) the pure-DP noise of Fact 3 and the Gaussian are close: their mean squared lengths are \(d(d+1)s^2 = 110\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(d\sigma^2 = 10 \times 3.7306^2\,(\Delta_2 f)^2 = 139.2\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\), which is why the pure-DP column is slightly better here. At \(d = 100\) they are \(10{,}100\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\) against \(1{,}392\,(\Delta_2 f)^2\): pure DP costs a factor that grows like \(d\), the price of \(\delta = 0\) that Lower bounds proves unavoidable.
Accuracy is forgiving. Excess risk is a fine measure, but you care about predictions. On held-out data the non-private model has accuracy 0.747 at \(n = 1{,}000\); output perturbation drops it to 0.681, noisy gradient descent to 0.695 and objective perturbation only to 0.736. By \(n = 10{,}000\) all four are within 0.002 of the non-private 0.753. A low-dimensional convex model on ten thousand records can be made private almost for free.
Training error is not test error. The excess risk in this chapter is measured on the training objective. A deployed model is judged instead by its population risk, the expected loss on a new record drawn from the same distribution as the training data. For convex losses with \(L\)-bounded gradients over a ball of radius \(R\), Bassily, Feldman, Talwar & Thakurta (2019) show that the best population excess risk under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is of order \[LR\Big(\frac{1}{\sqrt n} + \frac{\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}}{n\varepsilon}\Big). \tag{38.24}\] The first term is what any learner pays for seeing only \(n\) samples, private or not. The second is the price of privacy, and it is the smaller of the two once \(n\) exceeds about \(d\ln(1/\delta)/\varepsilon^2\). So, with enough data, privacy adds nothing to the error that sampling already causes, the same conclusion that Section 38.3 reached for strongly convex objectives.






Figure 38.5: Excess risk of the four private releases against the dataset size on the running example, log-log, with a line of slope \(-2\). All fall like \(1/n^2\); objective perturbation is about ten times better than output perturbation throughout.





38.7.5 Example: reading the rate
Equation 38.23 predicts how much data you need. Suppose an excess risk of \(10^{-4}\) is acceptable, and output perturbation gives \(9.274 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(n = 10{,}000\). The rate \(1/n^2\) says that multiplying \(n\) by \(\sqrt{9.274} = 3.05\) brings it to about \(10^{-4}\); Table 38.4 confirms it, with \(9.973 \times 10^{-5}\) at \(n = 30{,}000\). Equivalently, halving \(\varepsilon\) costs the same as halving \(n\), because \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\) appear only as the product \(n\varepsilon\): to keep the same accuracy at half the budget, you need twice the data.


38.7.6 Check yourself

In Equation 38.23, why do \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\) appear only as the product \(n\varepsilon\)? (Every sensitivity in this chapter is proportional to \(1/n\) and every noise to sensitivity over \(\varepsilon\), so the noise scale is proportional to \(1/(n\varepsilon)\).)
Objective perturbation beat output perturbation by a factor of ten. Name a problem on which it would not help at all. (Any problem whose data add no curvature beyond the ridge, such as a linear loss: then \(H = \lambda I\), \(h = \lambda\), and the ratio \((h/\lambda)^2\) is 1.)

title: 38  Private empirical risk minimization
section: 38.8 When the model is not convex
text:
38.8 When the model is not convex

38.8.1 Context
A neural network’s loss is not convex in its parameters. What survives of the three methods?


38.8.2 Statement
The privacy proofs of Section 38.3 and Section 38.4 do not carry over to non-convex objectives, because both need a unique minimizer that moves only a little when one record changes. Neither method becomes impossible. Output perturbation over a bounded set of weights is always private with noise scaled to the set’s diameter, but then the noise swamps the answer. Objective perturbation can be proved private without convexity (Neel, Roth, Vietri & Wu 2020), but only if the optimizer returns a global minimizer of the perturbed objective, which no practical optimizer for a neural network guarantees. Noisy gradient descent keeps its guarantee, Equation 38.17, for any loss whose per-record gradients have length at most \(L\), and loses only its accuracy guarantee. When no such \(L\) exists, clipping each per-record gradient to length \(C\) makes \(L = C\).


38.8.3 Derivation

The minimizer can jump. Optimization gives a one-dimensional loss with two wells, \(\frac14(\theta^2 - 1)^2 - y\theta\) with labels \(y = \pm1\), whose empirical minimizer sits in the well favoured by the majority label. With 501 labels \(+1\) and 500 labels \(-1\), changing one label flips the majority and moves the minimizer by 2.0010. No \(1/n\) appears: the sensitivity of the minimizer is a constant, so output perturbation would need noise with \(\sigma = 3.7306 \times 2.0010 = 7.465\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\), more than three times the distance between the wells, whatever the dataset size.
The objective-perturbation proof breaks at step 1. Without strong convexity the perturbed objective can have several minimizers, the map from noise to output is no longer invertible, and Fact 4 cannot be applied. Neel et al. (2020) replace the change of variables with a different argument. It shows that a variant of objective perturbation is private for bounded, Lipschitz losses, convex or not, when the perturbed objective is handed to an oracle that returns its global minimizer, or a point provably close to it. The guarantee is therefore about that minimizer, and it holds only for an optimizer that is certain to find it. Gradient descent on a neural network finds a local minimum that depends on the starting point, and the guarantee says nothing about that.
Gradient perturbation survives. Its derivation in Section 38.5 used only the gradient bound at the visited points (step 3 there).
Clipping supplies the bound. Replace each per-record gradient \(\nabla\ell(\theta; z_i)\) by \(\nabla\ell(\theta; z_i)\min(1, C/\|\nabla\ell(\theta; z_i)\|)\), which has length at most \(C\) and is unchanged when it is already shorter. The average of clipped gradients changes by at most \(2C/n\) when one record is replaced, and the derivation goes through with \(L = C\).



38.8.4 Interpretation
What the non-convex case loses is the guarantee of accuracy, not of privacy. Noisy gradient descent on a neural network is private whatever the network does; whether it learns anything is an empirical question, and the answer depends on the clipping norm, the noise and the number of steps, which the next chapter studies. Clipping also changes what is being optimized: the average of clipped gradients is not the gradient of \(\mathcal L\), so the algorithm no longer minimizes \(\mathcal L\), a bias that the next chapter measures.
Full-batch gradient descent is also too slow for large datasets: each step touches every record. Using a random minibatch at each step makes each step cheaper and, by Amplification by subsampling, more private per step, because each record is used only with probability \(q\). Clipping, noise, minibatches and a subsampled-Gaussian accountant together are DP-SGD.


38.8.5 Example: two wells and output perturbation
Take the double-well loss with \(n = 1{,}001\), whose minimizer sits in one of the two wells near \(\pm1\). Output perturbation with \(\sigma = 7.465\) releases a weight whose standard deviation is more than seven times the distance from either well to the origin; the released value carries almost no information about which well the data chose, which is exactly what privacy demands, since one record decides it. Noisy gradient descent with clipping still moves toward whichever well the noisy average gradient points to; on datasets where many records agree, the average gradient is large compared with the noise and the method finds the majority well with high probability.


38.8.6 Check yourself

Why does clipping not break the privacy proof, even though it changes the gradients? (The proof needs only that each step releases a function of the data with bounded sensitivity plus Gaussian noise. The clipped average is such a function, with sensitivity \(2C/n\), whatever it is the gradient of.)
Does noisy gradient descent on a non-convex loss need to find the global minimum to be private? (No. Privacy holds for every run, whatever point it reaches; finding a good point is a question of accuracy only.)

What to take from it. Three things. First, the privacy proofs can be checked numerically where the output distribution is computable: in one dimension the change-of-variables density is exact, and the log ratio stays inside its bound with room to spare. Second, the second-order predictions of excess risk match simulation to within the sampling error, so you can predict the cost of privacy before training. Without the ridge the guaranteed rate slows to \(1/n\), and the measured excess risk stays five to eight times below its bound.

Rules of thumb

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.1 Why this matters
Private empirical risk minimization ended with one method left standing for non-convex models: gradient descent with Gaussian noise on every step. Its privacy proof needs only that one record moves each step’s gradient by a bounded amount, and clipping each record’s gradient supplies that bound for any model. Two more changes make it practical for differential privacy (DP). Each step uses a random minibatch instead of the full dataset, which makes steps cheap and, by amplification, more private. And an accountant composes thousands of such steps into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). The result is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, introduced by Abadi et al. (2016). Nearly every private deep-learning system runs it, through libraries such as Opacus, TensorFlow Privacy and JAX Privacy.
Part 4 computed the privacy of DP-SGD without running it. Amplification by subsampling and Choosing an accountant report \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for a sampling rate \(q\) of 0.01, a noise multiplier \(\sigma\) of 1 and 10,000 steps. This chapter runs that configuration on a neural network, and asks what the noise and the clipping cost and how to choose the knobs that control them.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.1.1 The one idea: the analysis never looks inside the model
Each step of DP-SGD releases a noisy sum of clipped per-example gradients. Clipping rescales each record’s gradient to length at most \(C\), so adding or removing one record changes the sum by at most \(C\), whatever the network, the loss or the current parameters. The privacy proof stops there. Everything else, the architecture, the data, whether training converges, affects only accuracy.
That split organizes the chapter. The knobs divide into two groups. The noise multiplier \(\sigma\), the sampling rate \(q\) and the number of steps \(T\) determine \(\varepsilon\) through the accountant, and nothing else does. The clipping norm \(C\) and the learning rate \(\eta\) do not change \(\varepsilon\) at all; they change how much of the gradient survives clipping and how much the noise moves the weights. The cost of privacy comes in two forms: a bias from clipping, which changes the direction of the average gradient, and a variance from the noise, which makes each step partly random.

The baseline every later chapter improves on






Notation. A training set \(D\) has \(n\) records \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\). The model has \(d\) parameters, written \(\theta \in \mathbb R^d\), and \(g_i = \nabla_\theta\ell(\theta; z_i)\) is the gradient of record \(i\)’s loss, its per-example gradient. \(C\) is the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier (the noise standard deviation in units of \(C\)), \(q\) the sampling rate, \(B = qn\) the expected batch size, \(T\) the number of steps and \(\eta\) the learning rate. The learning rate is also called the step size. Neighbouring datasets now differ by adding or removing one record, \(D' = D \cup \{z\}\), because Poisson sampling pairs with that relation (Amplification by subsampling); the previous chapter used replacement.
The running example. Inputs are 50-dimensional standard normal vectors, and labels are the sign of the output of a fixed random teacher network with 8 hidden tanh units, so a perfect classifier exists. The student is a network with one hidden layer of 64 tanh units and a logistic loss, \(d = 3{,}329\) parameters including biases, trained on \(n = 10{,}000\) records and tested on 20,000 more. DP-SGD runs with \(q = 0.01\) (expected batch \(B = 100\)), \(C = 0.5\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, 100 epochs: exactly Part 4’s running example. The dataset is fixed; only the training randomness changes between runs.
How to read this chapter. Read the toolkit and Section 39.3, which states what the guarantee covers and what it assumes. Section 39.4 and Section 39.5 say how to set the knobs. Section 39.6 and Section 39.7 are about implementation and can be skipped on a first reading, except for the warning about microbatches. Section 39.8 puts the pieces together.

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
39.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

39.2.1 Fact 1 — A Gaussian mechanism is described by one ratio
Add noise \(\mathcal N(0, s^2I)\) to a vector-valued function whose value moves by at most \(\Delta\) in Euclidean length between neighbours. Its privacy depends only on \(\mu = \Delta/s\), the shift measured in noise standard deviations, because rotating the space puts the shift on one axis and leaves identical noise on the others (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). For a clipped sum with noise \(\sigma C\), \(\Delta = C\) and \(\mu = 1/\sigma\): the clipping norm cancels.


39.2.2 Fact 2 — The Poisson-subsampled Gaussian and its accountant
If each record enters the batch independently with probability \(q\), one step’s output with the record is a mixture: with probability \(1 - q\) the record was not drawn and the output is the same as without it, with probability \(q\) it was drawn and the output is shifted. In the worst case the two distributions to compare are the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) and \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), in one dimension. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair says only that the privacy loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\), not how far beyond \(\varepsilon\) that rare loss goes, and so it does not compose well. The accountant therefore tracks the whole distribution of the loss through its moments. That is the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve, the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) between the two distributions, which Abadi et al. (2016) introduced as the moments accountant. For integer \(\alpha\) it has the exact form \[\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^je^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}, \tag{39.1}\] and a numerical integral for other orders (Amplification by subsampling). RDP curves add under composition, even when each step depends on the previous outputs (Rényi DP), and the composed curve converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at the best order, \[\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}\alpha - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big] \tag{39.2}\] (Balle et al. 2020; From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)). For small \(q\) and orders that are not too large, only the \(j = 2\) term of Equation 39.1 matters beyond the first two, and the curve is close to \(\frac\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\).


39.2.3 Fact 3 — Post-processing
Any computation on a private output, which does not touch the data again, is as private as the output itself (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). Dividing a noisy sum by a public constant, taking a gradient step with it, and releasing the resulting weights are all post-processing.


39.2.4 Fact 4 — A dense layer’s gradient is an outer product
For a dense layer that maps an input \(a \in \mathbb R^{d_{\text{in}}}\) to \(Wa\), the gradient of a loss with respect to \(W\) is \(va^\top\), where \(v\) is the gradient with respect to the layer’s output, the back-propagated error. Each entry is \(\partial\ell/\partial W_{jk} = v_ja_k\), because \(W_{jk}\) multiplies \(a_k\) and contributes to output \(j\) only. Gradient inversion uses the same fact to reconstruct inputs from gradients; here it makes per-example gradient norms cheap.

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.3 The algorithm and its guarantee

39.3.1 Context
What exactly does DP-SGD compute, and which \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) does it satisfy? The answer has to be precise, because each detail of the algorithm is an assumption of the proof, and implementations that change a detail can lose the guarantee without any visible symptom.


39.3.2 Statement
Start from parameters \(\theta_0\) chosen independently of the data. For \(t = 0, \dots, T - 1\):

Sample. Put each record in the batch \(S_t\) independently with probability \(q\).
Per-example gradients. For each \(i \in S_t\), compute \(g_i = \nabla_\theta\ell(\theta_t; z_i)\).
Clip. Rescale each to length at most \(C\): \(\bar g_i = g_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\).
Noisy sum. \(G_t = \sum_{i\in S_t}\bar g_i + \xi_t\) with \(\xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\).
Step. \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,G_t/B\), with \(B = qn\) the expected batch size.

Releasing all of \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for add/remove neighbours, with \(\varepsilon\) given by Equation 39.2. Section C.5 in the appendices derives this from scratch, from clipping to the final \(\varepsilon\), with worked numbers. The guarantee does not depend on the loss, the model, \(C\) or \(\eta\).


39.3.3 Derivation

One record moves the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Fix the parameters \(\theta_t\) and the batch of the other records. If the record \(z\) is in the batch, the sum contains one extra term \(\bar g_z\), of length at most \(C\); every other term is the same for \(D\) and \(D'\), because each is computed from its own record alone.
One step is a subsampled Gaussian mechanism. With noise \(\sigma C\), Fact 1 gives the ratio \(1/\sigma\) for a step on which \(z\) is drawn. Under Poisson sampling, \(z\) is drawn with probability \(q\) independently of the other records, so the step’s output on \(D'\) is the mixture of Fact 2. Rescaling by \(C\) and rotating, the worst case over the direction and length of \(\bar g_z\) is the one-dimensional pair of Fact 2, a shift of exactly \(C\) along one axis; a shorter shift is the same pair with extra noise, which cannot be less private.
Dividing by \(B\) is post-processing. \(B = qn\) is a fixed public number, so \(\theta_{t+1}\) is computed from \(\theta_t\) and \(G_t\) alone (Fact 3).
Compose. Step \(t\) is evaluated at \(\theta_t\), which depends on the earlier noisy sums. RDP composition holds for such adaptive sequences, so the \(T\) steps together have RDP curve \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\).
Convert. Equation 39.2 turns the composed curve into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Every iterate is a function of the released noisy sums, so releasing all of them, or only the last, is covered.



39.3.4 Interpretation
What the proof assumes, and how implementations break it. Each step of the derivation is a condition on the code.

Step 1 needs per-example independence. Batch normalization computes means and variances over the batch, so one record changes every other record’s activations and gradients, and the sum can move by much more than \(C\). Private models use normalizations that act on one example at a time, such as group or layer normalization.
Step 1 needs a fixed \(C\). Choosing \(C\) as, say, the median gradient norm of the current batch makes the noise scale depend on the data. Choose \(C\) in advance, from public data or a private estimate.
Step 2 needs Poisson sampling. Shuffling the data and cutting it into fixed batches is a different mechanism, which Amplification by subsampling shows can be much less private than the Poisson accountant reports.
Step 3 needs a public denominator. Dividing by the actual batch size \(|S_t|\), which reveals how many records were drawn and changes when \(z\) is added, is not post-processing of \(G_t\). Divide by \(B\), or release a noisy count and spend budget on it.
Step 4 needs the accountant to see every step, including the steps of runs that were discarded during tuning: that is the subject of Hyperparameter tuning.

What it does not cover. The guarantee is for one record. A person with many records needs user-level privacy. Preprocessing that uses the data, such as normalizing features by their mean, must itself be private or use public statistics.


39.3.5 Example: the running example
With \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(T = 10{,}000\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the accountant gives \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), attained at order \(\alpha = 4.1\), the same value Part 4 reports. Table 39.2 gives the noise multiplier that the same \(q\) and \(T\) need for other budgets.

How large is the noise? The averaged update \(G_t/B\) carries noise with standard deviation \(\sigma C/B = 1 \times 0.5/100 = 0.005\) on each of the 3,329 coordinates. A Gaussian vector with \(d\) independent coordinates of standard deviation \(s\) has length close to \(s\sqrt d\), so the noise has length about \(0.005 \times \sqrt{3{,}329} = 0.288\). The averaged clipped gradient has length at most \(C = 0.5\), and in the run it is 0.070 at the first step and between 0.015 and 0.027 from step 1,000 on. The noise in every step is about ten times longer than the signal.
Training works anyway, because the signal points in roughly the same direction from one step to the next, while the noise is independent. Over \(t\) steps, the signals add up to about \(t\) times their length, and the noise to about \(\sqrt t\) times its length, since independent vectors add in squares. Signal overtakes noise when \(t \cdot 0.026 > \sqrt t \cdot 0.288\), that is after \(t > (0.288/0.026)^2 \approx 123\) steps. The final model reaches test accuracy 0.9589, against 0.9627 for non-private SGD.


39.3.6 Check yourself

A colleague’s implementation divides each noisy sum by the number of records actually in the batch. Which step of the derivation fails? (Step 3: the divisor depends on the data, so the update is no longer a function of the noisy sum alone, and the accountant’s analysis does not apply to it.)
Does changing \(C\) from 0.5 to 5 change \(\varepsilon\)? (No. The sum’s sensitivity and the noise both scale with \(C\), so their ratio \(1/\sigma\) and the accountant’s input are unchanged. It changes accuracy.)

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.4 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C
text:
39.4 Clipping: bias, noise and the choice of C

39.4.1 Context
The clipping norm does not affect privacy, but it controls both forms of cost. Small \(C\) clips more gradients, which biases the update; large \(C\) adds more noise, because the noise is \(\sigma C\). What does the update estimate, and how should \(C\) be chosen?


39.4.2 Statement
Averaged over the sampling and the noise, the update direction is a reweighted gradient: \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i, \tag{39.3}\] the true average gradient \(\frac1n\sum_ig_i\) with each record weighted by \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\). Its noise has standard deviation \(\sigma C/B\) per coordinate.
Scale invariance. If every per-example gradient in a run is clipped, that is \(\|g_i\| \ge C\) at every step, then the update is \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac{\eta C}{B}\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}\frac{g_i}{\|g_i\|} + \sigma\zeta_t\Big), \qquad \zeta_t \sim \mathcal N(0, I), \tag{39.4}\] which depends on \(\eta\) and \(C\) only through their product \(\eta C\).


39.4.3 Derivation

Average over the sampling. Each record is in the batch with probability \(q\), so \(\mathbb E\sum_{i\in S_t}\bar g_i = \sum_{i=1}^n q\,\bar g_i\). The noise has mean zero.
Divide by \(B = qn\). The \(q\) cancels and leaves \(\frac1n\sum_i\bar g_i\), which is Equation 39.3 by the definition of \(\bar g_i\). This is why the denominator is the expected batch size: with it, the update is an unbiased estimate of the average clipped gradient.
The noise. \(\xi_t/B\) has standard deviation \(\sigma C/B\) per coordinate.
Scale invariance. If \(\|g_i\| \ge C\), then \(\bar g_i = Cg_i/\|g_i\|\). Write the noise as \(\sigma C\zeta_t\) with \(\zeta_t\) standard normal. Then \(G_t = C(\sum_ig_i/\|g_i\| + \sigma\zeta_t)\), and \(\eta G_t/B\) is Equation 39.4. Two runs with the same \(\eta C\), the same seed and every gradient clipped produce the same parameters.



39.4.4 Interpretation
Below the gradient norms, only \(\eta C\) matters. When \(C\) is smaller than every per-example gradient, DP-SGD is normalized SGD, which averages unit vectors, plus noise, and its behaviour depends on the product \(\eta C\). Lowering \(C\) further changes nothing once \(\eta\) is scaled up to match. This is why practitioners often clip aggressively and tune only the learning rate; De et al. (2022) report that small clipping norms work well, which this explains.
Above them, noise grows and signal does not. Once \(C\) exceeds most gradient norms, the clipped average stops growing with \(C\), but the noise \(\sigma C/B\) keeps growing in proportion. The signal-to-noise ratio falls like \(1/C\). A large \(C\) is never better than the smallest \(C\) that clips almost nothing.
The bias reweights records, not uniformly. Equation 39.3 gives each record a weight that falls as its gradient grows. Records the model fits badly, such as rare examples, members of small groups or mislabelled points, have large gradients and are down-weighted, while well-fitted records keep their full weight. The update is not the gradient of the training loss but of a reweighted one, whose weights change as training proceeds. Disparate impact measures who pays for this.
Gradient norms change during training. In the DP-SGD run of the running example the median per-example gradient norm is 3.592 at the first step, 0.006 at step 1,000, and rounds to 0.000 from step 3,000 on; non-private training behaves the same way (Figure 39.1, right). The logistic loss flattens on records that are classified with a wide margin, so their gradients vanish. With \(C = 0.5\), every gradient is clipped at the start, and between 9% and 25% of the batch later: the few records still near the decision boundary. A fixed \(C\) is in the scale-invariant regime early and in the unbiased regime late.






Figure 39.1: Left: test accuracy of the running example at \(\sigma = 1\) (\(\varepsilon = 6.71\)) against the clipping norm, with the learning rate fixed at \(\eta = 0.5\) (circles) and with \(\eta C\) fixed at 0.25 (squares). Right: the median per-example gradient norm during non-private training, on a log scale; it falls by about five orders of magnitude.





39.4.5 Example: sweeping C
Table 39.3 trains the running example at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) with seven clipping norms, once with the learning rate fixed at 0.5 and once with \(\eta C\) fixed at \(0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\).
