With \(\eta C\) fixed, accuracy is flat for \(C \le 0.3\), as scale invariance predicts, and falls slowly for large \(C\), where the noise grows while the clipped gradients do not. The best accuracy, 0.9627 at \(C = 0.01\), equals the non-private model’s.


39.4.6 Check yourself

You double \(C\) and halve \(\eta\). When is the training run unchanged, and when not? (Unchanged in distribution if every gradient is clipped under both values of \(C\), by Equation 39.4. If some gradients are shorter than the new \(C\), they now keep more of their length relative to the others, and the update changes.)
Why does dividing by \(B\) rather than \(|S_t|\) make the expected update unbiased for the clipped average? (Because \(\mathbb E\sum_{i\in S_t}\bar g_i = q\sum_i\bar g_i\), and dividing by \(qn\) gives exactly the average. Dividing by \(|S_t|\) is a ratio of random quantities, whose expectation is not the ratio of expectations.)

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.5 Batch size and the number of steps at a fixed budget
text:
39.5 Batch size and the number of steps at a fixed budget

39.5.1 Context
Suppose the privacy budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and the compute budget, a number of epochs \(E\), are fixed. Each epoch is \(1/q\) steps, so \(T = E/q\). Should you take many small steps or few large ones? The accountant answers how much noise each choice needs, and the noise per averaged gradient decides how useful each step is.


39.5.2 Statement
In the regime where the small-\(q\) approximation of Fact 2 holds, keeping \(\varepsilon\) fixed while changing \(q\) at a fixed number of epochs requires \[\sigma \propto \sqrt q, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \frac{\sigma C}{B} \propto \frac{C}{\sqrt{qn}\,\sqrt n} = \frac{C}{\sqrt{Bn}}: \tag{39.5}\] the noise on the averaged gradient falls like \(1/\sqrt B\). Outside that regime, at small \(\sigma\), small batches need even more noise than Equation 39.5 says, so large batches do better than \(1/\sqrt B\).


39.5.3 Derivation

Per-step cost. By Fact 2, for small \(q\) the per-step RDP is about \(\frac\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), and for \(\sigma\) well above 1, \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1 \approx 1/\sigma^2\), so about \(\frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2}\).
Total cost. \(T = E/q\) steps add up to \(\frac{E}q\cdot\frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{\alpha Eq}{2\sigma^2}\). The conversion of Equation 39.2 depends only on this curve, so \(\varepsilon\) stays fixed when \(q/\sigma^2\) does, that is \(\sigma \propto \sqrt q\).
Noise per averaged gradient. \(\sigma C/B\) with \(B = qn\) and \(\sigma \propto \sqrt q\) is proportional to \(\sqrt q/q = 1/\sqrt q\), which is Equation 39.5.
Small \(\sigma\). When \(\sigma\) is near or below 1, \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) is much larger than \(1/\sigma^2\): the per-step cost is higher than step 1 says, by the factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\). Small batches are in this regime, because they need small \(\sigma\), so they pay this factor and need more noise than the \(\sqrt q\) law predicts.



39.5.4 Interpretation
Amplification is most efficient at large \(\sigma\). The ratio \(\sigma/\sqrt q\), which Equation 39.5 says is constant, falls from 22.3 at \(B = 10\) to 10.8 at \(B = 10{,}000\) in Table 39.4. The factor \(\sigma^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) explains most of it: 3.23 at \(\sigma = 0.704\), 1.33 at \(\sigma = 1.36\) and 1.04 at \(\sigma = 3.78\). Steps with little noise are expensive per unit of signal, because in the tail of the privacy loss, the high orders that the conversion uses, sampling buys little (Amplification by subsampling).
Large batches help, but not for free. For a fixed number of epochs, large batches give less noise per step and fewer steps. Fewer steps means less progress if the learning rate cannot grow in proportion, and the best learning rate grows with the batch: in Table 39.5 the best learning rate goes from 0.25 at \(B = 30\) to between 1 and 2 at \(B = 100\) to \(B = 1{,}000\). De et al. (2022) and Anil et al. (2022) train with batches of thousands to hundreds of thousands, and report that large batches are a main ingredient of accurate private models. Large batches also parallelize well, which matters more on accelerators than in this small example.

Left: the noise multiplier the accountant requires, against the \(\sqrt B\) law of Equation 39.5. Right: the noise standard deviation on the averaged gradient, in units of \(C\), against the \(1/\sqrt B\) law. Small batches need more noise than the law predicts.

title: 39  DP-SGD
section: 39.6 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients
text:
39.6 Per-example gradient norms without per-example gradients

39.6.1 Context
Ordinary backpropagation computes the gradient of the sum of the batch’s losses, never the gradient of each record. Clipping needs each record’s gradient norm. Forming all \(B\) per-example gradients costs \(B\) times the memory of the model’s gradient, which for large models is prohibitive. Can the norms, and the clipped sum, be had more cheaply?


39.6.2 Statement
For a dense layer with inputs \(a_i\) and back-propagated errors \(v_i\), record \(i\)’s gradient is \(v_ia_i^\top\) (Fact 4), and \[\big\|v_ia_i^\top\big\|_F = \|v_i\|\,\|a_i\|. \tag{39.6}\] The whole network’s per-example gradient norm is the square root of the sum of these squared norms over layers. The clipped sum is \(\sum_ic_iv_ia_i^\top = (c \circ V)^\top A\), where \(c_i = \min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\), \(V\) and \(A\) stack the errors and inputs as rows, and \(c \circ V\) multiplies row \(i\) of \(V\) by \(c_i\). For a layer applied to a sequence of length \(N\), the number of tokens, record \(i\)’s gradient is \(\sum_tv_{it}a_{it}^\top\), where \(t\) now indexes the tokens, and \[\Big\|\sum_tv_{it}a_{it}^\top\Big\|_F^2 = \sum_{t, s}(a_{it}\cdot a_{is})(v_{it}\cdot v_{is}). \tag{39.7}\]


39.6.3 Derivation

One token. The squared Frobenius norm is the sum of squared entries: \(\sum_{j,k}v_j^2a_k^2 = (\sum_jv_j^2)(\sum_ka_k^2) = \|v\|^2\|a\|^2\).
Layers. The full gradient is the concatenation of the layers’ gradients, so its squared length is the sum of theirs.
The clipped sum. \(\sum_ic_iv_ia_i^\top\) is linear in the errors: scale each record’s error by \(c_i\) and do the usual batch product of errors and inputs. One backward pass computes the errors, the norms come from Equation 39.6, and one more matrix product per layer gives the clipped sum.
Sequences. Expand the square: \(\|\sum_tv_ta_t^\top\|_F^2 = \sum_{t,s}\operatorname{tr}(a_tv_t^\top v_sa_s^\top) = \sum_{t,s}(v_t\cdot v_s)(a_s\cdot a_t)\), using \(\operatorname{tr}(uv^\top) = v\cdot u\). This is the entrywise product of two \(N \times N\) Gram matrices, summed.



39.6.4 Interpretation
This is ghost clipping (Goodfellow 2015 for the norms of single inputs; Lee & Kifer 2021 for clipping with them; Li et al. 2022 for sequences): the per-example gradients are “ghosts” that are never formed. For one token per record it stores \(B(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) numbers per layer instead of \(Bd_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\). For sequences the Gram matrices cost \(2BN^2\), which beats the explicit \(Bd_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) only when \(2N^2 < d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\), so long sequences in narrow layers favour forming the gradients. Bu, Mao & Xu (2022) choose per layer. Either way, privacy is untouched: these are exact computations of the same quantities.

For a random 16-token sequence, Equation 39.7 gives 33.144228 and the explicit gradient’s norm is the same. Table 39.6 compares the memory for several layers.

39.6.6 Check yourself

For a convolutional layer, is the per-example gradient an outer product? (Not of one pair of vectors. It is a sum over spatial positions of outer products, like the sequence case, so Equation 39.7 applies with positions in place of tokens.)

title: 39  DP-SGD
text:
39.7 Microbatches and vectorized per-example gradients

39.7.1 Context
Deep-learning frameworks are built to compute the gradient of a batch’s summed loss in one parallel pass, and per-example clipping breaks that pattern. Computed naively, one record at a time, DP-SGD can run tens or hundreds of times slower than ordinary training. Ghost norms (Section 39.6), which compute each record’s gradient length without forming the gradient, are one remedy. Two others are common in practice. One computes the per-example gradients in parallel after all. The other, microbatching, clips groups of records instead of single records. The first changes nothing about privacy or accuracy, so the question is what the second costs.


39.7.2 Statement
Fix in advance a rule that assigns every record to one of \(K = B/m\) groups, for example a hash of a record identifier taken modulo \(K\), so that a Poisson batch of expected size \(B\) splits into about \(K\) microbatches of about \(m\) records each. Microbatched DP-SGD clips the mean gradient of each microbatch, not each record’s gradient, and adds Gaussian noise to the sum of the clipped means. Under add/remove neighbours that sum has sensitivity \(2C\) as soon as a record can share its group with others, against \(C\) for per-example clipping. The accountant assumes noise \(\sigma\) times the sensitivity, so with the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) it gives the same \(\varepsilon\) only if the noise is \(2\sigma C\). The update divides the noisy sum by the expected number of microbatches, \(B/m\), so its noise has standard deviation \[\frac{2\sigma C}{B/m} = 2m\cdot\frac{\sigma C}{B} \tag{39.8}\] per coordinate, \(2m\) times that of per-example clipping.


39.7.3 Derivation

One record touches one microbatch. The assignment of records to groups is fixed before training and does not depend on which other records are present. A position in the dataset would not do, because adding a record shifts the positions of the records after it. So adding or removing record \(z\) changes only the microbatch of \(z\)’s group. Every other microbatch, and its clipped mean, is the same on both datasets.
That microbatch’s clipped mean moves by up to \(2C\). If the group had other sampled records, its clipped mean changes from one vector of length at most \(C\) to another, and the two can point in opposite directions, so they differ by up to \(2C\). Only when \(z\) is alone in its group does the change shrink to \(C\), the per-example case. A worst-case bound must take \(2C\).
The accountant. Step 2 of Section 39.3 needs the noise to be \(\sigma\) times the sensitivity, so the noise must be \(\sigma \cdot 2C\). The rest of the derivation is unchanged.
Per coordinate. The update divides the noisy sum by a public number, the expected number of microbatches \(B/m\). Dividing \(2\sigma C\) by it gives Equation 39.8.



39.7.4 Interpretation
Microbatching trades accuracy for speed, at a steep rate. Each microbatch is now the unit that is clipped, so a batch has only \(B/m\) clipped terms to carry signal instead of \(B\), while the total noise has doubled to \(2\sigma C\). The mean gradient of a microbatch is also shorter than its records’ gradients when they disagree, so clipping removes less of it, but that does not make up for a factor \(2m\) in the noise.
Check what your library assumes. Some libraries offer microbatches as a speed option. Whether their accounting uses sensitivity \(C\) or \(2C\) for a microbatch, and whether their microbatches are fixed in advance or cut from the shuffled batch, decides whether the reported \(\varepsilon\) is valid. If microbatches are cut by position within each sampled batch, adding one record shifts every later record into a different microbatch, and the bound of step 1 fails.
Vectorization costs nothing. The other remedy keeps per-example clipping and computes the per-example gradients in parallel. JAX’s vmap does it by vectorizing the gradient computation over the examples of a batch, and Opacus does it by attaching hooks that record the per-example quantities during back-propagation. These are exact computations of the same per-example gradients, so they change neither the privacy nor the accuracy. Subramani, Vadivelu & Kamath (2021) show that vectorization combined with just-in-time compilation in many cases brings DP-SGD’s running time close to that of ordinary training.


39.7.5 Example: microbatches on the running example
At the running example’s \(\sigma = 1\), \(C = 0.5\) and \(B = 100\), the noise on the averaged update is 0.0050 per coordinate with per-example clipping. With microbatches of \(m = 4\) records it is 0.0400, eight times more, and with \(m = 16\) it is 0.1600, thirty-two times more, at the same \(\varepsilon = 6.71\). The test accuracy falls with it, from 0.9589 for per-example clipping (Section 39.3) to 0.9336 with microbatches of 4 and 0.7459 with microbatches of 16, one run each.


39.7.6 Check yourself

Why is the sensitivity \(2C\) rather than \(C\), when one record changes only one microbatch? (Its microbatch’s clipped mean changes from one vector of length at most \(C\) to another, which may point the opposite way. Per-example clipping avoids this because, under add/remove, the record’s term goes from absent to present, a change of at most \(C\).)
Does computing per-example gradients with vmap instead of a loop change \(\varepsilon\)? (No. It computes exactly the same clipped sum, only faster.)

39.8.3 Derivation
Each row runs the algorithm of Section 39.3 from a fresh random initialization, with the noise multiplier from the accountant (Fact 2). The non-private baseline uses the same sampling and learning rate with neither clipping nor noise; its accuracy is already at its best after 1,000 steps (0.9627) and stays there (0.9617 after 10,000).


39.8.4 Interpretation
Clipping costs nothing here, noise costs everything. Clipping without noise reaches 0.9649, slightly above non-private SGD: on this problem clipping only limits the influence of the few records with large gradients. The whole loss comes from the noise, and it is steeply non-linear in \(\varepsilon\). From \(\varepsilon = 8\) to 4 the accuracy drops by half a point, from 2 to 1 by 2.7 points, and from 1 to 0.5 by almost 10.
Why the collapse at small \(\varepsilon\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise multiplier is 4.13, so the noise on the averaged gradient has length about \(4.13 \times 0.5/100 \times \sqrt{3{,}329} = 1.19\), against a signal of about 0.026. By the argument of Section 39.3, signal overtakes noise only after about \((1.19/0.026)^2 \approx 2{,}100\) steps, so the 10,000 steps contain only a few independent “useful” moves. Figure 39.4 shows the result: with \(\sigma = 4\) the model reaches its accuracy early and then wanders.
Run-to-run variation grows with the noise. The standard deviation over runs is 0.0019 at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and 0.018 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\). A single private run is a sample from a wide distribution, and comparing two configurations by one run each, as Table 39.3 does, is reliable only for differences well above that spread.
Architecture choices change under privacy. The running example uses tanh units, and that is deliberate. Papernot, Thakurta, Song, Chien & Erlingsson (2021) find that bounded activations such as tanh train better than ReLU under DP-SGD. With the same privacy guarantee, \((2.93, 10^{-5})\) on the handwritten digits of MNIST, their tanh network reaches 98.1% test accuracy against 96.6% for ReLU. On the CIFAR-10 images at \((7.53, 10^{-5})\) it reaches 66.2% against 61.6%. Model size changes too. The noise vector has length about \(\sigma C\sqrt d/B\), growing with the number of parameters \(d\), while the clipped signal cannot exceed \(C\). So the best private model is often smaller than the best non-private one, unless pretraining on public data has already done most of the work (Public data and private fine-tuning).
What the papers report. Larger models can still win when the other knobs scale with them. De, Berrada, Hayes, Smith & Balle (2022) train a 40-layer wide residual network from scratch on CIFAR-10 to 81.4% test accuracy at \((8, 10^{-5})\), with very large batches and small clipping norms, the two practices that Section 39.4 and Section 39.5 explain, among several others. These numbers come from the papers, not from this chapter’s script.






Figure 39.3: Test accuracy of DP-SGD on the running example at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) against \(\varepsilon\) (log scale), with the non-private model dashed. Accuracy is close to non-private above \(\varepsilon = 4\) and falls steeply below \(\varepsilon = 1\).









Figure 39.4: Left: test accuracy during training with clipping alone, with \(\sigma = 1\) (\(\varepsilon = 6.71\)) and with \(\sigma = 4\). Right: the length of the averaged clipped gradient at each step (solid, log scale) against the length of the noise on it (dotted). The noise is about ten times longer than the signal at \(\sigma = 1\), and about forty times at \(\sigma = 4\).





39.8.5 Example: what \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) buys
Part 4 asked how private the configuration \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), \(T = 10{,}000\) is, and answered \(\varepsilon = 6.71\). This chapter adds the other half: on this task it costs 0.4 points of accuracy, 0.9589 against 0.9627. To halve \(\varepsilon\) to about 3 you would need \(\sigma\) between 1.36 and 2.28 and accept about one more point of loss; to reach \(\varepsilon = 1\), four points. Choosing ε asks which of these trades is worth making, and Auditing checks whether the trained model is as private as the accountant says.


39.8.6 Check yourself

Why does the non-private baseline use 1,000 steps rather than 10,000? (Its accuracy is the same, 0.9627 against 0.9617, and the shorter run is the fair comparison: it is the non-private model at its best, not one that was given more steps.)
The training curve at \(\sigma = 4\) is flat after the first few hundred steps. Would more steps at the same \(\sigma\) help? (They would add signal, but they would also raise \(\varepsilon\). At a fixed budget, more steps require more noise per step, and the break-even calculation of the interpretation gets worse, not better.)

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.1 Why this matters
The previous chapter proved a guarantee for one training run. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, run once with a fixed learning rate, clipping norm, batch size and number of steps, satisfies differential privacy (DP) with the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) that the accountant reports; this algorithm is DP-SGD. Nobody trains once. A practitioner tries a grid of learning rates, perhaps several clipping norms and architectures, scores each trained model on a validation set, and ships the best one. The validation set and the training set are private data, and every run touched them. How much does the search leak, and how do you pay for it honestly?
The question has a sharp answer, and it is not “nothing” and not always “the sum of all runs”. Releasing the best of \(k\) private runs can cost exactly \(k\) times one run: there are mechanisms for which the best-of-\(k\) release is no better than releasing all \(k\) runs. That is what composition, the bound that adds up the costs of all runs in Rényi differential privacy (RDP), charges anyway, and for a grid of 10 DP-SGD runs of the running example it turns \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) into 27.23. But a small change to the procedure changes the answer completely. If the number of runs is random, drawn from a suitable distribution before the search starts, the best-of release costs a constant factor (two or three times one run for pure DP) plus a term that grows only with the logarithm of the expected number of runs. For 10 runs in expectation, the cost falls from 27.23 to between 10.08 and 13.67 depending on the distribution, and for 1,000 runs from 1,035.93 to 13.46.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.1.1 The one idea: the release is a function of every run, but a random number of runs hides which ones
The model you ship was chosen by comparing all the runs, so it is a function of all of them, and post-processing says its privacy is at most that of all the runs together. That is the composition bound. It can be tight because a fixed number of runs gives the adversary a sharp event to test for: “every one of the \(k\) runs came out badly”, whose probability multiplies \(k\) per-run likelihood ratios together. A random number of runs blurs that event. If \(K\) is random, the adversary does not know how many runs failed, and the event “all runs failed” is mostly explained by “there were few runs” rather than by the data. The mathematics of this is the generating function \(\mathbb E[x^K]\) of the number of runs, which turns “the best of \(K\) draws” into a formula, and the right choice of its distribution trades a slightly worse search for a much cheaper guarantee.
Table 40.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 40.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.





Result
Where it is used

Tuning DP-SGD with sublinear cost

Choosing among fixed candidates; protecting the validation set


Tuning the running example, and what to report
Every private training project; Choosing ε and Auditing






Notation. One run is a randomized algorithm \(Q\) that trains a model on the private data with hyperparameters drawn from a fixed set of candidates, and outputs the model together with its score, a number used to rank runs, such as a validation accuracy. The outputs of \(Q\) are totally ordered by score, so “the best” is well defined. \(Q(D)\) also denotes the distribution of one run’s output on dataset \(D\), and \(D \sim D'\) are neighbours. \(K\) is the number of runs, fixed (\(K = k\)) or random, and \(f(x) = \mathbb E[x^K]\) its generating function. The best-of-\(K\) algorithm \(M\) draws \(K\), runs \(Q\) independently \(K\) times, and releases the best output. \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is an RDP curve at order \(\alpha\) (the papers this chapter follows write \(\lambda\) for the order), and \(\varepsilon_M\) the curve of \(M\). The distribution of \(K\) has its own parameters. A Poisson number of runs is described by its mean \(\mathbb E[K]\). A geometric number of runs stops after each run with a probability \(\omega \in (0, 1)\), which is also a parameter of the truncated negative binomial distribution, and \(\nu\) denotes the shape of that distribution. Papernot & Steinke write the Poisson mean \(\mu\), the stopping probability \(\gamma\) and the shape \(\eta\). The running example is that of DP-SGD: a network with 3,329 parameters trained on \(n = 10{,}000\) records, with a sampling rate \(q\) of 0.01, a clipping norm \(C\) of 0.5 and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
How to read this chapter. The toolkit has the two facts every derivation uses, post-processing and the distribution of a maximum. Section 40.3 shows why tuning is not free, and Section 40.4 what the obvious fix costs. Section 40.5 is the key idea, in its simplest form, and Section 40.6 its version for DP-SGD; read the statements and the examples first, the derivations on a second pass. Section 40.7 covers the classical selection mechanisms, Section 40.8 runs everything on the running example, and Section 40.9 says what to do and what to report.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
40.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

40.2.1 Fact 1 — RDP curves add, and convert to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)
A mechanism \(M\) satisfies \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-Rényi differential privacy if, for all neighbours \(D \sim D'\), the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) between its output distributions is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\): \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\,\|\,M(D')\big) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_y \Pr_D[y]^\alpha \Pr_{D'}[y]^{1 - \alpha} \le \varepsilon(\alpha), \tag{40.1}\] where \(\Pr_D[y]\) is the probability that \(M(D)\) outputs \(y\). The sum is the average of the likelihood ratio \(\Pr_D[y]/\Pr_{D'}[y]\) raised to the power \(\alpha - 1\), averaged over outputs drawn from \(D\); large orders weight the rare, large ratios more. As \(\alpha \to \infty\) the divergence becomes the largest log ratio, so pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP is the point \(\alpha = \infty\). Three properties are used here (Rényi differential privacy). Running mechanisms in sequence, even adaptively, adds their curves. The divergence grows with the order, so a bound at order \(\alpha_2\) also holds at every \(\alpha_1 < \alpha_2\). And a curve converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP at the best order, \[\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big], \tag{40.2}\] or, read the other way, \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP gives \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP for every \(\hat\varepsilon\) with \(\hat\delta = e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \hat\varepsilon)}(1 - 1/\alpha)^{\alpha - 1}/\alpha\) (From RDP to (ε, δ)). DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and 10,000 steps has \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) by this conversion.


40.2.2 Fact 2 — Post-processing, and why “the best” is a post-processing of all runs
A computation that uses only a private output, and not the data, is as private as that output (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). The best of \(k\) runs is computed from the \(k\) outputs alone: compare their scores and keep the winner. So the best-of-\(k\) release is a post-processing of the \(k\) runs, and it is at least as private as releasing all of them, which by composition costs \(k\) times one run. The question of this chapter is whether it can be more private than that. Post-processing never makes things worse, but it does not promise to make them better.


40.2.3 Fact 3 — The best of \(K\) draws, and the generating function
Draw an output \(Y\) from a distribution \(Q\) on outcomes ordered from best to worst. The best of \(k\) independent draws is no better than \(y\) exactly when every draw is no better than \(y\), so \[\Pr[\text{best of } k \preceq y] = Q(\preceq y)^k, \tag{40.3}\] where \(Q(\preceq y)\) is the probability that one draw is no better than \(y\) and \(Q(\prec y)\) the probability that it is strictly worse. The best is exactly \(y\) when all draws are no better than \(y\) but not all are strictly worse: \(Q(\preceq y)^k - Q(\prec y)^k\). Now let the number of draws \(K\) be random, independent of the draws. Averaging over \(K\) replaces \(x^k\) by \(\mathbb E[x^K]\), which is the generating function of \(K\), written \(f(x) = \sum_k \Pr[K = k]\,x^k\). So \[\Pr[M = y] = f\big(Q(\preceq y)\big) - f\big(Q(\prec y)\big). \tag{40.4}\] A fixed \(K = k\) has \(f(x) = x^k\); a Poisson number of runs with mean \(\mathbb E[K]\) has \(f(x) = e^{\mathbb E[K](x - 1)}\); a geometric number on \(\{1, 2, \dots\}\), \(\Pr[K = k] = \omega(1 - \omega)^{k - 1}\), has \(f(x) = \omega x/(1 - (1 - \omega)x)\), by summing the geometric series.
A die. The best of two rolls of a fair die is a 6 unless both rolls are below 6: \(1 - (5/6)^2 = 11/36 = 0.3056\). In the form of Equation 40.4 with outcome \(y = 6\) the best, \(Q(\preceq 6) = 1\) and \(Q(\prec 6) = 5/6\), so \(P = 1^2 - (5/6)^2\). If instead you roll once or twice with probability \(\frac12\) each, \(f(x) = \frac12x + \frac12x^2\) and \(\Pr[\text{best} = 6] = f(1) - f(5/6) = 1 - \frac12\cdot\frac56 - \frac12\cdot\frac{25}{36} = 17/72 = 0.2361\), the average of the one-roll answer \(1/6\) and the two-roll answer \(11/36\).


40.2.4 Fact 4 — Disjoint parts of the data cost the larger of their costs
Suppose a dataset is split into two disjoint parts, a training set and a validation set, and each record lives in exactly one of them. An algorithm that is \(\varepsilon_1\)-DP in the training records (with the validation set fixed) and \(\varepsilon_2\)-DP in the validation records (with the training set fixed) is \(\max(\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2)\)-DP for neighbours that add or remove one record anywhere, because a pair of neighbours differs in one record, which sits in one part only. The same holds order by order for RDP curves: the curve is the pointwise maximum. This is the idea of parallel composition, and it is why a held-out validation set does not add its cost to training’s cost: it adds its own cost only where it is larger.

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.3 Best of k is k times worse
text:
40.3 Best of k is k times worse

40.3.1 Context
The intuitive argument for ignoring tuning goes: the release is one model, chosen among a handful by one comparison, and a choice among eight learning rates carries at most three bits. That argument is wrong in two ways. The released model is not the choice; it is a whole private run, picked because of how it came out. And the comparison is a function of every run. How bad can it be?


40.3.2 Statement
Let one run be randomized response on two outcomes, “good” and “bad” (best first). On \(D\) the run comes out good with probability \(\frac{1}{1 + e^\varepsilon}\), and on its neighbour \(D'\) with probability \(\frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}\). One run is exactly \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Releasing the best of \(k\) runs is exactly \(k\varepsilon\)-DP: \[\frac{\Pr_D[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]}{\Pr_{D'}[\text{best of } k \text{ is bad}]} = \frac{\big(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\big)^k}{\big(1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\big)^k} = e^{k\varepsilon}. \tag{40.5}\] In RDP, Papernot & Steinke (2022, Proposition 17) show that the same release has \(D_\alpha \ge k\varepsilon - k\ln(1 + e^{-\varepsilon})/(\alpha - 1)\), so at large orders it also costs about \(k\) times one run.


40.3.3 Derivation

Best of \(k\) is bad only if every run is bad. By Fact 3 with outcome “bad” the worst, \(\Pr[\text{best is bad}] = Q(\text{bad})^k\).
Each run’s ratio is \(e^\varepsilon\). \(Q_D(\text{bad}) = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and \(Q_{D'}(\text{bad}) = 1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), a ratio of \(e^\varepsilon\).
The \(k\) ratios multiply. Raising both to the power \(k\) gives Equation 40.5. The other outcome, “good”, has the ratio \((1 - Q_D(\text{bad})^k)/(1 - Q_{D'}(\text{bad})^k)\), which is between \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) and 1, so the largest log ratio over outcomes is \(k\varepsilon\).
The Rényi version. Keep only the “bad” term in the sum of Fact 1: \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha} \ge \Pr_D[\text{bad}]^\alpha \Pr_{D'}[\text{bad}]^{1 - \alpha} = e^{k\varepsilon\alpha}(1 + e^\varepsilon)^{-k}\), which is \((e^{k\varepsilon})^\alpha\) times \(\Pr_{D'}[\text{bad}]\). Taking logarithms and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives \(D_\alpha \ge (k\varepsilon\alpha - k\ln(1 + e^\varepsilon))/(\alpha - 1) = k\varepsilon - k\ln(1 + e^{-\varepsilon})/(\alpha - 1)\), using \(\ln(1 + e^\varepsilon) = \varepsilon + \ln(1 + e^{-\varepsilon})\).



40.3.4 Interpretation
Where the loss comes from. The whole loss sits on one event: every run failed. Its probability is small on both datasets, but its ratio is the product of \(k\) per-run ratios, because the runs are independent and the event requires all of them. Figure 40.1 (right) shows the privacy loss distribution for \(\varepsilon = 1\): one run has losses \(\pm1\); the best of 10 has a loss of \(-0.0446\) with probability 0.9564 and a loss of 10 with probability 0.0436. A test that looks for “the released model is bad” detects membership with a likelihood ratio of \(e^{10}\) whenever it fires.
This is not an artefact of a contrived mechanism. A DP-SGD run that sometimes diverges, a learning rate that sometimes produces a useless model, a candidate that rarely clears a threshold: each is a run with a “bad” outcome whose probability depends a little on the data. Best-of-\(k\) multiplies those small dependences. The example is extreme because it puts all of each run’s privacy loss on a single binary outcome. A particular DP-SGD search may leak much less, but no analysis that knows only each run’s guarantee can promise it, so the general bound for a fixed \(k\) is composition, which grows linearly (Section 40.4).
The bound for a fixed \(k\) is tight, so the procedure must change. Composition says best-of-\(k\) costs at most \(k\varepsilon\), and Equation 40.5 says some mechanism attains it. No better analysis of “the best of exactly \(k\) runs” exists for all mechanisms. A better guarantee needs a different procedure, and the next sections change one thing: the number of runs.
Non-private tuning leaks too. If you tune without any noise and then train privately once with the chosen hyperparameters, the hyperparameters are a non-private function of the data, and the final run’s \(\varepsilon\) does not cover them. Papernot & Steinke (2022, Section 2) build a support vector machine whose best regularization weight changes when a few outliers are added, so the chosen value reveals whether the outliers were in the training set, a membership inference through a single number.






Figure 40.1: Left: the exact \(\varepsilon\) of releasing the best of \(K\) randomized-response runs, each \(1\)-DP, against the expected number of runs, for a fixed number of runs, a Poisson, a geometric and a logarithmic number. A fixed number grows linearly; the geometric and logarithmic numbers stay below their bounds \(3\varepsilon\) and \(2\varepsilon\). Right: the privacy loss of the released outcome under \(D\) for one run, the best of 10 runs and the best of a Poisson number with mean 10; the best of 10 puts a loss of 10 on an event of probability 0.0436.





40.3.5 Example: the numbers for \(\varepsilon = 1\)
With \(\varepsilon = 1\) a run is good with probability 0.2689 on \(D\) and 0.7311 on \(D'\). The script computes the best-of-\(k\) distributions exactly. The largest log ratio is 2.0000 for \(k = 2\), 3.0000 for \(k = 3\) and 10.0000 for \(k = 10\), exactly \(k\varepsilon\). At order \(\alpha = 2\), the Rényi divergence of the best of 10 is 6.8683, between the lower bound of step 4, 6.8674, and composition’s upper bound, ten times one run’s 0.7353, which is 7.3533. Composition overstates the exact value by 7%; at order 2 it is nearly tight, as at order \(\infty\).


40.3.6 Check yourself

Releasing only the index of the best run, not the trained model, would it fix Equation 40.5? (No. In the example the output is “good” or “bad”, and the index of the best run carries the same event: if all runs are bad, every index is a bad run, and the chosen one reveals it. What matters is that the release depends on every run.)
Suppose each run is \(\varepsilon\)-DP and you release the best of \(k\) runs together with all \(k\) scores. What is the cost? (At most \(k\varepsilon\) by composition, the same as the best alone in the worst case; releasing more does not cost more here because the best of \(k\) already attains the bound.)

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
text:
40.4 Paying by composition

40.4.1 Context
The safe answer is to charge for every run. What does it cost on the running example, and how much more noise does each run need to keep the total fixed?


40.4.2 Statement
If each of \(k\) runs has RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), releasing anything computed from all of them, in particular the best, has curve at most \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le k\,\varepsilon(\alpha), \tag{40.6}\] converted to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) by Equation 40.2. For DP-SGD, \(k\) runs of \(T\) steps at noise multiplier \(\sigma\) cost the same as one run of \(kT\) steps, so keeping the total at a target \(\varepsilon\) means choosing \(\sigma\) for \(kT\) steps.


40.4.3 Derivation

The release is a post-processing of the \(k\) runs (Fact 2).
The \(k\) runs compose. Each run uses fresh randomness, and RDP curves add (Fact 1), so their joint output has curve \(k\varepsilon(\alpha)\). This holds even if the candidates are chosen adaptively, each after seeing the earlier results, since RDP composition covers adaptive sequences.
DP-SGD. One run of \(T\) steps has curve \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\), where \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}\) is one subsampled Gaussian step. \(k\) runs give \(kT\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\), the curve of one run of \(kT\) steps.



40.4.4 Interpretation
Composition is cheaper than \(k\varepsilon\), but still grows like \(k\). In \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) terms, \(k\) runs cost less than \(k\) times one run’s \(\varepsilon\), because the conversion of Equation 40.2 pays its \(\ln(1/\delta)\) term once, and because adding curves behaves like advanced composition, roughly \(\sqrt k\) at small \(\varepsilon\). On the running example, Table 40.2, 10 runs cost 4.06 times one run, not 10. But the curve grows linearly, and so does \(\varepsilon\) once the budget is large: from 30 to 100 runs, \(\varepsilon\) grows by a factor 2.5.
Raising the noise is the honest way to keep the budget. To keep the total at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\), each of 10 runs needs \(\sigma = 2.45\) instead of 1. DP-SGD showed what that costs on this task: more noise per step means fewer useful steps, and accuracy falls steeply below some budget.
When composition is the right tool. For a handful of candidates, two or three, composition costs little more than the alternatives below and needs no change to the procedure. Figure 40.2 shows that the random-\(K\) methods only pull away from composition from a few runs on.

Why does \(k\) runs of \(T\) steps cost exactly as much as one run of \(kT\) steps, if the runs start from different initializations? (The accountant does not look at the parameters. Each step costs \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) whatever it is applied to, and curves add.)

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.5 Random stopping: the best of a geometric number of runs
text:
40.5 Random stopping: the best of a geometric number of runs

40.5.1 Context
Liu & Talwar (2019) asked whether the best of many \(\varepsilon\)-DP runs can cost a constant multiple of \(\varepsilon\), independent of how many runs are made. They found that it can, with one change: after each run, flip a coin and stop with probability \(\omega\). The number of runs is then geometric with mean \(1/\omega\), and releasing the best run seen is \(3\varepsilon\)-DP whatever \(\omega\) is.


40.5.2 Statement
Algorithm (random stopping). Repeat: run \(Q\) on the data and keep its output; with probability \(\omega\), stop and release the best output kept so far.
If \(Q\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, the release is \(3\varepsilon\)-DP (Liu & Talwar 2019, Theorem 3.2). Its output distribution is explicit: for an outcome \(y\) with probability \(p\) under one run, \(p_>\) the probability that one run is strictly better than \(y\) and \(p_\ge = p_> + p\) the probability that it is at least as good, \[\Pr[M = y] = \frac{\omega\,p}{\big(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>\big)\big(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge\big)}. \tag{40.7}\] Its utility: for any fraction \(\pi\), the release falls below the top \(\pi\)-quantile of one run’s score with probability \[\Pr[\text{miss}] = \frac{\omega(1 - \pi)}{\omega + (1 - \omega)\pi} \le \frac{\omega}{\pi}. \tag{40.8}\]


40.5.3 Derivation
The idea: the probability of each output is a ratio built from three probabilities of one run, \(p\), \(p_>\) and \(p_\ge\). Each moves by at most \(e^\varepsilon\) between neighbours, and the parameter \(\omega\) enters in a way that cannot amplify those moves.

The number of runs. The algorithm stops after run \(j\) with probability \(\omega(1 - \omega)^{j - 1}\): it continued \(j - 1\) times and stopped once. So \(K\) is geometric with mean \(1/\omega\) and generating function \(f(x) = \omega x/(1 - (1 - \omega)x)\) (Fact 3).
Apply Equation 40.4. One run is no better than \(y\) with probability \(1 - p_>\) and strictly worse with probability \(1 - p_\ge\). So \(\Pr[M = y] = f(1 - p_>) - f(1 - p_\ge)\). Since \(1 - (1 - \omega)(1 - p_>) = \omega + (1 - \omega)p_>\), this is \[\frac{\omega(1 - p_>)}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>} - \frac{\omega(1 - p_\ge)}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge}. \tag{40.9}\]
Simplify. Over the common denominator, the numerator is \(\omega\) times \((1 - p_>)(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge) - (1 - p_\ge)(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>)\). Expanding, the terms with \(\omega\) give \(\omega(p_\ge - p_>) = \omega p\), and the terms with \(1 - \omega\) give \((1 - \omega)(p_\ge - p_>p_\ge - p_> + p_\ge p_>) = (1 - \omega)p\). Their sum is \(p\), which gives Equation 40.7.
Bound each factor. Write primes for the same quantities on \(D'\). Each of \(p\), \(p_>\) and \(p_\ge\) is the probability of an event about one run’s output, so \(\varepsilon\)-DP of \(Q\) gives \(p \le e^\varepsilon p'\), \(p'_> \le e^\varepsilon p_>\) and \(p'_\ge \le e^\varepsilon p_\ge\). The first bounds the numerator ratio. For the denominators, \(\omega + (1 - \omega)p'_> \le e^\varepsilon\big(\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>\big)\), because \(\omega \le e^\varepsilon\omega\) and \(p'_> \le e^\varepsilon p_>\); the same for \(p_\ge\).
Multiply. \(\Pr[M(D) = y]/\Pr[M(D') = y] = \frac{p}{p'}\cdot\frac{\omega + (1 - \omega)p'_>}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_>}\cdot\frac{\omega + (1 - \omega)p'_\ge}{\omega + (1 - \omega)p_\ge} \le e^{3\varepsilon}\). This holds for every outcome, so the release is \(3\varepsilon\)-DP.
Utility. The release is below the top \(\pi\)-quantile only if every run is: \(\sum_j\omega(1 - \omega)^{j - 1}(1 - \pi)^j = \omega(1 - \pi)/(1 - (1 - \omega)(1 - \pi))\), by the geometric series, which is the equality in Equation 40.8. It is at most \(\omega/\pi\) because \(\pi(1 - \pi) \le \omega(1 - \pi) + \pi\).



40.5.4 Interpretation
Why the fixed-\(k\) disaster disappears. In Equation 40.4 with \(f(x) = x^k\), the ratio for the worst outcome is \((Q(\preceq y)/Q'(\preceq y))^k\), a \(k\)-th power. The geometric generating function is a ratio of linear functions of \(x\), so the ratio of outputs is a product of three ratios of linear functions, each moved by at most \(e^\varepsilon\). The event “every run was bad” is now mostly the event “the coin stopped early”, which does not depend on the data.
The \(3\) is real. The bound is attained in the limit. Take three outcomes, best first, with probabilities \((a, b, 1 - a - b)\) on \(D\) and \((ae^\varepsilon, be^{-\varepsilon}, \dots)\) on \(D'\), with \(\omega \ll b \ll a\) small. For the middle outcome, the numerator ratio \(p/p' = e^\varepsilon\) and, since \(\omega\) is negligible next to \(p_>\) and \(p_\ge \approx p_>\), both denominator ratios approach \(e^\varepsilon\). The example below computes it.
Two outcomes give only \(2\varepsilon\). On randomized response, the “good” outcome has \(p_> = 0\), so one denominator factor is \(\omega\) on both datasets, and only two factors can move. Figure 40.1 (left) shows the exact \(\varepsilon\) of geometric stopping on randomized response rising toward \(2\varepsilon\) as the mean number of runs grows.
The utility guarantee is about quantiles, and it costs runs. Equation 40.8 does not promise the best candidate. It promises that, with probability at least \(1 - \omega/\pi\), the release is at least as good as the top \(\pi\) fraction of a single run’s outcomes. To find a candidate in the top \(1/m\) of a grid of \(m\) with probability 0.9, you need \(\omega/\pi \le 0.1\), so \(\omega = 0.1/m\), a mean of \(10m\) runs, ten times the grid. The exact miss probability is smaller than the bound, but not by much when \(\pi\) is small. This is the price of the method: you buy a constant privacy cost with extra runs, and the geometric distribution often stops after one or two.
Approximate DP and threshold variants. Liu & Talwar also give a version with a known score threshold, which stops as soon as a run clears it and costs \(2\varepsilon\) plus a small term (their Theorem 3.1), and versions for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP runs and with a hard cap on the number of runs (Theorems 3.4 and 3.5). For DP-SGD, which is analysed in RDP, Section 40.6 is the version to use.


40.5.5 Example: a 3ε pair, and the utility of stopping
On randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 1\), geometric stopping gives an exact \(\varepsilon\) of 1.3106 at \(\omega = 0.5\), 1.7957 at \(\omega = 0.1\), 1.9769 at \(\omega = 0.01\) and 1.9977 at \(\omega = 0.001\), approaching 2. On the three-outcome pair, with \(\varepsilon = 1\) for one run, Table 40.3 shows the exact \(\varepsilon\) of the release approaching 3, and the logarithmic distribution of Section 40.6 approaching 2.

For utility, suppose a grid of 8 candidates with one best. With \(\omega = 1/8\), a mean of 8 runs, the chance of never trying the top eighth is 0.4667, and the bound \(\omega/\pi = 1\) says nothing. With \(\omega = 1/80\), a mean of 80 runs, the chance falls to 0.0805 against a bound of 0.1. To have the same chance of hitting a top \(1/80\) fraction you would again need ten times more runs: with \(\omega = 1/80\) the miss probability for \(\pi = 1/80\) is 0.4969.


40.5.6 Check yourself

In step 4, why does \(\omega \le e^\varepsilon\omega\) matter? (The denominator is a mixture of the constant \(\omega\), which does not depend on the data, and \(p_>\), which does. Each part grows by at most \(e^\varepsilon\), so the sum does. The constant part is what blurs the “all runs failed” event.)
If you wanted to run exactly 8 candidates, could you emulate it by setting \(\omega = 1/8\)? (Only in mean. The geometric distribution stops after one run with probability 1/8 and after more than 16 runs with probability \((7/8)^{16} = 0.118\); Figure 40.3 shows how spread out it is. That spread is what buys the privacy.)

title: 40  Hyperparameter tuning and private selection
section: 40.6 Rényi bounds for a random number of runs
text:
40.6 Rényi bounds for a random number of runs

40.6.1 Context
DP-SGD is not usefully \(\varepsilon\)-DP for any small \(\varepsilon\); its guarantee is an RDP curve that converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Papernot & Steinke (2022) extended random stopping to RDP and to a family of distributions for \(K\), which lets you choose between more runs and less privacy cost. What do their bounds say, and what do they cost on the running example?


40.6.2 Statement
The generic bound (Papernot & Steinke 2022, Lemma 7). Let \(K\) have generating function \(f\), and let \(M\) release the best of \(K\) independent runs of \(Q\) (if \(K = 0\), an output that does not depend on the data). For neighbours with run distributions \(Q, Q'\) and best-of distributions \(M, M'\), \[D_\alpha(M\|M') \le D_\alpha(Q\|Q') + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big[f'(s)^\alpha f'(s')^{1 - \alpha}\Big] \tag{40.10}\] for some numbers \(s, s' \in [0, 1]\) that are the probabilities of one and the same randomized test accepting a run’s output, on \(D\) and on \(D'\).
Poisson (Theorem 6). If \(K\) is Poisson with mean \(\mathbb E[K]\), and \(Q\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP and \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP with \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\), then \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) + \mathbb E[K]\hat\delta + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{40.11}\]
Truncated negative binomial (Theorem 2). For \(\nu > -1\) and \(\omega \in (0, 1)\), let \(K\) on \(\{1, 2, \dots\}\) have \(\Pr[K = k] = \frac{(1 - \omega)^k}{\omega^{-\nu} - 1}\prod_{i = 0}^{k - 1}\frac{i + \nu}{i + 1}\), and for \(\nu = 0\) the logarithmic distribution \(\Pr[K = k] = \frac{(1 - \omega)^k}{k\ln(1/\omega)}\). The case \(\nu = 1\) is the geometric distribution. If \(Q\) is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP and \((\hat\alpha, \varepsilon(\hat\alpha))\)-RDP, then \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \varepsilon(\alpha) + (1 + \nu)\Big(1 - \frac1{\hat\alpha}\Big)\varepsilon(\hat\alpha) + \frac{(1 + \nu)\ln(1/\omega)}{\hat\alpha} + \frac{\ln\mathbb E[K]}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{40.12}\] for every \(\hat\alpha \ge 1\), with \(\mathbb E[K] = \frac{\nu(1 - \omega)}{\omega(1 - \omega^\nu)}\) (\(\nu \neq 0\)) or \(\frac{1/\omega - 1}{\ln(1/\omega)}\) (\(\nu = 0\)). For an \(\varepsilon\)-DP run, letting both orders go to infinity gives \((2 + \nu)\varepsilon\)-DP (their Corollary 3): \(3\varepsilon\) for the geometric distribution, as in Section 40.5, and \(2\varepsilon\) for the logarithmic.


40.6.3 Derivation
The generic bound comes from writing the best-of distribution of Fact 3 as a derivative, then pulling the derivative out of the Rényi sum. The Poisson bound then follows in a few lines. Take outputs finite and \(\Pr[K = 0] = 0\) for simplicity (the paper handles the general case).

The best-of probability is an average of \(f'\). By Equation 40.4 and the fundamental theorem of calculus, \(M(y) = f(Q(\preceq y)) - f(Q(\prec y)) = \int_{Q(\prec y)}^{Q(\preceq y)}f'(x)\,\mathrm dx\). The interval has length \(Q(y)\), so \(M(y) = Q(y)\,c(y)\), where \(c(y)\) is the average of \(f'\) over that interval, the expectation of \(f'(X)\) for \(X\) uniform on it. Likewise \(M'(y) = Q'(y)\,c'(y)\).
Put it in the Rényi sum. \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(M\|M')} = \sum_yA(y)^\alpha M'(y)^{1 - \alpha} = \sum_yQ(y)^\alpha Q'(y)^{1 - \alpha}\,c(y)^\alpha c'(y)^{1 - \alpha}\).
Bound the averages by a worst case. Couple \(X\) and \(X'\) at the same relative position \(t \in [0, 1]\) in their intervals. The function \((u, v) \mapsto u^\alpha v^{1 - \alpha}\) is jointly convex for \(\alpha > 1\), so by Jensen’s inequality \(c(y)^\alpha c'(y)^{1 - \alpha} \le \mathbb E[f'(X)^\alpha f'(X')^{1 - \alpha}]\), which is at most the largest value of \(f'(s)^\alpha f'(s')^{1 - \alpha}\) over \(t\), with \(s = Q(\prec y) + tQ(y)\) and \(s' = Q'(\prec y) + tQ'(y)\).
Pull the worst case out of the sum. Bounding every \(c^\alpha c'^{1 - \alpha}\) by the largest one over \(y\) and \(t\) leaves \(\sum_yQ(y)^\alpha Q'(y)^{1 - \alpha} = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(Q\|Q')}\) times that maximum. Taking logarithms and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives Equation 40.10.
\(s\) and \(s'\) come from one test. The test “accept an output worse than \(y\); accept \(y\) itself with probability \(t\); reject anything better” accepts with probability \(s\) on \(Q\) and \(s'\) on \(Q'\). Any privacy guarantee of \(Q\) therefore constrains the pair, by post-processing (Fact 2).
Poisson: compute \(f'\). \(f(x) = e^{\mathbb E[K](x - 1)}\), so \(f'(x) = \mathbb E[K] e^{\mathbb E[K](x - 1)}\) and \(\ln[f'(s)^\alpha f'(s')^{1 - \alpha}] = \ln\mathbb E[K] + \mathbb E[K]\big[\alpha(s - 1) + (1 - \alpha)(s' - 1)\big] = \ln\mathbb E[K] + \mathbb E[K]\big[(\alpha - 1)(1 - s') - \alpha(1 - s)\big]\).
Use \((\hat\varepsilon, \hat\delta)\)-DP on the rejection event. \(1 - s'\) and \(1 - s\) are the probabilities that the test of step 5 rejects, on \(D'\) and \(D\), so \(1 - s' \le e^{\hat\varepsilon}(1 - s) + \hat\delta\). The bracket is at most \((1 - s)\big[(\alpha - 1)e^{\hat\varepsilon} - \alpha\big] + (\alpha - 1)\hat\delta\).
The condition on \(\hat\varepsilon\) kills the first term. \(e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le 1 + \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\) is the same as \((\alpha - 1)e^{\hat\varepsilon} \le \alpha\), so the first term is not positive and the bracket is at most \((\alpha - 1)\hat\delta\). Divide by \(\alpha - 1\) and add \(D_\alpha(Q\|Q') \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\): that is Equation 40.11.
Truncated negative binomial. Here \(f'(x) = \omega^{\nu + 1}\mathbb E[K]\,(1 - (1 - \omega)x)^{-\nu - 1}\). The same steps apply, except that step 7 bounds the probabilities \(1 - s\) and \(1 - s'\) through the run’s RDP guarantee at a second order \(\hat\alpha\), again by post-processing, which gives Equation 40.12; Papernot & Steinke (2022, Appendix B.2) carry out the algebra, and Section M.3 in the appendices does it step by step, with their Corollaries 3 and 4.



40.6.4 Interpretation
What each term pays for. In Equation 40.11 and Equation 40.12 the first term, \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), is one run: you never pay less than one run, since the release contains a run. The last term, \(\ln\mathbb E[K]/(\alpha - 1)\), is the price of the number of runs, and it is logarithmic: multiplying the expected number of runs by 10 adds \(\ln 10/(\alpha - 1)\). The middle terms are the price of the tail of \(K\): how much the distribution of \(K\) lets the adversary tell “many runs, all bad” from “few runs”. For the truncated negative binomial it is a constant times the run’s own privacy at another order, so the total is a constant multiple of one run plus the logarithm. For the Poisson distribution it is \(\mathbb E[K]\hat\delta\), which is linear in \(\mathbb E[K]\) but multiplied by the run’s \(\hat\delta\) at a small \(\hat\varepsilon\), and so is small only when one run is very private.
Choosing \(\nu\): privacy against the shape of \(K\). Smaller \(\nu\) means a smaller multiple, \((1 + \nu)\), of the second term, so better privacy; the logarithmic distribution (\(\nu = 0\)) is the best of the family that keeps \(K \ge 1\) with a finite mean. But smaller \(\nu\) also means a more skewed distribution of \(K\). With mean 10, the logarithmic distribution has \(\omega = 0.02692\) and stops after a single run with probability 0.2692, against 0.1000 for the geometric (\(\nu = 1\)) and 0.1562 for \(\nu = 0.5\). The Poisson distribution is the limit \(\nu \to \infty\) at a fixed mean, and is concentrated near its mean: with mean 10, \(\Pr[K \le 1] = 4.99 \times 10^{-4}\). Figure 40.3 shows the four distributions with mean 8. A skewed \(K\) often runs few candidates, which Section 40.8 shows costs accuracy.
How tight are the bounds? They are upper bounds for every run with the given curve, so they can be loose for a particular one. On randomized response with \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and a logarithmic number of runs with mean 10, Table 40.4 compares the exact Rényi divergence of the release with Equation 40.12 and with composition of 10 runs. Randomized response is pure DP, so the bound keeps falling as \(\hat\alpha\) grows, and the table gives its limit, in which the two middle terms become \((1 + \nu)\varepsilon = 0.5\). At order 2, Equation 40.12 is worse than composition, because its constant terms dominate at small orders. At orders 5 and 20, where conversions to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) usually land, it is 2.6 and 4.3 times below composition, and 3.7 and 1.7 times above the exact value.

There the exact divergence is 0.4421, the bound 1.7654 and composition 2.7165.
What the theorems do not cover. Each run must draw its candidate independently from a fixed distribution, typically uniform on the grid: this is random search. Adaptive methods that pick the next candidate from the scores so far, such as Bayesian optimization, are not covered and need adaptive composition (Adaptive composition). The score must be part of each run’s private output: if it is computed on private validation data, it must be private too (Section 40.7). And for zero-concentrated DP runs, whose curve is a line \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), the paper’s Corollary 4 gives the closed form \(\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le 2\sqrt{\rho\ln\mathbb E[K]} + 2(1 + \nu)\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\omega)} - \nu\rho\) for orders up to \(1 + \sqrt{\ln\mathbb E[K]/\rho}\), when \(\rho \le \ln(1/\omega)\): the overhead grows like the square root of the logarithm of the expected number of runs.

The script evaluates Equation 40.11 and Equation 40.12 on the RDP curve of one DP-SGD run of the running example, at every order of the accountant, takes the best \(\hat\alpha\) for Equation 40.12 and, for Equation 40.11, the best \(\hat\delta\) that the curve gives at \(\hat\varepsilon = \ln(1 + 1/(\alpha - 1))\) by the conversion of Fact 1, uses that a bound at a larger order holds at a smaller one, and converts with Equation 40.2. In Equation 40.12, why can’t the cost fall below one run, \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), however few runs are expected? (The release is the output of one run. If \(K = 1\) it is exactly one run, so no bound can be below one run’s divergence.)

section: 40.7 Selecting by a noisy validation score
text:
40.7 Selecting by a noisy validation score

40.7.1 Context
The methods so far treat each run as a black box that outputs a model and its score. A different situation is common too: the candidates are already fixed, for example public pretrained checkpoints or models whose training is accounted for separately, and only the choice among them uses private data, a held-out validation set. That is a selection problem, and Selection solved it with the exponential mechanism and report-noisy-max. How do those tools apply to tuning, and what do they leave out?


40.7.2 Statement
Let the score of candidate \(r\) be its number of correct predictions \(u(r)\) on a private validation set of \(m\) records. Adding or removing one validation record changes every count by at most \(\Delta u = 1\). The exponential mechanism picks candidate \(r\) in \(\mathcal R\), the set of candidates, with probability proportional to \(e^{\varepsilon u(r)/(2\Delta u)}\); it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for the validation records, and its expected gap to the best count is at most \(\frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln|\mathcal R| + 1)\), an accuracy gap of \(\frac{2}{\varepsilon m}(\ln|\mathcal R| + 1)\). Report-noisy-max, which adds Laplace or Gumbel noise to each count and releases the index of the largest, has the same guarantee (with Gumbel noise it is the same mechanism).
If the candidates were trained on the private training set, with \(k\) runs whose RDP curves are \(\varepsilon_1(\alpha), \dots, \varepsilon_k(\alpha)\), and the validation set is disjoint from it, releasing the selected model costs \[\varepsilon_M(\alpha) \le \max\Big(\sum_{j = 1}^k\varepsilon_j(\alpha),\ \varepsilon_{\text{sel}}(\alpha)\Big), \tag{40.13}\] where \(\varepsilon_{\text{sel}}\) is the selection mechanism’s curve in the validation records.


40.7.3 Derivation

The exponential mechanism. One record changes each count by at most 1, so each weight \(e^{\varepsilon u(r)/2}\) by at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) and the normalizing sum by at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\); the ratio of probabilities is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) (Selection). Candidates more than \(c\) below the best have weight at most \(e^{-\varepsilon c/2}\) times the best’s, so the probability of picking one is at most \(|\mathcal R|e^{-\varepsilon c/2}\), and integrating the tail gives the expected gap (Utility of the exponential mechanism).
Training records. For a training record, the validation set and the selection noise are fixed and independent of it. The released model and index are a post-processing of the \(k\) trained models (Fact 2), which compose (Fact 1): \(\sum_j\varepsilon_j(\alpha)\).
Validation records. For a validation record, the trained models do not depend on it, and the release is the selection mechanism applied to fixed candidates: \(\varepsilon_{\text{sel}}(\alpha)\).
Combine. Each record is in one of the two sets, so Fact 4 gives the maximum.



40.7.4 Interpretation
Selection is cheap; training is not. On a validation set of thousands of records, selecting privately costs almost nothing: the scores differ by tens of correct predictions and the mechanism’s temperature, \(2/\varepsilon\), is a few. The expensive part of tuning is that each candidate was trained on private data, and Equation 40.13 still charges for all \(k\) trainings by composition. The exponential mechanism has nothing to say about it, because a trained model is not a low-sensitivity score: Liu & Talwar’s starting point was exactly that the candidates’ quality is only known through private, randomized runs.
When the classical tools are the right ones. If the candidates do not depend on the private training data, the training term in Equation 40.13 vanishes. Choosing which public checkpoint to fine-tune, which public model to deploy, or which hyperparameters to use from a list validated elsewhere, by their accuracy on a private validation set, is a pure selection problem, and the exponential mechanism or report-noisy-max is the tool, with \(\ln|\mathcal R|\) utility cost and no linear privacy cost.
The validation set needs protection under every method. The best-of methods of Section 40.5 and Section 40.6 assume that the score is part of each run’s private output. If it is an exact validation accuracy, the validation records are not protected at all: the choice and the released score depend on them with no noise. Adding Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma_{\text{val}}\) to each validation count makes each run’s score a Gaussian mechanism with RDP curve \(\alpha/(2\sigma_{\text{val}}^2)\), and by Fact 4 a run’s curve is the larger of its training curve and this one.
A cheaper score is not a cheaper run. Each noisy count adds to the cost in validation records, but by Fact 4 it adds nothing as long as it stays below the training curve at every order. With \(\sigma_{\text{val}} = 20\) correct predictions, one noisy count alone has \(\varepsilon = 0.182\) and eight composed have \(0.546\), well below the training runs in the example below.


40.7.5 Example: choosing a learning rate on 5,000 validation records
In the experiment of Section 40.8, eight DP-SGD runs at \(\sigma = 2.07\), with learning rates from 0.0625 to 8, get these counts out of \(m = 5{,}000\): 4,486, 4,604, 4,681, 4,694, 4,600, 4,470, 4,232 and 4,123. The best, learning rate 0.5, beats the second, 0.25, by 13 correct predictions. Table 40.6 selects among them with the exponential mechanism.

The training costs much more: each run at \(\sigma = 2.07\) and 1,000 steps has \(\varepsilon = 0.657\), and the eight together 1.994. 40.7.6 Check yourself

Why is the sensitivity of a count of correct predictions 1 under add/remove, while an accuracy has a sensitivity that depends on \(m\)? (Adding a record adds one prediction, which is right or wrong, so the count moves by at most 1. The accuracy is the count divided by the number of records, and both change; the count avoids dividing by a private number.)
Fifty public checkpoints, a private validation set of 2,000 records and \(\varepsilon = 0.5\): what expected accuracy gap does the exponential mechanism guarantee? (At most \(2(\ln 50 + 1)/(0.5 \times 2{,}000) = 0.0098\), about one point.)

40.8 Tuning the running example

40.8.1 Context
Put the strategies side by side on the running example: tune the learning rate of DP-SGD over a grid of eight values, at the same total budget, and compare what each strategy delivers. The budget must cover the training runs and the validation scores.


40.8.2 Statement
Each run trains the running example’s network with DP-SGD (\(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\)) for 1,000 steps instead of the 10,000 of DP-SGD, to keep the script’s runtime at a few minutes, with one of eight learning rates \(\eta \in \{0.0625, 0.125, \dots, 8\}\). The first 5,000 of the 20,000 held-out records are a private validation set, and the other 15,000 the test set. A run’s score is its number of correct validation predictions plus Gaussian noise with \(\sigma_{\text{val}} = 20\). The total budget is \(\varepsilon = 2\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and each strategy chooses its noise multiplier \(\sigma\) so that the whole procedure meets it, by the accountant of Section 40.4 or Section 40.6.

40.8.3 Derivation
The rows are computed as follows; each uses the facts and results named.

No tuning. One run with the learning rate the previous chapter used, at the noise multiplier for \(\varepsilon = 2\), \(\sigma = 1.03\) (the accountant rounds up, so the run costs 1.97).
The reporting bug. The same eight runs at \(\sigma = 1.03\), one per learning rate, best noisy validation count released, and the single-run \(\varepsilon\) reported. Its honest cost is the composition of eight runs, 5.60 (Equation 40.6).
Proxy data. A second task built the same way with a different random teacher stands in for public data from a related distribution. The grid is run there, the best learning rate by validation on the proxy task is kept, and one private run is trained with it at \(\sigma = 1.03\). The proxy runs touch no private data, so they cost nothing (Fact 2).
Composition. The eight runs at the \(\sigma\) for which eight runs together cost 2, which is 2.07 (Equation 40.6 with Fact 4 for the noisy counts).
Random search. \(K\) runs, each with a learning rate drawn uniformly from the grid, with \(K\) Poisson or logarithmic with mean 8, \(\sigma\) chosen by Equation 40.11 or Equation 40.12 so that the procedure costs 2.
Estimating accuracy. Training is the slow part, so the script trains three independent runs per learning rate for each \(\sigma\), and repeats each tuning procedure 4,000 times by drawing runs from this pool, with fresh validation noise and, for random search, a fresh \(K\). Drawing with replacement from three runs understates the variety of a real search a little.



40.8.4 Interpretation
The honest strategies cost about a point of accuracy here, and the bug hides it. At the same total budget, composition reaches 0.9430 and Poisson random search 0.9433, against 0.9509 without tuning. Reporting the single-run budget makes the grid search look free: it claims 1.97 and spends at most 5.60.
Tuning did not pay on this task, for an instructive reason. Even with the budget misreported, the grid search, 0.9479, is below the untuned learning rate of 0.5, 0.9509. The learning rate 0.5 is the best of the grid here, and the noisy validation count sometimes picks a neighbour. It is the best because DP-SGD chose its running example’s settings with knowledge of this very task, a leak of exactly the kind this chapter is about, which no accountant in the book has charged for. On a new task, you would not have such a guess, and a search would be needed.
Random search with a Poisson number of runs beats composition only slightly here. At a total of \(\varepsilon = 2\) and a mean of 8 runs, Poisson random search allows \(\sigma = 1.53\) instead of 2.07, each run costing 0.98 instead of 0.66. But it tries a given learning rate with probability only \(1 - e^{-1}\), since a candidate is missed with probability 0.3679, and its accuracy varies more from one search to the next, 0.0060 against 0.0022. The two effects roughly cancel at this small grid. With more candidates, Table 40.5 says the gap in \(\sigma\) grows.
The logarithmic distribution has the cheapest bound and the worst search. It allows the least noise of the honest strategies, \(\sigma = 1.36\), but with mean 8 it stops after a single run with probability 0.2907, and then releases a random learning rate. That is why its accuracy is lowest and most variable, \(0.9372 \pm 0.0200\). Papernot & Steinke report the same trade-off, and found the Poisson distribution best in their own small search. Figure 40.4 repeats the comparison at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 4 (one run per learning rate, so those points are noisier).
Tuning on proxy data is nearly free, when proxy data exist. The proxy task has a different teacher, so its best learning rate is not always the private task’s, and the released model reaches 0.9487 for a total cost of one private run. Its quality depends on how close the proxy is.






Figure 40.4: Test accuracy of the model released by each tuning strategy against the total \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) it costs (1,000 DP-SGD steps per run). The red dashed line places the grid search at the single-run \(\varepsilon\) that the reporting bug claims, and the arrows move each point to its honest cost by composition. Points at \(\varepsilon = 2\) use three runs per learning rate; those at 1 and 4 one run.





40.8.5 Example: what the bug changes in a paper’s table
A paper reports “test accuracy 0.948 at \(\varepsilon = 1.97\)” for a model chosen from eight learning rates. A reader comparing it with a paper that reports 0.943 at \(\varepsilon = 1.99\) after an honest grid search concludes that the first method is better at the same budget. In Table 40.7 both rows are the same algorithm; the difference is the accounting. At its honest cost of 5.60, the first row should be compared with other methods at \(\varepsilon = 5.60\), not at 1.97; DP-SGD shows how much accuracy a budget that large buys.


40.8.6 Check yourself

Why does the composition row use \(\sigma = 2.07\) while the logarithmic row can use 1.36, both at a total of 2? (Composition charges eight full runs; Equation 40.12 charges one run plus a constant multiple of one run at another order plus \(\ln 8/(\alpha - 1)\), which is less than seven more runs.)
The bootstrap draws runs with replacement from three per learning rate. Which strategy’s accuracy does this distort most? (Those that run the same learning rate many times, random search with large \(K\): repeated draws of the same three runs make the best of many runs look less good than independent runs would. With a mean of 8 runs over 8 learning rates, the effect is small.)

section: 40.9 What to do and what to report
text:
40.9 What to do and what to report

40.9.1 Context
The results of this chapter turn into a short procedure. What should a team training a private model actually do about hyperparameters, and what must a reported \(\varepsilon\) cover for a reader to rely on it?


40.9.2 Statement

Spend private runs only where you must. Tune on public data or on proxy data from a related distribution when it exists. Reuse hyperparameters that worked on similar tasks. Shrink the search: DP-SGD showed that below the typical gradient norm only the product of learning rate and clipping norm matters, so one of the two need not be searched.
Fix the search before touching the private data. Write down the candidate set, the distribution of the number of runs, the score and the validation set.
Make the score private. Use a held-out validation set and a noisy count, or spend part of the budget on a private score.
Account for the whole search. For a few candidates, compose. For more, run random search with a random number of runs and use Equation 40.11 (small per-run budget, moderate number of runs) or Equation 40.12 (many runs). Account for every run on the private data, including runs that crashed, runs for debugging, and evaluations used for early stopping.
Report both numbers. The \(\varepsilon\) of the released run, and the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole procedure with how it was computed: the candidate set, the distribution of \(K\), the accountant, \(\delta\) and the neighbouring relation.



40.9.3 Derivation
Each item follows from a result above.

Runs on public data cost nothing (Fact 2), and every private run costs something by Section 40.4 and Section 40.6. A smaller candidate set gives the same utility with fewer runs, which lowers \(\ln\mathbb E[K]\) or \(k\).
The theorems of Section 40.5 and Section 40.6 require that the candidates are drawn from a fixed distribution and that \(K\) is drawn from its distribution independently of the data. Choosing them after looking at results makes them functions of the data that no theorem covers.
Every best-of theorem assumes that the score is part of a private output (Section 40.7). An exact validation score makes the validation records unprotected.
Composition and the random-\(K\) bounds are both valid; which is smaller depends on the number of runs and the per-run budget (Table 40.5, Table 40.7). A crashed run still computed on the data, and if its failure influenced what was done next, it is part of the adaptive sequence.
The released run’s \(\varepsilon\) says how much the final model alone leaks if the hyperparameters were public; the procedure’s \(\varepsilon\) is what the release actually guarantees. Papernot & Steinke (2022) suggest stating both when the second is much larger.



40.9.4 Interpretation
The cheapest fix is usually upstream. In Table 40.7, the strategies that spend the whole budget on one private run, no tuning and proxy tuning, beat every honest search. That will not always hold, since a poor guess can be far worse than a noisy search, but it says where to start: get good hyperparameters without the private data, and search privately only over what remains uncertain.
Pre-registration is part of the guarantee. The random-\(K\) theorems are statements about a procedure. An engineer who looks at the first few results and decides to “try a few more” has changed the procedure, and the theorem no longer applies. Logging the search configuration before it runs is to tuning what fixing the clipping norm in advance is to DP-SGD.
Reporting standards exist. Ponomareva et al. (2023, Section 5.3.3) ask for the formal guarantee of the final model and of the tuning, and Choosing an accountant lists tuning among the checks of a reported \(\varepsilon\). Auditing cannot catch the bug: an audit tests the trained model, not how it was chosen.


40.9.5 Example: the report for the running example
For the Poisson row of Table 40.7, a complete report reads: “DP-SGD with Poisson sampling rate 0.01, clipping norm 0.5, noise multiplier 1.53, 1,000 steps; one run satisfies \((0.98, 10^{-5})\)-DP. The learning rate was selected by random search over \(\{0.0625, 0.125, \dots, 8\}\) with a Poisson number of runs with mean 8, scored by correct predictions on a disjoint validation set of 5,000 records with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 20; the whole procedure satisfies \((1.99, 10^{-5})\)-DP by the Rényi bound of Papernot & Steinke (2022, Theorem 6), add/remove neighbours, record level.”


40.9.6 Check yourself

A colleague tunes on the private data, then retrains the chosen configuration from scratch with fresh noise and releases only the retrained model. Does the retraining make the tuning free? (No. The chosen hyperparameters are a function of the tuning runs, so the release is a post-processing of the tuning runs plus the new run; the tuning must be accounted for, and the new run adds its own cost.)
Why can’t an audit of the released model detect that tuning was not accounted for? (An audit estimates how much the trained model reveals about its training records. The best-of-\(k\) leak is in the event “every run was bad”, which an audit of one released model at one fixed configuration does not replicate unless it reruns the whole search on neighbouring datasets.)

text:
40.10 Code: check every number by computation
The script code/hyperparameter_tuning.py computes the exact best-of-\(K\) distributions of Equation 40.4 for randomized response and the three-outcome mechanism, evaluates the bounds of Liu & Talwar and Papernot & Steinke on the RDP accountant of DP-SGD, whose model and accountant it imports from code/dp_sgd.py, and runs the tuning experiment. From the repository root:
uv run python code/part05-dp-ml/hyperparameter_tuning.py

The <η> of the last strategy is the shape \(\nu\).

The exact computations show that the bounds are attained in the worst case: \(k\varepsilon\) for a fixed number of runs, \(3\varepsilon\) and \(2\varepsilon\) for the geometric and logarithmic numbers. The experiment shows that on a small grid the accuracy gained by tuning can be smaller than the accuracy lost by paying for it, and that the cheapest strategy is to need fewer private runs.

40.11 References

Liu & Talwar, “Private Selection from Private Candidates” (STOC 2019; arXiv:1811.07971). Random stopping and the \(3\varepsilon\) bound of Section 40.5; threshold and \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) variants; the fixed-\(k\) counterexample (their Appendix B).
Papernot & Steinke, “Hyperparameter Tuning with Renyi Differential Privacy” (ICLR 2022; arXiv:2110.03620). The generic bound, the Poisson and truncated negative binomial theorems of Section 40.6, the lower bound of Section 40.3, and an experiment on image classification that recommends the Poisson distribution for small searches.
Chaudhuri & Vinterbo, “A Stability-Based Validation Procedure for Differentially Private Machine Learning” (NeurIPS 2013). The first improvement over composition for tuning, for learning algorithms that are stable.
Mohapatra, Sasy, He, Kamath & Thakkar, “The Role of Adaptive Optimizers for Honest Private Hyperparameter Selection” (arXiv:2111.04906, 2021). Honest tuning with composition, and optimizers that need less tuning.

Papernot, Thakurta, Song, Chien & Erlingsson, “Tempered Sigmoid Activations for Deep Learning with Differential Privacy” (arXiv:2007.14191, 2020). Architecture choices that are best without privacy are not best with it, so tuning cannot simply be done non-privately.

Rules of thumb

The best of \(k\) runs is not cheaper than \(k\) runs unless \(k\) is random. Report the cost of the search, not of the released run.
For DP-SGD, random search with a Poisson number of runs suits small searches at small per-run budgets; the logarithmic or \(\nu = 0.5\) distributions suit large searches, at the price of often running few candidates.
Validation scores on private data must be noisy; a few thousand validation records make the noise cheap.
The best tuning is the tuning you do not do on private data: public or proxy data, reused settings, fewer knobs.
Fix the candidate set and the distribution of the number of runs in advance; adaptive searches need adaptive composition.
