title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.1 Why this matters
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with differential privacy (DP), the DP-SGD of the previous chapter, gets its privacy from two sources. Clipping and Gaussian noise make each step a Gaussian mechanism, and Poisson sampling makes each step much more private than that: a record is in the batch only with probability \(q\), and the accountant credits the run for the uncertainty about whether the record was used. For the running example of this part, with \(q = 0.01\), that amplification is what turns a noise multiplier of 1 into \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) over 10,000 steps.
Many training pipelines cannot honestly claim Poisson sampling. Data loaders shuffle the dataset once, or once per epoch, and cut it into fixed batches; streaming pipelines read the data in the order it arrives; and in federated learning, where the records live on phones, the server cannot choose which devices check in, so it cannot sample them independently with a known probability. Amplification by subsampling shows that applying the Poisson accountant to such pipelines can understate \(\varepsilon\) considerably. The honest alternative is to give up amplification. Each step is then a plain Gaussian mechanism, and on the running example, for \(\varepsilon = 2\) over five passes through the data, the noise multiplier has to grow from 0.928 to 4.458, and test accuracy falls from 0.9460 to 0.8941.
This chapter asks: how do you train privately without trusting random batches, and can correlated noise beat independent noise? It can, by a lot, and the reason is a change of viewpoint. The first algorithm to exploit it ran the follow the regularized leader (FTRL) algorithm on noisy gradient sums and is called DP-FTRL; it adds its noise through a binary tree, a construction from the theory of private counters. The modern form, the matrix factorization mechanism, contains the tree as a special case, and on the running example it closes nearly all of the gap to amplified DP-SGD without any sampling at all.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.1.1 The one idea: training releases prefix sums, so put the noise where the prefix sums need it
Gradient descent without momentum adds up its steps. After \(t\) steps the weights are the starting point minus the learning rate times the prefix sum \(S_t = x_1 + \dots + x_t\) of the clipped gradient sums \(x_s\) of the batches seen so far. What the models reveal about the data is what these prefix sums reveal, and the error in a model is the error in its prefix sum. SGD with independent noise on every step, DP-SGD without amplification, makes the noise in \(S_t\) a random walk, whose standard deviation grows like \(\sqrt t\). Nothing forces the noise to be independent. If the noise added at step \(t\) partly cancels the noise added before it, the prefix sums stay accurate. The price is that each record’s gradient must then be hidden in several noisy quantities at once.
The bookkeeping is linear algebra. Releasing all \(T\) prefix sums is the linear map \(x \mapsto Ax\), with \(A\) the lower-triangular matrix of ones. Write \(A = LR\), add Gaussian noise to \(Rx\), and release \(L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz\). The encoder \(R\) sets the privacy, because the noise must hide one record’s effect on \(Rx\); the decoder \(L\) sets the error, because it is what multiplies the noise. Independent noise, the binary tree and the best known mechanisms are all choices of this factorization, and the question “how much noise does private training need without amplification?” becomes “how small can the sensitivity of \(R\) times the size of \(L\) be?”. Table 41.1 lists the results.

Notation. A run has \(T\) steps with a fixed batch size \(B\). At step \(t\) the model has parameters \(\theta_t \in \mathbb R^d\), and the clipped per-example gradients of the batch are summed into \(x_t \in \mathbb R^d\), one entry per weight; stacking the \(x_t\) as rows gives the \(T \times d\) matrix \(x\). \(C\) is the clipping norm, so each record adds a vector of length at most \(C\) to each \(x_t\) it takes part in. \(S_t = \sum_{s \le t}x_s\) is the \(t\)-th prefix sum and \(\hat S_t\) its private estimate. \(A\) is the \(T \times T\) lower-triangular matrix of ones. A factorization is \(A = LR\), with \(R\) an \(m \times T\) encoder and \(L\) a \(T \times m\) decoder; \(r_j\) is the \(j\)-th column of \(R\) and \(\ell_t\) the \(t\)-th row of \(L\). The noise \(z\) is \(m \times d\) with independent \(\mathcal N(0, s^2C^2)\) entries; \(s\) is the noise scale, in units of \(C\) like DP-SGD’s noise multiplier \(\sigma\). \(\mu\) is the ratio of sensitivity to noise standard deviation of a Gaussian mechanism, and \(E\) the number of epochs.
The running example. The part’s network from DP-SGD: 50-dimensional inputs, labels from a fixed random teacher network, a student with 64 tanh hidden units and \(d = 3{,}329\) weights, \(n = 10{,}000\) training and 20,000 test records, clipping norm \(C\) of 0.5, \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The fixed-order runs use one public random permutation of the record slots, drawn independently of the data and kept for every epoch, cut into 100 batches of \(B = 100\). Each epoch is 100 steps, and each record participates once per epoch, exactly 100 steps apart. The DP-SGD runs use Poisson sampling with \(q = 0.01\), so their expected batch is also 100.
How to read this chapter. Read the toolkit and Section 41.3, which sets up the problem, then Section 41.4, the general framework. Section 41.5 and Section 41.6 are two instances, the historical one and the one to use. Section 41.7 is needed as soon as you train for more than one epoch. Section 41.8 puts the pieces together on the running example.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 41.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
41.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

41.2.1 Fact 1 — A Gaussian mechanism is described by one ratio
Release \(f(D) + Z\), where \(f\) takes values in \(\mathbb R^{m \times d}\) and \(Z\) has independent \(\mathcal N(0, \varsigma^2)\) entries. Let \(\Delta_2 f\) be the largest change of \(f\) between neighbouring datasets, measured in the Frobenius norm: the square root of the sum of squared entries, the Euclidean length of the matrix read as one long vector. The privacy of the release depends only on \(\mu = \Delta_2 f/\varsigma\), because rotating the output space puts the shift on one axis, and the noise on every other axis has the same distribution under both datasets (The Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms). Such a mechanism is \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP), and it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \[\delta \ge \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big), \tag{41.1}\] with \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function (f-DP and Gaussian DP). The right side grows with \(\mu\), so each \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) has a largest admissible ratio \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\mu(2, \delta) = 0.502\) and \(\mu(8, \delta) = 1.666\). The noise standard deviation for sensitivity \(\Delta_2 f\) is then \(\varsigma = \Delta_2 f/\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\).


41.2.2 Fact 2 — Post-processing
Any computation on a private output that does not touch the data again is as private as the output (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). Multiplying a noisy matrix by a fixed matrix, and taking gradient steps with the result, are post-processing.


41.2.3 Fact 3 — A linear combination of independent Gaussian noise
If \(z\) has independent \(\mathcal N(0, \varsigma^2)\) entries and \(\ell\) is a fixed row vector, then \(\ell z\), one number for each of the \(d\) columns, has independent coordinates, each normal with variance \[\varsigma^2\|\ell\|^2 = \varsigma^2\sum_j\ell_j^2, \tag{41.2}\] because a weighted sum of independent normals is normal and the variances of independent terms add, each multiplied by its weight squared. Applied to the rows \(\ell_t\) of a decoder, the error of the \(t\)-th released prefix sum has standard deviation \(\varsigma\|\ell_t\|\) in each coordinate. Two rows give correlated errors, with covariance \(\varsigma^2\,\ell_t\cdot\ell_u\).


41.2.4 Fact 4 — Adaptive Gaussian steps compose into one Gaussian
If each of \(k\) steps is a Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(\mu_i\), and each step may depend on the outputs of the earlier ones, the run is \(\sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}\)-GDP (f-DP and Gaussian DP; Private empirical risk minimization restates the argument). Conditionally on the earlier outputs, each step’s privacy loss is normal with the mean and variance of a one-step Gaussian loss, so the losses add like independent normals, and their variances, which are the \(\mu_i^2\), add.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
section: 41.3 Training is a stream of prefix sums
text:
41.3 Training is a stream of prefix sums

41.3.1 Context
What does a training run actually have to release, and what does privacy cost when the data order is fixed and nothing is sampled? Pinning this down turns training into a classic problem, the private release of running sums, for which much better mechanisms exist than fresh noise on every step.


41.3.2 Statement
Run gradient descent with a constant learning rate \(\eta\) (also called the step size) and no momentum, \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \frac\eta B\hat x_t\), where \(\hat x_t\) is the possibly noisy clipped gradient sum of step \(t\). Then \[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_0 - \frac\eta B\hat S_t, \qquad \hat S_t = \sum_{s \le t}\hat x_s, \tag{41.3}\] so the whole run is a post-processing of the prefix sums \(\hat S_1, \dots, \hat S_T\), and the noise in \(\theta_{t+1}\) is \(\eta/B\) times the noise in \(\hat S_t\). FTRL with linearized losses and a quadratic regularizer, \(\theta_{t+1} = \arg\min_\theta\big(\langle\hat S_t, \theta\rangle + \frac B{2\eta}\|\theta - \theta_0\|^2\big)\), produces the same weights. Releasing all prefix sums is the linear workload \[S = Ax, \qquad A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & & & \\ 1 & 1 & & \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \\ 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1\end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb R^{T \times T}, \tag{41.4}\] where row \(t\) of \(Ax\) is \(S_t\). For a record that takes part in one step, two mechanisms suggest themselves, each with the noise that makes it \(\mu\)-GDP for its own sensitivity:

Independent noise on each step, \(\hat S_t = \sum_{u \le t}(x_u + z_u)\): sensitivity \(C\), and error standard deviation \(\sqrt t\) in units of \(C/\mu\) for \(\hat S_t\).
Independent noise on each prefix sum, \(\hat S_t = S_t + z_t\): sensitivity \(\sqrt TC\), and error standard deviation \(\sqrt T\) in the same units, for every \(t\).



41.3.3 Derivation

Unroll the recursion. Adding the updates \(\theta_{u+1} - \theta_u = -\frac\eta B\hat x_u\) for \(u = 1, \dots, t\) telescopes to Equation 41.3. The weights at every step are a fixed function of the released prefix sums, so releasing the prefix sums privately makes every model private (Fact 2).
FTRL. The FTRL objective is a linear term plus a quadratic; setting its gradient \(\hat S_t + \frac B\eta(\theta - \theta_0)\) to zero gives \(\theta = \theta_0 - \frac\eta B\hat S_t\), the same point.
Independent noise on each step: privacy. The record changes only \(x_\tau\), its step, by a vector of length at most \(C\). The released noisy gradients \(x_u + z_u\) are one Gaussian mechanism per step, and only step \(\tau\) moves, so the run is a Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity \(C\); the prefix sums are post-processing of the noisy gradients. Noise \(z_u \sim \mathcal N(0, C^2/\mu^2)\) per coordinate gives \(\mu\)-GDP.
Its error. \(\hat S_t - S_t = z_1 + \dots + z_t\), a sum of \(t\) independent normals with variance \(C^2/\mu^2\) each, so its standard deviation is \(\sqrt tC/\mu\) (Fact 3 with \(\ell = (1, \dots, 1, 0, \dots, 0)\)).
Independent noise on each prefix sum: privacy. The record’s gradient appears in every \(S_t\) with \(t \ge \tau\), so \(T - \tau + 1\) of the released vectors move by the same vector of length up to \(C\). The total Frobenius change is \(\sqrt{T - \tau + 1}\,C\), at most \(\sqrt TC\) for \(\tau = 1\). By Fact 1 the noise must be \(\sqrt TC/\mu\), and that is the error of every \(\hat S_t\).



41.3.4 Interpretation
DP-SGD without amplification is the first mechanism. Fixed-order noisy SGD adds independent noise to every step, so its model at step \(t\) carries a random walk of \(t\) noise vectors. At the end of a run of \(T\) steps the walk has standard deviation \(\sqrt T\) times the per-step noise. The second mechanism makes every prefix sum equally noisy, but no better than the worst prefix sum of the first. Neither exploits the structure of \(A\): the first ignores that the noise accumulates, the second ignores that most of \(S_t\) was already released in \(S_{t-1}\).
Why prefix sums, and not just the last model? If only the final model were released, one prefix sum, \(S_T\), would suffice, with sensitivity \(C\) and error \(C/\mu\). But training is adaptive: the gradient \(x_t\) is computed at \(\theta_t\), which depends on the earlier noisy prefix sums. The mechanism has to produce all the intermediate models anyway, and each must be private, because the later gradients are functions of them. So the workload is all \(T\) rows of \(A\), released one at a time as the stream arrives.
Other optimizers are other workloads. With momentum or a learning-rate schedule the weights are still fixed linear combinations of the noisy gradients, only with a different lower-triangular matrix in place of \(A\). Denisov, McMahan, Rush, Smith & Thakurta (2022) factor those matrices too. This chapter keeps plain gradient descent, so the workload is always \(A\).


41.3.5 Example: one epoch of the running example
Take one epoch, \(T = 100\) steps, and normalize \(\mu = 1\), \(C = 1\). Independent noise on each step gives a final prefix sum with error standard deviation \(\sqrt{100} = 10\) and a root-mean-square error over the 100 prefix sums of \(\sqrt{(1 + 2 + \dots + 100)/100} = \sqrt{50.5} = 7.11\). Independent noise on each prefix sum has error 10 on every one. At \(\varepsilon = 2\), \(\mu = 0.502\), so the first mechanism’s noise scale is \(1/0.502 = 1.994\) per step, in units of \(C\), and its final prefix sum carries noise of standard deviation 19.94 in units of \(C\). DP-SGD with Poisson sampling at the same \(\varepsilon\) and \(T\) needs only \(\sigma = 0.827\), and its final prefix sum carries \(0.827\sqrt{100} = 8.27\): amplification buys a factor of 2.4 here. The rest of the chapter shows that correlated noise can beat even that, without any sampling.


41.3.6 Check yourself

Why is the noise in the model after \(t\) steps of fixed-order noisy SGD of order \(\sqrt t\) and not \(t\)? (The per-step noises are independent with mean zero, so their variances add: the sum of \(t\) of them has variance \(t\) times one, and standard deviation \(\sqrt t\) times one.)
With momentum, are the weights still a post-processing of the prefix sums of noisy gradients? (Yes. Momentum combines the past noisy gradients linearly with fixed coefficients, and the noisy gradients are the differences of consecutive noisy prefix sums. A factorization of the momentum matrix itself can do better than going through prefix sums.)

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.4 The matrix mechanism

41.4.1 Context
The two naive mechanisms put noise at opposite ends: on the inputs, or on the answers. The matrix mechanism of Li, Hay, Rastogi, Miklau & McGregor (2010) puts it in between, on some linear transformation \(Rx\) of the inputs from which the answers can be recovered linearly. How private is such a release, how accurate, and what does it need to work on a stream whose inputs are chosen adaptively?


41.4.2 Statement
Let \(A = LR\), with \(R \in \mathbb R^{m \times T}\) and \(L \in \mathbb R^{T \times m}\), and release \[\hat S = L(Rx + z) = Ax + Lz, \qquad z_{jk} \sim \mathcal N(0, s^2C^2) \text{ independent}. \tag{41.5}\]
Privacy. If a record takes part in one step, at a position fixed in advance, the release is \(\mu\)-GDP with \[\mu = \frac{\Delta_2 R}{s}, \qquad \Delta_2 R = \max_j\|r_j\|, \tag{41.6}\] the largest Euclidean length of a column of \(R\). This holds even when each \(x_t\) is chosen after seeing \(\hat S_1, \dots, \hat S_{t-1}\), provided \(L\) and \(R\) are lower-triangular (streaming).
Error. Each coordinate of \(\hat S_t - S_t\) is normal with mean zero and standard deviation \(sC\|\ell_t\|\). At a fixed privacy level \(\mu\) this is \[\frac C\mu\,e_t, \qquad e_t = \Delta_2 R\,\|\ell_t\|, \tag{41.7}\] and \(e_t\), the error per unit of privacy, is unchanged if \(R\) is multiplied by any number \(c > 0\) and \(L\) divided by it. Two summaries are used below: the root-mean-square error \(\big(\frac1T\sum_te_t^2\big)^{1/2} = \Delta_2 R\,\|L\|_F/\sqrt T\), and the maximum error \(\max_te_t\).
Lower bound. For every factorization, \[\Big(\frac1T\sum_te_t^2\Big)^{1/2} = \frac{\Delta_2 R\,\|L\|_F}{\sqrt T} \ge \frac{\|A\|_*}T, \tag{41.8}\] where \(\|A\|_* = \sum_k\nu_k(A)\) is the sum of the singular values \(\nu_k(A)\) of \(A\), its trace norm. For the prefix-sum matrix, \(\nu_k(A) = 1/\big(2\sin\frac{(2k - 1)\pi}{4T + 2}\big)\) for \(k = 1, \dots, T\).


41.4.3 Derivation

The release is a function of \(Rx + z\). \(L\) is fixed, so \(\hat S\) is post-processing of \(Rx + z\) (Fact 2), and \(LRx = Ax\) by the factorization.
Sensitivity, non-adaptive inputs. Neighbouring streams differ in the record’s contribution \(g\) to \(x_\tau\), a vector of length at most \(C\): row \(\tau\) of \(x\) changes by \(g\) and nothing else. Then \(Rx\) changes by \(r_\tau g^\top\), column \(\tau\) of \(R\) times the row \(g\), whose Frobenius norm is \(\|r_\tau\|\,\|g\| \le \|r_\tau\|C\) (each entry is \(r_{j\tau}g_k\), and the sum of their squares factorizes). The worst position gives \(\max_j\|r_j\|\,C\), and Fact 1 with noise \(sC\) gives Equation 41.6.
Adaptive inputs, one participation. In training, \(x_t\) is computed at \(\theta_t\), which depends on the earlier outputs. With \(L\) and \(R\) lower-triangular, row \(j\) of \(Rx + z\) depends on \(x_1, \dots, x_j\) only, so the mechanism can release row \(j\) of \(Rx + z\) at step \(j\), and \(\hat S_j\) with it. Compare the two streams step by step. Before step \(\tau\) the record has contributed nothing, so the outputs before \(\tau\) have the same distribution under both. Condition on them: they fix \(\theta_\tau\), hence the record’s contribution \(g\). From then on, at any step, the other records’ gradients are the same functions of the earlier outputs in both runs, and the record contributes nothing more, so given the same history the mean of each later row of \(Rx + z\) differs between the two runs by the matching row of the fixed shift \(r_\tau g^\top\). Released row by row, these are Gaussian mechanisms whose squared shifts add up to \(\|r_\tau g^\top\|_F^2 \le \|r_\tau\|^2C^2\), so by Fact 4 the rest of the run is Gaussian with ratio at most \(\|r_\tau\|C/(sC)\), as in step 2. Averaging over the history before \(\tau\) keeps the bound. Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 2.1) prove the general statement: any factorization of a lower-triangular \(A\) that is \(\mu\)-GDP, or \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, for fixed streams stays so for adaptively chosen ones, with the same parameters. Section H.5 in the appendices proves the Gaussian case, for several adaptive participations.
Error. \(\hat S_t - S_t = \ell_tz\), so Fact 3 with noise \(sC\) gives standard deviation \(sC\|\ell_t\|\); substituting \(s = \Delta_2 R/\mu\) from Equation 41.6 gives Equation 41.7. Replacing \(R\) by \(cR\) and \(L\) by \(L/c\) multiplies \(\Delta_2 R\) by \(c\) and \(\|\ell_t\|\) by \(1/c\).
Lower bound, first half. For any matrix \(U\) whose largest singular value is at most 1, \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A) \le \|A\|_*\), with equality for \(U\) built from the singular vectors of \(A\); this is the dual description of the trace norm, which Section H.3 in the appendices proves in three lines. Write \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top LR) = \langle L^\top U, R\rangle_F \le \|L^\top U\|_F\|R\|_F \le \|L\|_F\|R\|_F\): the first step is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the Frobenius inner product. For the second, \(\|L^\top U\|_F = \|U^\top L\|_F\), and \(U^\top\) does not lengthen any vector, since its singular values are at most 1; applied to each column of \(L\) it gives \(\|U^\top L\|_F \le \|L\|_F\). So \(\|L\|_F\|R\|_F \ge \|A\|_*\).
Second half. \(R\) has \(T\) columns, each of length at most \(\Delta_2 R\), so \(\|R\|_F^2 \le T(\Delta_2 R)^2\). Combining, \(\Delta_2 R\|L\|_F \ge \|A\|_*/\sqrt T\); dividing by \(\sqrt T\) gives Equation 41.8. The singular values follow from \(A^{-1}\), which has 1 on the diagonal and \(-1\) just below it; the eigenvalues of \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) are \(4\sin^2\frac{(2k - 1)\pi}{4T + 2}\). Section H.3 in the appendices derives them: the product is the second-difference matrix with a 1 in its last diagonal entry, and its eigenvectors are sine waves. The script checks the closed form against a numerical singular value decomposition at \(T = 256\): they agree to \(2.0 \times 10^{-13}\).



41.4.4 Interpretation
Privacy lives in the columns, error in the rows. A column of \(R\) is where one step’s gradient ends up in the noisy quantities; its length says how much noise is needed to hide it. A row of \(L\) says which noisy quantities one prefix sum is assembled from; its length says how much of the noise lands in that answer. The best factorization balances the two, and the scale invariance of step 4 means only the product matters.
The two naive mechanisms are the extreme factorizations. Independent noise on each step is \(R = I\), \(L = A\): columns of length 1, rows of length \(\sqrt t\). Noise on each prefix sum is \(R = A\), \(L = I\): the first column has length \(\sqrt T\), rows have length 1. For \(T = 100\) their root-mean-square errors are 7.11 and 10, while Equation 41.8 says no factorization can go below 2.18. The rest of the chapter is about factorizations near that bound.
Streaming needs lower-triangular factors. If \(L\) or \(R\) had entries above the diagonal, \(\hat S_t\) would need noise or data from future steps. Honaker (2015) improved the tree’s estimates by using all of its nodes at the end, which is not lower-triangular, and for that reason his estimator cannot be used during training (Denisov et al. 2022 make this point). For any factorization there is a lower-triangular one with the same distribution of \(\hat S\) (Denisov et al. 2022, Proposition 2.2), so nothing is lost by insisting on it. Section H.5 in the appendices derives this by Gram–Schmidt and shows that the sensitivity does not grow.
When \(R\) is square and invertible, the mechanism is noisy SGD with correlated noise. Then \(L = AR^{-1}\) and \(\hat S = A(x + R^{-1}z)\): the mechanism adds the noise \(\zeta = R^{-1}z\) to the gradients and then sums. Each step’s noise \(\zeta_t\) is a fixed combination of \(z_1, \dots, z_t\), so implementations generate it on the fly from the stored \(z\)’s, without forming any \(T \times T\) matrix.
What neighbouring means here. The record’s slot in the fixed order is public, and the neighbouring stream has the slot empty, contributing zero gradient. If neighbours instead replace the record by another, the contribution changes by up to \(2C\), and every sensitivity doubles.

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.5 Tree aggregation and DP-FTRL

41.5.1 Context
The first mechanism with error far below \(\sqrt T\) was the binary tree, found independently by Dwork, Naor, Pitassi & Rothblum (2010) and Chan, Shi & Song (2010) for counting events in a stream. Kairouz, McMahan, Song, Thakkar, Thakurta & Xu (2021) used it to release the prefix sums of gradients, with FTRL as the optimizer, and called the result DP-FTRL. How does it work, and how good is it?


41.5.2 Statement
Build a binary tree over the steps \(1, \dots, T\). Level 0 has one node per step; each node at level \(l\) covers one of the blocks \(1, \dots, 2^l\), then \(2^l + 1, \dots, 2\cdot2^l\), and so on, of \(2^l\) consecutive steps; there are \(L_T = \lceil\log_2T\rceil + 1\) levels. Release each node’s sum of gradients plus independent noise. A prefix \(1, \dots, t\) is the union of one node for each 1 in the binary expansion of \(t\), so \[\hat S_t = \sum_{\text{nodes in the decomposition of }t}(\text{node sum} + \text{noise}), \qquad \Delta_2 R = \sqrt{L_T}, \qquad e_t = \sqrt{L_T}\sqrt{\operatorname{popcount}(t)}, \tag{41.9}\] where \(\operatorname{popcount}(t)\) is the number of 1s in the binary expansion of \(t\), at most \(L_T - 1\) for \(t \le T\). Both factors grow like \(\sqrt{\ln T}\), so the error grows like \(\ln T\).


41.5.3 Derivation

The factorization. \(R\) has one row per node, with 1 in the columns of the steps the node covers: \(R\) is \(m \times T\) with \(m\) about \(2T\). Row \(t\) of \(L\) has a 1 for each node of the decomposition of \(t\). Then \(LR = A\), because the decomposition’s nodes cover each step \(1, \dots, t\) exactly once.
The decomposition. Write \(t\) in binary. Going from the highest bit down, each 1 at bit \(l\) takes the next block of \(2^l\) steps, which starts right after the sum of the higher bits, a multiple of \(2^{l+1}\), so the block is a node of the tree. For example \(7 = 4 + 2 + 1\) uses the nodes covering steps 1 to 4, 5 and 6, and 7; \(8\) uses a single node covering 1 to 8.
Sensitivity. A step lies in exactly one node per level, so column \(j\) of \(R\) has \(L_T\) ones and length \(\sqrt{L_T}\).
Error. Row \(t\) of \(L\) has \(\operatorname{popcount}(t)\) ones, so \(\|\ell_t\| = \sqrt{\operatorname{popcount}(t)}\), and Equation 41.7 gives Equation 41.9.
Privacy during training. \(L\) and \(R\) can be ordered so that each node is released when its last step has arrived, and \(\hat S_t\) uses only completed nodes: the factorization is a streaming one, and Section 41.4 applies.



41.5.4 Interpretation
Why the tree helps. Independent noise sums \(t\) noise terms for the \(t\)-th prefix; the tree sums at most \(\log_2t + 1\) of them, each somewhat larger because every step is hidden in \(L_T\) nodes. Trading a factor \(\sqrt{L_T}\) in noise for a reduction from \(\sqrt t\) terms to \(\sqrt{\ln t}\) is a large win for long runs.
Why it is not the end. The tree’s error jumps around: at \(t = 127 = 1111111_2\) it uses seven nodes, at \(t = 128\) one (Figure 41.2, left). Its encoder is also wasteful: the nodes at the top levels are used by few prefixes, yet every step pays for being in them. Honaker (2015) showed how to combine all nodes with weights to reduce the variance, but not in a streaming way (Section 41.4). The square-root factorization of the next section has smaller error everywhere.
DP-FTRL. Kairouz et al. (2021) run FTRL, which by Equation 41.3 is gradient descent from \(\theta_0\) on noisy prefix sums, with the prefix sums released by the tree; they also add momentum and restart the tree after a number of steps. They report that DP-FTRL, without any amplification, compares favourably with DP-SGD with amplification in their experiments, and that it allows much more flexible data access. Xu et al. (2023) describe training production language models for the Gboard keyboard with DP-FTRL in federated learning, where Poisson sampling of devices is not available.


41.5.5 Example: \(T = 100\) and \(T = 10{,}000\)
For \(T = 100\), the tree has \(L_T = 8\) levels, so \(\Delta_2 R = \sqrt8 = 2.828\). The largest popcount up to 100 is 6 (at \(t = 63\)), so the largest error per unit of privacy is \(\sqrt8\sqrt6 = 6.93\), and the root-mean-square error is 5.05 (Table 41.2). For \(T = 10{,}000\) there are 15 levels, \(\Delta_2 R = 3.873\), the maximum error is 13.96 and the root-mean-square error 9.84, against 70.71 for independent noise.


41.5.6 Check yourself

Which prefix sums does the tree release most accurately? (Those whose length is a power of two, which use one node, such as \(t = 64\); their error is \(\sqrt{L_T}\) per unit of privacy.)
For \(T = 8\), is the tree better than independent noise? (No. With 4 levels, \(\Delta_2 R = 2\), and the root-mean-square error is \(2\sqrt{13/8} = 2.55\), against \(\sqrt{4.5} = 2.12\) for independent noise. The tree only pays off for longer runs; Exercise 1 finds the crossover.)

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.6 The square-root factorization

41.6.1 Context
The tree treats privacy and error asymmetrically: a tall, thin encoder and a sparse decoder. A natural symmetric choice is \(L = R\), a matrix whose square is \(A\). Is there a lower-triangular square root of \(A\), what does it look like, and how close is it to the best possible factorization?


41.6.2 Statement
The lower-triangular matrix \(R = A^{1/2}\) with \(R^2 = A\) is the Toeplitz matrix (constant along each diagonal) with entries \[R_{ij} = r_{i-j} \text{ for } i \ge j, \qquad r_k = \binom{2k}k4^{-k}: \quad r = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac38, \tfrac5{16}, \tfrac{35}{128}, \dots, \tag{41.10}\] the coefficients of the power series \((1 - x)^{-1/2} = \sum_kr_kx^k\), computed by \(r_0 = 1\), \(r_k = r_{k-1}\frac{2k - 1}{2k}\). With \(L = R\), \[(\Delta_2 R)^2 = \|\ell_T\|^2 = \sum_{k<T}r_k^2, \qquad 1 + \frac{\ln\frac{2T+1}3}\pi \le \sum_{k<T}r_k^2 \le 1 + \frac{0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5}\pi, \tag{41.11}\] and the largest error per unit of privacy is \(\max_te_t = e_T = \sum_{k<T}r_k^2\), which grows like \(\ln(T)/\pi\). As noisy SGD, the noise added to the gradients is \(\zeta = R^{-1}z\), with \(R^{-1}\) the Toeplitz matrix of the coefficients \(h_k\) of \((1 - x)^{1/2}\): \(h = 1, -\frac12, -\frac18, -\frac1{16}, -\frac5{128}, \dots\).


41.6.3 Derivation

Lower-triangular Toeplitz matrices are power series. Identify the matrix with first column \((c_0, c_1, \dots, c_{T-1})\) with the series \(c(x) = \sum_kc_kx^k\). The product of two such matrices has, in position \((i, j)\), the sum \(\sum_ka_{i-k}b_{k-j}\) over \(j \le k \le i\), which is the coefficient of \(x^{i-j}\) in \(a(x)b(x)\): products of matrices are products of series, truncated after \(x^{T-1}\).
\(A\) is the series \(1/(1 - x)\), since its first column is all ones and \(1 + x + x^2 + \dots = 1/(1 - x)\).
A square root. The series \(r(x) = (1 - x)^{-1/2}\) satisfies \(r(x)^2 = 1/(1 - x)\), so its Toeplitz matrix squares to \(A\). Its coefficients follow from the binomial series, \((1 - x)^{-1/2} = \sum_k\binom{-1/2}k(-x)^k\), with \((-1)^k\binom{-1/2}k = \frac{\frac12\cdot\frac32\cdots\frac{2k-1}2}{k!} = \frac{1\cdot3\cdots(2k - 1)}{2^kk!}\). Multiplying top and bottom by \(2\cdot4\cdots2k = 2^kk!\) gives \(\frac{(2k)!}{4^k(k!)^2} = \binom{2k}k4^{-k}\), and the ratio of consecutive terms is \(\frac{2k-1}{2k}\).
The inverse. \(R^{-1}\) corresponds to \(1/r(x) = (1 - x)^{1/2}\), whose coefficients are \(1, -\frac12, -\frac18, -\frac1{16}, -\frac5{128}, \dots\), by the binomial series again; all after the first are negative.
Sensitivity and error. Column \(j\) of \(R\) holds \(r_0, \dots, r_{T-j}\), so the first column is the longest, with squared length \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\). Row \(t\) of \(L = R\) holds \(r_{t-1}, \dots, r_0\), so its squared length is \(\sum_{k<t}r_k^2\), largest at \(t = T\). The product of the two at \(t = T\) is \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\).
Bounds. A Wallis-type inequality gives \(\frac1{\pi(k + 1/2)} \le r_k^2 \le \frac1{\pi(k + 1/4)}\) for \(k \ge 1\) (Fichtenberger, Henzinger & Upadhyay 2023 quote it with a reference). Section H.3 in the appendices proves it for every \(k\). Compare the sums with integrals of the decreasing functions \(1/(x + \frac12)\) and \(1/(x + \frac14)\): \(\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}\frac1{k + 1/2} \ge \int_1^T\frac{dx}{x + 1/2} = \ln\frac{2T + 1}3\), and \(\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}\frac1{k + 1/4} \le \frac1{5/4} + \int_1^{T-1}\frac{dx}{x + 1/4} = 0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5\). Adding the \(k = 0\) term, 1, gives Equation 41.11.



41.6.4 Interpretation
Correlated noise that cancels. The noise added to step \(t\)’s gradient is \(z_t - \frac12z_{t-1} - \frac18z_{t-2} - \dots\): fresh noise, minus a decaying share of the noise already injected. Each step’s noise is a little larger than independent noise, with standard deviation \(\sqrt{\sum_kh_k^2}\) times the noise scale, which tends to \(\sqrt{4/\pi} = 1.128\) (the script sums 100,000 coefficients: \(\sum h_k^2 = 1.2732 = 4/\pi\)). But the running sums of the noise no longer drift: the negative coefficients pull the accumulated noise back toward zero. Figure 41.1 shows one coordinate at \(\mu = 1\) for 1,000 steps. The per-step noises of the two mechanisms look alike; their running sums do not.






Figure 41.1: Left: one coordinate of the noise added to each of the first 60 steps’ gradients, independent (identity factorization) and square-root correlated, both calibrated to \(\mu = 1\) for one participation. Right: the noise in the prefix sums over 1,000 steps, for independent noise, the binary tree and the square root, with bands of two standard deviations. Independent noise drifts like a random walk; the square root’s stays within a narrow band.



How close to optimal. The lower bound Equation 41.8 is 2.18 at \(T = 100\) and 3.63 at \(T = 10{,}000\), and the square root’s root-mean-square error is 2.37 and 3.84, within 9% and 6%. Section H.3 in the appendices proves that this ratio tends to 1 as \(T\) grows. Fichtenberger, Henzinger & Upadhyay (2023) bound its maximum error with explicit constants and compare it with a lower bound that holds for every factorization, and Henzinger, Upadhyay & Upadhyay (2023) give almost tight bounds for its mean squared error; the factorization itself already appears in Bennett (1977), as they note. (The closed form printed in Theorem 1 of the arXiv version, \(1 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5/\pi\), omits the first term of the integral comparison of step 6 and is slightly below the true sum, 2.392 against 2.531 at \(T = 100\); the corrected form is the upper bound of Equation 41.11.) A finer expansion of \(r_k^2\) around \(1/(\pi k)\) gives the approximation \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2 \approx (\ln T + \gamma + 4\ln 2)/\pi\), with \(\gamma\) Euler’s constant, stated here without proof; the script finds 2.532 against the exact 2.531 at \(T = 100\).
The optimal factorization. For the root-mean-square error, the best encoder minimizes \(\|L\|_F\) subject to columns of length at most 1. Writing \(X = R^\top R\), the problem is to minimize \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1})\) over positive definite \(X\) with diagonal at most 1, which is convex. Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 3.2) show that the solution is \(X = V^{-1/2}(V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2})^{1/2}V^{-1/2}\), with \(V\) the diagonal matrix of a vector \(v\) that is the fixed point of \(v \mapsto \operatorname{diag}\big((V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2})^{1/2}\big)\), and they iterate that map. Setting the derivative of the Lagrangian \(\operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1}) + \sum_i\lambda_i(X_{ii} - 1)\) to zero gives \(X\Lambda X = A^\top A\), and the constraint \(X_{ii} = 1\) turns that into exactly this fixed point. Section H.4 in the appendices gives the full argument: convexity, the balance condition, why it identifies the global optimum, and that the optimal value is \(\sum_iv_i\). A lower-triangular \(R\) with \(R^\top R = X\) comes from a Cholesky factorization of \(X\) with rows and columns reversed. The script’s iteration converges in 155 steps at \(T = 100\) and 193 at \(T = 256\), to a root-mean-square error of 2.24 and 2.52, against 2.37 and 2.67 for the square root. The optimum costs a cubic-time computation per iteration, and the square root, which is free and nearly as good, is the usual default for long runs.
Figure 41.2 shows the error per unit of privacy across one run and against the horizon, and Figure 41.3 shows the factors for \(T = 16\). The square root and the optimal factorization look alike: lower-triangular, largest on the diagonal, decaying away from it.






Figure 41.2: Left: standard deviation of the error of each released prefix sum \(S_t\) for \(T = 256\), one participation, at \(\mu = 1\) and \(C = 1\), for five factorizations. Right: the root-mean-square error over a run against its length \(T\), with the trace-norm lower bound of Equation 41.8 dotted; the optimal factorization is computed up to \(T = 256\).









Figure 41.3: The encoder \(R\) (top) and decoder \(L\) (bottom) of three factorizations of the \(16 \times 16\) prefix-sum matrix. The tree’s encoder has one row per node (31 rows), and its decoder picks the nodes of each prefix. The square root uses the same matrix for both; the optimal factorization’s encoder has columns of length exactly 1.





41.6.5 Example: \(T = 4\) by hand
With \(r = (1, \frac12, \frac38, \frac5{16})\), \[R = \begin{pmatrix}1 & & & \\ \frac12 & 1 & & \\ \frac38 & \frac12 & 1 & \\ \frac5{16} & \frac38 & \frac12 & 1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{41.12}\] Row 3 times column 1 of \(R\) is \(\frac38 + \frac12\cdot\frac12 + \frac38 = 1\), and row 4 times column 1 is \(\frac5{16} + \frac38\cdot\frac12 + \frac12\cdot\frac38 + \frac5{16} = 1\), as \(R^2 = A\) requires; the script confirms \(R^2 = A\) exactly. The first column has squared length \(1 + \frac14 + \frac9{64} + \frac{25}{256} = \frac{381}{256} = 1.488\), so \(\Delta_2 R = 1.220\), and the last prefix sum has error \(1.488\) per unit of privacy, against \(\sqrt4 = 2\) for independent noise. At \(T = 100\) the same computation gives \(\sum r_k^2 = 2.531\), so \(\Delta_2 R = 1.591\) and the final prefix sum’s error is 2.53, a quarter of independent noise’s 10.


41.6.6 Check yourself

Why are the noise coefficients \(h_k\) after the first all negative, and what would happen to the prefix-sum noise if they were positive? (They are the coefficients of \((1 - x)^{1/2}\), whose binomial terms after the first are negative. Positive coefficients would add past noise again, so the prefix sums would drift faster than a random walk.)
The square root has \(\Delta_2 R = 1.591\) at \(T = 100\), so it needs 59% more noise per step than independent noise. Why is it still better? (Its decoder rows have length at most 1.591 instead of up to 10: each prefix sum collects a decaying, partly cancelling combination of the noise, not \(t\) independent terms.)

title: 41  DP-FTRL and matrix factorization
text:
41.7 Several participations

41.7.1 Context
So far each record took part in one step, as in a single pass over the data. Training usually makes several passes, and then a record’s gradient enters \(x\) at several steps, each time through a different column of \(R\). How large is the sensitivity then, and how should the factorization change?


41.7.2 Statement
Let a record take part at steps \(\tau_1 < \dots < \tau_k\), contributing vectors \(g_1, \dots, g_k\) of length at most \(C\), possibly chosen adaptively. Then the change in \(Rx\) is \(\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\), and \[(\Delta_2 R)^2 = \frac1{C^2}\max_{\text{patterns}}\ \sup_{\|g_i\| \le C}\Big\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\Big\|_F^2 = \max_{\text{patterns}}\Big\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}\Big\|^2 \quad\text{if } R^\top R \ge 0 \text{ entrywise}, \tag{41.13}\] the maximum over the possible participation patterns of the length of the sum of the participating columns. As before the sensitivity is in units of \(C\), and the release is \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = \Delta_2 R/s\). Two special cases:

Independent noise, \(R = I\): \(\Delta_2 R = \sqrt k\).
Banded encoders. If \(R\) is lower-triangular with nonzero entries only within \(b\) diagonals of the main one, \(R_{ij} = 0\) for \(i - j \ge b\), and any two participations are at least \(b\) steps apart (\(b\)-min-separation), then the columns of distinct participations do not overlap, and \(\Delta_2 R = \big(\sum_i\|r_{\tau_i}\|^2\big)^{1/2} \le \sqrt k\max_j\|r_j\|\).



41.7.3 Derivation

The change in \(Rx\). Row \(\tau_i\) of \(x\) changes by \(g_i\), so \(Rx\) changes by \(\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\), a sum of the same column-times-row products as in Section 41.4.
Expand the norm. \(\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\|_F^2 = \sum_{i,j}(r_{\tau_i}\cdot r_{\tau_j})(g_i\cdot g_j)\), because the Frobenius inner product of \(ab^\top\) and \(cd^\top\) is \((a\cdot c)(b\cdot d)\).
The worst gradients. Each \(g_i\cdot g_j\) lies in \([-C^2, C^2]\). If every \(r_{\tau_i}\cdot r_{\tau_j}\) is nonnegative, the sum is largest when every \(g_i\cdot g_j = C^2\), that is when all \(g_i\) are the same vector of length \(C\); the sum is then \(C^2\sum_{i,j}r_{\tau_i}\cdot r_{\tau_j} = C^2\|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}\|^2\). The entries of \(R^\top R\) are exactly the inner products of columns, so the condition is \(R^\top R \ge 0\), which holds for any \(R\) with nonnegative entries, such as the identity, the tree and the square root. Adaptive choices of the \(g_i\) cannot exceed this supremum; Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 2.1) state their adaptive result for exactly this sensitivity, the supremum over neighbouring streams. Section H.5 in the appendices proves it for Gaussian noise and a lower-triangular \(R\).
Independent noise. The columns of \(I\) are orthonormal, so \(\|\sum_ie_{\tau_i}\|^2 = k\).
Banded encoders. Column \(\tau\) of a \(b\)-banded \(R\) is nonzero only in rows \(\tau, \dots, \tau + b - 1\). Participations at least \(b\) apart have columns with disjoint supports, so their inner products are zero, the cross terms of step 2 vanish whatever the \(g_i\), and the sum is \(\sum_i\|r_{\tau_i}\|^2\|g_i\|^2\).



41.7.4 Interpretation
Correlated noise makes repeated participation more expensive. Under independent noise, \(k\) participations cost \(\sqrt k\), the usual composition of Gaussian mechanisms (Fact 4). Under the square root, the columns of nearby steps overlap and point in similar directions, so a record that appears again adds its contribution on top of its earlier one, and the sensitivity grows faster than \(\sqrt k\). Under the tree it is worse still: a record in two steps shares all the high-level nodes covering both, and in those nodes its two contributions add.
Banding restores \(\sqrt k\). Cutting the square root’s encoder to its first \(b\) diagonals, with \(b\) the separation between participations, removes the overlaps. The decoder \(L = AR^{-1}\) of the banded encoder is less accurate than the square root’s for a single participation, because the band no longer spreads the noise across the whole run, but with many participations the sensitivity saving dominates. Choquette-Choo, McMahan, Rush & Thakurta (2023) optimize the factorization directly under a participation constraint for multi-epoch training, and Choquette-Choo, Ganesh, McKenna, McMahan, Rush, Thakurta & Xu (2023) show that banded factorizations can also use amplification by sampling, so that they match DP-SGD where it is strong and beat it elsewhere.
The data order is part of the mechanism. The sensitivity depends on which steps a record can occupy. A fixed permutation repeated every epoch guarantees a separation of exactly \(n/B\) steps; reshuffling every epoch can put a record at the end of one epoch and the start of the next, one step apart, which breaks the banded bound. The order must be chosen independently of the data, and fixed in the analysis, but it need not be random.


41.7.5 Example: up to 20 epochs
Table 41.3 takes the running example’s order: 100 steps per epoch, separation \(b = 100\), \(E\) epochs, so \(T = 100E\) and every record takes part \(E\) times. The banded encoder keeps the first 100 coefficients of the square root. The last column is the error of the final prefix sum per unit of privacy, \(e_T\) of Equation 41.7 with the multi-epoch sensitivity.

41.8.3 Derivation
Each entry is computed as the earlier sections prescribe. For DP-SGD, the RDP accountant of DP-SGD finds the smallest \(\sigma\) for \(q = 0.01\), \(T = 100E\) steps and the target \(\varepsilon\); its final prefix sum carries \(T\) independent noises, \(\sigma\sqrt T\). For the fixed-order methods, the sensitivity of Equation 41.13 for \(E\) participations 100 steps apart (Table 41.3) is divided by \(\mu(\varepsilon, \delta)\) from Fact 1 to give the noise scale \(s\); for independent noise this is Fact 4, \(s = \sqrt E/\mu\). The final prefix sum’s noise is \(s\) times the length of the last row of the decoder (Fact 3). Training then runs Equation 41.3 with the noise of each factorization: the per-step noise \(R^{-1}z\) for the square-root and banded encoders, generated by a convolution in time, and the tree’s node noises summed along the binary decompositions, with consecutive differences taken as the per-step noise.


41.8.4 Interpretation
Without amplification, correlated noise is essential. At \(\varepsilon = 2\), fixed-order SGD with independent noise loses 2.8 points to DP-SGD after one epoch and 8.5 points after ten (0.8641 against 0.9493), and it gets worse with more epochs, because its noise grows like \(\sqrt E\) per step and accumulates like \(\sqrt T\). The tree recovers between a quarter and a half of the gap. The square root and the banded square root recover nearly all of it: at ten epochs the banded encoder reaches 0.9491, within 0.0002 of DP-SGD.
Matrix mechanisms can beat amplified DP-SGD. For short runs and large \(\varepsilon\), amplification gains little. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) and one epoch, DP-SGD needs \(\sigma = 0.501\) and independent noise without sampling \(0.600\), barely more, and the square root, whose final prefix sum carries 1.52 against DP-SGD’s 5.01, wins outright (0.9461 against 0.9371). At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the banded encoder has the highest mean accuracy at five and ten epochs. At \(\varepsilon = 2\) and one epoch the square root’s final noise, 5.05, is also below DP-SGD’s 8.27, and its accuracy is the same within the run-to-run spread.
Where DP-SGD keeps its lead. At small \(\varepsilon\) over many epochs, amplification is strongest: DP-SGD’s per-step noise grows only from 0.827 to 1.03 between one and ten epochs at \(\varepsilon = 2\), while every fixed-order mechanism pays for ten participations. The full square root then falls behind (0.9398 against 0.9493), because its overlapping columns make repeated participation expensive, and only banding keeps up. The final-prefix noise is a good guide: the method with the least of it is the most accurate or within the spread of the most accurate in every row.
The comparison is slightly tilted. DP-SGD is accounted with the RDP accountant, which overstates \(\varepsilon\) somewhat compared with a numerical accountant (Choosing an accountant), while the fixed-order mechanisms use the exact Gaussian curve of Fact 1. A tighter DP-SGD accountant would lower its noise somewhat. The learning rate was chosen per method from two values by test accuracy, which is itself a leak that Hyperparameter tuning accounts for; here it serves only to compare methods at their best. The runs are short, at most 1,000 steps, to keep the script under a few minutes. The noise gaps of Table 41.3 keep widening with the number of epochs, so longer runs should separate the methods more, not less.






Figure 41.4: Test accuracy of the running example after 5 epochs (500 steps of batch 100) at learning rate 1, against \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one run per point. DP-SGD uses Poisson sampling; the other four use a fixed data order and differ only in how their noise is correlated.



Figure 41.4 shows the same pattern across budgets at five epochs: independent noise collapses at small \(\varepsilon\), the tree is better, and the two square-root encoders track DP-SGD, with the banded one closest.


41.8.5 Example: what a federated deployment gains
In federated learning a “record” is a device, which checks in when it is idle, charging and on Wi-Fi; the server cannot sample devices independently with a known rate, so the Poisson accountant does not apply. Suppose the server can at least enforce that a device contributes at most once every \(b\) rounds, a \(b\)-min-separation. Then the banded matrix mechanism of Section 41.7 gives a provable guarantee with sensitivity \(\sqrt k\) times one column for \(k\) participations, and on the running example’s scale it is as accurate as DP-SGD with sampling would be. That is why production federated training of language models uses DP-FTRL (Xu et al. 2023), and why later work optimizes matrix factorizations for user-level training of language models (Choquette-Choo, McMahan, Rush & Thakurta 2023). The privacy unit there is a user, not an example, which User-level differential privacy treats.


41.8.6 Check yourself

In Table 41.5, independent noise at \(\varepsilon = 2\) gets worse from one epoch to ten. Why does more training hurt it? (Each extra epoch adds a participation, so the noise scale grows like \(\sqrt E\), from 1.994 to 6.305 between one and ten epochs: every update carries three times more noise, while each update’s signal stays the same size or shrinks as the model converges.)
When would you still choose DP-SGD over a matrix mechanism? (When you can implement Poisson sampling honestly and \(\varepsilon\) is small with many epochs, where amplification is strongest; or when the participation pattern is unknown, so no sensitivity for a correlated mechanism can be computed. Banded mechanisms with amplification combine both.)

Rules of thumb

If you cannot implement Poisson sampling, do not account as if you did. Fix the data order in advance and use a matrix mechanism.
For one pass over the data, use the square-root factorization: it is within about 10% of the best possible error and costs nothing to compute.
For several passes, fix the order so participations are evenly separated, and use a banded encoder whose band is at most the separation.
Compute the sensitivity for the participation pattern you actually have; reshuffling every epoch changes it.
Compare methods by the noise in the final prefix sum at equal \(\varepsilon\): on the running example, the method with the least of it was the most accurate, or within the run-to-run spread of the most accurate, in every configuration.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.1 Why this matters
Training a model with differential privacy (DP) by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with clipped and noisy gradients, DP-SGD (DP-SGD), makes the trained weights private. Every later use of the model is then free: anyone may download the weights and query them as often as they like, because releasing the weights was the private step and everything after it is post-processing. The price is paid during training. Every step adds noise to every gradient, the training code must compute and clip per-example gradients, and you must own the training loop.
Sometimes that price is the wrong one to pay, or cannot be paid at all. The model may be a large language model (LLM) behind an application programming interface, which you can prompt but not train. It may be a model that someone else trains, or one with no gradients, such as a forest of decision trees. Or it may answer only a few dozen questions in its whole life, a medical consultation tool for one study, for which a private training run is overkill. In each case there is another option: train ordinary, non-private models, never release them, and make each answer private instead. A query goes in, a differentially private answer comes out, and the models themselves stay behind a wall.
This chapter asks when that is the better choice and how to make it work. It answers with DP applied to predictions rather than to weights. Two questions organize it. How much does each private answer cost, and how many can you afford? And how do you turn a stream of private answers into a private model, so that the cost stops growing? The answer to the second question is private aggregation of teacher ensembles (PATE), introduced by Papernot, Abadi, Erlingsson, Goodfellow and Talwar (2017). Its modern descendant privatizes in-context learning: the private examples are placed in an LLM’s prompt rather than used for training.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.1.1 The one idea: one record, one vote
Split the private records into \(k\) disjoint shards, and train one model, a teacher, on each. To answer a query \(x\), let every teacher vote for a label and release only the label with the most votes after adding noise to the counts. A record lives in exactly one shard, so it influences exactly one teacher, and that teacher casts exactly one vote. Adding or removing the record can therefore move at most one vote from one label to another, whatever the teachers are, however they were trained, and however badly one of them overfits its shard. The privacy proof stops there. It is the subsample-and-aggregate idea of Beyond global sensitivity, with a vote as the aggregator.
Everything else is about accuracy, and it comes down to one comparison: the gap between the top two vote counts against the noise. When the teachers agree, the gap is large and the noisy winner is almost always the true plurality. When they disagree, the noise decides. And the noise must grow like the square root of the number of answered queries, because each answer spends budget. So private prediction is cheap for a few queries on which the teachers agree, and expensive otherwise. Table 42.1 lists the results.

Notation. A private dataset \(D\) has \(n\) records and is split into \(k\) disjoint shards of \(n/k\) records, one per teacher. A query \(x\) has \(m\) possible labels; \(N_i(x)\) is the number of teachers that vote for label \(i\), so \(\sum_iN_i(x) = k\), and \(i^*\) is the label with the most votes, the plurality. The gap is the difference between the top count and the runner-up; on two labels it is \(|N_1 - N_2|\). The noise on each count is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) for GNMax and \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) for LNMax. \(Q\) is the number of answered queries, \(\alpha > 1\) an order of Rényi differential privacy (RDP), and \(\tilde\beta\) an upper bound on the probability that the noisy winner differs from the plurality. Neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one record, as in DP-SGD, and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) throughout.
The running example. The part’s neural-network task (DP-SGD): 50-dimensional standard normal inputs labelled \(\pm1\) by a fixed random network, \(n = 10{,}000\) private training records. Its 20,000 test records are split in two. The first 10,000 form a public pool: their inputs are treated as public and unlabelled, as PATE requires, and their labels are used only to measure how good the private labels are. The last 10,000 form the evaluation set, on which every accuracy in this chapter is measured. The teachers are regularized logistic regressions, the model of Private empirical risk minimization, each fitted on one shard of consecutive records. Logistic regression is cheap and, on this task, as accurate as the part’s network on the same few records.
How to read this chapter. Read the toolkit and Section 42.3, which give the mechanism and its cost. Section 42.4 and Section 42.5 answer the question in the title: when private answers beat a private model. Section 42.6 builds PATE, and Section 42.7 the analysis that makes it competitive in practice; the second is the most technical section and can be skimmed for its statement and interpretation. Section 42.8 gives the alternative that needs no sanitizing, and why it is rarely used. Section 42.9 applies everything to in-context learning.

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
42.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

42.2.1 Fact 1 — One record changes one vote
Fix the partition of records into shards before looking at the data, by a hash of a record identifier rather than by position. Adding or removing a record then changes one shard, the one its hash points to, and leaves every other shard, and so every other teacher, exactly as it was. That teacher may now vote differently on a query: one count goes down by 1 and another goes up by 1, or nothing changes. The vote histogram \((N_1(x), \dots, N_m(x))\) therefore moves by at most 2 in \(\ell_1\) norm, the sum of absolute changes, and by at most \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt2\) in \(\ell_2\) norm, the Euclidean length of the change. This is the step of subsample-and-aggregate in Beyond global sensitivity: one record touches one block.
The partition rule matters. If shards were cut by position, inserting one record at the front would shift every later record into the next shard, change every shard, and possibly change every teacher. The derivations below assume a fixed hash; the script splits the records by position only because they are never added or removed in its experiments.


42.2.2 Fact 2 — The Gaussian mechanism in Rényi DP, and its accountant
Adding \(\mathcal N(0, s^2)\) noise to every coordinate of a vector-valued function \(f\) whose value moves by at most \(\Delta_2 f\) in \(\ell_2\) norm between neighbours gives a mechanism whose Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) between neighbours is at most \(\alpha(\Delta_2 f)^2/(2s^2)\) (Rényi DP). The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) between two distributions \(P\) and \(P'\) on a discrete set of outputs is \[D_\alpha(P\|P') = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\sum_yP(y)^\alpha P'(y)^{1 - \alpha}, \tag{42.1}\] and a mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP if this is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) for every pair of neighbours. Three properties make RDP the accountant here. Any computation on a private output that does not touch the data again, post-processing, cannot increase the divergence. RDP curves add under composition, even when each mechanism is chosen after seeing the earlier outputs. And a composed curve converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP at the best order, \[\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[\varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big] \tag{42.2}\] (Balle et al. 2020; From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)). When the curve is a line, \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), the result depends only on its slope \(\rho\): at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the largest slope that converts to \(\varepsilon = 1\) is \(\rho = 0.0306\), and to \(\varepsilon = 4\) it is \(\rho = 0.3731\). A pure Gaussian mechanism also has an exact conversion: its privacy is that of one Gaussian shift by \(\mu = \Delta_2 f/s\) standard deviations, Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\), and composing \(Q\) of them gives \(\mu\sqrt Q\) (f-DP and Gaussian DP).


42.2.3 Fact 3 — Report-noisy-max, and the RDP curve of any pure-DP step
Report-noisy-max adds independent Laplace noise \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) to every candidate’s score and releases only the index of the largest noisy score (Selection). If one record moves each score by at most \(\Delta u\), it is \((2\Delta u/b)\)-DP. The reason is that, with every other candidate’s noise held fixed, candidate \(i\) wins exactly when its own noise clears a bar, the best of the others’ noisy scores minus its own score. One record moves that bar by at most \(2\Delta u\), \(\Delta u\) through the maximum of the others and \(\Delta u\) through candidate \(i\)’s own score, and moving a Laplace threshold by \(s\) changes its tail probability by at most \(e^{s/b}\). When all scores move in the same direction, the factor 2 disappears. A vote histogram is not of that kind: one count goes up while another goes down.
An \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP mechanism also has an RDP curve. The worst \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP mechanism at every order is randomized response, which reports a bit truthfully with probability \(p = e^{\varepsilon_0}/(1 + e^{\varepsilon_0})\), so its curve, \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{RR}}(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\big(p^\alpha(1 - p)^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - p)^\alpha p^{1 - \alpha}\big), \tag{42.3}\] is a valid RDP curve for any \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP step (Concentrated differential privacy). This lets Laplace answers enter the same accountant as Gaussian ones.


42.2.4 Fact 4 — The difference of two independent Gaussians
If \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) are independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), then \(Z_1 - Z_2\) is \(\mathcal N(0, 2\sigma^2)\): variances of independent variables add, and subtracting does not change a variance. So \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > t] = \Phi(-t/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. In terms of the complementary error function \(\operatorname{erfc}\), which numerical libraries provide, \(\Phi(-u) = \frac12\operatorname{erfc}(u/\sqrt2)\), so \(\Pr[Z_1 - Z_2 > t] = \frac12\operatorname{erfc}(t/(2\sigma))\). Every accuracy statement about GNMax uses this, because whether a noisy vote picks label \(i\) over label \(j\) depends only on the difference of their two noises.

text:
42.3 The noisy vote: LNMax and GNMax

42.3.1 Context
A query arrives, the \(k\) teachers vote, and you must release one label. Which mechanism releases it, and how much does each answer cost? Two mechanisms are used in practice, and they differ in their noise: Laplace noise in the original PATE paper, Gaussian noise in its successor. The question is also how the cost of \(Q\) answers grows with \(Q\), since that is what limits private prediction.


42.3.2 Statement
LNMax releases \(\arg\max_i\big(N_i(x) + \mathrm{Lap}(b)\big)\) and GNMax releases \(\arg\max_i\big(N_i(x) + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\big)\), with independent noise on every count. Under add/remove neighbours and a fixed partition:

Each LNMax answer is \((2/b)\)-DP (Papernot et al. 2017).
Each GNMax answer is \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP for every \(\alpha > 1\) (Papernot, Song, Mironov, Raghunathan, Talwar & Erlingsson 2018, Proposition 8).
\(Q\) GNMax answers, even with queries chosen adaptively, are \((\alpha, Q\alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP. To meet a budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) the noise must therefore be \[\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{Q}{\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)}}, \tag{42.4}\] where \(\rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) is the largest slope whose line \(\rho\alpha\) converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) by Equation 42.2. The noise grows like \(\sqrt Q\).



42.3.3 Derivation

The histogram’s sensitivity. By Fact 1, one record moves the vote vector by at most 2 in \(\ell_1\) norm and \(\sqrt2\) in \(\ell_2\) norm.
LNMax is report-noisy-max. The counts are the scores, each moves by at most \(\Delta u = 1\), and they can move in opposite directions. Fact 3 with \(\Delta u = 1\) gives \((2/b)\)-DP.
GNMax is post-processing of a Gaussian histogram. Adding \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) to every count is the Gaussian mechanism on a vector with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt2\), so by Fact 2 its RDP is \(\alpha(\sqrt2)^2/(2\sigma^2) = \alpha/\sigma^2\). Taking the argmax and discarding the noisy counts is post-processing, which cannot increase it.
Compose. Each answer is \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP whatever the earlier answers were, so \(Q\) answers add up to \(Q\alpha/\sigma^2\) (Fact 2). This holds even if the analyst chooses query \(t\) after seeing answers \(1, \dots, t - 1\).
Calibrate. The composed curve is the line \(\rho\alpha\) with \(\rho = Q/\sigma^2\), and its \(\varepsilon\) depends only on \(\rho\). Setting \(Q/\sigma^2 = \rho(\varepsilon, \delta)\) and solving for \(\sigma\) gives Equation 42.4.



42.3.4 Interpretation
The cost is per answer, not per teacher. Neither the number of teachers nor what they are enters the privacy cost. A teacher can be a neural network trained without any noise, a decision forest, or a human annotator who saw one shard. The cost is set by the noise and the number of answers, and the noise can be large in absolute terms because the counts themselves are large: with 250 teachers, noise of standard deviation 40 on each count is noticeable but not overwhelming.
Gaussian noise wins for many queries, Laplace for very few. A Laplace answer is analysed as a pure-DP step, which pays for the worst case of every answer; a Gaussian answer has a privacy loss that is itself Gaussian and composes exactly. For one answer the pure-DP analysis is cheap, and as answers accumulate the Gaussian’s analysis wins. Table 42.2 compares the noise each needs, expressed as a standard deviation (\(\sqrt2b\) for Laplace). For a single answer, Laplace needs less noise. From 100 answers on, Gaussian noise is smaller by a factor close to 2 at both budgets, and the gap persists, since both grow like \(\sqrt Q\) once the composition is in its square-root regime.
Only the label is released. As in report-noisy-max, publishing the noisy counts as well would release a vector, and step 3 would no longer apply to the published output; the analysis would then have to pay for all \(m\) counts as a release in their own right. GNMax happens to have a valid analysis for the noisy counts too, since it is a Gaussian mechanism, but the data-dependent analysis of Section 42.7 needs the label alone.
How tight is the RDP accountant here? A Gaussian histogram has an exact conversion (Fact 2). At the \(\sigma\) the RDP accountant picks for \(\varepsilon = 1\), the exact \(\varepsilon\) is 0.915, and for \(\varepsilon = 4\) it is 3.698: the accountant overstates \(\varepsilon\) by about 9% and 8%. The ratio is the same for every \(Q\) because both depend only on \(Q/\sigma^2\).

Publishing the winner’s noisy count publishes that noise, which the proof assumed stays hidden.)

section: 42.4 How accurate is a noisy vote
text:
42.4 How accurate is a noisy vote

42.4.1 Context
The cost of an answer does not depend on the teachers. Its accuracy depends on little else. How likely is the noisy vote to return the plurality label, and how should you choose the number of teachers \(k\), given that more teachers means fewer records each?


42.4.2 Statement
On two labels, GNMax returns the plurality label with probability \[\Pr[\text{plurality}] = \Phi\Big(\frac{g}{\sqrt2\,\sigma}\Big), \tag{42.5}\] where \(g\) is the gap. On \(m\) labels, the probability that it returns anything other than the plurality \(i^*\) is at most \[\tilde\beta = \sum_{i \ne i^*}\frac12\operatorname{erfc}\Big(\frac{N_{i^*} - N_i}{2\sigma}\Big) \tag{42.6}\] (Papernot et al. 2018, Proposition 7). If a fraction \(a(x)\) of the \(k\) teachers vote for the correct label on a two-label query \(x\), the gap measured toward the correct label is \(k(2a(x) - 1)\), and the expected accuracy of the private answers is the average of \(\Phi\big(k(2a(x) - 1)/(\sqrt2\sigma)\big)\) over queries.


42.4.3 Derivation

Two labels. GNMax returns label 1 when \(N_1 + Z_1 > N_2 + Z_2\), that is when \(Z_2 - Z_1 < N_1 - N_2\). By Fact 4, \(Z_2 - Z_1\) is \(\mathcal N(0, 2\sigma^2)\), so this has probability \(\Phi((N_1 - N_2)/(\sqrt2\sigma))\). With label 1 the plurality, \(N_1 - N_2 = g\): Equation 42.5.
Many labels. GNMax returns some \(i \ne i^*\) only if \(N_i + Z_i > N_{i^*} + Z_{i^*}\) for at least one \(i\). The probability that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their probabilities (the union bound), and each has probability \(\frac12\operatorname{erfc}((N_{i^*} - N_i)/(2\sigma))\) by Fact 4: Equation 42.6.
Accuracy toward the truth. Measure the gap toward the correct label instead of the plurality: it is the number of teachers that are right minus the number that are wrong, \(ka - k(1 - a) = k(2a - 1)\), negative when most teachers are wrong. Step 1 with this signed gap gives the probability of a correct answer, and averaging over queries gives the expected accuracy.



42.4.4 Interpretation
The trade-off in \(k\). For a fixed number of answers and budget, \(\sigma\) is fixed (Equation 42.4), and the signal is \(k(2a - 1)\). More teachers multiply the signal by \(k\); but each teacher sees \(n/k\) records, is less accurate, and agrees less with the others, so \(2a - 1\) shrinks. Whether to add teachers depends on which effect wins. When the teachers’ accuracy falls slowly with shard size, as it does for a model that learns from few examples, more teachers win; when a teacher needs many records to be any good, fewer teachers are better.
The ceiling. Without noise, the plurality vote is an ensemble, and its accuracy is the best any private answer can reach. Noise can only pull answers toward a coin flip. On queries the teachers find hard, where \(a(x)\) is near \(\frac12\), any noise at all makes the answer close to random; this is the part of the accuracy that noise destroys first.
How tight is Equation 42.6? For two labels it is exact, since there is only one competitor. For many labels it adds the probabilities of beating the plurality one competitor at a time, which double-counts the outcomes where several competitors beat it. It is close when one competitor dominates the error and loose when many are nearly tied with the plurality.

section: 42.5 Private answers against a private model
text:
42.5 Private answers against a private model

42.5.1 Context
Here is the question of the title in its sharpest form. You have a budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). You can spend it on training one model with DP-SGD, whose answers are then free, or on answering queries one at a time with a teacher ensemble. Which gives more accurate answers, and how does the answer depend on how many queries you expect?


42.5.2 Statement
Let \(A_{\mathrm{model}}(\varepsilon)\) be the accuracy of a privately trained model at budget \(\varepsilon\); it does not depend on how many queries the model answers. Let \(A_{\mathrm{vote}}(Q, \varepsilon)\) be the expected accuracy of \(Q\) private answers at the same budget, with \(\sigma\) from Equation 42.4. Then \(A_{\mathrm{vote}}(Q, \varepsilon)\) decreases in \(Q\), from the noiseless vote’s accuracy toward \(\frac12\) (on two labels), and private answers are better exactly for \[Q < Q^*(\varepsilon) = \max\{Q : A_{\mathrm{vote}}(Q, \varepsilon) \ge A_{\mathrm{model}}(\varepsilon)\}, \tag{42.7}\] with \(Q^* = 0\) when even one answer is worse than the model.


42.5.3 Derivation

The model’s accuracy is constant in \(Q\). Every query to a released model is post-processing of its weights (Fact 2), so its answers cost nothing and are exactly as accurate as the model.
The vote’s accuracy falls with \(Q\). By Equation 42.4, \(\sigma\) grows like \(\sqrt Q\). Each query’s probability of a correct answer, \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\) with its signed gap \(g\), decreases in \(\sigma\) when \(g > 0\) and increases toward \(\frac12\) when \(g < 0\); as \(\sigma \to \infty\) every term tends to \(\frac12\). On this task the plurality is correct on most queries, and the average decreases in \(Q\) throughout the range shown here.
Break-even. A decreasing function crosses a constant at most once, at \(Q^*\).



42.5.4 Interpretation
Private prediction wins when the budget is small and the queries are few. DP-SGD pays a fixed price whatever the number of queries, and at small \(\varepsilon\) that price is a model much worse than the non-private one. The vote pays per query; its first answers are almost as good as the noiseless ensemble. So at small \(\varepsilon\) there is a range of \(Q\) where the vote wins, and at large \(\varepsilon\), where DP-SGD loses little, there may be none.
The ensemble’s ceiling sets the large-\(\varepsilon\) limit. Even one noiseless answer is only as good as the plurality vote. If the teachers, each trained on a small shard, cannot match one model trained on all the data, no amount of budget closes the gap. On the running example the ensemble of linear teachers reaches 0.9403 at best, below what DP-SGD reaches at \(\varepsilon = 2\).
What the comparison leaves out. It assumes you can run DP-SGD. When the teachers are LLMs behind an interface, models without gradients, or models trained by different parties who will not pool their data, the comparison is not with DP-SGD but with nothing, and private prediction is the only private option. It also ignores cost: DP-SGD trains once, while private prediction runs \(k\) models on every query.


42.5.5 Example: the running example
The DP-SGD baseline is the configuration of DP-SGD: \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\), learning rate 0.5, 10,000 steps, with the noise multiplier for each budget, retrained here and evaluated on this chapter’s evaluation set (two runs each). A product team expects a model to answer a million queries. Should it use private prediction? (Not query by query: a million answers need \(\sigma\) a hundred times that of 100 answers. It should either train privately or turn a few hundred private answers into a model, which is the next section.)

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
section: 42.6 PATE: from private answers to a private model
text:
42.6 PATE: from private answers to a private model

42.6.1 Context
Private answers cost budget forever; a private model costs it once. PATE combines them. Spend the budget on labelling a fixed number of public, unlabelled inputs with private answers, then train a new model, the student, on those inputs and labels. The student is released; the teachers never are. How private is the student, and how good can it be?


42.6.2 Statement
Let a student be trained, by any algorithm, on \(Q\) public inputs \(x_1, \dots, x_Q\) and their GNMax labels with noise \(\sigma\), and on any other public data, possibly unlabelled. Then the student, and every prediction it ever makes, is \((\alpha, Q\alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP with respect to the private data, and so \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon\) from Equation 42.2. The privacy cost depends on the number of labelled queries \(Q\) and on \(\sigma\), and on nothing about the student: not its size, its training algorithm or how many predictions it makes.


42.6.3 Derivation

The only private output is the labels. The student’s training algorithm sees the public inputs, which do not depend on the private data, and the \(Q\) labels. It never touches the teachers or the private records.
The labels are \(Q\) GNMax answers. The inputs to be labelled may be chosen adaptively, for example by the student asking about inputs it is unsure of, because RDP composition holds for adaptively chosen mechanisms. Their total cost is \(Q\alpha/\sigma^2\) (Section 42.3).
Post-processing. The student’s weights are a function of the labels and of public data, so they are as private as the labels (Fact 2), and so is every prediction computed from the weights.



42.6.4 Interpretation
Three things limit the student. It is trained on \(Q\) examples rather than \(n\), so it learns less than a model trained on all the private data. Its labels are noisy versions of the plurality vote, wrong on some fraction of the queries. And the plurality vote itself has the ensemble’s ceiling. Budget pulls these in opposite directions: more labels mean more noise per label by Equation 42.4, so for each \(\varepsilon\) there is a best \(Q\).
What PATE needs from you. Public, unlabelled inputs from the same distribution as the private data. In some domains this is easy (unlabelled images or text are plentiful; the labels are what is sensitive), in others impossible (there is no public pool of medical records). PATE also needs the public pool to be really public: an input that is itself a private record of someone else is protected by nothing in this analysis.
Semi-supervised students. The student may use every unlabelled public input, not only the \(Q\) it paid to label. Papernot et al. (2017) train the student as a semi-supervised generative adversarial network (GAN) on the labelled and unlabelled inputs, and Papernot et al. (2018) use semi-supervised methods for their image tasks. This chapter’s student uses only its \(Q\) labelled inputs, which is the simplest choice and the least favourable to PATE.
What PATE protects, and against whom. The guarantee covers the released student and its predictions. The teachers are non-private models of the data and must stay secret: an attacker who steals one can run any attack of Part 2 on its shard. PATE moves the trust from the training algorithm to the server that holds the teachers.


42.6.5 Example: students on the running example
Take \(k = 250\) teachers. Their plurality vote labels the public pool with accuracy 0.9322. The student is the part’s network (64 hidden units, 3,329 weights), trained non-privately on the first \(Q\) public inputs and their GNMax labels for 2,000 steps. Table 42.6 gives the results; the first two rows are references without privacy.

On this task PATE loses, and it is worth saying why, because the reasons are the conditions under which it wins elsewhere. The task is binary, so a wrong label is the other label and label noise is as damaging as it can be. The teachers are weak (0.7031 each with 40 records) and disagree on many queries, so many gaps are small against the noise. The student needs thousands of labels to learn the decision boundary. And DP-SGD does well on this task even at \(\varepsilon = 1\). PATE’s published successes are on tasks where teachers agree on most inputs and a student learns from few labels plus many unlabelled inputs: on a handwritten-digit benchmark (MNIST), Papernot et al. (2018, Table 1) report a student with 98.5% accuracy against a non-private 99.2%, at \(\varepsilon = 1.97\) with 286 answered queries. The next section explains the analysis behind such small \(\varepsilon\).


42.6.6 Check yourself

The student is trained with 2,000 steps of non-private SGD and has 3,329 weights. Does either number change its \(\varepsilon\)? (No. The student’s training is post-processing of the labels; only \(Q\) and \(\sigma\) enter.)
Could the student query the teachers about inputs it is uncertain about, after a first round of training? (Yes. The queries are public inputs chosen from earlier private answers, which adaptive composition allows; each answer still costs \(\alpha/\sigma^2\).)
