title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.7 Data-dependent analysis and Confident-GNMax

42.7.1 Context
The cost \(\alpha/\sigma^2\) of a GNMax answer is a worst case over all vote histograms, including those where the vote is tied and one teacher decides it. But when 249 of 250 teachers agree, one record, which changes one teacher, can hardly change the answer: the noisy vote returns the plurality with overwhelming probability, with or without that record. Can a query on which the teachers agree be charged less? And can a mechanism be designed to answer only such queries?


42.7.2 Statement
The pure-DP form (Papernot et al. 2017, Theorem 3, written in RDP). Let \(M\) be \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP and suppose that on the actual dataset \(D\) there is an output \(i^*\) with \(\Pr[M(D) \ne i^*] = \beta < e^{-\varepsilon_0}\). Then for every neighbour \(D'\), \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\|M(D')\big) \le \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big[(1 - \beta)^\alpha\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon_0}\beta\big)^{1 - \alpha} + \beta\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_0}\Big]. \tag{42.8}\] When only an upper bound \(\tilde\beta \ge \beta\) is known, the bound holds with the largest value of the right side over \(\beta \in (0, \tilde\beta]\). For LNMax, \(\varepsilon_0 = 2/b\).
The Gaussian form (Papernot et al. 2018, Theorem 6, with their orders from Proposition 10). For GNMax with noise \(\sigma\) and \(\tilde\beta\) from Equation 42.6, let \(\alpha_2 = \sigma\sqrt{\ln(1/\tilde\beta)}\), \(\alpha_1 = \alpha_2 + 1\), \(\varepsilon_1 = \alpha_1/\sigma^2\) and \(\varepsilon_2 = \alpha_2/\sigma^2\). If \(\alpha \le \alpha_1\), \(\alpha_2 > 1\) and \(\tilde\beta \le e^{(\alpha_2 - 1)\varepsilon_2}\big/\big(\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_1 - 1}\cdot\frac{\alpha_2}{\alpha_2 - 1}\big)^{\alpha_2}\), then for every neighbour \(D'\) \[D_\alpha\big(M(D)\|M(D')\big) \le \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\Big[(1 - \tilde\beta)A^{\alpha - 1} + \tilde\beta B^{\alpha - 1}\Big],\quad A = \frac{1 - \tilde\beta}{1 - (\tilde\beta e^{\varepsilon_2})^{(\alpha_2 - 1)/\alpha_2}},\quad B = \frac{e^{\varepsilon_1}}{\tilde\beta^{1/(\alpha_1 - 1)}}. \tag{42.9}\] Each answer is charged the smaller of this and \(\alpha/\sigma^2\), and the charges add up over answers.
Confident-GNMax (Papernot et al. 2018, Algorithm 1). For each query, release \(\bot\) (no answer) unless \(\max_iN_i + \mathcal N(0, \sigma_1^2) \ge \tau_1\); if the check passes, release a GNMax answer with noise \(\sigma_2\). With data-independent accounting, \(Q_{\mathrm{pool}}\) checks and \(Q_{\mathrm{ans}}\) answers cost \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \Big(\frac{Q_{\mathrm{pool}}}{2\sigma_1^2} + \frac{Q_{\mathrm{ans}}}{\sigma_2^2}\Big)\alpha, \tag{42.10}\] provided the total is kept below a budget fixed in advance.


42.7.3 Derivation
The pure-DP form shows where all data-dependent bounds come from; the Gaussian form follows the same plan with Rényi bounds at higher orders in place of the pure-DP ratio, and its proof is in Papernot et al. (2018, Appendix A). Section M.2 in the appendices derives it step by step.

Write the divergence as a sum over outputs. By Equation 42.1, \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha} = \sum_yP(y)^\alpha P'(y)^{1 - \alpha}\), with \(P = M(D)\) and \(P' = M(D')\). Split the sum into the likely output \(i^*\) and the rest. Write \(\beta = P(\text{not } i^*)\) and \(\beta' = P'(\text{not } i^*)\).
The unlikely outputs. For \(y \ne i^*\), \(P(y)^\alpha P'(y)^{1 - \alpha} = P(y)\big(P(y)/P'(y)\big)^{\alpha - 1} \le P(y)e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_0}\), because \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP bounds the ratio by \(e^{\varepsilon_0}\). Summed over \(y \ne i^*\), this is at most \(\beta\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_0}\).
The likely output. Its term is \((1 - \beta)^\alpha(1 - \beta')^{1 - \alpha}\). Pure DP, applied to the event “not \(i^*\)”, gives \(\beta' \le e^{\varepsilon_0}\beta\), so \(1 - \beta' \ge 1 - e^{\varepsilon_0}\beta > 0\). The exponent \(1 - \alpha\) is negative, so a larger base gives a smaller power: \((1 - \beta')^{1 - \alpha} \le (1 - e^{\varepsilon_0}\beta)^{1 - \alpha}\).
Collect. Adding the two parts and taking \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\) gives Equation 42.8 with the true \(\beta\). Since only a bound \(\tilde\beta\) is computable, take the largest value over all \(\beta\) the bound allows; the right side increases in \(\beta\) for every \(\beta < e^{-\varepsilon_0}\), because it is convex in \(\beta\) with a non-negative slope at 0 (Section M.2 in the appendices proves both), so the largest value is at \(\beta = \tilde\beta\).
Small \(\beta\). At \(\beta = 0\) the bracket is 1 and the bound is 0. Its derivative there is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_0} + (\alpha - 1)e^{\varepsilon_0} - \alpha\), so for small \(\beta\) the bound is about \(\beta\) times a constant: the cost of an answer is proportional to the probability that the noise overturns the plurality.
Confident-GNMax. The check releases a noisy version of \(\max_iN_i\), which one record changes by at most 1 (one count up or down by 1 moves the maximum by at most 1), so it is a Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity 1: \((\alpha, \alpha/(2\sigma_1^2))\)-RDP for every query, answered or not. The second step is GNMax, \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma_2^2)\)-RDP, run only when the check passes. Whether it runs is decided by a released output, so its cost is chosen adaptively. Both costs are lines in \(\alpha\), and the Rényi filter of Adaptive composition says that adaptively chosen RDP costs that stay below a fixed budget on every path compose as if fixed. Summing gives Equation 42.10.



42.7.4 Interpretation
Agreement is cheap, disagreement costs full price. Figure 42.4 draws the cost of one GNMax answer with \(\sigma = 40\) at order 8 against the gap. At gaps up to 100 the data-dependent bound is no better than the data-independent \(\alpha/\sigma^2 = 0.005\); then it falls steeply, to \(1.23 \times 10^{-3}\) at a gap of 150 and \(8.37 \times 10^{-5}\) at 200. The dashed curve is the exact data-dependent cost on two labels, which the script computes directly: the output is then a coin with probability \(\Phi(g/(\sqrt2\sigma))\), one record moves \(g\) by 2, and Equation 42.1 applies to two outcomes. It lies below the bound everywhere: at a gap of 150, \(2.42 \times 10^{-4}\), five times below. Theorem 6 is valid but not tight, and it is far from tight for small gaps, where on two labels even the data-independent cost overstates the truth.






Figure 42.4: The RDP cost at order 8 of one GNMax answer with \(\sigma = 40\), against the gap between the two vote counts, on a log scale: the data-independent \(\alpha/\sigma^2\), the data-dependent bound of Equation 42.9, and the exact data-dependent cost on two labels.



Why it helps little here and a lot elsewhere. The total is a sum over queries, so the saving depends on how many queries have large gaps. With 250 teachers on the running example, only 0.2879 of the public queries have a gap of at least 150, so most answers pay close to full price. On a task where nearly all teachers agree on nearly all inputs, as on handwritten digits, almost every answer is nearly free, and \(\varepsilon\) falls by a large factor.
The data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is itself private information. It is computed from the votes, so publishing it reveals something about the teachers and so about the data. Worse, its sensitivity is large: one record changes one teacher, and that teacher’s votes can change on every query, moving every term of the sum. Papernot et al. (2018, Appendix B) therefore release the data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) with Gaussian noise scaled to its smooth sensitivity, the device of Beyond global sensitivity for functions whose worst-case sensitivity is far above their typical one, and pay for that release too. On MNIST, with 250 teachers of 200 examples, 640 queries, \(\tau_1 = 200\), \(\sigma_1 = 150\) and \(\sigma_2 = 40\), they report an expected 283 answered queries and a data-dependent \(\varepsilon = 2.00\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), which becomes \(2.52 \pm 0.385\) once sanitized (their Table 2). Without that step, a data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is a measurement, not a guarantee.
A one-directional bound. Equation 42.8 and Equation 42.9 bound \(D_\alpha(M(D)\|M(D'))\) for the actual dataset \(D\) against every neighbour, the direction the accounting of Papernot et al. uses. The exact two-label computation above takes the worse of both directions, and is still below the bound.
Confident-GNMax answers what is cheap and correct. Queries with a strong consensus are cheap under the data-dependent analysis, and their plurality label is more likely to be right. The noisy check selects them. It costs something on every query, but with \(\sigma_1\) much larger than \(\sigma_2\) that cost is small per query, and the expensive, likely-wrong queries are mostly skipped. The price is that the student never sees labels for the hard inputs near the decision boundary.


42.7.5 Example: data-dependent costs on the running example
The pure-DP form. For an LNMax answer with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0.1\), at order 8 the data-independent cost is 0.0367. If the plurality fails with probability \(\tilde\beta = 0.1\), Equation 42.8 gives 0.0235; at \(\tilde\beta = 0.01\), 0.00248; at \(\tilde\beta = 0.001\), 0.00025. Below \(\tilde\beta = 0.1\) the cost falls in proportion to \(\tilde\beta\), as step 5 predicts.
GNMax on 250 teachers. Table 42.7 compares the costs of answering the first \(Q\) public queries with \(\sigma = 40\).

The data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) also has the instability described above: if one teacher among the 250 switched every one of its votes on the first 1,000 queries, the data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) would move from 4.375 to 4.389.

42.7.6 Check yourself

Why can’t the data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) simply be released with noise calibrated to its global sensitivity? (Its global sensitivity is huge. One record changes one teacher, whose votes may change on every query; on a histogram near a tie, each such change moves that query’s cost from almost 0 to the full \(\alpha/\sigma^2\), so the worst-case change of the sum is close to the data-independent total.)
In Confident-GNMax, why is \(\sigma_1\) chosen much larger than \(\sigma_2\)? (The check is paid on every query and the answer only on answered ones. A large \(\sigma_1\) makes the frequent cost small; the check only needs to separate strong consensus from weak, which a noisy maximum can do even with a lot of noise when \(\tau_1\) is set well.)

section: 42.8 Paying only for disagreement, with a worst-case guarantee
text:
42.8 Paying only for disagreement, with a worst-case guarantee

42.8.1 Context
The data-dependent analysis of Section 42.7 charges agreed answers less, but the \(\varepsilon\) it computes is itself a function of the votes, and publishing it needs a separate private release with smooth sensitivity. There is another way to make agreement cheap. Instead of measuring after the fact how much each answer cost, test privately, before answering, whether the vote is so lopsided that one record cannot overturn it. Release the plurality label exactly when the test passes, and nothing when it fails. Then let only the failures cost budget, by running the tests through the sparse vector technique of Selection. This is the stability-based aggregation of Thakurta & Smith (2013), which Bassily, Thakkar & Thakurta (2018) apply to PATE. Its guarantee is an ordinary \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) fixed before any vote is seen. What does it cost, and when does it pay?


42.8.2 Statement
For a query \(x\), the distance to instability is the largest number \(j\) such that changing the votes of any \(j\) teachers leaves the same label strictly on top. With \(g\) the gap between the top two counts, \[\operatorname{dist}(x) = \Big\lceil\frac g2\Big\rceil - 1, \quad\text{and } 0 \text{ when } g = 0. \tag{42.11}\] Stable aggregation goes through the public queries in order, and asks of each one whether its distance is clearly above a threshold \(\tau\). AboveThreshold halts at the first query whose value is high, and here the procedure should halt at the first query whose distance is low. So it runs AboveThreshold at a budget \(\varepsilon_0\) on the negated distances \(-\operatorname{dist}(x_i)\) with threshold \(-\tau\). The threshold gets noise \(\xi \sim \mathrm{Lap}(2/\varepsilon_0)\) and each query fresh noise \(\nu_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(4/\varepsilon_0)\).
A query with \(-\operatorname{dist}(x_i) + \nu_i \ge -\tau + \xi\) is unstable. It gets no label, and the run restarts with fresh threshold noise. Every other query is stable, and it gets the exact plurality label, with no noise. The procedure stops after \(c\) unstable answers or at the end of the pool of \(Q_{\mathrm{pool}}\) queries.
The total slack \(\delta\) is split in two. One part, \(\delta_{\text{bad}}\), bounds the chance that a query with no margin slips through the test, and the other, \(\delta'\), goes to the conversion from RDP. Choose the threshold \(\tau\) so that \[Q_{\mathrm{pool}}\cdot\Pr[\nu - \xi > \tau] \le \delta_{\text{bad}}, \qquad \Pr[\nu - \xi > \tau] = \frac{b_1^2e^{-\tau/b_1} - b_2^2e^{-\tau/b_2}}{2(b_1^2 - b_2^2)}, \tag{42.12}\] with \(b_1 = 4/\varepsilon_0\) and \(b_2 = 2/\varepsilon_0\) the two Laplace scales. Then all the released labels together are \((\varepsilon, \delta' + \delta_{\text{bad}})\)-DP, where \(\varepsilon\) is the better of basic composition, \(c\varepsilon_0\), and the conversion at \(\delta'\) of \(c\) composed \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP steps, \[\varepsilon = \min\Big\{c\varepsilon_0,\ \min_\alpha\Big[c\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{RR}}(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta' + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big]\Big\}, \tag{42.13}\] with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{RR}}\) the randomized-response curve of Fact 3 at \(\varepsilon_0\), the Rényi curve that bounds every \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP mechanism. The budget does not depend on how many stable labels are released.


42.8.3 Derivation

The distance. One changed teacher moves one vote from one label to another, so it lowers the gap by at most 2. After \(j\) changes the gap is at least \(g - 2j\), and the label stays strictly on top while \(g - 2j \ge 1\), that is for \(j \le (g - 1)/2\). The largest such whole number is \(\lceil g/2\rceil - 1\), which is Equation 42.11.
One record moves every distance by at most 1. Adding or removing a record changes one teacher (Fact 1), which changes each query’s distance by at most 1: if any \(j\) changes from \(D'\) keep the label on top, then any \(j - 1\) changes from \(D\) do, because \(D\) is one change away from \(D'\). This is the distance-to-a-set argument of Beyond global sensitivity. So the query values \(-\operatorname{dist}(x_i)\) have sensitivity 1, for every query at the same time.
The stable/unstable answers cost \(c\) runs. Each run of AboveThreshold on sensitivity-1 queries is \(\varepsilon_0\)-DP, however many queries it reads (Selection). There are at most \(c\) runs, each started after the previous one’s output. Basic composition gives \(c\varepsilon_0\) with no slack. Alternatively, Fact 3 gives each run the randomized-response RDP curve, the curves add, and the conversion of Fact 2 at \(\delta'\) gives the second term of Equation 42.13. Either bound is valid, so the smaller one is.
Exact labels are safe where the distance is at least 1. If \(\operatorname{dist}(x_i) \ge 1\) on \(D\), one change of teacher leaves the same label strictly on top, so the plurality of \(x_i\) is the same on \(D\) and on its neighbour \(D'\). So on such queries the released label is the same on \(D\) and \(D'\). Whenever every labelled query has distance at least 1 on \(D\), the whole output is therefore determined by which queries were declared stable, in the same way for both datasets.
The only danger is a passed test at distance 0. Call it the bad event. A query with distance 0 is declared stable when \(\nu_i < -\tau + \xi\), that is \(\nu_i - \xi < -\tau\). The difference of two independent symmetric variables is symmetric, so this has probability \(\Pr[\nu - \xi > \tau]\). A union bound over at most \(Q_{\mathrm{pool}}\) queries bounds the probability of the bad event by \(Q_{\mathrm{pool}}\cdot\Pr[\nu - \xi > \tau] \le \delta_{\text{bad}}\). The tail formula in Equation 42.12 comes from integrating the density of a sum of two Laplace variables (Section E.5 in the appendices does the integral), and the script checks it by simulation.
Put the two together. For any set \(S\) of outputs, the probability that the output lands in \(S\) on \(D\) is at most the probability that it lands in \(S\) without the bad event, plus \(\delta_{\text{bad}}\). Without the bad event, every labelled query has distance at least 1 on \(D\). So the output lands in \(S\) only if the stable/unstable answers land in a set \(S'\) of answer sequences, defined from \(D\), whose stable queries all have distance at least 1 on \(D\) and whose labels, the same on \(D\) and \(D'\) by step 4, put the output in \(S\). Step 3 bounds the probability of \(S'\) on \(D\) by \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability on \(D'\), plus \(\delta'\). On \(D'\), answers in \(S'\) produce an output in \(S\), because their labels are the same. That gives \((\varepsilon, \delta' + \delta_{\text{bad}})\)-DP.



42.8.4 Interpretation
Nothing needs sanitizing. The budget is fixed by \(c\), \(\varepsilon_0\) and the two \(\delta\)s before any vote is seen, so it can be published as it is. What depends on the data is how many labels you get for that budget, which is the reverse of the data-dependent analysis, where the labels are fixed and the cost depends on the data. The cutoff \(c\) must be fixed in advance for this to hold.
The labels are exact. A stable query gets the noiseless plurality, so the student’s labels are as good as the ensemble’s on every query it receives. Label noise, which hurt the students of Section 42.6, is gone. The hard queries near the boundary are skipped, as in Confident-GNMax.
The threshold is the obstacle. The test must almost never pass a query at distance 0, over the whole pool, so \(\tau\) grows like \(4\ln(Q_{\mathrm{pool}}/\delta_{\text{bad}})/\varepsilon_0\). At \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\) and a pool of 10,000 queries, that is \(\tau = 84.0\). So a query passes reliably only when the plurality leads by about \(2\tau \approx 170\) votes. On top of that, every unstable answer costs a whole \(\varepsilon_0\), and \(c\) runs compose almost linearly unless \(c\) is in the hundreds. So the method pays only when there are many teachers and they are nearly unanimous on almost every query. Bassily, Thakkar & Thakurta (2018) use it to prove accuracy guarantees for the student under such conditions. Deployed PATE systems use Confident-GNMax with data-dependent accounting instead, and pay for the sanitizing.


42.8.5 Example: the running example
Take \(\varepsilon_0 = 1\), and split the slack equally, \(\delta_{\text{bad}} = \delta' = 5 \times 10^{-6}\), so that the total \(\delta\) is \(10^{-5}\). For a pool of 1,000 queries Equation 42.12 gives the threshold \(\tau = 74.8\), and for 10,000 queries it gives 84.0. The tail formula is easy to check, since at \(\tau = 8\) it gives 0.0872 and a million simulated pairs give 0.0866. The budget of Equation 42.13 is \(\varepsilon = 5.00\) for \(c = 5\) unstable answers, and 20.00 for \(c = 20\), both from basic composition. The composition saves almost nothing at this scale: even 100 unstable answers cost 83.45 rather than 100.
The teachers rarely clear the bar. The running example’s pool has 10,000 queries, so the threshold is 84.0. With 250 teachers the largest distance on the pool is 124, and only 0.1996 of the queries have a distance of at least 84.0. With 500 teachers that share is 0.3923. On this task, where most queries fall short of the threshold, the worst-case-safe route is far more expensive than paying for the sanitizing.


42.8.6 Check yourself

Why is it safe to release the plurality with no noise at all when the test says “stable”? (If the query’s distance is at least 1, the neighbouring dataset has the same plurality, so the label carries no information that the stable/unstable answer did not. The only risk is a query at distance 0 that passes, which the threshold makes unlikely, at probability \(\delta_{\text{bad}}\) over the whole pool.)
Why must the cutoff \(c\) be fixed before the run? (The budget is set by \(c\). Choosing \(c\) after seeing how many queries turned out unstable would make the budget depend on the votes, the problem this construction avoids.)

title: 42  Private prediction: PATE and in-context learning
text:
42.9 Private in-context learning

42.9.1 Context
An LLM can learn a task from examples placed in its prompt, without any training: show it four labelled movie reviews and it will label the fifth. This in-context learning has its own privacy problem. If the examples, the exemplars, are private records, every answer is computed from them, and an attacker who can query the prompted model can learn about them. Duan, Dziedzic, Papernot and Boenisch (NeurIPS 2023) demonstrate this with a membership inference attack (MIA): querying GPT-3 prompted with one private example, the model’s probability for the correct label is markedly higher on the example that was in the prompt than on other records. Training the LLM with DP-SGD is not an option when it is only reachable through an interface. How do you answer privately from a prompt?


42.9.2 Statement
Private in-context learning (Wu, Panda, Wang & Mittal, ICLR 2024; Duan et al. 2023): split the private exemplars into disjoint groups by a fixed rule, prompt the model once per group with that group’s exemplars and the query, and release the GNMax label of the \(k\) answers. Each answer is \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP, exactly as in Section 42.3. If, as in Wu et al., each query first draws a fresh Poisson sample of the exemplars, each record included independently with probability \(q\), and the sample is split into groups by the fixed rule, then each answer’s RDP curve is that of the Poisson-subsampled Gaussian with sampling rate \(q\) and noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt2\), and \(Q\) answers add up: \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = Q\,\varepsilon_{q,\,\sigma/\sqrt2}(\alpha), \tag{42.14}\] with \(\varepsilon_{q, s}\) the subsampled-Gaussian curve of Amplification by subsampling, the same accountant DP-SGD uses. PromptPATE (Duan et al.) turns the answers into a public prompt instead: label a few public inputs with Confident-GNMax over an ensemble of prompted models, and use the labelled public inputs as the exemplars of a single prompt that is then deployed with no further cost, the student of PATE in prompt form.


42.9.3 Derivation

One exemplar, one prompt. With the groups fixed by a rule that does not depend on the data (a hash, as in Fact 1), adding or removing an exemplar changes the content of one group’s prompt and so at most one answer: one vote moves. The histogram has \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt2\).
Without subsampling. GNMax on this histogram is \((\alpha, \alpha/\sigma^2)\)-RDP (Section 42.3), whatever the language model computes from its prompt.
With Poisson subsampling. The record is in the query’s sample with probability \(q\), independently of the others. If it is not, the output is distributed as without it; if it is, the histogram shifts by a vector of length at most \(\sqrt2\) against noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) on each coordinate. Rotating the shift onto one axis and rescaling by \(\sqrt2\), this is the subsampled Gaussian of DP-SGD with sensitivity 1 and noise multiplier \(\sigma/\sqrt2\).
Compose. The \(Q\) answers use independent samples and add up in RDP: Equation 42.14.
PromptPATE. The deployed prompt contains public inputs and their private labels. It is post-processing of the labels, so its cost is that of the labels alone, however often it is used.



42.9.4 Interpretation
Answering from a prompt is private prediction. Everything in the previous sections carries over: the cost grows with the number of answered queries, the accuracy depends on how much the prompted models agree, and the data-dependent analysis applies. The difference is the teacher. A prompted LLM is a strong learner from very few examples, because most of what it knows comes from pretraining; its errors with different exemplars are correlated, so its votes agree far more than independently trained small models do. Duan et al. observe this high consensus and suggest that it may come from all teachers sharing the same underlying model. High consensus is exactly what makes data-dependent costs small.
Subsampling amplifies; disjointness is still needed. Subsampling lets a large exemplar set serve many queries cheaply, since each record takes part in a fraction \(q\) of them. But within one query the groups must be disjoint, or a record in two groups moves two votes.
Text generation needs another aggregator. Votes work for labels. For free text, Wu et al. map each group’s answer into a space where averaging makes sense, either sentence embeddings, which they privatize with the Gaussian mechanism, or keyword counts, from which they select keywords privately with propose-test-release or a joint exponential mechanism, and then ask the model to produce an answer from the private aggregate.
What the papers report. These numbers are from the papers, not from this chapter’s script. Duan et al. report, with GPT-3 as the base model, 92.7% accuracy on a movie-review sentiment task at \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (0.147, 10^{-6})\) with PromptPATE, against 95.2% without privacy. Wu et al. (arXiv version) report on the same sentiment task, with 10,000 queries each answered by a vote of ten 4-shot prompts, 91.97% at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 92.83% at \(\varepsilon = 3\) with GPT-3 Babbage, against 91.89% for a single non-private 4-shot prompt and 86.58% with no examples at all.


42.9.5 Example: a simulated in-context learner
No language model is available here, so the script simulates the mechanics with a stand-in: an “in-context learner” that, given exemplars \((x_j, y_j)\), labels a query by the sign of \(\langle\sum_jy_jx_j, x\rangle\). It has no pretraining at all, which makes it far weaker than an LLM; what carries over is the accounting and the dependence on agreement, not the accuracy.
The leak. An attacker who knows a candidate record \((x, y)\) scores it by \(y\langle\theta, x\rangle\), with \(\theta = \sum_jy_jx_j\) the learner’s parameter vector, its confidence in the right label. The area under the curve (AUC) of this attack, the probability that a random member scores above a random non-member, is 1.000 against a 1-shot learner, 0.996 against a 4-shot learner and 0.889 against a 16-shot learner (400 trials each). A prompt with few exemplars reveals them almost perfectly, as Duan et al. found for GPT-3.
Private answers. Each query draws a Poisson sample of the 10,000 private records at rate \(q = 0.04\), about 400 records, and splits it by record index into 25 groups of about 16. A developer puts 200 private exemplars into one long prompt and answers 1,000 user queries with it. Is anything private? What to take from it. The privacy of private prediction is easy: one record, one vote, a Gaussian histogram, an accountant. That is not a verdict on the method but a description of when to use it: when you cannot train privately, when the queries are few, and when the teachers agree, which is what pretrained models in in-context learning provide.

Rules of thumb

Private prediction costs per answer; private training costs once. Count your queries before choosing.
The noise grows like \(\sqrt Q\) and does not depend on the number of teachers; add teachers as long as their vote gaps grow.
Use Gaussian noise for more than a handful of answers, Laplace only for one or two.
A teacher ensemble is only as good as its noiseless vote; measure that ceiling first.
Data-dependent \(\varepsilon\) is not a guarantee until it is released privately; report the data-independent one, or pay for the release.
Stable aggregation avoids the sanitizing, but only pays with many, nearly unanimous teachers: check what share of your queries clears its threshold first.

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.1 Why this matters
The previous chapters trained models with differential privacy (DP) from random weights, by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, called DP-SGD, as in DP-SGD: every step adds Gaussian noise to a sum of clipped per-example gradients, and an accountant turns the steps into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). On the part’s running example it costs little at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and a great deal at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and below. The most accurate private models in the literature are not trained that way. They start from a model pretrained non-privately on a large public dataset, such as text or images collected from the web, and only fine-tune it privately on the sensitive data. Private image classifiers and private language models fine-tuned this way are far more accurate, at the same \(\varepsilon\), than the same models trained privately from scratch (Tramèr & Boneh 2021; Yu et al. 2022; Li et al. 2022; De et al. 2022).
This chapter asks why that helps so much, and why a second practice helps on top of it: fine-tuning only a small part of the model, such as the last layer or a low-rank update to each weight matrix, often beats fine-tuning all of it under DP, although without privacy it would usually be the other way round.
crumbs: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.1.1 The one idea: the noise is paid per trainable direction, the signal is not
DP-SGD adds noise of the same size to every coordinate it updates: with noise multiplier \(\sigma\), clipping norm \(C\) and expected batch size \(B\), the noise on the averaged gradient has standard deviation \(\sigma C/B\) in each of the \(d\) trainable coordinates, so its length is about \(\sigma C\sqrt d/B\). The useful part of the gradient, the average over the records, does not grow with \(d\): it has length at most \(C\) whatever the number of coordinates, and it is usually concentrated in a few directions. Every trainable coordinate that the task does not need is a coordinate that only collects noise.
Public data helps in two ways that both follow from this. First, it moves the starting point close to a good model, so that what remains to be learned privately is small and lies in few directions. Second, it tells you which directions those are, before you touch the private data and at no privacy cost: the last layer on top of good features, a low-rank update, or the top principal directions of public gradients. Restricting training to those directions cuts the noise without cutting the signal. Whether it is worth restricting depends on how much of the signal the restriction throws away, and that is what decides between fine-tuning all weights and fine-tuning a few.

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
43.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

43.2.1 Fact 1 — DP-SGD’s guarantee depends on the clipped sum, not on which weights it updates
Each step of DP-SGD releases \(\sum_{i \in S_t}\bar g_i + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\), where \(\bar g_i\) is record \(i\)’s gradient clipped to length at most \(C\) and \(S_t\) is a Poisson-sampled batch. Adding or removing one record changes the sum by one clipped gradient, of length at most \(C\), so the noise is \(\sigma\) times the sensitivity, and the accountant composes the steps into \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) from \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) alone (DP-SGD). Nothing in this argument depends on what the gradient is a gradient of: all weights, the last layer, the factors of a low-rank update, or a projection of the gradient onto a fixed subspace. The clipping simply applies to the vector of trainable coordinates, whatever it is. With \(q = 0.01\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), the accountant gives \(\sigma = 7.72\), 4.13, 2.28 and 0.917 for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), 1, 2 and 8 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).


43.2.2 Fact 2 — A Gaussian vector’s length grows like the square root of its dimension, and a projection keeps it Gaussian
If \(\xi \sim \mathcal N(0, s^2I_k)\), then \(\mathbb E\|\xi\|^2 = ks^2\), a sum of \(d\) squared coordinates each with mean \(s^2\), and \(\|\xi\|\) concentrates near \(s\sqrt d\) (Concentration inequalities). If \(P\) is the orthogonal projection onto a fixed \(m\)-dimensional subspace, then \(P\xi\) is again Gaussian, with standard deviation \(s\) along each of \(m\) orthonormal directions of the subspace and nothing outside it. The reason is rotation invariance: the density of \(\xi\) depends only on \(\|\xi\|\), so in any orthonormal basis its coordinates are independent \(\mathcal N(0, s^2)\), and the projection keeps \(m\) of them. So noise restricted to a subspace has length about \(s\sqrt m\).


43.2.3 Fact 3 — Public data is free, and so is anything computed from it
DP bounds how the output’s distribution changes when one private record changes. A computation that reads only public data, such as pretraining, choosing a subspace from public gradients or tuning on a public validation set, produces a fixed object as far as the private data are concerned, and using it as the starting point or a hyperparameter of a private algorithm costs nothing. In the DP-SGD proof this enters as the condition that the initial weights \(\theta_0\) are chosen independently of the private data (DP-SGD). Anything computed afterwards from the private algorithm’s output is post-processing (Post-processing, group privacy and composition).


43.2.4 Fact 4 — A dense layer’s per-example gradient is an outer product
For a layer that maps an input \(a \in \mathbb R^{d_{\text{in}}}\) to \(Wa\), the gradient of record \(i\)’s loss with respect to \(W\) is \(\nu_ia_i^\top\), where \(\nu_i\) is the gradient with respect to the layer’s output, and its length is \(\|\nu_i\|\,\|a_i\|\), because the squared entries \(\nu_{ij}^2a_{il}^2\) sum to \((\sum_j\nu_{ij}^2)(\sum_l a_{il}^2)\). Clipping can therefore compute each record’s gradient norm without forming the gradient, ghost clipping (DP-SGD).

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.3 Why dimension costs, and when it does not
text:
43.3 Why dimension costs, and when it does not

43.3.1 Context
Every bound on private learning in this part grows with the dimension. Private empirical risk minimization shows that the best excess risk achievable under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP grows like \(\sqrt d\) for convex Lipschitz losses and like \(d\) for strongly convex ones. Matching lower bounds hold up to logarithmic factors. The noise in DP-SGD has length \(\sigma C\sqrt d/B\), growing with the number of trainable weights. Yet large pretrained language models with hundreds of millions of weights are fine-tuned privately with good results. How much does each trainable direction really cost, and what decides it?


43.3.2 Statement
The noise on the averaged gradient, restricted to the \(d\) trainable coordinates, has length \[\|\xi_t\|/B \approx s\sqrt d = \frac{\sigma C\sqrt d}{B}. \tag{43.1}\] Near the starting point, model the loss as a quadratic with curvature \(H\). Then \(T\) steps of noisy gradient descent with learning rate \(\eta\) and noise of standard deviation \(s\) per coordinate raise the expected loss, compared with the same steps without noise, by \(\mathcal E\), the noise cost: \[\mathcal E = \sum_{j=1}^d\frac{\eta s^2}{2(2 - \eta h_j)}\Big(1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^{2T}\Big) \approx \frac{\eta s^2}{4}\,d_{\text{eff}}, \qquad d_{\text{eff}} = \sum_{j=1}^d\Big(1 - (1 - \eta h_j)^{2T}\Big), \tag{43.2}\] where \(h_j\) are the eigenvalues of \(H\) restricted to the trainable coordinates, \(0 \le h_j < 2/\eta\), and the approximation assumes \(\eta h_j \ll 1\). The effective dimension \(d_{\text{eff}}\) satisfies \[d_{\text{eff}} \le \min\Big(d,\ 2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H\Big). \tag{43.3}\]


43.3.3 Derivation
The idea is to follow the noise separately from the signal. On a quadratic, the dynamics are linear, so the noise’s contribution to the weights is a sum of independent Gaussian kicks, each shrunk by the curvature. Directions with high curvature forget old kicks quickly and reach a steady state; directions with almost no curvature keep accumulating kicks but charge very little for them.

Separate the noise. Write \(\mathcal L(\theta)\) for the training loss, the empirical risk on the fixed private dataset. On the quadratic \(\mathcal L(\theta) = \mathcal L(\theta^*) + \frac12(\theta - \theta^*)^\top H(\theta - \theta^*)\) the gradient is \(H(\theta - \theta^*)\). Let \(\theta_t\) follow the noisy steps \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta(H(\theta_t - \theta^*) + \xi_t)\) and \(\bar\theta_t\) the same steps without noise, from the same start. Their difference \(e_t = \theta_t - \bar\theta_t\) obeys \(e_{t+1} = (I - \eta H)e_t - \eta\xi_t\) with \(e_0 = 0\), because the terms with \(\theta^*\) are the same for both and cancel. So \(e_t\) is a linear function of the noise alone, a Gaussian with mean zero.
The loss increase. Expanding the quadratic around \(\bar\theta_T\), \(\mathcal L(\theta_T) = \mathcal L(\bar\theta_T) + \nabla\mathcal L(\bar\theta_T)^\top e_T + \frac12e_T^\top He_T\). The middle term has mean zero, because \(e_T\) has mean zero and is independent of the deterministic \(\bar\theta_T\). So \(\mathcal E = \frac12\mathbb E[e_T^\top He_T]\).
One direction at a time. In the eigenbasis of \(H\) the coordinates decouple, and by Fact 2 each coordinate of the noise is still \(\mathcal N(0, s^2)\), independently. Along an eigenvector with curvature \(h\), the coordinate \(e\) of the error obeys \(e_{t+1} = (1 - \eta h)e_t - \eta\xi\), so after \(T\) steps it is \(-\eta\sum_{t<T}(1 - \eta h)^{T - 1 - t}\xi_t\), with variance \[v_T = \eta^2s^2\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}(1 - \eta h)^{2t} = \eta^2s^2\,\frac{1 - (1 - \eta h)^{2T}}{1 - (1 - \eta h)^2}, \tag{43.4}\] a geometric sum.
Its cost. The direction contributes \(\frac12hv_T\) to \(\mathcal E\). Since \(1 - (1 - \eta h)^2 = \eta h(2 - \eta h)\), this is \(\frac{\eta s^2}{2(2 - \eta h)}(1 - (1 - \eta h)^{2T})\), and summing over the directions gives Equation 43.2. With \(\eta h \ll 1\) the first factor is \(\eta s^2/4\).
Two limits. For \(2\eta hT \gg 1\) the bracket is 1: the direction is at its steady state, the case Private empirical risk minimization analyses, and it costs \(\eta s^2/4\) whatever its curvature (stiffer directions wander less but charge more per unit of wandering). For \(2\eta hT \ll 1\) the bracket is about \(2\eta hT\), by \((1 - x)^{2T} \approx 1 - 2Tx\), and the direction costs about \(\frac{\eta s^2}{4}\cdot 2\eta hT\): the noise has random-walked a distance of variance \(T\eta^2s^2\), charged at rate \(h/2\), which is small when the direction is flat.
The bound. Each bracket is at most 1, which gives \(d_{\text{eff}} \le d\). And \(1 - (1 - x)^{2T} \le 2Tx\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\) (Bernoulli’s inequality, \((1 - x)^{2T} \ge 1 - 2Tx\)), so \(d_{\text{eff}} \le 2\eta T\sum_jh_j = 2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H\).



43.3.4 Interpretation
The count of trainable weights is an upper bound, not the price. Equation 43.2 says that noise in a direction the loss does not care about, \(h_j \approx 0\), costs nothing, however long it is. What you pay for is roughly the number of directions whose curvature exceeds \(1/(2\eta T)\), the directions the noise has time to fill. A large pretrained model whose loss is curved in only a few directions near the pretrained weights can be fine-tuned in all its weights at a cost set by those few. This is the explanation Li, Liu, Hashimoto, Inan, Kulkarni, Lee & Thakurta (2022) give for why private fine-tuning of large language models does not suffer from their size: the optimal rates of Private empirical risk minimization are worst cases over all losses with a given Lipschitz constant, and they replace the dimension \(d\) by a quantity that measures how the gradients spread over directions.
Fewer trainable weights still help, for two reasons. Freezing weights removes their directions from the sum, so \(d_{\text{eff}}\) can only fall. And clipping happens to the trainable gradient: with fewer coordinates, per-example gradients are shorter, fewer are clipped, and the average clipped gradient, the signal, can be longer. Both effects appear in the example below. Against them stands the bias of freezing: if the task needs a direction that is frozen, no amount of private data can move it.
The learning rate and the number of steps are part of the dimension. \(d_{\text{eff}}\) grows with \(\eta T\): a longer or more aggressive run fills more flat directions with noise. This is one reason private fine-tuning works best with smaller learning rates than private training from scratch, as Section 43.7 finds.
How good is the model? The quadratic is a local model, accurate while fine-tuning stays near its starting point; the loss of a network is not quadratic far from it. And the loss increase is not an accuracy loss: accuracy changes only when noise flips predictions. Use Equation 43.2 to compare strategies, not to predict accuracy.






Figure 43.1: Left: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (\(\sigma = 4.13\), \(B = 100\), \(C = 0.5\)), the noise length \(\sigma C\sqrt d/B\) (line) against the number of trainable weights \(d\), and the length of the average clipped gradient at the pretrained model (points) for the last layer, low-rank adapters of ranks 1 to 16, and all weights. Right: their ratio. The noise grows like \(\sqrt d\) while the signal shrinks, because longer gradient vectors are clipped more.

The signal is the average clipped gradient over the private records at the start of fine-tuning. From the pretrained weights its length is 0.0130 when all weights are trained, 0.0207 for the adapter and 0.0250 for the last layer alone (Figure 43.1). The last layer’s 65 coordinates carry a longer average clipped gradient than all 3,329 coordinates together, because each record’s gradient restricted to 65 coordinates is shorter and less often clipped. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the noise is 92.0 times the signal for all weights, 22.9 times for the adapter and 6.7 times for the last layer. By the break-even argument of DP-SGD, a signal of constant direction outgrows a random walk of noise after \((\text{noise}/\text{signal})^2\) steps: 8,455, 523 and 44 steps. From a random initialization the signal is 0.0618, five times longer than from the pretrained weights, because a random network gets many records wrong and their gradients are long; but it shrinks quickly as training proceeds, to 0.026 after 1,000 steps in DP-SGD.
The curvature tells a less pessimistic story. Take the Gauss–Newton curvature of the private loss at the pretrained weights: the Hessian of the logistic loss with the network replaced by its linearization around the current weights, the average over records of \(\pi_i(1 - \pi_i)\nabla f_i\nabla f_i^\top\), with \(f_i\) the network’s output on record \(i\) and \(\pi_i\) its predicted probability. It is positive semi-definite, and near a good fit it is close to the full Hessian, which is what the quadratic model needs. Estimated from 2,000 private records, it has largest eigenvalue 0.723 and trace 16.310 over all weights; for the last layer alone the largest eigenvalue is 0.142 and the trace 0.681. With \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), only 406 of the 3,329 directions have curvature above \(1/(2\eta T) = 5 \times 10^{-4}\), and \(d_{\text{eff}} = 451\); for the last layer, \(d_{\text{eff}} = 60.2\) of 65. The full model’s noise is \(\sqrt{3{,}329/65} = 7.2\) times longer than the last layer’s, but by Equation 43.2 it costs only \(451/60.2 = 7.5\) times more, not \(3{,}329/65 = 51\) times. At \(\varepsilon = 1\), where \(s = 0.0206\), Equation 43.2 predicts a loss increase of 0.0048 for all weights at \(\eta = 0.1\), against 0.0355 if every direction had reached its steady state, and 0.00064 for the last layer alone.


43.3.6 Check yourself

You double the number of steps at the same \(\sigma\) (ignoring that this would raise \(\varepsilon\)). Which directions’ noise cost changes? (Only the flat ones, \(2\eta hT \lesssim 1\), whose cost doubles roughly; directions already at their steady state cost the same.)
Why does \(d_{\text{eff}} \le 2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H\) not help much in the running example? (Because \(2\eta T\operatorname{tr}H = 2 \times 0.1 \times 10{,}000 \times 16.31 = 32{,}620\), far above \(d = 3{,}329\). The trace is dominated by a few large eigenvalues; the bound is useful only when the total curvature is small compared with \(1/(\eta T)\).)

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.4 Good features: the last layer as private convex ERM
text:
43.4 Good features: the last layer as private convex ERM

43.4.1 Context
The simplest way to use a pretrained model is to freeze everything except the last layer and train a linear classifier on the frozen features, linear probing. For the running example that is logistic regression on the 64 hidden activations plus a bias, 65 weights. It turns private deep learning back into the convex problem of Private empirical risk minimization, where the rates and the methods are known. Tramèr & Boneh (2021) showed that this simple recipe beats end-to-end private training of convolutional networks on standard image benchmarks at moderate budgets, even with handcrafted features (the ScatterNet wavelet transform), and that features learned on public data do better still. What does the private part of a linear probe cost, and what limits it?


43.4.2 Statement
Let \(\phi(x) \in \mathbb R^d\) be the frozen features, computed from public data only, and \(\ell(\theta; (x, y)) = \ln(1 + e^{-y\langle \theta, \phi(x)\rangle})\). Then:

The per-record gradient has length at most \(\|\phi(x)\|\). For \(d - 1\) tanh features and a constant 1, \(\|\phi(x)\| \le \sqrt d\), so the loss is \(\sqrt d\)-Lipschitz in \(\theta\) and clipping is optional.
The excess risk of a private probe splits into a feature gap and a privacy cost: \[\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\tilde\theta) - \mathcal L_{\text{best}} = \underbrace{\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta^\phi) - \mathcal L_{\text{best}}}_{\text{features}} + \underbrace{\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\tilde\theta) - \mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta^\phi)}_{\text{privacy}}, \tag{43.5}\] where \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}\) is the population risk, \(\mathcal L_{\text{best}}\) the best population risk of any model, \(\tilde\theta\) the private probe and \(\theta^\phi\) the best linear model on the features \(\phi\). The first term does not depend on \(n\) or \(\varepsilon\). The second is private convex ERM in \(d\) dimensions. Take losses that are \(L\)-Lipschitz over a ball of radius \(R\). Noisy projected gradient descent keeps the privacy cost below a constant times \(LR\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(n\varepsilon)\). No private algorithm can do better than order \(LR\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\) (Bassily, Smith & Thakurta 2014).



43.4.3 Derivation

The gradient bound. \(\nabla_\theta\ell = \ell'(m)\,y\,\phi(x)\) with \(m = y\langle \theta, \phi(x)\rangle\) the margin and \(\ell'(m) = -1/(1 + e^m) \in (-1, 0)\). So \(\|\nabla_\theta\ell\| \le \|\phi(x)\|\). Each tanh activation lies in \((-1, 1)\), so \(\|\phi(x)\|^2 < (d - 1) + 1 = d\).
The split. Add and subtract \(\mathcal L_{\mathcal D}(\theta^\phi)\). The first difference compares two non-private quantities and contains no noise.
The privacy term. By Fact 3, \(\phi\) is a fixed function, so the probe is an ordinary convex ERM problem on the transformed records \((\phi(x_i), y_i)\), with dimension \(d\) and Lipschitz constant \(\sqrt d\) or the clipping norm. The upper bound is the one Private empirical risk minimization derives for noisy projected gradient descent, and the lower bound is Bassily, Smith & Thakurta’s (2014). The Lipschitz constant and the dimension enter through the noise \(\propto L\sqrt d\) that every private method must add.



43.4.4 Interpretation
Features cap accuracy; privacy only decides how close you get to the cap. The feature gap is the price of freezing, paid even with infinite data and no privacy. The privacy cost falls like \(\sqrt d/(n\varepsilon)\). With few features and good ones, both are small; with few features and poor ones, the probe is private, cheap and bad. This is the trade-off behind the title of Tramèr & Boneh’s paper: private learning needs better features, or much more data. End-to-end training can eventually beat a probe, because it can learn better features, but it pays for every one of its weights to do so, and at small \(\varepsilon\) and small \(n\) it does not catch up.
Why linear probing is the safe first baseline. The problem is convex, so the optimizer cannot wander into a bad region, and the theory of Private empirical risk minimization applies: output perturbation, objective perturbation and noisy gradient descent all work, with known rates and no clipping bias if you use the Lipschitz bound. It has few hyperparameters, and with very few weights it can even be run full-batch. If a probe on public features is already within your accuracy target, there is little reason to fine-tune more.
Clipping below the Lipschitz bound still pays. The bound \(\sqrt d\) is a worst case: it is reached only by a record with every activation saturated and a large negative margin. Most records’ gradients are much shorter, because a record classified with a wide margin has \(|\ell'(m)|\) close to 0. Clipping at a smaller \(C\) biases the gradient of the few long ones and divides the noise by \(\sqrt d/C\); Exercise 3 compares the two on the running example.


43.4.5 Example: the ceiling and the cost on the running example
The pretrained network’s 64 hidden units plus a constant give \(d = 65\) features; the largest feature norm on the private training records is 7.035, below the bound \(\sqrt{65} = 8.062\). The pretrained network itself, with its public last layer, labels 0.9035 of the private test inputs correctly (the report half, Section 43.7). Fitting the last layer exactly and non-privately on the 10,000 private records, by Newton’s method, raises this to 0.9536: that is the probe’s ceiling, \(\theta^\phi\) in Equation 43.5. A network trained non-privately on the private data from scratch reaches 0.9606, so the feature gap is 0.007 in accuracy. The private probe reaches 0.9478 at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 0.9514 at \(\varepsilon = 8\) (Table 43.5): at every budget it is within 0.006 of its ceiling, and at no budget can it pass it.


43.4.6 Check yourself

The public features are replaced by 650 features of the same quality (same ceiling). What happens to the privacy cost of the probe? (The noise length grows by \(\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2\) at the same \(\sigma\), so the privacy term of Equation 43.5 grows by about that factor at a fixed \(n\varepsilon\); you need about 3.2 times more data for the same cost.)
Is the probe private if the features were computed by a network pretrained on data that included some of the private records? (The probe is private with respect to the private dataset given the features; but the features themselves are a function of those records and were not trained privately, so the released model as a whole has no guarantee for them. See Section 43.8.)

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.5 Low-rank adapters

43.5.1 Context
The last layer is often not enough: the features of a model pretrained on one task are not exactly right for another, and the probe stops at its ceiling. Training all weights fixes the features but pays for every weight. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) sits in between: it freezes each pretrained weight matrix \(W_0\) and learns a low-rank correction, \(W = W_0 + UV^\top\) with \(U \in \mathbb R^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}\) and \(V \in \mathbb R^{d_{\text{in}} \times r}\) (Hu et al. 2022). Yu et al. (2022) showed that private fine-tuning of language models with LoRA and similar parameter-efficient methods matches or beats private full fine-tuning at a fraction of the cost. How many weights does it train, what are its per-example gradients, and in which directions can it move \(W\)?


43.5.2 Statement
A rank-\(r\) adapter on a \(d_{\text{out}} \times d_{\text{in}}\) matrix has \[d = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}}) \tag{43.6}\] trainable weights, against \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) for the matrix. With \(\nu_i\) the gradient of record \(i\)’s loss with respect to the layer’s output and \(a_i\) its input, the per-example gradients are outer products, \[\nabla_U\ell_i = \nu_i\,(V^\top a_i)^\top, \qquad \nabla_V\ell_i = a_i\,(U^\top\nu_i)^\top, \tag{43.7}\] with lengths \(\|\nu_i\|\|V^\top a_i\|\) and \(\|a_i\|\|U^\top\nu_i\|\), so ghost clipping applies. One step with noisy gradient sums \(G_U = \sum_i\overline{\nabla_U\ell_i} + \xi_U\) and \(G_V = \sum_i\overline{\nabla_V\ell_i} + \xi_V\) and step \(\eta/B\) changes \(W\) to \(W'\), with \[W' - W = -\frac\eta B\big(G_UV^\top + UG_V^\top\big) + O\Big(\frac{\eta^2}{B^2}\Big). \tag{43.8}\] In particular, from the usual start \(U = 0\), the first step’s change has rank at most \(r\), and to first order its rows lie in the span of the columns of \(V\). The privacy guarantee is that of DP-SGD with the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\) (Fact 1).


43.5.3 Derivation

Counting. \(U\) has \(d_{\text{out}}r\) entries and \(V\) has \(d_{\text{in}}r\).
The chain rule through the product. By Fact 4 the gradient with respect to \(W\) is \(G_i = \nu_ia_i^\top\), and the loss depends on \(U\) and \(V\) only through \(W\). A small change \(dU\) changes \(W\) by \(dU\,V^\top\), which changes the loss by \(\operatorname{tr}(G_i^\top dU\,V^\top) = \operatorname{tr}(V^\top G_i^\top dU) = \langle G_iV, dU\rangle\), using the cyclic property of the trace. So \(\nabla_U\ell_i = G_iV = \nu_i(a_i^\top V) = \nu_i(V^\top a_i)^\top\). In the same way a change \(dV\) changes \(W\) by \(U\,dV^\top\) and the loss by \(\operatorname{tr}(G_i^\top U\,dV^\top) = \langle G_i^\top U, dV\rangle\), so \(\nabla_V\ell_i = G_i^\top U = a_i(\nu_i^\top U) = a_i(U^\top\nu_i)^\top\). This is Equation 43.7.
Norms. Each is an outer product of two vectors, so its length is the product of their lengths, as in Fact 4. The norm of record \(i\)’s whole gradient is the square root of the sum of the squared norms over \(U\), \(V\) and the other trainable layers, computed from vectors of length \(d_{\text{out}}\), \(d_{\text{in}}\) and \(r\) without forming any matrix.
The step. After the step, \(W' = W_0 + (U - \frac\eta BG_U)(V - \frac\eta BG_V)^\top\). Expanding the product, \(W' - W = -\frac\eta B(G_UV^\top + UG_V^\top) + \frac{\eta^2}{B^2}G_UG_V^\top\), which is Equation 43.8.
From \(U = 0\). Then \(\nabla_V\ell_i = 0\) for every record, so \(G_V = \xi_V\) is pure noise, and \(W' - W = -\frac\eta BG_UV^\top + \frac{\eta^2}{B^2}G_U\xi_V^\top\). The first term is a \(d_{\text{out}} \times r\) matrix times \(V^\top\), of rank at most \(r\), with rows that are combinations of the columns of \(V\). The second term is of order \(\eta^2/B^2\) and tilts those rows slightly. The whole change \(W' - W\) is a product of a \(d_{\text{out}} \times r\) and an \(r \times d_{\text{in}}\) matrix, so its rank is at most \(r\) exactly.



43.5.4 Interpretation
An adapter is DP-SGD in a smaller, moving space. The noise of DP-SGD on \((U, V)\) lives in \(d = r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) coordinates, so Equation 43.1 applies with that \(d\). Seen from \(W\), each step moves the matrix within a set of dimension about \(d\): the directions \(XV^\top + UY^\top\) for arbitrary \(X\) and \(Y\), which change as \(U\) and \(V\) change. The adapter restricts the update to that set; noise in the other \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}} - d\) directions of \(W\) never arises.
What the restriction costs. At the start, with \(U = 0\) and \(V\) random, the update is the true gradient \(G\) multiplied on the right by \(VV^\top\), which for a random \(V\) with small \(r\) is close to a multiple of the projection onto the span of its columns: the gradient is projected onto a random \(r\)-dimensional subspace of the inputs. Random subspaces capture a fraction of about \(r/d_{\text{in}}\) of a fixed vector’s energy, which for small \(r\) is little. As \(V\) moves (its gradient is no longer zero once \(U \neq 0\)) the subspace aligns with the useful directions. Low-rank adaptation works when the change from the pretrained weights that the new task needs is itself close to low rank, as Hu et al. (2022) observed for language models. The rank \(r\) trades bias against noise like the number of trainable weights does.
Full fine-tuning is not ruled out. Li, Tramèr, Liang & Hashimoto (2022) fine-tuned all the weights of pretrained language models with DP-SGD and matched or beat the parameter-efficient methods, once the hyperparameters were right: large batches, a learning rate tuned for private training, and a fine-tuning objective aligned with pretraining. Equation 43.2 explains why this can work: what full fine-tuning pays is \(d_{\text{eff}}\), not \(p\). Whether an adapter or full fine-tuning wins is an empirical question that depends on the model, the data and the tuning, and the published evidence goes both ways. The adapter’s advantages that do not depend on accuracy are certain: it stores and communicates only \(d\) numbers per task, and it computes and clips much smaller gradients.


43.5.5 Example: counting, and checking the gradients
The running example’s first layer maps 51 inputs (50 features and a constant) to 64 hidden units: 3,264 weights. A rank-4 adapter trains \(4 \times (51 + 64) = 460\) of them, plus the 65 weights of the last layer, \(d = 525\); rank 1 gives 180 and rank 16 gives 1,905. For a \(768 \times 768\) projection of a transformer, rank 8 trains \(8 \times 1{,}536 = 12{,}288\) weights instead of 589,824, a factor of 48 fewer, so the noise is \(\sqrt{48} = 6.9\) times shorter. On 256 private records, the ghost norms of Equation 43.7 agree with explicitly formed per-example gradients of the adapter to a relative difference of \(3.3 \times 10^{-16}\). Exercise 4 checks the rank of the first step.


43.5.6 Check yourself

Why does LoRA start with \(U = 0\) rather than both factors random? (So that \(W = W_0\) at the start: the fine-tuned model begins exactly at the pretrained one. With both random, the first forward pass would use a randomly perturbed matrix.)
An adapter of rank \(r = \min(d_{\text{in}}, d_{\text{out}})\) can represent any change of \(W\). Does it then have the same noise as training \(W\) directly? (No, more: it has \(r(d_{\text{in}} + d_{\text{out}})\) coordinates, more than \(d_{\text{in}}d_{\text{out}}\) when \(r\) is this large. Adapters save noise only at small rank.)

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
text:
43.6 Gradients near a public subspace

43.6.1 Context
Section 43.3 says the noise costs little in directions the loss does not use. If you knew the directions the private gradients do use, you could add noise only there. Public data gives an estimate: compute per-example gradients on public records at the current or pretrained weights, find their top principal directions, and project the private gradients onto them. Zhou, Wu & Banerjee (2021) do this as projected DP-SGD, and Yu, Zhang, Chen & Liu (2021) as gradient embedding perturbation, which also releases the residual outside the subspace with separate noise. Li et al. (2022) measured that the gradients of private fine-tuning are dominated by a few principal components. How much does a projection save, and what does it lose?


43.6.2 Statement
Let \(P_m\) be the orthogonal projection onto an \(m\)-dimensional subspace computed from public data only. Releasing \[P_m\Big(\sum_{i \in S_t}\bar g_i\Big) + \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2P_m) \tag{43.9}\] (noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) along each of \(m\) orthonormal directions of the subspace) at every step has the same \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) as DP-SGD with the same \(q\), \(\sigma\) and \(T\). If \(\bar m\) is the average clipped gradient and \(f_m = \|P_m\bar m\|^2/\|\bar m\|^2\) the fraction of its energy that the subspace captures, the kept signal has length \(\sqrt{f_m}\|\bar m\|\), the noise on the averaged gradient has length about \(s\sqrt m\), and signal outgrows noise after about \[T_{\text{even}}(m) = \Big(\frac{s\sqrt m}{\sqrt{f_m}\,\|\bar m\|}\Big)^2 \tag{43.10}\] steps, against \((s\sqrt p/\|\bar m\|)^2\) without projection. The lost fraction \(1 - f_m\) of the signal is a bias that no number of steps recovers.


43.6.3 Derivation

Sensitivity. A projection never lengthens a vector: \(\|P_mx\| \le \|x\|\), because \(x = P_mx + (x - P_mx)\) with the two parts orthogonal, so \(\|x\|^2 = \|P_mx\|^2 + \|x - P_mx\|^2\). Adding or removing one record changes the projected sum by \(P_m\bar g\), of length at most \(C\).
The mechanism. In an orthonormal basis of the subspace, Equation 43.9 is \(m\) coordinates of a vector of sensitivity at most \(C\) plus independent \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2)\) noise on each: a Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(1/\sigma\), exactly as in DP-SGD, and Poisson sampling makes it the same subsampled Gaussian. The subspace is fixed before the private data are read (Fact 3), so it is a public parameter of the mechanism. Equivalently, Equation 43.9 is the projection of the ordinary DP-SGD release onto the subspace (Fact 2), and projection is post-processing.
Signal and noise. Dividing by \(B\), the kept signal is \(P_m\bar m\), of length \(\sqrt{f_m}\|\bar m\|\) by the definition of \(f_m\), and the noise has \(m\) coordinates of standard deviation \(s\), length about \(s\sqrt m\) (Fact 2).
Break-even. As in DP-SGD, over \(j\) steps a signal of constant direction adds up to \(j\) times its length and independent noise to \(\sqrt j\) times; they are equal at Equation 43.10.



43.6.4 Interpretation
A projection trades bias for variance, and public data fix the exchange rate. The noise falls by \(\sqrt{p/m}\), the signal by \(\sqrt{f_m}\). If the private gradients lie near the public subspace, \(f_m\) is close to 1 for \(m \ll p\) and the trade is excellent. If the public data are unrelated, the subspace is no better than a random one, \(f_m \approx m/p\), and the projection removes as much signal as noise, gaining nothing. The quality of the public data appears here directly as \(f_m\).
A fixed subspace is a cap; methods refresh it or add the residual. Since \(P_m\) removes the part \(1 - f_m\) of the signal at every step, training with a fixed projection can only move the weights within the subspace. Projected DP-SGD recomputes the subspace from public gradients as training proceeds; gradient embedding perturbation releases the residual \(\bar g - P_m\bar g\) too, with its own noise, so the bias disappears at the price of a little more noise. LoRA, in this light, chooses a subspace by structure (low-rank changes of each matrix) and lets training move it.
Why this explains full fine-tuning. The same concentration that makes a public subspace useful makes \(d_{\text{eff}}\) small in Equation 43.2: gradients near a low-dimensional subspace are gradients of a loss curved in few directions. Projection makes the saving explicit and certain; full fine-tuning gets part of it implicitly, if the learning rate and number of steps are small enough that flat directions do not fill up with noise.






Figure 43.2: Left: eigenvalues of the Gauss–Newton curvature of the private loss at the pretrained weights, estimated from 2,000 private records, on log scales, with the thresholds \(1/(2\eta T)\) for \(\eta = 0.1\) and \(0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\); directions below a threshold contribute little noise cost. Right: the fraction of the energy of the private average clipped gradient that lies in the top \(m\) principal directions of 500 public per-example gradients (solid), and in \(m\) random directions (dashed).





43.6.5 Example: how concentrated the running example’s gradients are
At the pretrained weights the average clipped private gradient has length 0.0130. The top principal directions of 500 clipped public per-example gradients capture Table 43.3’s fractions of its energy; random subspaces of the same dimension capture about \(m/p\).

43.6.6 Check yourself

The public subspace is computed from the private data instead, by a non-private principal component analysis. Is Equation 43.9 still \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP? (No. The subspace then depends on the private records, the projection is no longer a fixed public map, and the subspace itself leaks information about them; it must be computed privately, at a cost in budget, or from public data.)

43.7 Pretraining and fine-tuning the running example

43.7.1 Context
How much does a related public dataset buy on the running example, at each budget, and which part of the model should be fine-tuned?


43.7.2 Statement
The public task. The private teacher has a first layer \(W_1^{\text{priv}}\) (8 hidden units, 51 inputs) and an output layer \(W_2^{\text{priv}}\). The public teacher has first layer \(W_1^{\text{priv}} + 0.15Z_1\) and output layer \(\cos(0.3)\,W_2^{\text{priv}} + \sin(0.3)\,Z_2\), where \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) are fixed standard normal draws: the same hidden units, each slightly perturbed, read out with weights turned by 0.3 radians toward a random vector. It labels 50,000 inputs drawn from the private input distribution. The design makes pretraining useful but not sufficient: the public student must learn features close to the ones the private task needs, but cannot learn the private task itself. The public teacher agrees with the private one on 0.9004 of the private test inputs.
Pretraining. The 64-unit student is trained on the public data by non-private SGD, 10,000 steps with batches of 100 and learning rate 0.5, to 0.9861 training accuracy on the public task. On the private task it reaches 0.9035 without any private data.
Fine-tuning. From the pretrained weights, DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) trains: all 3,329 weights (full); the last layer, \(d = 65\) (last layer); a rank-4 adapter \(W_1 = W_1^{\text{pre}} + UV^\top\) and the last layer, \(d = 525\) (adapter). The baseline trains all weights from a random initialization (scratch), the setting of DP-SGD. The private test set of 20,000 records is split in half: the learning rate of each method is chosen from three values on the first half at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (Table 43.4) and used at every budget, and accuracy is reported on the second half.

43.7.3 Derivation
Each entry is a measurement, and each method’s privacy follows from Fact 1 and Fact 3: the pretrained weights and the adapter’s random \(V\) are fixed before the private data are read, the clipped sum of each step has sensitivity \(C\) in the method’s trainable coordinates, and the accountant gives \(\sigma = 7.72\), 4.13, 2.28 and 0.917 for the four budgets, the same for every method because \(q\) and \(T\) are the same. The learning rates were chosen by looking at private data, the validation half, without paying for it; Hyperparameter tuning shows how to do that privately, and the comparison here is of methods at their best, as in DP-SGD.


43.7.4 Interpretation
Pretraining is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\). Every fine-tuning method at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) (0.9395 to 0.9478) beats training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (0.9246), and the best of them comes within 0.004 of training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 2\) (0.9518). The adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) (0.9616) matches training from scratch at \(\varepsilon = 8\) (0.9611) and the non-private model trained from scratch (0.9606), and full fine-tuning at \(\varepsilon = 2\) (0.9663) beats both. The public data carry information about the private task that 10,000 private records do not, and that information is free.
Which weights to train depends on the budget. At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the last layer is best: with 65 trainable weights its noise is \(\sqrt{3{,}329/65} = 7.2\) times shorter than full fine-tuning’s, and its ceiling, 0.9536, is not yet binding. From \(\varepsilon = 1\) on, the last layer is stuck near its ceiling (0.9497 to 0.9519) while the adapter and full fine-tuning keep improving: they can correct the features, and the noise is now small enough to let them. The adapter, with 525 weights, is never more than 0.0022 below the best method at any budget: the middle choice is the robust one. Full fine-tuning is behind at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), by 0.0083, but not far behind elsewhere once its learning rate is right, as Li et al. (2022) found for language models; at \(\varepsilon = 2\) and 8 it is the best, by 0.0010 and 0.0022. Figure 43.3, a separate set of single runs, shows the same overall picture, with the order of the three pretrained methods at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and 1 changed: differences of a few thousandths between them are within run-to-run variation.
Learning rates matter as much as the method. In Table 43.4 full fine-tuning loses 1.3 points at a learning rate three times too large, and the adapter 1.5 points. The best learning rate for full fine-tuning and the adapter, 0.1, is 2.5 times smaller than for training from scratch. That is the effective-dimension argument of Section 43.3 at work: a larger \(\eta\) fills more flat directions with noise and undoes what pretraining provided.
What the run-to-run spread says. The standard deviations over two runs are small for the pretrained methods, 0.0013 or less, but two runs estimate a spread only roughly: the rank sweep below repeats the adapter at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and finds a standard deviation of 0.0023, and a mean of 0.9624 against the table’s 0.9616. Differences between the pretrained methods smaller than about 0.005 should not be read as rankings.






Figure 43.3: Test accuracy of the four strategies against \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), one run each with the learning rates of Table 43.4 and a different seed from Table 43.5, with the pretrained model’s accuracy before fine-tuning (dotted). The pretrained methods are far ahead of training from scratch at small budgets; the last layer stays near its ceiling from \(\varepsilon = 1\) on, and training from scratch passes it at larger budgets.





43.7.5 Example: the adapter’s rank
At \(\varepsilon = 1\), with the adapter’s learning rate 0.1, two runs each give \(0.9590 \pm 0.0038\) at rank 1 (\(d = 180\)), \(0.9624 \pm 0.0023\) at rank 4 (\(d = 525\)) and \(0.9586 \pm 0.0031\) at rank 16 (\(d = 1{,}905\)). Rank 4 is best, but the differences are about the size of the run-to-run spread. Two forces pull in opposite directions: a higher rank lets the update follow more of the directions the task needs, and it adds noise, whose length grows like \(\sqrt d\) (Figure 43.1). On this problem neither dominates over a sixteenfold range of ranks, so the rank is a cheap hyperparameter to get roughly right.


43.7.6 Check yourself

Why is the last layer’s accuracy at \(\varepsilon = 8\) (0.9514) not higher than at \(\varepsilon = 2\) (0.9519)? (It is at its ceiling, the best linear model on the frozen features, 0.9536 non-privately. Less noise cannot help a model that cannot represent a better classifier.)
If the public teacher were identical to the private one, which strategy would you expect to win at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), and why? (The last layer, or no fine-tuning at all: the pretrained model would already be close to perfect, so there would be nothing for the extra weights to learn and only noise for them to collect. Exercise 5 measures it.)

title: 43  Public data and private fine-tuning
section: 43.8 What public data does not buy
text:
43.8 What public data does not buy

43.8.1 Context
Everything so far treated the public data as free. Formally that is right: the guarantee of a private fine-tuning run does not depend on what the public data are. But “public” is a label someone chose, and the guarantee says nothing about the records under that label. Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini (2024) argue that the field’s reliance on large web-scraped pretraining data needs scrutiny on several counts. What exactly is guaranteed, and what is not?


43.8.2 Statement
Let \(M(D_{\text{pub}}, D)\) pretrain on \(D_{\text{pub}}\) without privacy and fine-tune on \(D\) with an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm. Then for every fixed \(D_{\text{pub}}\), the map \(D \mapsto M(D_{\text{pub}}, D)\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. There is no guarantee of any kind with respect to \(D_{\text{pub}}\). A person with a record \(x\) in both datasets is protected only for the copy in \(D\): removing it from \(D\) changes the output’s distribution by at most \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), while the copy in \(D_{\text{pub}}\) can be revealed completely.


43.8.3 Derivation

Fixed public data. With \(D_{\text{pub}}\) fixed, pretraining produces fixed weights \(\theta_0\) (or a fixed distribution over them, if pretraining is randomized, independent of \(D\)). The DP-SGD proof of DP-SGD holds for any \(\theta_0\) chosen independently of the private data (Fact 3), so it holds conditionally on \(\theta_0\), and therefore for the mixture over \(\theta_0\).
Nothing for the public data. Changing one record of \(D_{\text{pub}}\) can change \(\theta_0\) arbitrarily, and the fine-tuned model inherits whatever \(\theta_0\) encodes; non-private training can memorize individual records (Memorization and extraction). No noise was calibrated to that change.
A record in both. The neighbouring datasets that DP compares are \(D\) and \(D\) without \(x\), with \(D_{\text{pub}}\) the same in both. A test of whether \(x\) was in \(D\) has true positive rate at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its false positive rate plus \(\delta\) (The definition). A test of whether \(x\) is in the training data at all can use the copy in \(D_{\text{pub}}\), which nothing bounds.



43.8.4 Interpretation
Overlap and contamination. Web-scale “public” datasets contain personal data: posts, profiles, documents put online by others, data that leaked. A private fine-tuning set of medical notes or emails may overlap with them, and the people whose records appear in both are protected only as well as the pretraining protects them, that is, not at all. Calling the resulting model “differentially private” is accurate about \(D\) and misleading about those people. Tramèr, Kamath & Carlini (2024) argue for this reason that the label should be used with care, and that the privacy of pretraining data deserves its own consideration.
Distribution shift. Public data help as much as they resemble the private task. Benchmarks in which the “private” set is a standard dataset whose distribution is close to well-curated public data, for example two collections of natural images, can overstate what the method will do on genuinely sensitive data, which is often unlike anything public: medical images, rare languages, internal logs. Table 43.5 used a public task close to the private one by design; Exercise 5 shows the gain shrinking, and for the last layer turning into a loss against training from scratch, as the public teacher drifts away.
Public is not the same as non-sensitive. Even when every pretraining record is public, a model trained on them can reproduce them, link them, or make inferences about people that the original publication did not allow. And large pretrained models are often too large to fine-tune locally, so the private data are sent to whoever has the compute, which is a trust question DP does not address (Trust models).
What to report. State what the public data are, how they were obtained, whether overlap with the private data was checked (deduplication against the private set is the minimum), and that the \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) covers the private dataset given the pretrained model. Any choice made by looking at private data, such as which public model to start from or the learning rate, is part of the private computation and must be accounted for.


43.8.5 Example: one record, two copies
At \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), any test of whether a record was in the private fine-tuning set that has false positive rate 0.01 has true positive rate at most \(e \times 0.01 + 10^{-5} = 0.0272\). If the same record is also in the public set, a membership test against the pretrained model, such as the likelihood-ratio attack of Membership inference, is bounded by nothing; it may still fail in practice, but no theorem says it will. If the record appears twice in the private set, group privacy gives \((2\varepsilon, 2e^\varepsilon\delta) = (2, 5.44 \times 10^{-5})\) for the pair (Post-processing, group privacy and composition), a weaker but real guarantee. A copy in the public set is worse than a duplicate in the private set.


43.8.6 Check yourself

You choose between three public pretrained models by fine-tuning each privately and keeping the one with the best private validation accuracy. What have you spent? (Three private training runs plus a selection on private data: the budget of all three, composed, or a private selection procedure from Hyperparameter tuning. Choosing by public validation data would have been free.)
A company deduplicates its private dataset against the public pretraining corpus by exact string matching. What can still go wrong? (Near-duplicates and paraphrases of the same personal information survive exact matching, and records about the same person need not be duplicates at all; the deduplication protects copies, not people.)

Rules of thumb

Start from a model pretrained on public data that resembles the private task. On the running example this is worth about a factor of eight in \(\varepsilon\).
