title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.1 Why this matters
Every differential privacy (DP) guarantee in this part so far protects one record. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, clips each record’s gradient, adds noise scaled to that clip, and reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) for the part’s running example: an adversary who sees the trained model learns little about whether any single training example was used. But the people behind the data do not contribute one record each. A user of a messaging app contributes hundreds of messages, a patient dozens of visits, a photographer thousands of photos. Each of those records is protected by DP, and the person is not, because what the adversary learns about all of a person’s records together can be much larger than what they learn about one.
This chapter asks two questions. What does a record-level \(\varepsilon\) say about a person who contributed \(k\) records? And how do you train a model with a guarantee for the person instead?

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.1.1 The one idea: the neighbouring relation is the privacy unit
A DP guarantee compares the outputs on two neighbouring datasets, and whatever differs between neighbours is what is protected. If neighbours differ in one record, records are protected; if they differ in all of one person’s records, people are. Nothing else in the definition changes. The work is to bound how much the unit, now a person, can move the computation, and to account for that bound.
There are two ways to get a guarantee for a person. The first keeps the record as the unit and pays for the person afterwards, by group privacy or by an accountant that knows the person has \(k\) records. It is cheap to implement and expensive in privacy, because the noise was calibrated to one record while the person moves the output by up to \(k\). The second makes the person the unit from the start: sample people instead of records, bound each person’s total contribution by clipping it, and run the usual accountant with people in place of records. On the running example the first route gives a useless model at any reasonable budget, and the second gives one within a few points of the non-private model.
Table 44.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 44.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.









Result

Notation. The training set has \(n\) records belonging to \(U\) users; user \(u\) owns \(n_u\) records. Two datasets are example-level neighbours if they differ by adding or removing one record, and user-level neighbours if they differ by adding or removing all the records of one user. \(k\) is the number of records a user contributes, or the cap on it. In a batch drawn by Poisson sampling at rate \(q\), \(H\) is the number of a given user’s records that are drawn. As in DP-SGD, \(C\) is the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(T\) the number of steps and \(B\) the expected batch size, now counted in whichever unit is sampled.
The running example. The part’s network (one hidden layer of 64 tanh units, 3,329 weights) learns labels produced by a fixed teacher network from 10,000 training records of 50 features, and is tested on 20,000 more. This chapter assigns the 10,000 records to \(U = 1{,}000\) users. Each user gets one record, and the other 9,000 are spread over users with probabilities proportional to log-normal weights, so user sizes are very uneven: the mean is 10 records, the median 4, and the largest user holds 348 (Figure 44.1). A user’s records are a nearest-neighbour cluster around a random record, so they resemble each other the way one person’s messages do: the label balance \(|\bar y|\) is 0.21 on average in the ten largest users, against 0.06 in the whole set. The population is fixed, like the dataset.






Figure 44.1: Left: the number of records per user in the running example’s population of 1,000 users, on log–log axes; 193 users have one record and the largest has 348. Right: the share of all records held by the largest users. The largest 10 users hold 17.9% of the records and the smallest half of the users 10.3%.



How to read this chapter. The toolkit restates three facts from earlier parts. Section 44.3 and Section 44.4 say what a record-level guarantee gives a person; the second has the chapter’s main derivation, the accountant for a user with \(k\) records. Section 44.5 and Section 44.6 are the two ways to train with a user-level guarantee, Section 44.7 asks what they do to heavy users, and Section 44.8 compares everything on the running example.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
section: 44.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses
text:
44.2 Toolkit: three facts every derivation uses

44.2.1 Fact 1 — Group privacy
If a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for neighbours that differ in one record, then for two datasets that differ in \(k\) records it satisfies, for every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon}\Pr[M(D'') \in S] + \delta_k, \qquad \delta_k = \delta\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}e^{j\varepsilon} = \delta\,\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}. \tag{44.1}\] The reason is a chain: \(D\) and \(D''\) are joined by a path of \(k\) steps, each between neighbouring datasets. Applying the one-record guarantee once per link multiplies the probability bound by \(e^\varepsilon\) each time, and each link’s slack \(\delta\) is then multiplied by the \(e^\varepsilon\) of every later link, which is where the geometric sum comes from. The bound is attained by some mechanisms, so no better one holds for every \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). For Rényi differential privacy (RDP) the chain is weaker still, because the Rényi divergence has no triangle inequality: an \((\alpha, \varepsilon)\)-RDP mechanism is \((\alpha/2^c, 3^c\varepsilon)\)-RDP for groups of \(2^c\) records, when \(\alpha \ge 2^{c+1}\) (Mironov 2017; Rényi DP). Each doubling of the group halves the order and triples \(\varepsilon\).


44.2.2 Fact 2 — The accountant of DP-SGD
One step of DP-SGD adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to a sum of clipped per-example gradients computed on a Poisson batch: each record enters independently with probability \(q\). In units of \(C\), the worst case for one record is the pair \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), the output without the record, and the mixture \((1 - q)P_0 + q\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\), the output with it. Its RDP curve at order \(\alpha\), the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) between the two, is \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha\), and for integer \(\alpha\) \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{j^2 - j}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{44.2}\] The sum comes from expanding \(\big((1 - q) + q\,r\big)^\alpha\), with \(r\) the Gaussian likelihood ratio, by the binomial theorem and averaging each power \(r^j\) under \(P_0\) (Amplification by subsampling). RDP curves add over the \(T\) steps, even when each step depends on earlier outputs, and the total converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at the best order: \[\varepsilon = \min_\alpha\Big[T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}\alpha - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{44.3}\] The terms \(j = 0\) and \(1\) carry no privacy cost, since their exponential factor is 1. For small \(q\) and moderate orders only the \(j = 2\) term matters beyond them, so \(A_\alpha \approx 1 + \binom\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\) and \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) \approx \frac\alpha2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\).


44.2.3 Fact 3 — The Gaussian moment generating function
If \(Y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), then \(\mathbb E[e^{sY}] = e^{s^2\sigma^2/2}\) for every real \(s\) (Distributions). Every Rényi divergence between Gaussians with the same variance reduces to it, because their likelihood ratio is the exponential of a linear function of the output: for \(P_m = \mathcal N(m, \sigma^2)\), \[\frac{P_m(y)}{P_0(y)} = \exp\Big(\frac{-(y - m)^2 + y^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) = \exp\Big(\frac{2my - m^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{44.4}\]

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.3 The privacy unit

44.3.1 Context
A model trained with record-level DP-SGD at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) is released. One of the people in the training set contributed \(k\) of its records. What, exactly, does the guarantee promise that person? The question has to be answered before a deployment can say “your data are protected”, because the promise is about whatever the neighbouring relation changes, and that relation was chosen by the engineer, not by the person.


44.3.2 Statement
A mechanism is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP if for every pair of datasets \(D\), \(D'\) that differ by adding or removing all the records of one user, and every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{44.5}\] It is example-level DP if the same holds for datasets that differ in one record. A mechanism that is example-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP is user-level \((k\varepsilon, \delta_k)\)-DP for users with at most \(k\) records, with \(\delta_k\) from Equation 44.1. Without more information about the mechanism, nothing better can be said.


44.3.3 Derivation

User-level neighbours are \(k\) example-level steps apart. If \(D'\) is \(D\) plus the \(k\) records of one user, add them one at a time. The datasets \(D, D \cup\{x_1\}, D\cup\{x_1, x_2\}, \dots, D'\) form a chain in which each is an example-level neighbour of the next.
Apply group privacy. Fact 1 along this chain gives Equation 44.1 with \(D'' = D'\), in both directions, since the chain can be walked either way.
Nothing better holds in general. The bound is attained by a mechanism built for the purpose, which outputs an alarm with probabilities chosen so that every link’s inequality is an equality (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). A guarantee that is only known as “\((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP” could come from that mechanism.



44.3.4 Interpretation
The definition is the same; the unit is not. User-level DP is not a new privacy notion. It is DP with a coarser neighbouring relation, so every property proved for DP holds for it: post-processing, composition and the accountants of Part 4. The only thing that changes is the sensitivity: how far one unit can move the computation. Records, users, households, devices and organizations are all possible units, and the choice should follow the question “whose participation do I want to hide?” A deployment that says “DP” without naming the unit leaves that question open, and Choosing an accountant lists the unit among the things a guarantee must report.
Group privacy is linear in \(\varepsilon\) and exponential in \(\delta\). For pure DP a user with \(k\) records gets \(k\varepsilon\), already weak: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) per record, a user with 10 records gets \(\varepsilon = 10\), a likelihood ratio of \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\). With \(\delta > 0\) it is worse. In Equation 44.1 each \(\delta\) is multiplied by up to \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\), so to keep the user’s \(\delta_k\) at \(10^{-5}\) the per-record \(\delta\) must be tiny, and a smaller \(\delta\) means a larger per-record \(\varepsilon\). For DP-SGD this trade can be made at any \(\delta\), because the accountant’s RDP curve converts to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at every \(\delta\): choose the per-record \(\delta\) so that \(\delta_k = 10^{-5}\) exactly.
For DP-SGD it can fail altogether. The per-record \(\varepsilon\) grows as the per-record \(\delta\) shrinks, so \(\delta_k = \delta\frac{e^{k\varepsilon} - 1}{e^\varepsilon - 1}\) is a race between a falling \(\delta\) and a rising \(e^{(k-1)\varepsilon}\). For small \(k\) the falling \(\delta\) wins. For larger \(k\) the rising \(\varepsilon\) wins at every \(\delta\), and no choice brings \(\delta_k\) down to \(10^{-5}\). Group privacy then gives no \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\) guarantee at all (Exercise 2 traces the race).


44.3.5 Example: the running example’s users
The running example’s model is example-level \((6.71, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Read naively as a user-level statement, a user with two records gets \(\varepsilon = 2 \times 6.71 = 13.42\) with \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}(1 + e^{6.71}) = 0.0082\): a probability of almost one in a hundred that the guarantee fails outright, which is no guarantee. Re-converting the accountant’s RDP curve at a smaller per-record \(\delta\) does better. The per-record \(\delta\) that makes \(\delta_2 = 10^{-5}\) gives a per-record \(\varepsilon\) of 9.30, so the user gets \((18.61, 10^{-5})\). For five records the same procedure gives a per-record \(\varepsilon\) of 23.62 and a user-level \(\varepsilon\) of 118.12. For ten records it gives nothing: no per-record \(\delta\) makes \(\delta_{10}\) as small as \(10^{-5}\). In the running example’s population, 244 of the 1,000 users have at least ten records (the median is 4), and 30 have at least 50.


44.3.6 Check yourself

A dataset has one row per hospital visit, and a mechanism is \(0.2\)-DP (pure) at the visit level. What does a patient with 7 visits get? (\(1.4\)-DP, by group privacy with \(k = 7\); for pure DP the bound is just \(k\varepsilon\).)
Why does a user-level guarantee still compose and survive post-processing? (Because it is DP with a different neighbouring relation, and those proofs hold for any fixed relation: they never use what a neighbour is.)

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
section: 44.4 A user with k records in example-level DP-SGD
text:
44.4 A user with k records in example-level DP-SGD

44.4.1 Context
Group privacy treats DP-SGD as a black box. It is not one: we know exactly how a user with \(k\) records enters each step. Each of the user’s records is drawn into the batch independently with probability \(q\), so in each step a random number of them, between 0 and \(k\), contributes to the noisy sum. An accountant that knows this can compute the user’s guarantee directly, as Amplification by subsampling did for one record. How large is that guarantee, and how does it grow with \(k\)?


44.4.2 Statement
Let \(H \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, q)\) be the number of the user’s records in a Poisson batch, and \(b_m = \binom km q^m(1 - q)^{k - m}\) its probabilities. In units of \(C\), one step of example-level DP-SGD compares \[P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \qquad\text{and}\qquad P_{(k)} = \sum_{m=0}^k b_m\,\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2), \tag{44.6}\] the output without the user and with the user, whose drawn records all push the sum by the full \(C\) in the same direction. Charles et al. (2024, Theorem 3) prove that this pair, composed over the \(T\) steps, bounds the user’s privacy loss, and that the bound is attained by a loss for which the user’s gradients are aligned. The user’s RDP curve is therefore \(\varepsilon_{k}(\alpha) = \max\{D_\alpha(P_{(k)}\|P_0), D_\alpha(P_0\|P_{(k)})\}\). The first divergence is \(\frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha\) with \[A_\alpha = \mathbb E\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum_{1\le i<j\le\alpha}H_iH_j\Big)\Big], \qquad H_1, \dots, H_\alpha \text{ independent copies of } H, \tag{44.7}\] for integer \(\alpha\). For small \(kq\) the curve is close to that of a single record sampled at rate \(kq\): \[\varepsilon_k(\alpha) \approx \frac\alpha2(kq)^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big). \tag{44.8}\] The user’s \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) after \(T\) steps is Equation 44.3 applied to \(T\varepsilon_k(\alpha)\).


44.4.3 Derivation
The derivation follows the one for a single record: find the distribution of one step’s output with and without the user, write the Rényi divergence as an average of a power of the likelihood ratio, and evaluate the average. The new ingredient is that the power of a mixture over \(m\) becomes a product of independent copies of \(H\), which makes the average computable by Fact 3.

How many of the user’s records are drawn. Poisson sampling draws each record independently with probability \(q\), so the number of the user’s \(k\) records in the batch is a sum of \(k\) independent coins: \(H \sim \mathrm{Bin}(k, q)\), independent of which other records are drawn.
What they do to the sum. Fix the other records’ contribution, which is the same with and without the user. Given \(H = m\), the user adds \(m\) clipped gradients, each of length at most \(C\), so their sum has length at most \(mC\), with equality when they all point the same way. In units of \(C\) and along that direction, the output is \(\mathcal N(m, \sigma^2)\) with probability \(b_m\): the mixture of Equation 44.6. That the aligned case is the worst over all configurations of the user’s gradients, and that the reduction to one dimension is valid, is the content of Charles et al.’s Theorem 3, which Section M.4 in the appendices proves for \(D_\alpha(P_{(k)}\|P_0)\) at integer orders; the intuition is that gradients pointing in different directions add in squares rather than in length, and spread the user’s influence over several coordinates where it is harder to detect.
The divergence as an average. By the definition of the Rényi divergence, \(e^{(\alpha-1)D_\alpha(P_{(k)}\|P_0)} = \mathbb E_{y\sim P_0}\big[(P_{(k)}(y)/P_0(y))^\alpha\big]\). Dividing the mixture by \(P_0\) term by term with Equation 44.4, \[\frac{P_{(k)}(y)}{P_0(y)} = \sum_m b_m\exp\Big(\frac{2my - m^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big) = \mathbb E_H\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{2Hy - H^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\Big], \tag{44.9}\] an average over the number of drawn records.
The power of an average is an average over independent copies. For integer \(\alpha\), \((\mathbb E_H[f(H)])^\alpha = \mathbb E[f(H_1)f(H_2)\cdots f(H_\alpha)]\) with \(H_1, \dots, H_\alpha\) independent copies of \(H\): multiplying out \(\alpha\) copies of the sum \(\sum_mb_mf(m)\) gives one term for every choice \((m_1, \dots, m_\alpha)\), with weight \(b_{m_1}\cdots b_{m_\alpha}\), which is the joint distribution of independent copies. The product of exponentials is the exponential of the sum, so with \(V = H_1 + \dots + H_\alpha\), the total over the copies, \[\Big(\frac{P_{(k)}(y)}{P_0(y)}\Big)^\alpha = \mathbb E\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{2Vy - \sum_iH_i^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\Big]. \tag{44.10}\]
Average over \(y\). Exchange the two averages, which is allowed because everything is positive. For fixed copies, Fact 3 with \(s = V/\sigma^2\) gives \(\mathbb E_{y\sim P_0}[e^{Vy/\sigma^2}] = e^{V^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), so \[A_\alpha = \mathbb E\Big[\exp\Big(\frac{V^2 - \sum_iH_i^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)\Big]. \tag{44.11}\] Expanding the square, \(V^2 = \sum_iH_i^2 + 2\sum_{i<j}H_iH_j\), and the squares cancel: this is Equation 44.7. Only products of different copies remain.
Check against one record. For \(k = 1\), each \(H_i\) is a coin, 0 or 1. If \(J\) of the \(\alpha\) coins are 1, the sum \(\sum_{i<j}H_iH_j\) counts the pairs among them, \(\binom J2 = (J^2 - J)/2\), and \(J \sim \mathrm{Bin}(\alpha, q)\). The average of \(e^{(J^2 - J)/(2\sigma^2)}\) over \(J\) is Equation 44.2.
Small \(kq\). When \(kq\) is small, most copies are 0. The terms of Equation 44.7 with at most one non-zero copy have \(\sum_{i<j}H_iH_j = 0\) and contribute their probability times 1. The first term that costs privacy has exactly two copies equal to 1, the most likely way for a product to be non-zero: there are \(\binom\alpha2\) pairs of copies, each copy is 1 with probability about \(kq\), and the factor is \(e^{1/\sigma^2}\). So \(A_\alpha \approx 1 + \binom\alpha2(kq)^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), the same as Equation 44.2’s first three terms with \(q\) replaced by \(kq\). Taking \(\ln(1 + x) \approx x\) and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives Equation 44.8.
Other orders and the other direction. For non-integer \(\alpha\), and for \(D_\alpha(P_0\|P_{(k)})\), there is no finite expansion. Compute both as one-dimensional integrals of \(P_0(y)\) times a power of the mixture ratio of step 3, on a grid of step \(\sigma/10\) wide enough to contain the bump near \(y = \alpha k\) that large orders create, with log-sum-exp to avoid overflow, exactly as for one record.



44.4.4 Interpretation
A user with \(k\) records looks like one record sampled \(k\) times as often. Equation 44.8 says that, in the regime where amplification works well, the only thing that matters is the probability that some record of the user is in the batch, about \(kq\). Halving the sampling rate exactly compensates doubling the user’s records. Since the per-step RDP grows like \((kq)^2\), and \(\varepsilon\) after conversion grows roughly like the square root of the RDP slope, the user’s \(\varepsilon\) grows roughly linearly in \(k\) while \(kq\) is small.
Beyond that regime it grows faster. Two things break the approximation. First, \(kq\) is no longer small: for \(k = 50\) and \(q = 0.01\), half of all steps include one of the user’s records, and subsampling, which helps only because the unit is usually absent, stops helping. Second, the higher terms of Equation 44.7 grow like \(e^{H_iH_j/\sigma^2}\), and \(H_iH_j\) can be as large as \(k^2\). A step that draws all \(k\) records shifts the sum by \(kC\), a mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\), whose privacy loss has a tail that no amount of rarity can hide at high orders. The accountant then uses orders close to 1, where the conversion is expensive.
Group privacy is the wrong tool for DP-SGD. It ignores both the structure of the mechanism and the fact that the RDP curve is known. The direct accountant gives a smaller \(\varepsilon\) for every \(k\) and a finite one for every \(k\).
The accountant is a worst case over gradients, not over users. It assumes the user’s drawn records push the sum in the same direction by the full \(C\). Real users’ gradients are partly aligned, which is precisely why their records are correlated, and the theorem says some loss attains the bound. An auditor should therefore treat it as the guarantee, not as a pessimistic estimate.






Figure 44.2: The user-level \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of the running example’s DP-SGD (\(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\), 10,000 steps; \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) per record) for a user with \(k\) records. The direct accountant of Equation 44.6 (black) is close to a single record sampled at rate \(kq\) (blue, dotted) and grows faster than linearly (grey). Group privacy from the record-level guarantee (red, dashed) is larger, and gives no guarantee at all for \(k = 10\) and above.

The first column checks the accountant: with one record it is the DP-SGD accountant, 6.72 against 6.71, the difference coming from the coarser grid of orders this chapter’s script uses (its best order is 4, against 4.1 on the finer grid). At \(\alpha = 4.1\) the two curves agree to all printed digits, \(3.733633 \times 10^{-4}\). For \(k = 2\) and 5 at \(\alpha = 2\), the numerical integral and the exact formula Equation 44.7, \(A_2 = \mathbb E[e^{H_1H_2/\sigma^2}]\), agree to seven digits (\(6.992273 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(4.626224 \times 10^{-3}\)), and the reverse direction is smaller (\(6.119238 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(3.412123 \times 10^{-3}\)).

The rate-\(kq\) approximation is within 1.5% at \(k = 2\) (15.32 against 15.54) and 8% at \(k = 10\) (134.50 against 146.20), so it is a quick estimate of the user’s exposure: rerun the record-level accountant with \(q\) replaced by \(kq\). In every row it errs on the low side, because it drops the terms in which several of the user’s records are drawn together.


44.4.6 Check yourself

Your model was trained with example-level DP-SGD at \(q = 0.001\), and its heaviest user has 20 records. Which single-record accountant run gives a quick estimate of that user’s \(\varepsilon\), and in which direction is it off? (The run with \(q = 0.02\) and the same \(\sigma\) and \(T\). It underestimates slightly, because it ignores steps that draw several of the user’s records at once.)
In Equation 44.7, why do only products of different copies appear? (Because the \(\sum_iH_i^2\) in the exponent of the likelihood ratio cancels the squares in \(V^2\) after the Gaussian average. Each copy alone averages to a ratio whose expectation under \(P_0\) is 1, as for one record.)

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.5 User-level DP-SGD

44.5.1 Context
Accounting for users after the fact charges a heavy user for every one of their records. The alternative changes the algorithm, so that the unit DP-SGD samples, clips and accounts for is the user. The idea is due to McMahan, Ramage, Talwar & Zhang (2018), who used it to train a language model with federated learning, where each user’s device computes an update on its own data and the server only sees the updates. What does the algorithm compute, and what does it guarantee?


44.5.2 Statement
Start from weights \(\theta_0\) chosen independently of the data. For \(t = 0, \dots, T - 1\):

Sample users. Put each user in the set \(S_t\) independently with probability \(q\).
Per-user update. For each \(u \in S_t\), compute one vector from user \(u\)’s records alone, for example the average gradient \(\bar g_u = \frac1{n_u}\sum_{i \in u}\nabla_\theta\ell(\theta_t; z_i)\), or the change in weights after a few local steps of SGD on those records.
Clip per user. \(\tilde g_u = \bar g_u\min(1, C/\|\bar g_u\|)\).
Noisy sum. \(G_t = \sum_{u\in S_t}\tilde g_u + \xi_t\) with \(\xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\).
Step. \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \eta\,G_t/(qU)\).

Releasing \(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_T\) is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon\) given by Equation 44.3 for the curve \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) of Fact 2: exactly the accountant of example-level DP-SGD, with users in place of records and \(q\) the user sampling rate.
A common variant replaces steps 2 and 3 by per-record clipping and a cap: keep at most \(k\) records per user, clip each record’s gradient to \(C\), and sum them. One user then moves the sum by at most \(kC\), and the guarantee is that of noise multiplier \(\sigma/k\): \[A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\exp\Big(\frac{k^2(j^2 - j)}{2\sigma^2}\Big), \tag{44.12}\] Equation 44.2 with \(\sigma\) replaced by \(\sigma/k\).


44.5.3 Derivation
The proof of DP-SGD used four properties of the clipped sum. Each holds with users in place of records.

One user moves the clipped sum by at most \(C\). Fix the weights \(\theta_t\) and the other sampled users. Each \(\tilde g_v\) is computed from user \(v\)’s records alone, so adding user \(u\) to the dataset leaves every other term unchanged and adds \(\tilde g_u\), of length at most \(C\) by step 3. However many records \(u\) has, they enter only through \(\tilde g_u\).
One step is a subsampled Gaussian mechanism over users. User \(u\) enters \(S_t\) with probability \(q\), independently of the other users. So the step’s output with \(u\) is a mixture: with probability \(1 - q\) the same as without \(u\), with probability \(q\) shifted by \(\tilde g_u\). After rescaling by \(C\) and rotating the shift onto one axis, the worst case is the pair of Fact 2, and the step’s RDP curve is \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\).
Dividing by \(qU\) is post-processing, since the number of users \(U\) is treated as public, as \(n\) is in example-level DP-SGD.
Compose and convert. RDP composition over the \(T\) adaptive steps and Equation 44.3 finish the proof, as before.
The capped-sum variant. With per-record clipping, user \(u\)’s contribution is a sum of at most \(k\) vectors of length at most \(C\), so its length is at most \(kC\), and the user is still sampled as a whole with probability \(q\). In units of \(C\) the pair is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) against \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\mathcal N(k, \sigma^2)\). Dividing the output by \(k\), an invertible map that changes no divergence, gives the pair with shift 1 and noise \(\sigma/k\), whose curve is Equation 44.2 with \(\sigma/k\): that is Equation 44.12. The script checks it at \(k = 2\), \(\alpha = 3\): both give \(8.219438 \times 10^{-2}\).



44.5.4 Interpretation
The count that matters is the number of units. User-level DP-SGD has the privacy of example-level DP-SGD on a dataset of \(U\) records. To keep the same expected batch of \(B\) units, the sampling rate must be \(B/U\), larger than \(B/n\) by the average number of records per user, and amplification is correspondingly weaker. On the running example, with 1,000 steps and an expected batch of 100 units, a record-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 0.778\) at \(q = 0.01\), and a user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\) needs \(\sigma = 3.78\) at \(q = 0.1\). The noise on the averaged update, \(\sigma C/B\), is 0.0189 against 0.00389, about five times larger. This is the honest price of protecting people: there are ten times fewer of them than records, and DP’s cost per unit is fixed.
Records inside a user are free. The guarantee does not depend on \(n_u\). A user’s records can be averaged, used for several local steps, or subsampled, all without changing \(\varepsilon\), as long as the result is one clipped vector computed from that user’s data alone. More records per user make each \(\bar g_u\) a better estimate of the user’s gradient, so the signal improves while the noise stays fixed. Levy et al. (2021) show that, when each user’s records come from the same distribution, user-level private learning gains from having more records per user.
Average, or sum then clip? Averaging before clipping gives every user a vector of the same kind regardless of size, which keeps the clipping norm meaningful across users. Clipping each record and summing at most \(k\) of them uses per-example gradient code that already exists, but pays a factor \(k\) in noise multiplier (Equation 44.12). Summing all of a user’s records and then clipping the sum is also valid (sensitivity \(C\)), and gives heavy users more weight than averaging does, as Section 44.7 shows.
What the proof assumes. Step 1 needs every user’s contribution to be computed from that user alone, which rules out cross-user normalization and requires that one user’s records are not spread across several “users” in the data. If one person has several accounts, the unit is the account, and the person is again a group. Step 2 needs users to be Poisson-sampled; an implementation that iterates over users in a fixed shuffled order is a different mechanism, as for records.


44.5.5 Example: the noise each strategy needs

The column “record-level” is not a user-level guarantee; it shows the noise the same schedule would need to protect only records. 44.5.6 Check yourself

In user-level DP-SGD, a user with 300 records runs five local steps of SGD on them and sends the clipped change in weights. Does that change \(\varepsilon\)? (No. The user’s contribution is still one vector computed from their records alone, clipped to \(C\); the local computation is invisible to the accountant.)
Why does user-level DP-SGD on 1,000 users need more noise than example-level DP-SGD on 10,000 records, at the same expected batch, steps and \(\varepsilon\)? (To keep the batch at 100 units it must sample at rate 0.1 instead of 0.01. Amplification by subsampling is weaker at a higher rate, so the same \(\varepsilon\) needs a larger \(\sigma\).)

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.6 Contribution bounding

44.6.1 Context
User-level DP-SGD needs a data pipeline that groups records by user and computes one vector per user. Many training pipelines are built around records: shuffled files of examples, per-example gradient code, fixed-length batches. Can you keep that pipeline and still protect users? You can, if you limit how many records each user contributes. The question is what limit to choose, because the limit trades the noise the accountant requires against the data you throw away.


44.6.2 Statement
Contribution bounding keeps at most \(k\) records of each user, chosen without looking at other users’ data, for example at random, and discards the rest. Run example-level DP-SGD on the \(n_k = \sum_u\min(n_u, k)\) remaining records with sampling rate \(q\). The result is user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon\) given by the accountant of Equation 44.6 for a user with \(k\) records. The trade-off:

the noise grows with \(k\): in the small-\(kq\) regime the user’s RDP is that of a record sampled at rate \(kq\) (Equation 44.8), so the noise multiplier must grow roughly in proportion to \(k\) at a fixed \(q\);
the bias shrinks with \(k\): the training set loses \(n - n_k\) records, all of them from users with more than \(k\) records, so the data are both smaller and reweighted toward light users.



44.6.3 Derivation

Bounding is applied per user. Write the bounded dataset as \(\Pi(D) = \bigcup_u\pi(D_u)\), where \(D_u\) is user \(u\)’s records and \(\pi\) keeps at most \(k\) of them using randomness that is independent of everything else. Adding user \(u\) to \(D\) adds \(\pi(D_u)\) to \(\Pi(D)\) and changes nothing else, so user-level neighbours map to datasets that differ in at most \(k\) records, all of one user.
Account for those records. Example-level DP-SGD on \(\Pi(D)\) sees the user’s at most \(k\) records, each drawn independently with probability \(q\). By Section 44.4, the pair for one step is Equation 44.6 with \(k\). A user with fewer records is covered too: they are a \(k\)-record user some of whose clipped gradients happen to be 0, and the worst case of Section 44.4 is over all gradients of length at most \(C\), including 0. Composition and conversion are as before.
The noise grows with \(k\). At fixed \(q\), Equation 44.8 depends on \(k\) and \(q\) through \(kq\) only. Keeping the user’s RDP fixed while \(k\) doubles therefore requires either halving \(q\), which halves the batch, or raising \(\sigma\). In the regime where the per-step RDP is about \(\frac\alpha2(kq)^2/\sigma^2\), holding it fixed means \(\sigma \propto kq\).
The bias. Before bounding, the expected update of DP-SGD averages over all \(n\) records; after it, over \(n_k\) records in which each user has weight \(\min(n_u, k)/n_k\) instead of \(n_u/n\). A user with \(n_u > k\) loses weight, and their records beyond \(k\) are not used at all.



44.6.4 Interpretation
Choosing \(k\) is a bias–variance trade-off. Amin, Kulesza, Muñoz Medina & Vassilvitskii (2019) studied exactly this choice for private empirical risk minimization, and showed that the best cap depends on the distribution of user sizes: a cap above most users’ sizes buys little data at a large noise cost, and a cap below them throws away most of the data. Their framing is the same as that of choosing the clipping norm in Beyond global sensitivity: a smaller bound means less noise and more distortion of what is computed. Because the cap depends on the data, it should be chosen from public knowledge of the population or privately; choosing it by trying several caps and looking at test accuracy, as the example below does to show the trade-off, spends privacy that the accountant does not see (Hyperparameter tuning).
Which records to keep matters. Random selection keeps the proof simple. Chua et al. (2024) compare selection rules for fine-tuning language models under contribution bounding and report that keeping each user’s longest records worked best on one of their datasets. Any rule that looks only at the user’s own records is allowed, by step 1.
Bounding plus user-level DP-SGD. The two techniques combine: cap each user at \(k\) records to bound compute, then compute one clipped vector per user. With user sampling, the cap no longer costs noise, only data, and users can contribute their full records again by subsampling them inside each step.

title: 44  User-level differential privacy
text:
44.7 Heterogeneous users

44.7.1 Context
User sizes are rarely equal. In the running example’s population, 30 users with at least 50 records each hold 30.6% of the records, while the smallest half of the users hold 10.3% (Figure 44.1). Example-level training weights each user by their number of records; user-level training does not. What objective does user-level DP-SGD optimize, and what does that mean for heavy users?


44.7.2 Statement
Averaged over the user sampling and the noise, the update direction of user-level DP-SGD is \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{qU}\Big] = \frac1U\sum_{u=1}^U\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|\bar g_u\|}\Big)\bar g_u, \tag{44.13}\] a sum in which each user has weight at most \(1/U\) whatever their number of records. Example-level DP-SGD gives user \(u\) weight \(n_u/n\) in its expected update, \(\frac1n\sum_u\sum_{i\in u}\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i\).


44.7.3 Derivation

Average over the sampling. User \(u\) is in \(S_t\) with probability \(q\), so \(\mathbb E\sum_{u\in S_t}\tilde g_u = q\sum_u\tilde g_u\). The noise has mean zero.
Divide by \(qU\). The \(q\) cancels, leaving \(\frac1U\sum_u\tilde g_u\), which is Equation 44.13 by the definition of \(\tilde g_u\).
The weight of one user. \(\|\tilde g_u\| \le C\) for every user, so each term has length at most \(C/U\), and the share of any group of users in the update is at most their share of the users.
Example-level. The same computation for DP-SGD over records (DP-SGD) gives each record weight \(1/n\), so user \(u\)’s records together have weight \(n_u/n\).



44.7.4 Interpretation
User-level training changes the objective, not only the noise. With averaged per-user gradients, the model minimizes (a clipped version of) the average over users of each user’s average loss, \(\frac1U\sum_u\frac1{n_u}\sum_{i\in u}\ell(\theta; z_i)\), rather than the average over records. Whether that is what you want depends on the application. For a keyboard model, weighting people equally keeps a few very active users from defining everyone’s suggestions. For a model meant to fit the overall distribution of records, it under-weights heavy users’ content, and the bias can matter when heavy users differ from light ones, for example by language, topic or device.
Clipping caps heavy users twice. A heavy user’s average gradient is a good estimate, typically short when the model already fits their data, and is rarely clipped. But if the user’s data are unusual, their gradient is long and is clipped to \(C\), so their influence is capped at that of any other user. This is the user-level analogue of what clipping does to records with large gradients (Disparate impact).
Sum-then-clip sits in between. Summing a user’s gradients before clipping makes a heavy user’s vector up to \(n_u\) times longer than one record’s, so heavy users are clipped first, and their influence rises with \(n_u\) until it reaches \(C\). It interpolates between record weighting, for users whose sum stays below \(C\), and user weighting, for those above it (Exercise 5).


44.7.5 Example: heavy users in the running example
The 30 users with at least 50 records hold 30.6% of the records, and so 30.6% of the weight in the expected example-level update. Under user-level DP-SGD their weight is at most \(30/1{,}000 = 3.0\%\). Does that hurt the model where heavy users’ data are? The script splits the test set by the owner of each test point’s nearest training record. Because a heavy user’s records were chosen as the nearest neighbours of one seed in 50 dimensions, they spread widely, and 68.3% of test points have a heavy user’s record as their nearest neighbour. At user-level \(\varepsilon = 4\), user-level DP-SGD reaches 0.9361 on those points and 0.9319 on the others; the non-private model, 0.9607 and 0.9622. On this task, down-weighting heavy users costs nothing measurable, because one teacher network labels every record, so the light users’ records teach the same function. On data where heavy users’ records follow their own patterns, the same reweighting would cost accuracy on those patterns.


44.7.6 Check yourself

A user-level model will be used to predict for each record equally, and you know that heavy users’ records differ from light users’. What can you change without changing \(\varepsilon\)? (How each user’s vector is computed: summing instead of averaging before clipping, or a larger \(C\) relative to typical averaged gradients. Both are inside the per-user computation and leave the sensitivity at \(C\).)
Why is each user’s share of the user-level update at most \(1/U\) rather than exactly \(1/U\)? (Because a user’s clipped vector has length at most \(C\); users whose average gradient is shorter than \(C\), typically those the model already fits, contribute less.)

44.8 Comparing the strategies on the running example

44.8.1 Context
Three ways to train the running example with a user-level guarantee are now on the table: (a) example-level DP-SGD on all records, with the user accountant for the heaviest user; (b) user-level DP-SGD; (c) contribution bounding to two records per user, then example-level DP-SGD. At the same user-level \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), which model is best?


44.8.2 Statement
Table 44.5 trains each strategy for 1,000 steps with an expected batch of 100 units, \(C = 0.5\) and \(\eta = 0.5\), at the noise multipliers of Table 44.3, one run each.

44.8.3 Derivation
Each strategy’s guarantee was derived above: (a) and (c) by the accountant of Section 44.4 with \(k = 348\) and \(k = 2\), and (b) by Section 44.5. The cap \(k = 2\) is the best cap at \(\varepsilon = 4\) in Table 44.4, tied with \(k = 1\); choosing it from test accuracy is a leak that a real deployment would have to pay for. Run-to-run variation is of the order of a point at these budgets: the cap \(k = 1\) and user-level DP-SGD restricted to one random record per user are the same algorithm with the same \(\sigma\), and two runs of it gave 0.8917 and 0.9070.


44.8.4 Interpretation
Keeping the record as the unit fails. Strategy (a) is at chance, between 0.53 and 0.57, at every budget up to \(\varepsilon = 8\). The heaviest user dictates the noise for everyone: \(\sigma\) between 70.3 and 449 drowns every gradient. That is the practical meaning of Figure 44.2: an example-level pipeline on data with heavy users needs either an enormous \(\varepsilon\) or a cap.
Changing the unit wins. User-level DP-SGD is the best strategy at every budget, 0.9347 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) against 0.9612 for the non-private model. It needs a little less noise than the cap of 2 (Table 44.3) and, unlike the cap, it uses every record, through the per-user average. Its advantage is largest at small budgets: 9.8 points at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 1.1 points at \(\varepsilon = 8\). Its cost is compute: each step processes all the records of about 100 users, about 1,000 records, ten times what the example-level strategies process.
Bounding is the fallback. Strategy (c) keeps the example-level pipeline and loses 5 to 10 points against (b) below \(\varepsilon = 8\). It comes close at \(\varepsilon = 8\), where the noise is small enough that the discarded data, not the noise, limits accuracy.
These findings agree with published comparisons on language models, which use different data, models and accountants. Chua et al. (2024) compare contribution bounding with group-privacy accounting (“Group Privacy”) against user-level DP-SGD with per-user averaging (“User-wise DP-SGD”) for fine-tuning, and report that user-wise DP-SGD generally does better, especially at small budgets. Charles et al. (2024), who call the two sampling schemes example-level and user-level sampling, report that user-level sampling usually does better when each user’s data are varied and when strong privacy is required, and that example-level sampling sometimes wins. Note that Chua et al. account for the cap with the generic group privacy of Equation 44.1; the direct accountant of Section 44.4 would give them less noise.






Figure 44.3: Test accuracy of the running example against the user-level \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), for the three strategies (1,000 steps, expected batch 100, one run each; the runs differ from Table 44.5 in their random seeds). User-level DP-SGD is best at every budget; example-level DP-SGD on all records, accounted for its heaviest user, stays near chance.





44.8.5 Example: what the user-level guarantee costs
At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the running example loses 2.7 points to protect users (0.9347 against 0.9612). The record-level model of DP-SGD at the same \(\varepsilon\), trained for 10,000 steps, reached 0.9548, and this chapter’s 1,000-step schedule would need only \(\sigma = 0.778\) for a record-level guarantee (Table 44.3). The difference is the price of the unit: 1,000 people instead of 10,000 records, and a guarantee that now covers the person with 348 records as well as the one with a single record.


44.8.6 Check yourself

Strategy (a) uses every record and the tightest available accountant. Why does it do worst? (Because the guarantee must hold for the heaviest user, whose 348 records put about 3.5 of them into every batch; the noise has to hide a shift of several clipping norms in almost every step, which takes \(\sigma\) in the hundreds.)
Would strategy (a) look better if the heaviest user were removed from the data? (Only a little: the accountant would be for the next-largest user, who has 258 records, so about 2.6 of them would still be in every batch. Removing a user because of their size is itself a data-dependent choice that must be made with public information or paid for, and it is a crude form of contribution bounding.)

What to take from it. The record-level accountant answers the wrong question when people contribute many records, and asking it the right question, about a user with \(k\) records, gives answers that grow faster than \(k\). Rules of thumb

Name the privacy unit with every \(\varepsilon\). A record-level \(\varepsilon\) says little about a person with many records.
To estimate what an example-level model gives a user with \(k\) records, rerun the accountant at rate \(kq\), and expect the truth to be a little worse.
Don’t use group privacy for DP-SGD; account for the user’s records directly, or better, sample and clip users.
Prefer user-level DP-SGD with per-user averaging. It pays for the number of people, not their records, and uses all their data.
If the pipeline must stay record-based, cap records per user, choose the cap from public knowledge, and account for the cap with the user accountant.
Decide deliberately how heavy users should count: averaging weights people equally, summing before clipping weights records until the clip.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.1 Why this matters
The chapter on private gradient descent showed that training the part’s running example with differential privacy (DP) at \(\varepsilon = 4\) costs less than one point of test accuracy: 0.9548 against 0.9610 without privacy. That number is an average over the test set. It says nothing about who loses the point. Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) asked that question and found an uncomfortable answer: when a network is trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, the accuracy it loses is concentrated on the classes and subgroups that are under-represented in the training data. In their gender classifier, for example, the drop in accuracy was much larger on Black faces than on white faces, and the gap between groups that the non-private model already had grew under DP. They called this the disparate impact of DP on model accuracy.
This matters in two ways. A model that is “less than a point worse” can be ten points worse on a group of people, and an average hides it. And the groups that pay are often the ones a privacy guarantee is meant to protect: small populations, rare conditions, unusual records. This chapter explains why it happens, from the two ingredients of DP-SGD, measures it on the running example, and asks what can be done about it.

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.1.1 The one idea: every record gets the same budget of influence, and every group gets the same noise
DP-SGD caps each record’s pull on the update at \(C\), then adds noise whose size depends only on \(C\) and \(\sigma\), not on the data. Both rules are blind to groups, and that is exactly why they are not neutral. A group’s pull on the expected update is at most its share of the records times \(C\), however badly the model fits it, so a group whose gradients are large is cut back more than a group whose gradients are small: that is the clipping mechanism. And the noise is the same for everyone, while a group’s signal is proportional to its size, so a small group’s signal-to-noise ratio is smaller by its share: that is the noise mechanism. Small groups and groups the model finds hard suffer from both, and the two compound, because clipping shrinks a group’s effective share and the noise then acts on the shrunk share.
Table 45.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 45.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.





Result
Where it is used




Measuring disparate impact: privacy cost per group
Reporting a private model; choosing ε


Clipping reweights groups and turns the update
Choosing \(C\); group-aware clipping


The noise floor of a small group
Deciding whether a group is large enough to train on privately


Confidence intervals for per-group accuracy
Every per-group evaluation, private or not


Mitigations and what each costs
Training a private model that serves every group






Notation. As in DP-SGD, \(n\) records \(z_i = (x_i, y_i)\) train a model with weights \(\theta\), \(g_i\) is record \(i\)’s gradient, \(C\) the clipping norm, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, \(q\) the sampling rate, \(B = qn\) the expected batch size, \(T\) the number of steps and \(\eta\) the learning rate. The records are split into groups \(g = 1, \dots, K\); group \(g\) has \(n_g\) records and share \(s_g = n_g/n\). A record’s clipping weight is \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\), the factor clipping multiplies its gradient by, and a group’s clipping weight \(w_g\) is its average over the group’s records. \(\mathrm{acc}_g\) is a model’s accuracy on test records of group \(g\). A subscript \(i\) always names a record and a subscript \(g\) or \(h\) a group, so \(g_i\) is a record’s gradient and \(\bar g_g\), defined below, a group’s average gradient.
The running example. The part’s running example classifies 50-dimensional inputs with a two-layer network (DP-SGD). This chapter adds a minority group. Of the \(n = 10{,}000\) training records, 9,500 are the first records of the running example’s fixed training set: standard normal inputs, labelled by the random teacher network. The other 500, a share of 5%, come from a different region and follow a different rule. Their inputs are \(x = 8u + z\), where \(u\) is a fixed unit vector and \(z\) is standard normal in a fixed 15-dimensional subspace orthogonal to \(u\), and their label is the sign of one coordinate of \(z\). So the minority’s records lie far from the majority’s, have larger inputs (average length 8.89 against 7.04), and need a rule that the majority does not teach. The non-private model learns both: it reaches 0.9529 on the majority and 0.9411 on the minority. Each group is tested on 20,000 fresh records of its own, so that the test error is small compared with the effects being measured. DP-SGD runs with the running example’s settings: \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\), \(\eta = 0.5\), \(T = 10{,}000\) steps and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
How to read this chapter. Section 45.3 defines what to measure and shows the effect. Section 45.4 and Section 45.5 explain it, one mechanism each; they are the core of the chapter. Section 45.6 is about measuring per-group accuracy honestly, and applies to any model. Section 45.7 discusses what can be done and what each fix costs.

title: 45  Disparate impact
section: 45.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
45.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

45.2.1 Fact 1 — The expected update is a reweighted average gradient
Each DP-SGD step adds up the clipped gradients of a Poisson batch, adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to each coordinate, and divides by the public expected batch size \(B = qn\). Each record is in the batch with probability \(q\), so the expected sum is \(q\) times the sum over all records, and dividing by \(qn\) gives \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\min\Big(1, \frac C{\|g_i\|}\Big)g_i, \tag{45.1}\] the average gradient with each record weighted by its clipping weight (DP-SGD). The noise on the averaged update has standard deviation \(\tau = \sigma C/B\) per coordinate, whatever the data. In the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\), \(\sigma = 1.36\) and \(\tau = 1.36 \times 0.5/100 = 0.0068\).


45.2.2 Fact 2 — A drift beats a random walk after (noise/signal)² steps
Suppose each step moves the weights by a signal of length \(\ell_{\text{sig}}\) that keeps pointing the same way, plus independent noise of length \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\). After a number \(t\) of steps the signals add up to length \(t\ell_{\text{sig}}\). The noise vectors are independent with mean zero, so their squared lengths add, and their sum has length about \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\sqrt t\). The signal is longer once \(t\ell_{\text{sig}} > \ell_{\text{noise}}\sqrt t\), that is after \[t > \Big(\frac{\ell_{\text{noise}}}{\ell_{\text{sig}}}\Big)^2 \tag{45.2}\] steps. DP-SGD uses this to explain why training works when every step’s noise is ten times longer than its signal: at \(\varepsilon = 4\) the noise on the averaged gradient has length \(\tau\sqrt{3{,}329}\) for the network’s 3,329 weights, and the signal emerges after a few hundred steps.


45.2.3 Fact 3 — A shrinking recursion with noise settles at a fixed variance
Let a number evolve as \(x_{t+1} = (1 - a)x_t + e_t\), where \(0 < a < 2\) and the \(e_t\) are independent with mean zero and variance \(v\). Each step shrinks \(x\) toward zero by the factor \(1 - a\) and adds fresh noise. Because the noise is independent of the current value, variances add: \(\operatorname{Var}x_{t+1} = (1 - a)^2\operatorname{Var}x_t + v\). Since \((1 - a)^2 < 1\), this converges, and the limit \(V\) solves \(V = (1 - a)^2V + v\): \[V = \frac{v}{1 - (1 - a)^2} = \frac{v}{a(2 - a)}. \tag{45.3}\] For example, with \(a = 0.1\) and \(v = 1\) the variance settles at \(1/(0.1 \times 1.9) = 5.26\): a weak pull toward zero lets the noise accumulate to more than five times one step’s variance. Halving the pull roughly doubles the stationary variance. The number of steps to forget the starting point is about \(1/a\), since \((1 - a)^t \approx e^{-at}\).


45.2.4 Fact 4 — An accuracy measured on \(m\) records is a binomial proportion
If a model classifies each test record of a group correctly with probability \(p\), independently, then the number correct out of \(m\) is binomial with mean \(mp\) and variance \(mp(1 - p)\), and the measured accuracy \(k/m\) has standard deviation \(\sqrt{p(1 - p)/m}\). The Clopper–Pearson interval (Hypothesis testing) inverts the binomial distribution exactly: at the 95% level its upper end \(u\) is the accuracy at which \(k\) or fewer correct answers would have probability 0.025, and its lower end \(l\) the accuracy at which \(k\) or more would have probability 0.025. It covers the true accuracy with probability at least 0.95. The smaller the group, the wider the interval, in proportion to \(1/\sqrt m\).

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.3 Disparate impact, measured

45.3.1 Context
What exactly should you measure to say that DP hurts one group more than another, and does it happen on the running example? An accuracy gap between groups is not enough, because the non-private model may already have one. The question is how much privacy adds to each group’s error.


45.3.2 Statement
The privacy cost of group \(g\) is the accuracy the group loses when the same training recipe is made private: \[\pi_g = \mathrm{acc}_g(\text{non-private}) - \mathbb E\big[\mathrm{acc}_g(\text{private})\big], \tag{45.4}\] where the expectation is over the randomness of private training (Esipova et al. 2023 use this definition; Bagdasaryan et al. 2019 compare the same differences). DP has disparate impact when the privacy costs of groups differ, \(\pi_a \ne \pi_b\), and the privacy cost gap \(|\pi_a - \pi_b|\) measures how much.
On the running example with a 5% minority, Table 45.2 gives each group’s accuracy over three training runs per row.

45.3.3 Derivation
This statement is a definition and a measurement, so its “derivation” is the experiment’s design, and each choice in it is there to make the comparison fair.

Same data, same recipe. Every row trains on the same 10,000 records with the same sampling rate, learning rate and number of steps. The only differences are the clipping (absent in the non-private row) and the noise multiplier, which the accountant of DP-SGD sets for each \(\varepsilon\).
Large test sets. Each group is tested on 20,000 records, so by Fact 4 a measured accuracy near 0.9 has a standard deviation of \(\sqrt{0.9 \times 0.1/20{,}000} = 0.0021\). The differences in the table are much larger than that.
Several runs. Private training is random, and its spread differs between groups. Each row averages three runs and reports their standard deviation; the privacy cost subtracts the average private accuracy from the average non-private accuracy.
A non-private model that serves both groups. The minority’s non-private accuracy, 0.9411, is within 1.2 points of the majority’s, 0.9529. Any large gap in the private rows is therefore caused by privacy, not inherited from the data.



45.3.4 Interpretation
The minority pays almost all of it. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the majority loses 0.59 points of accuracy and the minority 9.34, 15.7 times as much. At \(\varepsilon = 8\), a budget at which DP-SGD found the running example nearly as accurate as non-private training, the majority loses nothing (its accuracy is 0.20 points higher) and the minority loses 8.58 points. The ratio is smaller at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 4.6, only because there the majority starts to lose too: 7.07 points against the minority’s 32.78. An average over a test set drawn like the training set, 95% majority, would report a loss of \(0.95 \times 0.0059 + 0.05 \times 0.0934 = 0.0103\) at \(\varepsilon = 4\), about one point.
Both mechanisms are visible. The clipping-only row has no noise at all, yet the minority loses 4.04 points while the majority gains 0.51: clipping alone is disparate. Adding noise then widens the gap steadily as \(\varepsilon\) falls. The next two sections explain each part.
The minority’s runs also vary more. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the standard deviation over runs is 0.0211 for the minority and 0.0037 for the majority. A single private run says less about a small group than about a large one, a point Section 45.6 returns to.






Figure 45.1: Test accuracy of each group of the running example against \(\varepsilon\) (log scale, one run per point, \(\delta = 10^{-5}\)), with each group’s non-private accuracy dashed. The majority is close to its non-private accuracy down to \(\varepsilon = 2\); the minority falls far below it at every budget.





45.3.5 Example: what the published experiments found
Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov (2019) trained classifiers with DP-SGD on images and text and found the same pattern: the under-represented classes and subgroups, and the more complex ones, lost the most accuracy, and an existing gap between groups grew. Esipova et al. (2023) report, for MNIST digits where class 8 was undersampled to about 1% of the training set, a privacy cost of 8.9 points for the typical class 2 and 57.9 points for class 8 under DP-SGD (their Table 2, \(\varepsilon = 5.90\)). On the running example, Figure 45.1 shows the same shape: the majority’s curve is the curve of DP-SGD, the minority’s lies far below it.


45.3.6 Check yourself

Why is the privacy cost a better measure than the gap between the private model’s group accuracies? (Because part of the gap may be inherited from non-private training, which DP did not cause. The privacy cost subtracts each group’s own non-private accuracy.)
At \(\varepsilon = 4\), a test set with the training proportions shows an overall loss of under one point. What would a test set with equal numbers of both groups show? (The average of the two privacy costs, \((0.0059 + 0.0934)/2 = 0.0497\): about five points. The overall number depends on the test set’s mix as much as on the model.)

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.4 Clipping reweights the groups

45.4.1 Context
Clipping without noise changes nothing about privacy (without noise there is none), yet in Table 45.2 it costs the minority 4.04 points. How does a rule that treats every record the same way end up treating groups differently?


45.4.2 Statement
Split the expected update of Fact 1 by group. Write \(\bar g_g = \frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}g_i\) for group \(g\)’s average gradient and \(m_g = \frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\,g_i\) for its average clipped gradient. Then \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \sum_gs_g\,m_g, \qquad \|s_g\,m_g\| \le s_g\,C: \tag{45.5}\] each group pulls with its share times its average clipped gradient, and that pull is never longer than its share times \(C\), however large the group’s gradients are.
When the records within each group have parallel gradients, each group’s average clipped gradient is its average gradient scaled by a number, and the expected update becomes the gradient of a reweighted mixture of the groups: \[\mathbb E\Big[\frac{G_t}{B}\Big] = \Big(\sum_hs_h\,c_h\Big)\sum_g\tilde s_g\,\bar g_g, \qquad \tilde s_g = \frac{s_g\,c_g}{\sum_hs_h\,c_h}, \tag{45.6}\] where \(c_g = \|m_g\|/\|\bar g_g\|\) is the fraction of the group’s average gradient that survives clipping and \(\tilde s_g\) is its effective share. When all of a group’s records have the same norm, \(c_g\) is the group’s clipping weight \(w_g\).


45.4.3 Derivation

Split the sum. Fact 1’s expected update is \(\frac1n\sum_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i\). Group the records: \(\frac1n\sum_g\sum_{i\in g}(\cdots) = \sum_g\frac{n_g}n\cdot\frac1{n_g}\sum_{i\in g}(\cdots) = \sum_gs_gm_g\).
Bound the pull. Each clipped gradient has length at most \(C\), and the length of an average is at most the average of the lengths (the triangle inequality), so \(\|m_g\| \le C\) and \(\|s_gm_g\| \le s_gC\).
Parallel gradients. If every \(g_i\) in group \(g\) points along the same unit vector \(e_g\), then \(g_i = \|g_i\|e_g\) and \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i = \min(\|g_i\|, C)e_g\). Averaging, \(m_g\) and \(\bar g_g\) both point along \(e_g\), so \(m_g = c_g\bar g_g\) with \(c_g = \|m_g\|/\|\bar g_g\|\).
Factor out the total. \(\sum_gs_gc_g\bar g_g = (\sum_hs_hc_h)\sum_g\frac{s_gc_g}{\sum_hs_hc_h}\bar g_g\), which is Equation 45.6. The effective shares are non-negative and add up to 1.
Equal norms. If all of group \(g\)’s records also have the same norm \(\nu_g\), then \(c_g = \min(\nu_g, C)/\nu_g = \min(1, C/\nu_g) = w_g\).



45.4.4 Interpretation
Two errors: length and direction. Equation 45.6 separates what clipping does into two parts. The factor \(\sum_hs_hc_h\) shortens the update, which a larger learning rate can undo. The effective shares change which mixture of the groups is being descended, and no learning rate undoes that. Esipova et al. (2023) make this distinction for a whole batch: they compare training with the clipped batch gradient’s length but the true direction against the true length but the clipped direction, and find the direction error far more harmful, especially to the under-represented class (their Table 1). In Figure 45.2, clipping shortens the update and also turns it toward the majority.
Which groups are cut back. A group’s effective share falls when its clipping weight falls, that is when its gradients are long compared with \(C\). Gradients are long for two reasons. The model fits the group badly: for the logistic loss, the derivative with respect to the output is \(-y\,\mathrm{sigmoid}(-yf)\), close to 1 in size for a misclassified record and close to 0 for a record classified with a wide margin. And the group’s inputs are large: a dense layer’s per-example gradient is the outer product of the back-propagated error and the layer’s input, whose norm is the product of the two norms (DP-SGD), so at the same error a record with a longer input has a longer gradient. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) identify both factors, gradient norms and the input norms behind them, as the source of the clipping part of disparate impact. A small group the model has not yet learned has both.
A feedback loop. Early in training every record is clipped and every group has a similar weight. As the majority is learned, its gradients shrink below \(C\) and its weight rises toward 1, while the minority, not yet learned, keeps long gradients and a low weight. Its effective share falls below its true share, so it is learned more slowly, so its gradients stay long. The loop ends only when the minority’s gradients fall below \(C\) too.
Where training stops. Clipped gradient descent stops where the expected update is zero, \(\sum_gs_gm_g = 0\), not where the true average gradient \(\sum_gs_g\bar g_g\) is zero. If the groups’ gradients conflict, the stopping point is that of the reweighted objective, which has moved toward the majority.






Figure 45.2: The clipping example in two dimensions: 95 majority records with gradient (0.2, 0) and 5 minority records with gradient (0, 4). Without clipping the two groups pull about equally hard (black); clipping at C = 0.5 cuts the minority’s pull eightfold and turns the update toward the majority (red). Scaling every gradient by the same factor 1/8 instead keeps the direction (blue).





45.4.5 Example: two dimensions, then the running example
Take 95 majority records whose gradient is \((0.2, 0)\), already short, and 5 minority records whose gradient is \((0, 4)\), long because the model fits them badly. Without clipping the average gradient is \((0.95 \times 0.2, 0.05 \times 4) = (0.19, 0.2)\), of length 0.2759: the five minority records pull as hard as the ninety-five others, and the minority’s component is a fraction \(0.2/0.39 = 0.513\) of the sum of the two components. Clip at \(C = 0.5\). The majority’s gradients are untouched; the minority’s shrink to length 0.5. The average becomes \((0.19, 0.05 \times 0.5) = (0.19, 0.025)\), of length 0.1916, and the minority’s fraction falls to 0.116. The update has turned by 39.0 degrees toward the majority. Here \(c_{\text{maj}} = 1\) and \(c_{\text{min}} = 0.5/4 = 0.125\), and Equation 45.6 gives the minority an effective share of \(0.05 \times 0.125/(0.05 \times 0.125 + 0.95) = 0.0065\) instead of 0.05. Scaling every gradient by \(C/C_{\max}\) with \(C_{\max} = 4\), the largest norm, instead gives \((0.0238, 0.0250)\): eight times shorter, but at an angle of 0.0 degrees to the true average.

If you multiply the minority’s loss by 10, does its pull on the update grow tenfold? (Not for clipped records. Their gradients grow tenfold and are then rescaled back to length \(C\); only records whose upweighted gradient stays below \(C\) gain. Exercise 1 works it out.)
Why does a larger clipping norm reduce the clipping part of disparate impact? (It raises the clipping weights of the groups with long gradients more than those of groups whose gradients are already below \(C\), whose weight is already 1, so the effective shares move back toward the true shares.)

title: 45  Disparate impact
section: 45.5 The noise floor of a small group
text:
45.5 The noise floor of a small group

45.5.1 Context
Noise is added to the sum, the same for everyone. Why should it hurt a small group more than a large one? Because what the noise competes with is each group’s signal, and a group’s signal in the sum is proportional to its size.


45.5.2 Statement
A drift that is a fraction of the population’s. If the part of the expected update that serves group \(g\) is a fraction \(s_g\) of what the whole population’s signal would be, and the noise is unchanged, Fact 2 says that group’s signal emerges from the noise only after \[t_g = \frac1{s_g^2}\Big(\frac{\ell_{\text{noise}}}{\ell_{\text{sig}}}\Big)^2 \tag{45.7}\] steps, \(1/s_g^2\) times as many as for a signal the whole population shares.
A quadratic model of the noise floor. Suppose group \(g\)’s loss depends on its own block \(\theta_g\) of \(d_g\) weights, which the other groups’ losses do not touch, as \(L_g = \frac\lambda2\|\theta_g - \theta_g^*\|^2\), and the training objective is the share-weighted average \(\sum_gs_gL_g\). Run gradient descent with noise of standard deviation \(\tau\) per coordinate on the averaged gradient, as DP-SGD adds. Then group \(g\)’s excess loss settles at \[\mathbb E[L_g] = \frac{d_g\,\eta\,\tau^2}{2\,s_g\,(2 - \eta s_g\lambda)} \approx \frac{d_g\,\eta\,\tau^2}{4\,s_g}, \tag{45.8}\] and it takes about \(1/(\eta s_g\lambda)\) steps to get there. With clipping, \(s_g\) is replaced by \(s_gc_g\), the group’s share times the fraction of its gradient that survives clipping; when the majority is hardly clipped, this is close to the effective share \(\tilde s_g\) of Equation 45.6.


45.5.3 Derivation

The group’s gradient. The objective’s gradient with respect to \(\theta_g\) is \(s_g\lambda(\theta_g - \theta_g^*)\): only group \(g\)’s loss depends on these weights, and it enters with weight \(s_g\).
One step. With \(x = \theta_g - \theta_g^*\) and noise \(\tau\xi\) on the averaged gradient, \(\xi\) standard normal, the update \(\theta_g \leftarrow \theta_g - \eta(s_g\lambda x + \tau\xi)\) gives \(x \leftarrow (1 - \eta s_g\lambda)x - \eta\tau\xi\), coordinate by coordinate.
Stationary variance. This is Fact 3 with \(a = \eta s_g\lambda\) and \(v = \eta^2\tau^2\): each coordinate settles at variance \(\eta^2\tau^2/(a(2 - a)) = \eta\tau^2/(s_g\lambda(2 - \eta s_g\lambda))\).
Excess loss. \(L_g = \frac\lambda2\sum_jx_j^2\) over the \(d_g\) coordinates, so its expectation is \(\frac\lambda2d_g\) times the variance, which is Equation 45.8. For a small group \(\eta s_g\lambda\) is small and \(2 - \eta s_g\lambda \approx 2\).
Time scale. By Fact 3 the starting point is forgotten after about \(1/a = 1/(\eta s_g\lambda)\) steps.
The break-even law. If the population’s signal has length \(\ell_{\text{sig}}\) per step, the part that serves group \(g\) has length \(s_g\ell_{\text{sig}}\) and the noise length is still \(\ell_{\text{noise}}\); Fact 2 with \(s_g\ell_{\text{sig}}\) in place of \(\ell_{\text{sig}}\) gives Equation 45.7.
With clipping. By Equation 45.6, with parallel gradients within the group, group \(g\)’s term in the expected update is \(s_gc_g\bar g_g\) instead of \(s_g\bar g_g\), while the noise is unchanged. Treating \(c_g\) as constant over the steps considered, steps 1 to 6 apply with \(s_gc_g\) in place of \(s_g\). If the majority’s \(c\) is close to 1, then \(\sum_hs_hc_h\) is close to 1 and \(s_gc_g\) is close to \(\tilde s_g\).



45.5.4 Interpretation
The floor scales like one over the share. A group with a twentieth of the records sits at about twenty times the excess loss of a group with all of them. The curvature \(\lambda\) cancels: a group whose loss is sharper is pulled back harder, but each unit of noise also costs it more, and the two effects balance. What does not cancel is the share, because the noise is not scaled by it. It also takes the small group \(1/s_g\) times longer to reach even that floor.
Why waiting does not help. At a fixed budget, more steps require more noise per step. Under the small-\(q\) law of DP-SGD, multiplying the number of steps by \(m\) multiplies the noise variance per step by about \(m\), so the break-even count of Equation 45.7 grows as fast as the run (Exercise 3).
The two mechanisms compound. Clipping lowers a group’s pull from \(s_g\) to \(s_gc_g\); the noise floor scales like one over the pull. A group that is 5% of the data and whose gradients clipping halves pays the floor of a group of 2.5%.
How good is the model. The quadratic model is exact for what it assumes, as the simulation below confirms, but a network is not quadratic and its groups do not use disjoint weights. Where the minority’s task overlaps the majority’s, the majority’s gradient does part of the minority’s work, and the penalty is smaller. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) derive a related per-step decomposition for DP-SGD without assuming disjoint weights: the expected change in a group’s loss has a clipping term, driven by the group’s gradient norms, and a noise term proportional to \(\eta^2\sigma^2C^2\) times the trace of the group’s loss Hessian, which they relate to the group’s distance to the decision boundary and its input norms. Section M.5 in the appendices derives this decomposition, which is exact for quadratic losses, and shows that it contains Equation 45.8. The quadratic model makes the role of the share explicit, which their per-step terms leave implicit.






Figure 45.4: Left: each group’s test accuracy of the running example against the minority’s share of the 10,000 training records (one run per point), non-private and at \(\varepsilon = 4\). Right: the stationary excess loss of a group in the quadratic model, Equation 45.8, against its share, with the noise of \(\varepsilon = 4\), compared with simulation.

(By a factor of 4, since it is proportional to \(\tau^2\), for every group alike. The gap between groups grows by the same factor in absolute terms; the ratio between them, \(s_{\text{major}}/s_{\text{minor}}\), is unchanged.)
Why does the curvature \(\lambda\) drop out of the approximate noise floor? (The pull toward the optimum and the cost of a displacement are both proportional to \(\lambda\); the stationary variance falls like \(1/\lambda\) and the loss per unit of variance rises like \(\lambda\).)

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.6 Measuring per-group accuracy

45.6.1 Context
Every number so far was measured on 20,000 test records per group. Real evaluations are not so generous: a test split of 2,000 records with a 5% minority holds 100 minority records. How precisely can a group’s accuracy, and the gap between two groups, be measured, and how much does a single training run say?


45.6.2 Statement
The test-set error of a group’s accuracy is binomial (Fact 4): with \(k\) correct of \(m\) records, report the Clopper–Pearson interval. For the gap between two groups measured on disjoint test records, the two estimates are independent and their variances add, so an approximate 95% interval is \[(\hat p_a - \hat p_b) \pm 1.96\sqrt{\frac{\hat p_a(1 - \hat p_a)}{m_a} + \frac{\hat p_b(1 - \hat p_b)}{m_b}}, \tag{45.9}\] with \(\hat p_g\) the measured accuracies and \(m_g\) the numbers of test records. Training randomness is a second, separate source of variation: a group’s accuracy varies from run to run, more for small groups, and is estimated only by training several times.


45.6.3 Derivation

One group. Each test record is classified correctly or not, independently given the model, with probability equal to the group’s true accuracy \(p_g\). The count is binomial, and Clopper–Pearson inverts it exactly (Hypothesis testing).
The gap. The two counts come from disjoint test records, so they are independent given the model. The variance of a difference of independent estimates is the sum of their variances, \(p_a(1 - p_a)/m_a + p_b(1 - p_b)/m_b\). For large counts the difference is approximately normal by the central limit theorem, and 1.96 standard deviations on each side cover 95%.
Two sources. Conditional on the trained model, the spread comes from the test set alone. Over training runs, the model itself varies; by the law of total variance the spread of a single run’s measured accuracy is the test-set variance plus the run-to-run variance of the true accuracy. Only repeated training estimates the second.



45.6.4 Interpretation
Small groups need intervals. The width of the Clopper–Pearson interval falls like \(1/\sqrt m\) (Figure 45.5). A 5-point gap between groups can be seen only with a few hundred minority test records, and a 1-point gap only with thousands (Exercise 4). Report the interval, not only the point estimate, for every group.
Report the spread over runs. In Table 45.2 the run-to-run standard deviation at \(\varepsilon = 4\) is 0.0211 for the minority against 0.0037 for the majority, almost six times as large. A comparison of two training recipes on one run each can easily be reversed for the small group. This is the same lesson as for the overall accuracy of private models (DP-SGD), sharper for small groups.
The evaluation leaks too. Per-group accuracies computed on private test data are statistics of that data. If they are published, they need their own privacy analysis, which Choosing ε and the selection mechanisms of Hyperparameter tuning address.






Figure 45.5: Width of the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval for a group’s accuracy against the number of test records in the group, for observed accuracies 0.95 and 0.7, on log scales. The width falls like one over the square root of the number of records.





45.6.5 Example: one model, three test sets
Train the running example at \(\varepsilon = 4\) once. On all 20,000 minority test records its accuracy is 0.8641. Table 45.6 measures it on random subsets.
