With 100 minority records, the split a 2,000-record test set with a 5% minority would give, the estimate is 0.880, 1.6 points above the true 0.8641, and the interval is 13.6 points wide. The true accuracy is inside it, as it should be 95% of the time, and the non-private model’s 0.9411 from Table 45.2 lies only just above its upper end, 0.936: on this test set alone the minority’s privacy cost could be anywhere from about half a point to fourteen points. With 500 records the interval is 6.5 points wide and still contains the true value. The majority’s interval, from 1,900 records at a higher accuracy, is 2 points wide. By Equation 45.9 the gap between the groups, measured on the 1,900 and the 100 records, is \(0.954 - 0.880 = 0.074\) with a standard error of \(\sqrt{0.954 \times 0.046/1{,}900 + 0.88 \times 0.12/100} = 0.0329\), so its 95% interval is \(0.074 \pm 1.96 \times 0.0329 = 0.074 \pm 0.064\), from 0.010 to 0.138: the gap is real, but it could be anywhere from one point to fourteen. And this is one training run: by Table 45.2 the minority’s accuracy at \(\varepsilon = 4\) varies by 0.0211 from run to run on top of this.


45.6.6 Check yourself

A report gives a private model’s accuracy as 0.84 on a subgroup of 60 test records and 0.85 non-private on the same records. What can you conclude? (Almost nothing about this subgroup. Each accuracy’s 95% interval is about \(2 \times 1.96\sqrt{0.84 \times 0.16/60} = 0.19\) wide, nineteen times the one-point difference. Because both models were tested on the same records, the difference could be measured more precisely from the records on which they disagree, but the report does not say how many there are.)
Why doesn’t a larger test set fix the run-to-run variation? (It removes the test-set error for the model at hand, but a different training run produces a different model. Only repeated training estimates how much a group’s accuracy varies with the training noise.)

title: 45  Disparate impact
text:
45.7 Mitigations and what they cost

45.7.1 Context
Both mechanisms come from DP-SGD’s two knobs. Can you choose the knobs, or change the algorithm, so that small groups pay less, without spending more privacy? Each fix in this section moves cost around rather than removing it, and it is worth knowing where to.


45.7.2 Statement
Global scaling is a large clipping norm. Scaling every per-example gradient by \(C/C_{\max}\), where \(C_{\max}\) is a bound that no gradient’s norm exceeds, and adding noise \(\sigma C\), is the same algorithm as DP-SGD with the clipping norm set to \(C_{\max}\), the same noise multiplier and learning rate \(\eta C/C_{\max}\): \[\frac\eta B\Big(\frac C{C_{\max}}\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i + \sigma C\xi\Big) = \frac{\eta C/C_{\max}}B\Big(\sum_{i\in S_t}g_i + \sigma C_{\max}\xi\Big). \tag{45.10}\]
Oversampling a group costs that group’s privacy. If group \(g\)’s records are sampled at rate \(vq\) instead of \(q\), its pull on the update grows by the factor \(v\), and each of its records has the privacy of the subsampled Gaussian at rate \(vq\): \[\varepsilon_g = \varepsilon_{\text{acct}}(vq, \sigma, T, \delta) \;>\; \varepsilon_{\text{acct}}(q, \sigma, T, \delta), \tag{45.11}\] where \(\varepsilon_{\text{acct}}\) is the accountant of DP-SGD. The algorithm’s guarantee is the largest over records, so a fixed target \(\varepsilon\) requires the noise multiplier for rate \(vq\).


45.7.3 Derivation

Global scaling. Factor \(C/C_{\max}\) out of the left-hand side: \(\frac C{C_{\max}}\sum_ig_i + \sigma C\xi = \frac C{C_{\max}}(\sum_ig_i + \sigma C_{\max}\xi)\). With the clipping norm set to \(C_{\max}\) and no gradient longer than \(C_{\max}\), DP-SGD’s clipped sum is \(\sum_ig_i\) and its noise \(\sigma C_{\max}\xi\), which is the right-hand side. Both have sensitivity-to-noise ratio \(1/\sigma\), so the same accountant applies (Exercise 6).
Oversampling: the pull. The expected clipped sum is \(\sum_iq_i\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)g_i\), with \(q_i\) record \(i\)’s sampling rate. With \(q_i = vq\) for group \(g\) and division by the public \(B = qn\), group \(g\)’s term becomes \(vs_gm_g\).
Oversampling: the privacy. The add/remove analysis of record \(x\) in DP-SGD compares the output with and without \(x\); the mixture depends only on \(x\)’s own inclusion probability, because the other records’ terms are the same in both. A record sampled at rate \(vq\) therefore has the privacy of the subsampled Gaussian at rate \(vq\). The sampling rate may depend on the record’s own group, which is part of the record, but the rule must be fixed in advance, not chosen by looking at the data.
The guarantee. \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP must hold for every record, so it is the largest of the per-record values, which is Equation 45.11’s.



45.7.4 Interpretation
Global scaling trades direction for noise. By Equation 45.10, scaling all gradients by the same factor is the large-\(C\) end of the clipping-norm curve of DP-SGD with \(\eta C\) fixed: nothing is clipped, so the update points in the true direction (the blue arrow of Figure 45.2), but the noise \(\sigma C_{\max}\) is as large as possible relative to the gradients. Esipova et al. (2023) propose a version that clips the rare gradients above \(C_{\max}\) instead of discarding them and adapts \(C_{\max}\) during training from a privately estimated count of how many gradients exceed it; they report that it reduces the privacy cost gap and improves accuracy compared with DP-SGD and with earlier mitigations on MNIST, CelebA and two tabular datasets. Because it treats every record alike, it needs no group labels.
Group-aware methods need group labels. Xu, Du & Wu (2021) adjust each group’s contribution according to how much that group is being clipped, giving groups that are clipped more a larger clipping norm, so that the groups’ clipping biases are equalized. Tran, Dinh & Fioretto (2021) add to the training objective penalties on the differences between groups in the quantities their decomposition identifies. Both need each training record’s group, which is itself sensitive and may not be available or lawful to collect, and the per-group statistics they use must be computed privately.
Oversampling buys little at a fixed budget. Fixed at \(\varepsilon = 4\) for every record, sampling the minority four times as often requires \(\sigma = 4.71\) instead of 1.36: the minority’s pull grows by 4 and the noise by \(4.71/1.36 = 3.46\). Its signal-to-noise ratio improves by only \(4/3.46 = 1.16\), while the majority’s falls by 3.46, and the majority’s records are then far more private than the target, \(\varepsilon = 0.86\), which is wasted budget (Exercise 5). Oversampling without changing \(\sigma\) would silently give the minority \(\varepsilon = 20.96\): the group that is already disadvantaged in accuracy would also get the weakest privacy.
Some of the cost is unavoidable. Learning a group’s own rule privately is, in part, a private estimation problem on that group’s \(n_g\) records, and private estimation has a price that no algorithm avoids. Lower bounds proves it for the simplest case: releasing \(d\) attribute means with constant accuracy under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP needs at least about \(\sqrt d/(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) records, by the fingerprinting argument, whatever the mechanism. Put differently, the error that \(n_g\) records allow shrinks only like \(1/(n_g\varepsilon)\), and the Gaussian mechanism, with error about \(\sqrt{d\ln(1/\delta)}/(n_g\varepsilon)\), is close to the best possible. A smaller group is a smaller dataset, and no clever clipping makes it larger. Feldman (2020) argues the deeper point for any learner: when the data have a long tail of small subpopulations, fitting them well requires memorizing their few examples, which is exactly what DP forbids. What helps is more data from the group, a larger \(\varepsilon\) (with its own costs), or a starting point that already serves the group, such as a public pretrained model (Public data and private fine-tuning).


45.7.5 Example: the clipping norm and oversampling on the running example

None of the three changes helps the minority. A ten times smaller clipping norm clips the minority more, and its accuracy falls by 1.64 points while the majority’s rises by 0.71: the clipping mechanism of Section 45.4 at work. A ten times larger one clips almost nothing, so the update’s direction is right, but with \(\eta C\) fixed the noise in each step, \(\eta\sigma C/B\), is unchanged while the step along every gradient shorter than 0.5 is ten times smaller: the noise is ten times larger relative to that part of the signal, and the minority falls by 3.44 points: the noise mechanism of Section 45.5 at work. The running example’s \(C = 0.5\) sits between the two failures. These differences are of the size of the run-to-run spread, 0.0157 to 0.0211, so only their direction is clear, not their size.
Oversampling narrows the gap from 9.93 to 3.99 points, but by levelling down: the minority’s accuracy is 2.07 points lower than without it, and the majority’s 8.01 points lower. A smaller gap is not by itself a fairer model. Report both groups’ accuracy and privacy cost, never the gap alone.


45.7.6 Check yourself

Why does oversampling a group require more noise, while upweighting its loss does not? (Upweighting leaves every record’s contribution bounded by \(C\) and its sampling rate at \(q\), so the accountant is unchanged, but clipping undoes it. Oversampling raises the group’s sampling rate, which the subsampled Gaussian’s privacy depends on.)
A team proposes to fix disparate impact by setting \(C\) to the largest per-example gradient norm observed in the training data. What is wrong? (The clipping norm then depends on the data, and the sensitivity argument of DP-SGD assumes it is fixed in advance. A data-dependent \(C\) must itself be chosen privately, as in Esipova et al.’s adaptive threshold, and the estimate charged to the budget.)

Its two causes can be separated by switching the noise off, and each follows the arithmetic of this chapter: clipping lowers the group’s effective share while the majority is learned, and the noise penalizes a small share roughly in proportion to one over the share. Neither knob of DP-SGD removes the effect at a fixed budget; it only moves it between the groups and between the two mechanisms.

text:
45.9 References

Bagdasaryan, Poursaeed & Shmatikov, “Differential Privacy Has Disparate Impact on Model Accuracy” (NeurIPS 2019). The observation this chapter explains: DP-SGD’s accuracy loss falls on under-represented and complex groups, and existing gaps grow.
Tran, Dinh & Fioretto, “Differentially Private Empirical Risk Minimization under the Fairness Lens” (NeurIPS 2021). Per-step decompositions of a group’s excess risk into clipping and noise terms, for output perturbation and DP-SGD, and the role of gradient norms, input norms, the loss Hessian and the distance to the decision boundary.
Esipova, Ghomi, Luo & Cresswell, “Disparate Impact in Differential Privacy from Gradient Misalignment” (ICLR 2023). Separates clipping’s direction error from its length error, finds the direction error the main cause, and proposes global scaling with an adaptive threshold.
Xu, Du & Wu, “Removing Disparate Impact on Model Accuracy in Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent” (KDD 2021). Group-dependent clipping that equalizes the groups’ clipping bias.
Feldman, “Does Learning Require Memorization? A Short Tale about a Long Tail” (STOC 2020). Why fitting small subpopulations well requires memorizing their examples, and so conflicts with privacy.
Clopper & Pearson, “The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial” (Biometrika, 1934). The exact interval of Section 45.6.

Rules of thumb

Always report accuracy per group, with Clopper–Pearson intervals and the spread over several training runs, next to the non-private model’s.
Expect the privacy cost of a group to grow like one over its share of the data, and faster for groups with long gradients: large inputs or a rule the rest of the data does not teach.
Clipping alone is disparate. A larger clipping norm (with \(\eta C\) fixed) reduces the clipping part and raises the noise part.
Do not upweight a group’s loss to help it: clipping undoes it. Do not oversample a group without accounting at its higher sampling rate.
When a group is too small to learn privately, get more data from it or start from a public model that already serves it.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.1 Why this matters
Every model trained with differential privacy (DP) ships with a number, its budget \(\varepsilon\). DP is the guarantee that one record changes the probability of any output by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), up to a slack \(\delta\). Chapter 39 trained the part’s running example, a small neural network on 10,000 records, with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) made private by per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, DP-SGD, at five budgets, and measured what each costs in accuracy: test accuracy 0.9175 at \(\varepsilon = 1\), 0.9441 at \(\varepsilon = 2\), 0.9548 at \(\varepsilon = 4\) and 0.9604 at \(\varepsilon = 8\), against 0.9610 without privacy, all at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). That is half of a decision. The other half is what each budget means for the people in the data: what an attacker who sees the model can learn about one of them, and how sure it can be. Without that half, the choice of \(\varepsilon\) is made by habit (“everyone uses 8”) or by the accuracy curve alone, and neither survives a reviewer, a regulator or a data subject who asks what the number promises.
This chapter supplies the privacy half. It reads the guarantee in three operational ways: as a bound on any membership test, as a bound on how far an attacker’s belief can move, and as a bound on reconstructing a record. For each it compares two numbers: what the single pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) promises, and what the actual training algorithm, DP-SGD, really allows. It then turns to \(\delta\), to the budgets that real deployments have published and the units they are stated in, and to a procedure for choosing and defending a number.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.1.1 The one idea: ε is one line under a curve
An attacker who wants to know whether a record was in the training set runs a test, and every test has two error rates. The definition of DP is equivalent to a straight-line bound on those rates: at false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\), the true positive rate is at most \(e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta\). But a training algorithm has a whole trade-off curve, the best true positive rate at every false positive rate, and \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is only one line that lies above it, touching it at one point. Far from that point, the line can be useless: at \(\varepsilon = 8\) it allows a test that catches every member while almost never accusing a non-member, while the curve of DP-SGD at the same \(\varepsilon\) caps the true positive rate at 0.0589 when the false positive rate is \(10^{-3}\). Choosing \(\varepsilon\) well means computing and reporting the curve, not just the line, and reading it at the error rates that matter for your threat.
Table 46.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 46.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.





Result
Where it is used

Notation. A membership test sees the trained model (or the whole sequence of iterates) and says “member” or “non-member” about a target record \(z^*\). Its false positive rate (FPR) is the probability that it says “member” when \(z^*\) was not in the training set, and its true positive rate (TPR) is the probability that it says “member” when \(z^*\) was. \(Q\) is the distribution of the output when \(z^*\) is in the data, \(P\) the distribution when it is not, and \(L = \ln(Q(y)/P(y))\) is the privacy loss of an output \(y\). \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is the smallest \(\delta\) for which a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP at a given \(\varepsilon\), its privacy profile. For DP-SGD, \(q\) is the sampling rate, \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier and \(T\) the number of steps. The running example has \(q = 0.01\), \(T = 10{,}000\) and \(n = 10{,}000\) records, and its noise multiplier is the one the Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant of DP-SGD requires for each target \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\).
How to read this chapter. The toolkit and Section 46.3 restate what the definition of differential privacy proves, in the form this chapter needs. Section 46.4 is the core: the curve of DP-SGD against the line. Section 46.5 and Section 46.6 read the same curve as beliefs and as reconstruction. Section 46.7, Section 46.8 and Section 46.9 are about practice and can be read on their own.

title: 46  Choosing ε
section: 46.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
46.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

46.2.1 Fact 1 — A membership attacker is a test, and DP bounds the probability of every event
Fix the training set without the target, \(D^-\), and the target record \(z^*\). The attacker sees an output \(y\), drawn from \(Q = M(D^- \cup \{z^*\})\) if \(z^*\) is a member and from \(P = M(D^-)\) if not, and says “member” on some set \(S\) of outputs. Then \(\mathrm{FPR} = P(S)\) and \(\mathrm{TPR} = Q(S)\): both error rates are probabilities of one event. A mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when, for every pair of neighbouring datasets and every event \(S\), in both orders, \[Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta. \tag{46.1}\] So DP is a statement about tests before it is a statement about anything else. This chapter uses add/remove neighbours, as DP-SGD with Poisson sampling does (DP-SGD). An attacker that randomizes, saying “member” with probability \(\phi(y)\), has \(\mathrm{TPR} = \mathbb E_Q[\phi]\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = \mathbb E_P[\phi]\), and the same bound holds for it, because a randomized test is an average of events (The definition of differential privacy).


46.2.2 Fact 2 — The best test thresholds the privacy loss
Among all tests with a given FPR, the one with the largest TPR says “member” when the likelihood ratio \(Q(y)/P(y)\) is large, that is, when the privacy loss \(L(y)\) exceeds a threshold \(\tau\), randomizing at the threshold if needed. This is the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Hypothesis testing). The reason is an exchange argument: if a test said “member” on an output with a low ratio and “non-member” on one with a higher ratio, swapping the two (in equal amounts of \(P\)-probability) would keep its FPR and raise its TPR.
Two consequences follow. First, the best TPR at FPR \(\mathrm{FPR}\) depends only on the distribution of \(L\). Write \(\omega\) for the distribution of \(L\) when \(y \sim Q\), the privacy loss distribution (PLD). Then the best test with threshold \(\tau\) has \[\mathrm{TPR}(\tau) = Q[L > \tau], \qquad \mathrm{FPR}(\tau) = P[L > \tau] = \mathbb E_Q\big[e^{-L};\ L > \tau\big], \tag{46.2}\] where the second form is a change of measure: \(P(y) = e^{-L(y)}Q(y)\) by the definition of \(L\), so the \(P\)-probability of any event is the \(Q\)-average of \(e^{-L}\) over it. Second, the best achievable pairs \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{TPR})\) form a region whose upper boundary, the trade-off curve written here as \(\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR})\), is increasing and concave: increasing because a test with a higher FPR can always say “member” more often, concave because randomizing between two tests reaches every point of the segment between them.


46.2.3 Fact 3 — Beliefs multiply by the likelihood ratio
An attacker who believes beforehand that \(z^*\) is a member with probability \(p\), the prior, and then sees \(y\), believes afterwards \[\frac{\Pr[\text{member} \mid y]}{\Pr[\text{non-member} \mid y]} = \frac{p}{1 - p}\cdot\frac{Q(y)}{P(y)} = \frac{p}{1 - p}e^{L(y)}. \tag{46.3}\] This is Bayes’ rule in odds form: the posterior odds are the prior odds times the likelihood ratio, and the likelihood ratio is \(e^L\). Converting odds \(o\) back to a probability, \(o/(1 + o)\), gives the posterior \(p e^L/(p e^L + 1 - p)\).


46.2.4 Fact 4 — DP-SGD’s worst case is one pair of distributions, composed
Each step of DP-SGD adds Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\) to a sum of per-example gradients clipped to length \(C\), over a batch that contains each record independently with probability \(q\). DP-SGD showed that, for the target record, the worst case over models, data and directions is a one-dimensional pair in units of \(C\): without the record the step’s output is \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), with it the output is the mixture \((1 - q)\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The privacy loss of one step is \(L_1(y) = \ln\big((1 - q) + q\,e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}\big)\), and \(T\) steps release \(T\) outputs whose losses add, so the PLD of the whole run is the distribution of a sum of \(T\) such losses. Three accountants summarize it (Choosing an accountant):

the RDP accountant bounds the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) by \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) and converts it to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\); it is a valid upper bound, and it is what DP-SGD used to set \(\sigma\);
the numerical PLD accountant discretizes the one-step loss on a grid of spacing \(h\), rounding each loss up (pessimistic) or down (optimistic), and composes by fast Fourier transform (FFT) convolution; the truth lies between the two answers, which differ by at most a shift of \(Th\) in the total loss (Numerical accounting);
the Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) central limit theorem (CLT) approximates the run by a single Gaussian pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) with \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\); it is an approximation, not a bound (f-DP and Gaussian DP).

title: 46  Choosing ε
section: 46.3 What one (ε, δ) pair says about a membership test
text:
46.3 What one (ε, δ) pair says about a membership test

46.3.1 Context
A model card says “trained with \((\varepsilon, \delta) = (8, 10^{-5})\)”. Taken alone, what does that number forbid an attacker to do? This is the question to answer first, because it is the only one you can answer for a model whose algorithm you have not seen.


46.3.2 Statement
If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, every membership test, against every target, satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min\big\{1,\ e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta,\ 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\big\}, \tag{46.4}\] and its advantage, \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\), the amount by which it beats guessing, satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR} \le \frac{e^\varepsilon - 1 + 2\delta}{e^\varepsilon + 1}. \tag{46.5}\]


46.3.3 Derivation

The first line. Apply the definition (Fact 1) with \(D^- \cup \{z\}\) first and the event \(S\) on which the test says “member”: \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\), that is \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\).
The second line. Apply it in the other order to the complement \(S^c\), where the test says “non-member”: \(P(S^c) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S^c) + \delta\), that is \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta\). Solving for TPR gives \(\mathrm{TPR} \le 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\). A probability is at most 1, which is the third term of Equation 46.4.
The advantage. \(\mathrm{TPR} - \mathrm{FPR}\) is largest where the two lines of steps 1 and 2 cross, because below the crossing the first line rises faster than the diagonal (slope \(e^\varepsilon \ge 1\)) and above it the second line rises more slowly (slope \(e^{-\varepsilon} \le 1\)). Setting \(e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta = 1 - e^{-\varepsilon}(1 - \delta - \mathrm{FPR})\) and multiplying by \(e^\varepsilon\) gives \(\mathrm{FPR}(e^{2\varepsilon} - 1) = e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta - \delta e^\varepsilon\), so \(\mathrm{FPR} = (1 - \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\). There the TPR is \(e^\varepsilon(1 - \delta)/(e^\varepsilon + 1) + \delta\), and subtracting \(\mathrm{FPR}\) gives Equation 46.5.



46.3.4 Interpretation
The bound has three regimes. At small FPR the line \(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) binds, and the ratio TPR/FPR is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) plus \(\delta/\mathrm{FPR}\). Below \(\mathrm{FPR} \approx \delta e^{-\varepsilon}\) the \(\delta\) term dominates, and the guarantee rests on \(\delta\) alone. At large FPR the second line binds. And once \(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta \ge 1\), which at \(\varepsilon = 8\) happens from \(\mathrm{FPR} = (1 - 10^{-5})e^{-8} = 3.35\times10^{-4}\) on, the bound allows a perfect true positive rate: the pair says nothing at all at the false positive rates where attacks are usually evaluated.
Low FPR is where it matters. Membership inference evaluates attacks by their TPR at an FPR of \(10^{-3}\) or below, because an attack that flags members while almost never flagging non-members is one that confidently identifies people. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the pair caps that TPR at \(e \times 10^{-3} + 10^{-5} = 0.002728\), a real constraint. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the cap is 0.05461, at \(\varepsilon = 8\) it is 0.9997.
The advantage is an average, and DP’s guarantee is not about averages. Equation 46.5 bounds the advantage at a single point of the curve, the one with equal error rates. It is 0.4621 at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 0.9640 at \(\varepsilon = 4\), numbers that make \(\varepsilon = 4\) sound hopeless. They are tight only for the worst mechanism with this \(\varepsilon\), randomized response, whose curve is exactly the two lines. DP-SGD is not that mechanism, as the next section shows.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.4 The whole curve of DP-SGD

46.4.1 Context
The pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is one number out of a whole profile: the accountant could equally have reported \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-6}\) or \(10^{-3}\), and each of those pairs is another line that every test must satisfy. The best TPR an attacker can reach against DP-SGD is the curve that all those lines enclose, and for DP-SGD it can be computed. How far below the single line does it lie, and how well do cheaper accountants approximate it?


46.4.2 Statement
For a mechanism with PLD \(\omega\) (the law of \(L\) under \(Q\)), the best TPR at FPR \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is reached by thresholding the total loss (Fact 2), and equals the lower envelope of all the lines of its profile: \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = \inf_{\varepsilon \in \mathbb R}\big(e^\varepsilon \mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\big), \qquad \delta(\varepsilon) = Q[L > \varepsilon] - e^\varepsilon P[L > \varepsilon]. \tag{46.6}\] For DP-SGD the curve is traced exactly by \[\big(\mathrm{FPR}(\tau), \mathrm{TPR}(\tau)\big) = \big(\mathbb E_\omega[e^{-L};\ L > \tau],\ \omega(L > \tau)\big), \qquad \tau \in \mathbb R, \tag{46.7}\] where \(\omega\) is the \(T\)-fold convolution of the one-step PLD of Fact 4. Two cheaper curves bracket or approximate it. From the RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) of the whole run, every test satisfies \[\mathrm{TPR} \le \min_{\alpha > 1}\big(\mathrm{FPR}\cdot e^{\varepsilon(\alpha)}\big)^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}, \tag{46.8}\] a valid bound. The GDP central limit theorem approximates the curve by that of \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), \[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \approx 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu\big), \qquad \mu = q\sqrt{T\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}, \tag{46.9}\] with \(\Phi\) the standard normal distribution function; this is not a bound.


46.4.3 Derivation

Every line is valid. For each \(\varepsilon\), the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP in this direction by the definition of the profile, so by Equation 46.4 every test has \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta(\varepsilon)\). Taking the smallest right-hand side over \(\varepsilon\) gives “\(\le\)” in Equation 46.6.
The profile in terms of the loss. For the event \(\{L > \varepsilon\}\), \(Q(L > \varepsilon) - e^\varepsilon P(L > \varepsilon) = \mathbb E_Q[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L});\ L > \varepsilon]\) by the change of measure of Fact 2, and no other event does better, because adding an output with \(L \le \varepsilon\) adds \(Q(y) - e^\varepsilon P(y) = Q(y)(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}) \le 0\) and removing one with \(L > \varepsilon\) removes a positive amount. This is the formula for \(\delta(\varepsilon)\).
Each line touches the curve. Take the Neyman–Pearson test with threshold \(\tau\) and the line with \(\varepsilon = \tau\). By step 2, \(\delta(\tau) = \mathrm{TPR}(\tau) - e^\tau\mathrm{FPR}(\tau)\), so \(\mathrm{TPR}(\tau) = e^\tau\mathrm{FPR}(\tau) + \delta(\tau)\): the test lies on the line. Since the tests with thresholds \(\tau\) (and randomization between them) are the best ones by Fact 2, the infimum is attained and Equation 46.6 holds with equality.
Composition adds losses. The \(T\) steps of DP-SGD use independent noise, so the likelihood ratio of all \(T\) outputs is the product of the per-step ratios, and the total loss is the sum of the per-step losses. Even though each step’s input depends on the earlier outputs, the worst-case pair of Fact 4 is the same at every step, so the per-step losses are independent and identically distributed under \(Q\), and \(\omega\) is the \(T\)-fold convolution of one step’s PLD (Numerical accounting). Fact 2 then gives Equation 46.7.
Computing it with a guarantee. Round each one-step loss up to the grid \(h\mathbb Z\) and compose: the total loss is rounded up by at most \(Th\), and the resulting pair is less private than the true one, so its curve lies above the true curve. Rounding down gives a curve below it. The script uses \(h = 2\times10^{-6}\) for the three smallest budgets and \(h = 10^{-5}\) for the others, so that the total loss is pinned within 0.02 and 0.1.
The RDP bound. The Rényi divergence can only shrink when both distributions are passed through the same test (data processing, Rényi DP). After the test, the two distributions are coins with “member” probabilities TPR and FPR, so \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)} \ge \mathrm{TPR}^\alpha\mathrm{FPR}^{1 - \alpha} + (1 - \mathrm{TPR})^\alpha(1 - \mathrm{FPR})^{1 - \alpha}\). Dropping the second, non-negative term and solving for TPR gives \(\mathrm{TPR}^\alpha \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}\mathrm{FPR}^{\alpha - 1}\), which is Equation 46.8 after taking the power \(1/\alpha\); it holds at every order, so at the best one.
The GDP approximation. For \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) the best test thresholds the output at \(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR})\), and the shifted distribution exceeds that threshold with probability \(1 - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu)\). The value of \(\mu\) is the central-limit approximation of f-DP and Gaussian DP, which matches the mean and variance of the summed loss to leading order in \(q\).



46.4.4 Interpretation
The pair overstates the attacker, and more so the larger \(\varepsilon\). Table 46.5 puts the four curves side by side at FPR \(10^{-3}\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the pair allows 0.002728 and the true curve is between 0.002209 and 0.00225, a factor of about 1.2. At \(\varepsilon = 4\) the pair allows 0.05461 and the curve at most 0.01312, a factor of about 4. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the pair allows 0.9997 and the curve at most 0.0589, a factor of about 17. The reason is visible in Figure 46.1: the curve of DP-SGD is smooth and close to a Gaussian curve, and the line that the accountant reports at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) touches it only at a false positive rate of at most \(e^{-\varepsilon}Q[L > \varepsilon]\), below \(10^{-4}\) for every run here (Table 46.8). Everywhere else the line is a loose summary.
The RDP bound is the cheap middle ground. Equation 46.8 uses the same accountant that produced \(\varepsilon\), costs nothing extra, and is a guarantee. At \(\varepsilon = 8\) it caps the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) at 0.09016 instead of 0.9997. It is still looser than the exact curve, because one Rényi order summarizes the loss distribution by one moment, and because the conversion drops a term; the PLD keeps everything.
GDP is close, but not on the safe side. For budgets up to 8 the GDP curve lies inside the exact bracket at FPR \(10^{-3}\), and within 0.001 of it at the other operating points: 0.05719 at \(\varepsilon = 8\) and FPR \(10^{-3}\), against the bracket [0.05555, 0.0589]. At \(\varepsilon = 16\) it overshoots, 0.3234 against at most 0.2808, because \(\mu = 2.632\) is far from the small-\(q\sqrt T\) regime where the central limit theorem holds. Use it to explain, not to certify.
The curve is the worst case of a strong attacker. It is the best test of an attacker who knows every other record, the architecture, the initialization and every hyperparameter, sees every intermediate iterate, and targets a record whose clipped gradient is as large as clipping allows at every step on which it is sampled. Nasr et al. (2021) showed that an adversary who can choose the target’s gradient and see every iterate does reach the accountant’s guarantee, so the curve is attainable in that threat model. A typical record attacked through the final model alone is much safer. Table 46.4 measures it for one attack: the loss-threshold attack of Membership inference, which calls a training record a member when its loss is below a threshold, run on one model trained at each budget, with the 10,000 training records as members and the 20,000 test records as non-members.

(By step 3 it touches the curve at the Neyman–Pearson test with threshold \(\tau = \varepsilon\), whose FPR is \(P[L > \varepsilon] \le e^{-\varepsilon}Q[L > \varepsilon]\), because \(P = e^{-L}Q\) and \(L > \varepsilon\) on that event. The accountant chose \(\varepsilon\) so that the loss rarely exceeds it, so that FPR is tiny.)
A colleague proposes to report only the GDP \(\mu\) of a run with \(\mu = 2.6\). What do you tell them? (That the GDP curve is an approximation that can be too optimistic, as at \(\varepsilon = 16\) here, or too pessimistic. Report the PLD curve or the RDP bound as the guarantee, and \(\mu\) as an explanation.)

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.5 The Bayesian reading

46.5.1 Context
People who are not statisticians rarely think in error rates. They ask “if someone sees the model, how sure can they be that I was in the data?” That is a question about posterior probabilities. What do \(\varepsilon\), and the actual curve of DP-SGD, say about it, and why does the answer depend so much on the prior?


46.5.2 Statement
If every output has privacy loss at most \(\varepsilon\), then for every prior \(p\) the posterior probability of membership is at most \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid y] \le \frac{p\,e^\varepsilon}{p\,e^\varepsilon + 1 - p}. \tag{46.10}\] Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP this holds at a level \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\) except on outputs whose total probability is at most \(\delta/(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'})\). For DP-SGD the posterior after the run is exactly \(p\,e^L/(p\,e^L + 1 - p)\), with \(L\) drawn from the PLD \(\omega\). An attacker who acts only on a flag (“the test said member”) is right with probability \[\Pr[\text{member} \mid \text{flag}] = \frac{p\,\mathrm{TPR}}{p\,\mathrm{TPR} + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}} \le \frac{p\,(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta)}{p\,(e^\varepsilon\mathrm{FPR} + \delta) + (1 - p)\,\mathrm{FPR}}. \tag{46.11}\]


46.5.3 Derivation

The posterior is a function of the loss. By Fact 3, the posterior odds are \(\frac{p}{1 - p}e^{L(y)}\), and the posterior is \(pe^L/(pe^L + 1 - p)\). This is increasing in \(L\).
Pure bound. If \(L \le \varepsilon\), substitute \(\varepsilon\) for \(L\): Equation 46.10.
Rare outputs. Let \(S\) be the outputs with \(L > \varepsilon'\). On \(S\), \(P(y) < e^{-\varepsilon'}Q(y)\), so \(P(S) < e^{-\varepsilon'}Q(S)\). The definition gives \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta < e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}Q(S) + \delta\), so \(Q(S)(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}) < \delta\) (The definition of differential privacy).
The precision of a flag. Bayes’ rule with the event “flag” in place of \(y\): the flag has probability TPR for a member and FPR for a non-member, so the posterior odds are \(\frac{p}{1 - p}\cdot\frac{\mathrm{TPR}}{\mathrm{FPR}}\). Bounding TPR by Equation 46.4, which can only increase the odds, gives Equation 46.11. With \(\delta = 0\) the bound equals Equation 46.10: a flag can never be more convincing than the most convincing single output.



46.5.4 Interpretation

At \(\varepsilon = 4\) it can reach 35.55%, at \(\varepsilon = 8\) 96.79%: read through the pure bound, \(\varepsilon = 8\) permits near certainty.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.6 Reconstruction

46.6.1 Context
Membership is a demanding standard: the attacker is given the target record and only has to decide whether it was used. Many harms need more: recovering a record the attacker does not know, such as a patient’s diagnosis or a person’s face. Balle, Cherubin & Hayes (2022) formalize this as reconstruction robustness: an informed adversary knows every training record except the target \(Z\), knows a prior \(\pi\) from which \(Z\) was drawn, sees the trained model, and outputs a guess; it succeeds if the guess is within a distance \(\xi\) of \(Z\), its error radius. The baseline is the best success without seeing the model, \[\kappa = \sup_{z_0}\Pr_{Z \sim \pi}\big[\mathrm{err}(Z, z_0) \le \xi\big], \tag{46.12}\] for example \(\kappa = 1/m\) when \(Z\) is uniform over \(m\) candidates and only an exact guess counts. How much can the model raise the success above \(\kappa\)?


46.6.2 Statement
If every neighbouring pair of \(M\) has trade-off curve at or below \(\mathrm{TPR}^*\), then every reconstruction attack succeeds with probability at most \[\Pr[\text{success}] \le \mathrm{TPR}^*(\kappa). \tag{46.13}\] With the pair \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) this is \(e^\varepsilon\kappa + \delta\); with pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP, \(e^\varepsilon\kappa\), and with one RDP order, \((\kappa e^{\varepsilon(\alpha)})^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}\), which are Balle, Cherubin & Hayes’s bounds; with the exact curve of DP-SGD it is the bound of Hayes, Mahloujifar & Balle (2023), who write it as a “blow-up function”, the largest probability under \(Q\) of an event whose probability under \(P\) is at most \(\kappa\), which is the trade-off curve under another name.


46.6.3 Derivation

A reconstruction attack defines one test per candidate. Fix \(D^-\) and the attack \(\mathcal A\). For a candidate \(z\), let \(S_z\) be the set of models \(\theta\) for which \(\mathcal A(\theta)\) is within \(\xi\) of \(z\). The attack succeeds on \(z\) exactly when the model trained on \(D^- \cup \{z\}\) falls in \(S_z\).
Each test is bounded by the curve. “Say member when \(\theta \in S_z\)” is a membership test for \(z\) against the pair \(Q_z = M(D^- \cup \{z\})\), \(P = M(D^-)\). Its FPR is \(\mathrm{FPR}_z = P(S_z)\), so its TPR satisfies \(Q_z(S_z) \le \mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}_z)\).
Average over the prior. The success probability is \(\mathbb E_{Z\sim\pi}[Q_Z(S_Z)] \le \mathbb E_Z[\mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathrm{FPR}_Z)] \le \mathrm{TPR}^*(\mathbb E_Z[\mathrm{FPR}_Z])\), by Jensen’s inequality, since the curve is concave (Fact 2).
The average FPR is at most the baseline. \(\mathbb E_Z[\mathrm{FPR}_Z] = \Pr_{Z\sim\pi,\,\theta\sim M(D^-)}[\mathrm{err}(Z, \mathcal A(\theta)) \le \xi]\). Here \(\theta\) is trained without \(Z\), so it is independent of \(Z\), and for each fixed \(\theta\) the guess \(\mathcal A(\theta)\) is a fixed \(z_0\), which succeeds with probability at most \(\kappa\). So \(\mathbb E_Z[\mathrm{FPR}_Z] \le \kappa\), and since the curve is increasing, Equation 46.13 follows.
The special cases. Substitute the line of Equation 46.4, or the RDP bound Equation 46.8 at one order, for \(\mathrm{TPR}^*\).

The \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) form \(e^\varepsilon\kappa + \delta\) is this chapter’s corollary; Balle, Cherubin & Hayes state the pure-DP, RDP and zero-concentrated cases.


46.6.4 Interpretation
Reconstruction is membership at FPR κ. The derivation turns any reconstruction attack into a membership test whose false positive rate is the baseline. So the trade-off curve, read at FPR \(1/m\), answers “can the attacker pick the right one of \(m\) candidates?”. A large prior uncertainty is a small FPR, and that is where the curve of DP-SGD is far below the line.
Large budgets can still prevent reconstruction. Table 46.9 reads the curves of Figure 46.2 at \(\kappa = 1/m\). At \(\varepsilon = 8\) the pair gives no bound for any \(m\) up to 1,000, but the curve caps the success of choosing among 1,000 equally likely candidates at 0.0589, against 0.001 by guessing. Balle, Cherubin & Hayes observed the same in experiments: in their words, DP with large values of \(\varepsilon\) can protect against reconstruction attacks if the target is high-dimensional and the adversary’s prior contains a large degree of uncertainty. Hayes, Mahloujifar & Balle found their bound close to their best attack in all their settings, and that different DP-SGD hyperparameters with the same \(\varepsilon\) can give quite different reconstruction success: the curve, not \(\varepsilon\), is what matters.
Small priors are the honest assumption only if you can defend them. If the attacker can narrow the target to two candidates, \(\kappa = 0.5\) and reconstruction is as easy as membership at FPR 0.5. A defensible reconstruction claim states the prior: “an attacker who knows the target is one of \(m\) records”.
Guo, Karrer, Chaudhuri & van der Maaten (2022) bound reconstruction differently, for continuous targets: under RDP of order 2 at level \(\varepsilon\), any unbiased reconstruction of a target that ranges over an interval of width \(w\) has expected squared error at least \(w^2/(4(e^\varepsilon - 1))\), and Fisher information gives a tighter, data-dependent bound. The bound needs unbiasedness: for small \(\varepsilon\) a constant guess at the middle of the interval does better. Section N.4 in the appendices derives the bound and shows why it needs that condition.

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.7 Interpreting δ

46.7.1 Context
Every number so far was at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). What does \(\delta\) mean, how small must it be, and what does a smaller one cost in \(\varepsilon\) for DP-SGD?


46.7.2 Statement
The mechanism that publishes each record in full, independently with probability \(\delta\), is \((0, \delta)\)-DP and publishes at least one of \(n\) records with probability \[1 - (1 - \delta)^n \approx 1 - e^{-n\delta}. \tag{46.14}\] So \(\delta = 1/n\) permits exposing a record with probability about 0.63, and a meaningful guarantee needs \(n\delta \ll 1\). For a Gaussian-type mechanism such as DP-SGD, \(\delta\) is not a probability of catastrophe: the privacy loss has a light tail, \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le Q[L > \varepsilon]\), and shrinking \(\delta\) by orders of magnitude raises \(\varepsilon\) only moderately.


46.7.3 Derivation

The release mechanism is \((0, \delta)\)-DP. Run it on \(D^- \cup \{z^*\}\) by running it on \(D^-\) and tossing one more coin for \(z^*\). The two outputs differ only when that coin publishes \(z^*\), which has probability \(\delta\), so for every event \(S\) the two probabilities differ by at most \(\delta\) in either direction (The definition of differential privacy).
Exposure. Each record escapes with probability \(1 - \delta\), independently, so all escape with probability \((1 - \delta)^n = e^{n\ln(1 - \delta)} \approx e^{-n\delta}\), which gives Equation 46.14.
\(\delta\) is at most the tail of the loss. \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \mathbb E_Q[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+]\) (step 2 of Section 46.4), and the integrand is at most 1 and is 0 unless \(L > \varepsilon\).
Smaller \(\delta\) for DP-SGD. Run the RDP conversion of DP-SGD at several \(\delta\) for the same \(\sigma\); Table 46.10 and Figure 46.4 show the result.



46.7.4 Interpretation
Two kinds of \(\delta\). In the release mechanism, \(\delta\) is spent at infinite loss: the published record is identified with certainty. In DP-SGD it is spent at moderate losses, just above \(\varepsilon\), and the loss distribution has a Gaussian-like tail (Table 46.8). That is why NIST’s guidelines recommend, where possible, guarantees such as Rényi DP, zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) or GDP, which do not allow catastrophic failure, and why a full privacy profile, or the curve, is better than any one pair.
How small. Near, Darais, Lefkovitz & Howarth (NIST SP 800-226, 2025) write that a common recommendation is \(\delta \le 1/n^2\), that \(\delta \le 1/(n\ln n)\) is another sensible choice, and that values of \(\delta\) exceeding \(10^{-5}\) are suspicious and should be justified. The running example, with \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), has \(n\delta = 0.1\): acceptable for DP-SGD, whose \(\delta\) is not catastrophic, but not by the \(1/n^2 = 10^{-8}\) rule. Table 46.10 shows what the stricter rule costs: the \(\varepsilon = 4\) run is \((5.209, 10^{-8})\)-DP.
The unit decides n. If one person can contribute many records, \(n\) is the number of people and \(\delta\) must be small relative to that; and the per-record guarantee is not a per-person guarantee at all (User-level differential privacy).

46.7.5 Example: ten thousand records
For \(n = 10{,}000\), Equation 46.14 gives an exposure probability of 0.6321 at \(\delta = 10^{-4} = 1/n\), 0.09516 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and 0.00995 at \(10^{-6}\) for the release mechanism. For DP-SGD the same tenfold reductions of \(\delta\) cost little: from \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-6}\) the \(\varepsilon = 4\) run’s budget rises from 3.993 to 4.432, and down to \(10^{-10}\) it reaches 5.890. Every factor of 100 in \(\delta\) costs between about 0.2 and 0.9 in \(\varepsilon\) for these two runs. When in doubt, use a smaller \(\delta\); it is cheap.


46.7.6 Check yourself

A model is reported as \((1, 10^{-3})\)-DP on 50,000 records. What is wrong? (It allows \(n\delta = 50\): the release mechanism with this \(\delta\) would publish about 50 records. Unless the loss distribution is shown to be light-tailed, the guarantee permits catastrophic failure for some people.)
Why does the \(\varepsilon\) in Table 46.10 grow roughly like \(\sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\)? (For a nearly Gaussian loss with mean \(\bar L\) and variance \(v\), the tail beyond \(\varepsilon\) falls like \(e^{-(\varepsilon - \bar L)^2/(2v)}\), so reaching a tail of \(\delta\) needs \(\varepsilon - \bar L\) of order \(\sqrt{2v\ln(1/\delta)}\).)

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.8 Deployed values and their units

46.8.1 Context
“Industry uses \(\varepsilon\) between 1 and 10” is a common justification. What have real deployments published, and in which units? An \(\varepsilon\) means nothing without the privacy unit (what one neighbouring change is: one record, one user’s data for a day, one user’s data forever) and the period over which the budget is spent.


46.8.2 Statement
Table 46.11 lists deployments whose parameters are documented in a primary source. The privacy unit and period differ from row to row, and so do the accounting notions, so the \(\varepsilon\) values are not comparable without conversion. The zCDP guarantees convert to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) by the simple bound \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}, \tag{46.15}\] of Bun & Steinke (2016), and tighter numerical conversions give somewhat smaller values; pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP guarantees for independent reports compose by adding. The Gboard models were trained by follow the regularized leader (FTRL) with noise added to sums of gradients, DP-FTRL (DP-FTRL and matrix factorization), in federated learning, where the data stay on users’ devices.

46.8.3 Derivation: making the rows comparable

zCDP to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Equation 46.15 with \(\rho = 2.56\) and \(\delta = 10^{-10}\) gives \(2.56 + 2\sqrt{2.56 \times 23.026} = 17.915\), the persons’ figure of Kazan & Reiter (2022); the Bureau’s 17.14 comes from a tighter conversion. For the Spanish Gboard model, \(\rho = 0.81\) gives 9.447 by Equation 46.15, against the 8.9 Google reports from a numerical conversion. The Bureau’s 19.61 adds the \(\varepsilon\) of persons and housing units; converting the summed \(\rho = 2.63\) once would give a smaller number (18.194 by Equation 46.15).
Replace-one to add/remove. The Census guarantee is for replacing one person’s record, which is a removal followed by an addition, so its \(\varepsilon\) is not directly comparable with the add/remove \(\varepsilon\) of DP-SGD; an add/remove guarantee of \(\varepsilon\) implies a replace-one guarantee of \(2\varepsilon\) (The definition of differential privacy).
Local reports over time. A local randomizer with \(\varepsilon\) per donation, run a number \(k\) of times, has a total loss of at most \(k\varepsilon\) by basic composition, and a person whose data are correlated across reports can lose all of it. Apple’s documentation states \(\varepsilon\) per donation and the number of donations per day, so QuickType’s two donations of \(\varepsilon = 8\) are up to 16 per day. Tang, Korolova et al. (2017) measured macOS 10.12 independently, by reverse-engineering it. They found a privacy loss of 1 or 2 per submitted datum. Because many data are submitted each day, the loss reached 16 per day for four applications, namely Emojis, New words, Deeplinks and Lookup Hints. They also found that the budget renews every day, so the total grows with the number of days since a user opted in. Tang et al.’s figures are for macOS 10.12 and count each submitted datum, while Apple’s documentation states \(\varepsilon\) per donation, so the two need not match. RAPPOR’s memoization makes all the reports of a value that does not change cost at most its permanent level \(\varepsilon_\infty\), which depends on the number \(H\) of hash functions and the probability \(f\) of replacing a bit by a coin, \[\varepsilon_\infty = 2H\ln\frac{1 - f/2}{f/2}. \tag{46.16}\] With \(H = 2\) and \(f = 0.75\) that is \(4\ln(5/3) = 2.043\). But a value that changes is reported afresh (Local, shuffle and distributed trust models).
Microsoft’s rounds. Ding, Kulkarni & Yekhanin (2017) collect one bit per app every six hours at \(\varepsilon = 1\). To blur when a report changes, they flip each sent bit with a probability \(\nu = 0.2\). They report 0.686 for one round after the flip, which they call output perturbation. Their own bound for one round after the flip is \[\varepsilon' = \ln\frac{(1 - 2\nu)e^{\varepsilon}/(e^{\varepsilon} + 1) + \nu}{(1 - 2\nu)/(e^{\varepsilon} + 1) + \nu}, \tag{46.17}\] which gives 0.569 at these values. The paper does not explain the difference, and 0.686 is the more cautious figure. Their bound for all apps at once, whose usage adds up to at most the length of a round, is \(\varepsilon + e^{\varepsilon} - 1\), which is 1.672 from 0.686. Across rounds, memoization means that a user whose behaviour does not change reveals nothing new, while each change of behaviour can show. A user whose usage changes every round could lose up to \(4 \times 0.686 = 2.744\) per day.
Action to user level. The Facebook release adds Gaussian noise with standard deviation \(\sigma\) to counts of distinct user–URL pairs, separately for each kind of action. One action moves one count by 1, so it is \(\rho\)-zCDP with \(\rho = 1/(2\sigma^2)\). A user with \(k\) distinct URLs moves \(k\) counts by 1 each, so by composition of zCDP the user is \(k/(2\sigma^2)\)-zCDP. The release sets \(k\) at the 99th percentile of URLs per user for each kind of action. It then picks \(\sigma\) so that the user level is \(\varepsilon = 0.45\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), using a tighter conversion from the same paper of Bun & Steinke (2016), \[\varepsilon = \rho + \sqrt{4\rho\ln(\sqrt{\pi\rho}/\delta)}. \tag{46.18}\] For clicks the release uses \(k = 17\) and \(\sigma = 40\). So one click has \(\rho = 0.00031\), which is \(\varepsilon = 0.10\), and a user’s 17 clicks have \(\rho = 0.0053\), which is \(\varepsilon = 0.454\). For views, with \(k = 51{,}914\) and \(\sigma = 2{,}228\), one view costs almost nothing, while a user’s views still add up to \(\varepsilon = 0.450\). Users above the 99th percentile get proportionally more: twice the actions, twice the \(\rho\).
Per day versus total. A budget per user per day of \(\varepsilon = 1\) adds up to 365 over a year for someone whose behaviour is the same every day. NIST SP 800-226 uses exactly this example to warn that event-level and user-day units can be surprisingly weak.



46.8.4 Interpretation
The model rows are the comparable ones. For training a model on user data, the Gboard models are the best documented: device-level guarantees for a whole training run, \(\varepsilon\) between about 1 and 14 at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\). The running example’s budgets of 1 to 8 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) are in that range, but at a much larger \(\delta\) and with records, not users, as the unit.
Large published values are not rare. The Census Bureau published \(\varepsilon = 17.14\) for persons. Many local deployments spend several units of \(\varepsilon\) per day. NIST SP 800-226 notes that many deployments have used \(1 < \varepsilon \le 20\). These are facts about practice, not evidence that a value is safe; Dwork, Kohli & Mulligan (2019) found no clear consensus on how deployments choose \(\varepsilon\), and proposed an Epsilon Registry, a public record of deployed parameters, so that choices could be compared and criticized.
Compare like with like. Desfontaines’ list of real-world uses of DP converts guarantees to \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) and, for Apple, to a user-day unit, so its numbers differ from the primary sources on purpose. When you compare your budget with a deployment, convert both to the same unit, neighbouring relation, accounting and \(\delta\), or say that you did not.
The deployments also teach what a published \(\varepsilon\) leaves out. Five lessons recur, and each is a question to ask of any budget, including your own.
A budget that renews has no lifetime bound. The local deployments state \(\varepsilon\) per report, per donation or per day, and refresh it. Rogers et al. (2021, Table 2) put several of them on a monthly scale for a user whose records change, so that memoization never applies. One RAPPOR report every 30 minutes at \(\varepsilon_1 = 0.534\) then adds up to \(0.534 \times 48 \times 30 = 769\) per month. Microsoft’s four rounds a day at 0.686 add up to 82.3 per month. Apple’s Safari domains, with two donations a day at \(\varepsilon = 4\), add up to 240. These are upper bounds by basic composition, and memoization makes them much smaller for users whose data do not change, which is why the local deployments memoize. But no single number covers a user’s lifetime.
Some protections sit outside \(\varepsilon\). According to Apple’s Differential Privacy Team (2017), Apple’s devices send reports over an encrypted channel, Apple strips IP addresses before the reports are stored, and only a random sample of reports is sent. RAPPOR’s instantaneous randomized response also makes a user’s reports hard to link to each other, a benefit that \(\varepsilon_1\) does not express. These measures matter, but the stated \(\varepsilon\) does not cover them. A privacy statement should list them separately.
Some guarantees rest on assumptions that are not mathematical. LinkedIn’s Audience Engagements API answers queries chosen by outside analysts, such as advertisers, and keeps a budget per analyst per month (Rogers et al. 2021). Two analysts who pooled their answers would together exceed it. The guarantee therefore assumes that analysts do not collude, which LinkedIn enforces by vetting and by contract, not by noise. It does blunt one form of collusion, because every analyst who asks the same query on the same day receives the same noisy answer, so pooling identical answers reveals nothing new.
A value can be argued from a specific attack. LinkedIn chose its per-result \(\varepsilon = 0.15\) by modelling an analyst who asks the same count on each of the 30 days the data are kept and averages the noisy answers. With the API’s Laplace noise of scale \(2/\varepsilon\) on each answer, the source’s normal approximation gives a probability of 0.115 that the average lands within \(\frac12\) of the true count, which would reveal it after rounding. That is the “about 11%” chance the authors accepted. This is the procedure of Section 46.9 in miniature: name the attack, compute its success, and choose the number from it.
Partial user-level guarantees should say whom they cover. The Facebook URLs release protects each action strongly, and protects whole users at \(\varepsilon = 0.45\) for each kind of action only up to the 99th percentile of activity. Users above the 99th percentile get a weaker guarantee, whose \(\varepsilon\) grows with how far they exceed it (Exercise 7). That is an honest way to state a guarantee that cannot cover everyone, and User-level differential privacy explains why bounding each user’s contribution is the price of covering all of them.


46.8.5 Example: the Census as a training run
Could the running example’s \(\varepsilon = 8\) run be described as “less than half the Census budget”? The Census \(\varepsilon = 17.14\) is replace-one at \(\delta = 10^{-10}\); the run’s 7.997 is add/remove at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). At \(\delta = 10^{-10}\) the run is at 11.627 (Table 46.10), and replace-one doubles an add/remove guarantee in the worst case. After converting, the honest statement is that the two are of the same order, which is a weaker claim than the slogan.


46.8.6 Check yourself

A product reports “\(\varepsilon = 2\) per user per day” for data kept a year. What total should you assume for a user whose behaviour never changes? (Up to \(2 \times 365 = 730\) by basic composition, unless the mechanism memoizes or the accounting shows otherwise.)
Why can the Census Bureau’s 19.61 be larger than the \(\varepsilon\) of the combined \(\rho = 2.63\)? (Because adding two \(\varepsilon\) values computed at the same \(\delta\) is a valid but loose composition, while zCDP composes by adding \(\rho\) and converts once.)

title: 46  Choosing ε
text:
46.9 Justifying a choice

46.9.1 Context
You must pick a target for the running example and write a statement that a sceptical reviewer will check. What should the procedure be, and what does it give here?


46.9.2 Statement
A defensible choice of \(\varepsilon\) fixes the claim before the number:

The unit and the neighbouring relation. Record, user, device; add/remove or replace-one; the period over which the budget is spent, including every training run and hyperparameter search that touched the data (Hyperparameter tuning).
The threat. Membership, attribute inference or reconstruction; the attacker’s knowledge and prior; what it observes (the final model, the iterates, an API).
The whole guarantee. The privacy profile \(\varepsilon(\delta)\) or the trade-off curve, computed by a tight accountant, with \(\delta \ll 1/n\), and read at the operating points of the threat: TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) and below for membership, at FPR \(\kappa\) for reconstruction.
The evidence. An empirical audit (Auditing private training) whose lower bound is consistent with the claim, and a check of the implementation against the assumptions of the proof (DP-SGD).
The utility. The accuracy curve against \(\varepsilon\), and where it bends: the smallest budget past the bend is the natural candidate.
The comparison. The tiers of Ponomareva et al. (2023): \(\varepsilon \le 1\) gives strong formal guarantees; \(\varepsilon \le 10\) is the widely used goal they call a reasonable level of anonymization for many applications; above 10, the guarantee alone cannot be taken as sufficient evidence of anonymization and additional measures such as auditing may be necessary. NIST SP 800-226 offers no specific rule for choosing \(\varepsilon\), cites a study suggesting that \(\varepsilon\) of 0.1 generally provides strong protection and values below 1 are reasonable, and warns that large values may not provide meaningful privacy, that releases with \(\varepsilon\) of 10 or more can leave outliers vulnerable, and that organizations should evaluate the risk of the final data, especially for \(\varepsilon\) above 1. It also recommends publishing the parameters, which it says creates no additional risk.



46.9.3 Derivation: why each step is needed

Unit. Without it, the same number can mean protection of a single click or of a person’s whole history (Section 46.8).
Threat. The curve answers different questions at different points: a prior of 0.5 reads the curve near FPR 0.5, a thousand candidates read it at \(10^{-3}\) (Section 46.5, Section 46.6).
Whole guarantee. The single pair can overstate the attacker by a factor of 17 at FPR \(10^{-3}\) and \(\varepsilon = 8\) (Table 46.5), so a statement based on the pair alone either undersells the model or tempts the reader to dismiss DP as vacuous.
Evidence. The curve is a theorem about an algorithm; whether the code runs that algorithm is an empirical fact, and audits are how bugs that break the proof are found.
Utility. The accuracy curve is steeply non-linear (Figure 46.5), so the cost of halving \(\varepsilon\) varies by an order of magnitude along it.
Comparison. Tiers and practice give a reader a reference point; they cannot replace steps 1 to 5.



46.9.4 Interpretation
The accuracy curve and the risk curve together. Figure 46.5 puts the accuracies of DP-SGD against the largest membership TPR at FPR 1%, from the pair and from the exact curve. Going from \(\varepsilon = 1\) to 2 gains 2.66 points of accuracy (0.9175 to 0.9441) and moves the exact TPR at FPR 1% from at most 0.01893 to at most 0.03141. From 2 to 4 gains 1.07 points for a TPR of at most 0.0724. From 4 to 8 gains 0.56 points (0.9548 to 0.9604), the gap to the non-private model falling from 0.0062 to 0.0006, and nearly triples the TPR, to at most 0.2092. Past \(\varepsilon = 4\), each unit of accuracy is bought with a much larger increase in worst-case risk.
Rules of thumb are where the reasoning stops, not where it starts. “\(\varepsilon \le 1\) is strong” is true of every mechanism, because Equation 46.4 is already tight enough. “1 to 10 is common in machine learning” is true of practice, and this chapter shows why it can be reasonable for DP-SGD: at those budgets the actual curve is far below the line. “Above 10 needs justification” is true because there even the actual curve allows attacks with substantial power on worst-case records (TPR above 0.27 at FPR \(10^{-3}\) at \(\varepsilon = 16\)).






Figure 46.5: Left: test accuracy of the running example against \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), from the DP-SGD chapter’s table (three runs each), with the non-private model dashed. Right: the same accuracies against the largest TPR of a membership test at FPR 1%, from the exact curve (circles, labelled by \(\varepsilon\)) and from the pair alone (squares). The dotted vertical line is an attacker with no information.





46.9.5 Example: a privacy statement for the running example
Following the procedure, a team might choose the \(\varepsilon = 4\) run and write:

The model was trained with DP-SGD (Poisson sampling rate 0.01, noise multiplier 1.36, clipping norm 0.5, 10,000 steps) on 10,000 records, one record per person. The privacy unit is one record under add/remove neighbours; no other run touched the training data. The RDP accountant gives \((3.993, 10^{-5})\)-DP and \((5.209, 10^{-8})\)-DP; a PLD accountant gives \(\varepsilon \le 3.729\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Against an attacker who knows every other record and sees every iterate, any membership test has TPR at most 0.01312 at FPR \(10^{-3}\) and at most 0.0724 at FPR \(10^{-2}\), and any attack that picks a record out of 100 equally likely candidates succeeds with probability at most 0.0724. Test accuracy is 0.9548, against 0.9610 without privacy.

Every number in it is checkable, and each comes with its unit, its accountant and the attacker it refers to. A reviewer who thinks \(\varepsilon = 4\) is too large can now argue with the TPR at a specific FPR, which is the substance, rather than with the number.


46.9.6 Check yourself

Your accuracy curve is flat above \(\varepsilon = 2\). Which budget should you choose, and why? (About 2, or slightly above to leave room for run-to-run variation: past the bend, more budget buys almost no accuracy and raises the worst-case risk.)
A reviewer asks why you report the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) rather than the advantage. (Because an attack is dangerous when its flags are reliable, which is a low-FPR property, and because the advantage is read at one point near the middle of the curve, where it says little about confident identification.)

Rules of thumb

Report the curve, not just the pair: the TPR at FPR \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-2}\), computed with a PLD accountant or bounded with RDP.
State the unit, the neighbouring relation, the period and \(\delta\) with every \(\varepsilon\); convert before comparing with anyone else’s.
\(\varepsilon \le 1\) is strong for any mechanism. Between 1 and 10, DP-SGD’s actual curve is far below the pair’s line, and that curve is your justification. Above 10, show the curve and an audit, and expect worst-case records to be exposed.
Choose \(\delta\) well below \(1/n\) for the right \(n\); for Gaussian-type mechanisms a smaller \(\delta\) costs little \(\varepsilon\).
Put the accuracy curve next to the risk curve, and pick the smallest budget past the bend in accuracy.
Ask of every published budget how it grows over time, which protections sit outside it, which assumptions it rests on, and which users it covers.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.1 Why this matters
Every chapter of this part ended with a number: train with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) under differential privacy (DP), that is, with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise (DP-SGD), at a sampling rate \(q\) of 0.01, noise multiplier \(\sigma = 1\) and 10,000 steps, and the accountant reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). That number is the conclusion of a proof. The proof is about an algorithm on paper, and what ships is code. Between the two sit a dozen places where an implementation can quietly differ from the algorithm the proof analysed: noise scaled for the averaged gradient but added to the sum, the wrong dataset size handed to the accountant, batches sampled one way and accounted another, a random seed reused. None of these changes the accuracy much, so none is caught by the usual tests. Is the trained model as private as the accountant says?
An audit answers this the only way an empirical check can: it attacks. It plants records of its own, canaries, trains with and without them, runs a membership test, and counts how often the test is right. The definition of DP limits how often any test can be right, so the measured error rates imply a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\): the algorithm cannot be private with any smaller \(\varepsilon\). A lower bound cannot prove privacy. It can disprove a claim, when it lands above the claimed value, and it says how much of the accountant’s worst case a given attacker can actually realize.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.1.1 The one idea: privacy caps every test, so a measured test bounds privacy from below
An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm guarantees that every test, for every pair of neighbouring datasets, has a true positive rate (TPR) of at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its false positive rate (FPR) plus \(\delta\). Read backwards, a test with a measured FPR and TPR forces \(\varepsilon \ge \ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}\). Everything in this chapter is about making that inequality bite. The rates are estimated from a finite number of trials, so they come with confidence intervals, and the bound must use the pessimistic end of each; this caps what any audit with \(n\) trials can certify at about \(\ln n\). The test is only as strong as the attack, so the auditor chooses the most detectable canary and the most informative view of training; with the right canary and a view of every step, the audit faces exactly the pair of distributions the accountant analyses. And training thousands of models is unaffordable, so two tricks get many trials out of one or two runs: many canaries in one run, or one observation per step.
Table 47.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 47.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.









Result
Where it is used




A test’s FPR and TPR, with Clopper–Pearson intervals, give an \(\varepsilon\) lower bound
Every audit; reading audit results in papers


The ceiling: \(n\) trials certify at most about \(\ln(n/\ln(2/\beta))\)
Planning an audit; why audits of large \(\varepsilon\) are expensive

What a realistic attacker learns from a released model
