Testing DP-SGD implementations before release






Notation. The training algorithm is \(M\), the dataset without the canary \(D\) and with it \(D' = D \cup \{z^*\}\), where \(z^*\) is the canary; neighbours differ by adding or removing one record. A trial is one run of \(M\) on \(D\) or on \(D'\), with fresh randomness, followed by the attack’s score \(s\). The attack says “canary in” when \(s \ge \tau\), a threshold. Its false positive rate is \(\mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[s \ge \tau \mid D]\) and its true positive rate \(\mathrm{TPR} = \Pr[s \ge \tau \mid D']\); the false negative rate (FNR) is \(1 - \mathrm{TPR}\). With \(n\) trials of each kind, the counts are \(k_0\) false positives and \(k_1\) true positives. \(\beta\) is the probability that an audit’s bound is wrong (5% throughout), and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}\) is the bound itself. DP-SGD’s notation is that of DP-SGD: clipping norm \(C\), noise multiplier \(\sigma\), sampling rate \(q\), expected batch size \(B\) (the sampling rate times the number of records, 100 here), learning rate \(\eta\) and \(T\) steps. In this chapter \(n\) always counts trials, not records.
The running example. The part’s network: a two-layer tanh network trained on the 10,000 records of DP-SGD with \(q = 0.01\), \(C = 0.5\), \(\sigma = 1\), learning rate 0.5 and \(T = 10{,}000\) steps. The Rényi differential privacy (RDP) accountant reports \(\varepsilon = 6.71\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\); this is the claim every audit below tests.
How to read this chapter. Read the toolkit and Section 47.3, which turns an attack into a bound and says what it costs. Section 47.4 chooses the attack, Section 47.5 runs the strongest one many times and explains why even it stops short of 6.71. Section 47.6 and Section 47.7 audit a real training run in one go, and Section 47.8 uses audits to catch broken implementations. This chapter comes last in the part because it checks the claims of all the others.

title: 47  Auditing private training
section: 47.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
47.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

47.2.1 Fact 1 — Differential privacy caps every test, in both directions
\(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when, for all neighbours \(D, D'\) and every set of outputs \(S\), \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D) \in S] + \delta\), and the same with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped. A test that says “canary in” on the event \(S\) has \(\mathrm{TPR} = \Pr[M(D') \in S]\) and \(\mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[M(D) \in S]\), so the definition reads \(\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\). Applying the definition with the roles swapped to the complement of \(S\), where the test says “canary out”, gives \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta\): a test cannot be almost always right about absent canaries while rarely missing present ones. Together, \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta, \qquad 1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,(1 - \mathrm{TPR}) + \delta. \tag{47.1}\] These are the two lines of the hypothesis-testing interpretation of DP (The definition of differential privacy); they hold for randomized tests too.


47.2.2 Fact 2 — Clopper–Pearson bounds on a rate
If \(k\) of \(n\) independent trials succeed, each with unknown probability \(p\), then \(k\) is binomial, \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, p)\). The one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound at level \(\kappa\) is the rate \(u\) at which seeing \(k\) or fewer successes has probability exactly \(\kappa\), \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le k] = \kappa\); the lower bound \(l\) solves \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, l) \ge k] = \kappa\). Then \(\Pr[p \le u] \ge 1 - \kappa\) and \(\Pr[p \ge l] \ge 1 - \kappa\), for every true \(p\). The reason is that a true rate above \(u\) would make the observed count implausibly small, and the probability of an observation that implausible is at most \(\kappa\) (Hypothesis testing proves it, and Section F.3 in the appendices shows that \(u\) and \(l\) exist and are unique). With \(k = 10\) and \(n = 10{,}000\), the bounds at \(\kappa = 0.025\) are 0.00048 and 0.00184, the two ends of the usual two-sided 95% interval. With \(k = 0\) and \(n = 3{,}000\), the 95% upper bound is \(9.9808 \times 10^{-4}\), about \(3/n\): the rule of three.


47.2.3 Fact 3 — The best test thresholds the likelihood ratio
Among all tests with a given FPR, the one with the largest TPR says “canary in” when the likelihood ratio, the density of the observation under \(D'\) divided by its density under \(D\), exceeds a threshold. This is the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Hypothesis testing). The reason is a budgeting argument: each observation costs its probability under \(D\) in false positives and earns its probability under \(D'\) in true positives, and the best way to spend a fixed false-positive budget is on the observations with the best ratio of earnings to cost. The curve of the best TPR against FPR is the pair’s trade-off curve (written as best FNR against FPR in f-DP and Gaussian DP). For two unit-variance normals at distance \(\mu\), the best TPR at a given \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is \[\mathrm{TPR}_\mu(\mathrm{FPR}) = 1 - \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu\big), \tag{47.2}\] where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function; a mechanism whose curve is this one, or better, satisfies Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) with parameter \(\mu\), or \(\mu\)-GDP.


47.2.4 Fact 4 — One DP-SGD step, seen along one direction
A DP-SGD step releases \(G_t = \sum_{i\in S_t}\bar g_i + \xi_t\), the sum of the clipped gradients of the records in the batch \(S_t\) plus Gaussian noise \(\xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I)\). Project \(G_t\) on a fixed unit vector \(u\) and divide by \(C\). The noise becomes \(\sigma z_t\) with \(z_t\) standard normal, because the projection of an isotropic Gaussian vector on a unit vector is a one-dimensional Gaussian with the same standard deviation. A record whose clipped gradient is exactly \(Cu\) adds 1 when it is sampled, which under Poisson sampling happens with probability \(q\), independently at every step. So if no other record’s gradient has a component along \(u\), the projection is \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the record}, \qquad x_t \sim (1 - q)\,\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}, \tag{47.3}\] independently over steps, because both the sampling and the noise are drawn afresh at every step. This is the pair of distributions the accountant of Amplification by subsampling analyses: the worst case for one step under add/remove neighbours.

title: 47  Auditing private training
section: 47.3 From an attack to a lower bound on ε
text:
47.3 From an attack to a lower bound on ε

47.3.1 Context
You ran an attack: \(n\) training runs without the canary and \(n\) with it, a score per run, a threshold. You counted \(k_0\) false positives and \(k_1\) true positives. What can you conclude about \(\varepsilon\), with what confidence, and how much could you possibly conclude with \(n\) trials?


47.3.2 Statement
The measured rates are \(k_0/n\) and \(k_1/n\). Write \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) for the one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound on the FPR and lower bound on the TPR, each at level \(\beta/2\) (Fact 2). If the threshold was chosen without looking at these \(2n\) trials, then with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) the algorithm is not \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for any \(\varepsilon\) below \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = \max\Big\{\ln\frac{\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} - \delta}{\overline{\mathrm{FPR}}},\ \ln\frac{1 - \overline{\mathrm{FPR}} - \delta}{1 - \underline{\mathrm{TPR}}}\Big\}. \tag{47.4}\] The most that \(n\) trials per hypothesis can certify is the bound of a perfect attack, \(k_0 = 0\) and \(k_1 = n\): \[\varepsilon_{\max}(n) = \ln\frac{(\beta/2)^{1/n} - \delta}{1 - (\beta/2)^{1/n}} \approx \ln\frac{n}{\ln(2/\beta)}. \tag{47.5}\]


47.3.3 Derivation

The rates bound \(\varepsilon\). Solve the two inequalities of Equation 47.1 for \(\varepsilon\): \(e^\varepsilon \ge (\mathrm{TPR} - \delta)/\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(e^\varepsilon \ge (1 - \mathrm{FPR} - \delta)/(1 - \mathrm{TPR})\). Any \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm satisfies both, at the true rates of every test.
Both expressions grow with the TPR and shrink with the FPR. So replacing the true FPR by something larger and the true TPR by something smaller can only lower them.
The intervals hold together with probability \(1 - \beta\). By Fact 2, \(\mathrm{FPR} \le \overline{\mathrm{FPR}}\) fails with probability at most \(\beta/2\), and \(\mathrm{TPR} \ge \underline{\mathrm{TPR}}\) fails with probability at most \(\beta/2\). The probability that at least one of them fails is at most the sum, \(\beta\) (the union bound). This needs the counts to be binomial: independent trials, and a threshold fixed before the counting.
Combine. On the event that both intervals hold, step 2 gives \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} \le \max\{\ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}, \ln\frac{1 - \mathrm{FPR} - \delta}{1 - \mathrm{TPR}}\}\), and step 1 says this is at most the \(\varepsilon\) of any valid guarantee. So the event “\(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\varepsilon < \varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}\)” has probability at most \(\beta\).
The ceiling. With \(k_0 = 0\), \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, u) \le 0] = (1 - u)^n = \beta/2\) gives \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}} = 1 - (\beta/2)^{1/n}\). With \(k_1 = n\), \(\Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, l) \ge n] = l^n = \beta/2\) gives \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} = (\beta/2)^{1/n}\). Substituting in the first form of Equation 47.4 gives Equation 47.5; the second form gives the same value here. For large \(n\), \((\beta/2)^{1/n} = e^{-\ln(2/\beta)/n} \approx 1 - \ln(2/\beta)/n\), so \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}} \approx \ln(2/\beta)/n\), \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} \approx 1\) and \(\varepsilon_{\max} \approx \ln(n/\ln(2/\beta))\); with \(\beta = 0.05\), \(\ln(2/\beta) = \ln 40 = 3.69\).



47.3.4 Interpretation
A lower bound, and only that. \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}\) says “no smaller \(\varepsilon\) is possible”, never “this \(\varepsilon\) is enough”. A weak attack gives a small \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}}\) for a leaky model as easily as for a private one. That asymmetry is the whole logic of auditing: a bound above the claim refutes the claim, and a bound below it only says that this attacker, on this canary, could not do better.
The ceiling grows like \(\ln n\). Each factor of \(e\) in the bound costs a factor of \(e\) in trials, because a false positive rate cannot be distinguished from zero with fewer than about \(3/\mathrm{FPR}\) trials (the rule of three), and \(\varepsilon\) is about \(\ln(1/\mathrm{FPR})\) when the TPR is near 1. Table 47.2 shows what that means. Certifying the running example’s 6.71 needs at least 3,038 trials per hypothesis, so 6,076 training runs, even for an attack that never errs. Each run of the running example takes a few seconds; for a real network each is a full training job.



Table 47.2: The most a perfect attack can certify with \(n\) trials per hypothesis, at 95% confidence and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Conversely, certifying \(\varepsilon = 1\), 2, 4, 6.71 and 8 takes at least 12, 30, 204, 3,038 and 10,999 trials per hypothesis.

Choose the threshold on separate trials. Step 3 assumes the threshold does not depend on the counts. Sweeping the threshold over the same data and reporting the best bound is the norm in parts of the literature, and it makes the confidence level wrong: among many thresholds, one is lucky. Every audit in this chapter chooses its threshold on half of the trials and counts on the other half.
Both inequalities matter. The first form of Equation 47.4 rewards tests that flag few absent canaries; the second rewards tests that rarely miss present ones. A test that says “canary in” almost always, with FPR 0.5 and TPR 0.999, has a useless first form, \(\ln(0.999/0.5) = 0.69\), and a second form of \(\ln(0.5/0.001) = 6.21\). An audit should try both (Exercise 1).


47.3.5 Example: what confidence costs
Suppose 1,000 runs with the canary and 1,000 without give 500 true positives and 1 false positive. The point estimate is \(\ln\frac{0.5 - 10^{-5}}{0.001} = 6.21\). The Clopper–Pearson bounds at \(\beta/2 = 0.025\) are \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}} = 0.00556\) and \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} = 0.4685\): one false positive in 1,000 is consistent with a true FPR five times larger. The certified bound is \(\ln\frac{0.4685 - 10^{-5}}{0.00556} = 4.43\), almost two less than the point estimate. With ten times the trials and the same rates, 10 false positives and 5,000 true positives out of 10,000 each, \(\overline{\mathrm{FPR}} = 0.00184\), \(\underline{\mathrm{TPR}} = 0.4902\), and the bound rises to 5.59. The point estimate does not change; the price of confidence falls, slowly, as the counts grow.


47.3.6 Check yourself

An audit with 500 trials per hypothesis reports \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = 7\) at 95% confidence. What went wrong? (500 trials can certify at most about \(\ln(500/3.69) = 4.9\), by Equation 47.5. The threshold was probably chosen on the same trials, or the trials were not independent.)
Why does the bound use the upper end of the FPR interval and the lower end of the TPR interval? (Because the bound must hold whatever the true rates are within their intervals, and \(\ln\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}\) is smallest when the FPR is as large and the TPR as small as the data allow.)

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.4 Canaries and threat models

47.4.1 Context
DP is a promise about the worst pair of neighbouring datasets and the worst test. An audit must instantiate both: it picks the dataset, the canary record and what the attacker sees, then the score. A typical training record and a loss threshold give a valid but nearly useless bound (Membership inference shows that most records are barely exposed). What is the strongest audit of DP-SGD, and what does it face?


47.4.2 Statement
The auditor has two choices of canary and two threat models.
An input-space canary is a record \((x, y)\), inserted into the training data like any other: a mislabeled example, or one far from the data, so that its gradient is large and points where few others do. A gradient-space canary lets the auditor write the canary’s gradient directly, as if it controlled the training code; the strongest is a Dirac canary, a gradient equal to \(C\) on one coordinate and zero elsewhere (Nasr et al. 2023), on a coordinate where the other records’ gradients are zero. In the black-box threat model the attacker sees only the final model; in the white-box model it sees every iterate \(\theta_0, \dots, \theta_T\), and therefore every noisy sum \(G_t = -B(\theta_{t+1} - \theta_t)/\eta\).
For a Dirac canary seen white-box, the audit faces the accountant’s pair exactly. The projections \(x_t = G_{t,j}/C\) on the canary’s coordinate \(j\) follow Equation 47.3, independently over the \(T\) steps. The most powerful test at every FPR thresholds the likelihood-ratio statistic \[\Lambda = \sum_{t=1}^T\ln\Big(1 - q + q\,e^{(x_t - 1/2)/\sigma^2}\Big), \tag{47.6}\] and by the central limit theorem (CLT) its trade-off curve is close to that of \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\). The simpler sum of projections \(\sum_tx_t\), which is the canary coordinate of the total displacement \(\theta_0 - \theta_T\) times \(B/(\eta C)\), has a curve close to \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu_{\mathrm{sum}} = q\sqrt T/\sigma\).


47.4.3 Derivation

The canary is the only difference. With a Dirac canary on a coordinate \(j\) no other record’s gradient touches, every other record contributes 0 to \(G_{t,j}\). The canary’s clipped gradient is itself, since its norm is exactly \(C\), and it contributes \(C\) when sampled. Dividing by \(C\) gives Fact 4: \(x_t = \sigma z_t\) without the canary and \(\sigma z_t + b_t\) with it, \(b_t \sim \mathrm{Bern}(q)\).
The steps are independent. The sampling coin \(b_t\) and the noise \(z_t\) are fresh at each step, and the canary’s gradient is the same at every step whatever the weights are. So \((x_1, \dots, x_T)\) are independent and identically distributed under each hypothesis, even though training is adaptive.
The likelihood ratio of one step. The density of \(\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\) divided by that of \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) at \(x\) is \(e^{(2x - 1)/(2\sigma^2)} = e^{(x - 1/2)/\sigma^2}\), because the squares \(x^2\) cancel in the ratio of the two exponentials. The mixture’s density over the null’s is therefore \((1 - q) + q\,e^{(x - 1/2)/\sigma^2}\).
Multiply over steps. Independence (step 2) makes the joint likelihood ratio a product, and its logarithm the sum Equation 47.6. By Fact 3, thresholding \(\Lambda\) is the most powerful test at every FPR. No attacker, whatever it sees, can do better against this canary: the whole training run is a function of the projections \(x_t\) and of randomness that has the same distribution under both hypotheses (the other records’ sampling and the noise on the other coordinates), so it carries no evidence beyond the \(x_t\).
The two statistics in Gaussian terms. The CLT applied to the per-step privacy loss gives \(\mu = q\sqrt{T(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)}\) for \(\Lambda\) (f-DP and Gaussian DP derives it from the mean and variance of \(\ln(1 + qW)\), with \(W = e^{(x - 1/2)/\sigma^2} - 1\)). For the sum, the shift between the hypotheses is the expected number of times the canary is sampled, \(qT\), and the noise standard deviation is \(\sigma\sqrt T\); their ratio is \(q\sqrt T/\sigma\). (With the canary the sum has a little extra variance, \(Tq(1 - q)\), from the random number of samples.)



47.4.4 Interpretation
Why the likelihood ratio beats the sum. The sum treats every step alike. The likelihood ratio does not: a step with \(x_t = 3\) is much stronger evidence of the canary than three steps with \(x_t = 1\), because a value three noise standard deviations out is very unlikely without the canary. The exponential in Equation 47.6 weighs it accordingly. The two coincide when \(\sigma\) is large, since then the exponential is nearly linear, and differ most at small \(\sigma\); the ratio of their \(\mu\) is \(\sigma\sqrt{e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1}\), 1.311 at \(\sigma = 1\) (Exercise 4).
Why black-box audits are weaker. Three things separate a black-box audit with an input canary from the white-box Dirac audit. The final model is one function of all the noisy sums, so it carries at most as much information as all of them (post-processing), and usually much less: the noise of 10,000 steps is summed into the weights, and later steps partly overwrite earlier ones. An input canary’s gradient is not of norm \(C\) at every step: once the model fits it, or gives up on it, its gradient shrinks or turns. And it shares directions with the other records’ gradients, whose contributions act as extra noise. Nasr, Song, Thakurta, Papernot & Carlini (2021) built a ladder of such adversaries for DP-SGD and found the lower bound tight for the strongest, which sees every iterate and chooses a worst-case dataset and canary, and much weaker as the adversary was restricted towards a realistic one. Jagielski, Ullman & Oprea (2020), an early audit of DP-SGD, used black-box poisoning canaries crafted to have large gradients in a direction where the other data’s gradients are small (their ClipBKD), with Clopper–Pearson intervals; they report bounds about ten times better than standard membership inference and within about a factor of ten of the theoretical \(\varepsilon\).
Which threat model to audit. They answer different questions. A white-box gradient audit tests the mechanism: it asks whether the code adds the noise and clips the gradients the proof assumes, and its bound should match the accountant. A black-box input audit tests the deployment: it measures what an attacker with a released model and a planted record can do. A gap between the black-box bound and the accountant is not a bug; it is a measure of how far this attacker is from the proof’s worst case.


47.4.5 Example: the running example’s two statistics
At \(q = 0.01\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(T = 10{,}000\), the likelihood-ratio statistic has \(\mu = 0.01 \times \sqrt{10{,}000 \times 1.7183} = 1.3108\), and the sum of projections \(\mu_{\mathrm{sum}} = 0.01 \times 100 = 1.00\) (0.9951 with the extra variance). Read through the Gaussian privacy profile, the conversion from \(\mu\) to \(\varepsilon\) at a given \(\delta\) (f-DP and Gaussian DP), these are \(\varepsilon = 6.01\) and \(4.35\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Choosing the sum lowers \(\mu\) from 1.31 to 1.00, and the \(\varepsilon\) the audit can ever reach from 6.01 to 4.35, before a single trial is run.


47.4.6 Check yourself

Why must the Dirac canary sit on a coordinate the other records do not touch? (Otherwise their gradients add an unknown amount to \(x_t\), which acts as extra noise and as a bias that differs from step to step; the audit no longer faces Equation 47.3 but a harder problem, and its bound drops.)
An attacker sees only \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_T\) of a run with a Dirac canary. Which statistic can it compute, and what does it lose? (The total displacement on the canary coordinate, which is the sum of projections; it loses the per-step values, so it cannot weigh the large steps more, and its \(\mu\) falls from 1.31 to 1.00.)

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.5 Tight audits of the mechanism

47.5.1 Context
The white-box Dirac audit faces the accountant’s own pair. With enough trials, does it recover the accountant’s 6.71? With the trials an auditor can afford, how close does it get?


47.5.2 Statement
For any pair of distributions \(P\) (without the canary) and \(Q\) (with it), the smallest \(\varepsilon\) for which \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\) holds for every event \(S\) is \[\varepsilon^*(\delta) = \sup_S\ \ln\frac{Q(S) - \delta}{P(S)}, \tag{47.7}\] the supremum over events with \(Q(S) > \delta\), and the supremum may be taken over likelihood-ratio thresholds only. For a \(\mu\)-GDP curve the supremum is reached at the threshold whose false positive rate is \[\mathrm{FPR}^* = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\Big), \qquad \mathrm{TPR}^* = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{47.8}\] For the running example, \(\mu = 1.3108\) and \(\varepsilon = 6.01\) give \(\mathrm{FPR}^* = 8.1 \times 10^{-8}\) and \(\mathrm{TPR}^* = 4.3 \times 10^{-5}\): certifying the full \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) needs to measure a false positive rate below one in ten million.


47.5.3 Derivation

Equation 47.7 is the definition, solved for \(\varepsilon\). If \(\varepsilon\) is at least the supremum, then \(\ln\frac{Q(S) - \delta}{P(S)} \le \varepsilon\) for every \(S\), which rearranges to \(Q(S) \le e^\varepsilon P(S) + \delta\). If \(\varepsilon\) is below it, some event has \(\ln\frac{Q(S) - \delta}{P(S)} > \varepsilon\) and violates the inequality.
Only likelihood-ratio thresholds matter. For a fixed \(P(S) = \mathrm{FPR}\), the ratio grows with \(Q(S)\), and by Fact 3 the event with the largest \(Q(S)\) among those with \(P(S) = \mathrm{FPR}\) is a likelihood-ratio threshold.
So a perfect audit is exact. An audit that thresholds \(\Lambda\) (Equation 47.6) and measures FPR and TPR without error at every threshold computes Equation 47.7, the true \(\varepsilon^*(\delta)\) of the canary’s pair. For the Dirac canary this is the pair the accountant bounds, so the audit converges to DP-SGD’s true \(\varepsilon\) in this direction of neighbours.
The touching point. For a \(\mu\)-GDP curve, the ratio \(\frac{\mathrm{TPR} - \delta}{\mathrm{FPR}}\) is largest where the line \(\mathrm{TPR} = e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta\) touches the curve, that is where the curve’s slope is \(e^\varepsilon\). The slope of a trade-off curve at a threshold is the likelihood ratio there (Fact 3’s budgeting argument at the margin), which for two normals at distance \(\mu\) with threshold \(\tau\) is \(e^{\mu \tau - \mu^2/2}\). Setting it to \(e^\varepsilon\) gives \(\tau = \varepsilon/\mu + \mu/2\), whose FPR is \(1 - \Phi(\tau) = \Phi(-\tau)\) and TPR \(1 - \Phi(\tau - \mu)\): Equation 47.8.



47.5.4 Interpretation
The accountant’s number is not the audit’s target. The audit converges to the true \(\varepsilon^*\), not to what an accountant reports. The RDP accountant’s 6.71 is an upper bound, and a loose one: the numerical accountant of f-DP and Gaussian DP puts the true value of the running example between 6.14 and 6.24, and the CLT approximation gives 6.01. Even an audit with infinitely many trials stops about half a unit below 6.71. That gap belongs to the accountant, not to the audit.
\(\varepsilon\) at small \(\delta\) lives in the extreme tail. Equation 47.8 is the main reason audits fall short. With \(n\) trials you can measure false positive rates down to about \(3/n\); below that, the threshold admits no false positive and its rate is only bounded by the rule of three. At the rates you can measure, the curve’s ratio \(\mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR}\) is far below \(e^\varepsilon\). For \(\mu = 1.3108\) it is \(\ln(\mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR}) = 2.74\) at FPR \(10^{-2}\), 3.63 at \(10^{-3}\) and 4.38 at \(10^{-4}\), by Equation 47.2. Reaching 6 needs FPR near \(10^{-7}\), and about \(1.2\times10^{8}\) trials without the canary to see ten false positives there (Exercise 3). Figure 47.1 shows both sides: the measured trade-off curve sits well inside the \((6.71, 10^{-5})\) limit, and the \(\varepsilon\) each threshold certifies keeps rising until FPR \(10^{-7}\).
Assume the shape, and extrapolate. Nasr, Hayes, Steinke, Balle, Tramèr, Jagielski, Carlini & Terzis (2023) avoid the tail by assuming the trade-off curve has a known shape. If the mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP for some \(\mu\), a single test bounds \(\mu\) from below: by Equation 47.2, \(\mathrm{TPR} \le \mathrm{TPR}_\mu(\mathrm{FPR})\) rearranges to \[\mu \ge \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) - \Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR}), \tag{47.9}\] and a lower bound on \(\mu\) converts to a lower bound on \(\varepsilon\) through the Gaussian privacy profile. The rates can be measured at a moderate FPR, where trials are cheap, and the shape carries the bound into the tail. The statement “\(M\) is not \(\mu\)-GDP for any \(\mu\) below this” is rigorous; the conversion to \(\varepsilon\) is valid only if the curve really is Gaussian. For the subsampled Gaussian of DP-SGD it is not exactly: its tail is heavier, and the \(\mu\) that Equation 47.9 gives depends on where you read it. In the example below, the measured rates give 1.300 at FPR \(10^{-1}\), 1.303 at \(10^{-2}\), 1.371 at \(10^{-3}\) and 1.492 at \(2 \times 10^{-4}\), against the CLT’s 1.3108. Their audits mostly insert the canary at every step, so that each step is an exact Gaussian mechanism, and compose the per-step result with an accountant; Section 47.8 does the same.






Figure 47.1: Left: the trade-off of the white-box audit of the running example on log axes, from 30,000 trials per hypothesis. The black line is the most any test can achieve under \((6.71, 10^{-5})\)-DP; the dashed grey curve is \(\mu\)-GDP with the CLT’s \(\mu = 1.31\). The blue curve is the likelihood-ratio statistic, the orange one the sum of projections; boxes are 95% Clopper–Pearson regions at four thresholds. Right: the \(\varepsilon\) a threshold would certify if its rates were known exactly, \(\ln((\mathrm{TPR} - \delta)/\mathrm{FPR})\), against its false positive rate. The Gaussian curve reaches its \(\varepsilon\) of 6.01 only at FPR \(8 \times 10^{-8}\) (dotted line), far below the rates a feasible audit can measure.





47.5.5 Example: auditing the running example’s mechanism
The script simulates the white-box Dirac audit directly from Equation 47.3: each trial draws 10,000 projections, adds the canary on a \(\mathrm{Bin}(10{,}000, 0.01)\) number of steps when it is present, and computes \(\Lambda\). This is statistically identical to training the network with a Dirac canary on an untouched coordinate, and thousands of times cheaper.
With 50,000 trials per hypothesis, the measured curve is heavier-tailed than the Gaussian approximation. At the threshold that lets through 500 false positives (FPR \(10^{-2}\)) the TPR is 0.1530 and \(\ln((\mathrm{TPR} - \delta)/\mathrm{FPR}) = 2.73\), as the Gaussian predicts; at 10 false positives (FPR \(2.0 \times 10^{-4}\)) the TPR is 0.0203 and the point value 4.62, and at 5 false positives (FPR \(10^{-4}\)) it is 4.84, above the Gaussian’s 4.38. These are point estimates, without confidence intervals. Table 47.3 gives the certified bounds, each with the threshold chosen on the first half of the trials and the counts taken on the second.

The rigorous bound reaches 3.63 with 100,000 simulated training runs, about half the claim. With 10,000 runs per hypothesis its threshold lets through 6 false positives among 5,000 and catches 254 of 5,000 canaries; with 50,000 it lets through 3 among 25,000 and catches 368. The Gaussian-shape estimate climbs faster, to 5.33, and approaches the CLT’s 6.01 from below. The sum of projections needs far more trials for less: its rigorous bound is 1.97 with 10,000 trials per hypothesis and 3.26 with 100,000. With 1,000,000 it is 2.27 in this run, lower than with 100,000, because a threshold chosen on 500,000 trials to let through a handful of false positives let through more on the other half. Bounds read in the far tail are noisy, and Figure 47.2 shows the same scatter. Every number in Table 47.3 is below the claim, as it must be for a correct implementation.






Figure 47.2: The certified \(\varepsilon\) lower bound of the white-box audit of the running example against the number of trials per hypothesis, at 95% confidence and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\): the likelihood-ratio statistic (circles), the sum of projections (triangles) and the Gaussian-shape estimate from the likelihood ratio (squares), with the accountant’s 6.71 and the ceiling of a perfect attack. The bounds grow roughly like the logarithm of the number of trials.





47.5.6 Check yourself

A white-box audit with unlimited trials converges to 6.2, not 6.71. Is the implementation broken? (No. The audit converges to the true \(\varepsilon^*(\delta)\) of the pair, which the numerical accountant puts between 6.14 and 6.24; the RDP accountant’s 6.71 is an upper bound that is loose by about half a unit.)
Why does the Gaussian-shape estimate exceed the rigorous bound with the same trials? (It measures \(\mu\) where rates are well estimated and extrapolates to the tail using the Gaussian curve; the rigorous bound only uses what was measured. The estimate is a valid bound only if the curve really is Gaussian.)

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.6 One-run auditing

47.6.1 Context
The audits so far need one training run per trial, thousands of runs in all. For a model that takes a day to train, that is out of the question. Can one training run give a valid bound?


47.6.2 Statement
Insert \(m\) canaries, each independently with probability \(\frac12\): \(S_i = +1\) if canary \(i\) is in the training set and \(-1\) if not. Train once. Score every canary, and guess \(\hat S_i = +1\) (“in”) for the \(r/2\) highest scores, \(\hat S_i = -1\) (“out”) for the \(r/2\) lowest, and abstain (\(\hat S_i = 0\)) on the rest. Let \(W\) be the number of correct guesses. If training is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then for every \(v\) \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le \Pr\big[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v\big], \qquad p_\varepsilon = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{47.10}\] If training is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then with \(F(v) = \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon) \ge v]\), \[\Pr[W \ge v] \le F(v) + 2m\delta\max_{i = 1, \dots, m}\frac{F(v - i) - F(v)}{i} \tag{47.11}\] (Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski 2023, Corollary 5.4). Observing \(v\) correct guesses rejects every \(\varepsilon\) whose right-hand side is below \(\beta\); the largest such \(\varepsilon\) is the bound.


47.6.3 Derivation (pure DP; the δ term is in the paper)

Each inclusion bit is protected. Fix every inclusion bit except \(S_i\). Changing \(S_i\) adds or removes one record, so the training run, and the guesses computed from it (post-processing), are \(\varepsilon\)-DP as a function of \(S_i\): for every vector of guesses \(s\), \(\Pr[\hat S = s \mid S_i = +1, S_{-i}] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[\hat S = s \mid S_i = -1, S_{-i}]\).
Average over the later bits. Order the guessed canaries. Conditioning only on the earlier bits \(S_{<i}\), average step 1 over the later ones \(S_{>i}\): they are independent of \(S_i\), so the same weights appear on both sides, and \(\Pr[\hat S = s \mid S_i = +1, S_{<i}] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[\hat S = s \mid S_i = -1, S_{<i}]\).
No guess is right more than \(p_\varepsilon\) of the time. By Bayes’ rule with the prior \(\frac12\) on \(S_i\), \(\Pr[S_i = +1 \mid \hat S = s, S_{<i}] = \frac{x}{x + y}\) with \(x = \Pr[s \mid S_i = +1, S_{<i}]\) and \(y = \Pr[s \mid S_i = -1, S_{<i}]\). The fraction grows with \(x\), and step 2 says \(x \le e^\varepsilon y\), so it is at most \(\frac{e^\varepsilon y}{e^\varepsilon y + y} = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{e^\varepsilon + 1} = p_\varepsilon\). The same holds for \(S_i = -1\). So whichever way canary \(i\) is guessed, it is correct with probability at most \(p_\varepsilon\) given the guesses and the earlier bits, which fix whether the earlier guesses were correct.
A sum of such indicators is dominated by a binomial. Write the \(j\)-th guess’s correctness as \(\mathbf 1[U_j \le p_j]\) with \(U_j\) independent uniform numbers and \(p_j \le p_\varepsilon\) its conditional probability from step 3. Then \(\mathbf 1[U_j \le p_j] \le \mathbf 1[U_j \le p_\varepsilon]\), and the right-hand indicators sum to a \(\mathrm{Bin}(r, p_\varepsilon)\) variable. So \(W\) is at most a binomial variable, and Equation 47.10 follows. Section N.1 in the appendices builds this coupling step by step and proves the domination lemma it relies on.



47.6.4 Interpretation
Randomized response is the worst case, and that sets the scale. The binomial of Equation 47.10 is what you get when each guess is \(\varepsilon\)-randomized response on the true bit (The definition of differential privacy), so the bound is tight for that mechanism (Exercise 6). The paper’s worked example: 75 correct out of 100 is what \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\) produces on average, and Equation 47.10 gives the lower bound 0.702 at 95% confidence; the script reproduces it, and the paper’s 0.699 and 0.673 for \(\delta = 10^{-4}\) with 100 and 1,000 canaries.
The ceiling is again logarithmic. If all \(r\) guesses are right, the bound is the \(\varepsilon\) with \(p_\varepsilon^r = \beta\), about \(\ln(r/\ln(1/\beta))\): 3.49 for 100 canaries, 5.81 for 1,000 and 8.11 for 10,000, with \(\delta = 0\). Certifying 6.71 needs about 2,500 canaries guessed without a single error (Exercise 5). Each canary is a trial, so a one-run audit has the same \(\ln\) ceiling as the many-run audit with \(n \approx m\); it saves runs, not trials.
The \(\delta\) term grows with the number of canaries. The correction in Equation 47.11 is at most \(2m\delta\). With \(m = 1{,}000\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) that is 0.02, small next to \(\beta = 0.05\); with 10,000 canaries all guessed right the bound falls from 8.11 to 7.83. When \(2m\delta\) approaches the significance level, the correction can swallow the whole budget: no number of correct guesses rejects anything.
One run is not tight for DP-SGD. Even with white-box Dirac canaries, the one-run bound stays well below the many-run bound. Each canary is guessed once, at a fixed fraction of guesses, so the audit reads the trade-off curve near FPR \(1/m\) at best; and the binomial is calibrated to randomized response, whose curve has a sharp corner, while the curve of DP-SGD is smooth. Steinke et al. show that their bound is exact for randomized response; for DP-SGD their one-run bounds stay below the theoretical \(\varepsilon\) even with white-box gradient canaries.


47.6.5 Example: Dirac canaries in one run
Simulate one run of the running example with 1,000 Dirac canaries on distinct untouched coordinates, about half included, each scored by \(\Lambda\). The auditor tries six list lengths \(r\) and pays for trying them with a Bonferroni correction: each test runs at level \(\beta/6\), so that the chance that any of the six is wrong is at most \(\beta\). Table 47.4 gives the result.

All 50 most confident guesses are right, which certifies 2.22; the 100-guess list makes 8 mistakes and certifies less. With 5,000 canaries the best bound is 2.53, from 479 correct out of 500. There the \(\delta\) correction shows its teeth: \(2m\delta = 0.1\) exceeds the per-test level \(\beta/8\), and 20 correct guesses out of 20 certify nothing at all. One run certifies 2.22, against 2.84 for 10,000 runs per hypothesis in Table 47.3, at a twenty-thousandth of the cost.


47.6.6 Check yourself

Why must each canary be included by an independent fair coin, rather than, say, the first half included? (Step 3 uses the prior \(\frac12\) on \(S_i\) and step 2 the independence of the bits. With a deterministic split, the guesses could be right for reasons that have nothing to do with the training run, for example the order of the canaries.)
960 correct guesses out of 1,000 under pure DP: is \(\varepsilon = 2\) rejected? (Yes. Under \(\varepsilon = 2\), \(p_\varepsilon = 0.881\), so the binomial has mean 881 and standard deviation about \(\sqrt{1{,}000 \times 0.881 \times 0.119} = 10.2\); 960 is almost eight standard deviations above.)

title: 47  Auditing private training
section: 47.7 Black-box audit of the trained network
text:
47.7 Black-box audit of the trained network

47.7.1 Context
The white-box Dirac audit tests the mechanism. What does an attacker learn from the released network itself, with canaries that are ordinary records?


47.7.2 Statement: the protocol
Take 1,000 records from the held-out test set of the running example and flip their labels: mislabeled canaries, which the model can only fit by memorizing them. Include each in the 10,000 training records with probability \(\frac12\), train once with DP-SGD at the claimed configuration, and score each canary by minus its loss on the final model: a canary the model fits well was probably trained on. Guess with the six list lengths of Section 47.6 and bound \(\varepsilon\) with Equation 47.11, Bonferroni-corrected. As controls, run the same audit on a model trained with clipping but no noise, and on a model trained without clipping or noise.
The bound is valid for the add/remove neighbours of any canary, because including a canary is adding a record, and all the guarantees of DP-SGD hold for every dataset, including one with planted records.


47.7.3 Interpretation
Before the numbers, what to expect. The black-box attacker sees one function of the 10,000 noisy sums, the canary’s gradient changes as it is fitted, and its direction is shared with the gradients of the 10,000 real records, which pull the other way since the canary’s label is wrong. Each of these weakens the audit relative to Section 47.5. Nothing in the accountant knows about them: the accountant bounds the worst dataset, the worst record and an attacker who sees every step. So the black-box bound should be far below 6.71, and the gap measures this attacker, not the privacy of the algorithm.
The no-noise control separates the two. A model trained with clipping and no noise has no finite \(\varepsilon\) at all. If the black-box audit of that model also gives a small bound, then the audit’s weakness, not the noise, is what keeps the bound small.


47.7.4 Example: three training runs
Table 47.5 gives the three audits, one training run each.



Table 47.5: Black-box one-run audit of the running example’s network with 1,000 mislabeled canaries, one training run each, at 95% overall confidence and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Test accuracy is on the 19,000 test records not used as canaries.

The non-private model memorizes the canaries it trained on: their mean loss is 0.023 against 9.041 for those it did not see, 967 of 1,000 guesses are right, and the audit certifies 2.96; 1,000 perfect guesses would certify 5.78 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) even without the Bonferroni correction, so 33 mistakes cost almost three units. Memorizing 481 contradictory labels costs it almost five points of test accuracy, 0.9155 against the DP model’s 0.9645. DP-SGD does not memorize: the losses of included and excluded canaries differ by less than half a unit on average, 59 of the 100 most confident guesses are right, and the certified bound is 0.13 (from 293 of 500, the best list). The clipping-only model is barely easier, 0.24. So with \(\sigma = 1\) removed, the black-box attacker still learns almost nothing. Clipping alone bounds each canary’s pull on the weights to \(C\) per step, against the combined pull of 10,000 correctly labelled records, and that is what defeats this attacker. Figure 47.3 shows the loss distributions and how the fraction of correct guesses falls as the list grows.






Figure 47.3: One-run audits with 1,000 canaries. Left and middle: the loss of each mislabeled canary on the final model, for canaries in the training set (red) and left out (blue), without privacy and with DP-SGD at \(\varepsilon = 6.71\). Right: the fraction of the \(r\) guesses that are correct, against \(r\), for the non-private network (black box), the DP-SGD network (black box) and the mechanism with white-box Dirac canaries; the dashed line is the most a \(6.71\)-DP algorithm allows on average, \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\).



What this says about the claim. Nothing contradicts 6.71, and nothing confirms it. The black-box bound of 0.13 says that a realistic attacker, with one model and planted mislabeled records, extracts very little; the white-box audits of Section 47.5 say that an attacker who sees every step and controls a gradient extracts much more. Reporting both, with the threat model of each, is what an honest privacy statement does (Choosing an accountant lists what else it must contain).


47.7.5 Check yourself

The audit of the clipping-only model gives 0.24. Does that mean clipping alone is 0.24-DP? (No. The model has no finite \(\varepsilon\): a Dirac gradient canary seen white-box would identify membership perfectly. The bound says only that this black-box attack, with these canaries, cannot show more.)
Why mislabeled canaries rather than random test records? (A correctly labelled record from the data distribution has a small gradient and nearly the same loss whether or not it was trained on, so the audit would learn even less; a mislabeled one can only be fitted by memorizing it, which is the leakage the audit looks for.)

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.8 Finding bugs

47.8.1 Context
An audit bound below the claim proves nothing. A bound above it proves, with confidence \(1 - \beta\), that the claim is false. That makes audits a test suite for private training code: the test passes silently on a correct implementation and fails loudly on a broken one. Which bugs does it catch, and how cheaply?


47.8.2 Statement
A per-step audit inserts a Dirac canary at every step (a sampling rate of 1 for the canary, \(q_c = 1\)) in one run and leaves it out in another, and treats each step’s projection as one trial: \(T\) trials per hypothesis from two runs. In a correct implementation each step is a Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity \(C\) and noise \(\sigma C\), so the projections are \[x_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2) \text{ without the canary}, \qquad x_t \sim \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2) \text{ with it}, \tag{47.12}\] and each step is exactly \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = 1/\sigma\). The audit’s \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) from Equation 47.9 with Clopper–Pearson rates is a rigorous lower bound on the per-step \(\mu\). If \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}} > 1/\sigma\), the implementation does not add the noise it claims.
An end-to-end audit with the many-trial protocol of Section 47.5 tests everything at once, sampling and accounting included, but needs many runs.


47.8.3 Derivation

One step with the canary always present is a Gaussian mechanism. With \(q_c = 1\) there is no sampling coin for the canary, so Fact 4 gives Equation 47.12: a shift of 1 in noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\). By Fact 3 the best test thresholds \(x_t\) itself, and its trade-off curve is Equation 47.2 with \(\mu = 1/\sigma\).
The steps are independent trials. The noise is fresh at every step and the canary’s gradient is fixed, so the \(T\) projections of each run are independent, and the counts at a fixed threshold are binomial.
The bound on \(\mu\). For any threshold, a \(\mu\)-GDP step has \(\mathrm{TPR} \le 1 - \Phi(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu)\), which rearranges to Equation 47.9. Replacing the rates by their Clopper–Pearson bounds can only lower the right-hand side (it grows with the TPR and shrinks with the FPR), so with probability \(1 - \beta\) the true per-step \(\mu\) is at least \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\).
A refutation. A correct implementation has \(\mu = 1/\sigma\), so \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}} > 1/\sigma\) happens with probability at most \(\beta\). Observing it rejects the hypothesis that the code adds noise \(\sigma C\) to a sum with sensitivity \(C\).



47.8.4 Interpretation
Per-step audits test the noise and the clipping; they cannot see the sampling or the accountant. With the canary in every step, the audit never exercises the sampling code, and it compares the measured noise with the claimed \(\sigma\), not with the claimed \(\varepsilon\). A bug in how batches are drawn, or in what the accountant is told, passes it. Nasr et al. (2023) audit one step for this reason and say so; they caught clipping applied after averaging, noise drawn from a seed with only 100 possible values (a similar error appeared in a canonical JAX example of DP-SGD), and a wrong noise scale.
End-to-end audits see everything, but only large bugs. An end-to-end audit tests the claimed \(\varepsilon\) directly, so it catches an accounting bug as readily as a noise bug, provided the true \(\varepsilon\) exceeds the claim by more than the audit’s shortfall. From Section 47.5, that shortfall is about three units at 100,000 runs for the running example. Tramèr, Terzis, Steinke, Song, Jagielski & Carlini (2022) used such an audit to show that an open-source implementation of a differentially private deep-learning algorithm violated its claimed guarantee, at a confidence they report as \(1 - 10^{-10}\).
What no canary audit catches. An audit tests one dataset, one canary and one attack. A bug that only shows on datasets or records the audit did not try, or that raises \(\varepsilon\) by less than the audit’s shortfall, passes. Sampling bugs are the instructive case. Batches drawn by shuffling but accounted as Poisson can have an \(\varepsilon\) several times the reported one (Amplification by subsampling derives a lower bound that shows it), yet a per-step audit with the canary in every step never exercises the sampling, and an end-to-end audit sees the gap only where it exceeds the audit’s shortfall. Passing an audit is evidence, never a certificate.


47.8.5 Example: three implementations and an accounting bug
Table 47.6 audits three implementations of the running example’s noise, each with two runs of 10,000 steps, and an accounting bug.



Table 47.6: Per-step audits of three implementations of the running example’s DP-SGD step, from 10,000 steps with and 10,000 without a Dirac canary, at 95% confidence. The last column is what the RDP accountant would report for the noise the audit measured.

The correct implementation passes: 0.886 is below its claimed 1, and plugged into the accountant it gives 5.38, close to but below 6.71. The two noise bugs fail decisively. Passing \(\sigma^2C^2 = 0.25\) where the code expects a standard deviation halves the noise when \(C = 0.5\), and the audit measures \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}} = 1.745\) against the claimed 1. Scaling the noise for the averaged gradient, whose sensitivity is \(C/B\), and then adding it to the sum, whose sensitivity is \(C\), makes it \(B = 100\) times too small, and 10,000 steps separate the two hypotheses perfectly: 6.359 is the most Equation 47.9 can certify from 5,000 error-free trials per hypothesis, the evaluation half. The same bug also fails an end-to-end audit with the sum of projections: with 10,000 runs per hypothesis, the threshold catches all 5,000 canaries of the evaluation half with one false positive, and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} = 7.21 > 6.71\).
The accounting bug: the code is correct, but the accountant is told the dataset has 20,000 records instead of 10,000, as can happen when augmented copies are counted, so it computes \(q = 0.005\) and reports \(\varepsilon = 3.06\). The per-step audit measures the noise, which is right, and composing its \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}}\) at the claimed \(q = 0.005\) gives 2.47, which does not contradict 3.06. The end-to-end audit of Table 47.3 does: its 3.63 with 50,000 trials per hypothesis exceeds 3.06, so the claim is false with 95% confidence. Figure 47.4 shows why the two noise bugs are easy to see.






Figure 47.4: Per-step audits of three implementations: the projections of 10,000 steps on a Dirac canary, without it (blue) and with it at every step (red), in units of \(C\). A correct implementation has noise of standard deviation \(\sigma C\); the two bugs shrink it by a factor of 2 and of 100. The titles give the certified lower bound on the per-step \(\mu\); the claim is 1.





47.8.6 Check yourself

A per-step audit of your implementation gives \(\mu_{\mathrm{lo}} = 0.97\) for a claimed \(\sigma = 1\). Can you conclude the implementation is correct? (No. A lower bound on \(\mu\) can show that \(\mu\) is too large, never that it is small enough: 0.97 is consistent with the claimed \(\mu = 1\), and also with noise a little too small. And the audit says nothing about the sampling, the accountant or bugs that do not affect a Dirac canary.)
The opposite mistake adds noise \(\sigma C\) to the averaged gradient instead of to the sum. Would an audit flag it? (No. Noise \(\sigma C\) on the mean is noise \(\sigma CB\) on the sum, \(B\) times more than claimed: the implementation is more private than its claim and every audit passes. It is still a bug, since it wastes accuracy, but audits only catch errors in the unsafe direction.)

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.9 Code: run every audit
The script code/auditing.py implements the Clopper–Pearson bounds from the incomplete beta function, the bound of Equation 47.4 with thresholds chosen on half the trials, the white-box simulation of Equation 47.3 with both statistics, the one-run bound of Equation 47.11, the black-box audit of the running example’s network (importing the model and DP-SGD from code/dp_sgd.py) and the per-step audits. From the repository root:

It takes a few minutes, most of it simulating 100,000 white-box trials of 10,000 steps each and training three networks.

What to take from it. The bounds are valid but conservative, and they grow only like the logarithm of the effort. An audit is most useful as a test: the strongest attack you can mount, white-box with a gradient canary, aimed at the claim you want to check. A correct implementation passes it with room to spare, and the two noise bugs fail it with margins no amount of bad luck explains.

title: 47  Auditing private training
text:
47.10 References

Jagielski, Ullman & Oprea, “Auditing Differentially Private Machine Learning: How Private is Private SGD?” (NeurIPS 2020). An early audit of DP-SGD: poisoning canaries, Clopper–Pearson intervals, and the lower bound of Equation 47.4.
Nasr, Song, Thakurta, Papernot & Carlini, “Adversary Instantiation: Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Machine Learning” (IEEE S&P 2021). A ladder of threat models from black box to gradient canaries with every iterate visible; tight bounds for the strongest.
Nasr, Hayes, Steinke, Balle, Tramèr, Jagielski, Carlini & Terzis, “Tight Auditing of Differentially Private Machine Learning” (USENIX Security 2023). Dirac canaries, per-step audits with the canary at every step, Gaussian-shape bounds, and three bugs found.
Steinke, Nasr & Jagielski, “Privacy Auditing with One (1) Training Run” (NeurIPS 2023). The one-run audit of Section 47.6; Corollary 5.4 is Equation 47.11, and its appendix gives code for the bound.
Tramèr, Terzis, Steinke, Song, Jagielski & Carlini, “Debugging Differential Privacy: A Case Study for Privacy Auditing” (arXiv 2022). An audit that refuted the guarantee of a published implementation.
Carlini, Chien, Nasr, Song, Terzis & Tramèr, “Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles” (IEEE S&P 2022). The likelihood ratio attack (LiRA) and the case for reporting TPR at a low FPR, which an audit’s bound formalizes.
Dong, Roth & Su, “Gaussian Differential Privacy” (JRSS B 2022). Trade-off curves, \(\mu\)-GDP and the CLT for composition used in Section 47.5.
Kairouz, Oh & Viswanath, “The Composition Theorem for Differential Privacy” (ICML 2015). The hypothesis-testing reading of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP behind Equation 47.1.

Rules of thumb

An audit can refute a claim, never prove one. Report its threat model with its number.
Budget trials before you start: certifying \(\varepsilon\) needs at least \(e^\varepsilon\ln(2/\beta)\) trials per hypothesis, and in practice far more, because \(\varepsilon\) at small \(\delta\) lives at false positive rates you cannot measure.
To test an implementation, use the strongest attack: white box, Dirac gradient canary, likelihood ratio. Audit the noise per step and the claim end to end.
Choose thresholds and list lengths on separate data, or pay for the choice with a Bonferroni correction.
Read a small black-box bound as a statement about the attacker, not as the model’s privacy.

Practice. Exercises for this chapter, each with a worked solution, are in the exercise book.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.1 Why this matters
Every chapter so far has used differential privacy (DP) to protect the people in a dataset. This chapter uses it for a different purpose: to keep a data analysis honest. Machine learning reuses its evaluation data all the time. You tune hyperparameters on a validation set, look at the scores, and try new settings. Likewise, a competition shows a leaderboard score after every submission and teams adjust to it, while a benchmark test set is used by a whole field for a decade. In each case the next question asked of the data depends on the answers to the previous ones. How many such questions can one holdout set answer before its answers stop telling you anything about new data?
The answer depends on how the questions are answered. If you report exact averages on the holdout set, answers break quickly. When the holdout labels are coin flips, so that no model can beat 50% on new data, a thousand random submissions to a leaderboard of 1,000 records are enough to make one look 72% accurate. If you split the holdout set and answer each question on its own fresh part, the answers stay valid, but the data you need grows linearly with the number of questions. A DP mechanism does much better: adding Gaussian noise to each answer makes the data you need grow only like the square root of the number of questions. When there is also a training set to explore freely, the reusable holdout does better still: it adds noise, and pays privacy, only for the questions whose answers on the holdout set disagree with the training set.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.1.1 The one idea: an answer that reveals little about any one record cannot be overfitted
Overfitting a holdout set means choosing questions that fit its particular records. To do that, the analyst must learn something about those records from the earlier answers. A DP mechanism limits what any answer, and any sequence of answers, reveals about a single record, so it stops the overfitting. The proof reuses the main identity of Algorithmic stability and generalization in Part 1, which Section 48.5 restates. There, the expected gap between a chosen question’s value on the sample and on the population is an average, over records, of how much the chosen question’s value on a record changes when that record is replaced by a fresh one. Part 1 bounded each such term by the uniform stability of one fixed algorithm. DP bounds each term whatever the analyst does with the answers, because DP survives post-processing and adaptive composition, while uniform stability survives neither (Section 48.5 explains why).
Table 48.1 lists the results and where each is used.



Table 48.1: The results of this chapter and where each is used.









Result
Where it is used

What it means for practice
Hyperparameter search, leaderboards, benchmark reuse






Notation. The data are a sample of \(n\) records, the dataset \(D = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\). The records are drawn independently from a distribution \(\mathcal D\), the population, and each record \(x_i\) holds features and label together. A statistical query is a function \(q\) from one record to \([0, 1]\), such as “does this classifier get this record right?”. Its empirical value is its average over the sample, \(q(D) = \frac1n\sum_iq(x_i)\), and its population value is its average over the distribution, \(q(\mathcal D) = \mathbb E_{x\sim\mathcal D}\,q(x)\).
An analyst asks \(k\) queries, \(q_1\) to \(q_k\), one at a time. A mechanism \(M\) answers each of them, giving the number \(a_j\) for query \(q_j\). Because the analyst may choose each query from the earlier answers, the analysis is adaptive. Write \(D^{(i)}\) for the sample with \(x_i\) replaced by an independent fresh draw \(x_i'\). Samples that differ in one record, such as \(D\) and \(D^{(i)}\), are neighbours under the replace-one relation. Under this relation, every statistical query has sensitivity \(1/n\), since one record moves an average of \(n\) values in \([0, 1]\) by at most \(1/n\). The goal is accuracy against the population. The largest error \(\max_j|a_j - q_j(\mathcal D)|\) should be at most a target accuracy \(\alpha\), either on average or with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) for a small failure probability \(\beta\).
How to read this chapter. Section 48.3 shows the problem and Section 48.4 the simple fix. Section 48.5 is the key result, and its proof is short. Section 48.6 turns it into a rate, Section 48.7 into the reusable holdout, and Section 48.8 into advice for machine-learning practice.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
section: 48.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses
text:
48.2 Toolkit: four facts every derivation uses

48.2.1 Fact 1 — The largest of many averages: the maximal inequality
Each empirical value is an average of \(n\) independent values in \([0, 1]\), so its error, written \(Z = q(D) - q(\mathcal D)\), is rarely large. Hoeffding’s lemma (Concentration inequalities) makes this precise through the moment generating function. For a query fixed before the sample is drawn, and for every real \(\lambda\), \[\mathbb E\,e^{\lambda Z} \le e^{\lambda^2v/2}, \qquad v = \frac{1}{4n}. \tag{48.1}\] The value of \(v\) comes from applying the lemma to each of the \(n\) centred terms, each scaled by \(1/n\) and so lying in a range of length \(1/n\), which gives \(e^{\lambda^2/(8n^2)}\) per term. Independence multiplies the \(n\) bounds to \(e^{\lambda^2/(8n)}\). A variable with this property is called sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(v\), because a Gaussian variable with variance \(\sigma^2\) has the property with \(v = \sigma^2\), as an equality.
The fact this chapter uses is about the largest of many such variables. If \(Z_1, \dots, Z_m\) are each sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(v\), whatever their dependence, then \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j\le m}Z_j\Big] \le \sqrt{2v\ln m}. \tag{48.2}\] The reason is that the exponential of a maximum is at most the sum of the exponentials. For \(\lambda > 0\), Jensen’s inequality for the convex function \(e^x\) gives \(e^{\lambda\,\mathbb E\max_jZ_j} \le \mathbb E\,e^{\lambda\max_jZ_j}\). The exponential of the maximum is at most the sum of all \(m\) exponentials, and each has expectation at most \(e^{\lambda^2v/2}\), so the right side is at most \(m\,e^{\lambda^2v/2}\). Taking logarithms and dividing by \(\lambda\) gives \(\mathbb E\max_jZ_j \le \ln m/\lambda + \lambda v/2\), and the choice \(\lambda = \sqrt{2\ln m/v}\) gives Equation 48.2. For \(k\) queries, write \(Z_j = q_j(D) - q_j(\mathcal D)\) for the error of query \(j\). Applied to the \(2k\) variables \(\pm Z_j\), the inequality bounds the largest error in absolute value, with \(m = 2k\).


48.2.2 Fact 2 — Renaming a record and a fresh draw
The stability chapter’s main identity rests on one observation. Suppose \(x_i\) and the fresh draw \(x_i'\) are independent and have the same distribution, and both are independent of the other records and of an algorithm’s own coins. Then swapping them does not change the joint distribution of all these random quantities. So any expectation computed from \((D, x_i')\) equals the same expectation computed after the swap, from \((D^{(i)}, x_i)\). Write \(q_{W(D)}\) for the query that a randomized algorithm \(W\) outputs on the dataset \(D\) (the chapter shortens it to \(q_W\) when the sample is clear). Then \[\mathbb E\big[q_{W(D)}(x_i')\big] = \mathbb E\big[q_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)\big]. \tag{48.3}\] The left side is the population value of the chosen query, because \(x_i'\) is a new record that \(W\) never saw. Averaging over \(x_i'\) alone, with \(D\) and \(W\)’s coins fixed, gives \(q_{W(D)}(\mathcal D)\). The right side is the value of a query chosen without \(x_i\) on the record \(x_i\). The stability chapter walks through the swap on a table of every outcome.


48.2.3 Fact 3 — DP bounds the average of any bounded function of the output
Differential privacy has two parameters, a privacy level \(\varepsilon\) and a slack \(\delta\). A mechanism \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP when replacing a dataset \(D\) by a neighbour \(D'\) multiplies the probability of every set of outputs \(S\) by at most \(e^\varepsilon\), up to the slack \(\delta\) (The definition): \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{48.4}\] The derivations need the same bound for averages. For every function \(f\) of the output with values in \([0, 1]\), \[\mathbb E\big[f(M(D))\big] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E\big[f(M(D'))\big] + \delta. \tag{48.5}\] To see this, write the average of a quantity between 0 and 1 as the integral of its tail. For a random output \(Y\), the average of \(f(Y)\) is the integral, over thresholds \(t\) from 0 to 1, of the chance that \(f(Y)\) exceeds \(t\): \[\mathbb E[f(Y)] = \int_0^1\Pr[f(Y) > t]\,dt. \tag{48.6}\] Each tail is the probability of an event, so DP bounds it by \(e^\varepsilon\) times the tail for \(D'\), plus \(\delta\). Integrating over \(t\) from 0 to 1 gives Equation 48.5, because the \(\delta\) integrates to \(\delta\).
Two properties of DP make this useful against an analyst (Post-processing, group privacy and composition). Post-processing: any computation on the output that does not touch the data is as private as the output. Adaptive composition: a sequence of mechanisms, each chosen from the earlier outputs, is private with parameters that add up, or that grow more slowly under the accountants of Composition. The analyst’s choice of each query is post-processing of the earlier answers, and the answers to those chosen queries compose adaptively. So the whole transcript of queries and answers inherits the guarantee of the answering mechanism, however clever the analyst. The derivations swap one record for a fresh one, so the guarantees here are for the replace-one relation. A mechanism that is \(\varepsilon\)-DP for adding or removing a record is \(2\varepsilon\)-DP for replacing one. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism becomes \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\)-DP.


48.2.4 Fact 4 — The Gaussian mechanism in zero-concentrated DP
Zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) measures privacy by one number \(\rho\), which bounds the Rényi divergence between the outputs on neighbours by \(\rho\) times the order. Adding Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) to a query of sensitivity \(\Delta\) satisfies zCDP with \(\rho = \Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\). Under adaptive composition the values of \(\rho\) add, and a \(\rho\)-zCDP mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for every \(\delta > 0\) with \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)} \tag{48.7}\] (Concentrated differential privacy). For \(k\) statistical queries, with \(\Delta = 1/n\), the total is \(\rho = k/(2n^2\sigma^2)\). Because \(\varepsilon\) grows like \(\sqrt\rho\) when \(\rho\) is small, at a fixed noise level and sample size it grows like \(\sqrt k\) in the number of queries. That \(\sqrt k\) is the one this chapter’s rate inherits.

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.3 Reusing a holdout set overfits

48.3.1 Context
A holdout set gives an unbiased verdict on a model that was fixed before the holdout set was drawn. The trouble starts on the second question. In a hyperparameter search, a competition or a benchmark, the analyst sees an answer and lets it shape the next question. How quickly does that go wrong, and how many questions does it take?


48.3.2 Statement
Fixed queries. If the \(k\) queries are chosen before the sample is drawn, their empirical values are accurate, and the number of queries enters only through its logarithm. On average, \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j\le k}\big|q_j(D) - q_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sqrt{\frac{\ln(2k)}{2n}}, \tag{48.8}\] and all \(k\) errors are below \(\alpha\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\) once \[n \ge \frac{\ln(2k/\beta)}{2\alpha^2}. \tag{48.9}\] At \(\alpha = \beta = 0.05\), ten queries need 1,199 records. A thousand queries need 2,120, and a million need only 3,501.
One adaptive query, after many fixed ones, is enough to break this. Let the records be uniform on \(N\) values, labelled \(1, \dots, N\). The analyst asks the \(N\) point queries \(q_v(x) = \mathbf 1[x = v]\), one per value, which are fixed in advance. Their empirical values say exactly which values occur in the sample. Then the analyst asks one more query, chosen from those answers: “is this record’s value one of those that occur in the sample?”. Its empirical value is 1, while its population value is the fraction of the \(N\) values that the sample covers, at most \(n/N\). So with \(k = N + 1\) queries the largest error is \[\max_j\big|q_j(D) - q_j(\mathcal D)\big| \ge 1 - \frac nN = 1 - \frac{n}{k - 1}. \tag{48.10}\] With exact empirical answers, \(n\) must therefore grow linearly in \(k\) to keep the error below \(\frac12\), against \(\ln k\) for fixed queries.


48.3.3 Derivation

Fixed queries, on average. For a query fixed in advance, Fact 1 says the error \(q_j(D) - q_j(\mathcal D)\) is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy \(1/(4n)\), and so is its negative. The maximal inequality Equation 48.2 over these \(2k\) variables, with \(v = 1/(4n)\), gives \(\sqrt{2\ln(2k)/(4n)}\), which is Equation 48.8.
Fixed queries, with high probability. Hoeffding’s inequality bounds the chance that one error exceeds \(\alpha\) by \(2e^{-2n\alpha^2}\), so the union bound over \(k\) queries bounds the chance that any of them does by \(2ke^{-2n\alpha^2}\). Setting this equal to \(\beta\) and solving for \(n\) gives the sample size of the statement.
Where adaptivity enters. Step 1 needs \(q_j\) fixed while the records are drawn, so that \(q_j(x_1), \dots, q_j(x_n)\) are independent draws with mean \(q_j(\mathcal D)\). The final query of the attack is built from the sample, so its values on the sample’s records are all 1, whatever \(\mathcal D\) is.
The attack’s population value. The final query is 1 exactly on the distinct values in the sample, of which there are at most \(n\). Each value has probability \(1/N\), so the population value is at most \(n/N\). Averaged over samples, the population value is exactly \(1 - (1 - 1/N)^n\), because a given value is missed by all \(n\) draws with probability \((1 - 1/N)^n\).



48.3.4 Interpretation
The point queries are harmless one at a time: each of their errors is tiny. Together they reveal the sample, and the damage is done by one query that the revealed sample makes possible. That is the general shape of adaptive overfitting. Earlier answers carry information about individual records, and a later query exploits it.
Real analysts leak more slowly than this attack, but they leak. Freedman’s paradox (Freedman 1983) is the statistical version. Screen many candidate variables on a sample, keep those that look related to the outcome, and test the kept ones on the same sample, and the test looks significant even when every variable is noise. Part 1’s stability chapter runs this experiment on a holdout set (Choosing what to measure after looking). The boosting attack of Blum & Hardt (2015) is the leaderboard version. Its queries are random submissions, and it combines the ones that happened to score above chance by a majority vote.


48.3.5 Example: the point-query attack and a leaderboard
With \(n = 1{,}000\) records on \(N = 2{,}000\) values, the 2,000 point queries are all within 0.0035 of their population values in one run of the chapter’s script. The final query has empirical value 1 and population value 0.3905, against an expected \(1 - (1 - 1/2{,}000)^{1{,}000} = 0.3935\). So its error is about 0.61, while Equation 48.8 would bound the average largest error of 2,001 fixed queries by 0.0644. With \(N = 10{,}000\) values the error is about 0.90.
The boosting attack is closer to practice. The holdout labels are \(n\) fair coins, so no submission can beat 50% on new data. The attacker submits \(k\) random labellings and reads each one’s exact accuracy. Then it submits the majority vote of those that scored above 50%. Table 48.2 averages 20 runs.

The overfitting grows like \(\sqrt{k/n}\), and a short argument predicts its constant. A random submission’s accuracy is \(\frac12\) plus an error of standard deviation \(1/(2\sqrt n)\), approximately normal. Given that the error is positive, its average is \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt n}\sqrt{2/\pi}\), the mean of a half-normal. The accuracy is the average agreement over the records, and the records are interchangeable, so a kept submission agrees with each holdout label with probability \(\frac12 + \frac{1}{2\sqrt n}\sqrt{2/\pi}\). About \(k/2\) submissions are kept.
On each record the vote is then a sum of \(k/2\) terms of \(\pm1\). Each term has mean twice the excess agreement, \(\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sqrt{2/\pi}\), so the sum has mean \(k\sqrt{2/\pi}/(2\sqrt n)\), and its standard deviation is about \(\sqrt{k/2}\). Their ratio is \(\sqrt{k/n}/\sqrt\pi\). A normal sum with a small mean-to-spread ratio \(z\) is positive with probability \(\Phi(z) \approx \frac12 + z/\sqrt{2\pi}\), the first-order expansion of the normal distribution function. So the vote is right with probability about \(\frac12 + z/\sqrt{2\pi}\), which gives \[\text{overfitting} \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{k/n}}{\sqrt\pi} = \frac{\sqrt{k/(2n)}}{\pi}. \tag{48.11}\] The approximation matches the simulation until the overfitting is large, where the first-order expansion of \(\Phi\) overstates it, since an accuracy cannot pass 1 (Figure 48.1). Once \(k\) is a few dozen, the attack beats the bound for fixed queries, and with \(k = n\) submissions it reports 71% to 72% for a coin.
