The attack grows like \(\sqrt k\), the bound like \(\sqrt{\ln k}\).





48.3.6 Check yourself

In the point-query attack, which queries are adaptive? (Only the last one. The \(N\) point queries are fixed in advance and accurate. The attack needs only one adaptive round.)
A leaderboard rounds every score to the nearest 0.01. Does the boosting attack still work? (Yes, more slowly. Rounding hides small differences, but submissions that land above 0.5 after rounding still lean towards the labels. Blum & Hardt’s Ladder, in Section 48.8, goes further and releases a new score only when it beats the previous best by a margin.)

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.4 Sample splitting and its cost

48.4.1 Context
The attack works because a query can depend on the records that answer it. The obvious fix is to make that impossible: never let a record answer a query it helped to choose. How much data does this cost?


48.4.2 Statement
Split the sample into \(k\) parts \(D_1, \dots, D_k\) of \(n/k\) records each, and answer query \(j\) with its empirical value on part \(j\) only, \(a_j = q_j(D_j)\). Then, however the queries are chosen, \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j\le k}\big|q_j(D_j) - q_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sqrt{\frac{k\ln(2k)}{2n}}, \tag{48.12}\] and all errors are below \(\alpha\) with probability \(1 - \beta\) once \(n \ge k\ln(2k/\beta)/(2\alpha^2)\). The data needed grows linearly in \(k\).


48.4.3 Derivation

Condition on the past. Fix the parts \(D_1, \dots, D_{j-1}\) and the analyst’s own randomness. Query \(q_j\) depends only on the answers from those parts, so it is now fixed. Part \(D_j\) is independent of them, so its \(n/k\) records are fresh draws from \(\mathcal D\) as far as \(q_j\) is concerned.
One query. Given the past, Fact 1 applies to \(q_j(D_j) - q_j(\mathcal D)\) with \(n/k\) records, so its moment generating function is at most \(e^{\lambda^2k/(8n)}\). A bound that holds for every value of the past also holds on average over it, so the same bound holds without conditioning.
All queries. The maximal inequality Equation 48.2 needs only the bound of step 2 for each variable, not independence between them. With \(v = k/(4n)\) and \(m = 2k\) it gives Equation 48.12. The high-probability version follows in the same way from Hoeffding’s inequality and the union bound.



48.4.4 Interpretation
Splitting buys validity by using each record once, which is the same as collecting fresh data for every query. It is the right tool when the analysis has few rounds of adaptivity. If the queries come in \(r\) rounds, and each round is fixed before its answers are seen, one part per round suffices, and \(k\) becomes \(r\) in the factor in front of \(\ln(2k)\). A final test set, used once after all decisions are made, is the extreme case \(r = 1\).
When every query is adaptive, though, the cost is steep. At \(\alpha = 0.05\) and \(k = 1{,}000\) the expected-error bound Equation 48.12 needs 1,520,181 records, against 1,521 for the expected-error bound Equation 48.8 if the queries were fixed in advance (Table 48.5). The 2,120 records quoted earlier for 1,000 fixed queries are larger because they make every error small with probability 0.95, not just on average.


48.4.5 Example: a hyperparameter search
A team tries 1,000 configurations one after another, each chosen from the validation scores of the earlier ones, on a validation set of 10,000 records. If each score were a query fixed in advance, Equation 48.8 would bound the average largest error by 0.0195. The search is adaptive, so that bound does not apply. Splitting the validation set into 1,000 parts of 10 records restores validity but leaves Equation 48.12 at \(\sqrt{1{,}000\ln 2{,}000/20{,}000} = 0.6165\), which is useless for scores between 0 and 1.


48.4.6 Check yourself

Why does step 3 not need the parts to give independent answers? (The maximal inequality bounds the expected maximum through a sum of moment generating functions. A sum of expectations needs no independence.)
An analysis has 3 rounds of 100 queries each, each round fixed before its answers are seen. How many parts does it need? (Three, one per round. Within a round the queries are fixed with respect to that round’s part.)

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.5 Differential privacy implies generalization

48.5.1 Context
The attack learns individual records from the answers and then asks a query that fits them. A mechanism that hides individual records should therefore stop it, without throwing away any data. This section proves that it does. The proof is the replace-one argument of Part 1’s stability chapter, with the stability of the algorithm replaced by the privacy of the answers. The first result, the transfer lemma, says that a query chosen privately has nearly the same expected value on the sample as on the population. The second, the transfer theorem, turns this into accuracy against the population for every answer of a private mechanism. It follows Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold & Roth (2015) and the lecture notes of Kamath’s course (2020).


48.5.2 Statement
Transfer lemma. Let \(W\) be an \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP algorithm, under the replace-one relation, that takes a sample and outputs a statistical query \(q_W\). Then the chosen query’s empirical value and its population value have nearly the same expectation: \[\Big|\mathbb E\big[q_W(D)\big] - \mathbb E\big[q_W(\mathcal D)\big]\Big| \le e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta. \tag{48.13}\] The proof gives two one-sided bounds, which are sharper than Equation 48.13 when the expectations are small: \[\mathbb E[q_W(D)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)] + \delta, \qquad \mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[q_W(D)] + \delta. \tag{48.14}\]
Transfer theorem. Let \(M\) answer \(k\) adaptively chosen statistical queries, and let the whole interaction be \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP in the sample. Suppose its answers are accurate on the sample on average, \(\mathbb E[\max_j|a_j - q_j(D)|] \le \alpha\). Then they are accurate on the population, up to the lemma’s term: \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_{j\le k}\big|a_j - q_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \alpha + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta. \tag{48.15}\] For small \(\varepsilon\), \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \approx \varepsilon\), so privacy at level \(\varepsilon\) costs about \(\varepsilon\) in accuracy.


48.5.3 Derivation
The lemma first, in five steps.

The empirical value is an average over records. By definition, \(q_W(D) = \frac1n\sum_iq_W(x_i)\), so \(\mathbb E[q_W(D)] = \frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E[q_{W(D)}(x_i)]\), by linearity of expectation.
The population value is the same average after a swap. By Fact 2, \(\mathbb E[q_{W(D)}(\mathcal D)] = \mathbb E[q_{W(D)}(x_i')] = \mathbb E[q_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)]\) for every \(i\). In words, the population value of a query chosen from \(D\) equals the value on \(x_i\) of a query chosen without \(x_i\).
DP compares the two choices. Hold \(D\) and \(x_i'\) fixed. Then \(D\) and \(D^{(i)}\) are neighbours, and \(f(q) = q(x_i)\) is a function of \(W\)’s output with values in \([0, 1]\). Fact 3 gives \(\mathbb E_W[q_{W(D)}(x_i)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_W[q_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)] + \delta\), where \(\mathbb E_W\) averages over \(W\)’s coins. Averaging over \(D\) and \(x_i'\) keeps the inequality.
Combine. Average step 3 over \(i\), then use step 1 on the left and step 2 on the right: \(\mathbb E[q_W(D)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)] + \delta\). Subtracting \(\mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)]\) from both sides leaves \((e^\varepsilon - 1)\,\mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)] + \delta\), which is at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta\) because a query’s value is at most 1.
The other direction. The replace-one relation is symmetric, so step 3 also holds from \(D^{(i)}\) to \(D\): \(\mathbb E_W[q_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E_W[q_{W(D)}(x_i)] + \delta\). The same averaging gives \(\mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)] \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathbb E[q_W(D)] + \delta\), and the two directions together give Equation 48.13.

The theorem then follows by choosing the worst query privately.

Add the complements. For each query \(q_j\), also consider \(1 - q_j\), answered by \(1 - a_j\). These answers are computed from the original ones, so they cost nothing (post-processing, Fact 3). Their errors are the original errors with the sign flipped, \((1 - q_j(\mathcal D)) - (1 - a_j) = -(q_j(\mathcal D) - a_j)\). Over the \(2k\) queries, the largest signed error \(q(\mathcal D) - a\) is therefore the largest absolute error of the original \(k\).
Pick the worst query privately. Let \(W\) read the transcript of queries and answers and output the query, among the \(2k\), with the largest \(q(\mathcal D) - a\). \(W\) uses the distribution \(\mathcal D\), which is fixed and is not data, and the transcript, which is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. So \(W\) is post-processing, and it is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.
Split the worst error. Writing \(a_W\) for the answer to the chosen query, add and subtract its empirical value: \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_j\big|a_j - q_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] = \mathbb E\big[q_W(\mathcal D) - a_W\big] = \mathbb E\big[q_W(\mathcal D) - q_W(D)\big] + \mathbb E\big[q_W(D) - a_W\big]. \tag{48.16}\]
Bound each part. The first part is at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta\) by the lemma, since \(W\) is DP. The second is at most \(\mathbb E[\max_j|q_j(D) - a_j|] \le \alpha\), by the assumed accuracy on the sample. Adding them gives Equation 48.15.

Step 1 on a small case. The complements turn a largest absolute error into a largest signed one, so that a single query \(W\) can carry it. Table 48.3 takes two queries, one answered too high and one too low.

The largest absolute error is 0.12, on \(q_1\), whose answer is too high. Its signed error is negative, so the largest signed error among \(q_1\) and \(q_2\) alone would be 0.05. The complement \(1 - q_1\) has the same error with the opposite sign, \(+0.12\), and \(W\) picks it.


48.5.4 Interpretation
It is Part 1’s identity with a different bound on each term. Steps 1 and 2 of the lemma together say that \[\mathbb E\big[q_W(D)\big] - \mathbb E\big[q_W(\mathcal D)\big] = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb E\Big[q_{W(D)}(x_i) - q_{W(D^{(i)})}(x_i)\Big]. \tag{48.17}\] This is the stability chapter’s identity for the expected gap (Algorithmic stability and generalization), with the chosen query as the model and \(q(x)\) as the loss. That chapter bounded each term by the uniform stability of a fixed algorithm, the largest change in the loss when one record is replaced. Here each term’s expectation is bounded through the distribution of \(W\)’s output. Step 3 bounds one expectation by \(e^\varepsilon\) times the other plus \(\delta\), and since the values lie in \([0, 1]\) their difference is at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta\). DP is a form of stability: a bound on how much one record can change the distribution of an output.
Why this form of stability survives the analyst. Uniform stability is a property of one algorithm, and it does not survive what the analyst does next. Keeping the query with the largest of several values is a discontinuous choice. When two values are nearly tied, one record can change which query wins, and the chosen query’s value on that record can jump by a large amount. Part 1 showed the same instability in the 1-nearest-neighbour rule. DP survives post-processing and adaptive composition (Fact 3), so every query the analyst can build from private answers is chosen privately. That is the property the lemma needs.
How good the bound is. For small \(\varepsilon\) the lemma costs about \(\varepsilon\). A cost linear in \(\varepsilon\) is the right order in general. For example, take a single record that is a fair bit, keep it with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flip it otherwise, and choose the query “equals the result”. This choice already has a bias of about \(\varepsilon/4\) (Exercise 2). The sharper form in step 4, \((e^\varepsilon - 1)\,\mathbb E[q_W(\mathcal D)] + \delta\), is smaller when the chosen query has a small population value. The bound becomes useless once \(\varepsilon\) is near the accuracy you want, which ties the privacy level to the target accuracy: answering to within 0.05 needs \(\varepsilon\) around 0.05 or below. The theorem holds only on average. High-probability versions exist, with different proofs, and Section 48.6 states them.


48.5.5 Example: picking the best-looking query
Take \(k = 1{,}000\) queries that are all pure noise, each the rate at which a random feature agrees with a random label on \(n = 1{,}000\) records. Every population value is \(\frac12\), and the empirical values are independent with standard deviation \(1/(2\sqrt n) = 0.0158\). Choosing the query with the largest empirical value, with no privacy, overstates it by 0.0509 on average over 2,000 runs. That is close to the maximal inequality’s bound, 0.0616, which Equation 48.8 gives for 1,000 queries.
Now choose with the exponential mechanism of Selection, which picks query \(j\) with probability proportional to \(e^{\varepsilon nq_j(D)/2}\). Its score has sensitivity \(1/n\), so it is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. The script computes its selection bias exactly for each sample, as the probability-weighted average of the empirical values, and Table 48.4 compares it with the lemma.

For small \(\varepsilon\) the measured bias is \(\varepsilon/8\), a quarter of the sharper bound and half the \(\varepsilon/4\) of the one-record example above. A short calculation explains it. The mechanism weights the empirical values by \(e^{tq_j(D)}\) with \(t = \varepsilon n/2\). The derivative in \(t\) of an average with these weights is the weighted variance of the values, so for small \(t\) the weighted average exceeds the plain average by about \(t\) times their variance, which is about \(1/(4n)\). The product is \(\varepsilon n/2 \cdot 1/(4n) = \varepsilon/8\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\) the mechanism behaves like the argmax, and the lemma’s bound, 1.72, says nothing (Figure 48.2).

48.5.6 Check yourself

In step 2 of the theorem, \(W\) uses \(\mathcal D\), which nobody knows. Is that a problem? (No. The selector \(W\) exists only inside the proof, so no one has to run it. It only has to be a DP function of the transcript, and using \(\mathcal D\) costs no privacy because the distribution is fixed, not data.)
Why does the lemma need the replace-one relation rather than add or remove? (The swap in step 2 replaces \(x_i\) by \(x_i'\) and keeps \(n\) records, so step 3 compares two samples that differ by one replacement. An add-or-remove guarantee at \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) gives \((2\varepsilon, (1 + e^\varepsilon)\delta)\) for a replacement.)

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
section: 48.6 Answering with Gaussian noise: the \(\sqrt k\) rate
text:
48.6 Answering with Gaussian noise: the \(\sqrt k\) rate

48.6.1 Context
The transfer theorem turns any private mechanism that is accurate on the sample into one that is accurate on the population. The simplest choice is to add Gaussian noise to each empirical value. How many records does it need for \(k\) adaptive queries, and how does that compare with splitting?


48.6.2 Statement
Answer each query with \(a_j = q_j(D) + \xi_j\), where the \(\xi_j\) are independent Gaussian noises of standard deviation \(\sigma\). For every \(\delta > 0\), \[\mathbb E\Big[\max_j\big|a_j - q_j(\mathcal D)\big|\Big] \le \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)} + e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta, \qquad \varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}, \quad \rho = \frac{k}{2n^2\sigma^2}. \tag{48.18}\] Choosing \(\sigma\) and \(\delta\) to minimize the bound makes the error at most \(\alpha\). Step 4 below explains why \(\delta\) should then be of order \(\alpha\). With that choice, the number of records grows like the square root of \(k\): \[n = O\Big(\frac{\sqrt{k\,\ln k\,\ln(1/\alpha)}}{\alpha^2}\Big). \tag{48.19}\]
Three results go further, and this chapter states them with citations rather than proofs. The first is a high-probability version of the transfer theorem (Bassily, Nissim, Smith, Steinke, Stemmer & Ullman 2016). Suppose a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, and with probability \(1 - \beta\) all its answers are within \(\alpha\) of the empirical values. Suppose also that \(\varepsilon\) is at most a constant times \(\alpha\), and \(\delta\) at most a constant times \(\alpha\beta\). Then its answers are within a constant times \(\alpha\) of the population values, with probability at least \(1 - c\beta\) for a constant \(c\). Jung, Ligett, Neel, Roth, Sharifi-Malvajerdi & Shenfeld (2020) give a shorter proof with explicit constants. Section N.2 in the appendices derives it step by step, in a form that divides the sample’s failure probability by a free constant, which for Gaussian noise costs only a logarithm. With Gaussian noise this gives \(n = \tilde O(\sqrt k/\alpha^2)\) records with high probability, where \(\tilde O\) means “of this order, up to factors logarithmic in \(k\), \(1/\alpha\) and \(1/\beta\)”.
The second result helps when the number of queries is huge. Suppose the records take at most \(|\mathcal X|\) distinct values, a finite domain. Then private multiplicative weights (Query release) answers \(k\) adaptive queries with a number of records that grows only with \(\ln k\) (Bassily et al. 2016): \[n = \tilde O\Big(\frac{\sqrt{\ln|\mathcal X|}\,\ln k}{\alpha^3}\Big). \tag{48.20}\] It beats the Gaussian mechanism once \(k\) is large compared with \(\ln|\mathcal X|/\alpha^2\).
The third result is a lower bound. Once the records have enough dimensions, and assuming that one-way functions exist, no computationally efficient mechanism can answer more than about \(n^2\) adaptive queries accurately (Hardt & Ullman 2014; Steinke & Ullman 2015). Under that assumption, the \(\sqrt k\) rate is the best an efficient mechanism can reach in general.


48.6.3 Derivation

Privacy. Each answer is the Gaussian mechanism on a query of sensitivity \(1/n\), so by Fact 4 it is \(\rho_1\)-zCDP with \(\rho_1 = 1/(2n^2\sigma^2)\). The analyst chooses each query from earlier answers, and adaptive composition adds the \(\rho\) values to \(\rho = k\rho_1\). Equation 48.7 converts it to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).
Accuracy on the sample. The errors on the sample are the noises \(\xi_j\), Gaussian with variance \(\sigma^2\), so they are sub-Gaussian with \(v = \sigma^2\). The maximal inequality over the \(2k\) values \(\pm\xi_j\) gives \(\mathbb E\max_j|\xi_j| \le \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)}\).
Transfer. The transfer theorem with \(\alpha = \sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)}\) from step 2 and \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) from step 1 gives Equation 48.18.
The rate. For small \(\varepsilon\) the transfer term is about \(\varepsilon\), and for small \(\rho\) the conversion is dominated by its square-root term, so \[e^\varepsilon - 1 \approx \varepsilon \approx 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)} = \frac{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}}{n\sigma}. \tag{48.21}\] More noise lowers this term but raises the noise term of step 2. Write the bound as \(\sigma A + B/\sigma\), where the constant \(A = \sqrt{2\ln(2k)}\) comes from step 2 and the constant \(B = \sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta)}/n\) from the display above. Setting the derivative \(A - B/\sigma^2\) to zero gives the best noise level \(\sigma = \sqrt{B/A}\), and there the bound equals \(2\sqrt{AB}\). Setting \(2\sqrt{AB}\) equal to \(\alpha\), leaving the small \(\delta\) term aside for now, and solving for \(n\) gives the approximate size below. It slightly understates the exact optimum of Table 48.5, because \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) exceeds \(\varepsilon\) and the conversion’s \(\rho\) term was dropped. \[n \approx \frac{8\sqrt{k\ln(2k)\ln(1/\delta)}}{\alpha^2}. \tag{48.22}\] Taking \(\delta\) of order \(\alpha\), so that the \(\delta\) term stays below \(\alpha\), gives Equation 48.19.



48.6.4 Interpretation
The \(\sqrt k\) is the \(\sqrt k\) of composition. To hide each record across \(k\) answers, the total privacy loss must stay small, and under zCDP it grows like \(\sqrt k\) times the loss of one answer. Balancing the two terms, as in step 4, puts the best noise per answer at \(\sigma = \sqrt{B/A}\), which grows like \(k^{1/4}/\sqrt n\) up to logarithms. The error, the noise plus the transfer term, then grows like \(k^{1/4}\) and falls like \(1/\sqrt n\). Splitting pays \(\sqrt{k/n}\) instead. Answering empirically pays nothing for privacy, but it loses validity quickly. The boosting attack’s overfitting, about \(\sqrt{k/(2n)}/\pi\), reaches 0.05 after about \(0.05n\) adaptive queries, and the point-query attack pushes the error past \(\frac12\) after about \(2n\).
The constants are large. Table 48.5 solves each expected-error bound for the smallest \(n\) that reaches \(\alpha = 0.05\). For one query the Gaussian bound needs 7,300 records, against 139 for the other two expected-error bounds, because the transfer term must itself be below 0.05. Splitting stays cheaper up to a few hundred adaptive queries. Beyond that, the square root wins by a growing factor: at a million queries, 33 million records against 2.9 billion. Neither is close to the 2,902 records that a million fixed queries need.

At the optimum, the Gaussian bound splits the error almost equally between the noise, 0.0242, and the transfer term, 0.0258. The privacy parameters there are \(\varepsilon = 0.0236\) and \(\delta = 0.0019\), the same for every \(k\). They do not depend on \(k\) because, once the noise term \(\sigma\sqrt{2\ln(2k)}\) is fixed, \(k\) and \(n\) enter the transfer term only through \(k\ln(2k)/n^2\), and the \(n\) that reaches the target fixes that combination. Here \(\delta\) protects no one, because the goal is valid answers. It is only a parameter of the bound, where it adds to the error, so the optimizer sets it to whatever minimizes the total, here 0.0019. Figure 48.3 shows the three slopes.






Figure 48.3: Records needed for an expected largest error of 0.05 against the number of queries, for queries fixed in advance, sample splitting and Gaussian noise with the transfer theorem. The slopes on this log-log scale are about 0, 1 and \(\frac12\).





48.6.5 Example: 1,000 queries on 10,000 records
With \(n = 10{,}000\) and \(k = 1{,}000\) adaptive queries, the best Gaussian bound is 0.4095. It uses \(\sigma = 0.0513\), so that the noise contributes 0.2001 and the transfer term 0.2093, with \(\varepsilon = 0.1674\). Splitting gives 0.6165, and fixed queries would give 0.0195. So at this size the guarantee for adaptive queries is weak whichever method you use. The theorem is a worst-case statement, against an analyst who attacks the holdout set on purpose. Section 48.7 shows that a typical analyst is much easier to defend against.


48.6.6 Check yourself

Why does the noise per answer grow like \(k^{1/4}\) rather than \(\sqrt k\)? (Composition in zCDP makes \(\varepsilon\) grow like \(\sqrt k/(n\sigma)\), so keeping \(\varepsilon\) fixed needs \(\sigma \propto \sqrt k\). But the optimum balances \(\varepsilon\) against the noise, and the balance point is \(\sigma \propto k^{1/4}/\sqrt n\), up to logarithms.)
At \(k = 1\) the Gaussian bound needs 7,300 records, against 139 for the plain empirical answer. Why use it at all? (For one query you would not. The method pays a fixed overhead for a guarantee whose cost grows like \(\sqrt k\), which only pays off for many adaptive queries.)

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
text:
48.7 The reusable holdout: Thresholdout

48.7.1 Context
In machine learning the analyst usually has two sets: a training set to explore freely, and a holdout set only for confirming what the training set suggests. Most of the time the two agree, and then the holdout set’s answer adds nothing that the training set did not already say. Only disagreements, the sign of overfitting to the training set, carry information about the holdout set. The reusable holdout of Dwork, Feldman, Hardt, Pitassi, Reingold & Roth (2015), built on an algorithm called Thresholdout, answers from the training set when the two agree and pays privacy only when they do not. That is the pattern of the sparse vector technique of Selection.


48.7.2 Statement
Thresholdout holds a training set \(D_t\) and a holdout set \(D_h\) of \(n\) records, a threshold \(\tau\) and a noise scale \(b\). It starts with a noisy threshold \(\hat\tau = \tau + \zeta\), where \(\zeta\) is Laplace noise of scale \(2b\), and answers each query \(q\) in two steps.

Draw Laplace noise \(\nu\) of scale \(4b\), and compare the gap between the two sets with the noisy threshold: is \(|q(D_h) - q(D_t)| + \nu > \hat\tau\)?
If not, answer with the training value \(q(D_t)\). If so, count one overfitting detection, answer with \(q(D_h) + \xi\), where \(\xi\) is Laplace noise of scale \(b\), and redraw the threshold noise \(\zeta\).

The holdout set is protected by the detections alone. If a query changes by at most \(\Delta\) when one holdout record is replaced, then a run that stops at its \(B\)-th detection is \(\varepsilon\)-DP in the holdout records with \[\varepsilon = \frac{2B\Delta}{b}, \tag{48.23}\] however many queries were answered below the threshold. For statistical queries \(\Delta = 1/n\). Every answer is close to the holdout value, within the threshold plus noise for an answer below and within the noise \(\xi\) for an answer above. So the transfer theorem applies with the holdout set as the sample. The answers are accurate on the population to within their accuracy on the holdout set, about \(\tau\) plus noise, plus \(e^\varepsilon - 1\).


48.7.3 Derivation

One detection is one run of AboveThreshold. Between two detections, Thresholdout compares a stream of queries \(|q(D_h) - q(D_t)|\) with one noisy threshold and stops at the first that exceeds it. That is AboveThreshold from Selection. It is \((\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2)\)-DP when its threshold noise has scale \(\Delta/\varepsilon_1\) and its query noise scale \(2\Delta/\varepsilon_2\), for any number of answers below the threshold. The reason is that all the answers below are explained by one shift of the threshold noise.
The sensitivity of the compared quantity. The training set does not depend on the holdout set, so hold it fixed. Replacing one holdout record moves \(q(D_h)\) by at most \(\Delta\), so it moves \(|q(D_h) - q(D_t)|\) by at most \(\Delta\) too.
The cost of one detection. The threshold noise has scale \(2b = \Delta/\varepsilon_1\), so \(\varepsilon_1 = \Delta/(2b)\). The query noise has scale \(4b = 2\Delta/\varepsilon_2\), so \(\varepsilon_2 = \Delta/(2b)\). The noisy answer is the Laplace mechanism with scale \(b\), which costs \(\Delta/b\). The total is \(\Delta/(2b) + \Delta/(2b) + \Delta/b = 2\Delta/b\).
The answers below the threshold. They are training values, which do not depend on the holdout set. Their only link to it is the comparison, which step 1 already paid for.
All detections. Each detection closes one run, and the next run starts with fresh threshold noise. Basic composition over the \(B\) closed runs gives Equation 48.23. Queries after the last detection would form an unfinished run, which costs the threshold term \(\Delta/(2b)\) of step 3. That is why the holdout set stops at the \(B\)-th detection. If the analysis ends earlier, the unfinished run fits within the unused budget. Advanced composition would make the cost grow like \(\sqrt B\) rather than \(B\), at the price of a \(\delta\).



48.7.4 Interpretation
Only overfitting is charged. A query whose training and holdout values agree costs nothing, however many such queries there are. An analyst who overfits the training set triggers detections, and each detection spends a fixed amount of privacy. When the budget is spent, the holdout set must stop answering. This is the right accounting for confirmatory analysis, where most hypotheses either hold on both sets or fail on the training set first.
Accuracy means accuracy to within the threshold. Below the threshold, the answer is the training value, which can differ from the holdout value by about \(\tau\). So \(\tau\) sets the resolution of every answer. A smaller \(\tau\) gives sharper answers but more detections. Dwork et al. (2015) prove a high-probability guarantee for Thresholdout directly, in which the number of queries can grow exponentially with \(n\) as long as the number of detections stays small.
The formal guarantee needs large holdout sets. For the transfer term to be below the accuracy \(\alpha\) you want, \(\varepsilon = 2B/(nb)\) must be at most about \(\alpha\), so \(B\) detections need \(n\) of order \(B/(b\alpha)\) records. The experiment below runs far outside that regime and still works, because its analyst is not trying to attack the holdout set.


48.7.5 Example: selecting features on a training set and confirming them on a holdout set
This is the experiment of Dwork et al. (2015), scaled down. A training set and a holdout set each have \(n = 2{,}000\) records with \(d = 5{,}000\) features, each \(+1\) or \(-1\), and a label \(\pm1\). In the first setting, every feature is independent of the label, so no classifier can beat 50%. In the second, 20 features agree with the label with probability \(\frac12 + 1.5/\sqrt n\), a correlation of \(3/\sqrt n = 0.067\). The correlation of a \(\pm1\) feature with a \(\pm1\) label is the average of their product, twice the agreement rate minus 1. It lies between \(-1\) and 1, and one record moves it by at most \(2/n\). The analyst works as follows.

Compute each feature’s correlation with the label on the training set, and keep the features where it exceeds \(1/\sqrt n\) in size.
Ask the holdout set for the correlations of those features, and keep the ones whose holdout correlation also exceeds \(1/\sqrt n\) in size, with the same sign.
Rank them by training correlation. For each \(m\) from 10 to 200, build the classifier \(\mathrm{sign}(\sum_j s_jx_j)\) over the top \(m\), where \(s_j\) is the sign of feature \(j\)’s correlation, and ask the holdout set for its accuracy.

The holdout queries are answered in three ways: exactly, with Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(1/\sqrt n\) (the sampling error of one correlation), or by Thresholdout with \(\tau = 4/\sqrt n\) and \(b = 1/\sqrt n\). The script computes each classifier’s true accuracy exactly, from the distribution of the features. Table 48.6 averages 10 repetitions for \(m = 200\).

Answered exactly, the holdout set reports 68% for a classifier that cannot beat 50%. Gaussian noise of the size of the sampling error removes only part of the bias, because the selection still sees the holdout correlations through modest noise. Thresholdout reports 52%, within its threshold of the truth. That threshold is \(\tau = 4/\sqrt n\) on a correlation, and since an accuracy is (1 + correlation)/2, it is \(2/\sqrt n = 0.045\) on an accuracy. Thresholdout works in two ways. Most holdout correlations in step 2 come back as training values, so nearly every feature that passed on the training set is confirmed, and the selection barely depends on the holdout set. Then the accuracy queries of step 3 have training accuracies far above their holdout accuracies, so they trigger detections and come back as noisy holdout values. The training accuracy differs between the three rows because each way of answering confirms a different set of features. With 20 informative features, Thresholdout’s report, 0.5471, is close to the true accuracy of 0.5312, and its selection is about as good as the others (Figure 48.4).
The privacy accounting tells the other half of the story. Each repetition asks about 1,587 holdout queries, and Thresholdout records 325.8 detections on average. A correlation moves by at most \(\Delta = 2/n\) when one record changes, and each detection costs \(2\Delta/b = 0.0894\) by Equation 48.23. The 325.8 detections of an average repetition therefore cost \(\varepsilon = 29.1\), plus \(\Delta/(2b) = 0.022\) for the run left open at the end. The Gaussian answers, of standard deviation \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt n\), cost \(\rho = \Delta^2/(2\sigma^2) = 2/n\) each, so all of them together have \(\rho = 1.59\), which is \(\varepsilon = 10.1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Neither is anywhere near the small \(\varepsilon\) the transfer theorem needs. The guarantee is a worst case. This analyst only screens features, and does not attack the holdout set the way the boosting attack does.






Figure 48.4: Accuracy of a classifier built from the top \(m\) features against \(m\): on the training set, as reported by a holdout set reused as is, with Gaussian noise and through Thresholdout, and the true accuracy. Left: every feature is noise. Right: 20 features carry signal.





48.7.6 Check yourself

Why may Thresholdout use the training set without any noise? (The guarantee protects the holdout records. The training set is independent of them, so answering from it reveals nothing about the holdout set.)
What happens if an analyst keeps asking queries after the budget of detections is spent? (The holdout set must stop answering, or answer only from the training set. Every further detection would add \(2\Delta/b\) to \(\varepsilon\).)

title: 48  Adaptive data analysis
section: 48.8 What it means for machine-learning practice
text:
48.8 What it means for machine-learning practice

48.8.1 Context
Few machine-learning projects call their workflow “adaptive data analysis”, but most are. Hyperparameter search, early stopping on a validation loss, choosing an architecture after looking at errors, competition leaderboards and benchmark test sets all ask a fixed set of records many questions chosen from earlier answers. What should you do differently?


48.8.2 Statement
Five rules follow from the earlier sections.

Count adaptive rounds, not queries. Questions chosen before any answer was seen are cheap: \(k\) of them cost \(\ln k\) (Equation 48.8). Choosing the best of \(k\) models trained without the validation set is in this class. The bias of its validation score is at most \(\sqrt{\ln(2k)/(2n)}\). The cost grows with every round in which answers shape the next questions.
Keep a final test set and use it once. One query is never adaptive. If the analysis has a few rounds, give each round its own part of the data (Section 48.4).
Answer through noise when the rounds are many. Gaussian noise with the transfer theorem (Section 48.6), or Thresholdout when there is a training set to compare with (Section 48.7), lets one holdout set answer many more adaptive queries than splitting.
Private tuning generalizes for free. A hyperparameter search that is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP in the validation set, as in Hyperparameter tuning and private selection, chooses its winner privately. By the transfer lemma, the winner’s validation score overstates its true score by at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1 + \delta\) on average.
For leaderboards, release less. Blum & Hardt’s (2015) Ladder reports a new score only when a submission beats the best so far by a margin, rounded to that margin. Its error against the population is of order \(n^{-1/3}\), times a factor that grows only like the cube root of \(\ln(kn)\), and it stops the boosting attack.



48.8.3 Derivation
Rules 1 and 2 are Equation 48.8 and Equation 48.12. A score of a model trained elsewhere is a query fixed before the validation set was drawn, and the winner’s overstatement is at most the largest error among the \(k\) scores, which Equation 48.8 bounds. Rule 3 is Equation 48.18 and Equation 48.23. Rule 4 is the transfer lemma Equation 48.13 applied to the search, whose output, the winning configuration, is a DP choice of a query: “is this record classified correctly by the winner?”. Rule 5 is the Ladder paper’s theorem. Section N.3 in the appendices proves it with Hoeffding’s inequality and a union bound over the leaderboard’s possible histories. Its idea is that a leaderboard that changes rarely reveals few bits, and few bits cannot encode much about individual records.


48.8.4 Interpretation
Worst case against typical case. The theory guards against an analyst who attacks the holdout set. Real practice is usually milder, and the evidence agrees. Recht, Roelofs, Schmidt & Shankar (2019) collected new test sets for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet after years of reuse of the old ones. Accuracy dropped, by 3 to 15 points on CIFAR-10 and 11 to 14 points on ImageNet, but the ranking of models was largely preserved. The authors attribute the drop to small differences between the old and new test images rather than to adaptive overfitting. Roelofs et al. (2019) found little adaptive overfitting across more than a hundred Kaggle competitions. One proposed reason is that similar models ask similar questions, and a question close to an earlier one reveals little new about the records (Mania et al. 2019). The theory still explains when reuse is dangerous: few records, many truly adaptive rounds, and an incentive to climb the leaderboard.
Splitting is often the practical answer. A training, validation and test split is splitting with three rounds. It is cheap because a typical project has few true rounds. Noise-based reuse earns its keep when the rounds are many and the data are scarce, such as in a long interactive analysis of a fixed medical cohort.
The same mechanism serves both goals. A DP mechanism used for adaptive data analysis also protects the people in the holdout set. Thresholdout’s guarantee is a privacy guarantee. A team that already pays for privacy in its validation set gets protection against adaptive overfitting at no extra cost.


48.8.5 Example: what a search on 10,000 validation records can claim
A team on a validation set of 10,000 records reports the best of 1,000 configurations. If the configurations were all trained and fixed before the validation set was opened, rule 1 bounds the expected optimism of the winner’s score by 0.0195. If the search was sequential, with each configuration chosen from the earlier scores, that bound no longer holds, and the adaptive bounds of Table 48.5 show that 10,000 records are far too few to certify 1,000 adaptive scores to within 0.05. The honest options are a fresh test set for the final model, or a private search whose \(\varepsilon\) bounds the optimism by rule 4. With \(\varepsilon = 0.05\) and a negligible \(\delta\), that bound is \(e^{0.05} - 1 = 0.051\).


48.8.6 Check yourself

A team uses early stopping on a validation set, checking the loss after every epoch for 100 epochs. Is that adaptive? (Yes, mildly. Each decision to continue depends on earlier validation losses. Here the questions are few and similar, so the bias is small, but the validation loss at the stopping point is still optimistic.)
Why does rule 4 not make every private search’s reported score trustworthy to within \(\varepsilon\)? (The lemma bounds the bias on average, not for one search, and it assumes the reported score was computed on the same records the search was private in. A score on other data is a different question.)

48.9 Code: check every number by simulation
The script code/part05-dp-ml/adaptive_data_analysis.py computes every number in this chapter and draws its figures. It runs the point-query attack, the boosting attack against an exact leaderboard, and the selection-bias experiment. It solves the three expected-error bounds for the sample size each needs, and runs the reusable-holdout experiment with exact population accuracies. From the repository root:

What to take from it. Exact answers break quickly under adaptive queries: the boosting attack grows like \(\sqrt k\), as the short argument predicts. The transfer lemma is valid but loose by a factor of about 8 for small \(\varepsilon\) and useless for \(\varepsilon\) near 1. The rates are real but carry large constants, so splitting wins for small numbers of queries. Finally, a typical analyst is much easier to defend against than the worst case, and Thresholdout removes most of the overfitting at privacy levels far outside its theorem.

Rules of thumb

Count adaptive rounds, not queries. The records needed grow like \(\ln k\) for queries fixed in advance, and for adaptive ones like \(k\) with splitting and \(\sqrt k\) with noise.

On a leaderboard, release improvements, not scores.

title: Appendix A — How much noise to add
text:
A.1 What differential privacy promises, and the privacy loss
Every differentially private release in this book answers the same practical question. You have a number, or a list of numbers, computed from people’s data, and you want to publish it with random noise added. How much noise is enough? This appendix answers that question from scratch for the mechanisms the book uses most. They are Laplace noise for pure differential privacy (DP), Gaussian noise for approximate DP, which allows a small failure probability, randomized response for a single bit, and the exponential mechanism for choosing among candidates. It assumes only that you know what a probability density, an average, a logarithm and an exponential are. Everything else, including the definition of differential privacy itself, is built up on the page.
The results sit together because they all rest on one quantity, the privacy loss. It measures how much more likely an output is when one person’s record is in the data than when it is changed. Each mechanism is calibrated by bounding the privacy loss, everywhere for pure DP and except on outputs of small total probability for approximate DP. The chapters derive the same formulas with more general tools. Table A.1 shows where each one is stated and used, and its symbols are defined in the sections it points to.
crumbs: A  How much noise to add

title: Appendix A — How much noise to add
text:
A.1.1 The question
Before you can ask how much noise is enough, you need to know what “enough” means. What exactly must the noisy output satisfy, and how do you check it for one mechanism?


A.1.2 The answer
A dataset is a collection of records, one per person. Two datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours if they differ in one person’s record. The book uses two versions of this. Under add/remove, \(D'\) is \(D\) with one record added or removed, so the two have different numbers of records. The size \(n\) is then itself protected, because the output must not reveal which size is true. Under replace-one, \(D'\) is \(D\) with one record changed, so \(n\) is the same on both and treated as public. This appendix uses add/remove unless it says otherwise, as the chapters do for counts and histograms.
A mechanism \(M\) is a randomized algorithm: run on a dataset \(D\), it returns a random output \(M(D)\). Write \(p_D(y)\) for the probability (or density) that \(M(D)\) outputs \(y\), and \(p_{D'}(y)\) for the same on the neighbour. An event \(S\) is any set of outputs, such as “the released count is above 1240”. The privacy parameter \(\varepsilon \ge 0\) says how much one record may change the probability of an event: by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), so a small \(\varepsilon\) means a factor close to 1. Formally, \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private (\(\varepsilon\)-DP) if for every pair of neighbours and every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S]. \tag{A.1}\]
The weaker version allows a small slack \(\delta\) on top of the factor. A mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private if, for every pair of neighbours and every event \(S\), \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{A.2}\] Read it as “the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) holds, except for a \(\delta\) of probability”. Both definitions must hold with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped too, since a neighbour of \(D'\) is \(D\).
The quantity that decides both is the privacy loss of an output \(y\). It is the log of how much more likely \(y\) is on \(D\) than on \(D'\): \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p_D(y)}{p_{D'}(y)}. \tag{A.3}\] A loss of 0 means \(y\) is equally likely on both datasets and says nothing about which one was used. A loss of \(\varepsilon\) means \(y\) is \(e^\varepsilon\) times more likely on \(D\). Two facts, proved below, turn the definitions into statements about \(L\). First, if \(L(y) \le \varepsilon\) for every output \(y\) and every ordered pair of neighbours, the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Second, call the outputs where the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) the bad set, \(B = \{y : L(y) > \varepsilon\}\). The smallest \(\delta\) that works for one pair at a given \(\varepsilon\) is the probability of the bad set on \(D\), minus \(e^\varepsilon\) times its probability on \(D'\): \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Pr[M(D) \in B] - e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in B]. \tag{A.4}\]


A.1.3 A worked example
Take a mechanism with three possible outputs, and the probabilities in Table A.2 on a dataset \(D\) and its neighbour \(D'\).

The largest ratio is 2.5, at output 1, so this pair is \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\varepsilon = \ln 2.5 = 0.9163\) and with nothing smaller. The script that comes with this appendix (see the Code section at the end) checks all 7 non-empty events, and none has a larger ratio of probabilities than 2.5.
Now ask for a smaller \(\varepsilon\), so that the factor \(e^\varepsilon\) is 2 instead of 2.5. Output 1 then breaks the factor, because its ratio is 2.5. It is the only output in the bad set, because only there is the ratio above 2. So Equation A.4 gives \(\delta = 0.5 - 2 \times 0.2 = 0.1\). As a check, the script computes \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] - 2\Pr[M(D') \in S]\) for every event \(S\). The largest value is indeed 0.1000, reached by the event that holds output 1 alone. Figure A.1 draws it: \(\delta\) is the red part of the first bar, the probability that sticks out above \(e^\varepsilon\) times the neighbour’s.






Figure A.1: The three-output example. Blue bars are the probabilities on \(D\), orange bars are \(e^\varepsilon = 2\) times the probabilities on \(D'\). Only output 1 has more probability on \(D\) than the orange bar allows, and the excess, in red, is the exact \(\delta = 0.1\).



Note that \(\delta\) is not the probability of the bad set, which here is 0.5. Most of that probability is allowed by the factor \(e^\varepsilon\), and only the excess counts.


A.1.4 Why it works

A pointwise bound gives the event bound. Suppose \(L(y) \le \varepsilon\) at every output, that is \(p_D(y) \le e^\varepsilon p_{D'}(y)\). The probability of an event is the sum of the probabilities of its outputs, so summing this inequality over the outputs in \(S\) gives \(\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S]\). For a density, the sum is an integral, and the same step works. So bounding the loss at every output is enough for \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
The slack for one event is a sum over its outputs. Moving the \(e^\varepsilon\) term to the left in Equation A.2, the event \(S\) needs \(\delta \ge \Pr[M(D) \in S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S]\). The right side is the sum, over the outputs \(y\) in \(S\), of \(p_D(y) - e^\varepsilon p_{D'}(y)\).
The worst event takes exactly the outputs with a positive term. To make that sum as large as possible, include every output whose term is positive and leave out every other one. A term is positive exactly when \(p_D(y) > e^\varepsilon p_{D'}(y)\), that is when \(L(y) > \varepsilon\). So the worst event is the bad set \(B\), and the smallest \(\delta\) that covers every event is its sum, Equation A.4.
The probability of the bad set is always a valid \(\delta\). Dropping the term \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in B]\), which is never negative, gives \(\delta(\varepsilon) \le \Pr[M(D) \in B] = \Pr[L > \varepsilon]\), where the loss is computed at an output drawn from \(M(D)\). This simpler bound is what the classic Gaussian formula of Section A.6 uses.



A.1.5 Checking it
The script lists every event of the three-output example and confirms both numbers by brute force. The largest ratio over events is 2.5000, the same as the largest ratio over single outputs. The largest excess at \(e^\varepsilon = 2\) is 0.1000, the same as the sum over the bad set. The probability of the bad set, 0.5000, is five times larger than the exact \(\delta\), which shows how loose step 4 can be.


A.1.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To check a mechanism, write down its privacy loss for a pair of neighbours. If the loss never exceeds \(\varepsilon\), you have \(\varepsilon\)-DP. If it does, the exact \(\delta\) is the excess mass of Equation A.4, maximized over pairs of neighbours.
The most common mistake is to apply \(\delta\) to each output instead of each event. “Every output has \(p_D(y) \le e^\varepsilon p_{D'}(y) + \delta\)” pays the slack once per output, and with many outputs that allows a mechanism that reveals everything (Section 18.2 gives the example). The second mistake is to forget the neighbouring relation. A replacement is a removal followed by an addition, so a guarantee under replace-one can cost up to twice the \(\varepsilon\) of one under add/remove. Every guarantee should therefore say which relation it uses. Section 18.4 writes the same exact \(\delta\) as a divergence, and Section D.1 explains what \(\varepsilon\) means for an attacker.

title: Appendix A — How much noise to add
section: A.2 Sensitivity: how much one person can move the answer
text:
A.2 Sensitivity: how much one person can move the answer

A.2.1 The question
Noise has to hide the effect of any one person. So before choosing the noise you need to know how far one person can move the answer. How do you compute that for the queries you actually run?


A.2.2 The answer
Let \(f\) be the query, a function that takes a dataset and returns \(d\) numbers. The sensitivity of \(f\) is the largest change that one person can cause, over all pairs of neighbours. Because the answer is a list of numbers, the change \(v = f(D) - f(D')\) is a list too, and its size can be measured in two ways. The \(\ell_1\) norm \(\|v\|_1 = |v_1| + \dots + |v_d|\) adds up the absolute changes, and Laplace noise is calibrated to it. The \(\ell_2\) norm \(\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{v_1^2 + \dots + v_d^2}\) is the straight-line length of the change, and Gaussian noise is calibrated to it. So there are two sensitivities, one for each norm: \[\Delta_1 = \max_{D \sim D'}\|f(D) - f(D')\|_1, \qquad \Delta_2 = \max_{D \sim D'}\|f(D) - f(D')\|_2. \tag{A.5}\] Table A.3 gives them for the standard queries. Values are clipped to a range \([0, C]\): any value above \(C\) is replaced by \(C\) before the query runs, so no record can contribute more than \(C\).

A.2.3 A worked example
A study releases the mean age of \(n = 1000\) patients, with ages clipped to \([0, 100]\), under replace-one. One patient’s age can change from 0 to 100 at most, so the sum moves by at most \(C = 100\). The mean is the sum divided by the fixed \(n\), so it moves by at most \(100/1000 = 0.1\) years. That is the sensitivity, \(\Delta_1 = \Delta_2 = 0.1\), however old the patients actually are.


A.2.4 Why it works
Each row asks what the single worst record can do.

Count. Adding or removing a person changes the count by exactly 1. Replacing a person leaves it unchanged, which is why under replace-one the count of all records is public anyway.
Sum of clipped values. Adding a person with value \(x\) in \([0, C]\) changes the sum by \(x\), at most \(C\). Replacing \(x\) by \(x'\) changes it by \(|x - x'|\), again at most \(C\). Both bounds are reached with \(x = C\) and \(x' = 0\).
Mean. Under replace-one, the mean is the sum divided by the public \(n\), so its sensitivity is the sum’s divided by \(n\), which is \(C/n\). Under add/remove the divisor changes too, and the change depends on \(n\), which is private. The script finds that for datasets of 1 to 3 values in \([0, 3]\) one record can move the mean by 1.5, from the mean of \(\{0\}\) to the mean of \(\{0, 3\}\). The usual fix is to release a noisy sum and a noisy count separately and divide them.
Histogram. Under add/remove the person lands in one bin, so one bin changes by 1. Both norms of the change are 1. Under replace-one one bin loses 1 and another gains 1, so the \(\ell_1\) norm is \(1 + 1 = 2\) and the \(\ell_2\) norm is \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt2\).
Counts that one person can all touch. Suppose each person answers \(d\) yes/no questions and you release the number of “yes” answers to each. One person who says yes to all \(d\) moves every count by 1, so the \(\ell_1\) norm of the change is \(d\) and the \(\ell_2\) norm is \(\sqrt{d \cdot 1^2} = \sqrt d\).

The last row shows why the two norms matter. When one person spreads their effect over many coordinates, \(\Delta_1\) grows like \(d\) but \(\Delta_2\) only like \(\sqrt d\). Since the noise is scaled to the sensitivity, as the next sections show, this is why Gaussian noise wins for long vectors (Section 20.5).


A.2.5 Checking it
The script lists every dataset of 1 to 3 records and every neighbour under both relations, and takes the largest change. Values are in \(\{0, 1, 2, 3\}\), so \(C = 3\) and the histogram has 4 bins, and the vector query uses \(d = 3\) questions. It reproduces every row of Table A.3. For example, the histogram has \(\ell_1\) sensitivity 1 under add/remove and 2 under replace-one, with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity 1.4142 under replace-one. The three counts have 3 and 1.7321. For the mean of exactly 3 records under replace-one it finds \(3/3 = 1.0000\).


A.2.6 Recipe and pitfalls
First fix the neighbouring relation, then ask what the worst single record can do to each coordinate, and add the changes up in the norm your noise needs. Compute the sensitivity before you look at the data, because it is a worst case over everything the domain allows, not over the data you hold.
Unbounded data has infinite sensitivity. If ages, incomes or gradients can be as large as anyone likes, one record can move a sum by any amount, and no finite noise hides it. Clip every value to a fixed range first, and calibrate to the clipping norm. A second pitfall is a person who contributes many records: if one person can add 5 ratings, a count of ratings has sensitivity 5 per person, not 1. Section C.1 applies the same reasoning to clipped gradients.

title: Appendix A — How much noise to add
text:
A.3 Laplace noise: scale \(\Delta_1/\varepsilon\) gives \(\varepsilon\)-DP

A.3.1 The question
You want to publish a count, or a few numbers, with pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. How wide must the Laplace noise be, and how far will the published answer be from the truth?


A.3.2 The answer
The Laplace distribution is a two-sided exponential, peaked at 0. With scale \(b\), its typical size, it puts density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\) at each value \(z\). The Laplace mechanism adds independent Laplace noise to each of the \(d\) numbers, with the scale set to the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity divided by \(\varepsilon\): \[M(D) = f(D) + (Z_1, \dots, Z_d), \qquad Z_i \sim \mathrm{Lap}(b), \qquad b = \frac{\Delta_1}{\varepsilon}. \tag{A.6}\] It is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. For one number, the error is the noise itself, and it exceeds a threshold \(\tau\) with probability exactly \(e^{-\tau/b}\). So with probability 0.95 the error is at most \(b\ln 20\).


A.3.3 A worked example
A hospital has 1,234 patients with diabetes. On the neighbouring dataset \(D'\) there is one more, so the two true counts are 1234 and 1235, and \(\Delta_1 = 1\). With \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), the scale is \(b = 1/0.5 = 2\).
The privacy loss at an output \(y\) is the log of the ratio of the two Laplace densities. The factors \(\frac{1}{2b}\) cancel, and the log of a ratio of exponentials is the difference of the exponents, so \[L(y) = \frac{|y - 1235| - |y - 1234|}{b}. \tag{A.7}\] Table A.4 evaluates it at five outputs.

At \(y = 1230\) the loss is \((5 - 4)/2 = 0.5\), and at \(y = 1240\) it is \((5 - 6)/2 = -0.5\). Below both true counts the ratio is stuck at \(e^{0.5} = 1.6487\), above both it is stuck at \(e^{-0.5} = 0.6065\), and between them it moves from one to the other. It never goes further, however far out the output lands.
For accuracy, the 95% error bound is \(b\ln 20 = 2 \times 2.9957 = 5.99\). So the published count is within about 6 of 1234 in 95% of releases. The bound scales with \(1/\varepsilon\), so it is 29.96 at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), where the scale is 10, and 3.00 at \(\varepsilon = 1\).


A.3.4 Why it works

Only the shift matters. Write \(a = f(D)\) and \(a' = f(D')\) for the two true answers. For one number, the privacy loss at \(y\) is \((|y - a'| - |y - a|)/b\), as in the example.
Bound it with the triangle inequality. The distance from \(y\) to \(a'\) is at most the distance from \(y\) to \(a\) plus the distance from \(a\) to \(a'\), so \(|y - a'| - |y - a| \le |a - a'|\). In the example, with \(y = 1230\), this says \(5 - 4 \le 1\).
The shift is at most the sensitivity. So \(L(y) \le |a - a'|/b \le \Delta_1/b\), and with \(b = \Delta_1/\varepsilon\) that is \(\varepsilon\). This holds at every output \(y\).
Several numbers. With \(d\) coordinates and independent noise, the density of the output is the product of the \(d\) coordinate densities. The log of a product is a sum, so the privacy loss is the sum of the coordinate losses. Each is at most \(|a_i - a'_i|/b\) by step 2, and their sum is at most \(\|a - a'\|_1/b \le \Delta_1/b = \varepsilon\).
Conclude. The loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) at every output, for every pair of neighbours in either order. So by step 1 of Section A.1 the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.
Accuracy. The absolute error \(|Z|\) has density \(\frac{1}{b}e^{-z/b}\) for \(z \ge 0\), twice the Laplace density on one side. Its integral from \(\tau\) to infinity is \(e^{-\tau/b}\). Setting \(e^{-\tau/b} = 0.05\) and solving gives \(\tau = b\ln 20\). The same density has average \(\int_0^\infty z\frac1be^{-z/b}\,\mathrm dz = b\), so the typical error is \(b\).

The bound of step 2 is reached, with equality, at every output below both true answers. So with a smaller scale \(b\) the loss there would be \(1/b > \varepsilon\), and those outputs would break the factor \(e^\varepsilon\). For the count above, the event “the output is at most 1234” has probability 0.5 on \(D\) and \(\frac12e^{-1/b} = 0.3033\) on \(D'\), a ratio of exactly \(e^{0.5}\).


A.3.5 Checking it
Figure A.2 draws the two densities and their ratio for the example. The ratio is flat at \(e^{\varepsilon}\) on the left and at \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) on the right, and it never leaves that band. Figure A.3 draws the privacy loss itself. It is flat outside the two true answers and a straight line between them, and it stays between \(-0.5\) and \(0.5\). On a grid of 70,001 outputs from 1200 to 1270, the script finds the loss in exactly \([-0.5000, 0.5000]\).






Figure A.2: Top: the output densities of a count released with Laplace noise of scale 2, on a dataset with true count 1234 and on its neighbour with 1235. Bottom: their ratio on a log scale, which stays between \(e^{-0.5}\) and \(e^{0.5}\) at every output and reaches both ends.









Figure A.3: The privacy loss \(L(y)\) of the same count against the released value, for Laplace noise of scale 2 and for Gaussian noise of standard deviation 2. The Laplace loss is flat outside the two true answers and never leaves \([-0.5, 0.5]\). The Gaussian loss is a straight line that leaves any band.



For several numbers, the script takes three yes/no counts that one person can all raise by 1, so \(\Delta_1 = 3\) and \(b = 3/0.5 = 6\). Over 100,000 random outputs, the largest privacy loss is 0.5000, the \(\varepsilon\) that step 4 promises.
For accuracy, a million draws of \(\mathrm{Lap}(2)\) give a mean absolute error of 2.0026 against the exact 2. Their 95th percentile is 5.9938 against \(b\ln 20 = 5.9915\). The error exceeds 5.9915 in a fraction 0.0501 of draws.


A.3.6 Recipe and pitfalls

Compute the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity \(\Delta_1\) under your neighbouring relation.
Set \(b = \Delta_1/\varepsilon\) and add independent \(\mathrm{Lap}(b)\) noise to every coordinate.
Quote the error: \(b\) on average, and \(b\ln 20\) with probability 0.95 for each coordinate.

The noise does not depend on the number of people, so a count of a million people and a count of ten get the same noise. Small groups are therefore expensive. Use fresh noise for every release, because reusing the same noise draw lets an analyst subtract it out. Releasing the same count \(k\) times with fresh noise costs \(k\varepsilon\), which Section B.1 derives. Section 20.2 adds the bound on the largest error over \(d\) coordinates.

title: Appendix A — How much noise to add
text:
A.4 Randomized response: one bit, \(\varepsilon\)-DP

A.4.1 The question
Each person holds one sensitive bit, such as “I have used a drug”, and nobody is trusted to see the true bits. How often should each person tell the truth, and how do you estimate the fraction of ones from the noisy reports?


A.4.2 The answer
Each person reports their true bit with probability \(t\) and the flipped bit with probability \(1 - t\), where \[t = \frac{e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon}. \tag{A.8}\] This is \(\varepsilon\)-DP under replace-one. If \(\bar y\) is the fraction of reported ones among \(n\) people, an unbiased estimate of the true fraction \(\pi\) of ones is \[\hat\pi = \frac{\bar y - (1 - t)}{2t - 1}, \qquad \operatorname{sd}(\hat\pi) = \frac{\sqrt{t(1 - t)}}{(2t - 1)\sqrt n}. \tag{A.9}\]


A.4.3 A worked example
At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(t = e^{0.5}/(1 + e^{0.5}) = 0.6225\). A true 1 is reported as 1 with probability 0.6225, and a true 0 is reported as 1 with probability 0.3775. Their ratio is \(0.6225/0.3775 = 1.6487 = e^{0.5}\).
Survey \(n = 1000\) people, of whom a fraction \(\pi = 0.3\) have the bit. The expected fraction of reported ones is \(0.3 \times 0.6225 + 0.7 \times 0.3775 = 0.4510\). The estimate subtracts \(1 - t = 0.3775\) and divides by \(2t - 1 = 0.2449\), which turns this back into 0.3. Its standard deviation is \(\sqrt{0.6225 \times 0.3775}/(0.2449\sqrt{1000}) = 0.0626\).


A.4.4 Why it works

Privacy. There are two inputs and two outputs. A report of 1 has probability \(t\) if the bit is 1 and \(1 - t\) if it is 0, so its privacy loss is \(\ln(t/(1 - t))\). With \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), the ratio is \(t/(1 - t) = e^\varepsilon\). A report of 0 has the inverse ratio, so \(|L| \le \varepsilon\) at both outputs.
Many people. People flip their own coins independently, so the probability of all the reports is a product with one factor per person. Under replace-one, neighbours differ in one person’s bit, so every other factor is the same on both datasets and cancels in the ratio. The loss is that one person’s loss.
The expected report. A person with bit 1 reports 1 with probability \(t\), and a person with bit 0 with probability \(1 - t\). Averaging over the population gives \(\mathbb E[\bar y] = \pi t + (1 - \pi)(1 - t) = (1 - t) + \pi(2t - 1)\).
Unbias it. Solving that equation for \(\pi\) gives \(\hat\pi\). It is a linear function of \(\bar y\), so its average is the true \(\pi\).
The spread. Each report is a 0/1 variable with variance \(t(1 - t)\), whatever the true bit, and the reports are independent. So \(\bar y\) has variance \(t(1 - t)/n\). Dividing by \(2t - 1\) divides the standard deviation by \(2t - 1\).



A.4.5 Checking it
Ten thousand simulated surveys give a mean estimate of 0.2996 and a standard deviation of 0.0629, against 0.3 and 0.0626 from the formulas.


A.4.6 Recipe and pitfalls
Set \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), collect the reports, and compute \(\hat\pi\). Expect an error of about \(1/(\varepsilon\sqrt n)\) for small \(\varepsilon\). The reason is that \(e^\varepsilon \approx 1 + \varepsilon\) there, so \(t \approx (1 + \varepsilon)/2\), which makes \(2t - 1 \approx \varepsilon/2\) and \(t(1 - t) \approx \frac14\).
The price of trusting nobody is large. If one trusted party could see the true bits, it could add \(\mathrm{Lap}(1/\varepsilon)\) noise to their count instead, and the error on the fraction would fall like \(1/n\), not like \(1/\sqrt n\). The guarantee also holds only under replace-one. Under add/remove the neighbour has one report more or fewer, and the number of reports, which is published, shows the difference at once. Section 18.3 compares the two designs, and Warner’s original survey design is the same mechanism.

section: A.5 The exponential mechanism: choosing the best candidate
text:
A.5 The exponential mechanism: choosing the best candidate

A.5.1 The question
Sometimes the output is not a number but a choice: the best model, the most common diagnosis, the winner of a vote. Adding noise to a name makes no sense. How do you choose privately, and how good is the choice?


A.5.2 The answer
Fix a list of candidates \(\mathcal R\) in advance, and write \(|\mathcal R|\) for their number. For each candidate \(r\), a score \(u(D, r)\) says how good it is on dataset \(D\), where higher is better. Let \(\Delta u\) be the sensitivity of the score, the most that one person can change any one candidate’s score.
The exponential mechanism gives each candidate a weight \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D, r)/(2\Delta u))\), which grows with its score. It then picks a candidate with probability equal to its share of the total weight \(W(D)\), the normalizer: \[\Pr[M_E(D) = r] = \frac{\exp\big(\frac{\varepsilon\,u(D, r)}{2\Delta u}\big)}{W(D)}, \qquad W(D) = \sum_{s \in \mathcal R}\exp\Big(\frac{\varepsilon\,u(D, s)}{2\Delta u}\Big). \tag{A.10}\] Dividing by the normalizer makes the probabilities add up to 1. The mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, and its choice is rarely far below the best score \(\mathrm{OPT}(D)\). For every \(t > 0\), \[\Pr\Big[u(D, M_E(D)) \le \mathrm{OPT}(D) - \frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln |\mathcal R| + t)\Big] \le e^{-t}. \tag{A.11}\]


A.5.3 A worked example
Six people vote among options A, B, C and D. On \(D\) the counts are \((3, 2, 1, 0)\), and on the neighbour \(D'\) one more person votes for B, so the counts are \((3, 3, 1, 0)\). The score is the count, so \(\Delta u = 1\). Take \(\varepsilon = 1\), so each weight is \(e^{u/2}\).
On \(D\) the weights are \(e^{1.5} = 4.4817\), \(e^{1} = 2.7183\), \(e^{0.5} = 1.6487\) and \(e^0 = 1\), which sum to \(W(D) = 9.8487\). So A is chosen with probability \(4.4817/9.8487 = 0.4551\). On \(D'\) B’s weight rises to \(e^{1.5}\) and the normalizer to \(W(D') = 11.6121\). Table A.5 lists all four probabilities.



Table A.5: The exponential mechanism with \(\varepsilon = 1\) on a vote and its neighbour with one more vote for B.

For A, C and D the score did not change, so the ratio is just the change in the normalizer, \(11.6121/9.8487 = 1.1790\). For B, its own weight is also \(e^{1/2}\) times larger on \(D'\) than on \(D\), so its ratio is \(1.1790 \times e^{-1/2} = 1.1790 \times 0.6065 = 0.7151\). The largest privacy loss on this pair is \(|\ln 0.7151| = 0.3353\), well below \(\varepsilon = 1\).


A.5.4 Why it works
Privacy. The probability of \(r\) is a weight divided by a total, and one person can change both. So split the ratio of the probabilities on \(D\) and \(D'\) into two factors: \[\frac{\Pr[M_E(D) = r]}{\Pr[M_E(D') = r]} = \exp\Big(\frac{\varepsilon\big(u(D, r) - u(D', r)\big)}{2\Delta u}\Big) \cdot \frac{W(D')}{W(D)}. \tag{A.12}\]

The own-weight factor. One person changes \(r\)’s score by at most \(\Delta u\), so the exponent is at most \(\varepsilon\Delta u/(2\Delta u) = \varepsilon/2\). The factor is at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\).
The normalizer factor. Every candidate’s score on \(D'\) is at most \(\Delta u\) above its score on \(D\), so every term of \(W(D')\) is at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) times the matching term of \(W(D)\). Adding up the terms, \(W(D') \le e^{\varepsilon/2}W(D)\).
Multiply. The ratio is at most \(e^{\varepsilon/2} \cdot e^{\varepsilon/2} = e^\varepsilon\). The candidate and the pair were arbitrary, and the same argument works with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped, so by step 1 of Section A.1 the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP.

The 2 in the exponent is there because both factors can be large at once. One person can raise \(r\)’s score and lower all the others, so each factor needs its own half of the budget.
Utility. Call a candidate poor if its score is at least \(c\) below the best.

Poor candidates are light. Each has weight at most \(e^{\varepsilon(\mathrm{OPT} - c)/(2\Delta u)}\), since the weight grows with the score.
The normalizer is heavy. It contains the weight of a best candidate, so \(W(D) \ge e^{\varepsilon\,\mathrm{OPT}/(2\Delta u)}\).
Divide. There are at most \(|\mathcal R|\) poor candidates, so together they have probability at most \(|\mathcal R|\,e^{\varepsilon(\mathrm{OPT} - c)/(2\Delta u)}/e^{\varepsilon\,\mathrm{OPT}/(2\Delta u)} = |\mathcal R|\,e^{-\varepsilon c/(2\Delta u)}\).
Solve for \(c\). Setting \(|\mathcal R|\,e^{-\varepsilon c/(2\Delta u)} = e^{-t}\) and taking logs gives \(c = \frac{2\Delta u}{\varepsilon}(\ln |\mathcal R| + t)\).



A.5.5 Checking it
Figure A.4 shows the vote. On the right, each ratio is drawn as its two factors, and both stay below \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\). Only B’s score moved, so for A, C and D the own-weight factor is exactly 1.






Figure A.4: Left: the probability that the exponential mechanism with \(\varepsilon = 1\) chooses each option, on a vote with counts (3, 2, 1, 0) and on its neighbour with one more vote for B. Right: each ratio of the two probabilities, split into the change of the option’s own weight and the change of the normalizer. Each factor stays below \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\), so the ratio stays below \(e^\varepsilon\).



The utility bound is weak for so small an example. The probability of choosing C or D, at least \(c = 2\) below A, is 0.2689. Step 3 with \(|\mathcal R| = 4\) bounds it by \(4e^{-1} = 1.4715\), which says nothing. It helps when there are many candidates. Take 50 models scored by their correct predictions, \(900, 899, \dots, 851\), so that \(\Delta u = 1\). With \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(t = 3\), the bound says the gap exceeds \(2(\ln 50 + 3) = 13.82\) with probability at most \(e^{-3} = 0.0498\). The exact probability is \(9.12\times10^{-4}\), much smaller, because most models are far below the best and much lighter than the bound assumes.


A.5.6 Recipe and pitfalls

Fix the list of candidates before looking at the data, and choose a score \(u(D, r)\).
Find the score’s sensitivity \(\Delta u\).
Sample \(r\) with probability proportional to \(\exp(\varepsilon u(D, r)/(2\Delta u))\).

The candidate list must not depend on the data, because the proof compares the same list on \(D\) and \(D'\). Watch numerical overflow too: subtract the largest score before taking exponentials, which changes no probability. When every score moves the same way under each change of one person, as counts under add/remove do, the two factors cannot both be large, and the 2 can be dropped (Section 22.1). Section 22.2 adds the expected gap and the applications.

title: Appendix A — How much noise to add
section: A.6 Gaussian noise, the classic formula
text:
A.6 Gaussian noise, the classic formula

A.6.1 The question
Gaussian noise is calibrated to the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity, which is much smaller than the \(\ell_1\) sensitivity for long vectors such as gradients. But its privacy loss has no upper limit, so it can never give pure \(\varepsilon\)-DP. How much Gaussian noise gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, and where does the textbook formula come from?


A.6.2 The answer
Add independent normal noise with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\) to each coordinate. For \(0 < \varepsilon < 1\) and \(0 < \delta < 1\), the Gaussian mechanism with \[\sigma = \frac{\Delta_2\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}}{\varepsilon} \tag{A.13}\] is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The proof below needs \(\delta \le 0.7448\), which every useful \(\delta\) satisfies.


A.6.3 A worked example
Release the diabetes count with \(\Delta_2 = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Then \(\ln(1.25/10^{-5}) = \ln 125{,}000 = 11.7361\), and its double has square root \(c = \sqrt{23.4722} = 4.8448\). So \(\sigma = 4.8448/0.5 = 9.6896\). The 95% error of normal noise is 1.96 standard deviations, here 18.99, against 5.99 for Laplace noise at the same \(\varepsilon\). For a single count Laplace noise is better, and Gaussian noise pays off only for long vectors.


A.6.4 Why it works
The plan is to find the privacy loss, which turns out to be a normal random variable. Then show that it exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\), and that this is enough. Write \(\Phi(x)\) for the standard normal cumulative distribution function, the probability that a normal variable with mean 0 and standard deviation 1 is below \(x\), and \(\varphi(x) = e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\) for its density.

The privacy loss is a straight line in the noise. Take one number, with true answers \(a\) on \(D\) and \(a + s\) on \(D'\), where \(s\) is the shift between them. An output from \(M(D)\) is \(y = a + z\), where \(z\) is the noise. Its density on \(D\) is proportional to \(e^{-z^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) and on \(D'\) to \(e^{-(z - s)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), because \(y\) sits \(z - s\) away from \(D'\)’s answer. The log of the ratio is the difference of the exponents: \[L = \frac{(z - s)^2 - z^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{s^2 - 2sz}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{A.14}\]
So the loss is normal. The noise \(z\) is normal with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma\), and \(L\) is a constant minus a multiple of \(z\). So \(L\) is normal with mean \(s^2/(2\sigma^2)\) and standard deviation \(2s\sigma/(2\sigma^2) = s/\sigma\). Write \(\mu = s/\sigma\) for the shift measured in noise standard deviations. Then \(L\) has mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\). For a vector the same holds with \(s = \|f(D) - f(D')\|_2\). The reason is that expanding the squared distances in the same way leaves only the noise’s component along the direction of the shift, and that component is a single normal number with standard deviation \(\sigma\).
A small chance of a large loss is enough. Let \(B\) be the bad set, the outputs with \(L > \varepsilon\), and suppose its probability on \(D\) is at most \(\delta\). Split any event \(S\) into its part inside \(B\) and its part outside. The part inside has probability at most \(\delta\), because it is part of \(B\). On the part outside, every output has \(p_D(y) \le e^\varepsilon p_{D'}(y)\), so summing over it gives at most \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S]\). Adding the two parts gives \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta, \tag{A.15}\] which is Equation A.2. The pair in the other order has the same loss distribution, by the symmetry of the normal curve, so it needs nothing new.
The bad event is a normal tail. Standardize the loss by subtracting its mean \(\mu^2/2\) and dividing by its standard deviation \(\mu\). The result is a standard normal variable, and \(L > \varepsilon\) exactly when it exceeds the point \(t = (\varepsilon - \mu^2/2)/\mu = \varepsilon/\mu - \mu/2\). By the symmetry of the normal curve, \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(-t)\). A larger shift makes \(t\) smaller and the tail heavier, so the worst pair has the largest shift, \(s = \Delta_2\).
Put in the formula. Write \(c = \sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\), so Equation A.13 is \(\sigma = c\Delta_2/\varepsilon\). Then \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma = \varepsilon/c\), and \[t = \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2} = c - \frac{\varepsilon}{2c}. \tag{A.16}\]
Bound the normal tail. For \(t > 0\), every point \(z\) beyond \(t\) has \(z/t \ge 1\), so the tail \(\int_t^\infty\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz\) is at most \(\int_t^\infty\frac{z}{t}\varphi(z)\,\mathrm dz\). The derivative of \(\varphi(z)\) is \(-z\varphi(z)\), so the second integral equals \(\varphi(t)/t\). This is the Mills-ratio bound: \[\Phi(-t) \le \frac{e^{-t^2/2}}{t\sqrt{2\pi}}. \tag{A.17}\]
Expand \(t^2\). Squaring step 5 gives \(t^2 = c^2 - \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2/(4c^2)\), which is at least \(c^2 - \varepsilon\). So \(e^{-t^2/2} \le e^{-c^2/2}e^{\varepsilon/2}\). By the definition of \(c\), \(e^{-c^2/2} = \delta/1.25\). Together with step 6, \[\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le \delta \cdot \frac{e^{\varepsilon/2}}{1.25\sqrt{2\pi}\,t}. \tag{A.18}\]
This is where 1.25 and \(\varepsilon < 1\) come in. The bound is at most \(\delta\) when the fraction is at most 1, that is when \(t \ge e^{\varepsilon/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi})\). For \(\varepsilon < 1\), the right side is below \(e^{1/2}/(1.25\sqrt{2\pi}) = 0.5262\). It remains to show that \(t\) is that large. For \(\varepsilon < 1\), step 5 gives \(t = c - \varepsilon/(2c) \ge c - 1/(2c)\). This lower bound grows with \(c\), and it equals 0.5262 at \(c = 1.0176\), the positive root of \(c^2 - 0.5262c - \frac12 = 0\). Since \(c\) grows as \(\delta\) shrinks, \(c \ge 1.0176\) holds whenever \(\delta \le 1.25e^{-1.0176^2/2} = 0.7448\). So the constant 1.25 absorbs the factor \(e^{\varepsilon/2}/(t\sqrt{2\pi})\), and the condition \(\varepsilon < 1\) keeps \(e^{\varepsilon/2}\) below \(e^{1/2}\).

Step 3 is the reason a tail probability is enough. The rare outputs with a large loss are paid for by \(\delta\), and every other output keeps the factor \(e^\varepsilon\).


A.6.5 Checking it
The proof made three approximations in a row. Step 4 replaced the exact \(\delta\) by the bad-set probability, step 6 replaced that by the Mills bound, and step 7 loosened it further with the constants. Figure A.5 follows each of them for \(\varepsilon\) up to 1 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) the numbers are in Table A.6.



Table A.6: Each step of the classic proof at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), \(\Delta_2 = 1\), where \(t = 4.7932\).









Quantity at the classic \(\sigma = 9.6896\)
Value




Target \(\delta\)
\(10^{-5}\)


After expanding \(t^2\), step 7
\(8.55\times10^{-7}\)

\(8.54\times10^{-7}\)


Bad event \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(-t)\), step 4

So the classic \(\sigma\) delivers a \(\delta\) 622 times smaller than asked for. The constants of step 8 cost a factor of 11.7, and dropping the correction term of Equation A.4 costs a factor of 51.0. The Mills ratio itself costs almost nothing.






Figure A.5: The \(\delta\) that the classic \(\sigma\) delivers at each \(\varepsilon\) up to 1, for a target \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), at each step of the proof. The bound after step 7, the Mills bound and the bad-event probability nearly coincide, about ten times below the target. The exact \(\delta\) is a further 25.8 times smaller at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and 505.9 times smaller at \(\varepsilon = 0.05\).





A.6.6 Recipe and pitfalls

Compute the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2\).
For \(\varepsilon < 1\), set \(\sigma = \Delta_2\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}/\varepsilon\).
Add independent normal noise with that \(\sigma\) to every coordinate.

The formula is valid but wasteful, as the table shows. The proof says nothing for \(\varepsilon \ge 1\), and Section A.7 shows that the formula eventually becomes wrong there. Choose \(\delta\) much smaller than \(1/n\). A mechanism that publishes each person’s record in full with probability \(\delta\) satisfies the definition, and with \(n\) people and \(\delta = 1/n\) it publishes about one person’s record every time. Section 20.3 gives the same proof with the vector case in full.
