title: Appendix A — How much noise to add
section: A.7 Gaussian noise, the exact calibration
text:
A.7 Gaussian noise, the exact calibration

A.7.1 The question
The classic formula overshoots by a large factor, and it says nothing for \(\varepsilon \ge 1\). What is the smallest \(\sigma\) that gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, for any \(\varepsilon\)?


A.7.2 The answer
Measure the sensitivity in units of the noise, \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\). The Gaussian mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta \ge \delta(\varepsilon)\), where \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac{\Delta_2}{2\sigma} - \frac{\varepsilon\sigma}{\Delta_2}\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac{\Delta_2}{2\sigma} - \frac{\varepsilon\sigma}{\Delta_2}\Big) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{A.19}\] This \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) falls as \(\sigma\) grows. So the smallest \(\sigma\) for a target \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is the one solution of \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \delta\), which a computer finds by bisection.


A.7.3 A worked example
To see the two terms, take a case where both terms are large enough to see, \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\). The first term is \(\Phi(0.5 - 1) = \Phi(-0.5) = 0.3085\), the probability of the bad set on \(D\). The second is \(e \cdot \Phi(-1.5) = 0.1816\), the correction. Their difference is the exact \(\delta = 0.1269\).
Now the count again, with \(\Delta_2 = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Bisection finds \(\sigma = 7.0318\), and putting it back into Equation A.19 gives \(\delta = 1.000\times10^{-5}\). The classic formula gave 9.6896, which is 1.378 times more noise than needed. At the classic \(\sigma\) the true \(\delta\) is \(1.61\times10^{-8}\). With the exact \(\sigma\) the 95% error is \(1.96 \times 7.0318 = 13.78\), against 18.99 with the classic one.


A.7.4 Why it works

Start from the exact \(\delta\). By Equation A.4, the smallest \(\delta\) for one pair of neighbours is \(\Pr[M(D) \in B] - e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in B]\), where \(B\) is the set of outputs with \(L > \varepsilon\).
The first term. Step 4 of Section A.6 found \(\Pr[M(D) \in B] = \Phi(-t)\) with \(t = \varepsilon/\mu - \mu/2\), which is \(\Phi(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu)\).
The second term. Measure the output in units of \(\sigma\), starting from \(D\)’s true answer. The bad set is the outputs below \(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\), by step 4 of Section A.6. On \(D'\) the output is centred at \(\mu\) instead of 0, so it falls below that point with probability \(\Phi(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu - \mu) = \Phi(-\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu)\).
Combine. Subtracting \(e^\varepsilon\) times the second term from the first gives Equation A.19 for this pair.
The largest shift is the worst pair, and more noise always helps. The plan is to show that \(\delta\) grows with \(\mu\), by computing its derivative. Write \(\alpha = \mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\) and \(\beta = -\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\) for the two arguments, so that \(\delta = \Phi(\alpha) - e^\varepsilon\Phi(\beta)\). Their derivatives in \(\mu\) are \(\frac12 + \varepsilon/\mu^2\) and \(-\frac12 + \varepsilon/\mu^2\), which differ by exactly 1. Also \(\alpha^2 - \beta^2 = (\alpha - \beta)(\alpha + \beta) = \mu \cdot (-2\varepsilon/\mu) = -2\varepsilon\), so \(\varphi(\beta) = e^{-\varepsilon}\varphi(\alpha)\). The derivative of \(\delta\) in \(\mu\) is therefore \[\varphi(\alpha)\Big(\frac12 + \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu^2}\Big) - e^\varepsilon e^{-\varepsilon}\varphi(\alpha)\Big(-\frac12 + \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu^2}\Big) = \varphi(\alpha) > 0. \tag{A.20}\] So \(\delta\) grows with the shift \(\mu\), and the worst pair of neighbours is the one with the largest shift, \(\Delta_2\). And since \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\), a larger \(\sigma\) means a smaller \(\mu\) and a smaller \(\delta\).
“Exactly when.” The worst pair needs \(\delta \ge \delta(\varepsilon)\) by step 1, and every other pair needs less by step 5. So \(\delta \ge \delta(\varepsilon)\) is both necessary and enough.
Solve by bisection. As \(\sigma\) grows from near 0 to very large, \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) falls steadily from near 1 to near 0, so it crosses the target exactly once. Bisection keeps an interval of \(\sigma\) values with the crossing inside, evaluates \(\delta\) at its midpoint, and keeps the half that still contains the crossing. Each step halves the interval, and the script takes its midpoints in \(\ln\sigma\) because \(\sigma\) can range over many orders of magnitude.

Intuitively, step 5 says that adding more noise can only make the two datasets harder to tell apart. A Gaussian mechanism with a larger \(\sigma\) is the one with a smaller \(\sigma\) plus extra independent noise, and anything you can detect after adding that extra noise yourself, you could detect before.


A.7.5 Checking it
Figure A.6 draws the derivation at \(\mu = 1\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\). On the left, the bad set is the outputs left of \(-0.5\sigma\), where the density on \(D\) rises above \(e^\varepsilon\) times the density on \(D'\). The red area between the two curves is \(\delta\), and the orange area under it is the correction that the classic proof throws away. On the right, the same \(\delta\) appears as the part of the privacy loss distribution beyond \(L = \varepsilon\).






Figure A.6: The exact \(\delta\) of the Gaussian mechanism at \(\mu = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\). Left: the output density on \(D\) and \(e^\varepsilon\) times the density on \(D'\), with the output measured in units of \(\sigma\). On the bad set, left of the dotted line, the red excess is \(\delta = 0.1269\) and the orange area is the correction \(e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \in B] = 0.1816\). Right: the same excess in terms of the privacy loss, which is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and standard deviation \(\mu\) on \(D\).



The script checks the closed form in three ways. First, it integrates the excess \(p_D - e^\varepsilon p_{D'}\) over the bad set numerically (by Simpson’s rule, on a fine grid), and at \(\mu = 1\), \(\varepsilon = 1\) this gives 0.1269. The same \(\delta\) is also the average of \((1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\) over losses drawn on \(D\), where \((x)_+\) means \(\max(x, 0)\) (Section 18.4 shows why). A Monte Carlo average of it over a million random draws gives 0.1270. Second, over 22 pairs of \(\varepsilon\) and \(\mu\), the largest relative difference between the closed form and the numerical integral is \(3.1\times10^{-6}\). Third, a numerical derivative in \(\mu\) agrees with \(\varphi(\alpha)\) of step 5 to within \(10^{-9}\) on a grid of 16 pairs.

A.7.6 Recipe and pitfalls

Compute the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2\).
Solve \(\delta(\varepsilon) = \delta\) for \(\mu\) by bisection, using Equation A.19 with \(\Phi(x)\) computed as 0.5 * math.erfc(-x / math.sqrt(2)) in Python. Then set \(\sigma = \Delta_2/\mu\).
Check the answer by putting \(\sigma\) back into Equation A.19.

Because only \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\) enters, you can solve once for \(\Delta_2 = 1\) and scale: at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the noise is \(3.7306\,\Delta_2\). Never use the classic formula for \(\varepsilon \ge 1\). One Gaussian mechanism satisfies a whole curve of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pairs, so quote \(\mu\) or the curve rather than one pair. Section 20.4 derives the same formula through a divergence between the two output distributions, and Section B.3 shows that many Gaussian releases combine into one. Section A.8 works through the formula by hand and in code, and shows how the noise changes when you move \(\varepsilon\), \(\delta\) or the number of releases.

A.8 How ε, δ, σ and the sensitivity trade off

A.8.1 The question
The last section gave a formula for the exact \(\delta\) of the Gaussian mechanism and a way to solve it for \(\sigma\). In practice you start from what you can give up, a privacy budget of \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\), or from the noise you can afford, and you want to know how the four quantities move together. They are the privacy parameter \(\varepsilon\), the slack \(\delta\), the noise standard deviation \(\sigma\) and the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\Delta_2\). How do you compute \(\delta\) from normal probabilities, by hand and in code? And if you halve \(\varepsilon\), make \(\delta\) a thousand times smaller or release the answer ten times, how much more noise do you need?


A.8.2 The answer
Everything follows from the exact formula of Section A.7. Write \(\Phi(x)\) for the probability that a standard normal variable is below \(x\), and \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\) for the sensitivity measured in units of the noise. The mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta\) is at least \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big). \tag{A.21}\] Six facts about it answer the questions.

Only the ratio \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\) matters. The formula sees \(\Delta_2\) and \(\sigma\) only through \(\mu\). Doubling the sensitivity and doubling \(\sigma\) therefore gives the same guarantee, and you can solve once for \(\Delta_2 = 1\) and multiply the resulting \(\sigma\) by \(\Delta_2\).
One \(\sigma\) gives a whole curve. For a fixed \(\mu\), \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows. So a Gaussian mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon\) at once, not for one pair.
The noise falls roughly like \(1/\varepsilon\), then more slowly. Write \(z_\delta\) for the point a standard normal variable exceeds with probability \(\delta\), so that \(\Phi(-z_\delta) = \delta\). The exact \(\delta\) is never more than the probability of the bad set, a normal tail. So asking only that this tail be \(\delta\) gives a simple tail rule, which always gives enough noise: \[\sigma_{\text{tail}} = \Delta_2\,\frac{z_\delta + \sqrt{z_\delta^2 + 2\varepsilon}}{2\varepsilon}, \tag{A.22}\] The rule is about \(\Delta_2 z_\delta/\varepsilon\) when \(\varepsilon\) is small compared with \(z_\delta^2/2\), and about \(\Delta_2/\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\) when it is large. At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) it uses 1.39 times the exact noise for \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). The excess shrinks as \(\varepsilon\) grows, to 1.02 times at \(\varepsilon = 32\).
The noise grows only slowly as \(\delta\) shrinks. The point \(z_\delta\) grows like \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\), and by fact 3 the noise is roughly proportional to \(z_\delta\). Near \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), each factor of 10 in \(\delta\) adds only about 13% to 15% more noise at \(\varepsilon\) of 0.5 or 1.
Repeating costs \(\sqrt k\). Releasing \(k\) answers, each with sensitivity \(\Delta_2\) and its own independent noise \(\sigma\), gives exactly the guarantee of one release with \(\mu\sqrt k\). Then \(k\) releases need \(\sqrt k\) times the noise of one for the same \((\varepsilon, \delta)\).
Choose \(\delta\) from the number of people \(n\). Take \(\delta\) well below \(1/n\), for example \(1/n^2\). The reason, shown in step 7 below, is that a mechanism that publishes each record with probability \(\delta\) is \((0, \delta)\)-DP, and with \(\delta = 1/n\) it publishes someone’s record with probability about 0.63.



A.8.3 A worked example
By hand. Take \(\Delta_2 = 1\), \(\sigma = 4\) and \(\varepsilon = 1\). Table A.8 follows the formula one number at a time, for a dataset \(D\) and a neighbour \(D'\). First compute \(\mu\), then the two arguments of \(\Phi\), which Section A.7 called \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Then look up \(\Phi\) of each in a normal table or compute it, and finally combine them. The second term, \(e^\varepsilon\Phi(\beta)\), is the correction that turns the probability of the bad set into the exact \(\delta\).

By computer. Most languages have no \(\Phi\) built in, but they all have the complementary error function \(\operatorname{erfc}\), which Python calls math.erfc. In terms of it, \[\Phi(x) = \tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}\big(-x/\sqrt2\big), \qquad 1 - \Phi(x) = \tfrac12\operatorname{erfc}\big(x/\sqrt2\big). \tag{A.23}\] Use these forms, and never compute a small tail as 1 minus something close to 1. A double-precision number carries about 16 significant digits. So when \(\Phi(x)\) is within \(10^{-16}\) of 1, the subtraction \(1 - \Phi(x)\) keeps none of the digits that matter. Table A.9 shows this at \(x = 8\) and \(x = 9\). The textbook form \(\Phi(x) = \frac12(1 + \operatorname{erf}(x/\sqrt2))\), with the plain error function \(\operatorname{erf}\), has the same problem for negative \(x\), because \(\operatorname{erf}\) is then close to \(-1\).

Even with \(\operatorname{erfc}\), the formula subtracts two nearly equal terms, and a subtraction loses digits too. The last column says how many. When the first term is \(r\) times the difference, the subtraction loses about \(\log_{10} r\) digits. Here \(r\) is at most 72, and \(\log_{10} 72 = 1.86\), so the subtraction loses at most 2 of the 16 digits. To check this independently, the script also integrates the excess \(p_D - e^\varepsilon p_{D'}\) over the bad set directly. Measure the noise in units of \(\sigma\) as \(y\), so that its privacy loss is \(L(y) = \mu^2/2 - \mu y\). The integrand is then \(\varphi(y)\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L(y)})\), which is never a difference of two tails. That integral agrees with the \(\operatorname{erfc}\) formula to about one part in \(10^{12}\) at all four targets.
Scaling. Now take a sum of values clipped to \([0, 2]\), so that \(\Delta_2 = 2\), with \(\sigma = 8\). The ratio is still \(\mu = 0.25\), so \(\delta\) is again \(2.9243\times10^{-6}\), and the same holds for \(\Delta_2 = 0.5\) with \(\sigma = 2\).
The curve. The same \(\sigma = 4\) gives a whole curve of guarantees. It is \((1, 2.92\times10^{-6})\)-DP, and also \((2, 5.09\times10^{-17})\)-DP and \((0.9263, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Figure A.8 draws the curve for four noise levels. Each falls steeply as \(\varepsilon\) grows, and each crosses \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) at its own \(\varepsilon\).






Figure A.8: The exact \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of the Gaussian mechanism against \(\varepsilon\), on a log scale, for four noise levels \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\). A single \(\sigma\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta(\varepsilon))\)-DP for every \(\varepsilon\) on its curve. The dots mark the \(\varepsilon\) each one gives at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\): 0.93 for \(\sigma = 4\Delta_2\), 1.99 for \(2\Delta_2\), 4.38 for \(\Delta_2\) and 10.00 for \(\Delta_2/2\).





A.8.4 Why it works

Only \(\mu\) matters. In the formula, \(\Delta_2\) and \(\sigma\) appear only in \(\mu/2\) and \(\varepsilon/\mu\). So any sensitivity and noise with the same ratio give the same curve. In particular, the smallest \(\sigma\) for a target is \(\Delta_2\) times the smallest \(\sigma\) for a sensitivity of 1. The reason behind it is that measuring the output in units of \(\sigma\) turns every Gaussian mechanism into one with noise 1 and shift \(\mu\).
The curve falls. Write \(\alpha = \mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\) and \(\beta = -\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu\) as before, and \(\varphi\) for the standard normal density. Step 5 of Section A.7 showed that \(e^\varepsilon\varphi(\beta) = \varphi(\alpha)\). Both arguments fall by \(1/\mu\) for each unit of \(\varepsilon\), so differentiating in \(\varepsilon\) gives \[\frac{\mathrm d\delta}{\mathrm d\varepsilon} = -\frac{\varphi(\alpha)}{\mu} - e^\varepsilon\Phi(\beta) + \frac{e^\varepsilon\varphi(\beta)}{\mu} = -e^\varepsilon\,\Phi(\beta) < 0. \tag{A.24}\] The first and last terms cancel, and what is left is negative. So a larger \(\varepsilon\) always comes with a smaller \(\delta\), and one mechanism traces a curve. The same step 5 showed that \(\delta\) grows with \(\mu\). More noise means a smaller \(\mu\), so it lowers the whole curve.
A safe rule from the bad set alone. Step 4 of Section A.1 showed that the exact \(\delta\) is never more than the probability of the bad set, which step 4 of Section A.6 computed: \[\Pr[L > \varepsilon] = \Phi(\alpha). \tag{A.25}\] So any \(\sigma\) that makes \(\Phi(\alpha) = \delta\) is enough. Since \(\Phi(-z_\delta) = \delta\), that means \(\alpha = -z_\delta\), which is \(\mu/2 - \varepsilon/\mu = -z_\delta\). Multiplying by \(2\mu\) gives the quadratic \(\mu^2 + 2z_\delta\mu - 2\varepsilon = 0\), whose positive root is \(\mu = \sqrt{z_\delta^2 + 2\varepsilon} - z_\delta\). Then \(\sigma = \Delta_2/\mu\), and multiplying the top and bottom by \(\sqrt{z_\delta^2 + 2\varepsilon} + z_\delta\) gives Equation A.22. Solving the same equation for \(\varepsilon\) instead gives the matching rule for the \(\varepsilon\) of a given \(\sigma\): \[\varepsilon_{\text{tail}} = z_\delta\mu + \frac{\mu^2}{2}. \tag{A.26}\]
Its two regimes. When \(2\varepsilon\) is small compared with \(z_\delta^2\), the square root is close to \(z_\delta\), so \(\sigma_{\text{tail}} \approx \Delta_2 z_\delta/\varepsilon\), which is proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\). When \(2\varepsilon\) is large compared with \(z_\delta^2\), the square root is close to \(\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\) and dominates \(z_\delta\), so \(\sigma_{\text{tail}} \approx \Delta_2/\sqrt{2\varepsilon}\). The bend between the two is near \(\varepsilon = z_\delta^2/2\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), where \(z_\delta = 4.2649\), that is \(\varepsilon = 9.09\). The classic formula has the same \(1/\varepsilon\) shape with \(\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}\) in place of \(z_\delta\), but it never bends, which is why it fails at large \(\varepsilon\) (Section A.7).
Why \(\delta\) costs little. By the Mills-ratio bound of Section A.6, \(\Phi(-z_\delta)\) is close to \(e^{-z_\delta^2/2}/(z_\delta\sqrt{2\pi})\). So \(\delta\) shrinks like \(e^{-z_\delta^2/2}\), and \(z_\delta\) grows only like \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta)}\). Dividing \(\delta\) by 10 adds about \(2\ln 10 = 4.61\) to \(z_\delta^2\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) this makes \(z_\delta\) grow from 4.2649 to 4.7534, a factor of 1.115, and the tail rule’s noise of about \(\Delta_2 z_\delta/\varepsilon\) grows by the same factor. The exact noise grows a little faster, as the checks below show.
Repeating adds the losses. Suppose the \(k\) questions are fixed in advance, each answer has sensitivity \(\Delta_2\), and each gets independent noise \(\sigma\). Together the \(k\) answers are one vector, with \(\ell_2\) sensitivity \(\sqrt{k\Delta_2^2} = \sqrt k\,\Delta_2\). Step 2 of Section A.6 showed that a vector release behaves like one number shifted by the \(\ell_2\) length of the change. So the \(k\) releases have the exact curve of one release with \(\mu\sqrt k\). To keep \(\mu\sqrt k\) at the value one release needs, \(\sigma\) must grow by \(\sqrt k\). When a question may depend on earlier answers, the \(k\) answers are no longer one fixed vector query, so this argument does not apply as it stands. Section B.3 proves the same result for that case.
Why \(\delta\) must be below \(1/n\). Take the mechanism that publishes each record in full with probability \(\delta\), independently. One record changes the output only when its own coin publishes it, so the two probabilities of any event differ by at most \(\delta\), and the mechanism is \((0, \delta)\)-DP. Each of \(n\) records stays hidden with probability \(1 - \delta\), so someone is exposed with probability \(1 - (1 - \delta)^n\). With \(\delta = 1/n\) this is about 0.63. The reason is that \(n\ln(1 - 1/n)\) is close to \(-1\) for large \(n\), so \[(1 - 1/n)^n = e^{n\ln(1 - 1/n)} \approx e^{-1}, \tag{A.27}\] and \(1 - e^{-1} = 0.63\). A guarantee that allows this mechanism promises little, so \(n\delta\) must be far below 1.



A.8.5 Checking it
Table A.11 is the reference table of this section. It gives the exact \(\sigma/\Delta_2\) for five values of \(\varepsilon\) and four of \(\delta\), each found by bisection and checked by putting it back into the formula. Read along a row to see the cost of a smaller \(\delta\), and up a column to see the cost of a smaller \(\varepsilon\).

At \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), for example, a \(\delta\) ten thousand times smaller costs 1.518 times the noise. Halving \(\varepsilon\) instead, to 0.25, costs 1.889 times the noise (Table A.7 has the value at 0.25). Figure A.9 shows the whole plane. On the left each line is one noise level, and the lines are nearly vertical because \(\sigma\) depends mostly on \(\varepsilon\). The lines are nearly vertical, so \(\varepsilon\) decides the noise far more than \(\delta\) does. Right: the product \(\varepsilon\sigma/\Delta_2\) against \(\varepsilon\) for three values of \(\delta\), exact (solid) and by the tail rule (dashed). The tail rule is nearly flat for small \(\varepsilon\), where it is close to \(z_\delta/\varepsilon\), and the exact product sags below it there, because the correction term matters most at small \(\varepsilon\). Both rise at large \(\varepsilon\), where the noise falls more slowly than \(1/\varepsilon\).



Noise against \(\varepsilon\). Table A.12 compares the tail rule with the exact calibration at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). The rule is always enough, as step 3 promises. Its excess over the exact noise is 39% at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), and it shrinks steadily as \(\varepsilon\) grows. The reason is the correction term that the rule ignores. A.8.6 Recipe and pitfalls
Decide the quantities in this order, because the later steps use the earlier choices.

Fix the neighbouring relation and compute \(\Delta_2\), as in Section A.2. Clip first if the data are unbounded.
Pick \(\delta\) from the number of people \(n\), well below \(1/n\). The choice \(\delta = 1/n^2\) is cheap, as Table A.14 shows, and Section 46.7 discusses other rules.
Pick \(\varepsilon\). It decides the noise far more than \(\delta\) does, so spend your judgement here.
Count the releases \(k\) that must share the budget. If they are Gaussian releases of the same sensitivity, solve for one and multiply \(\sigma\) by \(\sqrt k\).
Solve for \(\sigma\) by bisection on the exact formula with \(\Delta_2 = 1\), computing \(\Phi\) with \(\operatorname{erfc}\), and multiply by \(\Delta_2\). Table A.11 gives a first estimate, and Equation A.22 gives a safe closed form if you cannot run bisection.
Check by plugging back. Put \(\mu = \Delta_2/\sigma\) into the formula and confirm that \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) is at most your target.
Report \(\mu\), or the curve, not only one pair, so that a reader can find \(\delta\) at any \(\varepsilon\).

The common mistakes follow from the facts above. Quoting \(\varepsilon\) without \(\delta\) says nothing, because one Gaussian mechanism has every \(\varepsilon\) on its curve. A \(\delta\) of \(1/n\) or more allows a mechanism that publishes a whole record. Computing \(1 - \Phi(x)\) by subtraction, or \(\Phi\) with \(\operatorname{erf}\), silently loses accuracy from about \(\delta = 10^{-12}\) and gives nonsense by \(10^{-18}\). The classic formula is unproved above \(\varepsilon = 1\) and wrong above 8.42 at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). And forgetting composition is the most expensive mistake of all, because \(k\) releases at the \(\sigma\) of one are only \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP for a much larger \(\varepsilon\). Splitting the budget evenly fixes that, but at about \(k\) times the noise of one release instead of \(\sqrt k\) times. Section B.3 and Section B.5 compare the ways to account for repeated releases.

title: Appendix B — Composing private releases
text:
B.1 Basic composition: the budgets add
A private system almost never releases one number. A dashboard publishes a hundred counts, an analyst asks one query after another, and a training run takes thousands of noisy steps. Each release on its own may be private, but an attacker sees all of them together, so this appendix answers the practical questions that follow. What is the total privacy cost of a number \(k\) of releases? Why is that answer correct? How much noise must each release get so that the whole set stays within a budget? And which of the several ways to add up the cost should you use?
Everything here rests on one quantity, so here it is in three sentences. A mechanism \(M\) is differentially private if changing one person’s record, which turns a dataset \(D\) into a neighbouring dataset \(D'\), barely changes the distribution of its output. The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the logarithm of how much more likely \(y\) is under \(D\) than under \(D'\). For a budget \(\varepsilon\), pure \(\varepsilon\)-differential privacy (DP) says this loss is between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\) for every output. Approximate \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP asks instead that every set \(S\) of outputs, for every pair of neighbours, satisfies \[\Pr_D[S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr_{D'}[S] + \delta, \tag{B.1}\] where \(\Pr_D[S]\) is the chance that the output lands in \(S\) when the data are \(D\). The small slack \(\delta\) lets rare outputs break the factor \(e^\varepsilon\). Section A.1 in the appendices states both definitions in full, with examples.
The one idea of this page is that the privacy loss of several releases is the sum of their separate losses. Basic composition bounds that sum by the largest value it can take. Advanced composition uses the fact that the terms partly cancel, like the steps of a random walk. For Gaussian noise the sum is again exactly Gaussian, and Rényi DP tracks a set of averages of the loss that add just as simply. A method that adds up the cost of many releases this way is called an accountant. Table B.1 lists the derivations and the chapter sections that use them.
Notation. The \(k\) mechanisms are \(M_1, \dots, M_k\), run on the same dataset, and their outputs are \(y_1, \dots, y_k\). For one mechanism, \(p(y)\) is the probability (or density) of the output \(y\) when the data are \(D\), and \(q(y)\) is the same when the data are \(D'\). The privacy loss is \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}. \tag{B.2}\] For Gaussian noise, \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the noise and \(\Delta\) is the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity. That is the largest ordinary (Euclidean) distance by which one record can move the true answer, which may be a vector of numbers. Their ratio, the shift in units of the noise, is \(\mu = \Delta/\sigma\). The accounting chapters take \(\Delta = 1\) and call \(\sigma\) the noise multiplier, so their \(\sigma\) is this page’s \(\sigma\) with \(\Delta = 1\). The standard normal cumulative distribution function is \(\Phi\), and logarithms are natural.
Neighbours can be defined in two ways: by adding or removing one record, or by replacing one record with another. The choice changes the sensitivity of a query, but not any argument on this page, as long as every release uses the same relation.

title: Appendix B — Composing private releases
text:
B.1.1 The question
You release \(k\) answers computed from the same dataset, each with its own fresh noise, and each private on its own. What guarantee holds for all \(k\) answers together, including when you choose each query after reading the earlier answers?


B.1.2 The answer
If release \(i\) is \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP, then the \(k\) releases together are \[\Big(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\ \sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\Big)\text{-DP}. \tag{B.3}\] Here \(\varepsilon_i\) is the budget of release \(i\), and \(\delta_i\) its slack. The same holds when release \(i\) is chosen using the earlier outputs, as long as its budget is fixed in advance. The chapter states this as Equation 19.11 in Section 19.3.


B.1.3 A worked example
A dashboard publishes 10 counts, such as the number of patients in each of 10 clinics. One person changes each count by at most 1, so each count has sensitivity 1. Laplace noise of scale \(b\) makes a release with sensitivity \(\Delta_1\) private at \(\varepsilon = \Delta_1/b\) (Section A.3). So each count gets Laplace noise of scale \(b = 1/0.1 = 10\), which makes it \(0.1\)-DP, and by Equation B.3 the 10 counts together are \(10 \times 0.1 = 1\)-DP.
It helps to see why one noisy count is \(0.1\)-DP. Say the true count is 0 on \(D\) and 1 on \(D'\). The Laplace density with scale \(b\) is \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|z|/b}\), and the two densities centred at 0 and 1 have the same constant \(\frac{1}{2b}\) in front. So the constants cancel in the ratio, and the privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the difference of the two exponents, \[L(y) = \frac{|y - 1| - |y|}{b}. \tag{B.4}\] For \(y \le 0\) this is \(\big((1 - y) - (-y)\big)/b = 1/b = 0.1\). For \(y \ge 1\) it is \(-0.1\), and in between it moves in a straight line from one to the other (Figure B.1, left). So the loss never leaves \([-0.1, 0.1]\).
The bound of 1 for the 10 counts is reached. Each count’s loss is \(+0.1\) exactly when its output is at most 0, its true value on \(D\). Under \(D\) the noise is symmetric around 0, so this happens with probability \(\frac12\), and all 10 counts do it at once with probability \((\frac12)^{10} = 0.000977\). A simulation of a million dashboards finds the largest total loss to be exactly 1.0000, reached in a fraction 0.000997 of them. So for pure DP, basic composition is exact in the worst case. But that case is rare, and the average total loss on \(D\) is only 0.0484, as the checking section below shows. The gap between the worst and the typical loss is what the next section exploits.


B.1.4 Why it works
Pure DP, outputs with independent noise. The plan is to write the probability of all \(k\) outputs as a product, so that the ratio of two such probabilities becomes a product of ratios, and the log of the ratio becomes a sum.

The joint probability is a product. Each release uses its own fresh noise, so with the dataset held fixed the outputs are independent. The probability of seeing \(y_1, \dots, y_k\) together is the product of the separate probabilities, \(p(y_1, \dots, y_k) = p_1(y_1)\cdots p_k(y_k)\), and the same holds for \(q\).
The ratio is a product of ratios. Dividing one product by the other, term by term, \[\frac{p(y_1, \dots, y_k)}{q(y_1, \dots, y_k)} = \frac{p_1(y_1)}{q_1(y_1)} \cdots \frac{p_k(y_k)}{q_k(y_k)}. \tag{B.5}\]
Each factor is bounded. Release \(i\) is \(\varepsilon_i\)-DP, so its ratio lies between \(e^{-\varepsilon_i}\) and \(e^{\varepsilon_i}\).
Multiply the bounds and take logs. The product lies between \(e^{-\sum\varepsilon_i}\) and \(e^{\sum\varepsilon_i}\). The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms, so the total loss is \(L = L_1(y_1) + \dots + L_k(y_k)\), and \(|L| \le \sum_i\varepsilon_i\) at every output. That is pure \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\)-DP.

Figure B.1 draws this for two counts. Each count’s loss is flat at \(+\varepsilon\) on one side, flat at \(-\varepsilon\) on the other, with a ramp in between, and the loss of the pair is the sum of the two. It reaches \(2\varepsilon\) only in the corner where both outputs favour \(D\), that is, where both have the largest loss.






Figure B.1: Left: the privacy loss of one count released with Laplace noise at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), as a function of the output, when the true count is 0 on \(D\) and 1 on \(D'\). It is flat at \(\pm\varepsilon\) outside \([0, 1]\). Right: the total loss of two such counts over the plane of the two outputs. It is the sum of two such steps, so it reaches \(2\varepsilon\) only in the lower-left corner, where both outputs favour \(D\). The figure uses \(\varepsilon = 0.5\) rather than 0.1 so that the shading is visible.



Adaptive releases. Now suppose you choose the second query after reading the first answer. The outputs are no longer independent, so step 1 needs a different reason. The chain rule of probability gives it. The chance of seeing \(y_1\) and then \(y_2\) is the chance of \(y_1\), times the chance of \(y_2\) given that the first output was \(y_1\): \[p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)\,p_2(y_2 \mid y_1). \tag{B.6}\] The ratio is again a product of two ratios, and the second one, \(p_2(y_2 \mid y_1)/q_2(y_2 \mid y_1)\), is the ratio of the mechanism you chose after seeing \(y_1\). If every mechanism you might choose is \(\varepsilon_2\)-DP, that ratio lies between \(e^{-\varepsilon_2}\) and \(e^{\varepsilon_2}\), whatever \(y_1\) was. So steps 2 to 4 go through unchanged. With \(k\) releases the chain rule has \(k\) factors, one per release.
A tiny case makes this concrete. Randomized response at level \(\varepsilon\) reports a person’s secret bit truthfully with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) and flips it otherwise. Ask once at level \(\ln 3\), which tells the truth with probability \(\frac34\). If the answer is 1, ask again at \(\ln 3\). If it is 0, ask again at \(\ln 2\), which tells the truth with probability \(\frac23\). Take \(D\) to be the dataset where the person’s bit is 1 and \(D'\) the one where it is 0. Table B.2 lists the four outcomes, as computed by this appendix’s script (see the Code section).

Each row’s loss is the first answer’s loss plus the second answer’s loss, where the second loss belongs to whichever mechanism was chosen. The largest loss is \(2.1972 = 2\ln 3\). That equals the basic bound \(\ln 3 + \ln 3\), in which the second budget is \(\ln 3\), the larger of the two levels the second step could use.
Approximate DP. An \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanism may have outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\), or is even infinite, as long as they are rare. The Gaussian mechanism is an example: its loss is a straight line in the output, so it has no largest value. So the product argument fails, and a different one is needed. It rests on a fact that this page uses again later, the bad-event fact: for any threshold \(\tau\) and any set \(S\) of outputs, \[\Pr_D[S] \le e^\tau\Pr_{D'}[S] + \Pr_D[L > \tau]. \tag{B.7}\] To see it, split \(S\) into the outputs whose loss is at most \(\tau\) and the rest. On the first part \(\ln(p/q) \le \tau\), so \(p \le e^\tau q\) output by output. Adding up over that part gives at most \(e^\tau\) times its probability under \(D'\), which is at most \(e^\tau\Pr_{D'}[S]\). The second part lies inside the event \(L > \tau\), so its probability is at most \(\Pr_D[L > \tau]\). So if the loss exceeds \(\tau\) with probability at most \(\delta\) when the data are \(D\), then \(\Pr_D[S] \le e^\tau\Pr_{D'}[S] + \delta\) for every \(S\). DP also asks for the same bound with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped, and the same argument gives it.
Now suppose each release satisfies a tail condition: whatever the earlier outputs were, its loss exceeds \(\varepsilon_i\) with probability at most \(\delta_i\). Then the composition is \((\sum\varepsilon_i, \sum\delta_i)\)-DP, in three steps.

A large total needs a large term. If every \(L_i\) is at most \(\varepsilon_i\), the sum is at most \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\). So the total can exceed \(\sum_i\varepsilon_i\) only if at least one term exceeds its own \(\varepsilon_i\).
Union bound. The chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances. So \[\Pr\Big[L > \sum_i\varepsilon_i\Big] \le \sum_i\Pr[L_i > \varepsilon_i] \le \sum_i\delta_i. \tag{B.8}\] In the adaptive case, the chance that term \(i\) exceeds \(\varepsilon_i\) is an average, over the earlier outputs, of a conditional chance that is at most \(\delta_i\). So it is at most \(\delta_i\) too.
Bad-event fact. Equation B.7 with \(\tau = \sum_i\varepsilon_i\) gives the result.

The tail condition is a sufficient condition: it is enough for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, but it asks for more. The classic Gaussian calibration proves exactly this condition (Section 20.3), so the argument covers it. But some \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP mechanisms do not satisfy it. For example, take a mechanism with two outputs. Output A has probability \(\frac12\) on \(D\) and \(\frac12 e^{-1.1} = 0.1664\) on \(D'\), and output B takes the rest, \(\frac12\) and \(0.8336\). Output A has loss 1.1, above 1, and it happens half the time, so the tail condition at \(\varepsilon = 1\) fails. Yet the only set that breaks the factor \(e\) is \(\{A\}\), and it breaks it by just \(\frac12 - e \times 0.1664 = 0.0476\). So the mechanism is \((1, 0.0476)\)-DP. Basic composition still holds for releases that are only known to be \((\varepsilon_i, \delta_i)\)-DP. Section 19.3 proves it with a two-step argument on events, and Section J.1 gives a second route through four-point randomized response.


B.1.5 Checking it
A simulation of a million runs of the 10-count dashboard backs up the worked example. The largest total loss is 1.0000, reached in a fraction 0.000997 of runs against the exact \((\frac12)^{10} = 0.000977\). The mean loss is 0.0484. That matches the exact value, which is 10 times the mean loss of one count, \(\varepsilon + e^{-\varepsilon} - 1\) at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), a formula you get by integrating the loss of Figure B.1 against the Laplace density. The script also recomputes Table B.2 from the two randomized-response steps, and the two-output pair above. So the bound is exact for the worst output, and very loose for the typical one.


B.1.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To share a total budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) among \(k\) releases with basic composition, follow three steps.

Give release \(i\) a share \(\varepsilon_i\) and \(\delta_i\), so that the shares add up to \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\). Equal shares \(\varepsilon/k\) and \(\delta/k\) are the simplest choice.
Calibrate each release to its share, for example with Laplace noise of scale \(\Delta_1/\varepsilon_i\), where \(\Delta_1\) is its \(\ell_1\) sensitivity, the largest total of the absolute changes one record can make to its answers.
Draw fresh, independent noise for every release.

Several things go wrong in practice. Reusing one noise draw for two different queries breaks step 1 of the derivation, because the outputs are no longer independent given the data. For example, subtracting two answers that share one noise draw cancels the noise exactly. Publishing the same noisy answer twice is fine, though, since the copy is computed from the output without touching the data. Choosing the budgets themselves from the answers, such as “stop when the answer looks good”, is not covered, because each budget must be fixed in advance (Section 36.4 handles it). The \(\delta_i\) add up, so \(k\) releases at \(\delta_i = 10^{-5}\) give \(k \times 10^{-5}\). And for many releases the bound is far too large, which is the subject of the next section.

title: Appendix B — Composing private releases
section: B.2 Advanced composition: \(\sqrt k\) instead of \(k\)
text:
B.2 Advanced composition: \(\sqrt k\) instead of \(k\)

B.2.1 The question
You publish 100 counts, each \(0.1\)-DP. Basic composition says the total is \(\varepsilon = 10\). That is almost no guarantee, because it allows some output to be up to \(e^{10} \approx 22{,}000\) times more likely on one dataset than on its neighbour. An attacker who sees that output can multiply their odds on which dataset it was by that much. If you accept a tiny slack \(\delta'\), can you claim a much smaller \(\varepsilon\)?


B.2.2 The answer
Yes. Take \(k\) releases that are each \(\varepsilon\)-DP and any slack \(\delta' > 0\). Together they are \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP with \[\varepsilon' = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')} + k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{B.9}\] The first term grows like \(\sqrt k\), and the second is small when \(\varepsilon\) is small, because \(e^\varepsilon - 1 \approx \varepsilon\). When each release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP instead, the total slack becomes \(k\delta + \delta'\). This is the theorem of Dwork, Rothblum and Vadhan, stated as Equation 21.9 in Section 21.2. The chapter also gives a sharper form whose second term is \(k\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\). Here \(\tanh(x) = (e^{2x} - 1)/(e^{2x} + 1)\) is the hyperbolic tangent, which is close to \(x\) for small \(x\), so this term is about half the one above.


B.2.3 A worked example
Take \(k = 100\), \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) and \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\). Then \(\ln(1/\delta') = 11.5129\), so the first term is \[0.1\sqrt{200 \times 11.5129} = 0.1\sqrt{2302.6} = 4.7985. \tag{B.10}\] The second term is \(100 \times 0.1 \times (e^{0.1} - 1) = 1.0517\). Their sum is \(\varepsilon' = 5.8502\), against 10 for basic composition. The sharper \(\tanh\) form gives 5.2981. The best bound that holds for every \(0.1\)-DP release, the optimal composition of Section 21.4, gives 4.3068.


B.2.4 Why it works
The idea: a random walk. The total loss is a sum of \(k\) terms, one per release, and each lies between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\). Basic composition assumes every term is \(+\varepsilon\) at once. But the terms are random and partly cancel, like the steps of a walk that goes up or down at random. After \(k\) steps such a walk is typically about \(\sqrt k\) steps from where it started, not \(k\). The reason is that the variances of independent steps add, so the variance after \(k\) steps is \(k\) times that of one step, and the typical distance, its square root, grows like \(\sqrt k\). The walk also drifts upward a little, because each term has a small positive average when the data are \(D\), as step 2 shows. So the total loss is a small drift plus a fluctuation of order \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\). A tail bound says how far above the drift the fluctuation can go except with probability \(\delta'\), and the bad-event fact turns that into \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP.
Randomized response shows the walk in its plainest form. At level \(\varepsilon\) each answer has loss exactly \(+\varepsilon\) if it is truthful and \(-\varepsilon\) if it is flipped. So the total loss of \(k\) answers is a walk with steps of \(\pm\varepsilon\), which Figure B.2 draws. The chapter shows that randomized response is the worst case among all \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanisms (Section 21.4). That is, no \(k\) releases that are each \(\varepsilon\)-DP need a larger \(\delta\), at any total \(\varepsilon\), than \(k\) randomized responses do. So it is the right one to look at.
The derivation has seven steps.

The loss is a sum of bounded terms. By Section B.1 the total loss is \(L = L_1 + \dots + L_k\), where \(L_i\) is the loss of release \(i\) given the earlier outputs. Each release is \(\varepsilon\)-DP whatever the history, so \(-\varepsilon \le L_i \le \varepsilon\).
Each term has a small average. Write \(m_i\) for the average of \(L_i\) on \(D\), given the earlier outputs. The claim is that, for one \(\varepsilon\)-DP release with output probabilities \(p\) and \(q\), \[m = \sum_y p(y)\ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)} \le \varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1). \tag{B.11}\] The proof uses one inequality about the logarithm of a positive number \(x\), \[\ln x \le x - 1. \tag{B.12}\] It holds because the line \(x - 1\) touches the curve \(\ln x\) at \(x = 1\) and the curve bends down away from it. There are three sub-steps. The first one adds a term to \(m\) so that the positive and negative losses can be paired up, output by output.

Add a term that is never negative. Apply \(\ln x \le x - 1\) with \(x = p/q\) and average under \(q\). This gives \(\sum_y q\ln(p/q) \le \sum_y q(p/q - 1) = \sum_y p - \sum_y q = 0\). Flipping the sign, and using \(-\ln(p/q) = \ln(q/p)\), the sum \(\sum_y q\ln(q/p)\) is never negative. Adding it to \(m\) can only make \(m\) larger, and the two sums combine term by term: \[m \le \sum_y p\ln\frac pq + \sum_y q\ln\frac qp = \sum_y (p - q)\ln\frac pq. \tag{B.13}\]
Use the bound on the loss. Each \(|\ln(p/q)|\) is at most \(\varepsilon\), so \(m \le \varepsilon\sum_y|p - q|\).
Bound the total difference. Write \(|p - q| = q\,|p/q - 1|\). The ratio \(p/q\) lies between \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) and \(e^\varepsilon\), so \(|p/q - 1|\) is at most \(e^\varepsilon - 1\), its value at the upper end. At the lower end it is only \(1 - e^{-\varepsilon}\), which is smaller. The \(q(y)\) add up to 1, so \(\sum_y|p - q| \le e^\varepsilon - 1\).

For randomized response, with two outputs, the average is easy to compute directly. Write \(t = e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\) for the chance of a truthful answer on \(D\), whose loss is \(+\varepsilon\), while a flipped answer has loss \(-\varepsilon\). So \(m = \varepsilon t - \varepsilon(1 - t) = \varepsilon(2t - 1)\). Substituting \(t\) gives \(2t - 1 = (e^\varepsilon - 1)/(e^\varepsilon + 1)\), which is \(\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\), so \(m = \varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\). At \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) this is 0.0050, while the bound of Equation B.11 is 0.0105. At \(\varepsilon = 1\) they are 0.4621 and 1.7183. So the bound holds and is about twice too large for small \(\varepsilon\), which is where the chapter’s sharper \(\tanh\) form comes from.
Centre the terms. Write \(X_i = L_i - m_i\). Given the earlier outputs, \(X_i\) has average zero, and it lies in an interval of length \(2\varepsilon\), from \(-\varepsilon - m_i\) to \(\varepsilon - m_i\). The total loss is the drift plus the sum of these centred terms, \(L = \sum_i m_i + \sum_i X_i\), and the drift is at most \(k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) by step 2.
One centred term has a small exponential average. The next two steps bound the average of \(e^{\lambda X}\) for a number \(\lambda > 0\) of our choosing, because an exponential magnifies large values, and step 6 turns that into a tail bound. Hoeffding’s lemma says that a variable \(X\) with average zero, which stays in an interval of length \(d\), satisfies \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda X}\big] \le e^{\lambda^2d^2/8} \qquad \text{for every real } \lambda. \tag{B.14}\] The proof compares \(X\) with a variable that sits only at the two ends of the interval, which has the largest exponential average, and then bounds that average. Concentration inequalities gives the details. With \(d = 2\varepsilon\) the right side is \(e^{\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/2}\).
The bounds multiply, even when releases adapt. Write \(W_j = X_1 + \dots + X_j\) for the running sum, so that \(e^{\lambda W_k} = e^{\lambda W_{k-1}}e^{\lambda X_k}\). Take the average of this product in two stages, first over the last output with the earlier ones fixed and then over the earlier ones. With the earlier outputs fixed, \(e^{\lambda W_{k-1}}\) is a fixed number, and step 4 bounds the average of \(e^{\lambda X_k}\) by \(e^{\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/2}\) whatever the history was. So \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda W_k}\big] \le e^{\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/2}\,\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda W_{k-1}}\big] \le \dots \le e^{k\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/2}. \tag{B.15}\] This is where adaptivity is handled. Each release may depend on the past, but the bound on its own term does not. This argument is Azuma’s inequality.
Turn the exponential average into a tail bound. Markov’s inequality says that a quantity that is never negative exceeds a level \(a\) with probability at most its average divided by \(a\). Apply it to \(e^{\lambda W_k}\) at the level \(a = e^{\lambda s}\), for a value \(s\) to be chosen. For \(\lambda > 0\) the event \(W_k \ge s\) is the event \(e^{\lambda W_k} \ge e^{\lambda s}\), so \[\Pr[W_k \ge s] \le e^{-\lambda s + k\lambda^2\varepsilon^2/2}. \tag{B.16}\] The exponent is a parabola in \(\lambda\). Its derivative \(-s + k\lambda\varepsilon^2\) is zero at \(\lambda = s/(k\varepsilon^2)\), where the exponent equals \(-s^2/(2k\varepsilon^2)\). Setting \(e^{-s^2/(2k\varepsilon^2)} = \delta'\) and solving gives the level \[s = \varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}. \tag{B.17}\]
Convert. If \(L > \varepsilon'\), then \(\sum_i X_i = L - \sum_i m_i > \varepsilon' - k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon - 1) = s\). So \(\Pr[L > \varepsilon'] \le \delta'\), and the bad-event fact Equation B.7 with \(\tau = \varepsilon'\) gives \((\varepsilon', \delta')\)-DP. The same argument with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped covers the other direction.

When each release is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \(\delta > 0\), its loss can exceed \(\varepsilon\) on rare outputs, so step 1 fails. The fix uses a fact proved in the chapter: every such release behaves like a processed version of a simple mechanism that, with probability \(\delta\), announces which dataset it ran on, and otherwise runs \(\varepsilon\)-DP randomized response. Then the \(k\) announcements cost at most \(k\delta\) by the union bound, and the rest is the argument above. Section 21.4 and Section J.1 carry this out.


B.2.5 Checking it
The script computes the loss of 100 randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) exactly, from the binomial count of truthful answers. Its mean is 0.4996 and its standard deviation 0.9988, so the bound \(\varepsilon' = 5.8502\) sits more than five standard deviations above the mean. The exact chance that the loss exceeds 5.8502 is \(1.022 \times 10^{-8}\), far below the \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\) the theorem promises. The exact \(\delta\) at that \(\varepsilon'\), the smallest slack that works (Section B.3, step 4, shows how to compute it), is smaller still, \(1.956 \times 10^{-9}\). So advanced composition is valid but conservative, for three reasons. Hoeffding’s lemma allows for a larger spread than the walk has, and step 2 doubles the drift. Then the bad-event fact counts every output above \(\varepsilon'\) in full.
Figure B.2 draws 25 runs of the walk over 1000 answers. Basic composition is the straight line \(i\varepsilon\), which leaves the plot at \(i = 400\). The runs stay in a band around the drift whose width grows like \(\sqrt i\). In 100,000 simulated runs of 1000 answers, the largest total loss was 18.4, while basic composition says 100 and advanced composition 25.6914.






Figure B.2: The total privacy loss of \(i\) randomized-response answers at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\), for 25 simulated runs (thin lines). The green line is the mean loss and the shaded band the mean plus or minus two standard deviations, whose width grows like \(\sqrt i\). The red curve is the advanced composition bound at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), and the dashed line is the basic bound \(i\varepsilon\).





B.2.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To spend a total budget \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}, \delta')\) on \(k\) releases that are each \(\varepsilon\)-DP, set the leading term of Equation B.9 equal to the target. That gives each release roughly \[\varepsilon \approx \frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{total}}}{\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}}. \tag{B.18}\] Then evaluate Equation B.9 with that \(\varepsilon\), and lower it a little if the second term pushes the total over the target.
Advanced composition is worse than basic composition when \(k\) is small. Its first term is \(\varepsilon\sqrt k\) times \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta')}\), which is 4.80 at \(\delta' = 10^{-5}\), while basic composition is \(\varepsilon k = \varepsilon\sqrt k \times \sqrt k\). So \(\sqrt k\) must beat 4.80 and more. Setting the two bounds equal and solving for \(k\) shows that at \(\varepsilon = 0.1\) advanced composition wins only once \(k\) exceeds \(2\ln(1/\delta')/(2 - e^\varepsilon)^2 = 28.76\). So always compute both and keep the smaller. For \(\varepsilon \ge \ln 2\) the second term alone is at least \(k\varepsilon\), so the \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) form never wins, and you need the \(\tanh\) form of the chapter. And when you know more than each release’s \(\varepsilon\), for example that the noise is Gaussian, the next two sections do much better.

title: Appendix B — Composing private releases
section: B.3 Gaussian releases: \(k\) of them are one
text:
B.3 Gaussian releases: \(k\) of them are one

B.3.1 The question
You add Gaussian noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\) to \(k\) answers, each with sensitivity \(\Delta\). What is the exact \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantee of all \(k\) together? And how much noise must each answer get so that the whole set meets a total budget?


B.3.2 The answer
The \(k\) releases are exactly as private as one Gaussian release whose sensitivity is \(\sqrt k\,\Delta\), with the same noise \(\sigma\). In units of the noise, that single release has the shift \[\mu_k = \frac{\sqrt k\,\Delta}{\sigma}. \tag{B.19}\] So the smallest valid \(\delta\) at a given \(\varepsilon\) is the exact Gaussian formula with \(\mu_k\) in place of \(\Delta/\sigma\): \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac{\mu_k}{2} - \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu_k}\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac{\mu_k}{2} - \frac{\varepsilon}{\mu_k}\Big). \tag{B.20}\] Read backwards, this gives the noise for \(k\) releases at a total budget. If \(\sigma_1\) is the noise that makes one release \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then \[\sigma_k = \sqrt k\,\sigma_1 \tag{B.21}\] makes \(k\) releases together \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. The single-release formula is Equation 20.17 in Section 20.4, and Section A.7 derives it.


B.3.3 A worked example
You want 10 counts with sensitivity 1 to be \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP together. One count at \((1, 10^{-5})\) needs \(\sigma_1 = 3.7306\), from the exact calibration. By Equation B.21 each of the 10 counts gets \(\sigma_{10} = \sqrt{10} \times 3.7306 = 11.797\). Putting \(\mu_{10} = \sqrt{10}/11.797\) back into Equation B.20 and solving for \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) gives 1.0000, as it should.
Compare this with basic composition. Splitting the budget evenly gives each count \((0.1, 10^{-6})\), and the exact calibration for that share needs \(\sigma = 36.305\). That is 3.08 times more noise for the same total guarantee. With 100 counts the two answers are \(\sigma_{100} = 37.306\) and 362.02, a factor of 9.70.


B.3.4 Why it works
The idea. The privacy loss of one Gaussian release is itself a normal random variable. Losses add, and a sum of independent normal variables is normal, with the means added and the variances added. The sum of \(k\) losses turns out to be exactly the loss of one release with \(\sqrt k\) times the shift. Since the smallest \(\delta\) depends only on the distribution of the loss, the two have the same \(\delta\) at every \(\varepsilon\).

The loss of one release is normal. Take one count whose true value is 0 on \(D\) and \(\Delta\) on \(D'\), and write the output on \(D\) as \(y = z\), where \(z\) is the noise. The same output \(y\) sits at distance \(z - \Delta\) from the centre on \(D'\). The normal density with standard deviation \(\sigma\) is proportional to \(e^{-z^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), so the loss is a difference of two exponents: \[L = \frac{(z - \Delta)^2 - z^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{\Delta^2 - 2\Delta z}{2\sigma^2}. \tag{B.22}\] This is a straight line in the noise \(z\). Its mean is \(\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2) = \mu^2/2\), because \(z\) has mean 0. Its variance is \((\Delta/\sigma^2)^2\sigma^2 = \mu^2\), because multiplying \(z\) by a constant multiplies the variance by its square. A straight-line function of a normal variable is normal, so on \(D\) \[L \sim \mathcal N\Big(\frac{\mu^2}{2},\ \mu^2\Big), \qquad \mu = \frac{\Delta}{\sigma}. \tag{B.23}\]
Add \(k\) independent losses. With fresh noise for each release, the \(k\) losses are independent, and the total loss is their sum (Section B.1). Means add, and so do variances of independent terms. A sum of independent normal variables is normal (Section E.1 proves it). So the total loss is normal with mean \(k\mu^2/2\) and variance \(k\mu^2\).
Recognize one release. A single release with shift \(\mu_k = \sqrt k\,\mu\) has, by step 1, a loss with mean \(\mu_k^2/2 = k\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu_k^2 = k\mu^2\). That is the same normal distribution as in step 2.
The exact \(\delta\) depends only on the loss. By the definition of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP in the opening, the smallest \(\delta\) at a given \(\varepsilon\) is the largest gap \(\Pr_D[S] - e^\varepsilon\Pr_{D'}[S]\) over sets of outputs. The gap is largest when \(S\) holds exactly the outputs with \(p > e^\varepsilon q\), so the smallest \(\delta\) is \(\sum_y(p - e^\varepsilon q)_+\), where \((x)_+ = \max(x, 0)\). Factor \(p\) out of each term, and note that \(e^\varepsilon q/p = e^{\varepsilon - L}\). This gives \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \sum_y p(y)\big(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L(y)}\big)_+ = \mathbb E_D\big[(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})_+\big]. \tag{B.24}\] The right side is an average over the loss alone. So two mechanisms whose losses have the same distribution on \(D\) have the same \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) for every \(\varepsilon\). By steps 2 and 3, the \(k\) releases have the \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) of one release at \(\mu_k\), which is Equation B.20. The other direction, with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped, gives the same value, because the Gaussian pair is symmetric.

There is a second way to see the same result. Stack the \(k\) answers into one vector. In the worst case, changing one record moves every answer by \(\Delta\), so the vector moves by \((\Delta, \dots, \Delta)\), whose length is \(\sqrt{k\Delta^2} = \sqrt k\,\Delta\). Gaussian noise with the same \(\sigma\) in every coordinate looks the same in every direction. So you can turn the axes until the shift points along the first one, and the other \(k - 1\) coordinates then carry no evidence at all. What is left is one Gaussian release with shift \(\sqrt k\,\Delta\).
Adaptive queries. Suppose each query is chosen after seeing the earlier answers, and each still has sensitivity \(\Delta\) and noise \(\sigma\). If every query moves by exactly \(\Delta\), step 1 gives the same normal distribution for each loss whatever the history was. A term whose distribution is the same whatever happened before is independent of what happened before, so steps 2 to 4 hold unchanged. Queries that move by less than \(\Delta\) can only help, but proving that for an adaptive sequence takes the composition theorem of Gaussian DP (Section 32.6, Section K.3), which this page does not repeat.


B.3.5 Checking it
To test this, the script simulates 400,000 runs of 16 counts with noise \(\sigma = 4\). Each count has \(\mu = 0.25\), so the 16 together should behave like one release with \(\mu_{16} = 4 \times 0.25 = 1\). Its loss should then have mean \(\frac12\) and variance 1, and the simulated total loss has mean 0.4971 and variance 1.0001. Averaging \((1 - e^{1 - L})_+\) over the simulated losses estimates \(\delta(1)\) as 0.1264. The formula Equation B.20 with \(\mu_{16} = 1\) gives 0.1269. Figure B.3 shows the simulated losses for 1, 4 and 16 counts against the normal curve of a single release.






Figure B.3: The total privacy loss of \(k\) Gaussian counts with noise \(\sigma = 4\) and sensitivity 1, for \(k = 1\), 4 and 16. Bars are simulated losses; lines are the normal distribution \(\mathcal N(k\mu^2/2, k\mu^2)\) of one release with shift \(\mu_k = \sqrt k/4\). The mean grows like \(k\) and the width like \(\sqrt k\).



The result is exact, not a bound. Nothing was approximated in steps 1 to 4.


B.3.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To release \(k\) answers with Gaussian noise under a total budget \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), follow three steps.

Find \(\sigma_1\), the exact noise for one release of sensitivity \(\Delta\) at \((\varepsilon, \delta)\), by solving Equation 20.17 (Section A.7).
Multiply by the square root of the number of releases, \(\sigma_k = \sqrt k\,\sigma_1\).
Add fresh noise \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma_k^2)\) to each answer.

The other way round, given \(\sigma\) and \(k\), put \(\mu_k = \sqrt k\,\Delta/\sigma\) into Equation B.20 and solve for \(\varepsilon\) at your \(\delta\). When the releases have different sensitivities \(\Delta_i\) or noise levels \(\sigma_i\), the same steps give one release with \(\mu^2 = \sum_i(\Delta_i/\sigma_i)^2\), because means and variances still add.
The sensitivity \(\Delta\) must be the \(\ell_2\) sensitivity of each release under the neighbouring relation you claim. For example, a sum of values between \(-C\) and \(C\), for a clipping norm \(C\), has sensitivity \(C\) under add/remove but \(2C\) under replace-one. The result needs plain Gaussian noise. With subsampling, where each step uses only a random subset of the records, as in private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), the loss of a step is no longer normal, and Section C.5 shows what to do instead. Laplace releases do not combine into one Laplace release, so for them you need advanced composition or the accountants below.

title: Appendix B — Composing private releases
section: B.4 Rényi DP: a summary of the loss that adds
text:
B.4 Rényi DP: a summary of the loss that adds

B.4.1 The question
Many pipelines mix mechanisms, or use noise whose loss is not normal, so the exact shortcut of the previous section does not apply. You want a summary of each mechanism that you can add up across releases, and convert to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) once at the end. What is that summary for the Gaussian mechanism, and why does it add?


B.4.2 The answer
Rényi differential privacy (RDP) summarizes the loss by averages of exponentials of it. A single number cannot capture both the typical and the rare large losses, so RDP keeps one such average for each order \(\alpha > 1\), a dial that sets how much weight large losses get. For each order, the Rényi divergence between the two output distributions \(P\) (on \(D\)) and \(Q\) (on \(D'\)) is \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\int p(y)^\alpha q(y)^{1-\alpha}\,\mathrm dy. \tag{B.25}\] The integral is the average, on \(D\), of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), because \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha} = p\,(p/q)^{\alpha - 1}\). So it weighs outputs with a large loss heavily, more so for larger \(\alpha\).
A mechanism is \((\alpha, \varepsilon(\alpha))\)-RDP when, for every neighbouring pair, \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) \le \varepsilon(\alpha). \tag{B.26}\] The function \(\alpha \mapsto \varepsilon(\alpha)\) is its RDP curve. The Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity \(\Delta\) and noise \(\sigma\) has a straight line for its curve, \[\varepsilon(\alpha) = \frac{\alpha\Delta^2}{2\sigma^2}, \tag{B.27}\] and RDP curves add under composition. So \(k\) Gaussian releases have the curve \(k\alpha\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\). The chapter states these as Equation 29.7 and Equation 29.10.


B.4.3 A worked example
Take \(\Delta = 1\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(\alpha = 2\). The formula gives \(D_2 = 2 \times 1/(2 \times 1) = 1\). Undoing the logarithm and the factor \(1/(\alpha - 1)\) in the definition, the integral inside is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha} = e^{(2-1) \times 1} = e = 2.7183\). You can check this with the derivation below, which shows the integrand is a normal bump with exactly that area (Figure B.4). Two such releases have \(D_2 = 1 + 1 = 2\).


B.4.4 Why it works
The Gaussian curve, by completing the square. Put \(p\) at centre 0 and \(q\) at centre \(\Delta\), both with standard deviation \(\sigma\). Write \(c = 1/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})\) for the constant in front of the normal density.

Combine the exponents. Since \(\alpha + (1 - \alpha) = 1\), the constants combine to a single \(c\), and \[p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha} = c\,\exp\Big(-\frac{\alpha y^2 + (1 - \alpha)(y - \Delta)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big). \tag{B.28}\]
Expand the numerator. Multiply out \((y - \Delta)^2 = y^2 - 2y\Delta + \Delta^2\) and collect terms: \[\alpha y^2 + (1 - \alpha)(y - \Delta)^2 = y^2 - 2(1 - \alpha)\Delta y + (1 - \alpha)\Delta^2. \tag{B.29}\]
Complete the square. The first two terms are the start of \(\big(y - (1 - \alpha)\Delta\big)^2\), which also contains \((1 - \alpha)^2\Delta^2\). Adding and subtracting that term gives \[y^2 - 2(1 - \alpha)\Delta y + (1 - \alpha)\Delta^2 = \big(y - (1 - \alpha)\Delta\big)^2 + (1 - \alpha)\Delta^2\big(1 - (1 - \alpha)\big). \tag{B.30}\] The last term simplifies to \((1 - \alpha)\alpha\Delta^2 = -\alpha(\alpha - 1)\Delta^2\).
Integrate. Putting this back into step 1, the exponent is \(-\big(y - (1 - \alpha)\Delta\big)^2/(2\sigma^2)\) plus the constant \(+\alpha(\alpha - 1)\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\), whose sign flips because of the minus in front of the fraction. So \[\int p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\,\mathrm dy = e^{\alpha(\alpha - 1)\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)}\int c\,e^{-(y - (1 - \alpha)\Delta)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,\mathrm dy = e^{\alpha(\alpha - 1)\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{B.31}\] The integral that remains is a normal density centred at \((1 - \alpha)\Delta\), so it equals 1.
Take the logarithm and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). This gives \(D_\alpha = \alpha\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\). The value grows with the shift, so the worst neighbouring pair is the one whose answers are \(\Delta\) apart, which gives Equation B.27.

Why the curves add. For two independent releases the joint density is a product, \(p(y_1, y_2) = p_1(y_1)p_2(y_2)\), and the same for \(q\). A power of a product is the product of the powers, so the integrand splits into a factor for \(y_1\) and a factor for \(y_2\). The double integral of such a product is the product of the two single integrals: \[\int\!\!\int p_1^\alpha q_1^{1-\alpha}\,p_2^\alpha q_2^{1-\alpha}\,\mathrm dy_1\,\mathrm dy_2 = \int p_1^\alpha q_1^{1-\alpha}\,\mathrm dy_1 \cdot \int p_2^\alpha q_2^{1-\alpha}\,\mathrm dy_2. \tag{B.32}\] Taking the logarithm turns this product into a sum, and dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives \(D_\alpha\) of the pair as the sum of the two divergences. When the second release is chosen from the first output, do the inner integral over \(y_2\) first, with \(y_1\) fixed. That inner integral is \(e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha}\) for the mechanism chosen after \(y_1\), so it is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_2(\alpha)}\) whatever \(y_1\) was. Replacing it by that bound leaves a constant times the first release’s integral. So the curves still add, now as an upper bound (Section 29.5). Unlike the composition of \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees, nothing like \(\delta\) is added at each step; the only slack comes in the one conversion at the end.
For \(k\) Gaussian releases the sum is \(k\alpha\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2) = \alpha(\sqrt k\,\Delta)^2/(2\sigma^2)\), the curve of one release with \(\sqrt k\) times the shift. That agrees with Section B.3. Other mechanisms have their own curves. The Laplace curve, for example, levels off at the pure \(\varepsilon\) of the mechanism (Equation 29.8).
Converting to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). At the end you convert the summed curve once. For any order \(\alpha\), the mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}, \tag{B.33}\] and you take the order that makes this smallest. The reason is the bad-event fact Equation B.7, with the tail \(\Pr[L > \tau]\) bounded by Markov’s inequality applied to \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\), whose average is what RDP controls. Section D.3 derives it. For example, take 1000 Gaussian steps with sensitivity 1 and noise \(\sigma = 20\). Their summed curve is \(1000\alpha/800 = 1.25\alpha\). At \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) you minimize \(1.25\alpha + 11.5129/(\alpha - 1)\) over the grid of orders that the accounting chapters use, which runs from 1.1 to 512. The best is \(\varepsilon = 8.838\), at \(\alpha = 4\). The exact answer from Section B.3 is 7.511, so the conversion costs 18%.


B.4.5 Checking it
A numerical integral of \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) on a fine grid, which uses no formula for the result, confirms the curve. It gives 1.0000 at \(\alpha = 2\) and 5.0000 at \(\alpha = 10\) with \(\sigma = 1\), and 0.0625 at \(\alpha = 2\) with \(\sigma = 4\). These match \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) to every digit shown. Figure B.4 shows why step 4 works. The product \(p^2q^{-1}\) is a normal bump centred at \((1 - \alpha)\Delta = -1\), on the far side of \(p\) from \(q\), and its area is \(e^1\).






Figure B.4: The two output densities of a Gaussian release with \(\Delta = 1\) and \(\sigma = 1\) (blue on \(D\), orange on \(D'\)), and the integrand \(p^\alpha q^{1-\alpha}\) for \(\alpha = 2\) (green). Completing the square shows that the integrand is a normal bump centred at \((1 - \alpha)\Delta = -1\), scaled up by \(e^{\alpha(\alpha - 1)\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)} = e\), so its area is \(e = 2.7183\) and \(D_2 = 1\).





B.4.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To account with RDP, follow three steps.

Write down each release’s RDP curve on a grid of orders, such as \(\alpha\Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\) for a Gaussian release.
Add the curves order by order.
Convert once, at the order that gives the smallest \(\varepsilon\).

Do not convert each release to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) first and then compose, because that throws away the curve and lands you back at basic or advanced composition. The grid of orders must reach small orders, because a steep summed curve makes large orders expensive, and the best order for many steps can be 2 or less. The converted \(\varepsilon\) overstates the exact one by an amount that shrinks slowly with \(k\), from 57% at one step to 10% at 10,000 steps in the comparison below. When every release is a plain Gaussian, use the exact result of Section B.3 instead.

title: Appendix B — Composing private releases
text:
B.5 Comparing the four accountants

B.5.1 The question
You now have four ways to add up the cost of \(k\) releases: basic, advanced, RDP and exact. For the same mechanism, how different are their answers, and which should you use?


B.5.2 The answer
Fix one mechanism, a Gaussian release with sensitivity 1 and noise \(\sigma = 20\), and a total \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Table B.3 gives the total \(\varepsilon\) of \(k\) releases under each accountant, from the script. Each accountant assumes something different. Two of them use the release’s exact privacy curve, the smallest \(\delta\) for each \(\varepsilon\) from Equation B.20 with \(k = 1\).

Basic gives each release the share \(\delta/k\), reads its \(\varepsilon_0\) off the release’s exact curve, and adds the \(k\) values of \(\varepsilon_0\).
Advanced spends a fraction \(\kappa\) of \(\delta\) on the releases, \(\kappa\delta/k\) each, and the rest on \(\delta'\). It reads \(\varepsilon_0\) off the exact curve, applies Equation B.9, and keeps the best \(\kappa\) on a grid from \(10^{-1/4}\) down to \(10^{-10}\).
RDP adds the curves Equation B.27 and converts once.
Exact is Equation B.20 with \(\mu_k = \sqrt k/20\).

B.5.3 A worked example
Take \(k = 1000\), the size of a short training run. Basic composition gives each step \(\delta = 10^{-8}\) and reports \(\varepsilon = 238.578\). Advanced composition reports 105.863, or 68.008 with the chapter’s sharper \(\tanh\) form. RDP reports 8.838, and the exact answer is 7.511. So the two accountants that see each release only as one \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) pair overstate \(\varepsilon\) by a factor of 9 to 32, while RDP overstates it by 18%.


B.5.4 Why it works
The order of the columns follows how much each accountant knows about a release. Basic and advanced composition know only one point \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\) of each release’s privacy curve. A Gaussian release has a whole curve of valid pairs, and collapsing it to one point throws away how the release behaves at every other point. Advanced composition still wins over basic for large \(k\), because it uses the cancellation of Section B.2. RDP keeps a whole curve of exponential moments, which adds exactly, and loses only in the one conversion at the end. The exact accountant keeps the whole distribution of the loss, which for Gaussian noise is a normal distribution described by two numbers.
At \(k = 1\) basic composition equals the exact answer, since there is nothing to add. Advanced composition is worst there, because its \(\sqrt{2\ln(1/\delta')}\) factor is paid even for one release. As \(k\) grows, basic composition grows like \(k\), advanced like \(\sqrt k\) until its drift term takes over, and RDP and exact both like \(\sqrt k\).


B.5.5 Checking it
Figure B.5 plots the four accountants for \(k\) from 1 to 10,000, on log axes, and their ratio to the exact answer. The basic line has slope 1, so it grows like \(k\). The RDP and exact lines run parallel, with slope one half, so they grow like \(\sqrt k\). RDP’s excess shrinks from 1.57 times the exact value at one release to 1.10 times at 10,000, because the conversion’s extra term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) matters less as the curve grows. The exact line is the true value, so every other line lies above it. The script’s value at \(k = 1000\), 7.511, is also the one the RDP chapter quotes for this mechanism.






Figure B.5: Left: the total \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of \(k\) Gaussian releases with sensitivity 1 and noise \(\sigma = 20\), on log axes, under basic composition (dashed), advanced composition with the best split of \(\delta\) (dash-dot), RDP converted once (orange) and the exact answer (thick blue). Right: each accountant’s \(\varepsilon\) divided by the exact one.





B.5.6 Recipe and pitfalls
Choose the accountant by what you know about each release.

Every release is a plain Gaussian. Use the exact result of Section B.3. It is a closed formula and the true answer.
The releases mix mechanisms, or are subsampled, as in private training. Use RDP, or a numerical accountant of the privacy loss distribution (PLD), which computes the exact answer to a chosen precision (Section 34.3). Section C.5 works through the subsampled case.
You know only each release’s \((\varepsilon_0, \delta_0)\). Use optimal composition (Section 21.4), with advanced composition as a quick check by hand.
Only a few releases, or pure DP with different budgets. Basic composition is simple and close enough, and it is exact for the worst case of pure DP.

Report one accountant, chosen before you look at the results, and state which one it was and what \(\delta\) it used. Every accountant needs the same neighbouring relation for every release, and none of them covers budgets chosen on the fly. For those cases, see Section 36.4.

B.7 References

Dwork, Rothblum & Vadhan, “Boosting and Differential Privacy” (2010). The original advanced composition theorem.
