title: Appendix C — Accounting for DP-SGD
text:
C.1 Clipping gives the sum a sensitivity
This appendix follows one training run from the clipped gradient to its final guarantee of differential privacy (DP). The run is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with per-example clipping and Gaussian noise, which is called DP-SGD. A training algorithm is differentially private when adding or removing one record changes the probability of any set of outcomes by at most a factor \(e^\varepsilon\), plus a small slack \(\delta\). The sensitivity of a computation is the most that one record can move its result. The Gaussian mechanism adds normal noise to such a result, and its privacy depends only on the sensitivity divided by the noise’s standard deviation. Appendix Section A.7 derives the Gaussian mechanism’s exact guarantee, and Section B.4 derives the Rényi divergence, the tool that adds up the cost of many steps. This page uses both and restates each where it is needed.
The five sections answer the questions a practitioner asks, in the order a training run raises them. Clipping fixes the sensitivity, and the noise then turns each step into a Gaussian mechanism. Random batches make each step cheaper, and a curve built from the Rényi divergence measures that cheaper step exactly. Finally, an accountant adds the steps up and converts the total into one \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Every number uses the book’s running example, so you can check each one against the chapters. It trains on 10,000 records for 100 epochs. Each batch is drawn at random and holds 100 records on average, and the run and reports its guarantee at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\). Table C.1 maps each section to the chapter sections that use its formula.
The notation is that of the DP-SGD chapter, and each symbol is introduced where it first appears. Two datasets are neighbours when one of them is the other with one record added. Write \(D\) for a dataset and \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\) for the same dataset with the record \(x\) added. This add/remove relation is the one the book uses for DP-SGD. The reason is the way DP-SGD draws its batches, by an independent coin flip for each record, so that adding a record simply adds one more coin (Section 18.1, and Section C.3).

title: Appendix C — Accounting for DP-SGD
text:
C.1.1 The question
The noise has to hide any one record’s contribution, so you need a bound on how far one record can move the sum of gradients. But a gradient can have any length. A mislabelled record far from the decision boundary can have a gradient a thousand times longer than a typical one, and nothing about the model bounds it. How do you get a bound that holds for every model and every record?


C.1.2 The answer
Write \(g_i\) for the per-example gradient of record \(i\), the gradient of that record’s own loss at the current weights. You rescale each one so that its length is at most a number \(C\) that you choose, the clipping norm. Rescaling keeps the direction and caps the length: \[\bar g_i = g_i\min\Big(1, \frac{C}{\|g_i\|}\Big), \qquad \bar G(D) = \sum_{i \in D}\bar g_i. \tag{C.1}\] Here \(\|g_i\|\) is the Euclidean length of the gradient and \(\bar G(D)\) is the clipped sum over the records of a dataset \(D\). Its \(\ell_2\) sensitivity is the largest length of \(\bar G(D') - \bar G(D)\) over neighbouring datasets, and it is \[\Delta_2 \bar G = C \quad\text{under add/remove}, \qquad \Delta_2 \bar G = 2C \quad\text{under replace-one}. \tag{C.2}\] Under replace-one, the other common relation, neighbouring datasets have the same size and differ in the value of one record. The book uses the add/remove relation for DP-SGD, so the sensitivity is \(C\).


C.1.3 A worked example
Take \(C = 1\) and a dataset \(D\) of two records with two-dimensional gradients. The first is \((3, 4)\), of length 5, so clipping divides it by 5 and gives \((0.60, 0.80)\). The second is \((0.3, -0.4)\), of length 0.5, which is shorter than \(C\) and stays as it is. The clipped sum is \(\bar G(D) = (0.90, 0.40)\).
Now add a third record \(x\) with gradient \((-2.4, 0.7)\), of length 2.5. Clipping divides it by 2.5 and gives \((-0.96, 0.28)\), so \(\bar G(D') = (-0.06, 0.68)\). The sum moved by \((-0.96, 0.28)\), which is exactly the new record’s clipped gradient. Its length is \(\sqrt{0.96^2 + 0.28^2} = 1.00\), which is \(C\).
Under the replace-one relation, change the first record’s gradient from \((3, 4)\) to \((-3, -4)\) instead. Its clipped term goes from \((0.60, 0.80)\) to \((-0.60, -0.80)\), so the sum becomes \((-0.30, -1.20)\). It moved by \((-1.20, -1.60)\), of length 2.00, which is \(2C\).


C.1.4 Why it works

A clipped gradient has length at most \(C\). If \(\|g_i\| \le C\), the factor \(\min(1, C/\|g_i\|)\) is 1 and the gradient is unchanged. Otherwise the factor is \(C/\|g_i\|\), and the length becomes \(\|g_i\| \cdot C/\|g_i\| = C\). Either way \(\|\bar g_i\| \le C\), and the direction is the same because the factor is positive.
The other records’ terms do not change. Each record’s gradient is computed from that record alone and from the current weights. The weights come from the earlier noisy steps, which are already released, so they are fixed when this step runs. Adding \(x\) therefore leaves every other term of the sum exactly as it was.
Add/remove: the sum moves by one clipped gradient. By step 2, \(\bar G(D') - \bar G(D) = \bar g_x\), and by step 1 its length is at most \(C\). That is the first half of Equation C.2.
Replace-one: the sum moves by a difference of two. If record \(x\) is replaced by \(x'\), the sum moves by \(\bar g_{x'} - \bar g_x\). The triangle inequality says that the length of a difference is at most the sum of the lengths, so it is at most \(C + C = 2C\). The worked example reaches \(2C\), because two gradients that point in opposite directions give the largest difference.

Nothing in these steps used the loss, the architecture or the data. That is why clipping gives a sensitivity for every model.


C.1.5 Checking it
This appendix’s script, described in the Code section at the end, draws 20,000 random datasets of five two-dimensional gradients, with lengths that are often far above \(C\), and a random new record for each. The largest change of the clipped sum, in units of \(C\), is 1.0000 when the record is added and 2.0000 when it replaces another. Both bounds are reached, so neither can be improved.
Figure C.1 shows the mechanism. On the left, each gradient outside the circle of radius \(C\) is pulled back onto it, along its own direction, and those inside are left alone. On the right, adding one record moves the clipped sum by that record’s clipped gradient, so the new sum always lands inside a circle of radius \(C\) around the old one.






Figure C.1: Left: nine random per-example gradients (grey) and the same gradients after clipping to norm \(C = 1\) (blue), with the ball of radius \(C\) dashed. Right: the clipped sum on \(D\) and on \(D\) plus one record, with the circle of radius \(C\) around the first, inside which the second must land.





C.1.6 Recipe and pitfalls
Clip every per-example gradient to a norm \(C\) that is fixed before training, and the sum has sensitivity \(C\) under add/remove. The clipping norm is not a privacy parameter. The next section sets the noise to \(\sigma C\), a fixed multiple \(\sigma\) of the clipping norm. So a larger \(C\) means more noise in the same proportion, and the two changes cancel in \(\varepsilon\) (Section C.2). The clipping norm affects only accuracy, which Section 39.4 studies.
Step 2 is where implementations break the argument. Batch normalization makes each record’s gradient depend on the other records in the batch, so one record can move every term of the sum. A clipping norm computed from the current batch, such as its median gradient length, has the same flaw in another place. The noise level then depends on the data, so it can itself reveal something about the records.
Two other cases double the sensitivity. Clipping the mean gradient of a group of records, a microbatch, has sensitivity \(2C\). The group’s clipped mean is a vector of length at most \(C\) both before and after one member is added, and the two vectors can point in opposite directions, as in the replace-one example above (Section 39.7). The replace-one relation also has sensitivity \(2C\). In both cases the program that adds up the privacy cost, the accountant, must be told, because it assumes \(C\) (Section 33.4).

title: Appendix C — Accounting for DP-SGD
section: C.2 One noisy step is a Gaussian mechanism
text:
C.2 One noisy step is a Gaussian mechanism

C.2.1 The question
Each step releases the clipped sum plus noise. How much noise makes that one step private, and what do the rest of the update and the later steps cost?


C.2.2 The answer
DP-SGD adds normal noise to the clipped sum, independently in every coordinate. Its standard deviation is \(\sigma C\), where the number \(\sigma\) is the noise multiplier, the noise’s standard deviation in units of the sensitivity. So step number \(t\) of training releases \[G_t = \bar G + \xi_t, \qquad \xi_t \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2I). \tag{C.3}\] Here \(I\) is the identity matrix, which says that the noise \(\xi_t\) has the same spread in every direction.
A Gaussian mechanism is described by one ratio, the sensitivity divided by the noise’s standard deviation, which the book calls \(\mu\). For one step it is \[\mu = \frac{\Delta_2 \bar G}{\sigma C} = \frac{C}{\sigma C} = \frac1\sigma. \tag{C.4}\] A larger ratio means the two output distributions overlap less, so an observer can tell them apart more easily. The exact trade-off between \(\varepsilon\) and \(\delta\) is the probability mass where the distribution with the record exceeds \(e^\varepsilon\) times the one without it. For the mechanism with ratio \(\mu\) that mass gives the condition \[\delta \ge \delta_\mu(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac\mu2 - \frac\varepsilon\mu\Big), \tag{C.5}\] where \(\Phi(z)\) is the probability that a standard normal variable is at most \(z\) (Section 20.4, and Section A.7 for a derivation from scratch). Without sampling, every record is used in every step. If the run has \(T\) steps, they act together like one Gaussian mechanism with ratio \[\mu_T = \frac{\sqrt T}{\sigma}. \tag{C.6}\]


C.2.3 A worked example
Take \(\sigma = 1\), so one step has \(\mu = 1\). Solving Equation C.5 for \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) gives \(\varepsilon = 4.38\) for a single step, which is already a large privacy cost. The cost grows quickly with the number of steps if every record is used in each one. For example, 100 steps have \(\mu_T = \sqrt{100} = 10\) and \(\varepsilon = 91.82\), and the running example’s 10,000 steps have \(\mu_T = 100\) and \(\varepsilon = 5425.51\). Nobody would report such a number, and the next two sections show how random batches bring it down to single digits.
The DP-SGD chapter has a full-batch row in Table 39.4, where every batch is the whole dataset, so its 100 epochs are 100 steps. For a target of \(\varepsilon = 4\) that row uses \(\sigma = 10.8\). So \(\mu_T = \sqrt{100}/10.8 = 0.926\), and the script gives \(\varepsilon = 4.005\), the target up to the rounding of \(\sigma\).


C.2.4 Why it works

Only the ratio matters. Compare the noisy sum on \(D\) and on \(D'\). The two are normal distributions with the same spread, centred \(s\) apart, where the shift \(s\) is the length of \(\bar G(D') - \bar G(D)\). Rotate the space so that this shift lies along the first axis. The noise has the same spread in every direction, so rotating it leaves it unchanged. Every other coordinate then has the same noise on both datasets and tells an observer nothing. What is left is one coordinate, \(\mathcal N(0, \sigma^2C^2)\) against \(\mathcal N(s, \sigma^2C^2)\). Dividing the output by \(\sigma C\) changes no probability of any event, so this is the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(s/(\sigma C), 1)\).
The worst shift gives ratio \(1/\sigma\). By Section C.1 the shift is at most \(C\), so the ratio is at most \(C/(\sigma C) = 1/\sigma\). A smaller ratio is never less private, because the two distributions then overlap more. Notice that the clipping norm cancels, which is why it is not a privacy parameter.
The rest of the update is free. The learning rate, the division by the expected batch size \(B\), momentum, Adam and the new weights are all computed from \(G_t\) and from earlier released values, without looking at the data again. Such a computation is called post-processing, and it cannot reveal more than its input. The reason is that an attacker who sees \(G_t\) could run the same computation herself, so any event about the processed output is an event about \(G_t\), and its probability obeys the same bound (Section 19.1).
Unsampled steps add up like one Gaussian. The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the logarithm of how much more likely \(y\) is on \(D'\) than on \(D\). For the pair \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\), the loss is \[\ln\frac{e^{-(y - \mu)^2/2}}{e^{-y^2/2}} = \mu y - \frac{\mu^2}2. \tag{C.7}\] With \(y \sim \mathcal N(\mu, 1)\), this is a normal variable with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\). Each step draws fresh noise, independent of the earlier steps. So over \(T\) steps the joint likelihood ratio is the product of the steps’ ratios, and the losses add. Each step’s loss has this same distribution whatever happened before, so the sum is normal with mean \(T\mu^2/2\) and variance \(T\mu^2\). That is exactly the loss of one Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(\sqrt T\mu = \sqrt T/\sigma\). Since \(\delta\) for a given \(\varepsilon\) is computed from the distribution of the loss alone, the two have the same guarantee, and Section B.3 proves it in full.



C.2.5 Checking it
The full-batch check above recovers the chapter’s \(\varepsilon = 4\) to three digits. It also confirms step 4, because the chapter solved its row for 100 composed steps, while here the 100 steps are one Gaussian with \(\mu_T = 10/\sigma\). The script solves Equation C.5 by bisection on \(\varepsilon\), working with logarithms, because at \(\mu_T = 100\) both terms underflow to zero in ordinary arithmetic. The value at 10,000 steps, 5425.51, agrees with the 5425.5 quoted in Amplification by subsampling.


C.2.6 Recipe and pitfalls
Set the noise to \(\sigma C\), and one step is a Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(1/\sigma\), whatever \(C\) is. Keep everything after the noise a function of the noisy sum and of public numbers. Dividing by the number of records actually in the batch is the common mistake here, because that count depends on the data and changes when \(x\) is added. Divide by the expected batch size \(B\) instead, the sampling rate times the number of records, which is public. And never compose unsampled steps for a long run, because \(\varepsilon\) grows at least like \(\mu_T^2/2 = T/(2\sigma^2)\), the average privacy loss, and reaches the thousands.

title: Appendix C — Accounting for DP-SGD
section: C.3 Random batches make each step cheaper
text:
C.3 Random batches make each step cheaper

C.3.1 The question
DP-SGD does not use every record in every step. Each step draws a random batch, and with \(q = 0.01\) your record is in it only one time in a hundred. How much cheaper is a step that probably did not see you?


C.3.2 The answer
Under Poisson sampling, each record enters the batch independently with probability \(q\), the sampling rate, by its own coin flip. If a step is \(\varepsilon\)-DP when it runs on whatever batch it is given, then the step run on a Poisson sample is \(\varepsilon'\)-DP under add/remove, with \[\varepsilon' = \ln\big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big). \tag{C.8}\] This is amplification by subsampling. When \(\varepsilon\) is small, \(e^\varepsilon - 1\) is close to \(\varepsilon\), and the logarithm of a number close to 1 is close to that number minus 1. So for small \(\varepsilon\) \[\varepsilon' \approx q\varepsilon, \tag{C.9}\] and the step becomes about \(1/q\) times cheaper. When the step also has a slack \(\delta\), the same argument shrinks that slack to \(q\delta\) (Equation 33.5).


C.3.3 A worked example
Take \(q = 0.01\) and a step with \(\varepsilon = 1\). Then \(e - 1 = 1.71828\), so \(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1) = 1.017183\) and \(\varepsilon' = \ln 1.017183 = 0.017037\). The step costs about 0.017 instead of 1, almost \(q\varepsilon = 0.01\). Table C.2 shows how the saving shrinks for larger \(\varepsilon\).



Table C.2: Amplification by Poisson sampling at rate \(q = 0.01\). For small \(\varepsilon\) the cost shrinks by about \(q\); for large \(\varepsilon\) it only drops by about \(\ln(1/q) = 4.6\).

C.3.4 Why it works
The idea is that with probability \(1 - q\) your record is not used, and then the output has exactly the distribution it would have without you. Only the remaining fraction \(q\) of the time can the output differ. So every likelihood ratio becomes a weighted average of 1, with weight \(1 - q\), and the old ratio, with weight \(q\).
A tiny case shows it. Suppose a step’s output \(y\) is three times as likely when your record is used. Under sampling, \(y\)’s probability with you in the dataset is \((1 - q) \cdot p + q \cdot 3p\), where \(p\) is its probability without you. With \(q = 0.01\) that is \(0.99p + 0.03p = 1.02p\), so the ratio has fallen from 3 to 1.02. Here are the steps in general.

Fix everyone else’s coin. Let \(U\) be the set of other records that were drawn. Each record has its own coin, so given \(U\), record \(x\) is drawn with probability \(q\), independently of \(U\).
Write both outputs given \(U\). Let \(P_0\) be the output distribution of the step run on \(U\), and \(P_1\) that of the step run on \(U \cup \{x\}\). On \(D\) the output is drawn from \(P_0\). On \(D'\) it is drawn from \(P_0\) when the coin of \(x\) says no, and from \(P_1\) when it says yes. So for every set of outputs \(S\), \[P_{D'}(S \mid U) = (1 - q)P_0(S) + qP_1(S). \tag{C.10}\]
Use the step’s own guarantee. The sets \(U\) and \(U \cup \{x\}\) are neighbours, and the step is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, so \(P_1(S) \le e^\varepsilon P_0(S)\) for every \(S\).
Put it into the mixture. Replacing \(P_1(S)\) by the larger \(e^\varepsilon P_0(S)\) gives \[P_{D'}(S \mid U) \le (1 - q)P_0(S) + qe^\varepsilon P_0(S) = \big(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\big)P_0(S). \tag{C.11}\]
Average over \(U\). Both datasets draw the other records’ coins with the same probabilities. The bound of step 4 holds for every \(U\) with the same factor, so it holds for the averages over \(U\) too. This is Equation C.8 in the direction “\(D'\) against \(D\)”.
Check the other direction. DP also needs \(P_D(S) \le e^{\varepsilon'}P_{D'}(S)\). The step’s guarantee holds with either dataset first, so it also gives \(P_1(S) \ge e^{-\varepsilon}P_0(S)\), so the mixture is at least \((1 - q + qe^{-\varepsilon})P_0(S)\). Dividing, \(P_0(S) \le P_{D'}(S)/(1 - q + qe^{-\varepsilon})\). To compare the two factors, write \(a = e^\varepsilon\) and multiply out: \[\big(1 - q + q/a\big)\big(1 + q(a - 1)\big) = 1 + q(1 - q)\frac{(a - 1)^2}{a} \ge 1. \tag{C.12}\] So \(1/(1 - q + qe^{-\varepsilon}) \le 1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\), and this direction is never the worse one.



C.3.5 Checking it
The script takes a count with Laplace noise, whose density falls like \(e^{-\varepsilon|y - \text{count}|}\), with \(\varepsilon = 1\). Adding the record moves the count by 1, so the noisy count’s density ratio between “used” and “not used” ranges from \(e^{-1}\) to \(e\). It computes the mixture’s likelihood ratio on a grid of outputs. At \(q = 0.01\) the largest log ratio, with the record against without it, is 0.017037, equal to Equation C.8, so the bound is reached and cannot be improved. The other direction’s largest log ratio is 0.006341, smaller, as step 6 says. Figure C.2 shows the same at \(q = 0.1\), where the effect is easier to see. The ratio without sampling climbs to \(e\), while the mixture’s ratio stays below \(1 + 0.1(e - 1) = 1.172\).






Figure C.2: Left: a Laplace count with \(\varepsilon = 1\) without the record (\(P_0\)), with the record used (\(P_1\)), and the Poisson-sampled output with the record, the mixture \(0.9P_0 + 0.1P_1\) (dashed). Right: the likelihood ratios \(P_1/P_0\) and mixture\(/P_0\) against the output, with the bounds \(e^\varepsilon\) and \(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1)\) dotted.





C.3.6 Recipe and pitfalls
For a step that is \(\varepsilon\)-DP on its batch, Poisson sampling at rate \(q\) makes it \(\ln(1 + q(e^\varepsilon - 1))\)-DP. For small \(\varepsilon\) this is about \(q\varepsilon\). For large \(\varepsilon\) it is about \(\varepsilon - \ln(1/q)\), because when the record is drawn, which happens with probability \(q\), it is fully exposed.
The proof needs Poisson sampling, because step 1 needs an independent coin for your record. A batch of exactly \(B\) records drawn at random has no such coin. When your record enters such a batch it pushes another one out, which is a replacement, so the analysis needs the replace-one relation and twice the sensitivity. Shuffling the data and cutting it into batches is worse, because then your record is in exactly one batch per epoch and is never “not used” (Section 33.4).
Finally, do not add up these per-step numbers over a long run. The slacks add up too, so with 10,000 steps each step may only have a tiny share of \(\delta\). A Gaussian step with a tiny \(\delta\) needs a large \(\varepsilon\), and there amplification only subtracts \(\ln(1/q)\). Section 33.7 shows that the total runs into the thousands, and the next section gives the quantity that composes well.

title: Appendix C — Accounting for DP-SGD
section: C.4 The Rényi curve of a sampled Gaussian step
text:
C.4 The Rényi curve of a sampled Gaussian step

C.4.1 The question
A single \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) pair says how often the privacy loss is large, but not how large it gets when it is, so pairs add up badly over 10,000 steps. A curve that summarizes the whole distribution of the loss composes by simple addition. What is that curve for one sampled Gaussian step?


C.4.2 The answer
The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) between two distributions \(P\) and \(Q\) is a log-average of a power of their likelihood ratio, \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_{y \sim Q}\Big[\Big(\frac{P(y)}{Q(y)}\Big)^\alpha\Big]. \tag{C.13}\] A mechanism has Rényi differential privacy (RDP) curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) when this divergence between its outputs on any two neighbouring datasets is at most \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\), for every order \(\alpha\). A larger order weights large ratios more heavily. For the plain Gaussian mechanism with noise multiplier \(\sigma\) the curve is the straight line \(\alpha/(2\sigma^2)\) (Section B.4).
For one DP-SGD step, divide the noisy sum by \(C\). Then the output without the record is \(P_0 = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\), and with the record it is the mixture \(P_q = (1 - q)P_0 + qP_1\) with \(P_1 = \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). This one-dimensional pair is the worst case, as the derivation below explains. Its RDP curve is \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) = D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0)\), and for integer \(\alpha\) it is a finite sum, \[\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln A_\alpha, \qquad A_\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^je^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{C.14}\] Here \(\binom\alpha j\) is the binomial coefficient, the number of ways to choose \(j\) of \(\alpha\) factors. For small \(q\) the curve is close to its leading term, \[\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) \approx \frac{\alpha q^2\big(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\big)}{2} \approx \frac{\alpha q^2}{2\sigma^2}\quad\text{for large }\sigma. \tag{C.15}\]


C.4.3 A worked example
Take the running example, \(q = 0.01\) and \(\sigma = 1\), at order \(\alpha = 2\). The sum has three terms, one for each \(j\) (Table C.3).

They add up to \(A_2 = 1.00017183\), so \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(2) = \ln A_2/(2 - 1) = 1.7181 \times 10^{-4}\). Without sampling the curve at \(\alpha = 2\) is \(2/(2\sigma^2) = 1\), so sampling made this order almost six thousand times cheaper.


C.4.4 Why it works
First, why one dimension and one shift of exactly 1 is enough. Given which other records were drawn, the step’s output with the record is a mixture of “not drawn” and “drawn”, as in Section C.3. As in Section C.2, rotating the space leaves one coordinate in which the two components differ, by at most \(C\), and a smaller shift is never worse. Averaging over the other records’ coins cannot increase the divergence. The reason is that the average of \((P/Q)^\alpha\) weighted by \(Q\) is a convex function of the pair \((P, Q)\), so a mixture of pairs is never further apart than the worst pair in it. Section 33.5 gives these reduction steps in full, so what remains is the pair \(P_q\) and \(P_0\). The derivation then takes five steps.

Write the mixture’s ratio. Dividing the mixture by \(P_0\) gives \(P_q/P_0 = (1 - q) + q\,r\), where \(r = P_1/P_0\) is the Gaussian likelihood ratio. The normalizing constants cancel, and \[r(y) = \frac{e^{-(y - 1)^2/(2\sigma^2)}}{e^{-y^2/(2\sigma^2)}} = e^{(2y - 1)/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{C.16}\] So by the definition, \(A_\alpha = \mathbb E_{y \sim P_0}\big[(1 - q + q\,r(y))^\alpha\big]\).
Expand the power. For a whole number \(\alpha\), the binomial theorem expands the power of a sum of two numbers into \(\alpha + 1\) terms. At \(\alpha = 2\) it is the familiar \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\). Here the two numbers are \(1 - q\) and \(qr\), so \[(1 - q + qr)^\alpha = \sum_{j=0}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^jr^j. \tag{C.17}\]
Average term by term. The average of a sum is the sum of the averages, and \((1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\) is a constant. So \(A_\alpha\) is the same sum with each \(r^j\) replaced by its average \(\mathbb E[r^j]\) under \(P_0\).
Each average is a Gaussian moment generating function (MGF). The MGF of a random variable \(y\) is the average of \(e^{\lambda y}\), as a function of a number \(\lambda\). For \(y \sim \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) it is \[\mathbb E[e^{\lambda y}] = e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}. \tag{C.18}\] To see why, complete the square in the exponent of the integrand, \(\lambda y - y^2/(2\sigma^2) = -(y - \lambda\sigma^2)^2/(2\sigma^2) + \lambda^2\sigma^2/2\). After you take out the constant \(e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\), what is left is a normal density centred at \(\lambda\sigma^2\), and it integrates to 1. Now \(r^j = e^{-j/(2\sigma^2)}e^{(j/\sigma^2)y}\), so taking \(\lambda = j/\sigma^2\) gives \[\mathbb E[r^j] = e^{-j/(2\sigma^2)}\,e^{j^2/(2\sigma^2)} = e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)}. \tag{C.19}\] For example, at \(j = 2\) and \(\sigma = 1\) this is \(e^{-1} \cdot e^{2} = e\), the factor in the last row of Table C.3.
Assemble. Putting each average back into the sum gives \(A_\alpha\) of Equation C.14, and dividing its logarithm by \(\alpha - 1\) gives the curve.

The small-\(q\) form comes from looking at which terms matter. Without the exponential factors, the terms add up to \((1 - q + q)^\alpha = 1\). The factors for \(j = 0\) and \(j = 1\) are \(e^0 = 1\), so those two terms cost nothing, and \[A_\alpha = 1 + \sum_{j=2}^\alpha\binom\alpha j(1 - q)^{\alpha - j}q^j\big(e^{(j^2 - j)/(2\sigma^2)} - 1\big). \tag{C.20}\] For small \(q\) the \(j = 2\) term dominates, because every later term carries \(q^3\) or a higher power. That term is about \(\frac{\alpha(\alpha - 1)}2q^2(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1)\), so \(A_\alpha\) is 1 plus a small number. The logarithm of 1 plus a small number is close to that small number, so dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) gives Equation C.15. Its second form follows because \(e^{1/\sigma^2} - 1\) is close to \(1/\sigma^2\) when \(\sigma\) is large. Both forms are approximations, not bounds. You will also see the curve quoted as \(q^2\alpha/\sigma^2\), which is the leading term of the upper bound Abadi et al. (2016) proved for small \(q\), and about twice Equation C.15 for large \(\sigma\) (Section 33.6).
Last, the direction. The guarantee must hold with either dataset first, so the curve is the larger of \(D_\alpha(P_q\|P_0)\) and \(D_\alpha(P_0\|P_q)\). The first one puts the dataset with the record first, and it is called the remove direction. It is always the larger for the subsampled Gaussian, which is why accountants compute only it. Appendix Section L.1 derives this step by step, and the script checks it below.


C.4.5 Checking it
The curve can be computed in two independent ways, and the script does both: by the binomial sum, and by averaging \((1 - q + qr)^\alpha\) numerically on a fine grid of outputs. At \(\alpha = 2\), 8 and 32 the two agree to all seven printed digits: \(1.718134 \times 10^{-4}\), \(8.936439 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(11.24628\). A Monte Carlo average of \(r^2\) over two million normal draws gives 2.7084, against the exact \(e = 2.7183\). The other direction is smaller at each of the three orders: \(1.6022 \times 10^{-4}\), \(5.7239 \times 10^{-4}\) and \(1.6923 \times 10^{-3}\).
Table C.4 compares the exact curve with its small-\(q\) form at the running example’s \(q\) and \(\sigma\).

Up to \(\alpha = 8\) the approximation is within 30%, but then it fails abruptly, and at \(\alpha = 16\) it is 2246 times too small. Figure C.3 shows why. The terms with large \(j\) grow like \(q^je^{j^2/(2\sigma^2)}\), and the last one overtakes the \(j = 2\) term near \(\alpha = 2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\) (Section 33.6). C.4.6 Recipe and pitfalls
For integer orders, compute Equation C.14 with logarithms, since the terms span many orders of magnitude. For orders between the integers, average \((1 - q + qr)^\alpha\) numerically, as the chapters’ accountants do. Use Equation C.15 only for estimates at orders below \(2\sigma^2\ln(1/q)\), never as the curve itself.
The curve assumes Poisson sampling and the add/remove relation, like Section C.3. It also assumes the sensitivity is exactly the clipping norm. If something in your code makes the sensitivity \(2C\), such as microbatches or the replace-one relation, give the accountant the noise multiplier \(\sigma/2\) instead of \(\sigma\), because the ratio is then \(2C/(\sigma C) = 1/(\sigma/2)\).

title: Appendix C — Accounting for DP-SGD
section: C.5 From batch, noise and epochs to the final ε
text:
C.5 From batch, noise and epochs to the final ε

C.5.1 The question
You train with \(n\) records, an expected batch of \(B\), noise multiplier \(\sigma\) and a number of epochs \(E\). What \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) do you report? And the reverse question, which a practitioner asks more often: for a target \(\varepsilon\), how much noise do you need?


C.5.2 The answer
The sampling rate is \(q = B/n\), and one epoch is \(n/B = 1/q\) steps, so there are \(T = E\,n/B\) steps in all. The RDP accountant multiplies the per-step curve by \(T\) and converts it to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) at the best order, using Mironov’s conversion: \[\varepsilon = \min_{\alpha}\Big[T\,\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}\Big]. \tag{C.21}\] The second term is the price of converting, which this page calls the conversion toll. The minimum runs over a grid of orders. The book’s grid has the orders from 1.1 to 10.9 in steps of 0.1, followed by whole orders up to 512. It takes \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) from Equation C.14 at whole orders and from the numerical average between them.


C.5.3 A worked example
The running example has \(n = 10{,}000\) records and \(B = 100\), so the sampling rate is \(q = 0.01\). Each of its 100 epochs has 100 steps, so \(T = 10{,}000\). The script finds that the best order is \(\alpha = 4.3\), where one step costs \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(4.3) = 3.9400 \times 10^{-4}\). Multiplying by the 10,000 steps gives a composed curve of 3.9400 at that order. The conversion then adds \(\ln(10^5)/(4.3 - 1) = 11.5129/3.3 = 3.4888\). So \(\varepsilon = 3.9400 + 3.4888 = 7.4287\), which you would report as \((7.43, 10^{-5})\). Table C.5 gives \(\varepsilon\) after each number of epochs.

Sampling turns thousands into single digits. The improved conversion of From Rényi DP to (ε, δ) subtracts two small corrections from the conversion term \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) and gives 6.71 at 100 epochs, the number the chapters report. A privacy loss distribution (PLD) accountant tracks the whole distribution of the loss instead of one curve, and Section 34.8 reports 6.2377 for the same run as its upper bound.


C.5.4 Why it works

The curves add. By the definition, the Rényi divergence of the whole run is set by the average of the \(\alpha\)-th power of its likelihood ratio, and step 2 below writes that as the average of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\) for the privacy loss \(L\). The run’s likelihood ratio is the product of the steps’ ratios, so \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\) is a product of per-step factors. Average this product one step at a time, starting from the last. With everything before it held fixed, the last step is a subsampled Gaussian step, so its factor averages to at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)}\), whatever the earlier steps did. That number is a constant, so it comes out of the average, and the next step is treated the same way. After \(T\) steps the average is at most \(e^{(\alpha - 1)T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)}\), so the composed curve is \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\), even though each step depends on the earlier ones (Section B.4).
The average of a power is the Rényi divergence. Let \(L\) be the privacy loss, \(\ln(P(y)/Q(y))\) with \(y\) drawn from \(P\), where \(P\) is the output distribution on the dataset with the record. Then \[\mathbb E_{y \sim P}\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] = \int P\Big(\frac PQ\Big)^{\alpha - 1}\mathrm dy = \int Q\Big(\frac PQ\Big)^\alpha\,\mathrm dy = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}. \tag{C.22}\]
Markov’s inequality bounds the chance of a large loss. For a variable that cannot be negative, the chance that it is at least \(a\) is at most its average divided by \(a\). Apply it to \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\) at the level \(a = e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\). With step 2 and the composed curve of step 1, this gives \[\Pr[L > \varepsilon] \le e^{(\alpha - 1)(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}. \tag{C.23}\]
A rare large loss is all that \(\delta\) has to cover. Split any set of outputs \(S\) into the outputs where the loss is at most \(\varepsilon\) and those where it is larger. On the first part, \(P\) is at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times \(Q\), by the definition of \(L\). The second part has probability at most the chance of a loss above \(\varepsilon\). Adding the two parts, \[P(S) \le e^\varepsilon Q(S) + \Pr[L > \varepsilon], \tag{C.24}\] so the run is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP as soon as the chance of a loss above \(\varepsilon\) is at most \(\delta\).
Solve for \(\varepsilon\). Set the bound of step 3 equal to \(\delta\), take logarithms and divide by \(\alpha - 1\). This gives \[\varepsilon = T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{C.25}\] It holds at every order, so the smallest value over the orders also holds, which is Equation C.21. Appendix Section D.3 derives the conversion, and its improved form, in more detail.

The minimum sits between the extremes because the two terms pull in opposite directions. Figure C.4 shows them for the running example. The composed curve \(T\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) rises with the order, slowly at first and then steeply past \(\alpha \approx 8\), where the curve leaves its small-\(q\) form. The conversion toll \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\) falls. Their sum is smallest at \(\alpha = 4.3\), where it is 7.43. A longer run makes the first term larger and pushes the best order down, from 8.9 after one epoch to 4.3 after 100.






Figure C.4: The two terms of Equation C.21 for the running example after \(T = 10{,}000\) steps, against the order \(\alpha\): the composed curve \(T\varepsilon(\alpha)\), the conversion toll \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), and their sum, with its minimum, \(\varepsilon = 7.43\) at \(\alpha = 4.3\), marked.





C.5.5 Checking it
The script’s accountant reproduces the chapters’ numbers to every printed digit: 7.4287 with Mironov’s conversion and 6.71 with the improved one, as in Section 33.7. Restricting the grid to whole orders, where Equation C.14 is exact, costs little, giving 7.4692 at \(\alpha = 4\). Figure C.5 plots \(\varepsilon\) against the number of epochs. Without sampling it grows nearly in proportion to the number of steps, while the RDP accountant grows slowly. The PLD upper bounds from Section 34.8, marked as crosses, sit below the RDP curves. A PLD bound is proved for every pair of neighbouring datasets, like the RDP bound, and it is the tightest such number for this run. Both are therefore valid guarantees, and with the improved conversion RDP overstates \(\varepsilon\) by about 8% at 100 epochs, since \(6.71/6.24 = 1.08\).






Figure C.5: The \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of the running example against the number of epochs, on log scales: every record in every step (exact Gaussian composition), the subsampled run with the RDP accountant under Mironov’s and the improved conversion, and the PLD upper bound that Part 4’s numerical accountant reports (crosses).





C.5.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To get \(\varepsilon\) from a training configuration, follow these steps.

Compute the sampling rate \(q\), which is \(B/n\), and the number of steps \(T = E\,n/B\).
Compute the per-step curve \(\varepsilon_{q,\sigma}(\alpha)\) on a grid of orders, with Equation C.14 at whole orders.
Multiply the curve by \(T\).
At each order add the toll \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), or use the improved conversion, and report the smallest value with its \(\delta\).

To go the other way, from a target \(\varepsilon\) to a noise multiplier, search over \(\sigma\). More noise never makes a step less private, so \(\varepsilon\) falls as \(\sigma\) grows, and bisection finds the smallest \(\sigma\) that meets the target. Table C.6 shows the result for the running example’s \(q\) and \(T\). The improved column matches Table 39.2 of the DP-SGD chapter.

Most mistakes in reported numbers come from a mismatch between the accountant and the code, not from the accountant itself. Five are common.

Sampling must be Poisson, or the analysis must match the sampler. The whole saving rests on the independent coin of Section C.3. If the code draws batches of exactly \(B\) records, a new record pushes another one out, so the sum has sensitivity \(2C\) and the accountant needs \(\sigma/2\). For the running example that gives \(\varepsilon = 47.42\) instead of 6.71, with the improved conversion. Shuffling and cutting into batches has no simple amplification at all (Section 33.4).
State the neighbouring relation. The numbers here are for adding or removing one record. A replace-one guarantee is a different statement and needs twice the sensitivity.
The clipping norm is not a privacy parameter. Changing \(C\) changes accuracy, not \(\varepsilon\), because the noise scales with it. A paper that reports \(C\) in place of \(\sigma\), \(q\) and \(T\) has not said how private the model is.
Report \(\varepsilon\) with \(\delta\). The same run is \((5.89, 10^{-3})\), \((7.43, 10^{-5})\) and \((8.71, 10^{-7})\) under Mironov’s conversion. An \(\varepsilon\) without its \(\delta\) means nothing, and \(\delta\) should be well below \(1/n = 10^{-4}\). A mechanism that published one random record in full would satisfy \(\delta = 1/n\), so a larger \(\delta\) allows a real leak.
Count every run, including tuning. Each training run that looks at the private data spends budget, including the runs you discard. Choosing the best of several runs by a score computed on private data leaks more than one run does (Section 40.3, and Section M.3 for the derivation).

C.6 Code
The script apx_core_dp_sgd.py computes every number on this page and draws its figures. It rewrites the accountant in a few dozen lines rather than importing the chapters’ code, so it is an independent check. title: Appendix D — What ε means, and converting between definitions
text:
D.1 What ε means for any test
A mechanism \(M\) is a randomized algorithm: it takes a dataset and returns a random output. Two datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours, written \(D \sim D'\), when one is the other with one person’s record added or removed. The definition of privacy has two parameters, a multiplicative limit \(\varepsilon\) and a small additive slack \(\delta\). The mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-differentially private when, for every pair of neighbours and every set \(S\) of outputs, \[\Pr[M(D) \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\,\Pr[M(D') \in S] + \delta. \tag{D.1}\]
The privacy loss of an output \(y\) is the log of how much more likely \(y\) is when the data are \(D\) than when they are \(D'\). Write \(p(y)\) and \(q(y)\) for the probability (or density) of \(y\) under \(M(D)\) and \(M(D')\). Then the privacy loss \(L\) is \[L(y) = \ln\frac{p(y)}{q(y)}. \tag{D.2}\] Pure differential privacy (DP), the case \(\delta = 0\), is written \(\varepsilon\)-DP. It is the same as asking that \(|L(y)| \le \varepsilon\) for every output. One direction holds because a single output is itself a set of outputs, and the other because a set’s probability is the sum over its outputs. The absolute value appears because neighbours come in both orders, so the definition also holds with \(D\) and \(D'\) swapped. Section A.1 builds these definitions slowly, with examples.
This appendix answers two practical questions. The first is what a number like \(\varepsilon = 1\) promises. The first two sections read the definition as a limit on any test an attacker can run, and as a limit on how far an attacker’s belief can move. The second question is how to report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) when your accountant tracks something else. An accountant is the code that adds up the privacy cost of many releases from the same data, which is called composition. Accountants track Rényi differential privacy (RDP), zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) or Gaussian differential privacy (GDP), because those compose more simply, and the last three sections convert each of them to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). Table D.1 lists the five results and the chapter sections that state or use them.
A running example. Most sections below use one mechanism, the Gaussian mechanism. It adds normal noise to a query, and the noise has standard deviation \(\sigma\). Here the query’s sensitivity \(\Delta\) is the most its value can move between neighbours, measured as a Euclidean distance when the query returns a vector.
Dividing the output by \(\sigma\), and then subtracting the query’s value on \(D\), changes nothing about privacy, because you can undo both steps. After them, the output on \(D\) is a unit normal centred at 0, and the output on \(D'\) is a unit normal centred a distance \(\mu = \Delta/\sigma\) away, for the neighbours whose query values are the full sensitivity apart. A smaller shift is harder to detect, so this pair is the worst one (Section D.5 shows why). So the two output distributions are \[P = \mathcal N(0, 1) \text{ on } D, \qquad Q = \mathcal N(\mu, 1) \text{ on } D'. \tag{D.3}\] Taking the log of the ratio of the two normal densities, the \(y^2\) terms cancel and the privacy loss is a straight line in the output, \[L(y) = -\frac{y^2}{2} + \frac{(y - \mu)^2}{2} = \frac{\mu^2}{2} - \mu y. \tag{D.4}\] When \(y\) is drawn from the distribution \(P\), so that \(y\) is standard normal, the loss is a shifted and scaled normal variable, which is again normal. It is therefore normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\). Throughout, the standard normal distribution function \(\Phi\) gives the probability that a standard normal variable \(Z\) is at most \(x\), \[\Phi(x) = \Pr[Z \le x], \tag{D.5}\] and \(\Phi^{-1}\) is its inverse. Unless a section says otherwise, the numbers use \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), and logarithms are natural.

title: Appendix D — What ε means, and converting between definitions
text:
D.1.1 The question
An attacker sees the output and must guess whether the data were \(D\) or \(D'\), for example whether your record was used. It may know everything else and compute anything. What does \(\varepsilon = 1\) stop it from doing?


D.1.2 The answer
Any guessing rule can be written as a set \(S\) of outputs: the attacker says “\(D'\)” when the output lands in \(S\), and “\(D\)” otherwise. It can be wrong in two ways. Its false positive rate (FPR) is how often it says “\(D'\)” when the data were \(D\), so \(\mathrm{FPR} = \Pr[M(D) \in S]\). Its false negative rate (FNR) is how often it says “\(D\)” when the data were \(D'\), so \(\mathrm{FNR} = \Pr[M(D') \notin S]\). If \(M\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, then every test, against every pair of neighbours, satisfies both \[\mathrm{FPR} + e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 - \delta \qquad\text{and}\qquad e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 - \delta. \tag{D.6}\] The chapter on the definition (Section 18.5) writes \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) for the two error rates. This page needs \(\alpha\) for a Rényi order, so it writes them \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\). There are two inequalities because the definition holds in both orders of the pair.


D.1.3 A worked example
Take \(\varepsilon = 1\) and \(\delta = 0\), and an attacker who accepts 5% false positives. The first inequality says \(0.05 + e\,\mathrm{FNR} \ge 1\), so \(\mathrm{FNR} \ge 0.95/e = 0.3495\). The second says \(e \times 0.05 + \mathrm{FNR} \ge 1\), so \(\mathrm{FNR} \ge 1 - 0.1359 = 0.8641\). Both must hold, so the attacker misses at least 86.4% of the time, and it catches \(D'\) at most 13.6% of the time.
Notice which inequality did the work. The first one alone would allow a miss rate as low as 35%. At a low FPR the second one is much stronger. Low FPR is exactly where attackers want to operate, because an attack that rarely raises a false alarm is one whose accusations can be trusted. For comparison, a coin that says “\(D'\)” 5% of the time, ignoring the output, catches \(D'\) 5% of the time. So \(\varepsilon = 1\) lets the best attacker catch \(D'\) at most \(0.136/0.05 = e \approx 2.7\) times as often as that coin.
Other false positive rates give other limits. At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.01\) the attacker misses at least 0.9728 of the time, and at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.25\) at least 0.3204. With \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) the limit at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.05\) drops only to 0.864076, because \(\delta\) lowers each of the two bounds by exactly \(\delta\).


D.1.4 Why it works
Each inequality is the definition applied to one set. The proof also uses one rule twice: the probability that the output is outside \(S\) is one minus the probability that it is inside, so \(\Pr[M(D) \notin S] = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] = 1 - \mathrm{FNR}\).

The first inequality. Apply the definition to the set of outputs where the test says “\(D\)”, the complement of \(S\). It gives \(\Pr[M(D) \notin S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D') \notin S] + \delta\). The left side is \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) and the probability on the right is \(\mathrm{FNR}\). So \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FNR} + \delta\), which rearranges to the first inequality.
The second inequality. If \(D\) and \(D'\) are neighbours, so are \(D'\) and \(D\), so the definition also holds with the two datasets swapped. Apply it in that order to \(S\) itself: \(\Pr[M(D') \in S] \le e^\varepsilon\Pr[M(D) \in S] + \delta\). The left side is \(1 - \mathrm{FNR}\) and the probability on the right is \(\mathrm{FPR}\), which gives the second inequality.
Tests that flip a coin. An attacker may also randomize, saying “\(D'\)” with some probability that depends on the output. In that case, think of its coin \(U\) as part of the output. Releasing \((M(D), U)\), with \(U\) independent of the data, is still \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, because for each value of \(U\) the inequality holds for the matching slice of the set, and averaging both sides over \(U\) keeps it. So steps 1 and 2 apply to randomized tests too.

A tiny case shows that the bound is reached. In randomized response, one person reports a bit: the true bit with probability \(e^\varepsilon/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), the flipped bit otherwise. Each report is exactly \(e^\varepsilon\) times as likely under one value of the bit as under the other, so the mechanism is \(\varepsilon\)-DP. Let the bit be 1 under \(D\) and 0 under \(D'\), and let the test say “\(D'\)” when the report is 0. It errs when the report is flipped, in either world, so \(\mathrm{FPR} = \mathrm{FNR} = 1/(1 + e^\varepsilon)\), which is 0.2689 at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Then \[\mathrm{FPR} + e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FNR} = \frac{1 + e^\varepsilon}{1 + e^\varepsilon} = 1, \tag{D.7}\] so the first inequality holds with equality, and by symmetry so does the second. So randomized response meets both bounds at once, and neither inequality can be strengthened if it is to hold for every \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism.


D.1.5 Checking it
The script for this page (see Section D.7) lists every possible test against three people who each run randomized response with \(\varepsilon = \ln 3\), for neighbours that differ in the first person’s bit. There are 8 report vectors, and a test is any subset of them, so there are \(2^8 = 256\) tests. The smallest slack, the amount by which a test clears the tighter of the two inequalities, is exactly 0: no test breaks the bound, and several tests meet it.
Figure D.1 draws the forbidden region, with the FPR across and the FNR up. Each pair of lines is the lower edge of where a test can be, and a smaller \(\varepsilon\) pushes that edge up towards the diagonal \(\mathrm{FPR} + \mathrm{FNR} = 1\), which is what a test that ignores the output achieves. The dots are randomized response, which sits on the corner of each region.






Figure D.1: The false positive and false negative rates that tests can reach under \(\varepsilon\)-DP with \(\delta = 0\), for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), 1 and 2. The shaded area below each pair of lines is forbidden for every test. The dots mark randomized response at the same \(\varepsilon\), the cross marks the worked example at 5% false positives, and the dotted diagonal is guessing without looking at the output.





D.1.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To turn a guarantee into an attack limit, pick the false positive rate you care about. The attacker’s true positive rate (TPR) is the fraction of the time it correctly says “\(D'\)”, so \(\mathrm{TPR} = 1 - \mathrm{FNR}\). The second inequality caps it at \[\mathrm{TPR} \le e^\varepsilon\,\mathrm{FPR} + \delta. \tag{D.8}\] Auditing, which tests a privacy claim by attacking the system, runs this in reverse. If an attack measures a TPR and an FPR against a trained model, the mechanism’s \(\varepsilon\) must be at least \(\ln\big((\mathrm{TPR} - \delta)/\mathrm{FPR}\big)\).
Three things go wrong in practice. The bound is for the worst mechanism with this \(\varepsilon\), and most mechanisms sit strictly inside it, so a weak attack says little about how private the mechanism really is. At very small FPR the \(\delta\) term dominates, since at \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0\) the bound still allows a TPR of \(\delta\), so \(\delta\) must be tiny. And the guarantee covers only the mechanism’s own kind of neighbours. A guarantee for neighbours that add or remove one record says less about neighbours that replace one record with another. Section 18.5 proves the converse, that the two inequalities for all tests are the same as \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, and Section 18.6 turns them into a bound on membership advantage.

title: Appendix D — What ε means, and converting between definitions
section: D.2 What ε means for an attacker’s belief
text:
D.2 What ε means for an attacker’s belief

D.2.1 The question
People often ask a different question: “after the release, how sure can someone be about my record?” Take the strongest attacker. It knows every record except yours, so it knows the data are one of two neighbours, \(D\) or \(D'\), which differ only in your record. Before the release it believes \(D\) with some prior probability \(\pi\). How large can its belief be afterwards?


D.2.2 The answer
The odds of \(D\) are its probability divided by the probability of \(D'\), so the prior odds are \(\pi/(1 - \pi)\). If \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-DP, then after any output \(y\) the posterior odds are within a factor \(e^\varepsilon\) of the prior odds, and the posterior probability is capped: \[\frac{\Pr[D \mid y]}{\Pr[D' \mid y]} \le e^\varepsilon\,\frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}, \qquad \Pr[D \mid y] \le \frac{e^\varepsilon\pi}{e^\varepsilon\pi + 1 - \pi}. \tag{D.9}\] The same argument with \(e^{-\varepsilon}\) gives the matching lower limits.


D.2.3 A worked example
Take \(\varepsilon = 1\) and a prior of 1%, so the prior odds are \(0.01/0.99 = 0.010101\). The output can multiply them by at most \(e\), which brings them to \(0.027457\). Any odds \(o\) turn back into a probability as \(o/(1 + o)\), so the posterior is at most \(0.027457/1.027457 = 0.0267\). In words, a suspicion of 1% can rise to at most 2.7%. With a prior of 50% the prior odds are 1, so the posterior odds are at most \(e\) and the posterior is at most \(e/(1 + e) = 0.7311\), or 73%.
Table D.2 gives the cap for other values. Small priors stay small unless \(\varepsilon\) is large: at \(\varepsilon = 4\) a prior of 1% can rise to 36%.

D.2.4 Why it works
The argument is Bayes’ rule written in odds. A table with the two hypotheses as rows shows it (Table D.3). Each row multiplies the prior by the chance of seeing \(y\) under that hypothesis, and the posterior divides each product by their sum \(c\).



Table D.3: Bayes’ rule for two hypotheses, where \(c = \pi\,p(y) + (1 - \pi)\,q(y)\) is the total chance of seeing \(y\).

Divide the two posteriors. The sum \(c\) is the same in both rows, so it cancels in the ratio. What is left is the prior odds times the ratio of the chances, which is \(e^{L(y)}\): \[\frac{\Pr[D \mid y]}{\Pr[D' \mid y]} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}\cdot\frac{p(y)}{q(y)} = \frac{\pi}{1 - \pi}\,e^{L(y)}. \tag{D.10}\]
Use pure DP. Under \(\varepsilon\)-DP, \(L(y) \le \varepsilon\) for every output, so \(e^{L(y)} \le e^\varepsilon\). This gives the odds bound of Equation D.9.
Turn odds into a probability. The map \(o \mapsto o/(1 + o)\) grows with \(o\), so the largest odds give the largest probability. Put in \(o = e^\varepsilon\pi/(1 - \pi)\) and multiply top and bottom by \(1 - \pi\) to get the probability bound.

With numbers, take randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\), your bit 1 under \(D\), and a report of 1. Then \(p(y) = e/(1 + e) = 0.7311\) and \(q(y) = 0.2689\). With a prior of 1%, the products are \(0.01 \times 0.7311 = 0.007311\) and \(0.99 \times 0.2689 = 0.266252\). Their sum is \(c = 0.273563\), so the posterior is \(0.007311/0.273563 = 0.0267\), exactly the cap.
With \(\delta\). Under \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP the privacy loss is not bounded everywhere, so the bound cannot hold for every output. It is tempting to say that it holds except on outputs of total probability \(\delta\), but that is false in general. For example, Section D.5 shows that the Gaussian running example with \(\mu = 1\) is \((4.3772, 10^{-5})\)-DP. Yet, when the data are \(D\), its privacy loss exceeds 4.3772 with probability \(5.284\times10^{-5}\), more than five times \(\delta\).
What does hold is the same bound at a larger level \(\varepsilon' > \varepsilon\), except on a set of outputs whose probability is a small multiple of \(\delta\). To prove it, let \(B\) be the set of outputs whose loss exceeds \(\varepsilon'\), and write \(\Pr_P[B]\) and \(\Pr_Q[B]\) for its probability under \(D\) and \(D'\).

The definition, applied to \(B\), says \(\Pr_P[B] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[B] \le \delta\).
On \(B\) each output has \(q(y) < e^{-\varepsilon'}p(y)\), because its loss exceeds \(\varepsilon'\). Adding over \(B\) gives \(\Pr_Q[B] < e^{-\varepsilon'}\Pr_P[B]\).
Put step 2 into step 1. Since \(\Pr_Q[B]\) is less than \(e^{-\varepsilon'}\Pr_P[B]\), replacing it by \(e^{-\varepsilon'}\Pr_P[B]\) makes the left side smaller, and the left side was already at most \(\delta\). So \(\Pr_P[B]\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}) < \delta\), and therefore \[\Pr_P[B] < \frac{\delta}{1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'}}. \tag{D.11}\]

Outside \(B\) the loss is at most \(\varepsilon'\), so steps 1 to 3 of the pure case go through with \(\varepsilon'\) in place of \(\varepsilon\). So the posterior bound holds at level \(\varepsilon'\), except on outputs whose probability under \(D\) is at most \(\delta/(1 - e^{\varepsilon - \varepsilon'})\). With \(\varepsilon' = \varepsilon + 1\) that exception is \(\delta/(1 - e^{-1}) = 1.582\times10^{-5}\). For the Gaussian example the true probability of a loss above \(4.3772 + 1\) is \(5.381\times10^{-7}\), well inside the bound.


D.2.5 Checking it
The script draws 2,000,000 people whose bit is 1 with probability 1% and runs randomized response at \(\varepsilon = 1\). Among the reports of 1, the fraction that came from a true 1 is 0.0267, the cap of Equation D.9. Randomized response reaches the cap, so the cap cannot be lowered.
Figure D.2 shows the mechanism of the proof. In log odds, the output adds \(L(y)\) to the prior’s log odds, so \(\varepsilon\)-DP keeps the posterior inside a band of half-width \(\varepsilon\) around the diagonal. In probabilities the same band bends. The reason is that turning log odds back into a probability squeezes large log odds towards 1 and very negative ones towards 0, while leaving the middle stretched.






Figure D.2: The largest (solid) and smallest (dashed) posterior of \(D\) after one output of an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism, for \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), 1, 2 and 4. Left: on the scale of log odds the posterior stays within a band of half-width \(\varepsilon\) around the prior (dotted diagonal). Right: the same band on the scale of probabilities, with the two worked examples at \(\varepsilon = 1\) marked.





D.2.6 Recipe and pitfalls
To explain \(\varepsilon\) to someone who thinks in probabilities, ask for their prior \(\pi\) and give them the cap \(e^\varepsilon\pi/(e^\varepsilon\pi + 1 - \pi)\). The guarantee limits the change in belief, not the belief itself. An attacker who is already 99% sure stays about that sure, and DP promises only that the output does not make it much surer. The bound is per person and per release. For correlated records, such as a household, first work out the guarantee for the whole group, and for repeated releases first add up their privacy cost. With \(\delta > 0\), quote the bound at a larger level \(\varepsilon'\) together with the exception of Equation D.11. Section 18.7 states the result and discusses weaker attackers.

title: Appendix D — What ε means, and converting between definitions
section: D.3 From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)
text:
D.3 From Rényi DP to (ε, δ)

D.3.1 The question
Your accountant tracks RDP because RDP composes by adding. At the end it hands you a curve, one number for each order \(\alpha\) (defined next), and you must report \((\varepsilon, \delta)\). How do you turn the curve into \(\varepsilon\)?
The Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha > 1\) is a log average of a power of the likelihood ratio \(p/q\). Written with the privacy loss, with \(y\) drawn from \(P = M(D)\), it is \[D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]. \tag{D.12}\] The expectation is the average of \((p/q)^{\alpha - 1}\) weighted by \(p\), which is the integral of \(p^\alpha q^{1 - \alpha}\), the form in which it is often defined. A mechanism has RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) when \(D_\alpha(M(D)\|M(D')) \le \varepsilon(\alpha)\) for every pair of neighbours. Multiplying by \(\alpha - 1\) and exponentiating, this says that \[\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big] \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{D.13}\] In words, the curve bounds the moment generating function (MGF) of the privacy loss, the average of \(e^{\lambda L}\), at the point \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\).


D.3.2 The answer
For every order \(\alpha > 1\), a mechanism with RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \frac{\ln(1/\delta)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{D.14}\] Every order gives a valid guarantee, so you report the smallest \(\varepsilon\) over the orders you have computed, usually a fixed grid. This is Mironov’s conversion.


D.3.3 A worked example
For the Gaussian running example with \(\mu = \Delta/\sigma = 1\), the curve is \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha/2\) (step 4 below derives it). With \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), the second term’s numerator is \(\ln(1/\delta) = 11.5129\). So at order 2 the conversion gives \(1 + 11.5129 = 12.5129\), and at order 32 it gives \(16 + 11.5129/31 = 16.3714\). Between the two, at order 5.8, it gives \(2.9 + 11.5129/4.8 = 5.2985\), which is the best possible (step 5). Yet the exact \(\varepsilon\) of this mechanism at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) is 4.3772 (Section D.5), so the conversion overstates it by 0.9213.


D.3.4 Why it works
The proof has two moves. Markov’s inequality turns the MGF bound into a bound on the chance that the loss is large. Then a small loss everywhere except on a rare set gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP.

Markov’s inequality on the loss. Fix a target level \(\varepsilon\). Markov’s inequality says that a quantity \(X\) that is never negative exceeds a level \(t\) with probability at most \(\mathbb E[X]/t\). The reason is that those outcomes alone already contribute at least \(t\) times their probability to the average. The quantity \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\) is never negative, and it exceeds \(e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}\) exactly when \(L > \varepsilon\), since \(\alpha - 1 > 0\). So, using Equation D.13 in the last step, \[\Pr_P[L > \varepsilon] \le \frac{\mathbb E_P\big[e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\big]}{e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon}} \le e^{(\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon)}. \tag{D.15}\]
Solve for \(\varepsilon\). Set the right side equal to \(\delta\) and take logs: \((\alpha - 1)(\varepsilon(\alpha) - \varepsilon) = -\ln(1/\delta)\). Solving for \(\varepsilon\) gives Equation D.14. So at that \(\varepsilon\), the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) with probability at most \(\delta\).
A rare large loss gives \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP. Take any set \(S\) of outputs and split it in two. On the part where \(L \le \varepsilon\), each output has \(p(y) \le e^\varepsilon q(y)\), so that part has \(P\)-probability at most \(e^\varepsilon\) times its \(Q\)-probability, which is at most \(e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[S]\). The other part lies inside the set where \(L > \varepsilon\), which has \(P\)-probability at most \(\delta\) by step 2. Adding the two parts gives \(\Pr_P[S] \le e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[S] + \delta\). RDP also bounds the divergence with the two datasets swapped, because swapped neighbours are still neighbours, so the same argument gives the other direction. Section A.6 uses the same split to calibrate the Gaussian mechanism. Note the direction: a rare large loss is enough for \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP, but Section D.2 showed that \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP does not force the large loss to be that rare.

A tiny case shows step 3 at work, before the Gaussian. Take three outputs with probabilities \(p = (0.6, 0.39, 0.01)\) under \(D\) and \(q = (0.6, 0.3999, 0.0001)\) under \(D'\), and \(\varepsilon = 0.1\). Only the third output has a loss above 0.1, namely \(\ln 100 = 4.605\), and its probability under \(D\) is 0.01. Step 3 then promises \((0.1, 0.01)\)-DP. Checking all 8 sets directly, the largest value of \(\Pr_P[S] - e^{0.1}\Pr_Q[S]\) is 0.00989, just below the promised 0.01.

The Gaussian’s curve. Under \(P\) the loss is normal with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\), so its MGF is that of a normal variable. For a normal variable \(X\) with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\), that MGF is \[\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}] = e^{\lambda m + \lambda^2v/2}. \tag{D.16}\] So with \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), \(m = \mu^2/2\) and \(v = \mu^2\), the exponent is \((\alpha - 1)\mu^2/2 + (\alpha - 1)^2\mu^2/2\), which factors as \((\alpha - 1)\,\alpha\mu^2/2\). Dividing by \(\alpha - 1\) then gives \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2\), a straight line through the origin. Section B.4 derives it in more detail and shows why curves add under composition.
The best order. The conversion is \(g(\alpha) = \alpha\mu^2/2 + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\), where \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\). The first term grows with the order and the second shrinks, so the best order is in between. The slope is \(g'(\alpha) = \mu^2/2 - \ell/(\alpha - 1)^2\), which is zero when \((\alpha - 1)^2 = 2\ell/\mu^2\). The first term is a straight line and the second curves upward, so their sum curves upward and this point is its minimum: \[\alpha^* = 1 + \frac{\sqrt{2\ell}}{\mu}, \qquad \varepsilon = \frac{\mu^2}{2} + \mu\sqrt{2\ell}. \tag{D.17}\] For the second formula, the first term at \(\alpha^*\) is \(\mu^2/2 + \mu\sqrt{2\ell}/2\), and the second is \(\ell\mu/\sqrt{2\ell} = \mu\sqrt{2\ell}/2\). At \(\mu = 1\), \(\sqrt{2 \times 11.5129} = 4.7985\), so \(\alpha^* = 5.7985\) and \(\varepsilon = 0.5 + 4.7985 = 5.2985\).

The improved conversion. Step 3 is wasteful. The smallest valid \(\delta\) is the largest value of \(\Pr_P[S] - e^\varepsilon \Pr_Q[S]\) over sets \(S\). That largest value comes from the set of outputs with \(L > \varepsilon\), and each such output adds \(p - e^\varepsilon q = p\,(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L})\). So the exact \(\delta\) counts an output with \(L > \varepsilon\) only in proportion \(1 - e^{\varepsilon - L}\), which is small when \(L\) is just above \(\varepsilon\), while step 3 charges it in full. The improved conversion (Balle et al. 2020; Canonne, Kamath & Steinke 2020) bounds that proportion by the smallest multiple of \(e^{(\alpha - 1)L}\) that lies above it, whose average Equation D.13 controls. It gives \[\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\alpha) + \ln\frac{\alpha - 1}{\alpha} - \frac{\ln\delta + \ln\alpha}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{D.18}\] Section 30.4 derives it. For the Gaussian with \(\mu = 1\) its best order is 5.43, where it gives 4.7284. It saves 0.5701 of the 0.9213 by which Mironov’s conversion overstates the exact 4.3772.


D.3.5 Checking it
The script averages \(e^{2L}\) over 2,000,000 Gaussian outputs; the log of that average, divided by 2, estimates the Rényi divergence of order 3 as 1.4965, against \(\alpha\mu^2/2 = 1.5\) from step 4. At Mironov’s \(\varepsilon = 5.2985\) the chance that the loss exceeds \(\varepsilon\) is \(7.992\times10^{-7}\), below the \(10^{-5}\) that step 1 guarantees. The exact \(\delta\) at that \(\varepsilon\) is smaller still, \(1.300\times10^{-7}\). So the true \(\delta\) is 76.9 times smaller than the \(10^{-5}\) you report. At the improved conversion’s 4.7284 the exact \(\delta\) is \(2.098\times10^{-6}\), so it too holds with room to spare.
Figure D.3 draws the conversion as a function of the order. The dashed line and the dashed hyperbola are its two terms, and their sum has a single minimum at \(\alpha^* = 5.80\). The improved conversion lies below at every order, and neither reaches the exact value. The reason is that the RDP curve keeps only the MGF values of the privacy loss, so a conversion from it must allow for every loss distribution with those values.






Figure D.3: The two terms of Mironov’s conversion for the Gaussian mechanism with \(\mu = 1\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\): the Rényi curve \(\alpha/2\), which grows, and \(\ln(1/\delta)/(\alpha - 1)\), which shrinks. Their sum (red) is smallest at \(\alpha^* = 5.80\). The improved conversion (purple) and the exact \(\varepsilon\) of the Gaussian (dotted) are shown for comparison.





D.3.6 Recipe and pitfalls
Compose in RDP, by adding the curves at each order of a fixed grid, such as the 154 orders from 1.1 to 512 that Part 4 uses. Then convert once, at the end, taking the smallest \(\varepsilon\) over the grid. Use the improved formula, because it is never worse and needs one more line of code. It can return a negative number when \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) is tiny, and then you report 0.
Three things go wrong. Converting each step to \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) and then adding the steps’ \(\varepsilon\)’s (basic composition) wastes most of the advantage of RDP. A grid can miss the best order. The conversion is flat near its minimum, so a grid point close to the best order loses little, but a grid with no point near it can lose a lot. And the curve must hold for every pair of neighbours under the relation you claim. Section 30.3 measures where each step of the proof loses, and Section 30.6 explains how to choose the grid.

title: Appendix D — What ε means, and converting between definitions
section: D.4 From zero-concentrated DP to (ε, δ)
text:
D.4 From zero-concentrated DP to (ε, δ)

D.4.1 The question
When every step adds Gaussian noise, the RDP curve is a straight line through the origin. A line is fixed by its slope, so you could keep one number instead of a curve. What is that number, and what \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) does it give?


D.4.2 The answer
A mechanism is \(\rho\)-zCDP when its RDP curve lies under the line of slope \(\rho\) through the origin: \(\varepsilon(\alpha) \le \rho\alpha\) for every order \(\alpha > 1\). The word “concentrated” in the name says that the privacy loss then has tails no heavier than a normal variable’s. Such a mechanism is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = \rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ln(1/\delta)}. \tag{D.19}\] Three facts make \(\rho\) easy to track. First, the Gaussian mechanism with sensitivity \(\Delta\) and noise \(\sigma\) is \(\rho\)-zCDP with \(\rho = \Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\). Second, running several mechanisms adds their \(\rho\)’s. Third, an \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism, such as a Laplace count, is \((\varepsilon^2/2)\)-zCDP (Bun & Steinke 2016, Proposition 1.4). For calibration, though, you need the reverse. Solving Equation D.19 for \(\rho\), a target \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) is met by any \[\rho \le \Big(\sqrt{\varepsilon + \ln(1/\delta)} - \sqrt{\ln(1/\delta)}\Big)^2. \tag{D.20}\]


D.4.3 A worked example
You answer ten count queries, each with \(\Delta = 1\) and Gaussian noise of \(\sigma = 5\). Each costs \(\rho = 1/(2 \times 25) = 0.02\), so the ten cost 0.2. You also release one Laplace count at \(\varepsilon = 0.5\), which costs \(0.5^2/2 = 0.125\). So the total is \(\rho = 0.325\), and the whole release is \((\varepsilon, 10^{-5})\)-DP with \[\varepsilon = 0.325 + 2\sqrt{0.325 \times 11.5129} = 4.1937. \tag{D.21}\] Going the other way, a single Gaussian query that must be \((1, 10^{-5})\)-DP can have \(\rho\) up to \((\sqrt{12.5129} - \sqrt{11.5129})^2 = 0.02082\). That means \(\sigma = 1/\sqrt{2\rho} = 4.901\) for a sensitivity of 1.


D.4.4 Why it works

Plug the line into the RDP conversion. By Equation D.14 with \(\varepsilon(\alpha) = \rho\alpha\), every order gives a valid \(\varepsilon\), namely \(g(\alpha) = \rho\alpha + \ell/(\alpha - 1)\), with \(\ell = \ln(1/\delta)\).
Find where the slope is zero. The slope is \(g'(\alpha) = \rho - \ell/(\alpha - 1)^2\). It is zero when \((\alpha - 1)^2 = \ell/\rho\), that is, at \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{\ell/\rho}\).
Check that it is a minimum. The term \(\rho\alpha\) is a straight line, and \(\ell/(\alpha - 1)\) curves upward for \(\alpha > 1\). Their sum curves upward, so its only flat point is its lowest point.
Evaluate. At \(\alpha^*\) the first term is \(\rho + \rho\sqrt{\ell/\rho} = \rho + \sqrt{\rho\ell}\). The second is \(\ell/\sqrt{\ell/\rho} = \sqrt{\rho\ell}\). Their sum is \(\rho + 2\sqrt{\rho\ell}\), which is Equation D.19.
The Gaussian’s \(\rho\). Step 4 of Section D.3 showed that the Gaussian’s curve is exactly the line \(\alpha\mu^2/2\) with \(\mu = \Delta/\sigma\). So \(\rho = \mu^2/2 = \Delta^2/(2\sigma^2)\).
Composition. RDP curves add at each order when mechanisms run one after another (Section B.4). Lines through the origin add to a line whose slope is the sum of the slopes, so the \(\rho\)’s add.
Pure DP. An \(\varepsilon\)-DP mechanism has a privacy loss between \(-\varepsilon\) and \(\varepsilon\). A variable confined to an interval has light tails, and Hoeffding’s lemma, which bounds the MGF of such a variable by a normal one’s, turns that into the line \(\alpha\varepsilon^2/2\). Section 31.4 proves it, along with the sharper slope \(\varepsilon\tanh(\varepsilon/2)\).
The inverse. Write \(x = \sqrt\rho\), so that Equation D.19 reads \(x^2 + 2x\sqrt\ell = \varepsilon\). Adding \(\ell\) to both sides then completes the square, \((x + \sqrt\ell)^2 = \varepsilon + \ell\), and taking the positive root and squaring it gives Equation D.20.

The one-step Gaussian with \(\Delta = 1\) and \(\sigma = 1\) is \(0.5\)-zCDP, and it shows that this section and the last agree. Step 2 gives \(\alpha^* = 1 + \sqrt{11.5129/0.5} = 5.7985\), and Equation D.19 gives \(0.5 + 2\sqrt{0.5 \times 11.5129} = 5.2985\), the same as the minimum found for the curve \(\alpha/2\) in Section D.3.


D.4.5 Checking it
For a Gaussian mechanism the zCDP line is exact, so the only slack is in the conversion. Table D.4 compares Equation D.19 with the improved RDP conversion on the same line, minimized over 20,001 orders, and with the exact \(\varepsilon\) of the Gaussian with \(\mu = \sqrt{2\rho}\). The simple formula is 13% to 27% above the exact value, more so at small \(\rho\). The improved conversion removes between 49% and 68% of that gap.

D.4.6 Recipe and pitfalls
Keep the budget in \(\rho\), add it up, and convert once at the end. Do not add up the \(\varepsilon\)’s of the parts instead. Because \(\varepsilon\) grows like the square root of \(\rho\), the \(\varepsilon\)’s of two halves add to more than the \(\varepsilon\) of the whole. Pure-DP steps enter at \(\varepsilon^2/2\), which is close to the best possible slope for small \(\varepsilon\) and wasteful for large ones.
The big pitfall is subsampling. Differentially private stochastic gradient descent (SGD), DP-SGD for short, runs each step on a random sample of the data, which makes each step much more private at small orders. But the sampled step’s RDP curve bends sharply upward at large orders. Any line that stays above the whole curve is then as steep as the line without sampling, so zCDP loses the whole gain. Accountants for DP-SGD therefore use RDP curves or numerical methods (Section 31.8). Section 31.5 states the conversion with its improved version.

title: Appendix D — What ε means, and converting between definitions
section: D.5 Gaussian DP and its exact (ε, δ) curve
text:
D.5 Gaussian DP and its exact (ε, δ) curve

D.5.1 The question
For the Gaussian mechanism, both conversions above leave slack. Is there one number that describes its privacy exactly, and turns into the exact \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)?


D.5.2 The answer
A mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP when no pair of neighbours is easier to tell apart than \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). In terms of errors, every test with false positive rate \(\mathrm{FPR}\) has a false negative rate of at least \[G_\mu(\mathrm{FPR}) = \Phi\big(\Phi^{-1}(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) - \mu\big). \tag{D.22}\] The Gaussian mechanism is \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = \Delta/\sigma\), with no slack. It is \((\varepsilon, \delta)\)-DP exactly when \(\delta\) is at least \[\delta(\varepsilon) = \Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} + \frac{\mu}{2}\Big) - e^\varepsilon\,\Phi\Big(-\frac{\varepsilon}{\mu} - \frac{\mu}{2}\Big). \tag{D.23}\] When several GDP mechanisms run one after another, their \(\mu\)’s add like the sides of a right-angled triangle, \(\mu = \sqrt{\mu_1^2 + \dots + \mu_k^2}\).


D.5.3 A worked example
Take \(\mu = 1\), the Gaussian mechanism with \(\sigma = \Delta\). The best test says “\(D'\)” when the output is above a threshold (step 1 below). An attacker who accepts 5% false positives uses the threshold \(\Phi^{-1}(0.95) = 1.6449\), and misses with probability at least \(G_1(0.05) = \Phi(1.6449 - 1) = 0.7405\). At \(\varepsilon = 1\), Equation D.23 gives \(\delta(1) = \Phi(-0.5) - e\,\Phi(-1.5) = 0.308538 - e \times 0.066807 = 0.126937\). To report \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\), solve Equation D.23 for \(\varepsilon\) by bisection, which repeatedly halves an interval that contains the answer. This works because \(\delta(\varepsilon)\) falls as \(\varepsilon\) grows: a larger \(\varepsilon\) asks less of every test. Table D.5 gives the result for three values of \(\mu\).



Table D.5: The exact \(\delta\) at \(\varepsilon = 1\) and the exact \(\varepsilon\) at \(\delta = 10^{-5}\) of \(\mu\)-GDP, from Equation D.23.
