title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
section: F.2 Chernoff’s exponent is exact, for tails and for tests
text:
F.2 Chernoff’s exponent is exact, for tails and for tests

F.2.1 What the chapter uses
Let \(X_1, \dots, X_n\) be independent copies of a variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\), and let \(S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n\). Write \(\psi(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E[e^{\lambda X}]\) for the log-MGF of one copy. The Chernoff method of Concentration inequalities bounds the chance that the sum reaches \(nt\), for a level \(t\) above the mean, by \[\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \le e^{-n\psi^*(t)}, \qquad \psi^*(t) = \sup_{\lambda > 0}\big(\lambda t - \psi(\lambda)\big). \tag{F.11}\] The chapter then says that “Cramér’s theorem says that … the probability of a large deviation decays exponentially in \(n\) with exactly the rate the optimized Chernoff bound gives, so no method can improve its exponent for large sums”. It does not prove this. In symbols, for every \(t\) between the mean \(\mu\) and the largest value \(x_{\max}\) that \(X\) can take, \[\lim_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge nt] = \psi^*(t). \tag{F.12}\]
Section 4.4 makes the same kind of claim about tests, and cites Cover & Thomas (chapter 11) for it. You observe \(n\) independent draws and test \(H_0\), that they come from \(P\), against \(H_1\), that they come from \(Q\). Hold the type I error at a level \(\mathrm{FPR}\) in \((0, 1)\), and write \(\mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR})\) for the smallest type II error of any test, randomized or not, whose type I error is at most \(\mathrm{FPR}\). The Chernoff–Stein lemma says that \[\lim_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q), \qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P\Big[\ln\frac{p(X)}{q(X)}\Big], \tag{F.13}\] where \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) is the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. The errors \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\) are the type I and type II errors of Section 4.4, renamed because this page needs \(\alpha\) for a Rényi order and \(\beta\) for a failure probability.


F.2.2 The idea
Chernoff’s bound shows that the probability is at most about \(e^{-n\psi^*(t)}\). To show that it is also at least about that, change the distribution so that the rare event becomes typical, and then pay for the change. The change is the tilted distribution of Divergences, which multiplies the probability of each outcome \(x\) by \(e^{\lambda x}\) and renormalizes. With \(\lambda > 0\) it moves mass toward large values. Pick \(\lambda\) so that the tilted mean sits just above \(t\), so that most of the tilted sums land in a narrow window just above \(nt\). Under the tilt, \(S_n\) then lands near \(nt\) most of the time, by Chebyshev’s inequality. The price of switching back is the ratio of the two distributions on those samples, which is about \(e^{-n(\lambda t - \psi(\lambda))}\), and that is the Chernoff exponent.
Here is a concrete case. A coin lands heads with probability 0.1, and you ask how likely 100 tosses are to give at least 20 heads, twice the expected number. Tilting by \(e^{\lambda x}\), with \(x = 1\) for heads and 0 for tails, turns it into a coin with heads probability \(0.1e^\lambda/(0.9 + 0.1e^\lambda)\). With \(\lambda = \ln 2.25 = 0.8109\) that probability is exactly 0.2, so for the tilted coin 20 heads in 100 is the typical outcome, not a rare one.
The Chernoff–Stein lemma uses the same trick, with the two distributions already given. Under \(P\), the evidence \(\sum_i\ln(p(x_i)/q(x_i))\) of a sample is close to \(n\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\), by the law of large numbers. So on most samples that \(P\) produces, \(Q\) gives a probability about \(e^{-nD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}\) times smaller. A test with a small type I error must accept \(H_0\) on most of \(P\)’s typical samples. So under \(Q\) it accepts with probability about \(e^{-nD_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)}\). No test can do better, because every test of small type I error must accept those samples. And the test that accepts exactly the samples with large evidence does that well.


F.2.3 Derivation
Two facts from the chapters do the work. The first is the change of measure (Fact 1 of Divergences, Fact 2 of Hypothesis testing). If \(P\) and \(Q'\) give positive probability to the same outcomes, then for any event \(A\), \[\Pr_P[X \in A] = \sum_{x \in A}p(x) = \sum_{x\in A}q'(x)\frac{p(x)}{q'(x)} = \mathbb E_{Q'}\Big[\frac{p(X)}{q'(X)}\mathbf 1[X \in A]\Big], \tag{F.14}\] because multiplying and dividing by \(q'(x)\) changes nothing. The second is the tilted distribution with parameter \(\lambda\), whose probabilities are \[q_\lambda(x) = p(x)\,e^{\lambda x - \psi(\lambda)}. \tag{F.15}\] They add up to 1 because \(e^{\psi(\lambda)} = \sum_xp(x)e^{\lambda x}\). Its mean is \(\psi'(\lambda)\) and its variance is \(\psi''(\lambda)\), as the Rényi section of Divergences shows for the log-likelihood ratio. Here you only need these facts for a bounded \(X\), where the sums are finite and the derivatives can be taken term by term.
Cramér’s lower bound. Assume that \(X\) is bounded and not constant, and that \(\mu < t < x_{\max}\).

Tilt to just above \(t\). Fix a small \(\kappa > 0\) with \(t + \kappa < x_{\max}\). The tilted mean \(\psi'(\lambda)\) equals \(\mu\) at \(\lambda = 0\). It increases with \(\lambda\), because its derivative is a variance, which is positive for a variable that is not constant. It tends to \(x_{\max}\) as \(\lambda \to \infty\), because the weight \(e^{\lambda x}\) favours the largest values more and more. So there is one \(\lambda > 0\) with \(\psi'(\lambda) = t + \kappa/2\).
Change the measure of the whole sample. Tilt each of the \(n\) copies. The ratio of the two probabilities of a sample is the product of the ratios of its draws, \(\prod_ip(x_i)/q_\lambda(x_i) = e^{-\lambda S_n + n\psi(\lambda)}\). The change of measure therefore gives, for any event \(A\) about the sample, \[\Pr[A] = \mathbb E_{Q_\lambda}\big[e^{-\lambda S_n + n\psi(\lambda)}\,\mathbf 1[A]\big]. \tag{F.16}\]
Restrict to a window. Let \(A\) be the event \(nt \le S_n \le n(t + \kappa)\). It is part of the event \(S_n \ge nt\). On \(A\), the sum is at most \(n(t + \kappa)\), and \(\lambda > 0\), so \(e^{-\lambda S_n} \ge e^{-\lambda n(t + \kappa)}\). Hence \[\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \ge \Pr[A] \ge e^{-n(\lambda(t + \kappa) - \psi(\lambda))}\,\Pr_{Q_\lambda}[A]. \tag{F.17}\]
The window is likely under the tilt. Under \(Q_\lambda\), the average \(S_n/n\) has mean \(t + \kappa/2\) and variance \(\psi''(\lambda)/n\). The window contains every average within \(\kappa/2\) of that mean. Chebyshev’s inequality bounds the chance of falling outside, so \[\Pr_{Q_\lambda}[A] \ge 1 - \frac{4\psi''(\lambda)}{n\kappa^2}, \tag{F.18}\] which tends to 1 as \(n\) grows.
Let \(n\) grow. Take logarithms in step 3 and divide by \(-n\). The term \(-\frac1n\ln \Pr_{Q_\lambda}[A]\) tends to 0, so \[\limsup_{n\to\infty}-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \le \lambda(t + \kappa) - \psi(\lambda). \tag{F.19}\]
Let \(\kappa\) shrink. As \(\kappa \to 0\), the chosen \(\lambda\) tends to the \(\lambda_0\) with \(\psi'(\lambda_0) = t\), because \(\psi'\) is continuous and increasing. The right side of step 5 then tends to \(\lambda_0t - \psi(\lambda_0)\). The function \(\lambda t - \psi(\lambda)\) is concave, since \(\psi\) is convex, and its slope \(t - \psi'(\lambda)\) is zero at \(\lambda_0\). So \(\lambda_0\) is where it is largest, and \(\lambda_0t - \psi(\lambda_0) = \psi^*(t)\).
Combine with Chernoff. Chernoff’s bound gives \(-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge nt] \ge \psi^*(t)\) for every \(n\). Step 6 gives the matching upper limit, which proves Equation F.12.

For the coin, \(\psi(\lambda) = \ln(1 - p + pe^\lambda)\) with \(p = 0.1\), and solving \(\psi'(\lambda_0) = t\) gives \(e^{\lambda_0} = t(1 - p)/\big(p(1 - t)\big)\). Substituting, the exponent is the binary KL divergence \[\psi^*(t) = \mathrm{kl}(t\|p) = t\ln\frac tp + (1 - t)\ln\frac{1 - t}{1 - p}. \tag{F.20}\] With \(t = 0.2\) this is \(\lambda_0 = \ln 2.25 = 0.8109\), \(\psi(\lambda_0) = \ln1.125 = 0.11778\), and \(\psi^*(0.2) = 0.2 \times 0.8109 - 0.11778 = 0.04440\).
Chernoff–Stein, achievability. Assume that \(P\) and \(Q\) give positive probability to the same outcomes. Write \(L(x)\) for the evidence \(\ln(p(x)/q(x))\) of one draw \(x\). Under \(P\) its mean is the divergence \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\), written \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) below, and assume that its variance \(V\) is finite. For a whole sample \(x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)\), write \(p^n(x)\) and \(q^n(x)\) for its probabilities under the two hypotheses. Each is a product over the draws, so the change of measure becomes \[q^n(x) = p^n(x)\,e^{-\sum_iL(x_i)}. \tag{F.21}\]

The test. Fix \(\kappa > 0\), and accept \(H_0\) exactly when the average evidence is at least \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa\). Call that set of samples \(A_n\).
Its type I error. It rejects when the average evidence falls more than \(\kappa\) below its mean \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\). The average has variance \(V/n\), so Chebyshev gives a type I error of at most \(V/(n\kappa^2)\), which is below \(\mathrm{FPR}\) once \(n\) is large.
Its type II error. On \(A_n\) the total evidence is at least \(n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)\), so \(q^n(x) \le p^n(x)\,e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}\). Summing over \(A_n\) gives \[\mathrm{FNR}_n = \Pr_{Q^n}[A_n] \le e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}\Pr_{P^n}[A_n] \le e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}. \tag{F.22}\]
The best test does at least as well. So \(\mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \le e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa)}\) for large \(n\), and \(\liminf_n -\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \ge D_{\mathrm{KL}} - \kappa\) for every \(\kappa > 0\).

Chernoff–Stein, converse. Now take any test, described by its probability \(\phi(x)\) of rejecting \(H_0\), with type I error \(\mathbb E_{P^n}[\phi] \le \mathrm{FPR}\).

Restrict to typical samples. Let \(B_n\) be the set of samples whose average evidence is at most \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa\). On \(B_n\), \(q^n(x) \ge p^n(x)\,e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa)}\). The type II error is the probability of accepting under \(Q\), and keeping only the samples in \(B_n\) can only lower it, so \[\mathrm{FNR}_n = \sum_x\big(1 - \phi(x)\big)q^n(x) \ge e^{-n(D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa)}\sum_{x\in B_n}\big(1 - \phi(x)\big)p^n(x). \tag{F.23}\]
The test must accept most typical samples. The last sum is the acceptance probability under \(P\), minus the part outside \(B_n\). That part is at most \(\Pr_{P^n}[B_n^c]\), which Chebyshev bounds by \(V/(n\kappa^2)\). So the sum is at least \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - V/(n\kappa^2)\).
Let \(n\) grow. Taking logarithms, \(-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n \le D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa - \frac1n\ln\big(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - V/(n\kappa^2)\big)\), and the last term tends to 0. (For large \(n\) the factor \(1 - \mathrm{FPR} - V/(n\kappa^2)\) is positive, so its logarithm is defined.) This holds for every test of level \(\mathrm{FPR}\), so \(\limsup_n-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*(\mathrm{FPR}) \le D_{\mathrm{KL}} + \kappa\). Since \(\kappa\) is arbitrary, steps 4 and 7 together prove Equation F.13.



F.2.4 Checking it
For the coin with \(p = 0.1\) and \(t = 0.2\), the script computes the exact exponent \(-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge 0.2n]\) from the binomial distribution. It is 0.06225 at \(n = 100\), 0.04728 at \(n = 1{,}000\) and 0.04481 at \(n = 10{,}000\), and it approaches \(\mathrm{kl}(0.2\|0.1) = 0.04440\) from above, as Chernoff’s bound requires. The right panel of Figure F.3 also draws the bound of steps 3 and 4 for each \(n\), with the window width \(\kappa = 4\sqrt{t(1 - t)/n}\). The factor 4 makes Chebyshev’s bound in step 4 leave about three quarters of the tilted mass in the window. It closes in from the other side, but slowly: 0.23163, 0.09152 and 0.05800 at the same three sizes. It is slow because the window must shrink like \(1/\sqrt n\), the size of the typical fluctuation. The left panel shows the tilt at \(n = 100\). The original count sits around 10, while the tilted count sits inside the window from 20 up.






Figure F.3: Left: the distribution of the number of heads in 100 tosses of a coin with heads probability 0.1, and of the tilted coin, with the window of step 3 shaded. Right: the exact exponent \(-\frac1n\ln\Pr[S_n \ge 0.2n]\) (black), the bound from the tilting argument (blue) and the Chernoff exponent \(\mathrm{kl}(0.2\|0.1)\) (dashed), against \(n\).



For the Chernoff–Stein lemma the script uses the spam example of Table 4.2. An email’s count of suspicious words, capped at 3, takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1 under ham (\(P\)) and 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 under spam (\(Q\)). There \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.4564\) and the variance of the evidence is \(V = 0.8348\). The evidence of one count is \(\pm\ln4\) or \(\pm\ln1.5\), so the evidence of a sample is \(i\ln4 + j\ln1.5\) for two whole numbers \(i\) and \(j\). The script tracks the exact distribution of \((i, j)\) under both hypotheses and builds the most powerful test of size exactly 0.05, as the Neyman–Pearson lemma prescribes. Table F.3 gives its type II error. Its last column gives the two bounds of the derivation. They use \(\kappa = \sqrt{V/(0.05\,n)}\) for achievability, so that step 2 gives size 0.05, and \(\kappa = \sqrt{2V/(0.95\,n)}\) for the converse, so that the factor in step 6 is \(0.95/2\). A negative lower bound says nothing, because an exponent is never negative.



Table F.3: Type II error of the most powerful size-0.05 test on \(n\) spam-example observations, its exponent, and the two bounds of the derivation with \(\kappa\) chosen for each \(n\). The limit is \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = 0.4564\).

The exponent creeps up toward 0.4564, as Figure F.4 shows. Both bounds tend to KL, at the slow rate \(1/\sqrt n\). The exact exponent is also far from its limit at moderate \(n\). With 200 observations it is still 18% below KL, because the test must leave room for fluctuations of the evidence of order \(\sqrt n\).






Figure F.4: The type II exponent \(-\frac1n\ln \mathrm{FNR}_n^*\) of the most powerful size-0.05 test on the spam example (black), between the achievability and converse bounds of the derivation, converging slowly to \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) (dashed).





F.2.5 What it does not cover
Cramér’s theorem holds without boundedness. The upper bound is always Chernoff’s, and the lower bound needs only a tilt with the right mean, which exists in more general settings; Dembo & Zeitouni prove it in full. The Chernoff–Stein argument above uses a finite variance \(V\) only for Chebyshev’s inequality. The weak law of large numbers gives the same two limits with only a finite KL divergence, which is the version Cover & Thomas prove. Neither proof says how fast the limit is reached. The examples above show that the approach is slow, with an error of order \(1/\sqrt n\) in the exponent.

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
section: F.3 The Clopper–Pearson limits exist and are unique
text:
F.3 The Clopper–Pearson limits exist and are unique

F.3.1 What the chapter uses
Section 4.11 builds the Clopper–Pearson interval for a rate from \(k\) successes in \(n\) independent trials. Write \(F_p(k) = \Pr[\mathrm{Bin}(n, p) \le k]\) for the probability of at most \(k\) successes when each trial succeeds with probability \(p\). Step 1 of the chapter’s derivation says that \(F_p(k)\) is continuous and strictly decreasing in \(p\) for \(k < n\), and concludes that for each \(k\) there is a single rate \(u(k)\) with \(F_{u(k)}(k) = \beta/2\). Here \(1 - \beta\) is the confidence level, which the chapter writes \(1 - \alpha\). The chapter gives a reason in one phrase, that a larger success probability makes small counts less likely, and points here for the proof. Fact 2 of Auditing relies on the same step for one-sided bounds, used in Section 47.3.
The precise statement is this. For \(0 \le k \le n - 1\), the function \(p \mapsto F_p(k)\) is continuous and strictly decreasing on \([0, 1]\), from \(F_0(k) = 1\) to \(F_1(k) = 0\). So for every level \(c\) in \((0, 1)\) exactly one rate \(u(k)\) in \((0, 1)\) solves \(F_{u(k)}(k) = c\). Moreover, \[F_p(k) = \int_p^1 n\binom{n-1}{k}s^k(1 - s)^{n-1-k}\,ds. \tag{F.24}\] For \(k = n\), \(F_p(n) = 1\) for every \(p\), and the chapter sets \(u(n) = 1\).


F.3.2 The idea
Picture all the trials driven by one set of random numbers. Draw \(n\) numbers \(U_1, \dots, U_n\) uniformly from \([0, 1]\), and say that trial \(i\) succeeds at rate \(p\) when \(U_i \le p\). Each trial then succeeds with probability \(p\), independently, so the count \(K_p\) of successes is \(\mathrm{Bin}(n, p)\). Now raise \(p\) while keeping the same numbers. A trial that succeeded still succeeds, and some new ones may join, so the count never goes down. For example, with \(n = 3\) and \(U = (0.15, 0.62, 0.40)\), Table F.4 shows the count as \(p\) grows.



Table F.4: One draw of three uniform numbers, and the count of successes they give at four rates. The count can only go up as \(p\) grows.

0.7

On every draw the event “at most \(k\) successes” can only stop happening as \(p\) grows. So its probability \(F_p(k)\) never increases. The count leaves that event when one more trial crosses over while exactly \(k\) of the other \(n - 1\) have already succeeded, and that has positive probability for every \(p\) strictly between 0 and 1. So the decrease is strict. The derivation makes this exact by differentiating.


F.3.3 Derivation

The endpoints. At \(p = 0\) no trial succeeds, so \(F_0(k) = 1\). At \(p = 1\) all \(n\) succeed, so \(F_1(k) = 0\) for \(k \le n - 1\).
Continuity. \(F_p(k) = \sum_{j=0}^k\binom njp^j(1 - p)^{n-j}\) is a polynomial in \(p\), so it is continuous and can be differentiated.
The derivative telescopes. Write \(g_j(p)\) for the probability of exactly \(j\) successes in \(n - 1\) trials, \(\binom{n-1}{j}p^j(1 - p)^{n-1-j}\), and set \(g_{-1} = 0\). Differentiate one term of the sum by the product rule, and then use the identities \(j\binom nj = n\binom{n-1}{j-1}\) and \((n - j)\binom nj = n\binom{n-1}{j}\). The result is \[\frac{d}{dp}\binom njp^j(1 - p)^{n-j} = n\big(g_{j-1}(p) - g_j(p)\big). \tag{F.25}\] Summing over \(j = 0, \dots, k\), each \(g_j\) appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, except \(g_{-1} = 0\) and the last one. So \[\frac{d}{dp}F_p(k) = -n\binom{n-1}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{n-1-k}. \tag{F.26}\] For example, with two trials and \(k = 0\), \(F_p(0) = (1 - p)^2\) has derivative \(-2(1 - p)\), which is what the formula gives. The formula also has a reading in words. When \(p\) rises a little, one of the \(n\) trials may cross over, and the count leaves “at most \(k\)” exactly when the other \(n - 1\) trials hold exactly \(k\) successes.
Strictly decreasing. The derivative is negative for \(0 < p < 1\). By the mean value theorem, for \(p < p'\) the difference \(F_{p'}(k) - F_p(k)\) equals \((p' - p)\) times the derivative at some point in between, which is negative.
Existence and uniqueness. A continuous function that goes from 1 to 0 takes every value \(c\) in between, by the intermediate value theorem. A strictly decreasing function takes each value at most once. So exactly one \(u(k)\) has \(F_{u(k)}(k) = c\). Strictness is also what the chapter needs when it turns the limit into a statement about the true rate: the true rate \(p\) is at least \(u(K)\) exactly when \(F_p(K) \le F_{u(K)}(K)\).
The lower end. For \(k \ge 1\), the probability of at least \(k\) successes is \(1 - F_p(k - 1)\). By steps 1 to 4 it is continuous and strictly increasing in \(p\), from 0 to 1. So the chapter’s lower limit \(l(k)\), the rate at which at least \(k\) successes have probability \(c\), also exists and is unique.
The Beta form. Integrate the derivative of step 3 from \(p\) to 1, and use \(F_1(k) = 0\). This gives Equation F.24. The integrand is the density of the \(\mathrm{Beta}(k + 1, n - k)\) distribution, because its normalizing constant \(1/B(k + 1, n - k) = n!/\big(k!\,(n - 1 - k)!\big)\) equals \(n\binom{n-1}{k}\). So \(F_p(k)\) is the probability that a \(\mathrm{Beta}(k + 1, n - k)\) variable exceeds \(p\). The upper limit \(u(k)\) is therefore the point that such a variable exceeds with probability \(c\). This is how statistical software computes Clopper–Pearson limits.



F.3.4 Checking it
Figure F.5 draws \(F_p(k)\) against \(p\) for \(n = 1{,}000\) and \(k = 0\), 1 and 10. Each curve falls from 1 to 0 and crosses the level \(0.025\) exactly once, at the upper limit: \(u(0) = 0.003682\), \(u(1) = 0.005559\) and \(u(10) = 0.018313\). The first has a closed form, because \(F_p(0) = (1 - p)^n\) gives \(u(0) = 1 - 0.025^{1/1000}\). The script checks the derivative of step 3 against finite differences, and the integral of step 7 by numerical integration. It also recomputes the limits that the chapters quote, by bisection. For 10 successes in 10,000 trials the interval is \([0.00048, 0.00184]\). For 1 success in 1,000 the one-sided 95% bound is 0.0047, and for none in 3,000 it is \(9.9808\times10^{-4}\).






Figure F.5: The probability \(F_p(k)\) of at most \(k\) successes in 1,000 trials, as a function of the true rate \(p\), for \(k = 0\), 1 and 10. Each curve crosses the level 0.025 (dotted) once, at the upper limit \(u(k)\).



Figure F.6 shows what the interval delivers. For \(n = 100\) it gives the exact coverage of the 95% Clopper–Pearson interval at each true rate \(p\), the probability that the interval built from a \(\mathrm{Bin}(100, p)\) count contains \(p\). The curve is a sawtooth, because it jumps each time \(p\) crosses an endpoint of one of the 101 intervals. It never drops below 0.95: its smallest value on the grid is 0.9504 and its average is 0.9645. The Wald interval \(\hat p \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat p(1 - \hat p)/n}\) of Section 4.11 falls far below 0.95 near the edges. At \(p = 0.01\) it covers only 63.34% of the time, against 98.16% for Clopper–Pearson.






Figure F.6: Exact coverage of 95% intervals for a rate from 100 trials, as a function of the true rate: Clopper–Pearson (blue) stays above the nominal 0.95 (dashed), and Wald (orange) falls far below it near 0 and 1.

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
section: F.4 Rényi divergence tends to KL at order 1
text:
F.4 Rényi divergence tends to KL at order 1

F.4.1 What the chapter uses
Section 3.4 writes the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) through the likelihood ratio \(r = p/q\) and the log-MGF of the evidence \(\ln r\) under \(P\), \[\psi(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P\big[r^\lambda\big], \qquad D_\alpha(P\|Q) = \frac{\psi(\alpha - 1)}{\alpha - 1}. \tag{F.27}\] That is Equation 3.12. Here \(\psi\) is the log-MGF of the evidence \(\ln r\), not of a sum as in the previous section. Property 1 there says that \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\) as \(\alpha \to 1\), where \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) = \mathbb E_P[\ln r]\) is the KL divergence. The chapter proves it as the slope of \(\psi\) at 0, by passing a derivative inside an average. It adds: “This needs \(\psi\) to be finite near 0. van Erven & Harremoës prove the limit in general.” Write \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\). This section proves two statements without derivatives: \[\lim_{\alpha \uparrow 1}D_\alpha(P\|Q) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \text{ always}, \qquad \lim_{\alpha\downarrow1}D_\alpha(P\|Q) = D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q) \text{ if } D_{\alpha_0}(P\|Q) < \infty \text{ for some } \alpha_0 > 1. \tag{F.28}\] The first holds even when the KL divergence is infinite.
Section 5.6 states the matching facts for the Rényi entropy \(H_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1 - \alpha}\log_2\sum_xp(x)^\alpha\), measured in bits, of a variable with finitely many values. It says that \(H_\alpha\) tends to the Shannon entropy \(H\) as \(\alpha \to 1\), and to the min-entropy \(H_\infty\) as \(\alpha \to \infty\). Both follow from the divergence limits.


F.4.2 The idea
The divergence \(D_{1+\lambda}\) is \(\psi(\lambda)/\lambda\), and two simple inequalities trap it between the KL divergence and a quantity whose limit is easy. The first is Jensen’s inequality for the concave logarithm: the log of an average is at least the average of the log. The second is the tangent-line bound \(\ln m \le m - 1\). Applied to the average \(\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda]\), they give \[\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \mathbb E_P[\ln r^\lambda] \le \psi(\lambda) \le \mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] - 1. \tag{F.29}\] Dividing by \(\lambda\), with care for its sign, puts \(D_{1+\lambda}\) between \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) and the average of the power slope \[h_\lambda(r) = \frac{r^\lambda - 1}{\lambda}. \tag{F.30}\] For each fixed value of the ratio \(r\), the power slope moves steadily toward \(\ln r\) as \(\lambda\) tends to 0. So its average moves toward the average of \(\ln r\), which is the KL divergence, and no derivative of \(\psi\) is needed.
On the die of Table 3.1, \(r\) is 3 on a six and 0.6 otherwise. Table F.5 shows \(h_\lambda\) at both values. Each row increases from left to right, and the middle column, \(\lambda = 0\), is \(\ln r\).

F.4.3 Derivation
The derivation uses one theorem about averages, the monotone convergence theorem. Suppose random variables \(Z_1 \le Z_2 \le \dots\) increase to a limit \(Z\) at every outcome, and \(\mathbb E[Z_1] > -\infty\). Then \(\mathbb E[Z_k] \to \mathbb E[Z]\), and the limit may be \(+\infty\). The same holds for a decreasing sequence if \(\mathbb E[Z_1] < \infty\). For finitely many outcomes this is just the limit of a finite sum. For densities, it is a standard theorem of integration.

The power slopes. For a number \(x > 0\), write \(z = \ln x\), so that \(x^\lambda = e^{\lambda z}\). Then the power slope is an integral, \[h_\lambda(x) = \frac{e^{\lambda z} - 1}{\lambda} = \int_0^z e^{\lambda s}\,ds, \tag{F.31}\] which runs backward when \(z < 0\). At \(\lambda = 0\) the integral is \(z = \ln x\), and it changes continuously with \(\lambda\). It is also non-decreasing in \(\lambda\). If \(z > 0\), every \(s\) in the integral is positive, so \(e^{\lambda s}\) grows with \(\lambda\). If \(z < 0\), the integral is \(-\int_z^0e^{\lambda s}\,ds\) with negative \(s\), so \(e^{\lambda s}\) shrinks with \(\lambda\) and its negative grows. So as \(\lambda \uparrow 0\), \(h_\lambda(x)\) increases to \(\ln x\), and as \(\lambda \downarrow 0\) it decreases to \(\ln x\).
Below order 1, an upper bound. Take \(\lambda \in (-1, 0)\). Then \(r^\lambda = (q/p)^{|\lambda|}\), and Jensen’s inequality for the concave power \(|\lambda| < 1\) gives \(\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] \le \big(\mathbb E_P[q/p]\big)^{|\lambda|} \le 1\), so \(\psi(\lambda)\) is not \(+\infty\). (If \(P\) and \(Q\) share no outcome, \(\psi(\lambda) = -\infty\) and every divergence is infinite, so there is nothing to prove.) Next, the logarithm is concave, so Jensen’s inequality gives \[\psi(\lambda) = \ln\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] \ge \mathbb E_P[\ln r^\lambda] = \lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}. \tag{F.32}\] Dividing by the negative \(\lambda\) flips the inequality, so \(D_{1+\lambda}\) is at most \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\). When the KL divergence is infinite this says nothing, and nothing is needed.
Below order 1, a lower bound. Since \(\ln m \le m - 1\), \(\psi(\lambda) \le \mathbb E_P[r^\lambda] - 1 = \lambda\,\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)]\). Dividing by the negative \(\lambda\) flips it again: \[\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)] \le D_{1+\lambda} \le D_{\mathrm{KL}}, \qquad -1 < \lambda < 0. \tag{F.33}\]
The limit from below. As \(\lambda \uparrow 0\), \(h_\lambda(r)\) increases to \(\ln r\) by step 1. The sequence starts above an integrable variable: at \(\lambda = -1\), \(h_{-1}(r) = 1 - 1/r\), and \(\mathbb E_P[1/r] = \sum_{x:\,p(x)>0}q(x) \le 1\), so \(\mathbb E_P[h_{-1}(r)] \ge 0\). So monotone convergence applies, and the average of the power slope tends to the average of \(\ln r\), which is the KL divergence. Both sides of step 3 tend to \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\), so \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) as \(\alpha \uparrow 1\). This includes an infinite KL divergence, where the lower bound alone grows without limit.
Above order 1. For \(\lambda > 0\) the same two inequalities hold, and dividing by the positive \(\lambda\) keeps their direction: \[D_{\mathrm{KL}} \le D_{1+\lambda} \le \mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)], \qquad \lambda > 0. \tag{F.34}\]
The limit from above. As \(\lambda \downarrow 0\), \(h_\lambda(r)\) decreases to \(\ln r\). Monotone convergence now needs a finite starting point. That is the assumption: if \(D_{\alpha_0} < \infty\) with \(\lambda_0 = \alpha_0 - 1 > 0\), then \(\mathbb E_P[r^{\lambda_0}] = e^{\lambda_0D_{\alpha_0}}\) is finite, and so is \(\mathbb E_P[h_{\lambda_0}(r)]\). Then \(\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)] \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) and \(D_\alpha \to D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) as \(\alpha \downarrow 1\).
Rényi entropy. Let \(U\) be the uniform distribution on the \(N\) values of \(X\), which gives each value probability \(1/N\). Measuring the divergence in bits too, with \(\log_2\) in place of \(\ln\), the definition gives \[D_\alpha(P\|U) = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\log_2\sum_xp(x)^\alpha N^{\alpha - 1} = \log_2 N - H_\alpha(X). \tag{F.35}\] The identity holds in any base used for both sides. In the same way, the KL divergence from the uniform distribution is \(\log_2 N\) minus the Shannon entropy \(H(X)\). On a finite set the likelihood ratio \(Np(x)\) is at most \(N\), so every \(D_\alpha(P\|U)\) is finite. Both limits of steps 4 and 6 then apply, and \(H_\alpha \to H\) as \(\alpha \to 1\). As \(\alpha \to \infty\), property 2 of Section 3.4 says that \(D_\alpha(P\|U)\) tends to the logarithm of the largest ratio, \(\log_2(N\max_xp(x))\). Subtracting it from \(\log_2 N\) leaves the min-entropy, \[\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}H_\alpha(X) = -\log_2\max_xp(x) = H_\infty(X). \tag{F.36}\]



F.4.4 Checking it
Figure F.7 draws the sandwich for the die and for the pair \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\), whose KL divergence is \(\frac12\). The black curve is \(D_{1+\lambda}\) and the blue curve is \(\mathbb E_P[h_\lambda(r)]\). The blue curve lies below the black on the left of 0 and above it on the right, and both meet the KL line at \(\lambda = 0\). On the die, where \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = 0.2939\), the divergence at \(\lambda = -0.01\) is 0.2907 with the lower bound 0.2902, and at \(\lambda = +0.01\) it is 0.2971 with the upper bound 0.2976.






Figure F.7: The Rényi divergence \(D_{1+\lambda} = \psi(\lambda)/\lambda\) (black) and the bound \(\mathbb E_P[(r^\lambda - 1)/\lambda]\) (blue) as functions of \(\lambda = \alpha - 1\), with the KL divergence (dashed). Left: the loaded die against the fair die. Right: \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) against \(\mathcal N(1, 1)\).



For the PIN example of Section 5.6, with 10% on one PIN and the rest uniform over the other 9,999, the Shannon entropy is \(H = 12.4278\) bits. The script finds \(H_{0.999} = 12.4310\) and \(H_{1.001} = 12.4246\) on either side of it. As the order grows, \(H_2 = 6.6322\) and \(H_{100} = 3.3555\) approach the min-entropy \(H_\infty = 3.3219\). The identity of step 7 holds to rounding error.


F.4.5 What it does not cover
Without the assumption of step 6, the limit from above can fail. Take outcomes \(k = 1, 2, \dots\) with \(p(k)\) proportional to \(e^{-\sqrt k}\), and let \(q(k) = p(k)e^{-k}\), with the rest of \(Q\)’s mass on an extra outcome that \(P\) never produces. Then \(\ln r(k) = k\), so \(D_{\mathrm{KL}} = \mathbb E_P[k]\) is finite. But \(\mathbb E_P[r^\lambda]\) sums \(e^{\lambda k - \sqrt k}\) times a constant, which diverges for every \(\lambda > 0\). So \(D_\alpha = \infty\) for every \(\alpha > 1\), while the limit from below is the finite KL divergence. van Erven & Harremoës (2014) treat the general case, including orders near 0 and \(\infty\).

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
section: F.5 Perspective functions are jointly convex
text:
F.5 Perspective functions are jointly convex

F.5.1 What the chapter uses
Let \(g\) be a convex function on \((0, \infty)\). Its perspective is a function \(G\) of two positive numbers \(x\) and \(y\). It applies \(g\) to their ratio and multiplies the result by the denominator: \[G(x, y) = y\,g(x/y). \tag{F.37}\]
The perspective has three properties. The first is that it is jointly convex. Take several points \((x_t, y_t)\), indexed by \(t\), and weights \(w_t \ge 0\) that add up to 1. The value of \(G\) at the weighted average of the points is at most the weighted average of its values: \[G\Big(\sum_tw_tx_t,\ \sum_tw_ty_t\Big) \le \sum_tw_t\,G(x_t, y_t). \tag{F.38}\] The second is that it is positively homogeneous, which means that scaling both arguments by a factor \(c > 0\) scales the value by \(c\). The third follows from the first two. The perspective is subadditive, so its value at a sum of two points is at most the sum of its values: \[G(x_1 + x_2,\ y_1 + y_2) \le G(x_1, y_1) + G(x_2, y_2). \tag{F.39}\]
The Rényi divergence uses \(g(t) = t^\alpha\) with \(\alpha > 1\), whose perspective is \(G(x, y) = x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\). Write the sum in the Rényi divergence as \[F(P, Q) = \sum_yP(y)^\alpha Q(y)^{1-\alpha} = e^{(\alpha - 1)D_\alpha(P\|Q)}. \tag{F.40}\] Several chapters assert one of the properties above for this function, without a proof:

Fact 3 of Conversions, the chapter on converting Rényi differential privacy (RDP) guarantees, says that a test cannot increase the Rényi divergence. Its short reason is the subadditivity of \(x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\), and it sends randomized tests to the general proof.
“Computing it” in Section 30.5 says that each constraint of Equation 30.11 is convex in the test’s errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\), so that the region they allow is convex and its lower boundary \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is a convex function. It also uses that each constraint is smallest, equal to 1, at \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\). Step 3 of Section 32.9 repeats the convexity claim.
Step 1 of Section 31.8 uses the joint convexity of \(F\) in the pair, for the pair \((Q, P)\) written as a mixture.
Step 2 of Section 33.5 uses it to show that a mixture of pairs with shared weights has a Rényi divergence no larger than the largest of its parts. It cites van Erven & Harremoës (2014, Theorem 13) for this quasi-convexity.

This section proves the three properties and these four uses.


F.5.2 The idea
The perspective is \(g\) of a ratio, weighted by the denominator. When you mix two points, the ratio of the mixture is an average of the two ratios, weighted by the denominators. A convex function of an average is at most the average of the function (Jensen), and multiplying back by the total denominator gives the joint convexity.
Take \(\alpha = 2\), so \(G(x, y) = x^2/y\), and the two points \((0.9, 0.3)\) and \((0.1, 0.9)\). Their values are \(0.81/0.3 = 2.70\) and \(0.01/0.9 = 0.0111\), and their ratios \(x/y\) are 3 and \(\frac19\). The midpoint is \((0.5, 0.6)\), whose ratio is \(0.5/0.6 = 0.833\). That is the average of 3 and \(\frac19\) with weights \(0.3/1.2 = \frac14\) and \(0.9/1.2 = \frac34\), the shares of the two denominators. At the midpoint \(G = 0.25/0.6 = 0.4167\), well below the average of the two values, \((2.70 + 0.0111)/2 = 1.3556\).
In the language of divergences, \(x\) is \(P\)’s probability of an output and \(y\) is \(Q\)’s. Merging two outputs replaces their likelihood ratios by an average weighted by \(Q\), as in the data-processing section of Divergences, and a convex summary of the ratios can only go down.


F.5.3 Derivation

Joint convexity. Fix the points \((x_t, y_t)\) and the weights \(w_t\), and let \(x = \sum_tw_tx_t\) and \(y = \sum_tw_ty_t\). The numbers \(v_t = w_ty_t/y\) are non-negative and add up to 1. They make the ratio of the mixture an average of the ratios, \[\frac xy = \sum_t\frac{w_ty_t}{y}\cdot\frac{x_t}{y_t} = \sum_tv_t\frac{x_t}{y_t}. \tag{F.41}\] Jensen’s inequality for the convex \(g\) gives \(g(x/y) \le \sum_tv_t\,g(x_t/y_t)\). Multiplying by \(y\) turns each \(y\,v_t\) back into \(w_ty_t\), which is Equation F.38.
Homogeneity. \(G(cx, cy) = cy\,g(cx/cy) = c\,y\,g(x/y)\), because the ratio does not change.
Subadditivity. By homogeneity with \(c = 2\), \(G(x_1 + x_2, y_1 + y_2) = 2\,G\big(\frac{x_1 + x_2}2, \frac{y_1 + y_2}2\big)\). By joint convexity with weights \(\frac12\), this is at most \(G(x_1, y_1) + G(x_2, y_2)\).
Zero probabilities. For \(G(x, y) = x^\alpha y^{1-\alpha}\), outputs where a probability is 0 follow the conventions \(G(0, y) = 0\) and \(G(x, 0) = \infty\) for \(x > 0\). Steps 1 to 3 still hold, case by case. If some point has \(y_t = 0 < x_t\), the right side is infinite, so there is nothing to check, while a point \((0, 0)\) adds nothing to either side. With \(x_t = 0 < y_t\), the formula \(y\,g(x/y)\) still applies, since \(g(0) = 0\) and \(g\) is convex on \([0, \infty)\).
Mixtures of pairs: quasi-convexity. Let \((P_t, Q_t)\) be pairs of distributions on the same outputs, and mix them with shared weights \(w_t\). Apply step 1 at each output \(y\), to the points \((P_t(y), Q_t(y))\), and add over \(y\). Then \[F\Big(\sum_tw_tP_t,\ \sum_tw_tQ_t\Big) \le \sum_tw_t\,F(P_t, Q_t) \le \max_tF(P_t, Q_t). \tag{F.42}\] For \(\alpha > 1\), \(D_\alpha = \frac{1}{\alpha - 1}\ln F\) increases with \(F\). So the Rényi divergence of the mixed pair is at most the largest \(D_\alpha(P_t\|Q_t)\). This is step 2 of Section 33.5. For densities, replace the sum over \(y\) by an integral, and the inequality survives because it holds at every \(y\).
The pair \((Q, P)\) for a subsampled Gaussian. In Section 31.8, \(Q = \mathcal N(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(P = (1 - q)Q + q\,\mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\). The pair \((Q, P)\) is the mixture \((1 - q)(Q, Q) + q\,(Q, \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2))\), with the shared weights \(1 - q\) and \(q\). The first inequality of step 5 gives \[F(Q, P) \le (1 - q)F(Q, Q) + q\,F\big(Q, \mathcal N(1, \sigma^2)\big) = (1 - q) + q\,e^{(\alpha - 1)\alpha\rho_0}, \tag{F.43}\] because \(F(Q, Q) = 1\), and \(D_\alpha\) between two normals with unit shift is \(\alpha\rho_0\), where \(\rho_0 = 1/(2\sigma^2)\). That is the bound the chapter states.
Tests cannot increase the divergence. A test rejects on output \(y\) with probability \(\phi(y)\), which may lie strictly between 0 and 1. Split each output \(y\) into two pieces, “\(y\) and reject” and “\(y\) and accept”. Their probabilities are \(\phi(y)P(y)\) and \((1 - \phi(y))P(y)\) under \(P\), and likewise under \(Q\). Both pieces keep the ratio \(P(y)/Q(y)\), so by homogeneity their two terms add up to \(G(P(y), Q(y))\), and \(F\) does not change. Now merge all the “reject” pieces into one output and all the “accept” pieces into another. By subadditivity, applied one merge at a time, \(F\) can only go down. The two merged outputs are the test’s coin. It rejects with probability \(\mathrm{FPR} = \sum_y\phi(y)P(y)\) under \(P\) and \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} = \sum_y\phi(y)Q(y)\) under \(Q\), where \(\mathrm{FPR}\) and \(\mathrm{FNR}\) are its type I and type II errors. So \[G(\mathrm{FPR}, 1 - \mathrm{FNR}) + G(1 - \mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) \le F(P, Q), \tag{F.44}\] which is Fact 3 of Conversions, randomized tests included. The same split-and-merge argument works for any processing that sends each output \(y\) to a random output \(z\), so it also proves the data-processing inequality for \(D_\alpha\).
The region of allowed tests is convex. The chapter’s RDP curve \(\varepsilon(\alpha)\) bounds the Rényi divergence of order \(\alpha\) in both directions, and the coin of step 7 inherits both bounds. Written with \(G\), the two constraints of Equation 30.11 are \[c_1(\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) = G(\mathrm{FPR}, 1 - \mathrm{FNR}) + G(1 - \mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}, \qquad c_2(\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR}) = G(1 - \mathrm{FNR}, \mathrm{FPR}) + G(\mathrm{FNR}, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}) \le e^{(\alpha - 1)\varepsilon(\alpha)}. \tag{F.45}\] Each term is \(G\) applied to numbers that depend linearly on \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\). Mixing two error pairs mixes those numbers with the same weights, so step 1 makes each term, and their sum, convex in \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\). The same holds for \(c_2\), which swaps the roles of the two distributions. If two error pairs satisfy a convex constraint, so does every mixture of them, because its value is at most the mixture of two values that are both within the limit. So each constraint allows a convex set of pairs, and so does their intersection.
The boundary is convex, and each constraint is smallest at \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\). Let \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) be the smallest allowed \(\mathrm{FNR}\) at type I error \(\mathrm{FPR}\). For allowed pairs \((\mathrm{FPR}_1, \mathrm{FNR}_1)\) and \((\mathrm{FPR}_2, \mathrm{FNR}_2)\), the mixture is allowed, so \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) at the mixed \(\mathrm{FPR}\) is at most the mixed \(\mathrm{FNR}\). Taking each \(\mathrm{FNR}_i\) as small as allowed shows that \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is convex. At \(\mathrm{FNR} = 1 - \mathrm{FPR}\), homogeneity gives \(c_1 = G(\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FPR}) + G(1 - \mathrm{FPR}, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}) = \mathrm{FPR} + (1 - \mathrm{FPR}) = 1\). Subadditivity merges the two terms, whose arguments add up to \((\mathrm{FPR} + 1 - \mathrm{FPR},\ 1 - \mathrm{FNR} + \mathrm{FNR}) = (1, 1)\), so \(c_1 \ge G(1, 1) = 1\) for every \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\), so 1 is the smallest value. A convex function of \(\mathrm{FNR}\) that is smallest at \(1 - \mathrm{FPR}\) decreases on \([0, 1 - \mathrm{FPR}]\), which is what the chapter needs to find \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(\mathrm{FPR})\) by bisection on \(\mathrm{FNR}\).



F.5.4 Checking it
At \(\alpha = 2\), the script draws 100,000 random pairs of points and weights. It finds no violation of joint convexity or of subadditivity. It also draws 20,000 random mixtures of three pairs of distributions on five outputs, and finds no mixture whose Rényi divergence exceeds the largest of its parts.
On the die, the loaded die gives a six probability 0.5 and each other face 0.1. Take the randomized test that rejects on a six, and with probability \(\frac12\) on a five. Its type I error is \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.5 + 0.05 = 0.55\), and it rejects under the fair die with probability \(1 - \mathrm{FNR} = \frac16 + \frac1{12} = 0.25\). Its coin has \(D_2 = 0.3920\), below \(D_2(P\|Q) = 0.5878\) for the full roll, as step 7 requires.
For the subsampled Gaussian of step 6, with \(q = 0.1\), \(\sigma = 1\) and \(\alpha = 2\), numerical integration gives \(F(Q, P) = 1.0115\), below the bound \(0.9 + 0.1e = 1.1718\). The bound is loose here because it charges the full Gaussian divergence to the fraction \(q\) of the mixture.
The right panel of Figure F.8 draws the region that order 2 alone allows for the Gaussian mechanism whose sensitivity equals its noise standard deviation (\(\mu = 1\) in the chapters), whose RDP curve gives \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\). At \(\mathrm{FPR} = 0.1\) the boundary is \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}(0.1) = 0.5068\), so the largest power is 0.4932, the order-2 value that Section 30.5 reports. The script checks convexity on a grid of 199 values of \(\mathrm{FPR}\): the smallest second difference of \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\) is positive. In the figure, the chord between two boundary points stays inside the region. The boundary has a kink where the binding constraint switches from \(c_2\) to \(c_1\), and convexity survives it.






Figure F.8: Left: contours of \(G(x, y) = x^2/y\), the perspective of \(g(t) = t^2\), with two points, the chord between them and its midpoint, where the function value is below the average of the two end values. Right: the pairs of type I and type II errors \((\mathrm{FPR}, \mathrm{FNR})\) that order \(\alpha = 2\) with \(\varepsilon(2) = 1\) allows (shaded), its lower boundary \(f_{\mathrm{RDP}}\), and a chord between two boundary points that stays inside.

title: Appendix F — Tail bounds, tests and divergences
section: F.6 A noisy count has an increasing likelihood ratio
text:
F.6 A noisy count has an increasing likelihood ratio

F.6.1 What the chapter uses
The example of Section 9.6 releases a noisy count of \(m = 100\) other records plus the target’s bit \(b\). The adversary sees \(K + b + Z\), where the unknown count \(K\) of the others is \(\mathrm{Bin}(m, \frac12)\) and the noise \(Z\) is normal with mean 0 and standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\). Write \(w_k = \binom mk2^{-m}\) for the binomial weights and \(\varphi_\sigma\) for the normal density with standard deviation \(\sigma\). In world 0 (\(b = 0\)) the observation has density \[p(y) = f(y), \qquad f(y) = \sum_{k=0}^mw_k\,\varphi_\sigma(y - k), \tag{F.46}\] and in world 1 (\(b = 1\)) it has the shifted density \(q(y) = f(y - 1)\).
The chapter says that the likelihood ratio increases with \(y\), so the best attack is a threshold, at \(m/2 + \frac12 = 50.5\) by symmetry. A tempting reason is that \(f\) is log-concave, because a binomial and a normal are both log-concave and so is their sum. That reason is not valid in general, because the rule it quotes concerns two variables that both have log-concave densities on the real line. A binomial count lives on the integers and has no density there, and for such sums the rule fails. For example, a Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) variable plus normal noise with \(\sigma = 0.2\) has two separate peaks, as the left panel of Figure F.9 shows, so it is not log-concave. With \(m = 100\) and \(\sigma = 1\) the density does happen to be log-concave, but with \(\sigma = 0.5\) it is not.
The attack needs less than log-concavity, and what it needs holds for every \(\sigma > 0\): \[\frac{q(y)}{p(y)} = \frac{f(y - 1)}{f(y)} \text{ is strictly increasing in } y. \tag{F.47}\] The proof below uses two properties. The weights \(w_k\) must form a log-concave sequence, \(w_k^2 \ge w_{k-1}w_{k+1}\), with no zero between two non-zero weights. The noise must be normal.


F.6.2 The idea
Both densities are mixtures over the unknown count of the others. Comparing the ratio at two observations \(y < y'\) therefore means comparing two double sums, over the count \(j\) in one world and the count \(k\) in the other. Pair each term \((j, k)\) with its mirror image \((k, j)\). Each pair turns into a product of two factors. One compares the binomial weights, and it is non-negative because the binomial is log-concave. The other compares normal densities, and it is non-negative because a larger observation favours a larger centre. A product of two non-negative factors is non-negative, and so is the sum.
For a single Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) record (\(m = 1\)), the weights are \(w_0 = w_1 = \frac12\), and \(w_k = 0\) for every other \(k\). The pairs with \(j > k\) whose weight factor \(w_{j-1}w_k - w_{k-1}w_j\) is not zero are listed in Table F.6. All three weight factors are positive, even though the density has two peaks.



Table F.6: The weight factors of step 4 for one Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) record, for the pairs \(j > k\) where they are not zero.

F.6.3 Derivation
Set \(w_i = 0\) for \(i\) outside \(0, \dots, m\), and write \(\varphi\) for \(\varphi_\sigma\). Substituting \(j = k + 1\) in \(q(y) = f(y - 1)\) writes both densities as sums over a centre: \[p(y) = \sum_kw_k\,\varphi(y - k), \qquad q(y) = \sum_jw_{j-1}\varphi(y - j). \tag{F.48}\]

What to show. The ratio increases exactly when \(q(y')/p(y') \ge q(y)/p(y)\) for every \(y < y'\). Multiplying by the positive \(p(y)p(y')\), this is \(\Delta = q(y')p(y) - q(y)p(y') \ge 0\).
Expand. Multiplying out the sums, \[\Delta = \sum_{j,k}a_{jk}b_{jk}, \qquad a_{jk} = w_{j-1}w_k, \qquad b_{jk} = \varphi(y' - j)\varphi(y - k) - \varphi(y - j)\varphi(y' - k). \tag{F.49}\]
Pair each term with its mirror. Swapping \(j\) and \(k\) swaps the two products in \(b_{jk}\), so \(b_{kj} = -b_{jk}\) and \(b_{jj} = 0\). Split the sum into the terms with \(j > k\) and those with \(j < k\), and rename the indices in the second part. Then \[\Delta = \sum_{j > k}\big(a_{jk} - a_{kj}\big)b_{jk} = \sum_{j>k}\big(w_{j-1}w_k - w_{k-1}w_j\big)\,b_{jk}. \tag{F.50}\]
The weight factor is non-negative. Take \(j > k\). If \(w_{k-1} = 0\) or \(w_j = 0\), the subtracted product is 0 and the factor is at least 0. Otherwise \(k - 1\) and \(j\) both carry weight, and so does every index between them, because there are no internal zeros. Log-concavity, \(w_i^2 \ge w_{i-1}w_{i+1}\), says that the ratio \(w_{i-1}/w_i\) never decreases as \(i\) grows. So \(w_{j-1}/w_j \ge w_{k-1}/w_k\), which is \(w_{j-1}w_k \ge w_{k-1}w_j\). For the binomial, \(w_{i-1}/w_i = i/(m - i + 1)\), which increases with \(i\).
The kernel factor is positive. Take \(j > k\) and \(y < y'\). Compare the logarithms of the two products in \(b_{jk}\). Expanding the squares in the normal densities, the terms in \(y^2\), \(y'^2\), \(j^2\) and \(k^2\) cancel, and \[\ln\frac{\varphi(y' - j)\varphi(y - k)}{\varphi(y - j)\varphi(y' - k)} = \frac{(y - j)^2 + (y' - k)^2 - (y' - j)^2 - (y - k)^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{(y' - y)(j - k)}{\sigma^2} > 0. \tag{F.51}\] So \(b_{jk} > 0\). In words, a larger observation is relatively more likely under the larger centre.
Conclude. Every term of step 3 is a non-negative weight factor times a positive kernel factor, so \(\Delta \ge 0\). The pair \((1, 0)\) has weight factor \(w_0^2 > 0\), so \(\Delta > 0\) and the ratio is strictly increasing. This proves Equation F.47.
The best attack is a threshold. By the Neyman–Pearson lemma (Section 4.4), the most powerful test rejects where the likelihood ratio \(q/p\) is above a cut-off. When the ratio increases with \(y\), that region is \(\{y > \tau\}\) for some threshold \(\tau\).
The threshold. The binomial weights are symmetric, \(w_k = w_{m-k}\), and so is the noise, so \(f(m/2 + s) = f(m/2 - s)\) for every \(s\). The ratio equals 1 where \(f(y - 1) = f(y)\). That happens when \(y - 1\) and \(y\) sit symmetrically around \(m/2\), at \(y = m/2 + \frac12\). Because the ratio is strictly increasing, it crosses 1 only there. The test with the best advantage rejects exactly where \(q > p\), that is, where the ratio is above 1 (Section 4.8), which is \(\{y > 50.5\}\) for \(m = 100\).



F.6.4 Checking it
For the Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) record with \(\sigma = 0.2\), the script finds two peaks in the density. On a grid of 4,001 points the log-ratio still increases at every step. It also evaluates the double sum of step 3 directly and matches \(\Delta\) to rounding error, both for this case and for \(m = 100\). For \(m = 100\) and \(\sigma = 1\), the ratio crosses 1 at 50.5000, and the advantage of that threshold is 0.0779, the exact value in Table 9.6. The largest second difference of \(\ln f\) on a grid is negative (\(-3.8\times10^{-6}\)) at \(\sigma = 1\) and positive (\(+5.5\times10^{-5}\)) at \(\sigma = 0.5\). So the density is log-concave in the chapter’s case but not for smaller noise. The ratio increases in both cases, as the right panel of Figure F.9 shows.






Figure F.9: Left: the densities of a Bernoulli(\(\frac12\)) bit plus normal noise with standard deviation 0.2, in world 0 and shifted by 1 in world 1; each has two peaks. Middle: the logarithm of their likelihood ratio still increases with the observation. Right: the log-likelihood ratio of the chapter’s noisy count of 100 records for three noise levels, increasing for each and crossing 0 at 50.5.





F.6.5 What it does not cover
The proof needs the kernel inequality of step 5 for the noise. Step 5 proves it for normal noise, and it holds for every log-concave noise density, such as the Laplace density (Karlin calls such shift kernels totally positive of order 2). For other noise the argument does not apply. It also needs log-concave weights without internal zeros. A count whose other records have unequal probabilities is a sum of independent Bernoulli variables, and such a count still has log-concave weights, so the result covers it too.
