Circles are Gaussian rows and squares are 0/1 rows rescaled by the diagonal of \(\Sigma^{-1}\). The black curve is \(m/(m - n - 1)\) and the dashed line is the naive value 1, from inverting the average Gram matrix.



Steps 4 and 5 can be checked one at a time. For one Gaussian matrix with \(m = 60\) rows, the script regresses the first column on the others and finds a squared residual of 4.931982. One over the first diagonal entry of the inverse is the same 4.931982, as Equation H.2 says. Figure H.2 repeats this for 20,000 matrices and compares the histogram with the \(\chi^2\) density with \(m - n + 1 = 11\) degrees of freedom. Step 6 for \(k = 11\) predicts \(1/9 = 0.1111\), and a million simulated \(\chi^2_{11}\) values give 0.1112. Finally, the symmetry of steps 2 and 3 shows up in simulation as an average inverse whose off-diagonal entries are tiny. With \(n = 10\), \(m = 30\) and 20,000 draws, their average size is 0.0013 of the diagonal for Gaussian rows. For 0/1 rows the ratio is 0.1000, because 0/1 entries have a nonzero mean and flipping a column’s sign is no longer a symmetry. That is still the shape the approximation predicts, since \(\Sigma^{-1}\) is proportional to \(I - \frac{1}{n + 1}\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top\), whose off-diagonal entries are \(\frac1n = 0.1\) times its diagonal ones.






Figure H.2: Histogram of \(1/[(Z^\top Z)^{-1}]_{11}\) over 20,000 Gaussian matrices with \(m = 60\) rows and \(n = 50\) columns, against the \(\chi^2\) density with \(m - n + 1 = 11\) degrees of freedom. The two agree, as steps 4 and 5 predict.





H.1.5 What it does not cover
The proof needs Gaussian rows in two places. Step 2 needs each column to keep its distribution when its sign flips, and step 5 needs rotation invariance. Rows of 0/1 entries have neither property, which is why the chapter calls the formula an approximation and checks the attack by simulation. There is also a technical gap for 0/1 rows. A 0/1 matrix is singular with a small but positive probability, for example when two columns happen to be equal, so the average of its inverse is not even defined. The rescaled values in Table H.2 are averages over draws that happened to be invertible, which at these sizes is every draw.
The condition \(m \ge n + 2\) is needed. At \(m = n + 1\) the residual is a \(\chi^2_2\) variable, whose inverse has an infinite average, because \(\chi^2_2\) puts too much probability near 0. Even for \(m \ge n + 2\), the diagonal entries of the inverse have a heavy right tail when \(m\) is close to \(n\), which makes simulations there noisy.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
section: H.2 A random subset matrix shrinks no direction much
text:
H.2 A random subset matrix shrinks no direction much

H.2.1 What the chapter uses
The worst-case bound of Section 17.5, Equation 17.9, says that least squares gets at most \(4mE^2/s_{\min}(A)^2\) bits wrong when every answer has error at most \(E\). Here \(s_{\min}(A)\), the smallest singular value, is the smallest length \(\|Ax\|\) over unit vectors \(x\). The bound is useful only if \(s_{\min}(A)\) is of order \(\sqrt m\). Step 5 there says that for a random matrix \(s_{\min}\) “concentrates near \(\sqrt m - \sqrt n\) times the scale of the rows” and cites Vershynin, High-Dimensional Probability, ch. 4. It then argues by a heuristic that \(s_{\min}(A) \approx \frac12(\sqrt m - \sqrt n)\) for random subsets, checks this at one size, and concludes that error \(E = o(\sqrt n)\) gives \(o(n)\) wrong bits with \(m = 4n\) queries.
This section proves a version with a worse constant and an extra logarithm, but a complete proof. Let \(A\) be an \(m \times n\) matrix whose rows are independent uniformly random subsets \(q_1, \dots, q_m\), so each entry is an independent fair 0 or 1. For a failure probability \(\beta\), \[s_{\min}(A) \ge \frac{\sqrt m}{14} \quad\text{with probability at least } 1 - \beta, \quad\text{once}\quad m \ge 128\Big(n\ln(80n + 1) + \ln\frac1\beta\Big). \tag{H.5}\] Substituted into Equation 17.9, this gives at most \(4mE^2 \cdot 196/m = 784E^2\) wrong bits. So with \(m = O(n\log n)\) queries, error \(E = o(\sqrt n)\) leaves \(o(n)\) wrong bits.


H.2.2 The idea
The proof reuses a lemma from the chapter’s linear-programming section, Section 17.4, in three moves. The lemma says that one random query catches any fixed direction: for any fixed vector \(x\), the squared answer \(\langle q, x\rangle^2\) exceeds \(\|x\|^2/16\) with probability at least \(\frac3{16}\). Over \(m\) independent queries, Hoeffding’s inequality then makes it nearly certain that a good share of the queries catch \(x\), and each caught query adds a fixed amount to \(\|Ax\|^2\). That handles one direction. To handle all directions at once, round every unit vector to a nearby point of a fine grid, use the union bound over the finitely many grid points, and pay for the rounding with a crude bound on how much \(A\) can stretch the small difference. Table H.3 lists the chain of constants.



Table H.3: How the lemma for one query becomes a bound on the smallest singular value.

The all-ones direction deserves a word, because subset queries have a nonzero mean. Every entry of \(A\) is \(\frac12\) on average, so \(A\) stretches the all-ones vector a lot: each answer \(\langle q, \mathbf 1\rangle\) is about \(n/2\). That direction gives the largest singular value, not the smallest, and the lemma already allows for it, since a nonzero mean only pushes \(\langle q, x\rangle\) away from 0.


H.2.3 Derivation

One query catches a fixed direction. This is the chapter’s lemma, whose proof holds for every vector \(x\) (the chapter adds an assumption about large coordinates only afterwards). Fix a nonzero \(x\) with \(n\) coordinates, and write a random subset as \(q_i = (1 + s_i)/2\) with independent fair signs \(s_i\), so that a person is in the subset when the sign is \(+1\). The answer \(Y = \langle q, x\rangle\) is then the constant \(\frac12\sum_ix_i\) plus the sum \(\frac12\sum_is_ix_i\) of terms with random signs. Write \(\tau\) for the standard deviation of that sum, so \(\tau^2 = \frac14\|x\|^2\). Counting which terms survive in the expansion of the fourth power shows that a random-sign sum has fourth moment at most 3 times its squared variance, as for a normal variable, and the chapter’s step 3 shows that adding the constant keeps \(\mathbb E Y^4 \le 3(\mathbb E Y^2)^2\). The Paley–Zygmund inequality (Equation 17.2) says that a non-negative variable \(W\) exceeds \(\xi\,\mathbb E W\) with probability at least \((1 - \xi)^2(\mathbb E W)^2/\mathbb E[W^2]\), for any level \(\xi\) between 0 and 1. Applied to \(W = Y^2\), the ratio of moments is at least \(\frac13\). Finally, \(\mathbb E Y^2\) is \(\tau^2\) plus the squared constant, so it is at least \(\tau^2\), and \[\Pr\big[|Y| > \sqrt\xi\,\tau\big] \ge \frac{(1 - \xi)^2}{3}. \tag{H.6}\] With \(\xi = \frac14\) the bound reads \[\Pr\Big[\langle q, x\rangle^2 > \frac{\|x\|^2}{16}\Big] \ge \frac{3}{16}. \tag{H.7}\]
Many queries catch it, by Hoeffding’s inequality. Call query \(j\) good for \(x\) when \(\langle q_j, x\rangle^2 > \|x\|^2/16\), and let \(N\) be the number of good queries. The queries are independent, so \(N\) is a sum of \(m\) independent 0/1 terms, each 1 with probability \(p \ge \frac3{16}\). Hoeffding’s inequality (Concentration inequalities) says that the average of \(m\) independent terms in \([0, 1]\) falls more than \(t\) below its mean with probability at most \(e^{-2mt^2}\). The event \(N \le m/8\) means the average falls at least \(p - \frac18 \ge \frac1{16}\) below its mean, so with \(t = \frac1{16}\) it has probability at most \(e^{-2m/256} = e^{-m/128}\).
Many good queries make \(\|Ax\|\) large. \(\|Ax\|^2 = \sum_j\langle q_j, x\rangle^2\) is a sum of non-negative terms, and each good query contributes more than \(\|x\|^2/16\). If \(N > m/8\), then \(\|Ax\|^2 > \frac m8\cdot\frac{\|x\|^2}{16} = \frac{m\|x\|^2}{128}\).
A finite grid. Every unit vector has its coordinates in \([-1, 1]\). Take the grid of points in \([-1, 1]^n\) whose coordinates are multiples of \(h = 1/(40n)\). Each coordinate takes \(2/h + 1 = 80n + 1\) values, so there are \((80n + 1)^n\) grid points. Rounding each coordinate of a unit vector \(x\) to the nearest multiple of \(h\) gives a grid point \(y\) with \(|x_i - y_i| \le h/2\), so \(\|x - y\| \le \frac h2\sqrt n = \frac{1}{80\sqrt n}\), and hence \(\|y\| \ge 1 - \frac{1}{80\sqrt n}\).
Union bound over the grid. By steps 2 and 3, each nonzero grid point fails \(\|Ay\|^2 > m\|y\|^2/128\) with probability at most \(e^{-m/128}\), and the point 0 does not matter, because no unit vector is rounded to it. The union bound says that the chance that at least one of several events happens is at most the sum of their chances. So every grid point satisfies it except with probability at most \((80n + 1)^ne^{-m/128}\). Taking logarithms, this is at most \(\beta\) exactly when \(m \ge 128\big(n\ln(80n + 1) + \ln(1/\beta)\big)\), the condition of Equation H.5.
A crude bound on stretching. Every entry of \(A\) is 0 or 1, so \(\|Av\|^2 = \sum_j\langle q_j, v\rangle^2 \le \sum_j\|q_j\|^2\|v\|^2 \le mn\|v\|^2\), by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and because each query has at most \(n\) ones, so \(\|q_j\|^2 \le n\). So \(A\) stretches any vector by at most \(\sqrt{mn}\).
From the grid to every unit vector. Outside the bad event of step 5, take any unit vector \(x\) and its grid point \(y\). By the triangle inequality and steps 3 to 6, \[\|Ax\| \ge \|Ay\| - \|A(x - y)\| \ge \sqrt{\frac{m}{128}}\Big(1 - \frac1{80\sqrt n}\Big) - \sqrt{mn}\cdot\frac{1}{80\sqrt n}. \tag{H.8}\] The right side equals \(\sqrt m\) times \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{128}} - \frac{1}{80}\big(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{128n}}\big)\), which grows with \(n\), so it is smallest at \(n = 1\), where it is \(\sqrt m\,\big(\frac{79}{80\sqrt{128}} - \frac1{80}\big) = 0.0748\sqrt m\), which is more than \(\sqrt m/14 = 0.0714\sqrt m\). The smallest \(\|Ax\|\) over unit vectors is \(s_{\min}(A)\), which gives Equation H.5.
The consequence for least squares. Substituting \(s_{\min}(A)^2 \ge m/196\) into Equation 17.9 bounds the number of wrong bits by \(4mE^2/(m/196) = 784E^2\). If \(E = o(\sqrt n)\), then \(E^2 = o(n)\), so the wrong bits are \(o(n)\).



H.2.4 Checking it
The proof is far from tight. Figure H.3 plots the simulated \(s_{\min}(A)/\sqrt m\) against \(m/n\) for \(n = 50\), 100 and 200. It falls below the proved floor of \(1/14\) only at \(m = 1.25n\), and from about \(m = 4n\) on it sits on the cited asymptotic \(\frac12(1 - \sqrt{n/m})\). At the chapter’s size, \(n = 500\) and \(m = 2000\), the script finds \(s_{\min}(A) = 11.44\), which is \(0.2558\sqrt m\). The asymptotic predicts \(\frac12(1 - \sqrt{1/4}) = 0.25\) times \(\sqrt m\), and the proof guarantees \(\sqrt m/14\). The price of the proof is the number of queries it asks for. For \(n = 100\) people and failure probability \(\beta = 0.01\), Equation H.5 asks for 115,627 queries, about 1,156 per person. The simulation shows the floor holding from \(m = 1.5n\) on.






Figure H.3: The smallest singular value of a random \(m \times n\) subset matrix, divided by \(\sqrt m\), against \(m/n\), for three values of \(n\) (three draws each). The black curve is the cited asymptotic \(\frac12(1 - \sqrt{n/m})\), and the dashed line is the floor \(1/14\) proved here, which the proof guarantees only once \(m\) is of order \(128\,n\ln(80n)\).



Figure H.4 shows where the slack comes from. For one matrix with \(n = 100\) and \(m = 400\), it plots \(\|Ax\|^2/m\) for 4,000 random unit directions. Random directions land between about 0.2 and 3. For a unit vector the average of \(\langle q, x\rangle^2\) is \(\frac14\big(1 + (\sum_ix_i)^2\big)\), the variance of one entry plus a share of the mean that grows with how far \(x\) points along the all-ones direction. The weakest direction is lower, and the all-ones direction is about a hundred times higher, because of the nonzero mean of the entries. The proof’s levels, \(\frac1{128}\) for a grid point and \(\frac1{196}\) for every direction, are well below all of them. The lemma itself has slack too. For the weakest direction of this matrix, 0.3075 of the queries are good, and no random direction of the 4,000 has fewer than 0.5550 good queries. The lemma guarantees only \(\frac3{16} = 0.1875\) on average.






Figure H.4: Histogram of \(\|Ax\|^2/m\) over 4,000 random unit vectors \(x\), for one random subset matrix with \(n = 100\) and \(m = 400\) (log scale). The vertical lines mark the weakest direction \(s_{\min}^2/m\), the all-ones direction, and the two levels of the proof: \(\frac1{128}\) for each grid point after Hoeffding’s inequality, and \(\frac1{196}\) for every direction.





H.2.5 What it does not cover
The proof gives \(m = O(n\log n)\), not \(m = 4n\). The logarithm comes from the union bound over a grid fine enough to absorb the crude stretching bound of step 6. For matrices whose entries have mean 0, called centred, a sharper argument bounds the stretching by about \(\sqrt m + \sqrt n\), so it can use a much coarser grid of directions (a net), and it needs only \(m = O(n)\) (Vershynin, ch. 4). For subset matrices it would also have to treat the all-ones direction separately, and this appendix does not carry that out. The sharp constant, \(s_{\min} \approx \frac12(\sqrt m - \sqrt n)\) for large \(m\) and \(n\) at a fixed ratio, is the Bai–Yin law for matrices with independent centred entries (Bai and Yin 1993; Vershynin, ch. 4). Subset matrices are not centred, but they differ from \(\frac12\) times a random-sign matrix by the rank-one matrix \(\frac12\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top\), and on vectors orthogonal to \(\mathbf 1\) the two act the same. Turning that observation into a proof of the sharp constant takes a perturbation argument for the one remaining direction, which stays cited. So the chapter’s statement with \(m = 4n\) rests on the cited asymptotics and on its simulation, while the \(O(n\log n)\) version is proved here.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
text:
H.3 The prefix-sum matrix

H.3.1 What the chapter uses
In DP-FTRL and matrix factorization, \(A\) is the \(T \times T\) prefix-sum matrix: lower-triangular, with every entry on and below the diagonal equal to 1, so that row \(t\) of \(Ax\) is the running sum \(x_1 + \dots + x_t\). A factorization \(A = LR\) releases \(L(Rx + z)\), where \(z\) is Gaussian noise. Its sensitivity \(\Delta_2 R\) is the largest length of a column of \(R\), and its error per unit of privacy at step \(t\) is \(e_t = \Delta_2 R\,\|\ell_t\|\), with \(\ell_t\) the \(t\)-th row of \(L\). The chapter uses four facts about this matrix.
The first two are in Section 41.4, steps 5 and 6. Every factorization has a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of at least \(\|A\|_*/T\) (Equation 41.8), where the RMSE is \(\big(\frac1T\sum_te_t^2\big)^{1/2}\), the typical error over the \(T\) released sums, where the trace norm \(\|A\|_*\) is the sum of the singular values. The proof uses the duality \[\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A) \le \|A\|_* \quad\text{for every } U \text{ whose largest singular value is at most } 1, \tag{H.9}\] which the chapter states without proof. It also states the singular values, with \(\omega_k = (2k - 1)\pi/(2T + 1)\), \[\sigma_k(A) = \frac{1}{2\sin\frac{(2k - 1)\pi}{4T + 2}} = \frac{1}{2\sin(\omega_k/2)}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, T, \tag{H.10}\] and says that the eigenvalues of \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) are \(4\sin^2(\omega_k/2)\), checking this numerically.
The other two are in Section 41.6. The square-root factorization uses the lower-triangular matrix with entries \(r_k = \binom{2k}{k}4^{-k}\) on its \(k\)-th diagonal, and step 6 bounds its sensitivity and largest error, \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\), with Equation 41.11. That step quotes the Wallis-type inequality \[\frac{1}{\pi(k + \frac12)} \le r_k^2 \le \frac{1}{\pi(k + \frac14)} \tag{H.11}\] from Fichtenberger, Henzinger and Upadhyay (2023) and checks it numerically for \(k < 100{,}000\). Finally, the chapter compares the square root with the lower bound at \(T = 100\) and \(T = 10{,}000\) and finds it within 9% and 6%. This section proves the duality, the singular values and the Wallis bounds, and it explains the comparison by proving that the ratio tends to 1: \[\frac{\ln(2T + 1)}{\pi} \le \frac{\|A\|_*}{T} \le \text{RMSE of any factorization}, \qquad \text{RMSE of the square root} \le 1 + \frac{0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}{5}}{\pi}. \tag{H.12}\]


H.3.2 The idea
The singular values of \(A\) are hard to see directly, but its inverse is simple. Taking running sums is undone by taking differences, so \(A^{-1}\) has 1 on the diagonal and \(-1\) just below it. Then \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) is the matrix of a second difference, \(-v_{j-1} + 2v_j - v_{j+1}\), the same matrix that describes a vibrating string. Its eigenvectors are sine waves, and the two ends of the matrix decide which frequencies fit. For \(T = 2\) the whole computation fits in a few lines: \[A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}, \qquad (A^{-1})^\top A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 1\end{pmatrix}. \tag{H.13}\] The eigenvalues of the second matrix are \((3 \pm \sqrt5)/2\), that is 2.618 and 0.382. The formula proved below gives the same two numbers, as \(4\sin^2(3\pi/10)\) and \(4\sin^2(\pi/10)\). The singular values of \(A\) are one over their square roots, the golden ratio 1.618 and its inverse 0.618.
The duality is a statement about lining up. The singular value decomposition writes \(A\) as a sum of simple pieces, one for each singular value \(\sigma_k\), and each piece maps one input direction \(v_k\) to one output direction \(u_k\). A matrix \(U\) that stretches no vector can line up with each piece at best perfectly, so it collects at most \(\sigma_k\) from each, and \(\|A\|_*\) in total. The Wallis bounds come from squeezing. Two sequences built from \(r_k^2\), one decreasing and one increasing, close in on the same limit \(1/\pi\), so each stays on its side. Finally, the near-optimality of the square root follows by putting the bounds side by side. The lower bound on every factorization and the upper bound on the square root both grow like \((\ln T)/\pi\), so their ratio tends to 1.


H.3.3 Derivation
The singular values.

The inverse. Write \(N\) for the matrix with ones just below the diagonal and zeros elsewhere, so that \(Nx = (0, x_1, \dots, x_{T-1})\) shifts a vector down by one. Taking the differences \(x_t - x_{t-1}\) of running sums gives back the \(x_t\), so \(A^{-1} = I - N\).
The product. \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1} = (I - N^\top)(I - N) = I - N - N^\top + N^\top N\). The matrix \(N^\top N\) is diagonal with entries \(1, \dots, 1, 0\), because \(N\) maps the last basis vector to 0 and every other basis vector to the next one. So the product \(M = (A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) is tridiagonal, with \(-1\) next to the diagonal and \(2\) on the diagonal, except for a 1 in the bottom-right corner.
Interior rows. Try \(v_j = \sin(j\omega)\) for \(j = 1, \dots, T\). Row \(j\) of \(Mv\), for \(1 < j < T\), is \(-v_{j-1} + 2v_j - v_{j+1}\). The identity \(\sin((j - 1)\omega) + \sin((j + 1)\omega) = 2\cos\omega\sin(j\omega)\) turns this into \((2 - 2\cos\omega)v_j = 4\sin^2(\omega/2)\,v_j\). So \(\nu = 4\sin^2(\omega/2)\) is the eigenvalue, if the first and last rows agree.
The first row. Row 1 is \(2v_1 - v_2\), which is the interior formula with \(v_0 = 0\). The sine satisfies \(\sin(0) = 0\), so row 1 holds for every \(\omega\).
The last row. Row \(T\) is \(-v_{T-1} + v_T\), which is the interior formula with \(v_{T+1} = v_T\). So the sine must take the same value at \(T\) and \(T + 1\), which means it must be symmetric about \(T + \frac12\), a peak or a trough there. That requires \((T + \frac12)\omega\) to be an odd multiple of \(\frac\pi2\), that is, \(\omega_k = (2k - 1)\pi/(2T + 1)\). The values \(k = 1, \dots, T\) give \(T\) different angles in \((0, \pi)\), where \(\sin^2(\omega/2)\) increases, hence \(T\) different eigenvalues, which is all of them.
Back to \(A\). The eigenvalues of \(M = (AA^\top)^{-1}\) are the squares of the singular values of \(A^{-1}\), which are one over the singular values of \(A\). So \(\sigma_k(A) = 1/\sqrt{4\sin^2(\omega_k/2)} = 1/(2\sin(\omega_k/2))\), which is Equation H.10, largest at \(k = 1\).

The duality. Write the singular value decomposition \(A = \sum_k\sigma_ku_kv_k^\top\), with orthonormal \(u_k\) and orthonormal \(v_k\). Since \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top u_kv_k^\top) = v_k^\top U^\top u_k = \langle Uv_k, u_k\rangle\), linearity of the trace gives \[\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A) = \sum_k\sigma_k\langle Uv_k, u_k\rangle \le \sum_k\sigma_k\|Uv_k\|\,\|u_k\| \le \sum_k\sigma_k = \|A\|_*. \tag{H.14}\] The middle step is the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, and the last uses \(\|Uv_k\| \le 1\), because \(U\) stretches no vector and \(v_k\) has length 1. Equality holds for \(U = \sum_ku_kv_k^\top\), which maps each \(v_k\) exactly onto \(u_k\). This is Equation H.9.
The Wallis bounds.

Two integrals. Let \(I_n = \int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^nx\,dx\). Integrating by parts gives \(I_n = \frac{n - 1}{n}I_{n-2}\), and \(I_0 = \frac\pi2\), \(I_1 = 1\). Unrolling the recursion, \(I_{2k} = \frac\pi2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac34\cdots\frac{2k - 1}{2k} = \frac\pi2r_k\), because the square root’s coefficients satisfy \(r_k = r_{k-1}\frac{2k - 1}{2k}\) (Equation 41.10). In the same way \(I_{2k+1} = \frac23\cdot\frac45\cdots\frac{2k}{2k + 1} = \frac{1}{(2k + 1)r_k}\).
The lower bound. On \([0, \frac\pi2]\), \(0 \le \sin x \le 1\), so higher powers are smaller and \(I_n\) decreases in \(n\). From \(I_{2k+1} \le I_{2k}\) you get \(\frac{1}{(2k + 1)r_k} \le \frac\pi2r_k\), that is, \(r_k^2 \ge \frac{2}{\pi(2k + 1)} = \frac{1}{\pi(k + \frac12)}\).
A first upper bound, and the limit. From \(I_{2k} \le I_{2k-1} = \frac{1}{2kr_k}\), the same way, \(r_k^2 \le \frac{1}{\pi k}\) for \(k \ge 1\). Together with step 2, \(k\,r_k^2\) is squeezed between \(\frac{k}{\pi(k + 1/2)}\) and \(\frac1\pi\), so it tends to \(\frac1\pi\). This is Wallis’s product in disguise.
Two monotone sequences. Let \(a_k = (k + \frac12)r_k^2\) and \(b_k = (k + \frac14)r_k^2\). Both tend to \(\frac1\pi\) by step 3. Using \(r_{k+1}/r_k = (2k + 1)/(2k + 2)\), \[\frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k} = \frac{(2k + 3)(2k + 1)}{(2k + 2)^2} = \frac{4k^2 + 8k + 3}{4k^2 + 8k + 4} < 1, \qquad \frac{b_{k+1}}{b_k} = \frac{(4k + 5)(2k + 1)^2}{(4k + 1)(2k + 2)^2} = \frac{16k^3 + 36k^2 + 24k + 5}{16k^3 + 36k^2 + 24k + 4} > 1. \tag{H.15}\] So \(a_k\) decreases and \(b_k\) increases.
Conclude. A decreasing sequence stays above its limit, so \(a_k \ge \frac1\pi\), which is the lower bound of Equation H.11 again. An increasing sequence stays below its limit, so \(b_k \le \frac1\pi\), which is the upper bound. Both hold for every \(k \ge 0\).

How close the square root is to optimal.

A floor under every factorization. For \(0 < x \le \frac\pi2\), \(\sin x \le x\), so each singular value in Equation H.10 is at least \(\frac{1}{\omega_k} = \frac{2T + 1}{(2k - 1)\pi}\). The function \(\frac1{2x - 1}\) decreases, so each term \(\frac1{2k - 1}\) is at least its integral from \(k\) to \(k + 1\). Adding these up, and then dividing the sum of the singular values by \(T\), \[\sum_{k=1}^T\frac1{2k - 1} \ge \frac12\ln(2T + 1), \qquad \frac{\|A\|_*}T \ge \frac{2T + 1}{2\pi T}\ln(2T + 1) \ge \frac{\ln(2T + 1)}{\pi}. \tag{H.16}\]
A ceiling over the square root. For the square root, \(L = R\). Row \(t\) holds \(r_{t-1}, \dots, r_0\), so each row of \(L\) is no longer than the last one, whose squared length is \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2 = (\Delta_2 R)^2\) (step 5 of Section 41.6). So every \(e_t \le (\Delta_2 R)^2\), and the RMSE, an average of the \(e_t^2\) under a square root, is at most the largest \(e_t\), which is \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2\), which Equation 41.11 bounds by \(1 + (0.8 + \ln\frac{4T - 3}5)/\pi\). With the Wallis bounds proved above, that step of the chapter is now complete.
The ratio tends to 1. By Equation 41.8, the optimal RMSE lies between \(\|A\|_*/T\) and the square root’s RMSE, so all three lie in the band of Equation H.12. Both ends of the band are \((\ln T)/\pi\) plus a constant, so the square root’s RMSE divided by the lower bound tends to 1 as \(T\) grows, like \(1 + O(1/\ln T)\).



H.3.4 Checking it
The script compares Equation H.10 with a numerical singular value decomposition at \(T = 256\), and the largest relative gap is \(2.7 \times 10^{-15}\). Each \(\sin(j\omega_k)\) vector satisfies \(Mv = \nu v\) to within \(1.4 \times 10^{-14}\). Figure H.5 draws the first three eigenvectors for \(T = 16\). Each starts from 0 just before position 1 and is flat across the mirror at \(T + \frac12\), which is how steps 4 and 5 select the angles.






Figure H.5: The first three eigenvectors \(v_j = \sin(j\omega_k)\) of \((A^{-1})^\top A^{-1}\) for \(T = 16\), as dots, with the sine curves they sample. Crosses mark the extra points \(j = 0\), where every curve is 0, and \(j = T + 1\), where every curve repeats its value at \(j = T\), because it is symmetric about the dotted line at \(T + \frac12\).



For the duality at \(T = 16\), the trace norm is 26.0552. The largest \(\operatorname{tr}(U^\top A)\) over 2,000 random matrices \(U\), each scaled so that its largest singular value is 1, is 4.9448, well below it, and the aligned choice \(U = \sum_ku_kv_k^\top\) attains 26.0552, the trace norm itself.
For the Wallis bounds, the script checks the two ratio inequalities of step 4 in exact integer arithmetic for every \(k < 10^6\), and Equation H.11 itself in floating point for every \(k < 10^4\). A floating-point check cannot go much further, because \(b_k\) approaches \(\frac1\pi\) like \(1/(32\pi k^2)\), which soon drowns in rounding error. At \(k = 9999\), \(a_k\) is still above \(\frac1\pi\) by \(8.0 \times 10^{-6}\) and \(b_k\) below it by \(9.9 \times 10^{-11}\). Figure H.6 shows the two sequences closing in on \(\frac1\pi\) from either side.






Figure H.6: The sequences \(a_k = (k + \frac12)r_k^2\) and \(b_k = (k + \frac14)r_k^2\) against \(k\) (log scale). The first decreases and the second increases, and both tend to \(1/\pi\) (dashed), which squeezes \(r_k^2\) between \(\frac{1}{\pi(k + 1/2)}\) and \(\frac{1}{\pi(k + 1/4)}\).



Table H.4 gives the band of Equation H.12 and the two curves inside it. The chapter’s “within 9% and 6%” are the ratios 1.089 and 1.056. The ratio keeps falling slowly, to 1.040 at \(T = 10^6\), as the \(1 + O(1/\ln T)\) of step 3 predicts. The proved band is wide. At \(T = 100\) the ceiling divided by the floor is 1.568, so the band only guarantees a ratio below that, while the actual ratio is 1.089, because both \(\sin x \le x\) and the bound of each row by the last one give away a constant. Figure H.7 shows the band and both curves from \(T = 10\) to \(10^6\). Every factorization has its RMSE above the blue curve, and the optimal one has its RMSE between the blue and the orange curve.

H.3.5 What it does not cover
The chapter also quotes the finer approximation \(\sum_{k<T}r_k^2 \approx (\ln T + \gamma + 4\ln2)/\pi\), with \(\gamma\) Euler’s constant. It follows from a longer expansion of \(r_k^2\) in powers of \(1/k\), and it stays unproved here, as in the chapter. The ratio of step 3 tends to 1 only slowly, so the comparison says that the square root is nearly optimal for the RMSE, not that it is optimal at any finite \(T\). The next section finds the optimum.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
section: H.4 The optimal factorization for the root-mean-square error
text:
H.4 The optimal factorization for the root-mean-square error

H.4.1 What the chapter uses
In Section 41.6, under “The optimal factorization”, the chapter looks for the factorization \(A = LR\) with the smallest RMSE. Scaling the encoder \(R\) up and the decoder \(L\) down by the same factor changes nothing. So the chapter fixes \(\Delta_2 R \le 1\), which means that every column of \(R\) has length at most 1. It then minimizes the Frobenius norm \(\|L\|_F\), the square root of the sum of the squared entries of \(L\), and the RMSE per unit of privacy is \(\|L\|_F/\sqrt T\). The encoder enters only through the matrix \(X = R^\top R\) of inner products of its columns, whose diagonal holds the squared column lengths. The chapter states that the problem is \[\text{minimize } \operatorname{tr}(A^\top AX^{-1}) \quad\text{over positive definite } X \text{ with } X_{ii} \le 1 \text{ for every } i, \tag{H.17}\] that it is convex, and that its solution is \[X = V^{-1/2}\big(V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}V^{-1/2}, \qquad v = \operatorname{diag}\Big(\big(V^{1/2}A^\top AV^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}\Big), \tag{H.18}\] with \(V\) the diagonal matrix of the vector \(v\), so that \(v\) is a fixed point of the map on the right. It cites Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 3.2) for this, sketches the Lagrangian step and iterates the map. A matrix is positive definite when it is symmetric and \(x^\top Xx > 0\) for every nonzero \(x\), and \(Y^{1/2}\) is the positive definite square root of such a \(Y\).


H.4.2 The idea
There are four steps. First, once the encoder \(R\) is chosen, the best decoder is forced. It is the one that undoes \(R\) with no wasted motion, and its size depends on \(R\) only through \(X = R^\top R\). That turns a problem about two matrices into one about \(X\). Second, the objective is convex in \(X\): along any straight line through the positive definite matrices it bends upward, in the same way that \(1/x\) does for positive \(x\). Third, at the optimum the gradient of the objective must be balanced by a price \(\kappa_i\) on each column-length constraint, and solving that balance gives Equation H.18. Fourth, convexity makes any balanced point the global minimum.
The smallest case shows the answer. At \(T = 2\), \(A^\top A\) has rows \((2, 1)\) and \((1, 1)\). A feasible \(X\) with both columns of length 1 has rows \((1, \rho)\) and \((\rho, 1)\), and the objective is \((3 - 2\rho)/(1 - \rho^2)\). Setting its derivative to zero gives \(\rho^2 - 3\rho + 1 = 0\), so \(\rho = (3 - \sqrt5)/2 = 0.382\) and the minimum is \(2.618\), the golden ratio squared. Table H.5 compares it with the other factorizations at \(T = 2\).

H.4.3 Derivation
Write \(B = A^\top A\). It is positive definite because \(A\) is invertible.

The best decoder for a given encoder. The encoder \(R\) has some number of rows and \(T\) columns. The equation \(LR = A\) can only hold if \(R\) has rank \(T\), because \(A\) has rank \(T\), and then \(X = R^\top R\) is positive definite. Let \(R^+ = X^{-1}R^\top\), so that \(R^+R = I\), and let \(\Pi = RR^+\), the orthogonal projection onto the column space of \(R\). Any decoder with \(LR = A\) satisfies \(L\Pi = LRR^+ = AR^+\). Split \(L = L\Pi + L(I - \Pi)\). Each row of \(L\Pi\) lies in the column space of \(R\) and each row of \(L(I - \Pi)\) is orthogonal to it, so the squared lengths add, and \(\|L\|_F^2 = \|AR^+\|_F^2 + \|L(I - \Pi)\|_F^2 \ge \|AR^+\|_F^2\), with equality for \(L = AR^+\). And \[\|AR^+\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}\big(AR^+(R^+)^\top A^\top\big) = \operatorname{tr}\big(AX^{-1}A^\top\big) = \operatorname{tr}(BX^{-1}), \tag{H.19}\] because \(R^+(R^+)^\top = X^{-1}R^\top RX^{-1} = X^{-1}\), and the trace does not change when a product is rotated. So the problem over \((L, R)\) is Equation H.17 over \(X\).
The objective is convex. Take positive definite \(X\), a symmetric direction \(H\), and \(X(t) = X + tH\). Differentiating \(X(t)X(t)^{-1} = I\) gives \(\frac{d}{dt}X^{-1} = -X^{-1}HX^{-1}\), and differentiating again gives \(2X^{-1}HX^{-1}HX^{-1}\). So the second derivative of \(f(t) = \operatorname{tr}(BX(t)^{-1})\) at \(t = 0\) is \[f''(0) = 2\operatorname{tr}\big(X^{-1}BX^{-1}\cdot HX^{-1}H\big). \tag{H.20}\] Both \(X^{-1}BX^{-1}\) and \(HX^{-1}H\) are positive semidefinite, and the trace of a product of two positive semidefinite matrices is at least 0, because \(\operatorname{tr}(GH) = \operatorname{tr}(G^{1/2}HG^{1/2})\) is a sum of non-negative diagonal entries. So \(f\) bends upward along every line. The positive definite matrices form a convex set, and the constraints \(X_{ii} \le 1\) are linear, so the problem is convex.
The balance condition. Give each constraint a price \(\kappa_i \ge 0\) and let \(K\) be the diagonal matrix of the prices. The gradient of \(\operatorname{tr}(BX^{-1})\) with respect to \(X\) is \(-X^{-1}BX^{-1}\), by step 2, and that of \(\sum_i\kappa_iX_{ii}\) is \(K\). At an optimum such prices exist, because the constraints are linear, and the two gradients balance: \[X^{-1}BX^{-1} = K, \qquad\text{that is,}\qquad XKX = B. \tag{H.21}\] Since \(B\) is positive definite, so is \(K = X^{-1}BX^{-1}\), so every price is positive. The optimality conditions also require each price times the slack of its constraint, \(\kappa_i(1 - X_{ii})\), to be 0, which is called complementary slackness. So a positive price forces \(X_{ii} = 1\), for every \(i\). All columns of the optimal encoder have length exactly 1.
Solving the balance. Multiply Equation H.21 by \(K^{1/2}\) on both sides: \((K^{1/2}XK^{1/2})^2 = K^{1/2}BK^{1/2}\). The matrix \(K^{1/2}XK^{1/2}\) is positive definite, and a positive definite matrix has only one positive definite square root, so \(K^{1/2}XK^{1/2} = (K^{1/2}BK^{1/2})^{1/2}\), which is the first half of Equation H.18 with \(V = K\). Its diagonal entries read \(\kappa_iX_{ii} = \big[(K^{1/2}BK^{1/2})^{1/2}\big]_{ii}\), and with \(X_{ii} = 1\) this is the fixed point \(v = \operatorname{diag}\big((V^{1/2}BV^{1/2})^{1/2}\big)\), the second half.
A balanced point is the minimum. A convex function lies above its tangent, so for any feasible \(Y\), \[\operatorname{tr}(BY^{-1}) \ge \operatorname{tr}(BX^{-1}) - \operatorname{tr}\big(X^{-1}BX^{-1}(Y - X)\big) = \operatorname{tr}(BX^{-1}) - \sum_i\kappa_i(Y_{ii} - 1) \ge \operatorname{tr}(BX^{-1}), \tag{H.22}\] using Equation H.21, \(X_{ii} = 1\), \(Y_{ii} \le 1\) and \(\kappa_i > 0\). So a fixed point of Equation H.18 gives the optimum.
The optimum exists, and its value is the sum of the prices. The feasible matrices have entries in \([-1, 1]\), since \(|X_{ij}| \le \sqrt{X_{ii}X_{jj}}\), and the objective grows without bound near a singular \(X\), so the minimum is attained at a positive definite matrix, where step 3 applies. Its value follows from Equation H.21, which gives \(BX^{-1} = XK\): \[\|L\|_F^2 = \operatorname{tr}(BX^{-1}) = \operatorname{tr}(XK) = \sum_iv_i, \qquad \text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac1T\sum_iv_i}. \tag{H.23}\]
A lower-triangular encoder. Any \(R\) with \(R^\top R = X\) gives the same RMSE, and streaming needs a lower-triangular one. Let \(J\) be the matrix that reverses the order of coordinates. The Cholesky factorization writes the positive definite matrix \(JXJ\) as \(GG^\top\) with \(G\) lower-triangular. Then \(R = JG^\top J\) is lower-triangular, because reversing both rows and columns turns the upper-triangular \(G^\top\) into a lower-triangular matrix, and \(R^\top R = JGJJG^\top J = J(JXJ)J = X\). The decoder \(L = AR^{-1}\) is lower-triangular too.

That the iteration \(v \leftarrow \operatorname{diag}\big((V^{1/2}BV^{1/2})^{1/2}\big)\) converges to the fixed point is shown by Denisov et al. (2022), and it stays cited. The script observes it.


H.4.4 Checking it
The script runs the iteration from \(v = \mathbf 1\) with the chapter’s stopping rule, a relative change below \(10^{-10}\). It reproduces the chapter’s counts, 155 iterations at \(T = 100\) and 193 at \(T = 256\), and the RMSE 2.2355 and 2.5244, against 2.3707 and 2.6688 for the square root. At \(T = 64\) it checks every step. The balance condition Equation H.21 holds to \(5.5 \times 10^{-13}\), the diagonal of \(X\) equals 1 to \(8.4 \times 10^{-11}\), the encoder has no nonzero entry above the diagonal, and \(LR = A\) to \(6.7 \times 10^{-16}\). The RMSE computed from \(L\), 2.0999, equals \(\sqrt{\sum_iv_i/T}\) as step 6 says. Moving \(X\) in 200 random feasible directions never lowers the objective: the smallest increase is 3.4857.
Figure H.8 shows the iteration and what it buys. On the left, the quantity \(\max_i|X_{ii} - 1|\) for the current \(v\) falls geometrically, and the number of iterations grows slowly with \(T\). On the right, the square root spends its privacy unevenly. Its first column is the longest and fixes the sensitivity, and its later columns are shorter, so the noise that hides them is larger than they need. The optimum makes every column exactly as long as the first, as step 3 requires.






Figure H.8: Left: the gap \(\max_i|X_{ii} - 1|\) of the fixed-point iteration against the iteration number, for \(T = 16\), 64 and 256 (log scale), down to the stopping tolerance \(10^{-10}\). Right: the column lengths of the encoder \(R\) for \(T = 64\), for the square root scaled so its longest column has length 1, and for the optimum, where every column has length 1.

title: Appendix H — Random matrices and factorizations
section: H.5 Streaming: triangular factors and adaptive participations
text:
H.5 Streaming: triangular factors and adaptive participations

H.5.1 What the chapter uses
Two facts in DP-FTRL and matrix factorization concern streams. There the mechanism must release its estimate \(\hat S_t\) of the running sum at step \(t\), and the gradients are chosen after seeing earlier outputs. Recall the setting. Each step’s gradient sum is a vector of \(d\) numbers, one per model weight, so \(x\) and the noise \(z\) are matrices with one row per step. One record adds a vector of length at most the clipping norm \(C\) to each step it takes part in, and the noise has standard deviation \(sC\), where \(s\) is the noise scale. Under “Streaming needs lower-triangular factors” in Section 41.4, the chapter says that for any factorization there is a lower-triangular one with the same distribution of the release \(\hat S = L(Rx + z)\), citing Denisov et al. (2022, Proposition 2.2). Precisely, if \(A = LR\) with \(L\) of size \(T \times m\) and \(R\) of size \(m \times T\), there are lower-triangular \(T \times T\) matrices \(L'\) and \(R'\) with \[L'R' = A, \qquad L'L'^\top = LL^\top, \qquad \Delta_2 R' \le \Delta_2 R. \tag{H.24}\] Here \(\Delta_2 R\) is the sensitivity when each record takes part in one step. When a record takes part at several steps \(\tau_1, \dots, \tau_k\), contributing \(g_1, \dots, g_k\), the encoder’s output changes by \(\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\), where \(r_\tau\) is column \(\tau\) of \(R\). The sensitivity of Equation 41.13 is the largest Frobenius norm of that change, over the allowed patterns and over all \(g_i\) of length at most \(C\), divided by \(C\). The same inequality holds for it.
Step 3 of Section 41.4 proves that a record that takes part in one step stays \(\mu\)-Gaussian differential privacy (GDP) when the inputs are chosen adaptively. In Section 41.7, step 3, a record takes part at several steps, and its later contributions \(g_i\) may depend on outputs it has already influenced. The chapter there says that such adaptive choices cannot do worse than the largest change over fixed \(g_i\), and it cites Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 2.1). This section proves that claim for Gaussian noise. With a lower-triangular \(R\), a fixed participation pattern, and the sensitivity of Equation 41.13, the release is \(\mu\)-GDP with \(\mu = \Delta_2 R/s\), however the contributions are chosen.
Recall what \(\mu\)-GDP means. The neighbouring datasets differ by adding or removing one record: \(D\) is the dataset without the record and \(D' = D \cup \{x\}\) the dataset with it. Let \(P\) be the distribution of all the outputs on \(D\), when the record is absent, and \(Q\) their distribution on \(D'\), when it is present. The release is \(\mu\)-GDP when telling \(P\) from \(Q\) is no easier than telling \(\mathcal N(0, 1)\) from \(\mathcal N(\mu, 1)\). The best trade-off between the two errors of a test for that normal pair is a curve called \(G_\mu\). By the Neyman–Pearson lemma, how easy that is depends only on the privacy loss \(L_{D,D'} = \ln(p/q)\), the log of the ratio of the two densities at the output, written with its pair of datasets because \(L\) alone is the decoder on this page, and on its distribution under \(P\) and under \(Q\) (f-DP and Gaussian DP). For the normal pair the privacy loss is normal, \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\) under \(P\).


H.5.2 The idea
For the triangular factors, the release depends on the decoder \(L\) only through the covariance \(LL^\top\) of its noise \(Lz\). Running Gram–Schmidt on the rows of \(L\), in order, writes each row as a combination of the first few orthonormal directions, which is a lower-triangular matrix of coefficients. The orthonormal directions can then be moved into the encoder, where they cannot lengthen any column.
For adaptivity, release the rows of \(Rx + z\) one at a time. Given what has been released so far, each new row is a Gaussian mechanism, and the record shifts its mean by some amount \(\mu_j\), measured in units of the noise. So the privacy loss of that row is a normal variable with mean \(\mu_j^2/2\) and variance \(\mu_j^2\). The shifts depend on the past, because the record’s later gradients do, but their squares always add up to at most \(\mu^2\). If they added up to exactly \(\mu^2\) on every path, the total privacy loss would be exactly \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\), the loss of a single Gaussian mechanism. To arrange that, imagine one extra output that tops the sum up to \(\mu^2\). Throwing that output away afterwards is post-processing, which cannot make privacy worse.


H.5.3 Derivation
Lower-triangular factors.

The decoder has full rank. \(A\) has rank \(T\) and \(A = LR\), so \(L\) has rank \(T\) and \(m \ge T\).
Gram–Schmidt on the rows. Orthonormalize the rows \(\ell_1, \dots, \ell_T\) of \(L\) in order, giving orthonormal rows \(o_1, \dots, o_T\), the rows of a \(T \times m\) matrix \(O\) with \(OO^\top = I\). By construction \(\ell_t\) is a combination of \(o_1, \dots, o_t\) only, so \(L = L'O\) with \(L'\) lower-triangular, and invertible because \(L\) has rank \(T\).
The new encoder. Set \(R' = OR\). Then \(L'R' = L'OR = LR = A\), and \(R' = L'^{-1}A\) is lower-triangular as a product of lower-triangular matrices. The noise covariance is unchanged, because \(L'L'^\top = L'OO^\top L'^\top = LL^\top\). So \(L'z'\), with \(z'\) of size \(T \times d\), has the same distribution as \(Lz\), and the release has the same distribution.
No more sensitivity. A matrix with orthonormal rows does not lengthen vectors: \(\|Ov\|^2 = \sum_t\langle o_t, v\rangle^2 \le \|v\|^2\), by Bessel’s inequality, because the \(o_t\) are orthonormal. Each column of \(R'\) is \(O\) times the matching column of \(R\), so \(\Delta_2 R' \le \Delta_2 R\). For several participations, the change \(\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\) becomes \(O\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\), whose Frobenius norm is no larger for the same reason. This gives Equation H.24.

Adaptive participations. Take \(R\) lower-triangular of size \(T \times T\), noise \(z\) with independent \(\mathcal N(0, \varsigma^2)\) entries where \(\varsigma = sC\), and release \(Y_j\), row \(j\) of \(Rx + z\), at step \(j\). The record takes part at fixed steps \(\tau_1 < \dots < \tau_k\), and its contribution \(g_i\) at step \(\tau_i\) may depend on \(Y_1, \dots, Y_{\tau_i - 1}\). The other records’ gradients at step \(t\) are functions of \(Y_1, \dots, Y_{t-1}\), the same functions with and without the record.

Each row is a Gaussian mechanism given the past. Given \(Y_1, \dots, Y_{j-1}\), the mean of \(Y_j\) is the same function of the past under \(P\) and \(Q\), except that under \(Q\) it is shifted by \(\Delta_j = \sum_iR_{j\tau_i}g_i^\top\). Only participations with \(\tau_i \le j\) contribute, because \(R\) is lower-triangular, and their \(g_i\) are already fixed by the past.
The privacy loss adds up. The density of all outputs is the product of the conditional densities, so the privacy loss is a sum \(L_{D,D'} = \sum_jL_j\) of the privacy losses \(L_j\) of the single rows. For one row, the normal densities give \(L_j = \frac{\|\Delta_j\|^2}{2\varsigma^2} - \frac{\langle\Delta_j, z_j\rangle}{\varsigma^2}\), with \(z_j = Y_j\) minus its mean under \(P\). Under \(P\), given the past, \(z_j\) is normal with independent coordinates, so \(L_j\) is normal with mean \(\mu_j^2/2\) and variance \(\mu_j^2\), where \(\mu_j = \|\Delta_j\|/\varsigma\).
The shifts are bounded on every path. The squared shifts add up to \(\sum_j\|\Delta_j\|^2 = \|\sum_ir_{\tau_i}g_i^\top\|_F^2\), the change in \(Rx\). The \(g_i\) have length at most \(C\), so this is at most \((\Delta_2 R)^2C^2\) by the definition Equation 41.13, whatever values the \(g_i\) took. Dividing by \(\varsigma^2\), \(\sum_j\mu_j^2 \le \mu^2\) with \(\mu = \Delta_2 R/s\).
Top up to exactly \(\mu^2\). Add one more output \(Y_{T+1}\), normal with variance 1, whose mean is 0 under \(P\) and \(\mu_{T+1} = \sqrt{\mu^2 - \sum_{j\le T}\mu_j^2}\) under \(Q\). Its shift depends on the past, which is allowed, because the argument below conditions on the past at every row. Now \(\sum_j\mu_j^2 = \mu^2\) exactly on every path. The original release is the padded one with \(Y_{T+1}\) thrown away, and by post-processing it is at least as private.
The total loss is exactly normal under \(P\). The tool is the moment generating function, the average of \(e^{\lambda L_{D,D'}}\) for a real number \(\lambda\). A normal variable with mean \(a\) and variance \(b\) has \(\mathbb E[e^{\lambda N}] = e^{\lambda a + \lambda^2b/2}\). So, given the past, step 2 gives \[\mathbb E\big[e^{\lambda L_j}\big] = e^{c\mu_j^2}, \qquad c = \frac{\lambda + \lambda^2}{2}. \tag{H.25}\] In other words, the factor \(e^{\lambda L_j - c\mu_j^2}\) has average 1 given the past, whatever \(\mu_j\) the past chose. Multiply these factors over all rows, averaging the last one first, then the one before, and so on: each average is 1, so the product has average 1. The product is \(e^{\lambda L_{D,D'} - c\sum_j\mu_j^2}\), and \(\sum_j\mu_j^2 = \mu^2\) is a constant on every path, so \[\mathbb E_P\big[e^{\lambda L_{D,D'}}\big] = e^{c\mu^2} = \exp\Big(\lambda\frac{\mu^2}2 + \lambda^2\frac{\mu^2}2\Big). \tag{H.26}\] This is the moment generating function of a normal variable with mean \(\mu^2/2\) and variance \(\mu^2\). A moment generating function that is finite for every \(\lambda\) determines the distribution, so \(L_{D,D'} \sim \mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\) under \(P\). Here the padding matters. Without it, the constant \(\mu^2\) would be the path-dependent \(\sum_j\mu_j^2\), and it could not be taken out of the average.
So is the loss under \(Q\), and the release is \(\mu\)-GDP. The distribution of \(L_{D,D'}\) under \(Q\) follows from that under \(P\), because \(q = e^{-L_{D,D'}}p\): for any set \(S\) of values, \(\Pr_Q[L_{D,D'} \in S] = \mathbb E_P\big[e^{-L_{D,D'}}\,\mathbf 1[L_{D,D'} \in S]\big]\). The single Gaussian mechanism with ratio \(\mu\) has the same law of \(L_{D,D'}\) under its \(P\), hence under its \(Q\) too. By Neyman–Pearson, the two pairs have the same trade-off curve \(G_\mu\). The padded release is therefore exactly \(\mu\)-GDP, and the release itself, by step 4, is \(\mu\)-GDP.



H.5.4 Checking it
For the triangular factors, the script starts from the binary tree of Section 41.5 at \(T = 64\), whose encoder has one row for each of its 127 nodes. Gram–Schmidt on the rows of its decoder gives \(64 \times 64\) lower-triangular factors with \(L'R' = A\) and \(L'L'^\top = LL^\top\), both exactly. The sensitivity stays 2.6458, which is \(\sqrt 7\), because the first column of the tree’s encoder already lies in the span of the decoder’s rows. So 64 noisy numbers can replace the tree’s 127 node sums, with the same distribution of every released prefix sum.
For adaptivity, the script simulates the square-root encoder at \(T = 8\), one coordinate, with \(C = 1\) and \(s = \Delta_2 R\), so that \(\mu = 1\). The record takes part at steps 1 and 5, with \(g_1 = 1\) and \(g_2 = \tanh(Y_4)\), a contribution chosen from an output the record has already influenced. Over a million runs under \(P\), the padded privacy loss has mean 0.4996 and variance 0.9985, against \(\mu^2/2 = 0.5\) and \(\mu^2 = 1\). Without the padding the loss has mean 0.2681 and variance 0.5207, smaller, because \(|g_2| < 1\) keeps the total shift below its worst case. Figure H.9 shows both histograms against the normal density.






Figure H.9: Histogram of the privacy loss \(\ln(p/q)\) under \(P\) for a two-participation run of the square-root mechanism at \(T = 8\), whose second contribution depends on an earlier output, with \(\mu = 1\). Filled: with the padding row of step 4, which matches \(\mathcal N(\mu^2/2, \mu^2)\) (black). Outline: the release itself, which is more concentrated, so more private.





H.5.5 What it does not cover
The adaptive proof assumes a square lower-triangular encoder released one row per step, a participation pattern fixed in advance, and Gaussian noise. The binary tree has more rows than steps. It fits after ordering its rows by the step at which each node is complete, and then the same argument applies with several rows released at some steps. Denisov et al. (2022, Theorem 2.1) prove a more general statement, which also covers \((\varepsilon, \delta)\) guarantees and non-Gaussian losses, and that version stays cited.

text:
H.6 Code
The script code/appendix-derivations/apx_matrices.py checks each derivation numerically and draws the figures. For the Wishart mean it simulates Gaussian and 0/1 matrices, checks the regression identity of step 4 and the \(\chi^2\) average of step 6. For the smallest singular value it measures \(s_{\min}\), the share of good queries and the number of queries the proof needs. For the prefix-sum matrix it checks the eigenvectors and singular values, the duality, the monotonicity of \(a_k\) and \(b_k\) for \(k < 10^6\), and the sandwich up to \(T = 10^6\). It also runs the fixed-point iteration, checks every condition of the optimum, and checks the triangular reduction and the adaptive privacy loss. Run it with
uv run python code/appendix-derivations/apx_matrices.py

title: Appendix I — Pseudorandom functions and learning with errors
text:
I.1 The GGM tree is a pseudorandom function
This appendix proves two results that Cryptography basics states without a full proof. The first is that the GGM tree, named after Goldreich, Goldwasser and Micali, is a pseudorandom function (PRF) whenever the pseudorandom generator (PRG) it is built from is secure. The second is about learning with errors (LWE), a problem in which a secret vector is hidden behind noisy linear equations. When the arithmetic is done modulo a prime, an algorithm that can only recognize such equations can be turned into one that finds the secret. Both proofs are reductions: each turns an algorithm that solves one problem into an algorithm that solves another. Both also rest on the same move. The new algorithm takes the input it must judge, called its challenge, and uses it to build exactly the situation the old algorithm expects to see. So the heart of each proof is a check that two distributions are identical. Table I.1 lists where each result comes from.
The notation is the chapter’s, with two letters changed. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is the length of keys and seeds in bits, and \(U_k\) stands for the uniform distribution on strings of \(k\) bits. An adversary is an algorithm that tries to break a scheme, usually by asking it questions called queries; it is written \(\mathcal A\), and a second adversary built from it in a reduction is written \(\mathcal B\). The number of queries \(Q\) and a bound \(\nu\) on an advantage get letters of their own. Cryptography texts often write these \(q\) and \(\varepsilon\), but in this book \(q\) is a sampling rate and \(\varepsilon\) a privacy parameter. The modulus in learning with errors is \(p\).
A distinguisher receives input from one of two distributions, its two “worlds”, and outputs a bit. Its advantage is the absolute difference between how often it outputs 1 in the two worlds. A procedure is efficient if its running time grows at most polynomially in \(\lambda\), and a quantity is negligible if it shrinks faster than one over any polynomial in \(\lambda\).

title: Appendix I — Pseudorandom functions and learning with errors
text:
I.1.1 What the chapter uses
A pseudorandom generator stretches a short random seed into a longer string that efficient algorithms cannot tell from random. Here the generator doubles the length: \(G\colon \{0,1\}^\lambda \to \{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\). Write its output as a left half \(G_0(s)\) followed by a right half \(G_1(s)\), each as long as the seed, so that \(G(s) = (G_0(s), G_1(s))\). A PRG distinguisher \(\mathcal B\) receives one \(2\lambda\)-bit string and outputs a bit, and its advantage is \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}(\mathcal B) = \big|\Pr[\mathcal B(G(U_\lambda)) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal B(U_{2\lambda}) = 1]\big|. \tag{I.1}\]
The GGM tree turns \(G\) into a keyed function on \(n\)-bit inputs. Picture a binary tree of depth \(n\) in which every node carries a \(\lambda\)-bit label. The root’s label is the key \(k\). A node’s left child gets the left half \(G_0\) of \(G\) applied to the node’s label, and its right child gets the right half \(G_1\). An input \(x = x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n\) is then read as directions from the root to a leaf. At level \(i\), the bit \(x_i\) says go left if it is 0 and right if it is 1, and the output is the label of the leaf you reach, \[F_k(x) = G_{x_n}\big(\cdots G_{x_2}\big(G_{x_1}(k)\big)\cdots\big). \tag{I.2}\] A node is named by the bits that lead to it, so node \(01\) is the right child of the left child of the root, and its depth is the length of its name.
In the PRF game, a fair coin decides what sits inside a box. It is either \(F_k\) with a uniform key, or a truly random function \(f\) from \(n\)-bit inputs to \(\lambda\)-bit outputs, which gives each input an independent uniform output. An adversary \(\mathcal A\) sends up to \(Q\) queries, each chosen after seeing the answers to the earlier ones, and then outputs a bit. The box that answers the queries is called an oracle, and \(\mathcal A^O\) means \(\mathcal A\) run with oracle \(O\). The adversary’s advantage is \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(\mathcal A) = \big|\Pr[\mathcal A^{F_k} = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A^{f} = 1]\big|, \tag{I.3}\] where the probabilities are also over the adversary’s own random choices.
The result says that any such adversary can be turned into a PRG distinguisher whose advantage is smaller by exactly the factor \(nQ\), and which is about as fast. Precisely, take any adversary \(\mathcal A\) that makes at most \(Q\) queries. Then there is a PRG distinguisher \(\mathcal B\) that runs \(\mathcal A\) once and, apart from that, evaluates \(G\) fewer than \(nQ\) times, such that \[\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(\mathcal A) = nQ\cdot\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}(\mathcal B). \tag{I.4}\] The running time matters because PRG security only limits fast distinguishers. So if no distinguisher with \(\mathcal B\)’s running time has PRG advantage above some \(\nu\), then no \(Q\)-query adversary has PRF advantage above \(nQ\,\nu\), which is the chapter’s \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}} \le nQ\cdot\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRG}}\). The chapter gives a proof sketch and cites Goldreich, Foundations of Cryptography, Vol. 1, §3.6, for the full proof.


I.1.2 The idea
The proof walks from the real function to a random one in \(n\) steps, one level of the tree at a time. Each intermediate world is called a hybrid, because it is part real and part random. The \(j\)-th hybrid, \(H_j\), gives every node at depth \(j\) a fresh uniform label and computes everything below it with \(G\) as usual. The first hybrid, \(H_0\), is the real \(F_k\), because the only node at depth 0 is the root and its uniform label is the key. The last, \(H_n\), is a random function, because every leaf gets its own uniform label. Going from \(H_{j-1}\) to \(H_j\) changes a single thing. In \(H_{j-1}\), the two children of a node at depth \(j - 1\) carry the two halves of \(G\) applied to a uniform label, while in \(H_j\) they carry two uniform labels. Telling these apart is the PRG’s game of output against uniform string, played once for every node at depth \(j - 1\) that the adversary’s queries pass through. Figure I.1 shows the four hybrids for \(n = 3\) and three queries.






Figure I.1: The GGM tree of depth 3 in the hybrids \(H_0\) to \(H_3\), for the queries 000, 001 and 100. Orange nodes get independent uniform labels, blue nodes are computed with \(G\) from their parent, and grey nodes lie on a query path but are never used. A red \(y_c\) marks the node at depth \(j - 1\) to which the reduction \(\mathcal B_j\) assigns its \(c\)-th challenge string.



The subtle part is that the adversary chooses its queries as it goes. A reduction \(\mathcal B_j\) that wants to use the adversary to break the PRG receives \(Q\) challenge strings, which are either all outputs of \(G\) on independent uniform seeds or all uniform. But it cannot know in advance which nodes at depth \(j - 1\) the queries will pass through. So it hands out its challenge strings like cloakroom tickets. The first time a query passes through a new node at depth \(j - 1\), that node gets the next unused string and keeps it for the rest of the game. If each \(y_c\) is \(G\) applied to its own uniform seed, then the labels at depth 2 are halves of \(G\) applied to independent uniform labels at depth 1, which is \(H_1\). If each \(y_c\) is uniform, the labels at depth 2 are uniform, which is \(H_2\). The one thing left to check is that handing out values on first use gives the adversary the same distribution of answers as drawing them all in advance. It does, because a value nobody has looked at yet is still a fresh draw, and step 4 below proves this carefully.


I.1.3 Derivation
The proof has four parts. Steps 1 to 3 set up the hybrids and show that two neighbouring hybrids differ only in the distribution of one table. Steps 4 and 5 build the reduction \(\mathcal B_j\), which judges \(Q\) strings at once, and show that it recreates either neighbour exactly. Steps 6 and 7 turn it into a distinguisher that judges a single string, and add up the levels. Step 8 restates the result for efficient adversaries.

Define the hybrids. For \(j = 0, 1, \dots, n\), hybrid \(H_j\) gives every node at depth \(j\) an independent uniform \(\lambda\)-bit label \(L(x_1\cdots x_j)\), all drawn before the game starts. It answers the query \(x\) by walking down from the depth-\(j\) node on its path: \[H_j(x) = G_{x_n}\big(\cdots G_{x_{j+1}}\big(L(x_1\cdots x_j)\big)\cdots\big). \tag{I.5}\] With \(j = 0\) the only label is the root’s, which is a uniform key, so \(H_0\) is \(F_k\). With \(j = n\) the answer is the leaf’s own label, independent and uniform for each input, so \(H_n\) is a random function. The table of \(2^j\) labels can be huge, but that does not matter. The hybrids are thought experiments, and only the reduction has to be efficient.
Split the advantage into levels. Write \(h_j = \Pr[\mathcal A^{H_j} = 1]\) for how often the adversary says 1 in hybrid \(H_j\). In the sum \(\sum_{j=1}^n (h_{j-1} - h_j)\), each intermediate \(h_j\) appears once with a plus sign and once with a minus sign, so the sum telescopes: \[h_0 - h_n = \sum_{j=1}^n (h_{j-1} - h_j). \tag{I.6}\] The chapter calls this telescoping Fact 3, where it is used with absolute values. The left side is \(\Pr[\mathcal A^{F_k} = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A^f = 1]\), whose absolute value is \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(\mathcal A)\).
Write two neighbouring hybrids as one table. Fix \(j \ge 1\) and look at a node \(w\) at depth \(j - 1\). In \(H_{j-1}\), its two children \(w0\) and \(w1\) get the two halves of \(G(L(w))\), so together they carry the string \(G(L(w))\). Different nodes \(w\) have independent uniform labels, so these strings are independent, each distributed as \(G(U_\lambda)\). In \(H_j\), the children carry two independent uniform labels, so together they carry a string distributed as \(U_{2\lambda}\), again independently for each \(w\). Below depth \(j\) both hybrids compute with \(G\) in the same way. So the two hybrids are one and the same world, except for the distribution \(P\) that the children’s strings come from. In that world, a table \(T\) gives each node \(w\) at depth \(j - 1\) its own independent draw \(T(w)\) from \(P\). The query \(x\) is answered by taking the half of \(T(x_1\cdots x_{j-1})\) that bit \(x_j\) selects and walking down with \(G\): \[W_j^{P}(x) = G_{x_n}\big(\cdots G_{x_{j+1}}\big(\text{half } x_j \text{ of } T(x_1\cdots x_{j-1})\big)\cdots\big). \tag{I.7}\] With \(P = G(U_\lambda)\) this world is \(H_{j-1}\), and with \(P = U_{2\lambda}\) it is \(H_j\). For \(j = 1\) the only node at depth 0 is the root, so the table has a single entry.
Lazy sampling gives the same view. There are two ways to fill the table \(T\). In the advance version, every entry is drawn before the game starts. In the lazy version, each entry is drawn from \(P\) the first time a query needs it, and reused afterwards. The adversary’s view is everything it sees: its own random choices (its coins) and all the answers it receives. The claim is that the view has the same distribution in both versions. Think of dice rolled earlier and hidden under cups: lifting a cup now shows a number that is exactly as random as rolling the die now, provided nobody peeked.
The proof goes one query at a time. Call the history after \(i\) queries the adversary’s coins together with the table entries used so far. Every answer, and therefore every next query, is a function of the history. If the next query needs an entry that was already used, both versions answer with that same entry, which is part of the history. If it needs a new entry, then in the advance version that entry was drawn independently of the other entries and of the adversary’s coins, so given the history it is still distributed as \(P\). In the lazy version it is a fresh draw from \(P\), so the same holds. So in both versions, the history after \(i + 1\) queries is the history after \(i\) queries plus one entry with the same conditional distribution. The probability of a whole history is the product of these conditional probabilities, one per query (the chain rule), so the histories have the same distribution after every query. The same then holds for anything computed from them, including the adversary’s output.
Build \(\mathcal B_j\), which judges \(Q\) strings at once. The reduction \(\mathcal B_j\) receives \(Q\) strings \(y_1, \dots, y_Q\) of \(2\lambda\) bits each. They are drawn independently from one distribution \(P\), which is either \(G(U_\lambda)\) or \(U_{2\lambda}\). It runs \(\mathcal A\) and keeps a ticket table, which starts empty. When a query \(x\) arrives, \(\mathcal B_j\) looks at the node \(w = x_1\cdots x_{j-1}\) at depth \(j - 1\) on its path, and if \(w\) has no ticket yet, gives it the next unused index \(c\). It then answers with the half of \(y_c\) that \(x_j\) selects, walked down with \(G\) exactly as in step 3. At the end, \(\mathcal B_j\) outputs whatever \(\mathcal A\) outputs. Each query passes through one node at depth \(j - 1\), so at most \(Q\) nodes ever need a ticket and the strings never run out.
Now compare this with step 4. The string \(y_c\) is first read when the \(c\)-th new node appears. Until then, everything \(\mathcal B_j\) has done depends only on \(y_1, \dots, y_{c-1}\) and on \(\mathcal A\)’s coins, and \(y_c\) is independent of all of them. So \(\mathcal B_j\) fills the table of step 3 lazily, in the sense of step 4, and \(\mathcal A\)’s view inside \(\mathcal B_j\) is exactly its view in \(W_j^{P}\). With step 3, this gives \[\Pr\big[\mathcal B_j(G(U_\lambda)^Q) = 1\big] = h_{j-1}, \qquad \Pr\big[\mathcal B_j(U_{2\lambda}^Q) = 1\big] = h_j, \tag{I.8}\] where \(G(U_\lambda)^Q\) means \(Q\) independent outputs of \(G\) on uniform seeds, and \(U_{2\lambda}^Q\) means \(Q\) independent uniform strings.
Go from \(Q\) strings to one. The chapter’s hybrid lemma for many samples does this, and here is its argument for this case. Write \(g_i\) for the probability that \(\mathcal B_j\) outputs 1 on a list of \(Q\) independent strings whose first \(i\) are uniform and whose other \(Q - i\) are outputs of \(G\). The two ends are the cases of step 5: \(g_0 = h_{j-1}\) (all from \(G\)) and \(g_Q = h_j\) (all uniform). The mixed lists in between match no hybrid, and they do not need to. The one-string distinguisher \(\mathcal B'_j\) takes a challenge string \(z\) and picks a position \(i\) uniformly from 1 to \(Q\). It puts uniform strings before position \(i\), puts \(z\) at position \(i\), and after it puts outputs of \(G\) on seeds it draws itself, which is possible because \(G\) is public. Then it outputs \(\mathcal B_j\)’s answer on the whole list. If \(z\) comes from \(G\), the list starts with \(i - 1\) uniform strings, so \(\mathcal B'_j\) says 1 with probability \(g_{i-1}\); if \(z\) is uniform, the probability is \(g_i\). Averaging over \(i\) gives \(\frac1Q\sum_{i=1}^Q (g_{i-1} - g_i)\), which telescopes as in step 2 to \(\frac1Q(g_0 - g_Q)\): \[\Pr[\mathcal B'_j(G(U_\lambda)) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal B'_j(U_{2\lambda}) = 1] = \frac1Q\,(h_{j-1} - h_j). \tag{I.9}\]
Pick the level at random and add up. The final distinguisher \(\mathcal B\) picks \(j\) uniformly from \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) and runs \(\mathcal B'_j\). Averaging step 6 over \(j\) and using Equation I.6, \[\Pr[\mathcal B(G(U_\lambda)) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal B(U_{2\lambda}) = 1] = \frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n \frac1Q\,(h_{j-1} - h_j) = \frac{h_0 - h_n}{nQ}. \tag{I.10}\] Taking absolute values gives Equation I.4. As for the cost, \(\mathcal B\) runs \(\mathcal A\) once. It computes at most \(Q - 1\) outputs of \(G\) for the list, and at most \(n - 1\) evaluations of \(G\) per query to walk down the tree. That is at most \((Q - 1) + Q(n - 1) = nQ - 1\) evaluations, fewer than \(nQ\).
Conclude for efficient adversaries. Suppose \(n\) and \(Q\) grow at most polynomially in \(\lambda\). Then an efficient \(\mathcal A\) gives an efficient \(\mathcal B\). If \(\mathcal A\)’s advantage were not negligible, it would be at least \(\lambda^{-c}\) for some exponent \(c\) and infinitely many \(\lambda\). Dividing by the polynomial \(nQ\) keeps it above one over a polynomial, so \(\mathcal B\)’s advantage \(\mathrm{Adv}_{\mathrm{PRF}}(\mathcal A)/(nQ)\) would not be negligible either, and \(G\) would not be a PRG. So if \(G\) is a PRG, the GGM tree is a PRF.

Adaptivity matters only in step 5. A reduction that fixed in advance which nodes get challenge strings would have to cover all \(2^{j-1}\) nodes at depth \(j - 1\). That can be exponentially many strings, and the loss factor would grow with it, from \(Q\) to \(2^{j-1}\). The ticket rule lets the adversary’s own queries decide where the \(Q\) strings go, and step 4 is why that changes nothing in what the adversary sees.


I.1.4 Checking it
The script runs the whole reduction on a toy with \(\lambda = 8\), \(n = 3\) and \(Q = 3\). Its PRG is broken on purpose, so that every advantage is large enough to measure: \(G(s) = (s, f(s))\) for a fixed random permutation \(f\) of the 8-bit strings. So the left half is the seed itself, and the right half is a public function of it. In the real \(F_k\), every left step keeps the label and every right step applies \(f\). So \(F_k(000) = k\), \(F_k(001) = f(k)\) and \(F_k(100) = f(k)\), while \(F_k(110) = f(f(k))\) because it takes two right steps.
The adversary uses these relations, and it chooses its third query adaptively so that the check also covers the subtle part of step 5. It asks 000 and then 001, and for its third query it asks 100 if the first answer starts with a 0 bit, and 110 otherwise. Check 1 asks whether the second answer is \(f\) of the first. Check 2 asks whether the third answer is \(f\) of the first, after 100, or \(f\) applied twice to the first, after 110. The adversary flips a coin to choose one check, and outputs 1, meaning “random function”, if that check fails. A uniform label passes a fixed equality only with probability \(2^{-8}\), so a check on labels that are independent fails with probability \(1 - 2^{-8}\). Both checks pass in \(H_0\), so \(h_0 = 0\). In \(H_1\) and \(H_2\), the first two leaves still hang below one node and are computed from it with \(G\), so check 1 passes. But check 2 compares labels from different branches of the tree, which are independent, so it fails with probability \(1 - 2^{-8}\). That gives \(h_1 = h_2 = \frac12(1 - 2^{-8}) = 0.4980\). In \(H_3\) both checks fail, so \(h_3 = 1 - 2^{-8} = 0.9961\). Table I.3 compares these with simulation.

Each \(\mathcal B_j\) lands on the hybrid that step 5 predicts, to within simulation noise of about 0.001, even though the adversary’s third query depends on what it has seen. Figure I.2 draws the same comparison. The single-sample distinguisher \(\mathcal B\) of step 7 says 1 with probability 0.5535 on outputs of \(G\) and 0.6641 on uniform strings. Its advantage is therefore 0.1105, against the predicted \(0.9961/9 = 0.1107\). Multiplying back by \(nQ = 9\) gives 0.995, which matches the adversary’s PRF advantage \(h_3 - h_0 = 0.9961\) as Equation I.4 says it should.






Figure I.2: How often the toy adversary says “random” in the hybrids \(H_0\) to \(H_3\), exactly and by simulation, and in each reduction \(\mathcal B_j\). Red triangles are \(\mathcal B_j\) fed outputs of \(G\), placed at \(H_{j-1}\); orange squares are \(\mathcal B_j\) fed uniform strings, placed at \(H_j\). Every marker sits on the curve.



Since Equation I.4 is an equality, the factor \(nQ\) between the two advantages is lost inside \(\mathcal B\) itself, in the averaging over levels and positions. The toy shows why. The adversary’s rate jumps by 0.498 at levels 1 and 3 and does not move at level 2, but \(\mathcal B\) spreads its effort evenly over all levels and all \(Q\) positions, most of which carry no signal. So the factor \(nQ\) comes from how the proof is organized, just like the factor for \(m\) samples in the chapter’s hybrid lemma.


I.1.5 What it does not cover
The proof needs every input to have the same length \(n\). With inputs of different lengths the GGM tree is not a PRF, because \(F_k(0)\) is the label of the node that \(F_k(00)\) hangs from. An adversary then checks whether \(F_k(00) = G_0(F_k(0))\), which always holds for the real function and almost never for a random one. The proof also assumes that \(G\) is deterministic, because a node’s label must give the same children every time a query passes through it. It assumes as well that \(G\) doubles its input exactly; a generator that stretches by only one bit can be applied repeatedly to its own output to reach double length. Finally, Equation I.4 compares advantages. To turn it into a concrete guarantee, such as “no attacker running for \(2^{128}\) steps succeeds”, you need a concrete bound on the advantage of PRG distinguishers with \(\mathcal B\)’s running time.

title: Appendix I — Pseudorandom functions and learning with errors
section: I.2 Search LWE reduces to decision LWE
text:
I.2 Search LWE reduces to decision LWE

I.2.1 What the chapter uses
Learning with errors hides a secret vector behind linear equations with small errors. Fix a dimension \(d\), a modulus \(p\) and an error distribution \(\chi\) on integers that are small compared with \(p\). Write \(\mathbb Z_p\) for the integers \(0, \dots, p - 1\) with arithmetic mod \(p\), and \(\mathbb Z_p^d\) for vectors of \(d\) such numbers. The secret \(s\) is a vector in \(\mathbb Z_p^d\). An LWE sample is a pair made of a uniform random vector \(a\) in \(\mathbb Z_p^d\) and a number \(b\). To make \(b\), draw an error \(e\) from \(\chi\) and set \[b = \langle a, s\rangle + e \bmod p, \qquad \langle a, s\rangle = \sum_{j=1}^d a_j s_j. \tag{I.11}\] Every sample has its own fresh \(a\) and \(e\), independent of the other samples, and the secret is the same in all of them.
Search LWE asks for \(s\), given as many samples as the algorithm needs. Decision LWE asks whether \(m\) given pairs are LWE samples or uniform pairs in \(\mathbb Z_p^d \times \mathbb Z_p\). The chapter shows that search is at least as hard as decision. For the converse it says only this: Regev, who introduced LWE, proves it for a prime \(p\) that is at most polynomial in \(d\), by guessing the coordinates of \(s\) one at a time and testing each guess with the decision algorithm.
Here is that converse in a form this appendix proves. Assume that \(p\) is prime. Assume also that a decision algorithm \(\mathcal A\), given \(m\) pairs, has advantage at least \(\nu\) for every secret, where the probabilities are over the pairs and over \(\mathcal A\)’s own random choices: \[\big|\Pr[\mathcal A(m \text{ LWE samples with secret } s) = 1] - \Pr[\mathcal A(m \text{ uniform pairs}) = 1]\big| \ge \nu \quad\text{for every } s \in \mathbb Z_p^d. \tag{I.12}\] Then, for any failure probability \(\beta\), there is a search algorithm that finds all of \(s\) with probability at least \(1 - \beta\). It calls \(\mathcal A\) at most \((dp + 1)N\) times and uses \(dpNm\) LWE samples, where the number of repetitions per test is \[N = \left\lceil \frac{8}{\nu^2}\ln\frac{2(dp + 1)}{\beta} \right\rceil. \tag{I.13}\] The advantage \(\nu\) is noticeable if it is at least one over some polynomial in \(d\). In that case, and when \(p\), \(m\) and \(\mathcal A\)’s running time are also polynomial in \(d\), the search runs in polynomial time. The value of \(N\) comes from step 6 of the derivation.


I.2.2 The idea
The test for one guess works like this. Take an LWE sample and a guess \(g\) for the first coordinate \(s_1\). Pick a random number \(r\), add it to the first coordinate of \(a\), and add \(r g\) to \(b\). If the guess is right, the change to \(b\) is exactly the change to \(\langle a, s\rangle\). So the new pair is again an LWE sample with the same secret and the same small error. If the guess is wrong, the error picks up the extra term \(r(g - s_1)\). When \(p\) is prime, that term is a random multiple of a nonzero number, so it is uniform. It drowns the error, and together with the shifted first coordinate it makes the whole pair uniform. Feeding the new pairs to \(\mathcal A\) therefore asks \(\mathcal A\) “LWE or uniform?”, and the true answer is “LWE” exactly when the guess is right. Repeating the test many times measures how often \(\mathcal A\) says 1, and comparing that rate with \(\mathcal A\)’s rate on uniform pairs, which the search draws itself, tells the right guess from the wrong ones. Trying all \(p\) guesses for each of the \(d\) coordinates recovers \(s\).
Table I.4 makes the wrong-guess case concrete with \(p = 5\), \(s_1 = 3\) and error \(e = 1\). After the change, the new \(b\) minus the inner product of the new \(a\) with \(s\) is \(e + r(g - s_1) \bmod 5\). With the right guess \(g = 3\) it stays at \(e = 1\) for every \(r\). With the wrong guess \(g = 1\) it becomes \(1 - 2r \bmod 5\), which takes each of the five values exactly once as \(r\) runs through \(0, \dots, 4\). Since \(r\) is uniform, the result is uniform.
